\# Optical tomography for in\-situ quality assurance in laser powder bed fusion\: From defect detection to closed\-loop control\: A critical review

\- Critical Review
\- Open access
\- Published\:

\#\# Abstract

Metal additive manufacturing has become a disruptive manufacturing method for producing components in critical applications\; therefore\, quality assurance is increasingly important for ensuring part reliability and performance\. Traditional methods for examining parts\, such as destructive testing and X\-ray computed tomography\, can be costly\, time\-consuming\, and impractical for inspecting every part in a production run\. In\-situ monitoring using optical tomography \(OT\) has gained increasing attention for quality control in processes such as laser powder bed fusion \(LPBF\) because it provides a relatively low\-cost monitoring solution with relatively simple hardware integration into commercial systems for full\-field\, layer\-wise monitoring of the build process\. This review provides a comprehensive overview of OT for in situ monitoring in LPBF processes\. It covers the fundamental principles\, sensor configurations\, research trends\, and applications for quality assurance and defect detection\. The discussion addresses the challenges and limitations these systems face\, such as data management\, signal interpretation\, and calibration\. The review highlights future opportunities to apply OT with machine learning to create digital twins or enable closed\-loop control\, thereby improving reliable build strategies in metal additive manufacturing\.

\#\# 1 Introduction

LPBF is a 3D printing process for metals that builds parts layer by layer from a CAD model\. Because of its high precision and small layer thickness\, LPBF is well\-suited for constructing lightweight parts and complex geometries\, such as biomedical implants with complex lattice structures\. The process works by spreading a thin layer of powder over a build plate\, which is then selectively melted by a laser to form a solid cross\-section\. The build plate is lowered\, another layer of powder is deposited\, and the process is repeated until the part is complete\.

LPBF\-processed parts often exhibit defects due to the process’s complexity and narrow processing window\. Common defects include porosity\, lack\-of\-fusion\, surface roughness issues\, cracking\, and geometric inaccuracies\. Traditionally\, post\-process characterization methods such as cross\-sectioning have been used to evaluate the type and density of defects\. However\, cross\-sectioning provides only localized information and fails to capture the full distribution of defects across the entire part \[1\]\.

More advanced techniques such as X\-ray micro\-computed tomography \(µCT\) can generate a three\-dimensional view of internal defects\, offering a more holistic assessment\. Yet\, these methods are costly and time\-intensive\, with expenses and time increasing significantly for larger parts\, which limits their widespread use in routine quality control\. In practical manufacturing environments\, it is not feasible to apply these post\-process characterization techniques to every part produced in one LPBF build\. Due to cost and time constraints\, only witness coupons or a small selection of parts are subjected to detailed inspection\. While this approach provides some indication of process quality\, it can leave undetected variability in the remaining parts on the build plate\.

Due to these limitations\, the additive manufacturing \(AM\) industry is increasingly adopting real\-time monitoring\, also known as in\-situ monitoring\, to assess part quality during the build process\. These approaches enable evaluation of material deposition as it occurs\, reducing reliance on post\-process characterization alone\. By integrating monitoring directly into the AM process\, it becomes possible not only to detect anomalies as they evolve\, but also to correct process instabilities on the fly before they lead to critical defects\.

One monitoring approach that has gained increasing attention in research and has also been adopted in commercial LPBF platforms is optical tomography \(OT\)\. OT systems used in LPBF utilize high\-speed optical\, near\-infrared\, or infrared sensors to capture time\-resolved intensity maps of the laser\-exposed regions for each layer of the build\. These maps can then be analyzed to identify irregular thermal patterns such as overheating\, lack\-of\-fusion indicators\, spatter\-related signatures\, and other process anomalies\. As a result\, OT provides a valuable method for assessing process stability and part quality throughout fabrication \[2\]\.

Although OT monitoring is mainly used to support post\-process part qualification\, this data can also enable closed\-loop control by guiding on\-the\-fly adjustments of process parameters during the build\. The overall workflow of OT\-based monitoring in LPBF\, from laser processing and in\-situ sensing to data acquisition\, analysis\, and final quality assurance\, is shown in Fig\. 1\.

In this review\, we provide a critical assessment of optical tomography for in\-situ quality assurance in LPBF\. We first introduce the fundamentals of OT\, including its working principles\, wavelength range\, sensor configurations\, and how it differs from other thermal and optical monitoring methods\. We then discuss reported applications of OT in defect detection\, surface roughness evaluation\, geometric monitoring\, digital twins\, and feedback control\. Beyond summarizing prior studies\, we evaluate the practical strengths and limitations of OT\, including its integration into commercial systems\, data\-processing requirements\, calibration challenges\, sensitivity to emissivity and optical interference\, and limited ability to detect subsurface defects directly\. Finally\, we discuss future opportunities for combining OT with machine learning\, sensor fusion\, digital twins\, and closed\-loop control to support more reliable certify\-as\-you\-build strategies in metal additive manufacturing\.

\#\# 2 Fundamentals of optical tomography in AM

\#\#\# 2\.1 Physics and working principles of optical tomography in LPBF

The term “tomography” is historically associated with medical computed tomography\, in which X\-rays are used to reconstruct cross\-sectional images\. In LPBF\, OT generally refers to layer\-wise optical or thermal emission imaging rather than internal 3D reconstruction of the part\. OT captures optical and near\-infrared emission intensity\, along with laser reflections\, from the powder bed and melt pool during laser exposure \[2\]\. These 2D images do not directly provide volumetric information comparable to computed tomography\. However\, because the layer\-wise data can be sequentially stacked\, OT can generate a spatial representation of the build history \[2\, 3\]\. The data are typically processed layer by layer to generate intensity maps of the build area\. Representative examples of these OT maps are shown in Fig\. 2\.

OT systems rely on radiative emission from the melt pool and surrounding heated material to monitor process behavior in real time \[8\, 9\]\. During LPBF\, the interaction between a focused laser beam and metal powder can generate localized melt pool temperatures approaching 3500 K \[10\]\, representing extremely severe thermal conditions\. While the melting points of most metals are typically above 1000 K\, vaporization and plume temperatures can be substantially higher \[11\]\. According to Planck’s radiation law\, an ideal black body emits electromagnetic radiation as a function of its temperature\, and the wavelength at which the emitted radiation reaches its maximum intensity can be estimated using Wien’s displacement law\:

\$\$\\\:\{\\lambda\\\:\}\_\{max\}\=\\\:\\frac\{b\}\{T\}\$\$

where λmax is peak\-emission wavelength \(m\)\, b is Wien’s displacement constant \(2\.897 × 10\-3 m\.K\)\, and T is Absolute Temperature \(K\)\. This relationship indicates that as temperature increases\, the peak emission wavelength shifts toward shorter wavelengths\. Under the high\-temperature conditions typical of LPBF\, the peak emission can shift toward the visible\-to\-near\-infrared range\, which explains why many OT systems use sensors sensitive to optical or near\-infrared radiation\. However\, materials in additive manufacturing rarely behave like ideal black bodies \[12\]\. Rather\, they are characterized by emissivity\, which describes how efficiently a real surface emits thermal radiation compared with a perfect black body\. Emissivity is difficult to define precisely during LPBF because it varies with material composition\, powder condition\, surface finish\, oxidation\, temperature\, viewing angle\, and observation wavelength \[11\]\. As a result\, OT is often more reliable for relative intensity mapping and anomaly detection than for direct quantitative temperature measurement\.

From a physical perspective\, optical radiation can broadly include the visible\, near\-infrared\, mid\-wave infrared\, and long\-wave infrared regions of the electromagnetic spectrum \[13\]\. In the additive manufacturing literature\, however\, the term optical tomography is typically used to refer to visible\-to\-near\-infrared imaging systems that generate layer\-wise emission intensity maps\. Systems operating in the mid\-wave infrared range \(typically 3–5 μm\) or the long\-wave infrared range \(typically 8–14 μm\) are more commonly classified as infrared thermography\, especially when designed for radiometric temperature measurement\. Therefore\, this review focuses on OT systems operating primarily in the visible\-to\-near\-infrared range\.

Within this spectral range\, visible wavelengths\, typically 380–700 nm\, can be affected by process\-related disturbances during LPBF\, including spatter\, metal vapor plume\, and reflected laser radiation\. These effects can introduce imaging artifacts\, reduce signal clarity\, or saturate the detector under certain conditions \[14\, 15\]\. To improve monitoring stability\, many OT systems extend detection into the near\-infrared range\, commonly around 750–900 nm\. In this range\, thermal emission from the melt pool and surrounding heated material can be captured more reliably\, while reducing sensitivity to some disturbances that strongly affect visible\-band imaging \[11\, 16\, 17\]\.

\#\#\# 2\.2 OT sensor configurations

OT systems can be implemented using different optical configurations\, as shown schematically in Fig\. 3\: on\-axis \(coaxial\) and off\-axis\. In the on\-axis or coaxial configuration shown in Fig\. 3 \(a\)\, the camera shares the optical path with the process laser\. It collects emitted radiation through the beam splitter and scan optics\. This arrangement provides a field of view that follows the laser optical path\, enabling high\-resolution monitoring of the melt pool and local process dynamics\. However\, the instantaneous field of view is limited to the region surrounding the laser spot\. As a result\, full\-layer visualization requires reconstruction by integrating data along the scan path rather than direct full\-field imaging\. A representative on\-axis configuration is demonstrated in Fig\. 4\, where melt\-pool radiation is collected coaxially through the laser optical path and directed to a high\-speed camera for thermal monitoring\.

In the off\-axis configuration shown in Fig\. 3 \(b\)\, the camera is mounted at an oblique angle relative to the build plate\. This arrangement provides a wider field of view and can capture a large portion\, or even the entirety\, of the build area within a single frame\. For this reason\, many OT systems are implemented in off\-axis configurations to enable layer\-wise intensity mapping over the entire build surface\. Examples of these configurations are shown in Fig\. 5\, where optical\, infrared\, and LWIR cameras are mounted either above the chamber\, outside the process chamber viewing through a process window\, or inside the chamber with appropriate thermal and optical protection\. The choice between coaxial and off\-axis configurations affects key metrological factors\, including field of view\, spatial resolution\, signal\-to\-noise characteristics\, and susceptibility to occlusion by the growing part geometry \[2\]\. Coaxial systems offer better optical alignment with the laser path and improved spatial consistency near the melt pool\. In contrast\, off\-axis systems are more mechanically simple\, easier to retrofit\, and lower in implementation cost\. However\, off\-axis imaging introduces perspective distortion\, which requires computational homographic rectification to map the oblique image plane onto the build coordinate system\. Therefore\, the selection between coaxial and off\-axis OT setups involves a trade\-off between optical alignment precision and practical implementation in real\-time process monitoring \[2\]\.

\#\#\# 2\.3 Spectral band selection for optical and infrared monitoring in LPBF

The wavelength range selected for optical monitoring strongly influences the thermal features that can be measured during LPBF\. Because the process involves both localized melt\-pool heating and broader part\-scale heat accumulation\, effective in\-situ monitoring requires careful selection of spectral bands\, including near\-infrared \(NIR\)\, mid\-wave infrared \(MWIR\)\, and long\-wave infrared \(LWIR\)\. This spectral selection is fundamentally governed by Wien’s displacement\, which dictates that the peak thermal emission wavelength \(\\\(\\\:\{\\lambda\\\:\}\_\{\\text\{max\}\}\\\)\) shifts inversely with temperature \(\\\(\\\:T\\\)\)\. At extreme melt\-pool temperatures \(\~ 1600–3000 °C\)\, thermal radiance peaks at shorter wavelengths\, making NIR \(0\.7–1\.1 \\\(\\\:\\mu\\\:\\\)m\) and MWIR \(3–5 \\\(\\\:\\mu\\\:\\\)m\) systems ideal for capturing high\-temperature\, rapid transient dynamics\. Conversely\, as solidified regions cool toward moderately elevated or near\-ambient surface temperatures \(150–600 °C\)\, the peak spectral radiance shifts toward longer wavelengths\, rendering LWIR systems \(8–14 \\\(\\\:\\mu\\\:\\\)m\) significantly more sensitive for monitoring part\-scale heat accumulation and layer\-by\-layer cooling \[2\, 3\, 25\]\. Therefore\, LWIR is less suitable for resolving the steep thermal gradients and rapid transient behavior directly associated with the active melt pool \[26\]\. In LPBF\, LWIR monitoring has instead been used to measure the end\-of\-cycle temperature\, which represents the minimum surface temperature reached at a given location before the next laser\-melting step begins\. This temperature can reflect the layer\-by\-layer thermal history and has been used to predict the resulting microstructure of the final part \[24\]\. In addition to wavelength selection\, the monitoring modality also determines the type of information obtained\. OT\-based monitoring generally provides an integrated intensity map for each layer\. It can be responsive to changes in processing parameters\. In contrast\, LWIR\-measured end\-of\-cycle temperature can be more sensitive to layer\-by\-layer part geometry and cross\-sectional area Fig\. 6 \[3\, 27\]\. Compared with LWIR\, MWIR thermography is generally better suited to measuring higher\-temperature regions in LPBF\, including the melt pool and surrounding heated material \[2\]\. Because MWIR captures thermal emission from elevated\-temperature process zones\, it can provide temperature\-related information closer to the active melting region\. However\, the measured values are often apparent temperatures\, which is the temperature calculated by the sensor\, rather than exact surface temperatures which differ due to emissivity changes\. MWIR data can also be analyzed over time to extract features such as time\-over\-threshold\, which describes how long a surface location remains above a selected apparent temperature \[25\]\. This makes MWIR useful for evaluating local cooling behavior\, heat accumulation\, and thermal signatures associated with defect formation\. Overall\, OT\, MWIR\, and LWIR provide complementary information\: OT captures layer\-wise integrated emission intensity\, MWIR provides time\-resolved temperature\-related data from higher\-temperature process regions\, and LWIR is more effective for tracking lower\-temperature surface conditions and layer\-to\-layer heat accumulation \[2\, 25\]\.

\#\# 3 Utility of optical tomography for defect detection and quality assessment in LPBF

Because many LPBF defects are linked to local thermal and process instabilities\, OT has been increasingly used to detect and interpret defect\-prone regions during the build\. For example\, lack\-of\-fusion conditions may appear as low\-intensity regions associated with insufficient energy input or incomplete melting\. In contrast\, local overheating\, unstable melting\, or keyhole\-prone conditions may appear as high\-intensity regions or hotspots\. OT\-derived signatures have also been correlated with post\-process X\-ray computed tomography data\, supporting its use as a quality assessment tool for identifying spatial patterns associated with porosity\, lack\-of\-fusion\, and geometric deviations \[28\,29\,30\,31\]\. Beyond internal porosity\-related defects\, OT has also been applied to monitor surface irregularities\, geometry inconsistencies\, and broader layer\-wise thermal patterns that may influence final part quality\. Therefore\, OT applications in LPBF have expanded from simple layer\-wise process observation toward defect detection\, quality assessment\, and process understanding\. The following subsections review key quality\-related anomalies investigated using OT monitoring\, including porosity and lack\-of\-fusion\, surface roughness\, geometric inconsistencies\, and microstructure\-related thermal signatures\. Table 1 presents a comprehensive overview of recent in\-situ optical monitoring literature\, categorized by the specific hardware configurations and analytical methods employed\. This matrix maps camera sensor types and targeted wavelength regimes to the corresponding machine learning algorithms used to classify specific process anomalies\.

\#\#\# 3\.1 Porosity and lack\-of\-fusion

In LPBF\, part density and mechanical integrity are primarily limited by the formation of internal voids\, broadly categorized into keyhole porosity\, and lack\-of\-fusion defects\. The transition between these defect regimes is governed by the volumetric energy density \(VED\)\, which is a function of both the laser power and scanning speed \[37\]\. Lack\-of\-fusion occurs in the low\-energy\-density regime\, characterized by insufficient laser power or excessively high scan speeds\. This results in insufficient melt pool penetration to remelt the solidified track\, or in the non\-melted powder particles being retained within the build volume\, as seen in Fig\. 7 \(a\)\. Highly tortuous and sharp\-edged cavities characterize the morphology of lack\-of\-fusion defects \[38\]\. Due to the sharpness of the defect geometries\, the fatigue life and tensile strength of the component are significantly compromised \[38\, 39\]\. Thermally\, the region where lack\-of\-fusion occurs is characterized by lower radiance and greater thermal gradients due to inadequate energy input to establish a stable and steady\-state melt pool \[13\, 40\]\. This observation is consistent with the previously established physics\; the formation of a lack\-of\-fusion pore is due to inadequate laser energy input and an abnormal cooling gradient\. Similarly\, there can be a correlation made on the other side of the intensity spectrum\, where regions exhibiting extreme\, high\-intensity OT values are strongly prone to over\-melting and vaporization \[5\, 7\]\. These correlations have been validated using X\-ray computed tomography \(XCT\)\. This post\-process inspection provides high\-resolution accuracy in the locations of density and porosity\, as shown in Fig\. 7 \(b\)\. The LPBF process’s ability to engineer and intentionally introduce a defect allows researchers to leverage OT data to identify patterns and behaviors that can be correlated one\-to\-one with a specific defect morphology\.

The fundamental challenge of directly correlating an intensity reading to a defect morphology like a lack\-of\-fusion or a keyhole pore\, is the calibration of intensity against the true melt pool temperature\. The moment the solid metal melts into a liquid\, the surface becomes much more reflective\, causing the emissivity to drop extremely\. Additionally\, the emissivity varies with the metal temperature\. This dynamic emissivity caused by temperature and phase change can compromise the fidelity of the intensity data \[3\, 11\, 16\, 41\]\. Even if the dynamic emissivity could be perfectly mitigated\, OT still struggles with spatial resolution\. While OT can map macroscopic lack\-of\-fusion regions\, if a high\- or low\-intensity reading causing micro\-porosity falls below the optical setup’s pixel pitch\, it will evade detection\. This creates discrepancies between OT and high\-resolution µCT measurements\. As shown in Fig\. 7\(c\)\, keyhole pores with decreasing volumes of 1000 μm³\, 500 μm³\, and 250 μm³ were intentionally produced and evaluated using both OT and µCT\. The comparison shows that smaller pores become progressively more difficult for OT to detect\, while µCT can still resolve these defects with higher spatial fidelity\. These results confirm that OT sensitivity is constrained by spatial resolution\, meaning that defects below a critical size may become effectively invisible to the sensor \[7\]\.

\#\#\# 3\.2 Surface roughness

Numerous factors\, including material\, design\, and process parameters\, influence surface roughness in AM parts \[39\]\. Factors such as part orientation within the build chamber\, the geometry of overhangs and downskin surfaces\, and the need for support structures can lead to variations in thermal gradients and cooling rates\, resulting in different surface finishes across a single component\. Specific process parameters such as heat source power\, scan speed\, layer thickness\, overhang angles\, and scan path strategy can all contribute to surface irregularities\. For instance\, improper energy input may lead to incomplete melting\, producing partially fused particles or visible scan tracks on the surface\. Phenomena like balling\, lack\-of\-fusion between layers\, and striations along melting tracks are commonly observed surface defects that stem from these processing variables \[38\, 39\, 42\, 43\]\.

Post\-processing steps are often necessary to achieve the surface quality demanded by high\-end applications\. These may include mechanical operations such as machining\, grinding\, tumbling\, peening\, or polishing\, as well as chemical treatments designed to smooth or refine the surface\.

Measurement and quantification of surface roughness are typically carried out using profilometers\, which record surface height variations along a specified profile length\, or by imaging and analysis with scanning electron microscopy\. One common metric used to quantify these irregularities is the arithmetic average surface roughness \(Ra\)\, calculated as the average absolute deviation of the surface height from a mean line\, measured at ‘N’ discrete points along the evaluation profile\.

Surface roughness estimation using OT has been demonstrated by correlating layer\-wise emission intensity with post\-process surface roughness measurements under different surface angles\, scan strategies\, and energy input conditions \[8\]\. In this approach\, samples are printed under controlled variations in processing conditions to generate differences in surface quality\. The corresponding OT images are divided into selected regions or quadrants\, and the average gray value within each region is calculated to quantify local brightness differences\. As illustrated in Fig\. 8 \(a\)\, scan strategies such as continuous scanning and time\-homogenization scanning can be compared to evaluate their influence on the OT response\. Representative OT images under different energy and scan conditions are shown in Fig\. 8 \(b\)\, where variations in brightness indicate changes in local thermal emission\. These brightness metrics are then compared with measured surface roughness values\, as shown in Fig\. 8 \(c\)\. The observed statistical correlation indicates that OT can serve as a layer\-wise indicator of surface quality\, particularly when scan strategy\, laser energy input\, and surface angle are considered\. This approach also highlights several limitations of OT\-based surface quality assessment\. The correlation was strongest under the time\-homogenization scan strategy\, where more uniform layer heating produced clearer brightness differences between selected regions of the overhang geometry\. However\, the 90° condition was excluded from the correlation analysis because symmetric image segmentation yielded a nearly zero brightness difference\, suggesting that OT may be less sensitive when the geometry does not provide sufficient spatial contrast\. Moreover\, OT brightness should be interpreted as an emission\-intensity feature rather than a direct temperature measurement unless proper calibration is performed\. Because OT provides layer\-wise two\-dimensional emission maps\, it can identify surface\-related thermal anomalies and overheating trends\. Still\, it does not directly resolve melt pool depth or subsurface defects\.

Although OT brightness can be correlated with surface roughness under controlled processing conditions\, its interpretation as an independent predictor of surface morphology requires careful validation\. The reported correlations suggest that OT can indicate roughness trends for specific scan strategies\, laser energy inputs\, and surface angles\; however\, the reliability of this relationship is constrained by the angular dependence\, spatial resolution\, and segmentation approach used in the analysis\. In addition\, optical emission maps may be influenced by factors unrelated to surface roughness\, including spatter\, soot\, plume effects\, recoater\-induced disturbances\, and local changes in emissivity\. These factors can alter the brightness field and may complicate the generalization of OT\-based roughness prediction across different materials\, geometries\, and process conditions\. Nevertheless\, the study demonstrates that\, when processing parameters and image analysis procedures are carefully controlled\, OT can serve as a semi\-quantitative tool for linking layer\-wise emission history with surface morphology\.

\#\#\# 3\.3 Geometric inconsistencies

Geometric inconsistencies remain a major challenge in LPBF\, where fabricated parts can deviate from the intended CAD geometry due to machine limitations\, process resolution\, and the difficulty of reproducing fine features\, thin walls\, sharp corners\, and complex overhangs \[44\]\. These deviations are often linked to local thermal behavior during the build\. Rapid heating and cooling generate steep thermal gradients\, which can cause localized expansion\, contraction\, residual stress\, and thermal distortion \[45\]\. Solidification shrinkage can further contribute to dimensional errors\, particularly in overhanging regions and thin\-walled features where heat conduction is limited \[46\]\. Because geometric defects can affect dimensional accuracy\, assembly performance\, and mechanical reliability\, early detection is important for LPBF quality assurance \[47\]\.

Although OT is commonly treated as a two\-dimensional layer\-wise intensity map\, it can also be used to extract geometric information during the build\. Figure 9 \(c\) illustrates an example workflow for converting OT intensity images into layer\-wise geometric data\. First\, a threshold\-based segmentation step is applied to separate the fabricated region from the surrounding powder bed and reduce image noise\. Edge detection is then used to identify the boundary of the printed cross\-section at each layer\. This process isolates the two\-dimensional layer\-wise contour of the fabricated part from the surrounding powder bed and enables OT to function as an indirect metrology tool \[23\]\. The extracted geometric boundaries can then be directly compared with the nominal CAD geometry for each layer\. Figure 9 \(a\) demonstrates this capability by superimposing OT\-derived contours onto the corresponding CAD slice and measuring the deviation between the fabricated and intended geometries\. In this way\, local dimensional errors can be quantified continuously throughout the build \[9\]\. By stacking these layer\-wise deviation maps through the build height\, OT can also support a three\-dimensional reconstruction of geometric fidelity across the fabricated part\.

This mapping approach can also link localized OT anomalies to macroscopic build failures\. Overhanging regions are especially susceptible to thermal distortion due to limited heat dissipation\, leading to heat accumulation\. Figure 9 \(b\, i–iii\) demonstrates the real\-time progression of this failure mechanism \[23\]\. In this case\, OT captures localized thermal accumulation near the unsupported overhang before or during the onset of physical curling due to residual stress\. By monitoring the geometric index of the distorted edge shown in Fig\. 9 \(c\)\, the system can identify when deformation becomes severe enough to cause recoater interference \[23\]\.

\#\#\# 3\.4 Optical tomography for microstructural assessment

Although OT does not directly image the microstructure\, it can provide indirect information about microstructural development because the recorded emission intensity reflects local thermal behavior during LPBF\. Microstructural features such as grain morphology\, cellular or dendritic spacing\, phase transformation behavior\, and texture are strongly influenced by thermal gradients\, cooling rate\, remelting\, and heat accumulation\. Since these thermal conditions also affect the layer\-wise OT response\, OT can serve as an indirect indicator of microstructure\-relevant process conditions\. Figure 10 shows a multimodal framework in which in\-situ thermal signatures are correlated with physical metallurgy by integrating OT data\, thermal imaging\, and physics\-based simulations \[24\]\. By integrating layer\-wise OT data\, specifically mean melt pool intensity and inter\-layer time\, with macroscopic thermal imaging and physics\-based simulations\, the researchers built a comprehensive thermal history profile \[41\]\. This multi\-sensor data was subsequently used to train a hierarchical k\-Nearest Neighbors \(kNN\) machine learning model\. In the first echelon\, the algorithm classified the presence of lack\-of\-fusion porosity\. More importantly\, in the second echelon\, the model successfully utilized the OT and thermal data to quantitatively predict specific microstructural characteristics\, including melt pool depth\, primary grain size\, and microhardness\. These findings demonstrate that\, when integrated with complementary thermal measurements\, physics\-based modeling\, and robust machine learning frameworks\, OT\-derived thermal signatures can serve as effective indicators of microstructural evolution and resulting mechanical properties\, thereby reducing reliance on destructive characterization methods\.

\#\#\# 3\.5 Machine learning \& feedback control

Beyond passive process monitoring\, OT also provides a foundation for implementing closed\-loop feedback control\. Although most current OT systems primarily function as open\-loop monitoring tools\, the layer\-wise information they generate could be used to adjust process parameters dynamically between successive layers\. Because OT captures a full\-field emission map after each layer is completed\, it can identify regions associated with under\-melting\, overheating\, or geometric swelling before the recoater deposits the next powder layer\. This interval between completing one layer and depositing the next provides an opportunity for layer\-wise corrective action\, such as applying a remedial remelting pass to reduce the risk of lack\-of\-fusion or adjusting laser power in subsequent layers to compensate for local heat accumulation \[33\]\. This transition from defect detection to defect prevention represents one of the key advantages of OT\, extending its role beyond process monitoring to closed\-loop control and quality assurance\.

However\, achieving closed\-loop operation requires more than monitoring alone\; it requires rapid interpretation of OT data and timely intervention in the LPBF process\. Raw OT intensity images must be translated into defect classifications\, process\-state indicators\, or corrective control commands\. Deep learning algorithms have shown strong potential for interpreting the complex spatial and thermal patterns captured by in\-situ sensors\. Figure 11 illustrates a data\-driven framework that employs the convolutional neural network ResNet50 to predict porosity directly from layer\-wise OT grayscale images \[33\]\. By registering OT emission data with X\-ray CT measurements\, the model learned the relationship between layer\-wise melt pool signatures and final volumetric porosity \[33\]\. Prediction accuracy was further improved by using multi\-frame inputs\, in which OT images from the preceding\, current\, and subsequent layers were combined to account for cross\-layer thermal interactions and remelting effects \[33\]\. This approach demonstrates how machine learning can convert OT data from qualitative emission images into quantitative defect predictions\. Despite these promising developments\, implementing true closed\-loop control remains challenging because the complete decision pipeline\, including OT image acquisition\, preprocessing\, defect classification\, control decision\, and machine response\, must be completed within the time available before the subsequent layer is processed\.

An alternative approach to closed\-loop control avoids the computational cost of deep learning by using OT signals directly as process feedback\. Nahr et al\. \[48\] demonstrated this concept using the Smart Fusion feedback\-control strategy to reduce thermal inhomogeneities in structures containing down\-skin and up\-skin features\. The control architecture is illustrated in Fig\. 12 \(a\)\. Following each layer exposure\, the OT camera records the near\-infrared \(NIR\) process emission and generates an integral gray\-value \(GV\) image\. This measured GV distribution is compared with a predefined target GV\, producing a spatial deviation map\. The controller converts this deviation into a laser correction\-factor image\, which is then used to locally increase or decrease the laser power during subsequent exposure\. In this manner\, the system provides spatially resolved\, layer\-to\-layer process correction directly from OT measurements without requiring machine learning\-based defect classification\. Figure 12 \(b\) compares the resulting thermal response for open\-loop and feedback\-loop processing of Ti\-6Al\-4 V and MS1\, showing that feedback control reduces the increase and spatial spread of the measured mean gray values during the build\.

\#\# 4 Current challenges and research gaps

\#\#\# 4\.1 Optical signal interpretation challenges

Both emissivity variations and optical interference during the build process complicate the interpretation of OT data\. Emissivity differs among powder\, liquid melt\, and solidified metal\, causing the recorded OT intensity to change even when the underlying temperature field is similar \[11\]\. As a result\, raw OT intensity values cannot be directly interpreted as absolute temperature\. Because OT relies on capturing thermal radiation or light intensity\, interpretation in metals is especially challenging because metallic emissivity is nonlinear and noisy\. This can cause models to struggle during phase transitions\, where emissivity may change rapidly\. In particular\, the solid\/liquid transition can generate signals that resemble defects but may instead reflect thermal gradients \[25\]\. Current research is therefore moving toward emissivity\-independent pyrometry and expanded\-wavelength camera systems that can improve temperature estimation despite emissivity variation \[16\]\.

Optical interference can further complicate signal interpretation\. Metal vapor plumes and spatter generated near the laser\-material interaction zone can absorb and scatter the optical signal\, obscuring the true thermal response of the process \[27\, 49\]\. As a result\, software algorithms may misinterpret these disturbances as process anomalies\. Advanced filtering algorithms are therefore needed to reduce plume\- and spatter\-related noise in OT images\.

\#\#\# 4\.2 Data processing\, computation\, and latency

The large volume of image data generated during a build\, often reaching gigabytes per build\, creates a “big data” bottleneck that makes manual interpretation impractical\. Because high\-resolution OT cameras\, such as those used in EOS OT systems\, can operate with high spatial and temporal resolution\, the resulting datasets require advanced processing methods for quality control and analysis\. As a result\, the effective use of OT increasingly depends on automated data\-processing pipelines\. Convolutional neural networks and unsupervised learning models are becoming important tools for segmenting OT images and automatically classifying anomalies in real time\.

At the same time\, the computational requirements of OT analysis must be balanced with real\-time process\-control needs\. Large image datasets and machine\-learning models can introduce latency\, especially when standard CPUs cannot process convolutional neural networks fast enough for layer\-wise control\. This poses a challenge for closed\-loop implementation\, in which data processing\, anomaly classification\, and corrective action must occur before the next layer is deposited or scanned\. These requirements must also be considered alongside hardware constraints\, such as line\-of\-sight obstruction by the recoater mechanism and tradeoffs between spatial resolution and field of view\.

\#\#\# 4\.3 Indirect defect measurement and subsurface limitations

OT is not a direct defect measurement technique\; it is a light\-intensity\-based monitoring method\. Therefore\, there is no universal way to transfer a single intensity pixel into a specific pore shape or size \[7\, 50\]\. To correlate OT intensity with defect characteristics\, machine learning algorithms or digital twin models are needed to estimate where pores may form and approximate their size\. Some defects are also difficult to observe using OT\. For example\, keyhole pores that form at unstable keyhole depths can be challenging to detect because they are located below or within the melt pool\. Therefore\, OT\-based monitoring needs to be correlated with other monitoring or inspection methods that can capture subsurface defects\. Despite these limitations\, OT remains a viable candidate for macro\-scale monitoring of geometric and thermal consistency in LPBF\.

\#\# 5 Future direction

\#\#\# 5\.1 Physics\-informed and generative machine learning

The future development of OT will likely depend strongly on its integration with machine learning algorithms\. However\, many existing algorithms require large\, labeled datasets\, which can be expensive and cumbersome to generate experimentally\. In the future\, physics\-informed machine learning may help address this limitation by embedding physical principles and governing theories directly into the algorithm\. This would allow models to use sparse OT data more effectively while remaining calibrated by physics\-based constraints\. In addition\, generative networks could be used to create synthetic OT datasets that replicate difficult\-to\-produce defect scenarios\, such as regions where pore formation is highly likely but difficult to generate consistently through experiments\.

\#\#\# 5\.2 OT\-enabled digital twins

For a digital twin to be more than a static CAD file or a pre\-process simulation\, it requires a continuous stream of real\-time data that reflects the actual state of the build\. OT is well positioned to serve as this live link because it captures layer\-wise thermal history during fabrication\. Bevans et al\. developed a digital twin strategy using in\-situ data and computational thermal modeling \[24\]\. However\, a key challenge is that much OT data is currently stored in formats that do not communicate easily with simulation software\. There is no universal data language that allows sensor data to update a digital model instantly\. Addressing this limitation will require standardized data architectures\, such as HDF5\, a format for organizing and storing large scientific datasets\, along with compatible data interfaces that allow OT data to feed directly into the digital twin\. This would enable a “shadow” simulation to run in parallel with the actual build\, in which OT data continuously updates the thermal history of the digital part to match the real process better\.

\#\#\# 5\.3 Toward volumetric OT inference

Current OT systems are limited because they mainly provide a two\-dimensional\, top\-view image of each layer\. As a result\, they can capture surface\-level emission patterns but cannot directly observe subsurface features such as the depth of keyhole pores or the morphology of internal defects\. A future direction is to use OT data to indirectly infer three\-dimensional information\. For example\, surface cooling behavior and layer\-wise emission history could be combined with machine learning models to estimate melt pool depth or the likelihood of subsurface keyhole porosity\. This would extend OT from a surface\-sensitive monitoring tool toward a more predictive method for assessing internal part quality\.

\#\# 6 Conclusion

Optical tomography stands as one of the most promising tools for in\-situ monitoring because it offers a non\-contact\, layer\-by\-layer record of the thermal history of the build that post\-process inspection cannot provide\. Unlike X\-ray CT\, which is used after the part is completed\, OT provides an opportunity to observe process stability in real time\. However\, the potential of OT is currently limited because it is often used as a qualitative tool for tasks that require quantitative assessment\. The advantage of capturing high\-speed thermal data is reduced if that data cannot be reliably converted into actionable pass\/fail criteria without extensive calibration\. Therefore\, a key future need is to shift OT from a passive observation camera toward a calibrated metrology instrument that can be trusted to assess part quality rather than only infer it\.

As the industry moves from prototyping to serial production\, the role of OT is shifting from a research tool to a potential gatekeeper of quality assurance\. Current certification still relies heavily on destructive testing and expensive offline NDT\, which can bottleneck production and increase part cost\. OT offers a path toward “certify\-as\-you\-build” by creating a digital birth record for each part\, where layer\-wise thermal data are associated with the build history\. However\, for OT to support or replace traditional testing\, the industry must overcome the “trust gap” in which operators still rely on CT scans to validate OT data\. The growing role of OT will depend on the development of standardized transfer functions that enable engineers to map specific optical signatures to safe and reliable part states\.

The future adoption of OT will not be driven only by better sensors\, but also by better interpretation of the data already being collected\. The hardware can capture more data than can currently be processed effectively\; therefore\, the main bottleneck is the lack of robust\, physics\-informed models capable of separating meaningful process signals from noise\. Industrial adoption will remain limited until closed\-loop capability is demonstrated\, where the machine not only detects abnormal process behavior but also determines how to correct it with minimal human intervention\. In this role\, OT can move beyond a standalone add\-on feature and become an embedded sensing system in the next generation of metal AM printers\, continuously feeding data into digital twins to ensure that the physical part matches the digital design\.

records.summary: This Semiconductor Engineering expert roundtable discusses the test and failure-analysis challenges of co-packaged optics (CPO) and near-packaged optics (NPO) as photonics moves into advanced packages. Participants from Teradyne, Advantest, ISE Labs (ASE Group) and Keysight describe how engineers use reference planes, de-embedding, known-good substitute components and loopback/monitor photodiodes to localize faults in electro-optical signal paths. They note that retimed NPO with its own DSP can be compliance-tested like a pluggable, whereas linear-drive NPO and CPO merge electrical and optical paths, making fault isolation harder. Reported economics include test cost for optical components approaching manufacturing cost (per IPSR surveys cited by ISE Labs' Armstrong), and the argument that an inexpensive optical engine must not scrap a $40,000–$50,000 GPU or ASIC, justifying heavy pre-assembly screening. The discussion is expert opinion and industry commentary, not peer-reviewed experimental data; a Meta reliability presentation is referenced but not detailed.
records.why_it_matters: Because a low-cost optical engine can destroy a very expensive ASIC/GPU package, test strategy shifts toward over-testing and pre-assembly screening of known-good optical engines rather than relying on final package test.

records.body_text:
Bringing Down Test Costs For Co-Packaged Optics
Pinpointing failures, ensuring known-good optical engines, and controlling test costs become increasingly critical as photonics moves into advanced packages.
Key Takeaways:
- For FA, engineers need to identify boundaries and be able to decouple individual components to identify the root cause of problems.
- Underperforming lasers are a substantial issue, making the “golden reference” a hot topic in test.
- Training in electro-optics is critical to understanding tradeoffs in design and test.
Experts At The Table: Testing cost for optical components is high, approaching the manufacturing cost. Loopback capability is an important part of failure diagnosis. Semiconductor Engineering sat down with Matt Griffin, senior product manager for optoelectronics test at Teradyne; Ira Leventhal, vice president of research and venture at Advantest America; Dave Armstrong, fellow at ISE Labs, a subsidiary of ASE Group; and Kazuo Yamaguchi, silicon photonics researcher and engineer at Keysight Technologies. What follows are excerpts of that conversation. To view part one, click here. Part two is here.
Fig. 1: (L-R): Teradyne’s Griffin; Keysight’s Yamaguchi; ISE Labs’ Armstrong; Advantest’s Leventhal
SE: How do you determine where failure originates in electro-optical systems?
Yamaguchi: We always look at the reference plane. For the testing, these are the physical, electrical, and optical boundaries at each of the measurement planes — for example, determining where this boundary sits. Is it at the die pad, package balls, the connectors, or the fiber interface? We also need to think about de-embedding everywhere between the boundaries — for instance, probe, socket, trace, connectors, patch cord — whatever we are introducing, and making sure the same boundaries are used at testing insertions 1, 2, and 3. We need to align those boundary conditions, as well. So then we emulate the missing half. For example, to test the optical engine alone, you replace the neighbors with a known characterized substitute. If we have a golden reference laser source, that can be used.
Griffin: We are seeing customers add monitor photodiodes into their light paths, so that if they see an unexpected result from the transmit or receive path, they can trace it back. Some customers doing loopback testing want tap capability so they can route to characterization instrumentation or simply monitor power. That’s useful if they aren’t planning to do a full characterization test and just want to do loopback or mission-mode testing. The downside is that if it fails and you don’t meet your bit error rate or you have a functional issue with the program, you may not know why. So being able to tap into that loopback capability could be important.
Leventhal: I wanted to follow up about having a golden reference for a laser source. Really, the job at the end of the day is not to test the laser source. We’re looking for how to test the part. That laser source is basically the functional equivalent of the device power supply on the electrical side, and we don’t call that a golden reference. We call it a device power supply, and it’s a given that thing is supposed to work as it should, just like everything else in the test system. Customers want to default to getting the laser source out of the equation and to use the same one that they’re using in mission mode, but that laser source is not an ATE instrument, so things are going to need to evolve. As Dave talked about, FA is following your nose, and you need to be able to discern the scent of things that should be in the equation of causing trouble and things that should be just off the table because it’s a given they’re known-good.
SE: In what ways is co-packaged optics (CPO) failure diagnosis harder than near-packaged optics (NPO) FA?

The two share similar challenges, in that module test requires alignment of multiple optical connectors, and we still need to deliver power to the device. Some customers will say, ‘With NPO, I can detach the optical engines.’ That might be a key distinction. So you could argue that the test coverage before that attachment becomes less valuable, because if I detect a failure caused by a bad optical engine, I can just remove it. But we’ve also heard from customers that reworking and reattaching further downstream is a real pain point, which means they still want known-good optical engines, regardless of detachability.
Leventhal: With CPO, you have a lot more stuff integrated onto the package, and you need to have ways of decoupling them. And so many of the themes that we’ve talked about over the course of this discussion come into play here. DFT would help, as Dave discussed — understanding what information you need to get out of the testing on the individual pieces so you can correlate it to what’s going to fail in the package.
Yamaguchi: A retimed NPO has its own DSP, so the optical engine can be compliance-tested on its own, like a pluggable, and a failure is easy to locate. A linear-drive NPO removes the DSP, and the host ASIC SerDes drives the optics directly through linear drivers and TIAs (transimpedance amplifiers). The electrical and optical sides then form one signal path, so a failed link can’t easily be traced to either side. The test complexity is the same as for CPO.
Armstrong: Another concern is high power dissipation. For CPO, your electrical signals can’t drive very far, and hopefully with an NPO they can. And because you have higher reach in the electrical, you have to manage that. The thermal of all these optical parts is a big deal.
SE: How does the economics of tests change when you have an inexpensive photonics device integrated with a very expensive ASIC or GPU?
Leventhal: You can’t have an inexpensive optical engine taking down a $40,000 or $50,000 GPU or ASIC, so it’s an interesting change in terms of your test budget. We tend to look at test costs as a certain percentage of the manufacturing cost of that chip, but this blows that completely out of the water. Now you essentially have like an infinite test budget for these chips that are going to surround your big ASIC. Of course, you always look for ways to reduce test cost, but you do have the ability to over-test at the beginning to make sure that you’re not throwing away the really expensive chip. And then, over time, we will get the yield learning information as we scale.
Yamaguchi: The device value is increasing, the scrap cost is increasing, the test complexity is increasing, the package complexity is increasing. So, given this situation, additional wafers or optimal engine-level testing become more justifiable, and that’s how the economics are shifting toward pre-assembly screening rather than packaging test, which we have traditionally served in the industry.
Griffin: I completely agree. I would add that the end customers for these AI accelerator and network switch devices are highly motivated to deploy as many of these as possible into data centers so they can generate more tokens. These are some of the most complex semiconductor devices ever made. If you look at the cost of an optical engine in isolation, you get a different answer than if you look at the extremely complex package that it’s going to be integrated into, and the core functionality it provides. It reduces power and enables disaggregated compute architectures, which makes that device extremely critical. So we’re going to see continued focus on testing these systems efficiently.
Leventhal: For the industry, it’s no longer a challenge to prove that CPO works. Meta presented strong reliability data earlier this year showing it’s actually quite reliable. It works. Now the question is, ‘How do you take what we have today to high-volume manufacturing?’ That’s an ecosystem problem. It’s not just a problem in a single piece of the puzzle. So we’ll deal with that in the shorter term by relying on additional testing, screen-in, burn-in, more insertions, more engineering controls, while the ecosystem gets dialed in and matures. NPO plays a really important role in this. It’s a lower hurdle to jump over to get up and running. Learnings that come out of that will bootstrap efforts to bring CPO to HVM. But it won’t be a slam dunk. And you asked what we haven’t talked about at this point. The answer is standards. The industry is moving so fast that standards bodies can’t keep up. Where standards come into play is not to invent the technology, but to be able to manufacture at scale, where we have multiple sources for parts.
Yamaguchi: The industry is looking into standards and MSAs to enable the technology and collaborate with ecosystem partners. Standards don’t change the measurement science itself, but they align the platforms, and that is where the industry can help most. Some of the test criteria also include questions like how much optical power needs to be transmitted and what kind of bias you need to apply. That helps us prepare the manufacturing requirements and the deliverables.
Griffin: With almost every customer we talk to, there are two different groups within that company — the photonics group, which has been testing devices but typically not at the scale of semiconductor high-volume manufacturing, and the semiconductor high-volume test group. The test group is really concerned about uptime, software support, service support, ensuring they can deploy many test cells in high volume, and there are a lot of decisions you would make about a test cell for flexibility, modularity, and serviceability that may force a trade-off on optical performance. So from an ecosystem perspective, these groups have to talk to each other within the company to make educated decisions regarding acceptable trade-offs. No one knows their device better than the customer, the designers, and the manufacturing teams, so they need to understand that if I choose a certain connector type for more flexibility or higher channel count, but it results in slightly lower optical power at the DUT, that may impact the design. These conversations require multiple groups at the same company with vastly different backgrounds talking to each other, and I think we’re just now starting to see that happen because the production ramp is starting. Those conversations will do more to move the industry forward than anything else.
Armstrong: According to the surveys we’ve done in the IPSR, the cost to test an optical component is approaching the cost of manufacturing, and as the complexity rises, it may exceed the cost of manufacturing. That means the industry will have to realize that they’re going to have to pay for quality and known-good die, and as Ira alluded to, there should be money on the table because the reality is the cost of testing the GPU on a percentage basis is peanuts compared to the cost of testing the optical components. So the economies have to shift a little bit, and there could be different companies involved. Also, it takes a community. Each of us needs to work with partners to grow a structure that makes sense for all of us to help the industry move forward in a unified, consistent fashion that is scalable and high-volume production-capable.

For example\, to test the optical engine alone\, you replace the neighbors with a known characterized substitute\. If we have a golden reference laser source\, that can be used\.

Griffin\: We are seeing customers add monitor photodiodes into their light paths\, so that if they see an unexpected result from the transmit or receive path\, they can trace it back\. Some customers doing loopback testing want tap capability so they can route to characterization instrumentation or simply monitor power\. That’s useful if they aren’t planning to do a full characterization test and just want to do loopback or mission\-mode testing\. The downside is that if it fails and you don’t meet your bit error rate or you have a functional issue with the program\, you may not know why\. So being able to tap into that loopback capability could be important\.

Customers want to default to getting the laser source out of the equation and to use the same one that they’re using in mission mode\, but that laser source is not an ATE instrument\, so things are going to need to evolve\. Scaling Test Infrastructure for Silicon Photonics
How the semiconductor sector is solving high-volume optical testing bottlenecks for AI data centers.
The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and high-performance computing is accelerating the demand for high-speed data movement. Traditional electrical interconnects are increasingly hitting physical ceilings regarding power usage, latency, and operational reach. Consequently, technologies such as silicon photonics, near-packaged optics, and co-packaged optics are gaining critical importance for next-generation data center infrastructure.
While significant industry focus has centered on creating advanced photonic integrated circuits, transforming these designs into commercially viable, high-volume products requires robust test methodologies. Unlike standard semiconductor manufacturing, which relies on mature automated electrical testing, optics introduces complex variables including fiber alignment, coupling efficiency, and polarization management alongside conventional electrical characterization.
Automating Precision Optical Alignment
Establishing a repeatable optical connection remains a primary hurdle in production environments. Unlike straightforward physical electrical probing, optical testing depends on accurately channeling light into microscopic structures. Minor deviations in fiber positioning or angle can alter insertion loss, complicating efforts to differentiate true device variations from test setup inconsistencies.
To address this, high-volume production lines implement active alignment techniques. These systems use visual positioning to place fiber arrays near grating couplers, followed by gradient searches and feedback loops across six degrees of freedom—three positional axes and three rotational axes—to maximize coupling efficiency. As component channels multiply, alignment protocols must guarantee uniform light distribution across multiple pathways simultaneously while managing light polarization states.
Integrating Electrical and Optical Operations
Photonic integrated circuits frequently feature photodetectors and modulators requiring both electrical and optical evaluation. Conducting these measurements sequentially creates significant production delays. To maintain output velocity, manufacturers are moving toward concurrent testing models where electrical continuity checks run during automated optical probe alignment, and multi-instrument laser and power-meter controls operate in parallel.
Collaborative Ecosystem Development
No single vendor possesses all components needed for complete high-volume testing of photonic integrated circuits. Building an effective production workflow demands close cooperation across automated test equipment makers, probe and positioning specialists, foundries, and optical instrument developers. For instance, companies like Advantest and FormFactor have cooperated to merge electrical instrumentation, automated fiber alignment, wafer handling, and optical tools into unified wafer-level testing environments.
Impact analysis
As regional data center operators scale capacity to support heavy computational workloads, adopting advanced optical interconnects will dictate infrastructure efficiency. Regional technology investors must monitor how equipment integration and testing costs influence the commercial deployment timelines of silicon photonics.

records.body_text:
Been thinking about this one as it's relevant to my boat setup. I'm running a similar-ish arrangement — two MPPT controllers feeding into a 48V lithium bank, and getting the wiring right to the battery bank is something I spent ages mulling over.
The core question here is whether you connect both MPPTs directly to the battery terminals (or a busbar) versus daisy-chaining them. Short answer: busbar every time. Without one, you're relying on the battery's own terminals and cable runs to balance everything out, which gets messy fast, especially under load.
On a boat I've got limited space so I used a compact busbar from Victron — keeps things tidy and means both the 150/70s are seeing the same voltage reference point. If you've got two batteries in parallel as your bank, I'd also strongly recommend connecting the busbars at opposite corners of the parallel bank (positive from battery 1, negative from battery 2). Balances the current draw across both cells much better.
The "master" battery setting you mention — I'm guessing that's a BMS thing? Worth clarifying which BMS you're running, because that affects how you configure the charge profile on each Victron. Both MPPTs should ideally be getting the same charge parameters and ideally talking to each other via VE.Smart networking so they share current sensing data.
Anyone else running dual MPPTs into a parallel lithium bank on here? Curious whether others have gone down the VE.Smart route or just set them independently. I found the networked approach made a noticeable difference to how evenly they shared the load.

@EssexCruiser the suspense is killing me too, but while we wait for the cliffhanger resolution — one thing nobody's mentioned yet is inter-pack fusing.
Running dual packs without individual fuse protection on each battery is where people get caught out. If one pack develops a fault, you want that pack isolated, not both of them attempting to resolve their differences through your cabling at several hundred amps.
On my garden office setup (two Fogstar Drift 48V units into a Victron Multiplus-II), each pack has its own MEGA fuse rated appropriately before the positive lands on the busbar. Adds maybe £40 to the build, saves the entire shed.
Torque wrench as @SamFrost says — absolutely. But also check your torque after 2-3 thermal cycles. Connections settle. Learned that one the warm way. 🔥

records.summary: This is a Victron Community forum thread (publication number not applicable) about expanding an existing DIY battery bank with new batteries. The abstract and body text describe practical wiring and voltage-matching approaches: connecting new batteries directly to the DC busbar, or grouping batteries in parallel pairs and connecting them 'diagonally' (positive of one battery and negative of the other to the busbar). Forum participants discuss matching old and new packs by measuring terminal voltage with a multimeter, targeting within roughly 0.1–0.2 V, and note that most new batteries ship at roughly 60% state of charge where the voltage curve is flat. Every time I had to expand an existing system, measuring the battery voltage with a multimeter was the chosen way.
I did my best to match old/new packs within 0.1-0.2V and all was perfect. Of course, a little current will flow between old/new packs.
Sometimes, old packs were at 100% SOC, in this case, switched off the system, disconnected old one, connected new one, switched on the system and charge it to 100% SOC. After that, switched off the system, set the DIP switches as required (defined the master) and switched ON all packs and the system.
Other times when old pack were not fully charged I opted to discharge it and voltage match with new pack, followed by system shutdown, DIP switch setup and turn ON all.
由 BjoernK 于 5 小时前 发布
Most batteries are supplied at roughly 60% SIC, as they can be stored for a long time at that level. Since the voltage curve is very flat in that range, newly purchased batteries can be connected almost straight away.
A) Switch on each battery individually and measure the voltage at its terminals, then charge or discharge the system to the same voltage, e.g. via the ESS/Grid Setpoint.
B) Buy a small 60V/5A bench power supply and use it to charge them. Depending on the BMS, however, the batteries may shut down if they don’t receive a heartbeat via the BMS data connection. I don’t know Pytes.

records.body_text:
High-quality and efficient liquid phase exfoliation of zirconium disulfide in aqueous imidazolium-based ionic liquid solutions for efficient electrocatalytic hydrogen evolution reaction
- Energy materials
- Published:
Abstract
Zirconium disulfide (ZrS2) nanosheets, as a member of transition metal dichalcogenides, have exhibited potential applications in a variety of fields such as the fabrication of the field effect transistors, sensors, laser fiber. Liquid-phase exfoliation is considered to be a simple, low-cost, and large-scale method to prepare ZrS2 nanosheets. However, in this method, most of the organic solvents commonly employed are toxic, and the overall exfoliation yield remains relatively low. In this work, we have successfully exfoliated bulk ZrS2 into nanosheets with single and few layer through a simple, efficient and green liquid-phase exfoliation in water-imidazolium-based ionic liquids ([C14mim]Br, [C14mim][C8H7O3], [C14mim][CHN4], [C14mim][C6H4N3], or [C14mim][C8H10NO2]) solutions. It is found that exfoliation yield is up to 82.5%, which surpasses most of the reported values obtained by liquid-phase exfoliation method. The exfoliation yield of ZrS2 nanosheets decreased with the increase in pKa of ionic liquid anions. The ZrS2 nanosheets exhibited a thickness of 1–2 nm and lateral dimension of 100–200 nm. The high yield is primarily attributed to the strong interactions between C=O or C–OH groups in ionic liquid anions and ZrS2, which effectively weakens the van der Waals forces among layers under the assistance of ultrasound, enabling efficient preparation of ZrS2 nanosheets. Furthermore, the prepared ZrS2 nanosheets were applied in the hydrogen evolution reaction as electrocatalysts, and demonstrated stronger electrocatalytic activity compared to bulk ZrS2. Therefore, the liquid-phase exfoliation method reported has great potential in large-scale production of ZrS2 nanosheets for high activity hydrogen evolution reaction.

records.body_text:
Metal 3D printing for under $5,000? Global Laser Box says hundreds have already shipped
Jiangsu Global Laser Box Digital Technology (江苏铬莱铂数字科技有限公司) will launch a global crowdfunding campaign for its third-generation compact metal 3D printer, the GLB-M1, at the end of November. The company says it has already shipped several hundred units of its first-generation compact machine, priced at $4,988, to international customers.
Company chairman Wang Binhua gave a detailed account of pricing, factory construction, overseas shipments and the GLB-M1 in an interview with Nanjixiong at TCT Shenzhen on 14 October 2026. The interview came a month after the company announced a Series A round of nearly RMB200 million.
Three generations of compact metal machines
The GLB-M1, displayed behind the company’s stand in Shenzhen ahead of its crowdfunding launch, is built around voice interaction. Operators can give spoken instructions and hear live updates on how a print is progressing. Combined with cloud slicing and global data management, these features underpin the company’s pitch of the GLB-M1 as an “AI 3D printer”.
The new model builds on two earlier compact systems. The first, introduced at a consumer electronics show in June, sells abroad for $4,988, and Wang put overseas shipments at several hundred units. A second model, the DP-C2, is meant for buyers in China. Wang said it needs no more setup than a power supply and a source of nitrogen, either a generator or rented cylinders. It also carries eight AI-based tools, among them residual stress analysis and slicing in the cloud.
To back up its claims on print quality, the company put out a set of small parts, metal turtles among them, straight from the machine. None had been sandblasted, annealed or finished in any other way. Staff explained that the aim was to let visitors judge the raw accuracy and surface quality a sub-$5,000 metal printer can achieve.
Sales activity at the show was also brisk, according to Wang. A prize draw gave visitors the chance to win discounts worth as much as RMB24,888, and he said several buyers who had put down deposits on day one went on to complete purchases once they secured a reduced price.
On the industrial side, the company is promoting the RMB298,000 GLB-330M, which debuted at TCT Shanghai this year. Wang said prototyping and mould-making firms make up much of the company’s South China customer base, and these buyers typically opt for a 400 mm machine. His pitch is that the same money can buy a pair of GLB-330Ms instead, delivering greater combined build area and higher output.
Factories, funding and a Genesis joint venture
The Series A round was jointly backed by Qifu Capital, Changxing Investment and Genesis Investment. According to public reports, the company develops and produces its core components in-house, including lasers, control systems and software, and has sold products to more than 60 countries.
Wang said production is expanding quickly following the round. The company’s base in Huzhou, Zhejiang covers more than 50 acres and includes a self-built 40,000 m² factory scheduled to begin production in December 2026. Production bases are already operating in Yancheng, Jiangsu, and Changsha, Hunan.
In Shenzhen, the company has formed a joint venture with machine-tool producer Genesis (创世纪, 300083), a Tier 1 supplier to the 3C electronics industry. The venture will focus on metal additive manufacturing of high-end components for consumer electronics, robotics and AI infrastructure, mainly liquid-cooled copper structural parts. Genesis will handle key customers, while Global Laser Box will be responsible for custom machine development and process verification. At the time of the interview, the Shenzhen facility was under renovation and due for completion by the end of the month.
A Cheaper Road Into Metal AM
The company’s approach targets one of metal additive manufacturing’s longest-standing gaps: the cost of getting started. Instead of competing on high-end industrial machines, it pairs affordable equipment with Chinese component production to keep hardware costs down, adds software integration so the system works as a complete workflow, and builds out a network of manufacturing sites that turns installed machines into real production capacity. Buying a printer becomes only one part of the offer.
Recent launches show how fast the low-cost segment is moving. Colorado-based Scrap Labs unveiled the Scrap 1 low-cost LPBF metal 3D printer at the Rocky Mountain RepRap Festival 2026, with kit pricing starting at $9,600 for a limited time. The company says the savings come from engineering and manufacturing efficiencies rather than stripped-down capabilities. At the industrial end, Mastrex introduced the MX300 affordable LPBF metal 3D printer, priced at $185,000 and pitched as the industry’s most affordable LPBF system. Mastrex presents it as a long-term production platform rather than a machine limited to prototyping.
The network side of the strategy also matches where the industry expects metal AM to go. In 3D Printing Industry’s additive manufacturing expert forecasts for 2026, contributors predicted that digital inventories, distributed manufacturing networks and qualified additive workflows will keep replacing brittle, offshore-dependent supply models. Related future of 3D printing predictions describe a shift toward distributed printing networks where digital files are fulfilled at the nearest available print location, cutting logistics friction and lead times.
Cheap metal printers are no longer the hard part. What will set companies apart is turning low-cost machines into reliable, networked production capacity.
Paloma Duran holds a BA in International Relations and an MA in Journalism. Specializing in writing, podcasting, and content and event creation, she works across politics, energy, mining, and technology. With a passion for global trends, Paloma is particularly interested in the impact of technology like 3D printing on shaping our future.

records.title: Swiss-Polish team skips the solvent bath, gets printed aluminium to 98% density
records.abstract: In material extrusion (MEX-AM), a printer lays down a “green” part made of metal powder held in a thermoplastic binder, which must be removed before the part is sintered. Binder is usually removed with a solvent bath followed by burn-off in air.
records.summary: This 3D Printing Industry news article reports on a Swiss-Polish research effort to improve material extrusion additive manufacturing (MEX-AM) of aluminium AA6061 by replacing conventional solvent debinding with a capillary wicking step. In MEX-AM, metal powder is held in a thermoplastic binder that must be removed before sintering; aluminium is difficult because it oxidises readily, and thermal analysis reportedly showed the 6061 powder begins oxidising near 400 °C, below the ~500 °C binder suppliers recommend. The team mixed gas-atomised AA6061 at 60 vol.% with commercial binders (EnCeram, Kcmix3.3, EmbemouldCC; the last separated during extrusion and was dropped) and printed 20 mm discs on a Tumaker Voladora NX+ pellet-screw printer. Solvent debinding followed by air thermal debinding at 350 °C removed at least 96% of binder but gave poor sintered density (EnCeram ~75% after water soaking; Kcmix ~94% after acetone). Dropping the solvent step and using a porous alumina powder bed to wick out binder during a 24-hour air heat treatment at 350 °C removed over 97% of binder without cracking, blistering or deformation; after sintering in nitrogen at 635 °C for two hours, Kcmix parts reached 96.7% and EnCeram 93.6% density, rising to 97.9% and 96.8% with a 10-hour hold. The article states the authors measured only density and microstructure and that mechanical properties must be evaluated before industrial use.
records.why_it_matters: The reported results suggest that for MEX-AM aluminium the debinding step, rather than the alloy or binder alone, may be the main barrier to densification, pointing to a low-equipment capillary-wicking route that runs in air on standard extrusion hardware with commercially available binders.

Measured outcomes are given (96.7%/93.6% density at 2 h hold; 97.9%/96.8% at 10 h), plus a quantified oxidation result (~0.25% mass gain at 400 °C). records.body_text:
In material extrusion (MEX-AM), a printer lays down a “green” part made of metal powder held in a thermoplastic binder, which must be removed before the part is sintered. Binder is usually removed with a solvent bath followed by burn-off in air. Aluminium complicates both steps because it oxidises readily, and the resulting surface oxide blocks sintering. Thermal analysis showed the 6061 powder begins to oxidise at around 400 °C, below the roughly 500 °C program the binder suppliers recommend.
The team mixed gas-atomised AA6061 at 60 vol.% with three commercial binders: EnCeram from Chemische Fabrik Budenheim, Kcmix3.3, and EmbemouldCC from KRAHN Chemie. EmbemouldCC separated during extrusion and was dropped. The remaining two feedstocks were pelletised and printed into 20 mm discs on a Tumaker Voladora NX+ pellet-screw printer.
Solvent baths left an oxidised shell
Following the suppliers’ instructions, the researchers first used solvent debinding followed by thermal debinding in air at 350 °C. This removed at least 96% of the binder, but sintered density was poor. EnCeram parts, soaked in water, reached only about 75%. The water had turned the powder surface into hydroxide, which converted to oxide on heating and left a porous outer layer of unbonded particles. Kcmix parts treated in high-purity acetone reached around 94%, but their edges still failed to densify fully.
The team then dropped the solvent step. Instead, printed parts were placed in a porous alumina powder bed that draws out the liquid binder by capillary action during one 24-hour heat treatment in air. At 350 °C, this removed over 97% of the binder with no cracking, blistering or deformation. Raising the temperature to 400 °C backfired. In a separate test, the aluminium powder gained about 0.25% in mass from oxidation after 24 hours at that temperature, and parts wick-debound at 400 °C sintered to lower density.
A ten-hour hold pushes density to 98%
After wicking at 350 °C and sintering in nitrogen at 635 °C for two hours, Kcmix parts reached 96.7% density and EnCeram parts 93.6%. Extending the hold to 10 hours raised these to 97.9% and 96.8% respectively, with even densification from centre to edge. The authors note these values exceed most reported for additively manufactured aluminium feedstocks. They add that the same feedstocks could also be warm-pressed, extruded or injection moulded.
The best result still requires 24 hours of debinding and 10 hours of sintering in nitrogen. The team measured only density and microstructure, and says mechanical properties must be evaluated before the method can move toward industrial use.
The long road to sintered aluminium
The Swiss-Polish team is taking a low-equipment approach to an alloy that metal AM has struggled to sinter. Rather than developing new binders or specialised powders, it focuses on the step between printing and the furnace. The goal is a debinding route that runs in air on standard extrusion hardware, using binders anyone can buy.
Powder makers have shown that aluminium can be sintered to high density. The Swiss result suggests the debinding step, not the alloy, may be what has held extrusion back. Mechanical data will decide whether it matters.
