records.body_text:
How to Adjust Laser Welding Parameters for Thin Aluminum Sheets
Reference machine: LaserMen LM-2000 4-in-1 / 5-in-1 handheld fiber laser welder | Author: Zhou Dong | Reading time: 12 minutes
Thin aluminum sheet, from 0.5 to 3 mm, is the material behind a large share of today's fabrication: kitchen sinks and range hoods, electrical cabinets, advertising channel letters, battery trays and enclosures for new-energy vehicles. Handheld fiber laser welding has moved into this work quickly because it puts a stable, concentrated heat source in an operator's hand without the long learning curve of AC TIG. But the same properties that make aluminum useful also make it the least forgiving metal on the shop floor. Miss the heat balance by a fraction, and a 1 mm panel either burns through or refuses to fuse.
This guide is built around the LaserMen LM-2000 4-in-1 / 5-in-1 platform (1,200 to 3,000 W, 1,080 nm fiber, double-wobble head) and the parameter logic our application team uses to commission machines for real production lines. Every value below is a field-verified starting point, not a gospel number. Your alloy, joint fit-up and gas setup will move the settings, so weld a coupon first, every time.
Why Thin Aluminum Fights Back
Before touching a single parameter, it helps to understand what the beam is up against. Four physical facts explain almost every aluminum welding defect you will see.
- Reflectivity. At room temperature aluminum reflects roughly 90% of a 1,080 nm beam. The first milliseconds of every weld are spent fighting to couple the light into the metal; once the molten pool forms, absorption jumps and the same power suddenly feels too hot. This is why cold starts and stutter appear on aluminum far more than on steel. The Raycus, Maxphotonics and BWT fiber sources fitted to the LM-2000 carry back-reflection protection, which matters on aluminum more than on any other common metal.
- Thermal conductivity. Aluminum conducts heat three to five times faster than carbon steel. A slow, cautious weld simply pours energy into the whole panel, producing distortion and sag instead of penetration. Aluminum wants power density delivered quickly, not a long warm-up.
- The oxide film. Aluminum oxide (Al2O3) melts at about 2,072 °C, while the aluminum underneath melts at 660 °C. A mill-finish surface carries a tenacious oxide layer that resists fusion and traps gas. Weld over it and the bead looks acceptable from the top while hiding lack-of-fusion and pinholes.
- Shrinkage and hydrogen. Aluminum has one of the highest solidification shrinkages of any commercial metal, about 6% by volume, and hydrogen dissolved in the liquid pool comes out of solution as the metal freezes. That combination is the source of most porosity, crater cracks and end-of-seam depressions.
On a 0.8 mm sheet there is no heat buffer at all. The line between "not fused" and "hole" is narrower than the weld bead itself, which is why parameter discipline matters more on aluminum than on any other material the LM-2000 welds.
Choose the Right Power Class First
The LM-2000 is rated across a 0.5 to 8 mm welding thickness range, but that envelope is dominated by carbon and stainless steel. Single-pass aluminum sits at the lower end, and buying headroom is cheaper than buying short. Use this as the sizing reference before fine-tuning any seam.
Laser power | Practical single-pass aluminum (flat butt) | Typical work | Shop power supply
---|---|---|---
1,200 W | 0.5 to 1.5 mm | 0.8 to 1.2 mm kitchenware, sign cabinets, thin ducts | 220 V, single-phase
1,500 W | 0.5 to 2.0 mm | HVAC boxes, enclosures, general light fabrication | 220 V / 380 V
2,000 W | 0.8 to 3.0 mm | Battery trays, brackets, mixed-gauge shops | 380 V, 3-phase
3,000 W | 1.5 to 5.0 mm | Structural fabrications, thick-to-thin assemblies | 380 V, 3-phase
Spec the machine so your thickest everyday job runs at 70 to 80% of rated power. A laser that lives at 100% on every seam gives away diode life and leaves no margin for a dirty surface, a slightly wider gap or a cold shop in winter.
LM-2000 4-in-1 / 5-in-1 Handheld Fiber Laser Welding Cutting Cleaning Machine
- Model: LM-2000 4-in-1 / 5-in-1
- Laser power: 1200W/1500W/2000W/3000W
- Working range: Welding, Cutting, Weld seam cleaning, Cleaning, Battery welding
- Application: Welds, cuts, cleans various metals; supports weld seam cleaning & new energy battery welding; widely used in advertising, kitchen, automotive, machinery and elevator industries.
The Starting Parameter Sheet
The table below is the exact starting point our engineers hand to customers. Reference conditions: flat position, cleaned 3000 / 5000 / 6000 series sheet, argon shielding, 1.0 mm 4043 or 5356 filler wire, double-wobble head, red-dot visual alignment.
Sheet thickness | Laser power | Travel speed | Defocus | Wobble amplitude | Wobble frequency | Wire feed speed
---|---|---|---|---|---|---
0.5 mm | 550 to 700 W | 45 to 60 mm/s | +2 mm | 0.8 mm | 150 Hz | 0.6 to 0.9 m/min (often no wire)
0.8 mm | 800 to 1,000 W | 35 to 45 mm/s | +1.5 mm | 1.0 mm | 150 to 180 Hz | 0.8 to 1.1 m/min
1.0 mm | 1,000 to 1,200 W | 30 to 40 mm/s | +1 mm | 1.2 mm | 150 to 200 Hz | 1.0 to 1.4 m/min
1.5 mm | 1,300 to 1,500 W | 22 to 30 mm/s | 0 to +1 mm | 1.5 mm | 120 to 180 Hz | 1.2 to 1.6 m/min
2.0 mm | 1,600 to 1,900 W | 18 to 25 mm/s | 0 to -1 mm | 1.8 to 2.0 mm | 100 to 150 Hz | 1.4 to 1.9 m/min
3.0 mm | 2,200 to 2,600 W | 12 to 18 mm/s | -1 to -2 mm | 2.0 to 2.5 mm | 80 to 120 Hz | 1.8 to 2.4 m/min
For a 0.5 mm sheet with a tight, gap-free butt joint, filler wire is often unnecessary. Run the bead autogenous and keep the positive defocus. Above 1.5 mm, the wire is doing real work: it fills the joint, replaces solidification shrinkage and breaks the crack sensitivity of 6000-series alloys.
These values move with the alloy. 5052 and 5083 conduct heat faster and need roughly 5 to 10% more power than 3003; 6061 should always take 4043 filler; anodized material must have the coating stripped at the seam, and the machine's cleaning mode does this in one pass rather than with a grinder.
How Each Setting Actually Behaves
Power and travel speed work as a pair
Heat input per unit length is roughly power divided by speed, expressed in joules per millimeter. On thin aluminum the correct direction is high power with fast travel: a fast pool solidifies before heat can spread, so distortion stays low and the bead stays bright. Resist the instinct to turn the power down and crawl along, because that is precisely how thin sheets sag and grain structure grows. When a bead is wrong, change travel speed first, in steps of about 10%, and only then adjust power.
Defocus sets the shape of the pool
Positive defocus moves the focal point above the sheet, widening and softening the pool, which is right for 0.5 to 1.5 mm. Negative defocus drives a keyhole deeper for 2 to 3 mm. Move in 0.5 mm increments. A single millimeter of defocus changes the bead more than most operators expect, and chasing a defect with power when defocus is the real cause wastes a lot of coupons.
Wobble is your gap tolerance and your porosity defense
The double-wobble head on the LM-2000 sweeps the spot across a 0 to 5 mm width and stirs the pool in two directions, letting trapped gas escape and giving aluminum its most porosity-resistant bead. Amplitude is also what bridges fit-up gaps that a static spot cannot. Set amplitude at roughly 1 to 1.5 times the sheet thickness; anything wider on thin gauge pulls cold shuts at the bead edges. Frequency shapes the surface: higher frequency smooths the fish-scale pattern but slightly reduces effective penetration.
Filler wire and gap limits
Use 4043 (AlSi5) for 6000-series and general work; it flows well and suppresses hot-crack tendency. Use 5356 (AlMg5) for 5000-series where weld strength matters, keeping in mind it colors differently after anodizing. Match wire diameter to the sheet: 0.8 mm wire for 0.5 to 0.8 mm sheet, 1.0 mm for 1 to 2 mm, 1.2 mm at 3 mm. Hold fit-up gaps under 0.1 mm up to 1 mm sheet and under 0.2 mm at 2 to 3 mm. Wobble plus wire cannot rescue a badly gapped joint, no matter how the parameters are tuned.
Shielding Gas: Use Argon on Aluminum
The LM-2000 accepts both nitrogen and argon, and nitrogen saves money on stainless steel jobs. On aluminum it is a false economy.
Factor | Argon | Nitrogen
---|---|---
Behavior on aluminum | Fully inert; clean wetting and a stable pool; the standard for aluminum | Reacts at aluminum pool temperatures; nitride films and scattered porosity follow
Typical use | All aluminum, including 3000 / 5000 / 6000 series | Cost-saving on selected stainless and steel jobs
Purity and flow | 99.99%+; 15 to 20 L/min thin sheet, 20 to 25 L/min at 3 mm | Not recommended for aluminum
Keep 3 to 5 seconds of post-flow after the trigger releases. A bead that cools under argon stays bright silver; a bead that cools in air turns dull and sooty. Note that too much flow is also a defect. A turbulent jet drags shop air into the pool and creates the very pinholes you are trying to avoid, so turn the flow up only as far as the joint actually needs.
Commissioning Routine, Step by Step
- Strip the seam. Clean both sides of the joint and the filler wire. On the LM-2000, switch to the cleaning lens and use cleaning mode, with a sweep up to 35 mm, to remove oxide, rust and anodizing. Otherwise wipe with solvent and a stainless brush kept exclusively for aluminum.
- Fit, gap and back. Clamp tightly, hold the gaps listed above, and place a copper backing bar under thin butt joints. Copper pulls heat from the back, stops sag and produces a consistent, shallow back bead. It is the single biggest difference between a test coupon and a production-quality seam.
- Set gas and wire. Argon on, feed the wire, purge the line and run a wire-feeding test away from the part.
- Weld a coupon. Use the same alloy and thickness, trace the seam with the red-dot pointer and run the table values. The 9 m standard cable, with 14 m optional, makes it easy to work on a bench or directly on a finished assembly.
- Read the bead and adjust. A good bead is bright silver with uniform scales and a consistent back bead. Specific corrections are listed below.
- Ramp in and out. Use the start and end power ramps and fill the crater at the end of the seam. A 6061 seam that ends with a sharp trigger release is exactly where most crater cracks begin.
- Clean the finished seam. The weld-seam cleaning mode, with a 0 to 12 mm sweep, removes the dull oxide ring on a finished bead in seconds and replaces hand polishing. This is one of the reasons the 4-in-1 platform pays back fastest in aluminum shops.
When the coupon is wrong, adjust in this order:
- Burn-through or sag: speed up 10 to 15%, reduce power 5 to 10%, move defocus positive, check the backing bar.
- Cold lap or lack of fusion: add power, slow slightly, move defocus negative, re-clean the seam.
- Porosity: re-clean, check gas purity and flow, block drafts, lengthen post-flow.
- Undercut: narrow the wobble, add wire, soften the end ramp.
Handheld Laser vs AC TIG on Thin Aluminum
For a shop deciding between processes, the numbers on thin gauge are not close:
Factor | LM-2000 handheld fiber laser | AC TIG
---|---|---
Travel speed on 1 mm sheet | 30 to 40 mm/s | 3 to 8 mm/s
Heat-affected zone | Narrow; minimal distortion | Broad; frequent straightening
Operator ramp-up | Productive within days | Competent after months
Filler delivery | Automatic wire feeder | Hand-fed rod
Post-weld finishing | Little to none; seam cleaning on board | Grinding and polishing typical
Best domain | 0.5 to 5 mm thin and mid gauge | Heavy plate, critical pipe, code work
In our customers' kitchenware and enclosure shops, the laser runs 4 to 8 times the seam length per shift on 1 to 2 mm aluminum. TIG still owns heavy, code-critical pipe work, and anyone selling a handheld laser as a universal TIG replacement is overselling. The two processes are complementary in a mature shop.
Defect Troubleshooting at a Glance
Symptom | Likely cause | Correction
---|---|---
Pinholes or porosity | Oxide film, damp or low-purity gas, drafts, short post-flow | Re-clean the seam, check gas purity and flow, block drafts, extend post-flow
Burn-through | Too much heat, slow travel, excessive gap, no backing | Speed up, reduce power, add a copper bar, move defocus positive
Sagging or undercut | Heat soak, wobble too wide, no filler | Reduce power and amplitude, add wire, fit a backing bar
Cold lap, no fusion | Too fast, too little power, oxide under the bead | Add power, slow slightly, clean, move defocus negative
Hot cracks on 6061 | 6000-series crack sensitivity, no filler, sharp crater | Run 4043 wire, ramp out the end, reduce restraint
Black, sooty bead | Wrong gas or air in the shield, low flow | Switch to argon, raise flow, check hose seals
Intermittent start | High reflectivity, contaminated surface | Clean the start point, use a power ramp on an anti-reflection source
Final Notes
Thin aluminum rewards a disciplined sequence: a clean surface, a tight fit-up, a copper backing bar, argon shielding, and a high-power, fast-travel weld that was tuned on a coupon first. The parameter sheet is the first ten minutes of the job, not the whole job. Every shop eventually develops its own numbers around its fixtures, its alloys and its operators.
The LM-2000 platform keeps the entire loop on one cart: pre-weld cleaning, welding and post-weld seam cleaning without moving the part. If you are setting up a new line, send us your alloy, thickness and joint drawing. Our application lab will weld your coupons and return the exact parameter set before the machine ships, so production starts on day one instead of week three.
Zhou Dong (周东)
Senior Welding Process Engineer, LaserMen
Zhou Dong has spent 13 years on fiber laser welding applications and leads the handheld-welding process group at LaserMen, where he develops the default parameter libraries shipped with every LM-2000 machine.
He has commissioned handheld laser lines for kitchenware, automotive battery, enclosure and advertising fabricators in more than 30 countries, and has personally run several thousand weld coupons on 3003, 5052, 5083, 6061 and cast aluminum. His work focuses on turning laboratory welding parameters into repeatable shop-floor settings that survive real gaps, real surfaces and real operators.

2\.0 mm \| 1\,600 to 1\,900 W \| 18 to 25 mm\/s \| 0 to \-1 mm \| 1\.8 to 2\.0 mm \| 100 to 150 Hz \| 1\.4 to 1\.9 m\/min 
3\.0 mm \| 2\,200 to 2\,600 W \| 12 to 18 mm\/s \| \-1 to \-2 mm \| 2\.0 to 2\.5 mm \| 80 to 120 Hz \| 1\.8 to 2\.4 m\/min 

For a 0\.5 mm sheet with a tight\, gap\-free butt joint\, filler wire is often unnecessary\. Run the bead autogenous and keep the positive defocus\. Above 1\.5 mm\, the wire is doing real work\: it fills the joint\, replaces solidification shrinkage and breaks the crack sensitivity of 6000\-series alloys\.

These values move with the alloy\. 5052 and 5083 conduct heat faster and need roughly 5 to 10\% more power than 3003\; 6061 should always take 4043 filler\; anodized material must have the coating stripped at the seam\, and the machine\'s cleaning mode does this in one pass rather than with a grinder\.

\#\# How Each Setting Actually Behaves

\#\#\# Power and travel speed work as a pair

Heat input per unit length is roughly power divided by speed\, expressed in joules per millimeter\. On thin aluminum the correct direction is high power with fast travel\: a fast pool solidifies before heat can spread\, so distortion stays low and the bead stays bright\. Resist the instinct to turn the power down and crawl along\, because that is precisely how thin sheets sag and grain structure grows\. When a bead is wrong\, change travel speed first\, in steps of about 10\%\, and only then adjust power\.

\#\#\# Defocus sets the shape of the pool

Positive defocus moves the focal point above the sheet\, widening and softening the pool\, which is right for 0\.5 to 1\.5 mm\. Negative defocus drives a keyhole deeper for 2 to 3 mm\. Move in 0\.5 mm increments\. A single millimeter of defocus changes the bead more than most operators expect\, and chasing a defect with power when defocus is the real cause wastes a lot of coupons\.

\#\#\# Wobble is your gap tolerance and your porosity defense

The double\-wobble head on the LM\-2000 sweeps the spot across a 0 to 5 mm width and stirs the pool in two directions\, letting trapped gas escape and giving aluminum its most porosity\-resistant bead\. Amplitude is also what bridges fit\-up gaps that a static spot cannot\. Set amplitude at roughly 1 to 1\.5 times the sheet thickness\; anything wider on thin gauge pulls cold shuts at the bead edges\. Frequency shapes the surface\: higher frequency smooths the fish\-scale pattern but slightly reduces effective penetration\.

\#\#\# Filler wire and gap limits

Use 4043 \(AlSi5\) for 6000\-series and general work\; it flows well and suppresses hot\-crack tendency\. Use 5356 \(AlMg5\) for 5000\-series where weld strength matters\, keeping in mind it colors differently after anodizing\. Match wire diameter to the sheet\: 0\.8 mm wire for 0\.5 to 0\.8 mm sheet\, 1\.0 mm for 1 to 2 mm\, 1\.2 mm at 3 mm\. Hold fit\-up gaps under 0\.1 mm up to 1 mm sheet and under 0\.2 mm at 2 to 3 mm\. Wobble plus wire cannot rescue a badly gapped joint\, no matter how the parameters are tuned\.

\#\# Shielding Gas\: Use Argon on Aluminum

The LM\-2000 accepts both nitrogen and argon\, and nitrogen saves money on stainless steel jobs\. On aluminum it is a false economy\.

Factor \| Argon \| Nitrogen 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Behavior on aluminum \| Fully inert\; clean wetting and a stable pool\; the standard for aluminum \| Reacts at aluminum pool temperatures\; nitride films and scattered porosity follow 
Typical use \| All aluminum\, including 3000 \/ 5000 \/ 6000 series \| Cost\-saving on selected stainless and steel jobs 
Purity and flow \| 99\.99\%\+\; 15 to 20 L\/min thin sheet\, 20 to 25 L\/min at 3 mm \| Not recommended for aluminum 

Keep 3 to 5 seconds of post\-flow after the trigger releases\. A bead that cools under argon stays bright silver\; a bead that cools in air turns dull and sooty\. Note that too much flow is also a defect\. A turbulent jet drags shop air into the pool and creates the very pinholes you are trying to avoid\, so turn the flow up only as far as the joint actually needs\.

\#\# Commissioning Routine\, Step by Step

\- Strip the seam\. Clean both sides of the joint and the filler wire\. On the LM\-2000\, switch to the cleaning lens and use cleaning mode\, with a sweep up to 35 mm\, to remove oxide\, rust and anodizing\. Otherwise wipe with solvent and a stainless brush kept exclusively for aluminum\.
\- Fit\, gap and back\. Clamp tightly\, hold the gaps listed above\, and place a copper backing bar under thin butt joints\. Copper pulls heat from the back\, stops sag and produces a consistent\, shallow back bead\. It is the single biggest difference between a test coupon and a production\-quality seam\.
\- Set gas and wire\. Argon on\, feed the wire\, purge the line and run a wire\-feeding test away from the part\.
\- Weld a coupon\. Use the same alloy and thickness\, trace the seam with the red\-dot pointer and run the table values\. The 9 m standard cable\, with 14 m optional\, makes it easy to work on a bench or directly on a finished assembly\.
\- Read the bead and adjust\. A good bead is bright silver with uniform scales and a consistent back bead\. Specific corrections are listed below\.
\- Ramp in and out\. Use the start and end power ramps and fill the crater at the end of the seam\. A 6061 seam that ends with a sharp trigger release is exactly where most crater cracks begin\.
\- Clean the finished seam\. The weld\-seam cleaning mode\, with a 0 to 12 mm sweep\, removes the dull oxide ring on a finished bead in seconds and replaces hand polishing\. This is one of the reasons the 4\-in\-1 platform pays back fastest in aluminum shops\.

When the coupon is wrong\, adjust in this order\:

\- Burn\-through or sag\: speed up 10 to 15\%\, reduce power 5 to 10\%\, move defocus positive\, check the backing bar\.
\- Cold lap or lack of fusion\: add power\, slow slightly\, move defocus negative\, re\-clean the seam\.
\- Porosity\: re\-clean\, check gas purity and flow\, block drafts\, lengthen post\-flow\.
\- Undercut\: narrow the wobble\, add wire\, soften the end ramp\.

\#\# Handheld Laser vs AC TIG on Thin Aluminum

For a shop deciding between processes\, the numbers on thin gauge are not close\:

Factor \| LM\-2000 handheld fiber laser \| AC TIG 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Travel speed on 1 mm sheet \| 30 to 40 mm\/s \| 3 to 8 mm\/s 
Heat\-affected zone \| Narrow\; minimal distortion \| Broad\; frequent straightening 
Operator ramp\-up \| Productive within days \| Competent after months 
Filler delivery \| Automatic wire feeder \| Hand\-fed rod 
Post\-weld finishing \| Little to none\; seam cleaning on board \| Grinding and polishing typical 
Best domain \| 0\.5 to 5 mm thin and mid gauge \| Heavy plate\, critical pipe\, code work 

In our customers\' kitchenware and enclosure shops\, the laser runs 4 to 8 times the seam length per shift on 1 to 2 mm aluminum\. TIG still owns heavy\, code\-critical pipe work\, and anyone selling a handheld laser as a universal TIG replacement is overselling\. The two processes are complementary in a mature shop\.

\#\# Defect Troubleshooting at a Glance

Symptom \| Likely cause \| Correction 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Pinholes or porosity \| Oxide film\, damp or low\-purity gas\, drafts\, short post\-flow \| Re\-clean the seam\, check gas purity and flow\, block drafts\, extend post\-flow 
Burn\-through \| Too much heat\, slow travel\, excessive gap\, no backing \| Speed up\, reduce power\, add a copper bar\, move defocus positive 
Sagging or undercut \| Heat soak\, wobble too wide\, no filler \| Reduce power and amplitude\, add wire\, fit a backing bar 
Cold lap\, no fusion \| Too fast\, too little power\, oxide under the bead \| Add power\, slow slightly\, clean\, move defocus negative 
Hot cracks on 6061 \| 6000\-series crack sensitivity\, no filler\, sharp crater \| Run 4043 wire\, ramp out the end\, reduce restraint 
Black\, sooty bead \| Wrong gas or air in the shield\, low flow \| Switch to argon\, raise flow\, check hose seals 
Intermittent start \| High reflectivity\, contaminated surface \| Clean the start point\, use a power ramp on an anti\-reflection source 

\#\# Final Notes

Thin aluminum rewards a disciplined sequence\: a clean surface\, a tight fit\-up\, a copper backing bar\, argon shielding\, and a high\-power\, fast\-travel weld that was tuned on a coupon first\. The parameter sheet is the first ten minutes of the job\, not the whole job\. Every shop eventually develops its own numbers around its fixtures\, its alloys and its operators\.

The LM\-2000 platform keeps the entire loop on one cart\: pre\-weld cleaning\, welding and post\-weld seam cleaning without moving the part\. If you are setting up a new line\, send us your alloy\, thickness and joint drawing\. Our application lab will weld your coupons and return the exact parameter set before the machine ships\, so production starts on day one instead of week three\.

Zhou Dong \(周东\)

Zhou Dong has spent 13 years on fiber laser welding applications and leads the handheld\-welding process group at LaserMen\, where he develops the default parameter libraries shipped with every LM\-2000 machine\.

He has commissioned handheld laser lines for kitchenware\, automotive battery\, enclosure and advertising fabricators in more than 30 countries\, and has personally run several thousand weld coupons on 3003\, 5052\, 5083\, 6061 and cast aluminum\. His work focuses on turning laboratory welding parameters into repeatable shop\-floor settings that survive real gaps\, real surfaces and real operators\.

Copper Busbar: The Numbers Behind Every Busbar
Every copper busbar is measured against one number: 100 percent. Since 1913, annealed copper has defined 100 percent on the International Annealed Copper Standard (IACS), the scale every other conductor is graded on. Modern busbar copper scores about 101 percent, so it beats the very standard that defines it. So why is copper used for busbars when aluminum is lighter and often cheaper? In short, copper packs the most current into the smallest bar, stays strong enough to bolt and bend, and forms bolted joints that last for decades with little upkeep. This page collects the numbers for electrical copper in one place: conductivity, strength, temper, heat, weight, grades, ampacity and plating. Then it shows what each number means on the shop floor, where bars get cut, punched and bent every day.
⏱ ...
Share:
Take a Look at Our Products
Click
If you’d rather listen than read, feel free to play the audio file below for the rest of this article.
What Is a Copper Busbar?
A copper busbar is a solid copper bar or strip that carries and distributes electric current inside switchboards, panelboards, switchgear, busways and battery systems. Installers also spell it copper bus bar; both names mean the same part.
Ask what is copper busbar in a panel shop, and you will hear a simpler answer: the backbone that feeds every breaker. Typical uses include:
- Main and branch bars in switchboards and panelboards
- Phase, neutral and ground bars in switchgear
- Busway and bus duct runs in buildings and plants
- Battery, UPS and inverter links, including laminated copper busbar packs
- Grounding bars in telecom sites
Built for processing larger conductors, the HBC-B200 machine performs cutting, punching, and bending operations on busbars up to 200 × 20 mm. Its sequential operating system is designed for accurate fabrication of heavy-duty electrical connections.
Why Copper: The Core Numbers
The table lists typical copper busbar material values for C11000, the grade most ASTM B187 bus bar uses, and what each number does in a real panel.
Property | Typical value (C11000) | Why it matters
---|---|---
Conductivity | 101% IACS | Less heat per amp
Resistivity | 1.7241 µΩ·cm defines 100% IACS | Sets voltage drop
Density | 0.322 lb/in³ (8.91 g/cm³) | Weight and cost
Thermal conductivity | 226 Btu/ft·h·°F (391 W/m·K) | Spreads joint heat
Thermal expansion | 9.4 × 10⁻⁶/°F (16.9 × 10⁻⁶/K) | Moves bolted joints
A copper bar is only one part of the wider system that moves power from the incomer to every load. For busbar types, design and applications across modern facilities, see our guide to electrical busbar systems.
Electrical: Conductivity, Resistivity and %IACS
What is the conductivity of copper busbar? For C11000, the Copper Development Association lists 101 percent IACS at 68 °F (20 °C). The %IACS scale compares any metal with annealed copper, which defines 100 percent: a conductivity of 58.0 MS/m, or a resistivity of 1.7241 µΩ·cm at 20 °C.
Modern refining easily beats that 1913 reference. As a result, electrolytic tough pitch (ETP) and oxygen-free grades meet or exceed 100 to 101 percent. Each extra point means slightly less heat for the same current, which adds up across a long switchboard run.
Impurities work the other way. Even small amounts of phosphorus, iron or other elements scatter electrons and lower conductivity, so bus copper is refined to very high purity. For example, phosphorus-deoxidized copper (C12200) drops to roughly 85 percent IACS, which is why ASTM B187 lists it for general use rather than for bus bar. For the full resistivity story, including temperature and alloy effects, see our copper resistivity guide.
Good busbar design starts with the conductor, so the copper industry publishes its own guidance. The Copper Alliance covers current rating, joints, short-circuit effects and coatings in its busbar design guide.
Mechanical: Tensile Strength, Hardness and Temper
ASTM B187/B187M-26 covers copper bus bar in two tempers: O60 (soft annealed) and H04 (hard). Temper describes how much cold work the bar carries, and it changes strength far more than chemistry does.
The Copper Development Association’s data for C11000 shows the gap. Annealed rod typically reaches about 32 ksi (221 MPa) tensile strength, with a low 10 ksi (69 MPa) yield and 55 percent elongation. Hard (H04) bar and rod typically reach 45 to 48 ksi (310 to 331 MPa) tensile, with yield near 40 to 44 ksi and 16 to 20 percent elongation. These are typical values, not specification minimums, so always check the mill certificate for the bar you buy.
In practice, the copper busbar temper O60 vs H04 choice is a trade-off. Soft bar bends tightly and forgives mistakes, but it dents and sags more easily. Hard bar stays straight and resists dents, because the cold work that adds strength also adds hardness. However, it needs larger bend radii and more press force.
Thermal: Conductivity, Expansion and Temperature Rise
Copper’s high thermal conductivity spreads heat away from hot spots, especially bolted joints, where contact resistance concentrates losses into a small area. Consequently, a copper bar runs more evenly along its length than a poorer conductor would.
Copper busbar thermal expansion matters at every load cycle. At 9.4 × 10⁻⁶ per °F, a 10 ft run that heats up by 90 °F (50 K) grows by about 0.1 in (2.5 mm). That movement pushes on supports and flexes bolted joints each time the load changes, so long runs need expansion joints or flexible links, and supports should let the bar slide.
Temperature rise ties these numbers together. UL 891 for switchboards and IEC 61439-1 for low-voltage assemblies set temperature-rise limits for busbars and terminals. Those limits, not the copper itself, fix the design current. Meanwhile, copper industry ampacity tables list ratings at 30, 50 and 65 °C rise, and they favor 30 °C for energy efficiency.
Density and Weight
Density drives both freight and copper cost, and the weight formula is simple: weight = width × thickness × length × density.
For example, a common 4 × 1/4 in bar has a 1 in² cross-section. At 0.322 lb/in³, each foot (12 in) weighs about 3.9 lb. In metric terms, a 100 × 10 mm bar holds 1,000 cm³ per meter, so it weighs about 8.9 kg/m at 8.91 g/cm³.
Tin plating adds very little weight, so the bare-copper figure is close enough for quotes, stock planning and shipping. For any other width, thickness or length, use our copper weight calculator.
Recommended machine
HBC-A120
Cuts, punches and bends the exact copper and aluminium bar sizes in this guide — up to 120 × 12 mm, three stations at once.
120 × 12 mm
3 power packs
Cut · Punch · Bend
Copper Grades Used for Busbar
ASTM B187 allows more than a dozen coppers for bus applications. In practice, busbar copper in the US usually means C11000 ETP, with oxygen-free copper grades for special cases.
Grade | Type | Typical busbar use
---|---|---
C11000 (ETP) | Electrolytic tough pitch, 101% IACS | Most switchboard and panel bars
C10200 (OF) | Oxygen-free | Brazed or welded bars
C10100 (OFE) | Oxygen-free electronic, highest purity | Vacuum and high-purity uses
ETP contains a trace of oxygen, so heating it in a hydrogen-rich flame can embrittle it. That is why brazed and welded assemblies often switch to C10200, and why ASTM B187 includes embrittlement among its tests. Bolted panels, by contrast, rarely need anything beyond standard ETP. For a full grade comparison, read our copper grades guide.
The standard names every copper allowed for bus bar, rod and shapes. The ANSI store page lists the covered coppers, from C10100 to C12000, in its ASTM B187 summary.
Grade is only one of the rules a busbar must meet before it goes into a panel. For the main specifications on material, ratings and testing, see our overview of busbar standards.
Ampacity: How Much Current Can a Copper Busbar Carry?
Copper bus bar ampacity has no single answer, because heat, not copper, sets the limit. Five factors decide the rating:
- Cross-section: more copper means less resistance.
- Temperature rise: a 50 °C rise allows more current than 30 °C.
- Enclosure and ventilation: closed panels trap heat and cut the rating.
- Orientation and finish: edgewise bars and painted surfaces shed heat better.
- AC skin effect: alternating current crowds toward the surface, so thick bars gain less than expected.
So, how to calculate current capacity of copper bus bar? Start from a rating table, then derate for enclosure and ambient.
What size copper busbar is required for a 250 amp rating? Example — verify with the rating table: in still air with a 35 °C rise, a 25 × 3 mm (about 1 × 1/8 in) bar rates near 285 A. Inside a closed panel, however, 1.2 to 1.8 A/mm² points to 140 to 210 mm², such as 30 × 5 mm. Use our current rating table and busbar calculator for sizing.
Ampacity tables state their assumptions, which decide whether a rating fits your panel. The Copper Development Association explains its 30, 50 and 65 °C rise basis in its busbar ampacity tables.
Continuous current is only half the sizing story, because fault current also stresses the bar and its supports. Our article explains how peak forces and heating are checked under short-circuit withstand.
Plating: Bare, Tin or Silver
Copper busbar plating protects the contact surfaces, not the whole bar. Bare copper oxidizes in air, and that oxide raises joint resistance over time. A plated surface stays cleaner, and tin also makes copper safer to join with aluminum.
Finish | Benefit | Watch-out
---|---|---
Bare | Lowest cost, best for clean dry rooms | Oxidizes; clean before assembly
Tin plating | Resists humidity, suits aluminum contact | Soft; wears on sliding contacts
Silver plating | Lowest contact resistance at high current | Costly; tarnishes in sulfur-rich air
When choosing tin plated vs silver plated copper busbar, start with the duty. Tin suits bolted joints in general and humid sites, which covers most industrial panels. Silver, by contrast, suits high-current contacts, plug-in joints and switchgear that must slide or wipe.
Coating standards set thickness classes by severity of service, so plating specs should name one. ASTM’s tin coating standard describes the low contact resistance, corrosion protection and service classes of electroplated tin in its tin coating specification.
Silver deserves a closer look wherever contact resistance must stay as low as possible. Our guide covers its benefits, costs and best uses in detail under silver plated busbar.
Copper vs Aluminum Busbar
The copper vs aluminum busbar choice trades size against weight. Aluminum carries less current per square inch, so it needs a larger bar, but that bar still weighs about half as much.
Property | Copper (C11000) | Aluminum (1350)
---|---|---
Conductivity | 101% IACS | About 61–62% IACS
Density | 0.322 lb/in³ (8.91 g/cm³) | 0.0975 lb/in³ (2.70 g/cm³)
Bar size for same resistance | 1× | About 1.6×
Weight for same resistance | 1× | About 0.5×
Joint care | Simple; plating optional | Oxide removal, compatible hardware
Main cost driver | Metal price | Larger bar and joint labor
As a result, an aluminum busbar suits large busway and utility runs where weight matters. Copper, in contrast, wins where space is tight and joints must stay trouble-free.
So, are buss bars better than wiring? For high currents, busbars usually beat wiring: they are compact, rigid and easy to tap off.
Aluminum bus conductors follow their own specification, separate from copper. ASTM’s aluminum bus bar standard covers 1350 bars for electrical purposes and requires resistivity and conductivity tests in its aluminum bus specification.
The choice of metal also shapes the final quote for every busbar run. For the factors that drive cost, from metal price to fabrication, see our guide to busbar prices.
What the Numbers Mean on the Shop Floor
The same numbers decide how a bar bends, punches and joins in production.
When a rigid bar cannot bend to fit, a flexible copper busbar or a laminated stack often solves it; see our flexible busbar guide.
Application engineer’s note: Before quoting a busbar machine, we ask for three numbers: maximum thickness, maximum width and temper. Together they set the force, the tooling and the machine size.
Press force follows a simple rule. The Fabricator explains how perimeter, thickness and shear strength set punching tonnage in its punching force guide.
Accurate bends start with the right flat length, long before the bar reaches the press. Our step-by-step method with bend allowance shows how to calculate busbar bending.
Bending: Temper, Radius and Springback
Temper decides how a bar bends. Soft O60 copper bends around a tight inside radius and holds its shape. Hard H04 copper, by contrast, needs a larger radius to avoid cracking on the outside face, and it springs back more after the press releases.
Bend direction matters too. A flat bend is the easiest, while an edgewise (vertical) bend stretches the outer edge most and is the hardest to do without cracking. Therefore, edgewise bends need wider radii and slower, well-supported tooling.
ASTM B187 includes bend requirements for each temper, so check the mill certificate before setting up. Then compensate for springback by overbending a few degrees and checking the first part against the drawing. Hard bar usually needs more overbend than soft bar, so set it up separately. For minimum radii by thickness, see our guide to busbar bending techniques.
Punching and Cutting: Force and Burr
Punching force follows one formula: force = hole perimeter × bar thickness × shear strength. For example, a 1/2 in hole in a 3/8 in hard bar has a 1.57 in perimeter. At 26 ksi shear strength, it needs about 15,300 lb, or roughly 7.7 US tons. The same hole in annealed bar, at about 22 ksi, needs about 6.5 tons.
Tensile strength tracks shear strength, so harder temper always means more force. It also changes the ideal punch-to-die clearance and the edge quality. Soft copper tends to roll over and leave a larger burr, while hard copper shears cleaner but wears punches and dies faster.
Next, deburr every hole and cut edge, since burrs damage plating, cut insulation and reduce contact area at joints. For tonnage tables and tooling tips, read our busbar punching guide.
Joints: Surface Prep and Torque
A joint is only as good as its contact surfaces. First, clean bare copper just before assembly to remove oxide, and keep contact faces flat so pressure spreads evenly. Tin plating helps here, because it stays clean in storage and humid sites.
Next, hold the clamp force. Thermal expansion moves the joint every time the load changes, so the bolts can loosen over time. Belleville (conical spring) washers keep the pressure steady through those heating and cooling cycles.
Finally, torque every bolt to the manufacturer’s values, not by feel, and mark it once checked. Over-torque can deform soft copper and crush plating, while under-torque raises joint resistance and heat. For cable connections to bars, see our cable lug guide.
Recommended machine
HBC-C200
Cuts, punches and bends the exact copper and aluminium bar sizes in this guide — up to 120 × 12 mm, three stations at once.
120 × 12 mm
3 power packs
Cut · Punch · Bend
Conclusion: Copper Busbar
Five numbers explain electrical copper: 101 percent IACS conductivity, 0.322 lb/in³ density, 9.4 × 10⁻⁶/°F expansion, 32 versus 45-plus ksi tensile strength by temper, and a rating set by temperature rise. Together, they decide how a copper busbar carries current, how much it weighs and how it behaves on the press. Get them right at the design stage, and fabrication and testing go smoothly. For deeper detail, use our weight calculator, resistivity guide, grades guide, punching guide and cable lug guide.
Material numbers are the first step, but the finished bar must also fit the panel with safe spacing. For the minimum distances between phases and to earth, see our guide to busbar clearances.
Frequently Asked Questions about Copper Busbar
What is a copper busbar used for?
It carries and distributes current inside switchboards, panelboards, switchgear, busways and battery systems. Breakers, feeders and loads connect to it, so one rigid bar replaces many heavy cables and their terminations. Grounding and neutral bars use the same idea on a smaller scale.
Why is copper used for busbars?
Copper offers the highest conductivity of any common metal at a practical price, about 101 percent IACS for C11000. It is also strong, easy to bend and punch, and forms reliable bolted joints that resist creep and stay cool for decades of service.
How much current can a copper busbar carry?
It depends on cross-section, allowed temperature rise, enclosure, orientation and AC frequency. A larger bar and a higher permitted rise both raise the rating, while a closed panel lowers it. Check our copper busbar current ratings table for specific sizes.
What size copper busbar is required for a 250 amp rating?
Example — verify with the rating table: in open air at a 35 °C rise, a 25 × 3 mm (about 1 × 1/8 in) bar rates near 285 A. In a closed panel, plan for roughly 140 to 210 mm², such as 30 × 5 mm.
Are busbars better than wiring?

\# Copper Busbar\: The Numbers Behind Every Busbar

Every copper busbar is measured against one number\: 100 percent\. Since 1913\, annealed copper has defined 100 percent on the International Annealed Copper Standard \(IACS\)\, the scale every other conductor is graded on\. Modern busbar copper scores about 101 percent\, so it beats the very standard that defines it\. So why is copper used for busbars when aluminum is lighter and often cheaper\? In short\, copper packs the most current into the smallest bar\, stays strong enough to bolt and bend\, and forms bolted joints that last for decades with little upkeep\. This page collects the numbers for electrical copper in one place\: conductivity\, strength\, temper\, heat\, weight\, grades\, ampacity and plating\. Then it shows what each number means on the shop floor\, where bars get cut\, punched and bent every day\.

⏱ \.\.\.

Share\:

Take a Look at Our Products

Click

If you’d rather listen than read\, feel free to play the audio file below for the rest of this article\.

\#\# What Is a Copper Busbar\?

A copper busbar is a solid copper bar or strip that carries and distributes electric current inside switchboards\, panelboards\, switchgear\, busways and battery systems\. Installers also spell it copper bus bar\; both names mean the same part\.

Ask what is copper busbar in a panel shop\, and you will hear a simpler answer\: the backbone that feeds every breaker\. Typical uses include\:

\- Main and branch bars in switchboards and panelboards
\- Phase\, neutral and ground bars in switchgear
\- Busway and bus duct runs in buildings and plants
\- Battery\, UPS and inverter links\, including laminated copper busbar packs
\- Grounding bars in telecom sites

Built for processing larger conductors\, the HBC\-B200 machine performs cutting\, punching\, and bending operations on busbars up to 200 × 20 mm\. Its sequential operating system is designed for accurate fabrication of heavy\-duty electrical connections\.

\#\# Why Copper\: The Core Numbers

The table lists typical copper busbar material values for C11000\, the grade most ASTM B187 bus bar uses\, and what each number does in a real panel\.

Property \| Typical value \(C11000\) \| Why it matters 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Conductivity \| 101\% IACS \| Less heat per amp 
Resistivity \| 1\.7241 µΩ·cm defines 100\% IACS \| Sets voltage drop 
Density \| 0\.322 lb\/in³ \(8\.91 g\/cm³\) \| Weight and cost 
Thermal conductivity \| 226 Btu\/ft·h·°F \(391 W\/m·K\) \| Spreads joint heat 
Thermal expansion \| 9\.4 × 10⁻⁶\/°F \(16\.9 × 10⁻⁶\/K\) \| Moves bolted joints 

A copper bar is only one part of the wider system that moves power from the incomer to every load\. For busbar types\, design and applications across modern facilities\, see our guide to electrical busbar systems\.

\#\#\# Electrical\: Conductivity\, Resistivity and \%IACS

What is the conductivity of copper busbar\? For C11000\, the Copper Development Association lists 101 percent IACS at 68 °F \(20 °C\)\. The \%IACS scale compares any metal with annealed copper\, which defines 100 percent\: a conductivity of 58\.0 MS\/m\, or a resistivity of 1\.7241 µΩ·cm at 20 °C\.

Modern refining easily beats that 1913 reference\. As a result\, electrolytic tough pitch \(ETP\) and oxygen\-free grades meet or exceed 100 to 101 percent\. Each extra point means slightly less heat for the same current\, which adds up across a long switchboard run\.

Impurities work the other way\. Even small amounts of phosphorus\, iron or other elements scatter electrons and lower conductivity\, so bus copper is refined to very high purity\. For example\, phosphorus\-deoxidized copper \(C12200\) drops to roughly 85 percent IACS\, which is why ASTM B187 lists it for general use rather than for bus bar\. For the full resistivity story\, including temperature and alloy effects\, see our copper resistivity guide\.

Good busbar design starts with the conductor\, so the copper industry publishes its own guidance\. The Copper Alliance covers current rating\, joints\, short\-circuit effects and coatings in its busbar design guide\.

\#\#\# Mechanical\: Tensile Strength\, Hardness and Temper

ASTM B187\/B187M\-26 covers copper bus bar in two tempers\: O60 \(soft annealed\) and H04 \(hard\)\. Temper describes how much cold work the bar carries\, and it changes strength far more than chemistry does\.

The Copper Development Association’s data for C11000 shows the gap\. Annealed rod typically reaches about 32 ksi \(221 MPa\) tensile strength\, with a low 10 ksi \(69 MPa\) yield and 55 percent elongation\. Hard \(H04\) bar and rod typically reach 45 to 48 ksi \(310 to 331 MPa\) tensile\, with yield near 40 to 44 ksi and 16 to 20 percent elongation\. These are typical values\, not specification minimums\, so always check the mill certificate for the bar you buy\.

In practice\, the copper busbar temper O60 vs H04 choice is a trade\-off\. Soft bar bends tightly and forgives mistakes\, but it dents and sags more easily\. Hard bar stays straight and resists dents\, because the cold work that adds strength also adds hardness\. However\, it needs larger bend radii and more press force\.

\#\#\# Thermal\: Conductivity\, Expansion and Temperature Rise

Copper’s high thermal conductivity spreads heat away from hot spots\, especially bolted joints\, where contact resistance concentrates losses into a small area\. Consequently\, a copper bar runs more evenly along its length than a poorer conductor would\.

Copper busbar thermal expansion matters at every load cycle\. At 9\.4 × 10⁻⁶ per °F\, a 10 ft run that heats up by 90 °F \(50 K\) grows by about 0\.1 in \(2\.5 mm\)\. That movement pushes on supports and flexes bolted joints each time the load changes\, so long runs need expansion joints or flexible links\, and supports should let the bar slide\.

Temperature rise ties these numbers together\. UL 891 for switchboards and IEC 61439\-1 for low\-voltage assemblies set temperature\-rise limits for busbars and terminals\. Those limits\, not the copper itself\, fix the design current\. Meanwhile\, copper industry ampacity tables list ratings at 30\, 50 and 65 °C rise\, and they favor 30 °C for energy efficiency\.

\#\#\# Density and Weight

Density drives both freight and copper cost\, and the weight formula is simple\: weight \= width × thickness × length × density\.

For example\, a common 4 × 1\/4 in bar has a 1 in² cross\-section\. At 0\.322 lb\/in³\, each foot \(12 in\) weighs about 3\.9 lb\. In metric terms\, a 100 × 10 mm bar holds 1\,000 cm³ per meter\, so it weighs about 8\.9 kg\/m at 8\.91 g\/cm³\.

Tin plating adds very little weight\, so the bare\-copper figure is close enough for quotes\, stock planning and shipping\. For any other width\, thickness or length\, use our copper weight calculator\.

Recommended machine

HBC\-A120

Cuts\, punches and bends the exact copper and aluminium bar sizes in this guide — up to 120 × 12 mm\, three stations at once\.

120 × 12 mm

3 power packs

Cut · Punch · Bend

\#\# Copper Grades Used for Busbar

ASTM B187 allows more than a dozen coppers for bus applications\. In practice\, busbar copper in the US usually means C11000 ETP\, with oxygen\-free copper grades for special cases\.

Grade \| Type \| Typical busbar use 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
C11000 \(ETP\) \| Electrolytic tough pitch\, 101\% IACS \| Most switchboard and panel bars 
C10200 \(OF\) \| Oxygen\-free \| Brazed or welded bars 
C10100 \(OFE\) \| Oxygen\-free electronic\, highest purity \| Vacuum and high\-purity uses 

ETP contains a trace of oxygen\, so heating it in a hydrogen\-rich flame can embrittle it\. That is why brazed and welded assemblies often switch to C10200\, and why ASTM B187 includes embrittlement among its tests\. Bolted panels\, by contrast\, rarely need anything beyond standard ETP\. For a full grade comparison\, read our copper grades guide\.

The standard names every copper allowed for bus bar\, rod and shapes\. The ANSI store page lists the covered coppers\, from C10100 to C12000\, in its ASTM B187 summary\.

Grade is only one of the rules a busbar must meet before it goes into a panel\. For the main specifications on material\, ratings and testing\, see our overview of busbar standards\.

\#\# Ampacity\: How Much Current Can a Copper Busbar Carry\?

Copper bus bar ampacity has no single answer\, because heat\, not copper\, sets the limit\. Five factors decide the rating\:

\- Cross\-section\: more copper means less resistance\.
\- Temperature rise\: a 50 °C rise allows more current than 30 °C\.
\- Enclosure and ventilation\: closed panels trap heat and cut the rating\.
\- Orientation and finish\: edgewise bars and painted surfaces shed heat better\.
\- AC skin effect\: alternating current crowds toward the surface\, so thick bars gain less than expected\.

So\, how to calculate current capacity of copper bus bar\? Start from a rating table\, then derate for enclosure and ambient\.

What size copper busbar is required for a 250 amp rating\? Example — verify with the rating table\: in still air with a 35 °C rise\, a 25 × 3 mm \(about 1 × 1\/8 in\) bar rates near 285 A\. Inside a closed panel\, however\, 1\.2 to 1\.8 A\/mm² points to 140 to 210 mm²\, such as 30 × 5 mm\. Use our current rating table and busbar calculator for sizing\.

Ampacity tables state their assumptions\, which decide whether a rating fits your panel\. The Copper Development Association explains its 30\, 50 and 65 °C rise basis in its busbar ampacity tables\.

Continuous current is only half the sizing story\, because fault current also stresses the bar and its supports\. Our article explains how peak forces and heating are checked under short\-circuit withstand\.

\#\# Plating\: Bare\, Tin or Silver

Copper busbar plating protects the contact surfaces\, not the whole bar\. Bare copper oxidizes in air\, and that oxide raises joint resistance over time\. A plated surface stays cleaner\, and tin also makes copper safer to join with aluminum\.

Finish \| Benefit \| Watch\-out 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Bare \| Lowest cost\, best for clean dry rooms \| Oxidizes\; clean before assembly 
Tin plating \| Resists humidity\, suits aluminum contact \| Soft\; wears on sliding contacts 
Silver plating \| Lowest contact resistance at high current \| Costly\; tarnishes in sulfur\-rich air 

When choosing tin plated vs silver plated copper busbar\, start with the duty\. Tin suits bolted joints in general and humid sites\, which covers most industrial panels\. Silver\, by contrast\, suits high\-current contacts\, plug\-in joints and switchgear that must slide or wipe\.

Coating standards set thickness classes by severity of service\, so plating specs should name one\. ASTM’s tin coating standard describes the low contact resistance\, corrosion protection and service classes of electroplated tin in its tin coating specification\.

Silver deserves a closer look wherever contact resistance must stay as low as possible\. Our guide covers its benefits\, costs and best uses in detail under silver plated busbar\.

\#\# Copper vs Aluminum Busbar

The copper vs aluminum busbar choice trades size against weight\. Aluminum carries less current per square inch\, so it needs a larger bar\, but that bar still weighs about half as much\.

Property \| Copper \(C11000\) \| Aluminum \(1350\) 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Conductivity \| 101\% IACS \| About 61–62\% IACS 
Density \| 0\.322 lb\/in³ \(8\.91 g\/cm³\) \| 0\.0975 lb\/in³ \(2\.70 g\/cm³\) 
Bar size for same resistance \| 1× \| About 1\.6× 
Weight for same resistance \| 1× \| About 0\.5× 
Joint care \| Simple\; plating optional \| Oxide removal\, compatible hardware 
Main cost driver \| Metal price \| Larger bar and joint labor 

As a result\, an aluminum busbar suits large busway and utility runs where weight matters\. Copper\, in contrast\, wins where space is tight and joints must stay trouble\-free\.

So\, are buss bars better than wiring\? For high currents\, busbars usually beat wiring\: they are compact\, rigid and easy to tap off\.

Aluminum bus conductors follow their own specification\, separate from copper\. ASTM’s aluminum bus bar standard covers 1350 bars for electrical purposes and requires resistivity and conductivity tests in its aluminum bus specification\.

The choice of metal also shapes the final quote for every busbar run\. For the factors that drive cost\, from metal price to fabrication\, see our guide to busbar prices\.

\#\# What the Numbers Mean on the Shop Floor

The same numbers decide how a bar bends\, punches and joins in production\.

When a rigid bar cannot bend to fit\, a flexible copper busbar or a laminated stack often solves it\; see our flexible busbar guide\.

Application engineer’s note\: Before quoting a busbar machine\, we ask for three numbers\: maximum thickness\, maximum width and temper\. Together they set the force\, the tooling and the machine size\.

Press force follows a simple rule\. The Fabricator explains how perimeter\, thickness and shear strength set punching tonnage in its punching force guide\.

Accurate bends start with the right flat length\, long before the bar reaches the press\. Our step\-by\-step method with bend allowance shows how to calculate busbar bending\.

\#\#\# Bending\: Temper\, Radius and Springback

Temper decides how a bar bends\. Soft O60 copper bends around a tight inside radius and holds its shape\. Hard H04 copper\, by contrast\, needs a larger radius to avoid cracking on the outside face\, and it springs back more after the press releases\.

Bend direction matters too\. A flat bend is the easiest\, while an edgewise \(vertical\) bend stretches the outer edge most and is the hardest to do without cracking\. Therefore\, edgewise bends need wider radii and slower\, well\-supported tooling\.

ASTM B187 includes bend requirements for each temper\, so check the mill certificate before setting up\. Then compensate for springback by overbending a few degrees and checking the first part against the drawing\. Hard bar usually needs more overbend than soft bar\, so set it up separately\. For minimum radii by thickness\, see our guide to busbar bending techniques\.

\#\#\# Punching and Cutting\: Force and Burr

Punching force follows one formula\: force \= hole perimeter × bar thickness × shear strength\. For example\, a 1\/2 in hole in a 3\/8 in hard bar has a 1\.57 in perimeter\. At 26 ksi shear strength\, it needs about 15\,300 lb\, or roughly 7\.7 US tons\. The same hole in annealed bar\, at about 22 ksi\, needs about 6\.5 tons\.

Tensile strength tracks shear strength\, so harder temper always means more force\. It also changes the ideal punch\-to\-die clearance and the edge quality\. Soft copper tends to roll over and leave a larger burr\, while hard copper shears cleaner but wears punches and dies faster\.

Next\, deburr every hole and cut edge\, since burrs damage plating\, cut insulation and reduce contact area at joints\. For tonnage tables and tooling tips\, read our busbar punching guide\.

\#\#\# Joints\: Surface Prep and Torque

A joint is only as good as its contact surfaces\. First\, clean bare copper just before assembly to remove oxide\, and keep contact faces flat so pressure spreads evenly\. Tin plating helps here\, because it stays clean in storage and humid sites\.

Next\, hold the clamp force\. Thermal expansion moves the joint every time the load changes\, so the bolts can loosen over time\. Belleville \(conical spring\) washers keep the pressure steady through those heating and cooling cycles\.

Finally\, torque every bolt to the manufacturer’s values\, not by feel\, and mark it once checked\. Over\-torque can deform soft copper and crush plating\, while under\-torque raises joint resistance and heat\. For cable connections to bars\, see our cable lug guide\.

Cut · Punch · Bend

\#\# Conclusion\: Copper Busbar

Five numbers explain electrical copper\: 101 percent IACS conductivity\, 0\.322 lb\/in³ density\, 9\.4 × 10⁻⁶\/°F expansion\, 32 versus 45\-plus ksi tensile strength by temper\, and a rating set by temperature rise\. Together\, they decide how a copper busbar carries current\, how much it weighs and how it behaves on the press\. Get them right at the design stage\, and fabrication and testing go smoothly\. For deeper detail\, use our weight calculator\, resistivity guide\, grades guide\, punching guide and cable lug guide\.

Material numbers are the first step\, but the finished bar must also fit the panel with safe spacing\. For the minimum distances between phases and to earth\, see our guide to busbar clearances\.

\#\# Frequently Asked Questions about Copper Busbar

\#\#\# What is a copper busbar used for\?

It carries and distributes current inside switchboards\, panelboards\, switchgear\, busways and battery systems\. Breakers\, feeders and loads connect to it\, so one rigid bar replaces many heavy cables and their terminations\. Grounding and neutral bars use the same idea on a smaller scale\.

\#\#\# Why is copper used for busbars\?

Copper offers the highest conductivity of any common metal at a practical price\, about 101 percent IACS for C11000\. It is also strong\, easy to bend and punch\, and forms reliable bolted joints that resist creep and stay cool for decades of service\.

\#\#\# How much current can a copper busbar carry\?

It depends on cross\-section\, allowed temperature rise\, enclosure\, orientation and AC frequency\. A larger bar and a higher permitted rise both raise the rating\, while a closed panel lowers it\. Check our copper busbar current ratings table for specific sizes\.

\#\#\# What size copper busbar is required for a 250 amp rating\?

Example — verify with the rating table\: in open air at a 35 °C rise\, a 25 × 3 mm \(about 1 × 1\/8 in\) bar rates near 285 A\. In a closed panel\, plan for roughly 140 to 210 mm²\, such as 30 × 5 mm\.

\#\#\# Are busbars better than wiring\?

For high currents\, usually yes\. Buss bars\, as many installers spell them\, are compact and rigid\, and they make tap\-offs easy anywhere along their length\. However\, cable still suits long\, flexible or low\-current runs where a rigid bar would be awkward to route\.

\#\#\# What is the conductivity of copper busbar\?

C11000 ETP copper\, the standard grade\, conducts at about 101 percent IACS at 68 °F \(20 °C\)\. That equals a resistivity just below 1\.7241 µΩ·cm\, the 100 percent reference\. See our copper resistivity guide for temperature effects and other grades\.

records.title: Covalent organic framework/graphene oxide hybrids via in situ polymerization as high-performance lubricant additives
records.abstract: Abstract Covalent organic frameworks/graphene oxide (COFs/GO) hybrid nanocomposites were synthesized via an in-situ polymerization strategy and evaluated as lubricant additives in polyalphaolefin (PAO 10) under severe operating conditions. Two hybrids, TATP/GO and TADM/GO, were prepared and their tribological performance was systematically investigated. Structural characterization revealed that the in situ growth of TADM increased the interlayer spacing of GO and improved its dispersion behavior in PAO 10. At the optimal concentration of 0.05 wt.%, TADM/GO reduced the friction coefficient and wear volume by 30.43% and 95.58%, respectively, compared with neat PAO 10 in reciprocating sliding tests. Under four-ball conditions with an applied load of 392 N, TADM/GO maintained effective lubrication for 4 h, reducing the friction coefficient and wear volume by 35.71% and 69.37%, respectively. The wear volume after 4 h is only 47.54% higher than that measured in the independent 1 h test, demonstrating sustained anti-wear performance under prolonged severe contact conditions. The superior tribological performance of TADM/GO is attributed to the synergistic effects of surface filling, interlayer sliding, and tribochemical film formation. Raman analysis of the worn surface further revealed improved retention of the conjugated carbon structure in the TADM/GO-derived tribofilm under severe shear. These findings demonstrate the potential of molecularly engineered COF/GO hybrids as lubricant additives for severe contact conditions.

Covalent organic framework/graphene oxide hybrids via in situ polymerization as high-performance lubricant additives
Yue Liua, XiangLi Shena, ChangSheng Chena, Xiaoqiang Fana(), ZhiHui Xieb(), Minhao Zhua,c
a Key Laboratory of Advanced Technologies of Materials (Ministry of Education), School of Materials Science and Engineering, Southwest Jiaotong University, Chengdu 610031, China.
b Chemical Synthesis and Pollution Control Key Laboratory of Sichuan Province, College of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, China West Normal University, Nanchong, 637002, China.

Show Author Information Hide Author Information
Abstract
Covalent organic frameworks/graphene oxide (COFs/GO) hybrid nanocomposites were synthesized via an in-situ polymerization strategy and evaluated as lubricant additives in polyalphaolefin (PAO 10) under severe operating conditions. Two hybrids, TATP/GO and TADM/GO, were prepared and their tribological performance was systematically investigated. Structural characterization revealed that the in situ growth of TADM increased the interlayer spacing of GO and improved its dispersion behavior in PAO 10. At the optimal concentration of 0.05 wt.%, TADM/GO reduced the friction coefficient and wear volume by 30.43% and 95.58%, respectively, compared with neat PAO 10 in reciprocating sliding tests. Under four-ball conditions with an applied load of 392 N, TADM/GO maintained effective lubrication for 4 h, reducing the friction coefficient and wear volume by 35.71% and 69.37%, respectively. The wear volume after 4 h is only 47.54% higher than that measured in the independent 1 h test, demonstrating sustained anti-wear performance under prolonged severe contact conditions. The superior tribological performance of TADM/GO is attributed to the synergistic effects of surface filling, interlayer sliding, and tribochemical film formation. Raman analysis of the worn surface further revealed improved retention of the conjugated carbon structure in the TADM/GO-derived tribofilm under severe shear. These findings demonstrate the potential of molecularly engineered COF/GO hybrids as lubricant additives for severe contact conditions.

Photonics coalition publishes five optical manufacturing specifications
—
The Advanced Photonics Coalition has published five optical manufacturing documents. They cover co-packaged optics, silicon photonics testing and fabrication, and four-core fibre interfaces, with the aim of improving component interoperability and manufacturing repeatability.
IN Brief:
- The Advanced Photonics Coalition has released five specifications and recommended-practice documents developed through collaboration involving 60 member organisations.
- The portfolio addresses co-packaged optics, silicon photonics manufacturing and testing, and four-core multicore fibre cables, connectors and fibre-array units.
- The documents provide common design and manufacturing references; adoption, product qualification and demonstrated cost reductions remain dependent on implementation.
The Advanced Photonics Coalition has published five specifications and recommended-practice documents covering optical networking components, manufacturing processes and system interfaces. Developed through collaboration involving 60 member organisations, the portfolio addresses co-packaged optics, silicon photonics fabrication and testing, and four-core multicore fibre connections used in high-capacity networking equipment.
Released on 20 October 2026, the documents establish common references for companies designing, manufacturing and integrating optical hardware. The coalition’s work brings together semiconductor and photonic circuit designers, foundries, laser suppliers, packaging specialists, test-equipment manufacturers and connector developers, reflecting the different processes involved in producing a complete optical networking assembly.
The five publications are the System Level Architecture Overview for Co-Packaged Optics; Co-Packaged Optics Informative Outlook and Recommended Practices; Silicon Photonics for Co-Packaged Optics Recommended Test Practices; 4-Core Multicore Fiber Cable, Connector and Fiber Array Unit Specification; and Silicon Photonics Manufacturing Specification. They form the coalition’s initial published standards portfolio, with additional work continuing through its specialist groups.
Co-packaged optics places optical communication devices close to electronic processors or network switching circuits, allowing part of a high-speed data connection to be carried optically after travelling a comparatively short distance through an electrical interface. The arrangement differs from conventional pluggable transceivers, which are commonly positioned at the equipment panel and connected to the main switching silicon by longer electrical paths.
At increasing data rates, those electrical paths can impose substantial signal integrity requirements. Attenuation, reflections and interference affect the waveform received at the far end, potentially increasing the equalisation and retiming needed to maintain reliable communication. Shorter connections can reduce some of those demands, although the result depends on the electrical architecture and package design.
Moving optical conversion closer to the processor introduces different manufacturing constraints. Photonic integrated circuits, lasers, optical coupling structures and electronic chips may need to operate within a tightly integrated assembly, where heat removal, mechanical tolerances and electrical connections have to be managed together.
The coalition’s system architecture and recommended-practice documents address these integration challenges from different directions. An architectural reference helps define the constituent interfaces, while guidance on practical implementation can reduce unnecessary differences between assemblies supplied by separate manufacturers. Components still require individual validation against the electrical, optical and environmental requirements of their intended systems.
Silicon photonics production presents another collection of manufacturing variables. Photonic circuits use structures such as waveguides, modulators and optical couplers to route and control light, with performance determined partly by the geometry and material properties established during fabrication.
Variations in waveguide dimensions or material composition can change optical loss and wavelength response. Subsequent assembly processes must position the photonic device relative to fibres, lasers or other optical components closely enough to maintain the intended transfer of light. Electrical continuity alone is insufficient to demonstrate that the optical interface performs correctly.
The Silicon Photonics Manufacturing Specification provides a common manufacturing reference, while the separate recommended test-practices document concerns assessment of photonic components intended for co-packaged systems. Establishing compatible production and measurement approaches can make results easier to compare between suppliers, provided the relevant methods and conditions are applied consistently.
Optical measurements may be influenced by source wavelength, temperature, connection geometry and the calibration of the instruments used. A reported insertion-loss figure, for example, has limited value unless the measurement boundaries and conditions are defined. Comparable test procedures help separate variation in the component from variation introduced by the measurement arrangement.
The multicore fibre specification extends the work beyond individual semiconductor packages. Conventional single-core optical fibre contains one principal light-guiding core, whereas a multicore structure places several cores within a common cladding. The coalition’s document addresses a four-core configuration together with associated cable, connector and fibre-array components.
Four cores can carry separate optical channels within one fibre structure, but successful transmission depends on maintaining acceptable coupling into the intended core and limiting unwanted interaction between channels. The geometry of the fibre and its connection hardware consequently becomes an important part of system design.
Rotational alignment presents a particular problem. Where a connector joins two multicore fibres, the positions of the individual cores must correspond sufficiently closely for light to pass between them. An angular or lateral mismatch can introduce losses that differ between channels, even when the fibres appear mechanically connected.
Multicore interfaces also require attention to crosstalk, connector repeatability and the relationship between fibre assemblies and optical equipment. Common mechanical and optical requirements can support the development of compatible components from more than one supplier, although interoperability must still be demonstrated through appropriate testing.
The coalition is separately examining optical circuit switching for network installations, including reliability and configuration requirements for rack-level deployment. An optical circuit switch establishes a selectable optical connection between ports, potentially allowing network paths to be rearranged without performing electronic packet switching at every intermediate connection.
Such equipment must manage insertion loss, switching behaviour and connection state while remaining compatible with the surrounding optical network. Reliability becomes especially important when a switching operation changes the connectivity available to computing equipment, as a failed or incorrectly configured path can interrupt communication between systems.
Manufacturing consistency also affects sourcing. When components depend on proprietary connection geometries or incompatible test definitions, replacing a supplier may require changes to the surrounding assembly and another qualification programme. Shared interfaces can reduce that dependency, but commercial adoption still depends on the specifications being implemented in actual products.
The coalition’s documents are available through a registration-based download service. They remain copyrighted works, with public redistribution subject to permission. Their publication establishes technical references for the participating industry, while measurable reductions in cost, manufacturing variation and integration effort will depend on subsequent use by equipment and component suppliers.

Ceryx Medical has produced its first implantable heart failure pacemaker. The device was manufactured at King’s College London’s MAISI facility and will undergo preclinical testing before any study involving the implanted system.

records.summary: This 财富号 (Caifuhao) industry report article surveys the state of co-packaged optics (CPO) for AI data centers, arguing that the bottleneck for volume manufacturing has shifted from photonic devices themselves to opto-electronic test, packaging yield and automation. It describes NVIDIA's Quantum-X Photonics InfiniBand switch shipping in early 2026 and Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics entering full production in August 2026, with CPO expected to extend from scale-out switch networking toward scale-up GPU interconnect (Rubin Ultra NVL576 in 2H2027, Feynman in 2028). It outlines TSMC's COUPE/SoIC platform for integrating PIC and EIC into optical engines, a five-insertion test flow spanning wafer, bonded die, optical engine, packaged device and full system, and FAU evolution from roughly 40 to 80 channels as engines move from 3.2T to 6.4T. The article also presents scenario-based yield and output projections (e.g., ~1.56亿 PICs and ~7387万 optical engines in 2028 under assumed 95% SoIC bond yield and 50% downstream packaging yield), which the report itself labels as forecasts rather than achieved production results.
records.why_it_matters: For CPO manufacturing engineering, the article frames post-bond wafer-level optical-electrical test (Insertion 2) and packaged-device joint optical/electrical final test (Insertion 4) as the gating steps, implying that test parallelism, fiber auto-alignment and detachable FAU interfaces must be designed in early rather than added after packaging.

This is relevant adjacent-to-core technology for a high-speed connectivity team, but it is a secondary industry report with garbled tables, unverified vendor claims, and scenario forecasts rather than measured engineering data.

从NVIDIA Spectrum-X、Quantum-X到Rubin Ultra，CPO光互连架构持续演进
PIC/EIC混合键合、FAU精密耦合与光电联合测试成为规模化制造关键
随着AI计算集群规模不断扩大，传统电互连在带宽密度、功耗、信号完整性和传输距离方面面临越来越大的挑战。CPO（Co-Packaged Optics，光电共封装）通过将光引擎与交换芯片进行高密度集成，为下一代AI数据中心提供了新的高速互连技术路线。
报告重点研究CPO从技术验证走向规模化部署过程中，面临的光子芯片制造、光电混合键合、精密光纤耦合、封装测试与系统级可靠性等关键挑战。
报告最核心的判断是：CPO技术已经进入实际部署阶段，但决定下一阶段规模化发展的关键，正在从光器件本身转向光电测试、封装良率以及自动化制造能力。
尤其值得关注的是，报告将台积电COUPE/SoIC平台、NVIDIA Spectrum-X与Quantum-X光子交换机，以及未来Rubin Ultra NVL576的Scale-up光互连联系起来，揭示了CPO从交换机走向GPU计算集群内部互连的技术路线。
一、CPO从技术验证走向实际部署，下一阶段将向GPU Scale-up互连扩展
报告指出，CPO已经不再停留在实验室或概念验证阶段。NVIDIA Quantum-X Photonics InfiniBand交换机于2026年初开始出货，并在2026年中进入客户生产环境；Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics则于2026年8月进入全面生产阶段。
目前，CPO主要用于AI数据中心交换机的Scale-out网络，通过将光引擎与交换ASIC进行高密度集成，改善高速光通信系统的互连方式。
下一阶段的重要变化，是CPO有望从交换机网络进一步进入AI计算集群的Scale-up互连。报告预计，Rubin Ultra NVL576将在2027年下半年引入相关CPO方案，而2028年的Feynman平台可能推动更大规模部署。
这意味着，CPO的应用场景有望从数据中心交换设备扩展至更高密度的GPU互连系统，对光引擎数量、封装精度、测试量以及系统级可靠性提出更高要求。
从技术演进来看，CPO正在经历从交换机光互连向GPU计算系统内部高速互连的扩展，其核心目标是满足下一代AI集群对更高带宽密度、更低功耗和更高集成度的要求。
二、台积电COUPE与SoIC推动光电异构集成，PIC与EIC成为CPO制造核心
CPO的重要技术基础，是将光子集成电路（PIC）与电子集成电路（EIC）进行高密度集成，形成具备光电转换能力的光引擎（Optical Engine，OE）。
报告介绍，台积电COUPE平台通过SoIC相关工艺，将EIC与PIC集成，使光电转换功能能够与先进封装流程相结合。
其中，PIC主要承担光信号调制、探测及传输等功能；EIC则负责相应的电子驱动、信号处理和接收电路。两者集成后，必须验证完整的电光转换与光电转换性能，而不能仅依赖独立芯片测试。
报告特别强调，EIC与PIC完成键合后的晶圆级测试，是CPO制造中技术难度很高的环节。
测试设备不仅需要从一侧与EIC建立电气接触，还需要从另一侧将光纤精确对准PIC上的光耦合结构。整个过程容易受到振动、温度变化和晶圆翘曲影响。
由于光波导尺寸远小于传统光纤结构，微小的对准误差就可能导致明显的插入损耗变化。因此，光电芯片集成不仅要求先进的混合键合工艺，还需要高精度光学定位、稳定的机械结构和可靠的测试环境。
CPO制造的难点不仅是实现光电芯片集成，更在于如何在集成过程中及时筛选合格器件，避免缺陷进入后续复杂的封装流程。

三、光电测试成为CPO量产关键瓶颈，五个测试阶段贯穿整个制造流程
这是整份报告最值得关注的技术内容。
报告认为，当前CPO光学测试仍然较慢，且较多依赖人工操作，行业尚未形成完全统一的测试规范。随着光引擎数量增加，测试量、自动化程度和良率控制将直接影响CPO的规模化生产。
流程图将CPO制造划分为从晶圆级到系统级的多个测试插入点：

报告指出，现阶段部分CPO产品的封装后终测主要覆盖电气功能，未来还需要逐步完善光电联合终测和系统级测试。
与传统半导体测试相比，CPO不仅需要检测电压、电流、频率和数字信号，还需要同步测量光功率、光损耗、调制性能、接收灵敏度及光链路稳定性。
此外，测试过程中还必须控制温度变化、机械振动和光纤对准误差，避免测试环境本身影响器件性能判断。
CPO的测试逻辑正在从传统的电学测试，升级为覆盖晶圆、光引擎、封装器件和完整系统的多阶段光电联合测试体系。
四、光引擎良率决定CPO产能，2028年OE出货量预计接近7400万个
除了测试设备，报告还重点分析了PIC制造、EIC/PIC混合键合以及下游封装良率对光引擎产能的影响。
报告指出，台积电PIC生产能力仍然是CPO制造体系的重要约束，而光电芯片完成混合键合后，还需要经过切割、光纤耦合、封装和测试等工序。任何一个环节的良率下降，都可能明显减少最终可交付的光引擎数量。

从制造工艺角度来看，未来CPO的核心任务是建立稳定的PIC制造、EIC/PIC混合键合、FAU精密耦合和光电测试流程，通过提升各环节良率，实现光引擎的规模化生产。

五、FAU光纤阵列从40通道迈向80通道，光耦合精度与自动化成为制造难点
FAU（Fiber Array Unit，光纤阵列单元）是连接光纤与PIC、光引擎的重要组件，其制造精度直接影响光信号的插入损耗和传输稳定性。
报告指出，随着单个光引擎带宽提高，FAU需要集成更多光纤通道。
以并行光互连架构为例，3.2T光引擎采用16×200G通道时，需要32根收发信号光纤，加上外部激光相关光纤，FAU总通道数约为40。
当光引擎带宽提升至6.4T时，32×200G架构需要64根收发信号光纤，加上外部激光光纤，FAU总通道数可能达到约80。
CPO光纤阵列正在从单排一维（1D）结构向多排二维（2D）结构演进。住友电工已经展示72芯二维光纤阵列，部分厂商也在开发多层堆叠方案。
与此同时，CPO还存在两条重要技术路线。
光栅耦合（Grating Coupling）：从PIC表面引入光信号，是报告所述台积电COUPE生态的重要路线。这种结构有利于从芯片表面完成光纤连接和光学测试。
边缘耦合（Edge Coupling）：从芯片侧面耦合光信号，例如康宁GlassBridge所探索的玻璃波导方案。该路线通过不同的光学耦合结构实现芯片与外部光纤之间的连接。
光纤接口也正在从永久固定式向可拆卸、可返工结构演进，以改善封装后的测试、维修和器件更换能力。
随着通道密度提高，亚微米级对准、自动化耦合、插入损耗控制以及长期可靠性，将成为FAU制造的重要技术挑战。
尤其是在高密度二维光纤阵列中，光纤数量增加会显著提高装配难度，因此需要将高精度机械定位、机器视觉、主动光学对准和自动化装配技术结合起来。
FAU技术正在从传统光纤连接组件，向高密度、精密化、自动化的光电封装关键组件演进。
六、CPO制造进入光电联合测试时代，台积电、ASE与设备厂商共同完善制造体系
CPO与传统半导体封装的重要区别，是封装过程不仅涉及电气连接，还需要完成高精度光学对准和光电性能验证。
测试流程图展示了从晶圆制造到系统级测试的分工：台积电主要负责晶圆级PIC/EIC集成与测试，ASE/SPIL等封测厂商承担光引擎和封装后的相关工序。
在设备层面，报告重点介绍了多个技术方向。
MPI正在推进晶圆级光电测试设备、Die-to-Die探针设备和EIC探针卡相关方案。
Hon Precision开发适用于光电联合终测的Handler设备，帮助完成封装器件的自动化搬运、定位和测试。
AllRing通过六轴对准平台和机器视觉，实现FAU与光芯片之间的自动化耦合，提高光纤阵列与光引擎之间的装配精度。
此外，Advantest、Teradyne、TEL、FormFactor、Chroma、Winway等企业分别参与测试机、探针、光学检测、测试接口和系统级测试设备等环节。
报告认为，未来CPO制造体系需要将半导体ATE测试技术与精密光学测量能力结合，并进一步解决温度控制、光纤自动对准、测试标准化和多通道并行测试问题。其中，多通道并行测试尤其重要。随着单个光引擎集成的光学通道数量增加，如果仍然依靠逐通道测试，将显著增加测试时间。
因此，CPO测试设备需要向更高并行度、更高自动化程度和更稳定的光学测量能力发展。
与此同时，系统级测试也将成为重要环节。由于CPO器件在实际工作中同时受到温度、电气负载和光信号变化影响，仅通过晶圆级或单器件测试，难以完全验证最终系统的运行可靠性。
CPO的制造能力不仅取决于光子芯片设计，还取决于晶圆制造、先进封装、精密光学设备与自动化测试之间的协同水平。
七、CPO将从交换机延伸至Optical I/O，NPO成为另一条重要技术路线
报告对下一代光互连架构提出了两个值得关注的判断。
首先，CPO的长期发展方向不只是交换机光互连，还可能进一步进入GPU、XPU及多芯片模块的Optical I/O（光学输入输出）架构。
当光引擎与计算芯片、HBM等组件进行更紧密的封装集成时，光纤连接、封装返工和系统可靠性的重要性将进一步提高。
报告提到，部分企业已经展示结合XPU与HBM的多芯片光互连封装方案，说明光互连技术正在向计算封装内部延伸。不过，这些方案仍处于不同程度的开发、验证和导入阶段。
其次，报告认为，中国AI计算系统可能采取与海外大型GPU平台不同的光互连发展路径。
报告预测，从2027年开始，NPO（Near-Packaged Optics，近封装光学）可能先于CPO成为中国AI计算系统的重要光互连方式。
NPO将光学组件放置在计算芯片封装附近，而不是像CPO那样进行更紧密的共封装。这种方案为光电集成提供了另一条技术路线。
从技术结构来看，NPO与CPO在光学组件集成位置、封装复杂度、光纤连接方式以及维护便利性等方面存在差异。
未来AI光互连可能呈现多种架构并行发展的局面：交换机CPO、近封装NPO以及面向GPU/XPU的Optical I/O，根据系统带宽、制造工艺和部署要求选择不同的实现方式。
随着GPU集群规模扩大，光互连技术将逐步从传统交换机端口向计算系统内部延伸，推动光子芯片、先进封装和高速互连架构进一步融合。
小编总结
下一代CPO的核心挑战，正在从“能否实现光电共封装”，转向“如何通过COUPE、SoIC、FAU精密耦合、光电联合测试与先进封装，实现高良率、高量和高可靠性的规模化制造”。
