Analysis of Gold-Plating Anomalies in Pogo Pins (Spring-Loaded Pins)
Henry Clark
Henry is a testing engineer. He conducts various tests on Pogo Pin connectors to ensure their performance in special scenarios. His accurate test results are crucial for product improvement and the development of new solutions.
An unusual gold-plating color is a reason to investigate the coating and production process. Reddish deposits, dark patches, or differences between parts can result from several conditions, including bath contamination, unsuitable current distribution, inconsistent surface preparation, or variations in coating thickness.
Appearance alone cannot identify the cause. The investigation should connect the visible change with measurements of thickness, adhesion, surface condition, and the finished contact's electrical and mechanical performance.
Pogo pin plungers and barrels commonly use copper alloys, including brass. These materials offer useful combinations of conductivity and machinability, but exposed surfaces can oxidize or corrode. A suitable coating system helps protect the functional contact surfaces. Gold is a common choice, often applied over a nickel underlayer, although the appropriate finish depends on the application.
We can develop pogo pin contacts and magnetic connector assemblies from customer drawings, coordinating machined dimensions, coating requirements, insulating carriers, and mating features. Defining these requirements together helps prevent a surface-treatment change from creating an assembly or contact-performance problem.
Gold-plated parts do not necessarily have one identical shade. Deposit composition, thickness, substrate finish, and surface texture can influence appearance. Lighting and viewing angle also affect the comparison, particularly on small curved components.
The first step is therefore to compare parts with the same specified finish under consistent inspection conditions. An approved reference sample can help identify a process change, but measurable acceptance criteria remain necessary.
Observed condition | Possible explanations | Useful verification
---|---|---
Consistent shade difference between batches | Deposit composition, thickness, surface texture, or inspection conditions | Confirm the coating specification, thickness results, and process records
Dark or patchy areas | Surface residue, incomplete preparation, bath imbalance, or contamination | Review pretreatment, bath analysis, rinsing, and affected locations
Reddish areas with rough deposits | Excessive local current density, solution-access limitations, or bath problems | Check current settings, loading, surface area calculations, and deposit condition
Different appearance inside bores | Local thickness variation, preparation, wetting, or solution exchange | Inspect internal coverage and measure designated critical areas
Contamination can enter the plating bath through chemical additions, carryover from preceding stages, inadequately cleaned parts, fixtures, or equipment. Once present, its effects depend on the bath chemistry, contaminant, and concentration.
Organic contamination can contribute to dullness or uneven deposits. Metallic contamination can change deposit characteristics and the range of current densities that produces acceptable results. Neither type has a single appearance that reliably identifies it.
Dark patches therefore do not prove organic contamination, and a red or black deposit does not identify a particular metallic impurity. Those observations should guide sampling and testing rather than determine the corrective treatment by themselves.
Intentional bath ingredients must also be distinguished from contamination. Some gold processes contain controlled alloying additions and additives that influence hardness or deposition behavior. Their presence can be part of the specified process. The relevant question is whether the chemistry remains within its established control limits.
Bath management should follow the requirements of the selected chemistry. Relevant records may include metal concentration, temperature, pH, additive additions, filtration, and contamination analysis. Uncontrolled chemical additions made solely to improve color can obscure the original cause and introduce further variation.
A Hull cell test can be useful where it is suitable for the plating chemistry. It allows deposit behavior to be examined across a range of current densities and can help reveal changes in the bath's operating range.
Its results require interpretation alongside other evidence. A test panel does not reproduce the geometry of a miniature barrel bore or every electrical-contact condition in a production load. Chemical analysis may still be required to establish whether contamination is present and what treatment is appropriate.
Excessive current density is another potential contributor to abnormal deposits. For a simplified average calculation:
Average current density = applied current ÷ plated surface area
If the surface area is overestimated and the applied current is calculated from that value, the actual average current density will exceed the intended value. Part quantity, dimensions, masking, and exposed surfaces therefore need to be included correctly.
This average does not describe the entire component. Local current distribution varies with geometry, positioning, and the plating arrangement. Exposed edges and projections can behave differently from recessed surfaces and internal bores.
Increasing current to improve weak coverage inside a bore may create excessive buildup or poor deposit quality elsewhere. The correction should consider current distribution, solution access, bath condition, and loading together.
Part movement is relevant in barrel and vibratory processes. Movement influences electrical contact, solution access, and how components are exposed during plating. Inadequate movement or unsuitable loading can contribute to variation.
Vibration amplitude alone is not a complete process specification. Component size, shape, load quantity, equipment configuration, and motion all influence the result. Changes should be evaluated for both coating consistency and the possibility of mechanical damage from contact between parts.
Small internal features deserve separate attention. A barrel may have an acceptable external finish while its bore has incomplete coverage or a different surface condition. Restricted solution exchange, poor wetting, trapped residue, and current distribution can all contribute.
Inspection should identify which internal surfaces are functionally important. A plunger-to-barrel contact area may influence electrical resistance and movement, while another surface may primarily require corrosion protection. The coating specification should reflect those roles.
Surface preparation and underlayer quality must remain part of the investigation. Oil, machining residue, oxides, or particles can interfere with deposition and adhesion. Rough machining marks or burrs can also remain significant after coating.
Where nickel is specified beneath gold, its continuity, adhesion, thickness, and surface condition affect the complete finish. A problem originating in the substrate or underlayer may remain visible after gold plating.
Dimensional checks are equally important. Plating increases external dimensions and reduces the space available on coated internal surfaces. Excessive buildup or rough deposits can cause a plunger to bind even when the gold color appears acceptable.
A practical investigation should preserve the failed samples and their production records, then proceed through a controlled comparison:
Identify whether the anomaly affects a whole batch, selected parts, or particular locations.
Confirm the substrate, underlayer, gold specification, and inspection conditions.
Review pretreatment, bath records, loading, current calculations, and part movement.
Measure thickness and inspect adhesion, roughness, internal coverage, and finished dimensions.
Check contact resistance and plunger movement under the specified conditions.
Verify the proposed correction on a controlled production trial before releasing the process.
The acceptance decision should combine appearance with functional evidence. A visible difference may require correction, but a uniform gold color is not sufficient proof that the coating will provide reliable contact, smooth movement, or the required durability.
1. Does reddish gold plating mean the current density was too high?
It can be one contributing factor, particularly when roughness is also present. Bath composition, contamination, coating thickness, and underlayer condition can produce similar observations. Confirm the cause through process review and deposit inspection.
2. Can gold-plated parts have different shades and still meet the specification?
Yes, depending on the specified finish and permitted appearance variation. Compare parts under consistent conditions and check the required thickness, adhesion, electrical performance, and other acceptance criteria.
3. Why can the inside of a pogo pin barrel look different from the outside?
Internal geometry affects preparation, wetting, solution exchange, and current distribution. These differences can influence coverage and thickness. Critical internal surfaces should have defined inspection requirements.
4. Can adding more gold solve a plating anomaly?
Additional thickness only addresses certain conditions. It will not reliably correct contamination, poor adhesion, unsuitable preparation, or uneven current distribution. It can also reduce internal clearance, so the cause should be established before changing the coating specification.

What issues should be considered during the electroplating of pogo pins?
Alice Smith
Alice is a senior R&D engineer at Dongguan Xinteng Electronics Co., Ltd. With over 8 years of experience in the field of Pogo Pin connectors, she specializes in the research of high - current and miniaturization scenarios. She has contributed to many of the company's patented products and more than 300 solutions.
Pogo pin electroplating affects contact resistance, corrosion protection, wear, solderability, and the fit between moving components. A finish that looks uniform can still be unsuitable if it changes the plunger clearance, adheres poorly, or provides inadequate coverage at a functional surface.
The process should therefore begin with a defined coating specification. The plunger tip, internal sliding surfaces, barrel exterior, and soldering tail may have different requirements. Inspection needs to reflect those differences.
Gold over a suitable nickel underlayer is a common finish for electrical contacts. Other systems, including silver, tin, and palladium-based coatings, can serve particular contact or termination requirements. Platinum, rhodium, and ruthenium finishes require application-specific justification; they should not be treated as interchangeable upgrades.
Selecting the coating material is only the starting point. Surface preparation, current distribution, bath condition, part movement, rinsing, and dimensional control determine whether the finished contact performs as intended.
Current density is one of the principal controls in electrolytic plating. Its average value relates the applied current to the surface area being plated:
Average current density = applied current ÷ plated surface area
If the plated area is overestimated and the current is calculated from that value, the actual average current density can exceed the intended setting. Changes in part quantity, exposed surfaces, masking, or loading arrangement can therefore affect the result.
Average current density does not describe every location on a component. Edges, projections, recesses, and internal surfaces can receive different local current densities. A setting that produces an acceptable external finish may still leave a recessed area with inadequate coverage.
Excessive local current density can contribute to rough or otherwise defective deposits. However, a reddish, dark, or uneven gold surface does not prove that current density is the cause. Bath composition, contamination, coating thickness, underlayer condition, and surface preparation also need examination.
Part movement matters in barrel or vibratory plating. It influences solution access, exposure, and electrical contact during processing. Insufficient movement or unsuitable loading can contribute to inconsistent results, but simply increasing vibration is not a reliable correction. Movement should suit the component geometry and equipment without causing excessive part-to-part damage.
Observed condition | Possible contributing factors | What to verify
---|---|---
Rough or discolored gold deposit | Local current density, bath condition, contamination, or inadequate solution movement | Current calculation, loading, bath analysis, and deposit condition
Patchy or dull areas | Uneven preparation, residue, additive imbalance, or contamination | Cleaning and activation stages, bath controls, and rinsing
Uneven finish in recesses or bores | Limited solution access, current distribution, or incomplete preparation | Local coverage and thickness at the specified surfaces
Peeling or flaking | Poor surface preparation, unsuitable underlayer condition, or deposit stress | Adhesion, pretreatment records, and coating structure
Plunger sticking after plating | Excessive buildup, roughness, particles, or inadequate dimensional allowance | Finished bore and plunger dimensions, surface condition, and cleanliness
Bath contamination is another important investigation area. Impurities can enter through chemical additions, carryover from earlier stages, inadequately cleaned parts, fixtures, or equipment.
Organic contamination may affect deposit appearance and behavior. Metallic contamination can alter the operating range or deposit characteristics. The effect depends on the bath chemistry, contaminant, and concentration, so appearance alone cannot identify the substance responsible.
It is also important to distinguish contamination from intentional bath constituents. Some gold plating systems contain controlled alloying additions or additives that influence the deposit. Their presence is not automatically a defect; the relevant question is whether the bath remains within its specified control limits.
Process records should track the parameters required by the plating chemistry supplier. Depending on the system, these may include metal concentration, temperature, pH, additives, filtration, and contamination levels. Corrective treatment should follow a confirmed diagnosis rather than an attempt to adjust the bath until the color looks acceptable.
Where appropriate for the bath, a Hull cell test can help compare deposit behavior across a range of current densities. It is useful for investigating changes in appearance or the usable operating range.
The test has limits. A panel does not reproduce every recessed surface, internal bore, loading condition, or electrical contact condition found in production. It also does not replace chemical analysis when the identity or concentration of an impurity needs to be established.

Burrs and rough machining marks should also be addressed before plating. A coating cannot be relied upon to correct an unsuitable base surface. On a precision sliding interface, an underlying defect can remain significant after the finish has been applied.
The nickel underlayer, where specified, forms part of the functional coating system. It can provide a barrier between the copper-alloy substrate and the gold surface, while also influencing the support and condition of the top coating. For custom projects, we can work from customer drawings to coordinate the pogo pin geometry, material, coating system, and assembled fit. Samples or small batches can then be evaluated before the design is released for larger production orders.

Thickness at designated locations, including critical contact surfaces.
Adhesion and evidence of peeling, roughness, or particulate contamination.
Finished dimensions and assembly clearance.
Smooth plunger movement and reliable return.
Contact resistance at the specified working compression.
Solderability of designated termination surfaces.
Performance after the required wear or environmental exposure.
Thickness measurements also need an appropriate method and setup. Small diameters, curved surfaces, and multilayer finishes can affect measurement interpretation. The specification should identify where measurements are taken and how the results relate to the acceptance requirement.
Appearance remains useful for detecting process changes, but it should be assessed alongside these measurements. An attractive gold finish is not sufficient evidence of electrical or mechanical reliability.

Not necessarily. Current density is one possible contributor, but bath composition, contamination, thickness, underlayer condition, and preparation can also affect appearance. Review the process records and inspect the deposit before assigning a cause.

No. The thickness must suit the required wear and environmental performance while remaining compatible with the component dimensions. Excessive buildup can reduce clearance, increase cost, or interfere with movement.

No. It can help reveal deposit behavior across a current-density range when suitable for the bath. Production geometry, adhesion, local coverage, and chemical contamination may require additional inspection or analysis.

\# What issues should be considered during the electroplating of pogo pins\?

Alice Smith

Alice is a senior R\&D engineer at Dongguan Xinteng Electronics Co\.\, Ltd\. With over 8 years of experience in the field of Pogo Pin connectors\, she specializes in the research of high \- current and miniaturization scenarios\. She has contributed to many of the company\'s patented products and more than 300 solutions\.

Pogo pin electroplating affects contact resistance\, corrosion protection\, wear\, solderability\, and the fit between moving components\. A finish that looks uniform can still be unsuitable if it changes the plunger clearance\, adheres poorly\, or provides inadequate coverage at a functional surface\.

The process should therefore begin with a defined coating specification\. The plunger tip\, internal sliding surfaces\, barrel exterior\, and soldering tail may have different requirements\. Inspection needs to reflect those differences\.

Gold over a suitable nickel underlayer is a common finish for electrical contacts\. Other systems\, including silver\, tin\, and palladium\-based coatings\, can serve particular contact or termination requirements\. Platinum\, rhodium\, and ruthenium finishes require application\-specific justification\; they should not be treated as interchangeable upgrades\.

Selecting the coating material is only the starting point\. Surface preparation\, current distribution\, bath condition\, part movement\, rinsing\, and dimensional control determine whether the finished contact performs as intended\.

Current density is one of the principal controls in electrolytic plating\. Its average value relates the applied current to the surface area being plated\:

Average current density \= applied current ÷ plated surface area

If the plated area is overestimated and the current is calculated from that value\, the actual average current density can exceed the intended setting\. Changes in part quantity\, exposed surfaces\, masking\, or loading arrangement can therefore affect the result\.

Average current density does not describe every location on a component\. Edges\, projections\, recesses\, and internal surfaces can receive different local current densities\. A setting that produces an acceptable external finish may still leave a recessed area with inadequate coverage\.

Excessive local current density can contribute to rough or otherwise defective deposits\. However\, a reddish\, dark\, or uneven gold surface does not prove that current density is the cause\. Bath composition\, contamination\, coating thickness\, underlayer condition\, and surface preparation also need examination\.

Part movement matters in barrel or vibratory plating\. It influences solution access\, exposure\, and electrical contact during processing\. Insufficient movement or unsuitable loading can contribute to inconsistent results\, but simply increasing vibration is not a reliable correction\. Movement should suit the component geometry and equipment without causing excessive part\-to\-part damage\.

Uneven finish in recesses or bores \| Limited solution access\, current distribution\, or incomplete preparation \| Local coverage and thickness at the specified surfaces 
Peeling or flaking \| Poor surface preparation\, unsuitable underlayer condition\, or deposit stress \| Adhesion\, pretreatment records\, and coating structure 
Plunger sticking after plating \| Excessive buildup\, roughness\, particles\, or inadequate dimensional allowance \| Finished bore and plunger dimensions\, surface condition\, and cleanliness 

Bath contamination is another important investigation area\. Impurities can enter through chemical additions\, carryover from earlier stages\, inadequately cleaned parts\, fixtures\, or equipment\.

Organic contamination may affect deposit appearance and behavior\. Metallic contamination can alter the operating range or deposit characteristics\. The effect depends on the bath chemistry\, contaminant\, and concentration\, so appearance alone cannot identify the substance responsible\.

It is also important to distinguish contamination from intentional bath constituents\. Some gold plating systems contain controlled alloying additions or additives that influence the deposit\. Their presence is not automatically a defect\; the relevant question is whether the bath remains within its specified control limits\.

Process records should track the parameters required by the plating chemistry supplier\. Depending on the system\, these may include metal concentration\, temperature\, pH\, additives\, filtration\, and contamination levels\. Corrective treatment should follow a confirmed diagnosis rather than an attempt to adjust the bath until the color looks acceptable\.

records.body_text:
Reel-to-Reel Plating: Continuous Finishing for High-Volume Stamped Strip
Quick Answer
TL;DR
Reel-to-reel plating runs stamped metal strip continuously through cleaning, plating, and rinsing stations while it stays on the carrier. It supports stripe, spot, and full-surface plating with finishes such as nickel, tin, silver, and gold. The method suits high-volume electrical parts because it limits handling, keeps coverage consistent, and fits directly after high-speed stamping.
High-speed stamping can produce millions of small parts, but a bare stamped contact is rarely finished. It needs a plated surface that resists corrosion, solders well, or conducts reliably at the mating point. Plating parts one batch at a time would slow the whole operation. Reel-to-reel plating solves that by finishing the strip itself in a continuous flow.
This article explains how reel-to-reel plating works, what it can do, and why it pairs so naturally with high-volume stamping.
How Reel-to-Reel Plating Works
In reel-to-reel plating, stamped parts remain attached to a continuous carrier strip. The strip unwinds from one reel, travels through a sequence of process stations, and winds onto a take-up reel at the end. Along the way it passes through cleaning, activation, plating, rinsing, and drying.
Because the parts never leave the strip, they are not tumbled, sorted, or loaded into racks. That reduces handling damage and gives each part nearly identical exposure to the plating solution. The result is consistent thickness and coverage across very large quantities.
Continuous In-Line Processing
The continuous design means the line can run for long periods with the same settings. Operators monitor solution chemistry, current, and strip speed rather than loading and unloading batches. For high-volume programs, that stability is a major advantage over batch methods.
Compatible Base Metals
Composidie’s reel-to-reel plating lines process base metals including copper alloys, stainless steel, and phosphor bronze. The base metal affects cleaning, activation, and the underlayers needed, so it should be defined at the start of a program.
What Reel-to-Reel Plating Can Do
Reel-to-reel plating covers a wide range of finishes and coverage patterns. It can plate the entire strip surface or target specific zones, and it can combine more than one finish on the same part.
- Full-surface plating for corrosion resistance or solderability
- Stripe plating for a continuous band of finish along the strip
- Spot plating for finish in defined locations
- Multi-layer systems, such as nickel underlayers with gold, silver, or tin top finishes
Available Finishes
Composidie lists nickel in sulfamate, bright, and matte forms, matte and bright tin, hard and soft gold, silver, and palladium-nickel, among other finishes. A longer list of materials is available on the material and finishes page. Each finish has a different job. Tin supports solderability, gold supports low contact resistance, silver supports conductivity, and nickel provides a barrier and wear surface.
Selective Application
Applying precious metal only where it is needed keeps cost under control. Selective approaches are a core strength of reel-to-reel plating, especially for connectors and contacts where the mating area is small compared with the whole part.
Why Plating Pairs Well With High-Speed Stamping
Stamping and reel-to-reel plating share the same format. Both work on continuous strip, so the output of a high-speed press can feed a plating line without being broken into loose parts. This keeps parts organized and protects delicate features.
Composidie operates stamping presses at up to 1,800 strokes per minute and runs plating in house, so a stamped strip can move straight into finishing. Reading the reel-to-reel plating and electroplating overview shows how the two services connect.
Strip registration is the link between stamping and plating. If the carrier and pitch are designed with the plating line in mind, stripe and spot locations land where the finished part needs them. Composidie designs its tooling in house with that alignment as an input.
Fewer Handoffs
Every handoff between suppliers adds time and risk. When stamping, plating, and inspection are under one roof, the team can solve problems across process boundaries. A plating issue that traces back to burr direction or strip layout can be fixed with a single conversation instead of a chain of emails.
Typical Reel-to-Reel Plating Applications
The process is used wherever small metal parts need a precise finish at volume. Common examples include electrical contacts, connectors, terminals, and EMI shields. Industries range from electronics and automotive to medical and telecommunications. Composidie’s electronics industry page shows how these parts are used in practice.
Quality Checks
Plating quality depends on measurement. Thickness is typically verified with XRF, and adhesion and appearance are checked against the print. Consistent monitoring across the run catches drift before it affects a large quantity of parts.
Packaging and take-up also matter. Finished strip is typically wound onto a reel with protective measures so plated surfaces are not scratched in storage or shipping, and the reel format feeds directly into automated assembly equipment at the customer’s site.
Preparing a Program for Reel-to-Reel Plating
A good plating program begins with a clear specification. The steps below outline a practical order.
- Choose the base metal, temper, and thickness of the strip.
- Define the finish system, including underlayer and top finish.
- Decide on full-surface, stripe, or spot coverage.
- Set thickness ranges and the critical zones that must be covered.
- Design the carrier and strip layout for registration through plating.
- Validate thickness and adhesion on first pieces before releasing production.
With more than five decades of plating experience, Composidie can help review these choices before tooling is built. Getting the finish specification right up front is one of the most effective ways to protect schedule and cost.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is reel-to-reel plating?
Reel-to-reel plating is a continuous process in which stamped strip travels from one reel to another through cleaning, plating, and rinsing stations. Parts stay on the carrier throughout, which limits handling and keeps coverage consistent.
What finishes can be applied with reel-to-reel plating?
Composidie plates nickel, tin, silver, hard and soft gold, and palladium-nickel, among other finishes, either across the full surface or selectively with stripe and spot patterns.
Why is reel-to-reel plating suited to high volume?
The process runs continuously on strip, so the same settings hold over long runs. It also avoids loading and unloading batches, which reduces handling and variation.
What parts are typically plated this way?
Electrical contacts, connectors, terminals, and EMI shields are common examples, particularly where a precise finish is needed over very large quantities.

Composidie lists nickel in sulfamate\, bright\, and matte forms\, matte and bright tin\, hard and soft gold\, silver\, and palladium\-nickel\, among other finishes\. A longer list of materials is available on the material and finishes page\. Each finish has a different job\. Tin supports solderability\, gold supports low contact resistance\, silver supports conductivity\, and nickel provides a barrier and wear surface\.

\#\#\# Selective Application

Applying precious metal only where it is needed keeps cost under control\. Selective approaches are a core strength of reel\-to\-reel plating\, especially for connectors and contacts where the mating area is small compared with the whole part\.

\#\# Why Plating Pairs Well With High\-Speed Stamping

Stamping and reel\-to\-reel plating share the same format\. Both work on continuous strip\, so the output of a high\-speed press can feed a plating line without being broken into loose parts\. This keeps parts organized and protects delicate features\.

Composidie operates stamping presses at up to 1\,800 strokes per minute and runs plating in house\, so a stamped strip can move straight into finishing\. Reading the reel\-to\-reel plating and electroplating overview shows how the two services connect\.

Strip registration is the link between stamping and plating\. If the carrier and pitch are designed with the plating line in mind\, stripe and spot locations land where the finished part needs them\. Composidie designs its tooling in house with that alignment as an input\.

\#\#\# Fewer Handoffs

Every handoff between suppliers adds time and risk\. When stamping\, plating\, and inspection are under one roof\, the team can solve problems across process boundaries\. A plating issue that traces back to burr direction or strip layout can be fixed with a single conversation instead of a chain of emails\.

\#\# Typical Reel\-to\-Reel Plating Applications

The process is used wherever small metal parts need a precise finish at volume\. Common examples include electrical contacts\, connectors\, terminals\, and EMI shields\. Industries range from electronics and automotive to medical and telecommunications\. Composidie’s electronics industry page shows how these parts are used in practice\.

\#\#\# Quality Checks

Plating quality depends on measurement\. Thickness is typically verified with XRF\, and adhesion and appearance are checked against the print\. Consistent monitoring across the run catches drift before it affects a large quantity of parts\.

Packaging and take\-up also matter\. Finished strip is typically wound onto a reel with protective measures so plated surfaces are not scratched in storage or shipping\, and the reel format feeds directly into automated assembly equipment at the customer’s site\.

\#\# Preparing a Program for Reel\-to\-Reel Plating

A good plating program begins with a clear specification\. The steps below outline a practical order\.

\- Choose the base metal\, temper\, and thickness of the strip\.
\- Define the finish system\, including underlayer and top finish\.
\- Decide on full\-surface\, stripe\, or spot coverage\.
\- Set thickness ranges and the critical zones that must be covered\.
\- Design the carrier and strip layout for registration through plating\.
\- Validate thickness and adhesion on first pieces before releasing production\.

With more than five decades of plating experience\, Composidie can help review these choices before tooling is built\. Getting the finish specification right up front is one of the most effective ways to protect schedule and cost\.

\#\# Frequently Asked Questions

What is reel\-to\-reel plating\?

Reel\-to\-reel plating is a continuous process in which stamped strip travels from one reel to another through cleaning\, plating\, and rinsing stations\. Parts stay on the carrier throughout\, which limits handling and keeps coverage consistent\.

What finishes can be applied with reel\-to\-reel plating\?

Composidie plates nickel\, tin\, silver\, hard and soft gold\, and palladium\-nickel\, among other finishes\, either across the full surface or selectively with stripe and spot patterns\.

Why is reel\-to\-reel plating suited to high volume\?

The process runs continuously on strip\, so the same settings hold over long runs\. It also avoids loading and unloading batches\, which reduces handling and variation\.

What parts are typically plated this way\?

Electrical contacts\, connectors\, terminals\, and EMI shields are common examples\, particularly where a precise finish is needed over very large quantities\.

Marvell Technology Ph.D. Intern – AI / ML & Design Automation
Marvell Technology is hiring a Ph. D. Intern – AI/ML & Design Automation for an internship focused on applied research in semiconductor engineering. You will work on problems that connect doctoral research with production-scale chip design or enterprise AI systems. The role gives you access to real design data, active engineering workflows, and research challenges that do not have off-the-shelf solutions.
Job Snapshot
Company: Marvell Technology
Role: Ph. D. Intern – AI/ML & Design Automation
Location: Westlake Village, CA
Work Type: Internship.
Why Marvell’s AI Research Work Stands Out
Marvell gives doctoral researchers a chance to apply machine learning research to the silicon behind cloud and AI infrastructure, including custom XPUs, 224G and 448G SerDes, silicon photonics interconnects, and co-packaged optics platforms. The hardware track reaches into EDA automation, design space exploration, timing, power, placement, routing, and verification at 3nm and 2nm process nodes. The enterprise track focuses on LLM integration, agentic workflows, and internal AI systems used by engineering and operations teams. That combination can prepare you for research engineering, semiconductor automation, applied AI, or enterprise AI implementation work while keeping your projects connected to academic research. You will also present findings, model performance, or adoption results to engineering and cross-functional leadership.
AI, EDA, and LLM Tools in This Internship
The listing covers two technical tracks, so your relevant experience will depend on whether your research is closer to chip design or enterprise AI systems.
- Machine Learning: Graph neural networks, reinforcement learning, and generative approaches
- Chip Design: EDA tool flows, placement, routing, timing closure, power estimation, and design rule checking
- Enterprise AI: Large language models, Claude, agentic workflows, and AI-assisted engineering systems
- AI Implementation: Retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, fine-tuning workflows, and prompt engineering frameworks
- Production Evaluation: Model performance, safety, reliability, user feedback, and adoption metrics
What You Will Work On at Marvell
You will join one of two connected tracks: AI and machine learning for hardware and chip design, or enterprise AI tools and implementation. The work involves collaboration with design engineers, IT, security, engineering, and operations stakeholders.
- Develop and apply ML models to chip design tasks such as placement, routing, timing closure, power estimation, and design rule checking.
- Work with production EDA flows and design data from active tapeouts in advanced process nodes.
- Build predictive models that reduce design iteration cycles and improve first-pass silicon success rates.
- Collaborate with analog, digital, and physical design engineers to identify automation targets and validate model outputs against ground-truth silicon results.
- Present hardware research findings and model performance to engineering leadership.
- Design, implement, and evaluate LLM-based tools and agentic workflows for global engineering and operations teams.
- Build RAG pipelines, fine-tuning workflows, and prompt engineering frameworks using Marvell’s internal knowledge and tooling ecosystem.
- Evaluate model performance, safety, and reliability in enterprise environments.
- Iterate on AI systems using feedback from engineering teams.
- Work with IT, security, and engineering stakeholders on responsible and scalable AI deployment.
- Present implementation results and adoption metrics to cross-functional leadership.
Who This Ph. D. Internship Is For
- Be a doctoral candidate whose academic research connects to machine learning, computer science, or electrical engineering.
- Be prepared to apply doctoral research to production-scale problems in semiconductor design or enterprise AI.
- Bring research relevant to at least one of the two tracks: AI/ML for hardware and chip design, or enterprise AI tools and implementation.
- For the hardware track, be prepared to work on chip design challenges including EDA automation, design space exploration, predictive modeling, physical design, or verification.
- For the enterprise tools track, be prepared to work with LLM integrations, agentic workflows, RAG pipelines, fine-tuning, or prompt engineering.
- Be able to present research findings, model performance, implementation results, or adoption metrics to technical and cross-functional audiences.
The Two Tracks and Your Day-to-Day Work
The hardware track connects ML research with advanced silicon development, while the enterprise tools track connects AI systems with Marvell’s global engineering and operations workflows. Across both tracks, the work is research-driven but tied to production data, engineering use cases, model evaluation, and technical communication.
This internship is based in Westlake Village, California.
How to Present Your Research for Marvell
Choose Your Track: Make it clear whether your research fits AI/ML for hardware and chip design or enterprise AI tools and implementation.
Show Technical Depth: Connect projects to graph neural networks, reinforcement learning, EDA automation, LLMs, RAG, agentic workflows, or another technique named in the listing.
Quantify Evaluation: Include evidence of model performance, reliability, iteration-cycle improvements, silicon-related validation, user feedback, or adoption metrics where applicable.
How to Apply
Apply through the company’s own careers portal with a current resume ready that clearly presents your doctoral research, technical focus, and relevant project results.

records.summary: This is a DIY Solar Power Forum thread in which a homeowner planning an off-grid 48 V power shed asks where to find a UL/ETL/CSA-listed battery bus bar with studs. The planned system uses two SRNE ASP48160U300-H 16 kW inverters in parallel and three SRNE EOS15B (51.2 V, UL 1973) batteries on one common floating bus, with the dealer recommending an 800 A busbar. The poster needs seven ring-lug connections per pole (three battery leads with SC50-8 lugs and four inverter cables, two 3/0 per terminal per SRNE's manual) inside a UL-listed steel NEMA 1 enclosure under the 2023 NEC. The thread lists candidate parts and their stated listings: NSi Polaris IPLD250-8/IPLD350-8 multi-taps (UL 486A/B, set-screw ports requiring pin adapters), Burndy BDBLCS7R1DW (UL 1953, 1,456 A per pole, ~$1,034 each), Mersen MPDB66262/66263 (UL 1953, 400 A, one stud in/out per pole), Marathon BFPB stud blocks (UL Recognized only), and MidNite MNBCB 1000/50 (listing not found by the poster). No part is confirmed by the thread as meeting all requirements, and no inspection outcome is reported.

Follow-up to my Class T holder thread:
I've since gone with SRNE's own wiring for the inspection: no external fuses, relying on the
built-in breakers in the batteries (240 A) and the inverters. So the only open part now is the bus.
Setup: off-grid power shed in North Idaho, homeowner permit, 2023 NEC. Two SRNE ASP48160U300-H
(16 kW, 48 V) in parallel, three SRNE EOS15B (51.2 V, UL 1973) on one common bus. Floating
(ungrounded) battery bank per SRNE's manuals. One-line attached.
My inspector's rule: "As long as all your equipment is listed for solar installations, and is
done exactly how your one line diagram is drawn up you should be good to go." So the bus needs
a real NRTL listing (UL, ETL or CSA).
What the bus has to do:
- The dealer recommends an 800 A busbar for two ASP 16 kW in parallel.
- 7 cables per pole: 3 battery leads (SRNE's 1.5 m fine-strand leads with SC50-8 ring lugs)
and 4 inverter cables (SRNE's manual calls for two 3/0 per terminal).
- It mounts inside a UL-listed steel NEMA 1 box (Saginaw 30x24x8), closed and padlocked.
What I've found so far:
- NSi Polaris IPLD250-8 / IPLD350-8 insulated multi-taps (UL 486A/B), about $330 for both.
That's what's on my one-line now. The ports are set-screw, so the battery leads need pin
adapters (Burndy KAPO1/0) instead of their ring lugs.
- Burndy BDBLCS7R1DW (UL 1953, 1,456 A per pole). Takes fine strand directly, but $1,034 each
and special order.
- Mersen MPDB66262/66263 (UL 1953, 400 A). Listed with studs, but only one stud in and one
out per pole.
- Marathon BFPB stud blocks: UL Recognized only, not Listed.
- MidNite MNBCB 1000/50 battery combiner (1000 A bars with 3/8" studs): I can't find a listing
for the box or the bars.
- Blue Sea, Victron and the Amazon bars: no NRTL listing.
Questions:
1. Is there a UL/ETL/CSA-listed bus bar or battery combiner with studs that can take 7 ring
lugs per pole at 600-800 A, 48 V DC? Model numbers would be great.
2. Is the MidNite MNBCB 1000/50 (or any MidNite battery combiner) ETL or UL listed? Anyone
have a photo of the label?
3. Has anyone used a listed DC panel from OutBack (FLEXware), Schneider (Conext PDP) or Magnum
as the battery bus with other-brand inverters, and passed inspection?
4. If you passed an inspection with a 48 V battery bus, what did you use, and did the
inspector check its listing?
5. Polaris taps with pin adapters on fine-strand battery leads: has anyone had that accepted?
Thanks!

How to Choose Copper Busbars for 2026 Energy Storage PACKs: Top 10 Brand Guide
As global battery energy storage systems (BESS) scale toward higher capacities and denser PACK architectures in 2026, the copper busbar has moved from a commodity component to a critical performance and safety element. For European and international B2B buyers, the challenge is no longer simply finding a supplier who can cut and bend copper — it is selecting a partner who can guarantee conductivity, dimensional tolerance, plating quality, documentation and delivery reliability across multi-year framework agreements. This guide outlines the industry trends, procurement steps, maintenance practices and compliance risks that should shape your 2026 busbar sourcing strategy.
Three trends dominate the 2026 landscape. First, higher current densities in 300+ Ah cells are pushing designs toward thicker, wider busbars and laminated or multi-layer configurations, which places greater demands on flatness and hole-position accuracy. Second, the EU Batteries Regulation and the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) are increasing documentation requirements around material origin, recycled content and embedded carbon, so buyers increasingly request declarations that go beyond a simple mill certificate. Third, localization of supply is accelerating: European buyers are balancing Asian cost advantages against lead-time risk, tariff exposure and the need for rapid engineering changes, often qualifying two suppliers per part number.
From a technical standpoint, specify the alloy and temper explicitly — T2 or TU1 oxygen-free copper for high-conductivity applications, with hardness and temper matched to your bending and welding process. Define surface treatment clearly: bare, tin-plated, nickel-plated or silver-plated, with plating thickness tolerances and adhesion test methods. Insulation, if required, should be specified by dielectric strength, flame rating and temperature class. Most importantly, align acceptance criteria with recognized standards such as EN 13601 for copper rod and bar, IEC 61439 where applicable to assemblies, and your own PPAP or first-article inspection process.
Selection Criterion | What to Specify | Typical Risk if Ignored | Verification Method
---|---|---|---
Material grade | T2 / TU1 oxygen-free copper, temper and hardness | Hot spots, reduced conductivity, cracking at bends | Mill certificate, spectrometer check, conductivity test
Dimensions & tolerance | Thickness, width, hole position, flatness, burr limits | Assembly fit issues, torque loss, vibration loosening | CMM inspection, first-article report
Surface treatment | Tin/nickel/silver plating thickness, adhesion, appearance | Corrosion, contact resistance rise, solderability problems | Coating thickness gauge, cross-section, salt spray
Insulation | Dielectric strength, flame rating, temperature class | Short circuits, thermal runaway propagation risk | Hi-pot test, UL94 / IEC flame test reports
Compliance & documentation | EN 13601, RoHS, REACH, CBAM data, material origin | Customs delays, fines, tender disqualification | Supplier audit, declaration review
Process capability | Cpk for key dimensions, welding/plating in-house or subcontracted | Batch-to-batch variation, field failures | Process audit, SPC data review
Logistics & packaging | Protective packaging, VCI, moisture barrier, Incoterms | Oxidation, transit damage, hidden costs | Pre-shipment inspection, packaging spec
Capacity & lead time | Monthly capacity, buffer stock, dual-site options | Line stoppages during demand peaks | Capacity audit, contract clauses
On the supplier side, the market segments into several recognizable types. Vertically integrated copper mills and busbar fabricators offer material traceability and large-volume stability, and are often the preferred choice for framework agreements. Specialist precision stamping and CNC busbar houses excel at complex geometries, laminated bars and fast prototyping. Plating specialists add value where contact resistance and corrosion resistance are critical. Regional European fabricators provide short lead times and engineering proximity, while Asian manufacturers remain competitive on cost and volume but require robust quality surveillance and clear Incoterms. When shortlisting, include recognized industry names where they fit your specification — for example, established copper producers and fabricators such as Aurubis, KME, Wieland, Luvata and Elektrokoppar are commonly referenced in European technical discussions, alongside specialist busbar processors. Always verify current capabilities, certifications and references directly with each supplier rather than relying on brand reputation alone.
A practical procurement workflow for 2026 looks like this: define the electrical and mechanical requirements with your cell and PACK engineers; issue an RFQ that includes drawings, standards, test methods and documentation requirements; audit two to three shortlisted suppliers for process capability and compliance; run first-article inspection and a pilot batch before full release; then lock in quality agreements, change-notification clauses and dual-source or buffer-stock arrangements. Include a total-cost-of-ownership model that accounts for freight, duties, CBAM costs, inspection and the risk of line stoppages — not just unit price.
Maintenance and lifecycle management deserve equal attention. During incoming inspection, check plating integrity, burrs and flatness before parts reach the assembly line. In service, monitor torque values on bolted joints, inspect for oxidation or discoloration at contact points, and use thermal imaging during commissioning and periodic service to detect hot spots early. Keep spare busbars and fasteners for critical part numbers, and document torque and inspection intervals in your maintenance plan. For outdoor or high-humidity installations, confirm that plating and insulation choices match the environmental class, and include corrosion inspection in scheduled service routines.
Compliance and risk management should be built into the contract, not added afterward. Confirm RoHS and REACH conformity, request material origin and recycled-content data for CBAM reporting, and ensure the supplier can provide updated declarations on request. Address counterfeit or substituted copper risk through incoming material testing and supplier audits. Clarify warranty terms, liability for field failures and change-notification obligations. Finally, plan logistics carefully: specify packaging that prevents oxidation and transit damage, agree Incoterms and customs documentation in advance, and build lead-time buffers for long-haul shipments. Buyers who combine rigorous specifications, verified suppliers and disciplined maintenance will be best positioned to secure reliable copper busbar supply for their 2026 energy storage PACK programs.

Business Management Track Expands SUR/FIN Educational Curriculum
Targeted seminars to focus on platers’ day-to-day operational issues.
WASHINGTON, D.C., April 2 — Owners and managers of plating shops now have another compelling reason to attend SUR/FIN 2007, which kicks off Aug. 13–16 at the Cleveland Convention Center in Ohio. Conference organizers have expanded the show's traditional technology-based educational offering with a new Business Management Track, a well-rounded program that focuses keenly on the finisher's critical day-to-day operational issues.
Developed predominately by platers for platers, the Business Management Track is comprised of relevant and timely seminars tailored toward virtually every level of a metal finishing operation—from employee to manager and financial officer all the way up to the business owner. Following is a snapshot of some of the topics on tap:
-Retirement Planning
- OSHA Safety Training
-Truth… or Blowing Smoke? Business Insurance – What Do You Really Need and What are Your alternatives?
-Employee Satisfaction
-Metals Update
-Succeeding with OEMs in the “Exponential Economy”
-Seven Steps to a Successful Exit Strategy
-Disaster Planning Panel
-Preventative Maintenance and Asset Management
“From the standpoint of coming up with the curriculum for the courses, it was very important to the Management Committee that we had bits and pieces that appealed to all levels of the business,” said Matt Kirchner, vice-chair of the NASF Management Committee, and president and CEO of ABQC Corp., a Milwaukee, Wis.-based plater. “We didn’t want it all to be directed at the owners and CEOs, or just at the employees of metal finishing facilities. Instead, we wanted to come up with something that had a broad appeal, and I think we were really successful in putting that together.”
Successful, indeed. According to Kirchner, the committee worked tirelessly with platers as well as other industry members around the country in developing strong, issue-specific content that reflected the challenges and concerns central to finishing operations today. For instance, he cited the “Preventative Maintenance and Asset Management” seminar, which will be conducted by a panel of operations managers representing some of the most sophisticated surface finishing facilities in the U.S. Specifically, they will discuss how equipment uptime, reliability and performance are three of the most important factors in the efficiency of any metal finishing operation. The panelists are also expected to share their individual company philosophies on predicting problems and solving them before they occur.
Kirchner cited other seminars, such as the “Employee Satisfaction” course, which will be conducted by Steven Bauer of Nebraska-based Lincoln Plating. “That should be a very good presentation, because I know Lincoln Plating has a strong track record of dealing with employees and creating a great environment,” he said. Another example is the seminar on metals pricing, “which looks into the challenges that come along with a volatile metals market. That's something we all deal with on a daily basis.”
The examples don't end there. In fact, Kirchner himself is set to deliver a presentation on a topic of critical importance to any finisher, regardless of their size: serving original equipment manufacturers. In “Succeeding with OEMs in an Exponential Economy,” Kirchner plans to discuss the dynamics of keeping up with the pace of a fast-changing business environment. Relative to OEMs, this means understanding shrinking product life-cycles, corporate re-engineering, dealing with shorter order lead times, and global regulation, to name a few. Kirchner will also share examples of the trend toward OEMs rewarding their employees for performance and innovation in finishing technology.
Regardless of the subject matter—and there are variety of worthwhile seminars from which to choose—organizers say the business management courses will provide attendees with tangible, real-world information they can apply to their operational strategies after the show. “We had to make sure that—at least for a lot of these segments—there was usable take-home value at the end of the program,” Kirchner said. “It was really important that we offered a first-class list of topics that people could really use when they leave SUR/FIN.”
SUR/FIN 2007 is sponsored by the newly formed National Association for Surface Finishing (www.nasf.org). At SUR/FIN 2007, you’ll find a technical program that includes sessions focused on OEM and captive platers, as well as the expansion of exhibitors and attendees to reflect the entire supply chain. SUR/FIN 2007’s technical program will occur on Aug. 13–16; the exhibition takes place Aug. 14–15 at the Cleveland Convention Center in Cleveland, Ohio. For more information, visit www.sur-fin.net or contact Cheryl Clark at 202-457-8403; (e-mail) cclark@nasf.org.

In fact\, Kirchner himself is set to deliver a presentation on a topic of critical importance to any finisher\, regardless of their size\: serving original equipment manufacturers\. In “Succeeding with OEMs in an Exponential Economy\,” Kirchner plans to discuss the dynamics of keeping up with the pace of a fast\-changing business environment\. Relative to OEMs\, this means understanding shrinking product life\-cycles\, corporate re\-engineering\, dealing with shorter order lead times\, and global regulation\, to name a few\. Kirchner will also share examples of the trend toward OEMs rewarding their employees for performance and innovation in finishing technology\.

Regardless of the subject matter—and there are variety of worthwhile seminars from which to choose—organizers say the business management courses will provide attendees with tangible\, real\-world information they can apply to their operational strategies after the show\. “We had to make sure that—at least for a lot of these segments—there was usable take\-home value at the end of the program\,” Kirchner said\. “It was really important that we offered a first\-class list of topics that people could really use when they leave SUR\/FIN\.”

SUR\/FIN 2007 is sponsored by the newly formed National Association for Surface Finishing \(www\.nasf\.org\)\. At SUR\/FIN 2007\, you’ll find a technical program that includes sessions focused on OEM and captive platers\, as well as the expansion of exhibitors and attendees to reflect the entire supply chain\. SUR\/FIN 2007’s technical program will occur on Aug\. 13–16\; the exhibition takes place Aug\. 14–15 at the Cleveland Convention Center in Cleveland\, Ohio\. For more information\, visit www\.sur\-fin\.net or contact Cheryl Clark at 202\-457\-8403\; \(e\-mail\) cclark\@nasf\.org\.

E-Archive
Cover Page
in Vol. 3 - November Issue - Year 2002
Sample Processing Proves Value of Automated Blasting
Author Herb Tobben manages the sample processing lab at Clemco Industries Corp.
A roller system mounted on powered work car allows simultaneous internal and external blasting of this tubular weldment.
A pivoting/oscillating arm maintains precise nozzle angle and distance while depainting this curved aircraft skin section.
An eight-nozzle array removes tooling marks, burrs, and casting lines to leave a uniform satin finish on these pistol components prior to plating.
In the Spotlight
Clemco Industries Corp. manufacturers automated blast cabinets, blast rooms, blast cabinets, portable blast machines, and a complete line of nozzles and other blast components. The company has a worldwide network of licensees, subsidiaries, and distributors.
Clemco Industries Corp. offers a free sample processing service to help customers of its ZERO brand equipment determine if automated blast cleaning or shot peening would improve their operations.
Obviously the benefit of free sample processing service comes from the potential for a sale, but sample processing provides clear advantages as well for the company owner, project manager, or engineer.
First, this company based in Washington does the R & D work in their lab, using experienced technicians operating their own equipment. As a customer, one does not need to buy a blast system, learn to use it, then try to create a process for ones own application. Clemco has designed systems to efficiently handle everything from fragile silicon wafers to massive space shuttle fuel tanks. This experience gives a head start narrowing down the parameters for parts handling and blasting.
Second, the American manufacturer has the resources to do the work without compromise. Creating custom fixtures is easy, because their engineers and technicians have direct access to machine tools, metal fabrication equipment, and a urethane mold shop. They do not sell blast media, but stock just about every type, in every mesh size imaginable exclusively for sample processing.
And third, after processing representative samples of actual parts, their expertise can evaluate, not just the best way to do the job, but what production rate one can realistically expect. The customers also know what the equipment will cost to purchase and to operate.
The sample processing technicians test blast or shot peen representative parts, provided by customers, while modifying the variables to get the best results. These variables include:
-suction or pressure blasting
-number and size of nozzles or guns
-position of nozzles or guns (distance, angle, spacing)
-blast pressure
-dwell (amount of blast time a surface receives)
-nozzle oscillation speed
-part movement
-media composition and size
The goal is to design an automated system to get the desired finish, consistently, and economically. Many customers ask what criteria is used to determine if an application could benefit from automation. Customers are surprised all the time with unique applications, but a few common characteristics usually indicate that a part is a candidate for automation.
The simplest automated blast applications take parts of relatively consistent size, shape, and condition, and apply a predetermined process to produce identical results over a long production run. With the help of quick-change fixtures and programmable controllers, however, one can build machines to handle an assortment of parts over short or long production runs.
So how does one know if sample processing will be a benefit? If one or more of the following issues is of importance, it might be worth evaluating a sample processing:
-Surface preparation has become a bottleneck in the production line. This includes chemical processes, hand sanding, or manual blasting.
-Two or more employees spend more than half of each day cleaning parts. An automated blast system will speed production and can significantly reduce the risk of repetitive-motion injuries.
-A surface preparation involves toxic chemicals. (When one factors in the health and safety issues, environmental compliance requirements, and disposal costs for chemicals, an automated blast system can usually pay for itself in less than a year.)
-A current process produces inconsistent results or causes excessive rework. This is especially true for shot peening, where verifiable and repeatable results are critical to part performance.
-A current process takes too long. Or, drying the parts after chemical processing takes too long.
-In the past year, one has worn out a manual blast cabinet or has spent more than half the cost of a new manual cabinet keeping your old one running.
For many people, blasting conjures images of aggressive abrasives cleaning rust and paint from steel. But, the American manufacturer has sold systems to automatically blast just about every material one can imagine – aluminum, plastics, glass, fiberglass, silicon wafer, cloth, titanium, ceramics, wood, brass and yes, tons of steel.
ZERO automated systems clean thermos bottles, degloss fiberglass boat hulls, relieve stress in glass ingots, deburr dental braces, satin finish automotive trim, prepare aluminum baseball bats for coatings, etch cookware to accept non-stick coatings, refurbish brass water meters, and so much more.
Clemco can help to evaluate a current process, and show how automated blasting can save time and money, while improving the overall quality of a company’s products.

Mo 63090
USA

Materials | Highly Cited Papers in 2025 in the “Manufacturing Processes and Systems” Section
23 October 2026
The Section “Manufacturing Processes and Systems in Materials”, of Materials (ISSN 1996-1944), covers a wide range of manufacturing processes, from traditional methods to more advanced technologies. It emphasizes the importance of selecting the appropriate manufacturing process based on the desired material properties, the complexity of the parts design, and economic factors. Understanding, optimizing, monitoring, controlling, modelling, and simulating these different processes and systems is essential for efficient and cost-effective production, ensuring that materials are processed and converted into finished products with the required quality and functionality.

records.summary: This study investigates whether the heat introduced when joining reinforcement segments by welding during Selective Paste Intrusion (SPI) printing impairs the steel–concrete bond. Sixteen 16 mm ribbed bars embedded vertically in a particle bed were produced in two series: eight with segments joined by manual gas tungsten arc welding (seven joints per bar, a stud-welding-like approximation of WAAM) and eight with adhesively bonded segments as a no-heat reference. Thermography with a grey-body estimate (assumed steel emissivity 0.20–0.30) indicated bar-surface temperatures of at least 214–277 °C near joints immediately after welding and 125–162 °C after 2–3 min. In push-through tests at 28 days, welded bars reached a mean maximum bond stress of 20.5 MPa versus 22.4 MPa for the adhesively bonded reference; the 1.9 MPa (9%) difference lay within scatter (CV 22% and 21%), with a 95% confidence interval of −7.0 to +3.1 MPa, so a reduction of up to 31% cannot be excluded. All specimens failed by bar push-through, none by splitting.
records.why_it_matters: For integrating reinforcement into SPI by segment welding, the results suggest that repeated short welding-induced thermal cycles at roughly 200–280 °C near joints did not produce a detectable bond loss under short-term compressive loading, but the small sample cannot rule out reductions up to about 31%, so the approach is not yet proven equivalent to unheated reinforcement.

Evidence is strong: 16 specimens, two series, quantified bond stresses (20.5 vs 22.4 MPa), thermographic temperatures, and explicit confidence intervals. Novelty is moderate—first manual approximation of WAAM segment joining within SPI—but authors themselves frame it as a stud-welding-like approximation, not genuine WAAM.
