Selective Paste Intrusion—Effect of Process-Integrated Welding of Reinforcement Segments on Bond Strength
,
and
Chair of Materials Science and Testing, Centre for Building Materials (cbm), School of Engineering and Design, Technical University of Munich, 85748 Garching, Germany
Author to whom correspondence should be addressed.
Abstract
Integrating Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) into the Selective Paste Intrusion (SPI) process enables the fully additive fabrication of reinforced concrete structures with complex geometries. However, the WAAM process transfers thermal energy into the reinforcement and the surrounding concrete matrix, which may affect the bond between steel and concrete. This study addresses whether the heat introduced by the welding of reinforcement segments impairs the bond between reinforcing steel and SPI-fabricated concrete. To isolate this thermal effect from the geometric process effects covered in a companion study, two groups of 16 mm reinforcing bars embedded in SPI-fabricated concrete were compared: bars whose segments were joined during printing by manual welding at seven joints per bar (process-integrated thermal exposure), and bars with adhesively bonded segments without heat input as the reference. Eight specimens per group from two production series were tested in push-through. A grey-body estimate based on the thermography and an assumed steel emissivity of 0.20 to 0.30 indicates approximate bar-surface temperatures of at least 214 to 277 °C near the joints immediately after welding and of 125 to 162 °C after 2 to 3 min. Despite these temperatures and the repeated heating and cooling cycles during printing, no discernible difference in bond capacity from the adhesively bonded reference group was detected: the welded group reaches a mean maximum bond stress of 20.5 MPa, the adhesively bonded reference 22.4 MPa, and the difference of 1.9 MPa (9%) lies within the scatter of the two groups (coefficients of variation 22% and 21%). With a 95% confidence interval of −7.0 to 3.1 MPa for this difference, a reduction of up to 31% cannot be excluded with this sample. All specimens of both groups failed by bar push-through, with a similar slip at maximum bond stress. Because the weld beads also change the joint geometry, the thermal exposure cannot be fully separated from the joint geometry. Since the procedure investigated here resembles a stud welding process rather than genuine WAAM fabrication, the results indicate that joining reinforcement segments by stud-welding-like processes during printing is a feasible route for integrating reinforcement into SPI with respect to the bond under short-term compressive loading. For genuine WAAM, further investigations are required, since welding occurs far more frequently than in the present procedure because of the smaller layer heights, so that heat accumulates and overlapping thermal cycles can produce even higher sustained temperatures at the steel–concrete interface.
1. Introduction
Selective Paste Intrusion (SPI) is an additive manufacturing method for producing concrete elements with complex geometries. Aggregates are sequentially spread to form a particle bed, and cement paste is selectively applied to bind them, while the unbound surrounding aggregates act as temporary support, so that freeform components can be fabricated without formwork (Figure 1) [1,2].
Figure 1. Schematic representation of the combined SPI and WAAM process (renderings), modified after [3]. (a) Printing a reinforcing bar. (b) Spreading an aggregate layer. (c) Applying cement paste. (d) Curing the finished reinforced concrete element. (e) Excavating the component.
Strategies for integrating reinforcement into digitally fabricated concrete are the subject of ongoing research [4,5]. Combining SPI with Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) has been proposed as a strategy to produce custom-shaped reinforcement directly within the particle bed [6]. WAAM reinforcement reached upper yield strengths of 316 to 348 MPa, tensile strengths of 454 to 481 MPa, and uniform elongations of 14.4 to 17.5% in the valid tensile tests, and its bond performance is comparable to conventional B500B reinforcement [7]. B500B denotes a characteristic yield strength
Bond between ribbed reinforcement and concrete is transferred by adhesion, mechanical interlock of the ribs, and friction, which dominate successively with increasing slip [12,13,14,15]. Damage to the matrix around the bar, whether thermal or from impaired material deposition, can therefore affect both the early bond response and the bond capacity.
A challenge of this combination is the heat generated during the WAAM process. In WAAM, every deposited layer reheats the material below it, and with short interlayer times the heat accumulates over successive layers, which raises the interlayer temperature and changes the microstructure and mechanical properties of the deposit [16]. Interlayer dwell times and active or forced interpass cooling are therefore used to control this thermal history [17,18]. In a combined SPI-WAAM process, the accumulated heat would also act on the fresh cement paste and on the forming steel–concrete interface. The thermal load transferred from the welding point into the reinforcement and the surrounding particle bed can alter the rheological properties of the cement paste and impair the mechanical performance of the hardened concrete. Cement-paste rheology is sensitive to temperature, with changes in yield stress and plastic viscosity reported within 20 to 50 °C [19,20,21].
For the SPI system considered here, the relevant thermal limits were established in a sequence of preceding studies. The fresh-state limit was identified by measuring how rising cement paste temperatures affect yield stress and viscosity. A sharp transition was observed at 60 to 70 °C, above which penetration of the cement paste into the particle bed deteriorates [22]. The hardened-state limit was established by examining the effect of fresh-state thermal exposure on the compressive and flexural strength of the resulting concrete, which decline at a fresh-state temperature of 80 °C and above [23]. The actual temperatures occurring during WAAM at varying distances from the welding point, and corresponding cooling strategies, were then quantified [24]. Depending on the distance to the welding point, the reinforcement reached temperatures of 100 to 450 °C at an interlayer cooling time of 60 s [24]. Bar temperatures of 164 to 206 °C were measured by thermocouples embedded in the bar at a distance of 40 mm between measuring point and process zone [24]. These temperatures exceed the identified rheological and hardened-state thresholds.
To reduce the thermal load on the particle bed, one strategy is to increase the vertical distance between the welding point and the bed surface. Print quality is unimpaired up to 40 mm, and a first strength reduction of about 16% sets in at 50 mm [3]. This vertical protrusion of the reinforcement gives rise to shadowing effects, a process-induced disturbance of material deposition in the vicinity of the protruding bar. A companion study [25] investigates these geometric effects systematically, covering bar diameters of 8 mm, 16 mm, and 25 mm and inclination angles of 0 to 90° in 15° increments. The present work addresses the welding of segments within the SPI process, in which the thermal exposure and the weld bead arise from the same operation, and leaves the geometric process effects to the companion study.
To isolate the effect of thermal exposure on bond strength, a controlled laboratory study was conducted prior to the present work. Conventionally cast pull-out specimens with WAAM-fabricated reinforcing bars heated to 20 °C, 60 °C, 80 °C, and 200 °C by means of an internal cartridge heater were tested according to RILEM RC6 [26]. The results revealed a displacement-dependent thermal effect that runs counter to the expectation of a uniform bond reduction across all slip levels. At small slip values (0.001 mm and 0.01 mm), the 200 °C specimens exhibited higher bond stresses than those at 60 °C and 80 °C, attributed to heat-induced water evaporation at the steel–concrete interface, which locally reduces the water-to-cement ratio and increases matrix stiffness. The 200 °C specimens showed a reduction of 29% in maximum bond stress relative to the unheated reference at 20 °C (13.99 versus 19.67 MPa). Complementary microstructural analyses by X-ray diffraction (XRD), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and mercury intrusion porosimetry (MIP) confirmed partial dehydration of calcium silicate hydrate (C-S-H) phases, an increased content of unhydrated tricalcium silicate (C3S), which indicates a locally reduced degree of hydration due to premature water loss, and a shift of the pore size distribution towards larger radii at 200 °C [26].
These findings establish the thermal sensitivity of the bond interface under controlled conditions. Independent evidence from cyclic thermal loading tests on reinforced concrete beams (7, 14, 21, and 28 heating and cooling cycles with peak temperatures of 100 °C, 200 °C, and 300 °C) shows that lap-splice bond strength is close to or above that of the unheated control at 100 °C and 200 °C but is reduced by up to 44% at 300 °C, and that the effect of the thermal cycles generally increases with their number [27]. For oven-heated specimens, bond losses additionally increase with heating rate and target temperature [28], and depend non-monotonically on the concrete age at exposure for ages of 3 to 28 days [29]. The thermal exposure considered here, by contrast, acts within the first hours after intrusion, before the interface has fully formed. The controlled study used conventionally cast specimens with a cartridge heater to apply a defined, uniform temperature over the bond length. In the actual combined SPI-WAAM process, the thermal exposure differs in character: it arises from the layer-by-layer deposition of reinforcement directly in the particle bed, producing a transient, spatially non-uniform temperature field. The cement paste surrounding the reinforcement is not conventionally cast but formed by selective intrusion into a granular packing.
The preceding studies thus established the thermal limits of the SPI system and the sensitivity of the bond to sustained heating, but they used defined, uniform temperatures in conventionally cast specimens or did not include bond tests. None of them joined reinforcement by welding within the SPI process itself. The present study takes this step as a first, manual approximation of WAAM. During SPI printing, segments of 16 mm reinforcing bars embedded vertically in the particle bed were joined by manual gas tungsten arc welding, a stud-welding-like procedure that exposes the bond zone to repeated welding-induced heating and cooling cycles. The thermal exposure was recorded by thermography, and the bond was determined in push-through tests. As the reference without heat input, segments of the same bars were joined by an adhesive under the same printing conditions. Segmentation is required for both groups, since the bar can protrude above the particle bed only by a limited distance during printing without colliding with the print heads (Section 2.2). Based on the controlled study, the hypothesis was that the welding-induced thermal exposure reduces the bond capacity of the welded bars relative to the adhesively bonded reference, as observed after sustained heating to 200 °C [26]. Sixteen specimens were produced in two production series, eight welded and eight adhesively bonded.
2. Materials and Methods
2.1. Materials
The concrete was produced using ordinary Portland cement (CEM I 42.5 N, Heidelberg Materials, Heidelberg, Germany) and quartz sand (Quarzwerke, Frechen, Germany) with a particle size ranging from 1.0 to 2.2 mm and a median particle size
2.2. Specimen Geometry and Reinforcement Configuration
The bond length was
Figure 2. Specimen geometry and holder assembly. (a) Segment sequence and specimen geometry (to scale). (b) Holder assembly: (1) steel rails, (2) reinforcement segments, (3) transverse struts, (4) co-printed ground bar for the welding process.
Two joining methods were compared. In the welded group, the segments were joined by gas tungsten arc welding (GTAW) using a power source (REHM Invertig.Pro digital 240DC, Uhingen, Germany) with an air-cooled torch (R-Tig 200/35) and a steel filler rod (W3Si1 according to DIN EN ISO 636 [34]) under a pure argon (I1 according to DIN EN ISO 14175 [35]) shielding gas atmosphere. The welding was performed in direct current electrode negative (DCEN) polarity at a machine-set welding current of 120 A with a filler rod diameter of 1.0 mm. Torch and filler rod were guided manually, as is characteristic of manual GTAW, so that arc duration and filler addition varied from joint to joint. In each joining cycle, one segment was welded onto each bar of the welded rail in the order P01 to P04 and one onto the ground bar. Consecutive bars were welded about 1.1 min apart, measured between the ΔT peaks of P02 to P04 (Section 2.5). The mean interval between the joining cycles was 17.6 and 15.4 min in series 1 and 2. All welds were made by the same operator. Prior to each welding operation, the exposed bar end and the joint faces were cleaned to remove adhering aggregate particles, dust, and cement paste from the particle-bed environment. In the adhesively bonded group, the segments were butt-joined using a low-viscosity ethyl cyanoacrylate adhesive (Loxeal Instant Adhesive 32, Cesano Maderno, Italy). The joint faces of this group were cleaned prior to joining in the same manner as those of the welded group.
The reinforcing bars were fixed in the particle bed by welding them onto a holder consisting of two steel rails. Each rail carried four bars at a spacing of approximately 180 mm along the rail, and the two rails were mounted approximately 180 mm apart. The rails were connected by transverse steel struts for stability. A vertical ribbed bar (diameter 28 mm) was the ground connection for the welding process. This bar was co-printed with the specimens and segmented in the same manner as the reinforcing bars, so that a fresh segment was always available above the bed surface for attaching the welding clamp. Figure 2 shows the specimen geometry and the holder assembly.
2.3. Specimen Fabrication
The specimens were fabricated on a laboratory SPI printer with a build volume of 600 × 350 × 350 mm. The aggregate was spread in layers of 3 mm thickness using the spreading roller of the printer, followed by a doctor blade. After each aggregate layer, cement paste was selectively applied by two print heads with eight nozzles each (nozzle diameter 1 mm) at a print speed of 300 mm s−1 and a nozzle distance of 20 mm above the bed surface. Assuming that the paste fills the void volume of the layer, the paste quantity was approximately 1.3 L m−2 of printed area per layer. Without segment joining, one layer took about 55 s. The printing took place at (20 ± 1) °C and a relative humidity of 44 to 50%. For printing, the holder was placed on the printer platform and both rails were overprinted simultaneously in the same printing sequence, so that the welded and adhesively bonded groups received identical cement paste and aggregate conditions.
The printing started with the first 10 mm segment protruding above the particle bed. With each successive 3 mm layer of aggregate and cement paste, the protrusion decreased until the upper end of the segment approached the level of the bed surface. The printer was then paused, and a new segment was joined to the existing bar using the respective joining method (see Section 2.2), restoring the protrusion. This cycle of printing and segment joining was repeated until the full bond length of 80 mm was reached.
The setup produced a continuous block of printed concrete along each rail, embedding all four specimens per rail in a single monolithic body. This fabrication was performed in two production series of identical configuration, so that eight specimens per group were obtained. In both series, the adhesively bonded segments were mounted on the left and the welded segments on the right rail (Figure 3b). The bar positions are designated P01 to P04 on the welded rail and P05 to P08 on the adhesively bonded rail (Figure 3c), and the series is added as a suffix, for example P03.2 for position P03 in series 2. Both series used the same materials, mix design, and printing parameters.

(a) Holder assembly in the particle bed before printing: (1) spreading roller, (2) particle bed, (3) initial segments protruding 10 mm above the bed surface, (4) ground bar. (b) Top view after printing: (1) printed block along the adhesively bonded rail, (2) printed block along the welded rail, (3) ground bar. (c) Bar positions P01 to P04 (welded) and P05 to P08 (adhesively bonded) in the particle bed shown in (b), at the same scale, drill cores dashed, ground bar grey.
After 24 h of curing in the particle bed, the blocks together with their holders were excavated. Since the embedded bars still connected the blocks to the holder rails, the reinforcement stubs were separated directly upon excavation to release the blocks for storage. The stubs were cut with a rotary tool (Dremel, Mount Prospect, IL, USA) and a thin cutting disc to limit vibration-induced loading of the early-age bond at the steel–concrete interface. The blocks were then stored at 20 °C and 65% relative humidity.
Since the SPI process produces a monolithic block rather than individual cylindrical specimens, each specimen had to be isolated by core drilling. At an age of 21 days, four cylindrical specimens with a diameter of 80 mm were extracted from each block by wet core drilling, with the reinforcing bar centred within each core. All specimens were stored at 20 °C and 65% relative humidity until testing at an age of 28 days in both production series. Figure 3 shows the key stages of the fabrication process.
2.4. Mechanical Testing
Push-through tests were conducted following a procedure adapted from RILEM RC6 [33], as in the companion study [25] (Figure 4). The specimens were placed on a spherical seat to compensate for angular misalignment between bar axis and load axis and to ensure axial load application. The reinforcing bars protruded vertically upwards, and the specimens were tested inverted relative to the printing orientation: the former rail-side bar end pointed upwards for load application, while the displacement transducer engaged the opposite bar end (the final segment) below the specimen. Force-controlled loading was applied at the loading rate of RILEM RC6 [33], which was adopted for comparability. It was computed as

(b) Instrumented specimen: (1) loaded bar end, (2) steel confinement ring, (3) polymer holder clamped to the ring, (4) free bar end, (5) linear displacement transducer.
Displacement was recorded at the free (unloaded) bar end using a potentiometric linear displacement transducer (Ahlborn FWA025TR, Holzkirchen, Germany, measuring range 25 mm, resolution 0.001 mm as specified by the manufacturer) mounted in a polymer holder clamped to the steel confinement ring. Because the displacement is measured at the free end, it does not contain the elastic shortening of the bar or the deformation of the segment joints between the loaded and the free end, in the same way as the free-end slip of a pull-out test according to RILEM RC6 [33] does not contain the elastic elongation of the bar. The bond stress
The configuration deviates from RILEM RC6 [33] in several respects. Loading is applied in compression rather than tension (Section 2.2), so that lateral expansion of the bar due to the Poisson effect increases the radial pressure at the interface instead of reducing it. Over the full specimen height, the bar is bonded, without the bond-free pre-length of the RC6 specimen. The concrete cover of the RC6 cube is replaced by a steel confinement ring, whose radial stiffness exceeds that of a typical concrete cover. Finally, the concrete is built up layer-wise along the bar axis rather than cast transverse to it. The absolute bond stresses reported here therefore characterise this confined push-through configuration, and the two groups are compared within it. Both groups were fabricated and tested in the identical configuration, but the configuration can interact with the joint type, since the entire load is transferred through the segment joints in compression (Section 3.4). The RC6-derived bond length, loading rate, and slip-level evaluation were retained for comparability with the preceding controlled study [26] and with the pull-out characterisation of WAAM reinforcement [7].

Infrared video was recorded during each production series using a thermal imaging camera (VarioCAM Research 976S, InfraTec, Dresden, Germany, long-wave infrared 8 to 14 μm) with a 30 mm objective (Jenoptik, Jena, Germany). 2.6. Data Evaluation
All results are reported as group means with standard deviations (SD) and coefficients of variation (CV), and the individual values are listed in Appendix A (Table A1). The joining method was assigned to a complete holder rail. The four specimens of a rail therefore share the printed block, the curing, and, in the welded group, the welding sequence of the series, so that they are not fully independent of each other. To quantify the uncertainty of the comparison, the difference between the group means (welded minus adhesively bonded) is given with its 95% confidence interval, calculated with Welch’s t-test for unequal variances. The interval contains the differences that are compatible with the measured scatter. If it includes zero, no difference is detected, and its lower bound indicates the largest reduction that the data cannot exclude. Because the specimens of a rail share the production, the difference between the groups is also reported separately for each series.

3.3. Weld Geometry, Heat-Affected Zone, and Interface Microstructure
The adhesively bonded segments are the reference without heat input that can be produced under the same SPI conditions, since segmentation is required by the process (Section 2.2). However, they are not an ideal unheated counterpart of the welded bar. Each welded joint carries a weld bead that protrudes from the bar surface (Figure 10) and may act as an additional bearing element, whereas the adhesively bonded butt joints are flush with the bar surface and contain a thin adhesive layer. The joints also differ in axial stiffness and continuity. A thermally induced bond reduction could therefore be partly offset by mechanical interlock at the weld beads, and the comparison reflects the welding procedure as a whole, in which the thermal exposure cannot be fully separated from the joint geometry. For the joining of reinforcement segments by welding during printing, this combined effect is the one that acts, since heat input and weld bead arise from the same operation.
Figure 10. Close-up of a segment joint during fabrication, taken directly after a welding cycle. The weld bead protrudes from the bar surface, forming a localised geometric discontinuity.
Three joint-related mechanisms may influence the bond of the welded bars. First, the weld bead changes the bar surface at each joint and may act as a bearing element in addition to the ribs. Second, the heat-affected zone may have changed the steel properties and the rib geometry close to each joint. Because the joints were loaded in compression in the push-through test, such changes are more relevant for the tensile and fatigue performance of the joints than for the present bond results (Section 3.4). Third, the matrix at the interface close to the joints was exposed to the highest temperatures. After sustained heating to 200 °C, the controlled study found the changes in hydration and pore structure summarised in Section 1 [26]. In the present process, the short, repeated exposure together with the weld beads did not lead to a discernible bond reduction (Section 3.1).
WAAM-fabricated reinforcement, whose entire surface consists of successive weld beads, achieves bond performance comparable to conventionally ribbed B500B bars [7]. Bond degradation after elevated-temperature exposure of hardening or hardened concrete has been reported in multiple independent studies [27,28,29,42,43,44], and the controlled thermal-exposure study with the same cement paste mixture identified a bond reduction under sustained 200 °C [26]. In the present comparison, the mean difference of 9% is smaller than this reduction of 29%, which lies within the confidence interval of the difference (Section 3.1).
3.4. Limitations of the Push-Through Configuration
Because of the compression loading and the steel confinement ring (Section 2.4), the measured bond capacities refer to a confined bar under compression. The displacement at the free bar end excludes the elastic shortening of the bar and the joints, but a different joint stiffness may still change the distribution of slip along the bond length. Since the segments were butt-joined and the joints were loaded in compression, the cut faces were pressed against each other, so that the joined bars are expected to behave approximately like the continuous bar of a RILEM RC6 test in this respect. The results therefore characterise the bond of the joined bars under short-term compressive loading.
3.5. Transfer to WAAM
The present procedure resembles stud welding rather than genuine WAAM. Short segments of 10 mm (final segment 20 mm) were joined in single welding operations, which were separated by several printed layers. A similar stud-welding-like approach is used for segmented reinforcement in the extrusion-based AMoRC process [10,11]. Over the bond length of 80 mm, the present bars contain seven joints, each made once per joining cycle at intervals of 15.4 to 17.6 min. A WAAM-deposited bar with a mean layer height of 1.25 mm [24] consists of 64 layers over the same length, each a weld bead and a thermal cycle, deposited at much shorter intervals. In genuine WAAM, heat therefore accumulates over successive layers [16], and the overlapping thermal cycles in a given bar cross-section can produce higher sustained temperatures at the steel–concrete interface than in the present procedure, of the kind shown to degrade bond under controlled heating [26] and under cyclic thermal loading [27]. The present results thus represent the low-exposure end of the range between single joining operations and continuous WAAM deposition. For full WAAM integration, active cooling strategies [17,18] or a lower heat input per weld are therefore necessary. Drawn-arc stud welding, which completes a joint in a sub-second welding cycle [45], is one option for automating the segment-joining route with a defined heat input.
A further transfer aspect concerns joint cleanliness. In the present study, the joint faces were cleaned before each welding cycle, so that contamination by particles or cement paste was largely excluded. Moisture is a known source of diffusible hydrogen in arc welds, shown for example for moist stick electrode coatings [46], and contamination of the weld has been shown to change its microstructure and reduce its strength, for example in friction stir spot welds of steel [47]. In an automated SPI-WAAM process without intermediate cleaning, this adds to the qualification requirements for the welded joints, independently of the concrete-side bond behaviour measured here.
The heat input per joint depended on the manual procedure, since arc duration and filler addition varied from joint to joint (Section 2.2). Because the thermal exposure is the variable of interest, this variability of the manual procedure limits the present study. The thermography documents the resulting exposure of the bed surface (Section 3.2).
4. Conclusions
This study investigated the bond behaviour between reinforcement and concrete fabricated by Selective Paste Intrusion (SPI) under process-integrated thermal exposure from welding of steel segments, with adhesively bonded segments without heat input as the reference. Reinforcing bars with a diameter of 16 mm embedded vertically in the particle bed were tested in push-through (eight specimens per group from two production series). Under short-term compressive push-through loading, the welded bars reached a mean bond capacity close to that of the adhesively bonded reference, for the stud-welding-like scenario investigated here with seven joints per bar at 10 mm spacing and approximate bar-surface temperatures of at least 214 to 277 °C immediately after welding and 125 to 162 °C after 2 to 3 min. The results therefore indicate that joining reinforcement segments by stud-welding-like processes during SPI printing is a feasible route with respect to the bond under short-term compressive loading. Longer segments, within the clearance below the print heads (Section 2.2), reduce the number of welding cycles per bond length. For reinforcement produced by genuine Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM), further investigations are required, in particular regarding heat accumulation, and questions of joint cleanliness are still to be addressed separately as a process-engineering task.
The welded and the adhesively bonded groups reach comparable bond capacities (20.5 MPa and 22.4 MPa). At 1.9 MPa (9%), the difference is smaller than the standard deviation of either group, and the coefficients of variation of the two groups are 22% and 21%. No discernible difference was therefore detected in this sample, while the 95% confidence interval of the difference (−7.0 to 3.1 MPa) shows that a reduction of up to 31% cannot be excluded with eight specimens per group from two production series. The scatter exceeds the range reported for pull-out testing. Since it is of the same size in both groups, it more likely originates from the fabrication steps common to both groups (SPI intrusion, manual segmentation and joining, core drilling) than from the thermal exposure, which only the welded group received.
Bond stress values at very small slips (s ≤ 0.01 mm) approach the resolution limit of the displacement measurement and show no consistent difference between the groups. All specimens failed by bar push-through and none by splitting, and the slip at maximum bond stress is similar in both groups. Because the weld beads change the joint geometry, the thermal exposure cannot be fully separated from the joint geometry in this comparison (Section 3.3). For the joining of segments by welding during printing, this combined effect is the one that acts. The results characterise the steel–concrete bond under short-term compressive loading (Section 3.4).
5. Outlook
Three steps follow from the present results. First, automated joining with a defined heat input per weld, for example by stud welding, where the process variant (drawn-arc versus capacitor-discharge according to DIN EN ISO 14555 [48]) governs the actual heat input, would eliminate the variability of the manual procedure and allow the remaining scatter to be attributed to the process rather than to the preparation. Second, the welded joints are to be characterised for structural use, in tension according to DIN EN ISO 17660-1 [49], under fatigue loading, and with respect to durability. Measurements of the bead geometry, hardness profiles across the joints, and microstructural analyses of the interface zone would separate the joint-related mechanisms discussed in Section 3.3. Third, the step towards in situ WAAM deposition combined with SPI, with its higher welding frequency and cumulative thermal load, is still to be taken. The temperature thresholds established in the controlled study [26] and the temperature measurements and cooling strategies quantified in the concept study [24] define the design space for this step.

\# Selective Paste Intrusion—Effect of Process\-Integrated Welding of Reinforcement Segments on Bond Strength

Author to whom correspondence should be addressed\.

\#\# Abstract

Integrating Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing \(WAAM\) into the Selective Paste Intrusion \(SPI\) process enables the fully additive fabrication of reinforced concrete structures with complex geometries\. However\, the WAAM process transfers thermal energy into the reinforcement and the surrounding concrete matrix\, which may affect the bond between steel and concrete\. This study addresses whether the heat introduced by the welding of reinforcement segments impairs the bond between reinforcing steel and SPI\-fabricated concrete\. To isolate this thermal effect from the geometric process effects covered in a companion study\, two groups of 16 mm reinforcing bars embedded in SPI\-fabricated concrete were compared\: bars whose segments were joined during printing by manual welding at seven joints per bar \(process\-integrated thermal exposure\)\, and bars with adhesively bonded segments without heat input as the reference\. Eight specimens per group from two production series were tested in push\-through\. A grey\-body estimate based on the thermography and an assumed steel emissivity of 0\.20 to 0\.30 indicates approximate bar\-surface temperatures of at least 214 to 277 °C near the joints immediately after welding and of 125 to 162 °C after 2 to 3 min\. Despite these temperatures and the repeated heating and cooling cycles during printing\, no discernible difference in bond capacity from the adhesively bonded reference group was detected\: the welded group reaches a mean maximum bond stress of 20\.5 MPa\, the adhesively bonded reference 22\.4 MPa\, and the difference of 1\.9 MPa \(9\%\) lies within the scatter of the two groups \(coefficients of variation 22\% and 21\%\)\. With a 95\% confidence interval of −7\.0 to 3\.1 MPa for this difference\, a reduction of up to 31\% cannot be excluded with this sample\. All specimens of both groups failed by bar push\-through\, with a similar slip at maximum bond stress\. Because the weld beads also change the joint geometry\, the thermal exposure cannot be fully separated from the joint geometry\. Since the procedure investigated here resembles a stud welding process rather than genuine WAAM fabrication\, the results indicate that joining reinforcement segments by stud\-welding\-like processes during printing is a feasible route for integrating reinforcement into SPI with respect to the bond under short\-term compressive loading\. For genuine WAAM\, further investigations are required\, since welding occurs far more frequently than in the present procedure because of the smaller layer heights\, so that heat accumulates and overlapping thermal cycles can produce even higher sustained temperatures at the steel–concrete interface\.

\#\# 1\. Introduction

Selective Paste Intrusion \(SPI\) is an additive manufacturing method for producing concrete elements with complex geometries\. Aggregates are sequentially spread to form a particle bed\, and cement paste is selectively applied to bind them\, while the unbound surrounding aggregates act as temporary support\, so that freeform components can be fabricated without formwork \(Figure 1\) \[1\,2\]\.

Figure 1\. Schematic representation of the combined SPI and WAAM process \(renderings\)\, modified after \[3\]\. \(a\) Printing a reinforcing bar\. \(b\) Spreading an aggregate layer\. \(c\) Applying cement paste\. \(d\) Curing the finished reinforced concrete element\. \(e\) Excavating the component\.

Strategies for integrating reinforcement into digitally fabricated concrete are the subject of ongoing research \[4\,5\]\. Combining SPI with Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing \(WAAM\) has been proposed as a strategy to produce custom\-shaped reinforcement directly within the particle bed \[6\]\. WAAM reinforcement reached upper yield strengths of 316 to 348 MPa\, tensile strengths of 454 to 481 MPa\, and uniform elongations of 14\.4 to 17\.5\% in the valid tensile tests\, and its bond performance is comparable to conventional B500B reinforcement \[7\]\. B500B denotes a characteristic yield strength

Bond between ribbed reinforcement and concrete is transferred by adhesion\, mechanical interlock of the ribs\, and friction\, which dominate successively with increasing slip \[12\,13\,14\,15\]\. Damage to the matrix around the bar\, whether thermal or from impaired material deposition\, can therefore affect both the early bond response and the bond capacity\.

A challenge of this combination is the heat generated during the WAAM process\. In WAAM\, every deposited layer reheats the material below it\, and with short interlayer times the heat accumulates over successive layers\, which raises the interlayer temperature and changes the microstructure and mechanical properties of the deposit \[16\]\. Interlayer dwell times and active or forced interpass cooling are therefore used to control this thermal history \[17\,18\]\. In a combined SPI\-WAAM process\, the accumulated heat would also act on the fresh cement paste and on the forming steel–concrete interface\. The thermal load transferred from the welding point into the reinforcement and the surrounding particle bed can alter the rheological properties of the cement paste and impair the mechanical performance of the hardened concrete\. Cement\-paste rheology is sensitive to temperature\, with changes in yield stress and plastic viscosity reported within 20 to 50 °C \[19\,20\,21\]\.

For the SPI system considered here\, the relevant thermal limits were established in a sequence of preceding studies\. The fresh\-state limit was identified by measuring how rising cement paste temperatures affect yield stress and viscosity\. A sharp transition was observed at 60 to 70 °C\, above which penetration of the cement paste into the particle bed deteriorates \[22\]\. The hardened\-state limit was established by examining the effect of fresh\-state thermal exposure on the compressive and flexural strength of the resulting concrete\, which decline at a fresh\-state temperature of 80 °C and above \[23\]\. The actual temperatures occurring during WAAM at varying distances from the welding point\, and corresponding cooling strategies\, were then quantified \[24\]\. Depending on the distance to the welding point\, the reinforcement reached temperatures of 100 to 450 °C at an interlayer cooling time of 60 s \[24\]\. Bar temperatures of 164 to 206 °C were measured by thermocouples embedded in the bar at a distance of 40 mm between measuring point and process zone \[24\]\. These temperatures exceed the identified rheological and hardened\-state thresholds\.

To reduce the thermal load on the particle bed\, one strategy is to increase the vertical distance between the welding point and the bed surface\. Print quality is unimpaired up to 40 mm\, and a first strength reduction of about 16\% sets in at 50 mm \[3\]\. This vertical protrusion of the reinforcement gives rise to shadowing effects\, a process\-induced disturbance of material deposition in the vicinity of the protruding bar\. A companion study \[25\] investigates these geometric effects systematically\, covering bar diameters of 8 mm\, 16 mm\, and 25 mm and inclination angles of 0 to 90° in 15° increments\. The present work addresses the welding of segments within the SPI process\, in which the thermal exposure and the weld bead arise from the same operation\, and leaves the geometric process effects to the companion study\.

To isolate the effect of thermal exposure on bond strength\, a controlled laboratory study was conducted prior to the present work\. Conventionally cast pull\-out specimens with WAAM\-fabricated reinforcing bars heated to 20 °C\, 60 °C\, 80 °C\, and 200 °C by means of an internal cartridge heater were tested according to RILEM RC6 \[26\]\. The results revealed a displacement\-dependent thermal effect that runs counter to the expectation of a uniform bond reduction across all slip levels\. At small slip values \(0\.001 mm and 0\.01 mm\)\, the 200 °C specimens exhibited higher bond stresses than those at 60 °C and 80 °C\, attributed to heat\-induced water evaporation at the steel–concrete interface\, which locally reduces the water\-to\-cement ratio and increases matrix stiffness\. The 200 °C specimens showed a reduction of 29\% in maximum bond stress relative to the unheated reference at 20 °C \(13\.99 versus 19\.67 MPa\)\. Complementary microstructural analyses by X\-ray diffraction \(XRD\)\, thermogravimetric analysis \(TGA\)\, and mercury intrusion porosimetry \(MIP\) confirmed partial dehydration of calcium silicate hydrate \(C\-S\-H\) phases\, an increased content of unhydrated tricalcium silicate \(C3S\)\, which indicates a locally reduced degree of hydration due to premature water loss\, and a shift of the pore size distribution towards larger radii at 200 °C \[26\]\.

These findings establish the thermal sensitivity of the bond interface under controlled conditions\. Independent evidence from cyclic thermal loading tests on reinforced concrete beams \(7\, 14\, 21\, and 28 heating and cooling cycles with peak temperatures of 100 °C\, 200 °C\, and 300 °C\) shows that lap\-splice bond strength is close to or above that of the unheated control at 100 °C and 200 °C but is reduced by up to 44\% at 300 °C\, and that the effect of the thermal cycles generally increases with their number \[27\]\. For oven\-heated specimens\, bond losses additionally increase with heating rate and target temperature \[28\]\, and depend non\-monotonically on the concrete age at exposure for ages of 3 to 28 days \[29\]\. The thermal exposure considered here\, by contrast\, acts within the first hours after intrusion\, before the interface has fully formed\. The controlled study used conventionally cast specimens with a cartridge heater to apply a defined\, uniform temperature over the bond length\. In the actual combined SPI\-WAAM process\, the thermal exposure differs in character\: it arises from the layer\-by\-layer deposition of reinforcement directly in the particle bed\, producing a transient\, spatially non\-uniform temperature field\. The cement paste surrounding the reinforcement is not conventionally cast but formed by selective intrusion into a granular packing\.

The preceding studies thus established the thermal limits of the SPI system and the sensitivity of the bond to sustained heating\, but they used defined\, uniform temperatures in conventionally cast specimens or did not include bond tests\. None of them joined reinforcement by welding within the SPI process itself\. The present study takes this step as a first\, manual approximation of WAAM\. During SPI printing\, segments of 16 mm reinforcing bars embedded vertically in the particle bed were joined by manual gas tungsten arc welding\, a stud\-welding\-like procedure that exposes the bond zone to repeated welding\-induced heating and cooling cycles\. The thermal exposure was recorded by thermography\, and the bond was determined in push\-through tests\. As the reference without heat input\, segments of the same bars were joined by an adhesive under the same printing conditions\. Segmentation is required for both groups\, since the bar can protrude above the particle bed only by a limited distance during printing without colliding with the print heads \(Section 2\.2\)\. Based on the controlled study\, the hypothesis was that the welding\-induced thermal exposure reduces the bond capacity of the welded bars relative to the adhesively bonded reference\, as observed after sustained heating to 200 °C \[26\]\. Sixteen specimens were produced in two production series\, eight welded and eight adhesively bonded\.

Two joining methods were compared\. In the welded group\, the segments were joined by gas tungsten arc welding \(GTAW\) using a power source \(REHM Invertig\.Pro digital 240DC\, Uhingen\, Germany\) with an air\-cooled torch \(R\-Tig 200\/35\) and a steel filler rod \(W3Si1 according to DIN EN ISO 636 \[34\]\) under a pure argon \(I1 according to DIN EN ISO 14175 \[35\]\) shielding gas atmosphere\. The welding was performed in direct current electrode negative \(DCEN\) polarity at a machine\-set welding current of 120 A with a filler rod diameter of 1\.0 mm\. Torch and filler rod were guided manually\, as is characteristic of manual GTAW\, so that arc duration and filler addition varied from joint to joint\. In each joining cycle\, one segment was welded onto each bar of the welded rail in the order P01 to P04 and one onto the ground bar\. Consecutive bars were welded about 1\.1 min apart\, measured between the ΔT peaks of P02 to P04 \(Section 2\.5\)\. The mean interval between the joining cycles was 17\.6 and 15\.4 min in series 1 and 2\. All welds were made by the same operator\. Prior to each welding operation\, the exposed bar end and the joint faces were cleaned to remove adhering aggregate particles\, dust\, and cement paste from the particle\-bed environment\. In the adhesively bonded group\, the segments were butt\-joined using a low\-viscosity ethyl cyanoacrylate adhesive \(Loxeal Instant Adhesive 32\, Cesano Maderno\, Italy\)\. The joint faces of this group were cleaned prior to joining in the same manner as those of the welded group\.

The reinforcing bars were fixed in the particle bed by welding them onto a holder consisting of two steel rails\. Each rail carried four bars at a spacing of approximately 180 mm along the rail\, and the two rails were mounted approximately 180 mm apart\. The rails were connected by transverse steel struts for stability\. A vertical ribbed bar \(diameter 28 mm\) was the ground connection for the welding process\. This bar was co\-printed with the specimens and segmented in the same manner as the reinforcing bars\, so that a fresh segment was always available above the bed surface for attaching the welding clamp\. Figure 2 shows the specimen geometry and the holder assembly\.

\#\#\# 2\.3\. Specimen Fabrication

The specimens were fabricated on a laboratory SPI printer with a build volume of 600 × 350 × 350 mm\. The aggregate was spread in layers of 3 mm thickness using the spreading roller of the printer\, followed by a doctor blade\. After each aggregate layer\, cement paste was selectively applied by two print heads with eight nozzles each \(nozzle diameter 1 mm\) at a print speed of 300 mm s−1 and a nozzle distance of 20 mm above the bed surface\. Assuming that the paste fills the void volume of the layer\, the paste quantity was approximately 1\.3 L m−2 of printed area per layer\. Without segment joining\, one layer took about 55 s\. The printing took place at \(20 ± 1\) °C and a relative humidity of 44 to 50\%\. For printing\, the holder was placed on the printer platform and both rails were overprinted simultaneously in the same printing sequence\, so that the welded and adhesively bonded groups received identical cement paste and aggregate conditions\.

The printing started with the first 10 mm segment protruding above the particle bed\. With each successive 3 mm layer of aggregate and cement paste\, the protrusion decreased until the upper end of the segment approached the level of the bed surface\. The printer was then paused\, and a new segment was joined to the existing bar using the respective joining method \(see Section 2\.2\)\, restoring the protrusion\. This cycle of printing and segment joining was repeated until the full bond length of 80 mm was reached\.

The setup produced a continuous block of printed concrete along each rail\, embedding all four specimens per rail in a single monolithic body\. This fabrication was performed in two production series of identical configuration\, so that eight specimens per group were obtained\. In both series\, the adhesively bonded segments were mounted on the left and the welded segments on the right rail \(Figure 3b\)\. The bar positions are designated P01 to P04 on the welded rail and P05 to P08 on the adhesively bonded rail \(Figure 3c\)\, and the series is added as a suffix\, for example P03\.2 for position P03 in series 2\. Both series used the same materials\, mix design\, and printing parameters\.

The configuration deviates from RILEM RC6 \[33\] in several respects\. Loading is applied in compression rather than tension \(Section 2\.2\)\, so that lateral expansion of the bar due to the Poisson effect increases the radial pressure at the interface instead of reducing it\. Over the full specimen height\, the bar is bonded\, without the bond\-free pre\-length of the RC6 specimen\. The concrete cover of the RC6 cube is replaced by a steel confinement ring\, whose radial stiffness exceeds that of a typical concrete cover\. Finally\, the concrete is built up layer\-wise along the bar axis rather than cast transverse to it\. The absolute bond stresses reported here therefore characterise this confined push\-through configuration\, and the two groups are compared within it\. Both groups were fabricated and tested in the identical configuration\, but the configuration can interact with the joint type\, since the entire load is transferred through the segment joints in compression \(Section 3\.4\)\. The RC6\-derived bond length\, loading rate\, and slip\-level evaluation were retained for comparability with the preceding controlled study \[26\] and with the pull\-out characterisation of WAAM reinforcement \[7\]\.

\#\#\# 2\.6\. Data Evaluation

All results are reported as group means with standard deviations \(SD\) and coefficients of variation \(CV\)\, and the individual values are listed in Appendix A \(Table A1\)\. The joining method was assigned to a complete holder rail\. The four specimens of a rail therefore share the printed block\, the curing\, and\, in the welded group\, the welding sequence of the series\, so that they are not fully independent of each other\. To quantify the uncertainty of the comparison\, the difference between the group means \(welded minus adhesively bonded\) is given with its 95\% confidence interval\, calculated with Welch’s t\-test for unequal variances\. The interval contains the differences that are compatible with the measured scatter\. If it includes zero\, no difference is detected\, and its lower bound indicates the largest reduction that the data cannot exclude\. Because the specimens of a rail share the production\, the difference between the groups is also reported separately for each series\.

\#\#\# 3\.3\. Weld Geometry\, Heat\-Affected Zone\, and Interface Microstructure

The adhesively bonded segments are the reference without heat input that can be produced under the same SPI conditions\, since segmentation is required by the process \(Section 2\.2\)\. However\, they are not an ideal unheated counterpart of the welded bar\. Each welded joint carries a weld bead that protrudes from the bar surface \(Figure 10\) and may act as an additional bearing element\, whereas the adhesively bonded butt joints are flush with the bar surface and contain a thin adhesive layer\. The joints also differ in axial stiffness and continuity\. A thermally induced bond reduction could therefore be partly offset by mechanical interlock at the weld beads\, and the comparison reflects the welding procedure as a whole\, in which the thermal exposure cannot be fully separated from the joint geometry\. For the joining of reinforcement segments by welding during printing\, this combined effect is the one that acts\, since heat input and weld bead arise from the same operation\.

Figure 10\. Close\-up of a segment joint during fabrication\, taken directly after a welding cycle\. The weld bead protrudes from the bar surface\, forming a localised geometric discontinuity\.

Three joint\-related mechanisms may influence the bond of the welded bars\. First\, the weld bead changes the bar surface at each joint and may act as a bearing element in addition to the ribs\. Second\, the heat\-affected zone may have changed the steel properties and the rib geometry close to each joint\. Because the joints were loaded in compression in the push\-through test\, such changes are more relevant for the tensile and fatigue performance of the joints than for the present bond results \(Section 3\.4\)\. Third\, the matrix at the interface close to the joints was exposed to the highest temperatures\. After sustained heating to 200 °C\, the controlled study found the changes in hydration and pore structure summarised in Section 1 \[26\]\. In the present process\, the short\, repeated exposure together with the weld beads did not lead to a discernible bond reduction \(Section 3\.1\)\.

WAAM\-fabricated reinforcement\, whose entire surface consists of successive weld beads\, achieves bond performance comparable to conventionally ribbed B500B bars \[7\]\. Bond degradation after elevated\-temperature exposure of hardening or hardened concrete has been reported in multiple independent studies \[27\,28\,29\,42\,43\,44\]\, and the controlled thermal\-exposure study with the same cement paste mixture identified a bond reduction under sustained 200 °C \[26\]\. In the present comparison\, the mean difference of 9\% is smaller than this reduction of 29\%\, which lies within the confidence interval of the difference \(Section 3\.1\)\.

\#\#\# 3\.4\. Limitations of the Push\-Through Configuration

Because of the compression loading and the steel confinement ring \(Section 2\.4\)\, the measured bond capacities refer to a confined bar under compression\. The displacement at the free bar end excludes the elastic shortening of the bar and the joints\, but a different joint stiffness may still change the distribution of slip along the bond length\. Since the segments were butt\-joined and the joints were loaded in compression\, the cut faces were pressed against each other\, so that the joined bars are expected to behave approximately like the continuous bar of a RILEM RC6 test in this respect\. The results therefore characterise the bond of the joined bars under short\-term compressive loading\.

\#\#\# 3\.5\. Transfer to WAAM

The present procedure resembles stud welding rather than genuine WAAM\. Short segments of 10 mm \(final segment 20 mm\) were joined in single welding operations\, which were separated by several printed layers\. A similar stud\-welding\-like approach is used for segmented reinforcement in the extrusion\-based AMoRC process \[10\,11\]\. Over the bond length of 80 mm\, the present bars contain seven joints\, each made once per joining cycle at intervals of 15\.4 to 17\.6 min\. A WAAM\-deposited bar with a mean layer height of 1\.25 mm \[24\] consists of 64 layers over the same length\, each a weld bead and a thermal cycle\, deposited at much shorter intervals\. In genuine WAAM\, heat therefore accumulates over successive layers \[16\]\, and the overlapping thermal cycles in a given bar cross\-section can produce higher sustained temperatures at the steel–concrete interface than in the present procedure\, of the kind shown to degrade bond under controlled heating \[26\] and under cyclic thermal loading \[27\]\. The present results thus represent the low\-exposure end of the range between single joining operations and continuous WAAM deposition\. For full WAAM integration\, active cooling strategies \[17\,18\] or a lower heat input per weld are therefore necessary\. Drawn\-arc stud welding\, which completes a joint in a sub\-second welding cycle \[45\]\, is one option for automating the segment\-joining route with a defined heat input\.

A further transfer aspect concerns joint cleanliness\. In the present study\, the joint faces were cleaned before each welding cycle\, so that contamination by particles or cement paste was largely excluded\. Moisture is a known source of diffusible hydrogen in arc welds\, shown for example for moist stick electrode coatings \[46\]\, and contamination of the weld has been shown to change its microstructure and reduce its strength\, for example in friction stir spot welds of steel \[47\]\. In an automated SPI\-WAAM process without intermediate cleaning\, this adds to the qualification requirements for the welded joints\, independently of the concrete\-side bond behaviour measured here\.

The heat input per joint depended on the manual procedure\, since arc duration and filler addition varied from joint to joint \(Section 2\.2\)\. Because the thermal exposure is the variable of interest\, this variability of the manual procedure limits the present study\. The thermography documents the resulting exposure of the bed surface \(Section 3\.2\)\.

\#\# 4\. Conclusions

This study investigated the bond behaviour between reinforcement and concrete fabricated by Selective Paste Intrusion \(SPI\) under process\-integrated thermal exposure from welding of steel segments\, with adhesively bonded segments without heat input as the reference\. Reinforcing bars with a diameter of 16 mm embedded vertically in the particle bed were tested in push\-through \(eight specimens per group from two production series\)\. Under short\-term compressive push\-through loading\, the welded bars reached a mean bond capacity close to that of the adhesively bonded reference\, for the stud\-welding\-like scenario investigated here with seven joints per bar at 10 mm spacing and approximate bar\-surface temperatures of at least 214 to 277 °C immediately after welding and 125 to 162 °C after 2 to 3 min\. The results therefore indicate that joining reinforcement segments by stud\-welding\-like processes during SPI printing is a feasible route with respect to the bond under short\-term compressive loading\. Longer segments\, within the clearance below the print heads \(Section 2\.2\)\, reduce the number of welding cycles per bond length\. For reinforcement produced by genuine Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing \(WAAM\)\, further investigations are required\, in particular regarding heat accumulation\, and questions of joint cleanliness are still to be addressed separately as a process\-engineering task\.

The welded and the adhesively bonded groups reach comparable bond capacities \(20\.5 MPa and 22\.4 MPa\)\. At 1\.9 MPa \(9\%\)\, the difference is smaller than the standard deviation of either group\, and the coefficients of variation of the two groups are 22\% and 21\%\. No discernible difference was therefore detected in this sample\, while the 95\% confidence interval of the difference \(−7\.0 to 3\.1 MPa\) shows that a reduction of up to 31\% cannot be excluded with eight specimens per group from two production series\. The scatter exceeds the range reported for pull\-out testing\. Since it is of the same size in both groups\, it more likely originates from the fabrication steps common to both groups \(SPI intrusion\, manual segmentation and joining\, core drilling\) than from the thermal exposure\, which only the welded group received\.

Bond stress values at very small slips \(s ≤ 0\.01 mm\) approach the resolution limit of the displacement measurement and show no consistent difference between the groups\. All specimens failed by bar push\-through and none by splitting\, and the slip at maximum bond stress is similar in both groups\. Because the weld beads change the joint geometry\, the thermal exposure cannot be fully separated from the joint geometry in this comparison \(Section 3\.3\)\. For the joining of segments by welding during printing\, this combined effect is the one that acts\. The results characterise the steel–concrete bond under short\-term compressive loading \(Section 3\.4\)\.

\#\# 5\. Outlook

Three steps follow from the present results\. First\, automated joining with a defined heat input per weld\, for example by stud welding\, where the process variant \(drawn\-arc versus capacitor\-discharge according to DIN EN ISO 14555 \[48\]\) governs the actual heat input\, would eliminate the variability of the manual procedure and allow the remaining scatter to be attributed to the process rather than to the preparation\. Second\, the welded joints are to be characterised for structural use\, in tension according to DIN EN ISO 17660\-1 \[49\]\, under fatigue loading\, and with respect to durability\. Measurements of the bead geometry\, hardness profiles across the joints\, and microstructural analyses of the interface zone would separate the joint\-related mechanisms discussed in Section 3\.3\. Third\, the step towards in situ WAAM deposition combined with SPI\, with its higher welding frequency and cumulative thermal load\, is still to be taken\. The temperature thresholds established in the controlled study \[26\] and the temperature measurements and cooling strategies quantified in the concept study \[24\] define the design space for this step\.

Air cooling at those currents is not practical for cable ergonomics or connector thermal management, so all production MCS implementations use liquid cooling throughout.
records.summary: This Hongjiali (HG Power) buyer-guide article compares air-cooled and liquid-cooled DC fast-charging architectures at 240 kW per gun and above, distinguishing liquid-cooled cables/connectors from liquid-cooled power modules. It argues that a ~95 mm² liquid-cooled CCS2 cable can sustain 500 A within EN 50620/IEC 62196-3 touch-temperature limits, whereas an uncooled equivalent needs 150–185 mm² copper and is roughly twice as heavy at the handle. The article states air-cooled modules typically derate above ~45 °C intake air while liquid-cooled modules hold rated power to ~50–55 °C, and that back-to-back duty above ~60% removes the recovery window air-cooled connectors rely on. It presents an illustrative 180–240 kW crossover (dropping to ~150 kW in hot climates) and a 10-year maintenance comparison of fan/filter service versus coolant/pump service. The content is vendor-authored marketing and engineering guidance, not peer-reviewed measurement; reported figures are presented as typical values without cited test data.
records.why_it_matters: For sites with high ambient temperatures or high duty cycle, the cooling choice should be specified per subsystem (cable vs module) with a written full-power ambient envelope and a continuous-load test report, rather than inferred from nameplate kW alone.

[gtranslate]
Liquid-Cooled vs Air-Cooled DC Fast Chargers: Which to Buy at 240 kW and Above
DC FAST CHARGING · COOLING COMPARISON
Liquid-Cooled vs Air-Cooled DC Fast Chargers: Which to Buy at 240 kW and Above
HG PowerAir · Hybrid · LiquidBuyer guide
Crossover
Below ~180–240 kW per gun, air-cooled is cheaper and simpler. Above it, liquid-cooled wins on cable weight, sustained power, and lifetime.
Cable Physics
A liquid-cooled 500 A CCS2 cable uses ~95 mm² copper; the air-cooled equivalent needs 150–185 mm² and is twice as heavy at the handle.
Duty Cycle
Air-cooled connectors derate after sustained high-current sessions; liquid-cooled holds rated current back-to-back at 40 °C ambient.
HG Power Lineup
Air-cooled: Genesis 40–480 kW, Aurora Split 180 kW–2.6 MW. Liquid-cooled: Glacier 160–480 kW, Deepsea 600 kW–2 MW (MCS-capable).
Direct answer: Air-cooled DC fast chargers remain the economic choice up to about 180–240 kW per gun. Above that threshold, liquid-cooled cables and modules deliver higher sustained current in a lighter handle and hold efficiency flat under back-to-back sessions. The four cost drivers are cable copper mass, connector derating under duty cycle, module thermal headroom, and 10-year maintenance mix. HG Power’s Glacier 160–480 kW and Deepsea 600 kW–2 MW cover the liquid-cooled range (Deepsea is MCS-capable); Genesis 40–480 kW and Aurora Split 180 kW–2.6 MW cover the air-cooled baseline where ambient and duty cycle allow.
1. What is a liquid-cooled DC fast charger and what exactly is cooled
A “liquid-cooled DC fast charger” refers to one or both of two independently engineered subsystems. First is the liquid-cooled charging cable and connector, where a glycol-water coolant loop runs through the cable alongside the power conductors to carry away I²R heat at the handle and the CCS2 (or NACS, GB/T) pins. Second is the liquid-cooled power module, where the rectifier stack inside the cabinet uses a coolant loop instead of forced air to pull heat from the IGBTs and inductors.
Vendors routinely conflate the two. A charger marketed as “liquid-cooled” may have liquid cables but air-cooled modules (common in 350–480 kW units) or full liquid everywhere (standard above 600 kW and in MCS platforms). The decision for a buyer is which subsystem is justified at the chosen power rating, not whether to flip a single switch.
2. The four cost drivers side-by-side
Driver | Air-cooled | Liquid-cooled | Impact at ≥240 kW
---|---|---|---
Cable copper & weight | 150–185 mm² to carry 500 A continuously; handle ~2.3–3.0 kg | ~95 mm² with coolant loop; handle ~1.3–1.8 kg | Driver experience and ergonomic compliance (EN 50620)
Sustained current under duty | Current derates after ~15–20 min continuous at 500 A, 40 °C ambient | Holds 500 A continuously; 600–1000 A possible with uprated handle | Highway hubs and depots cannot absorb mid-session derate
Module thermal headroom | Fans + heatsinks; derates above ~45 °C intake air | Coolant loop + heat exchanger; stable to ~50–55 °C ambient | Hot climates, dust ingress, 24/7 duty
10-year lifetime maintenance | Fan replacement every 3–5 years, filter cleaning quarterly | Coolant replacement every 3–5 years, pump/heat-exchanger service | Operator OPEX, SLA uptime commitments
Both approaches have scheduled maintenance; neither is maintenance-free. The decision is which failure mode and OPEX profile the operator prefers for the site’s climate and traffic.
3. Cable physics: why 95 mm² of copper outperforms 185 mm² when it is cooled
CCS2 is rated to 500 A continuous. Pushing 500 A through copper generates I²R losses proportional to resistance; resistance scales inversely with cross-sectional area. An uncooled cable at 500 A reaches handle temperatures that exceed the handle-surface limits set by EN 50620 and IEC 62196-3 (50 °C on grasped surfaces, 60 °C on other touchable surfaces during normal use) unless the copper mass is increased to 150–185 mm² — which pushes handle weight above the ergonomic one-handed-insertion threshold cited in the same standards.
Liquid cooling flips the thermodynamics: the cable’s coolant jacket actively removes heat, so the copper only needs to carry the current, not also dissipate the heat. A ~95 mm² copper conductor paired with a glycol-water loop sustains 500 A within the standard touch-temperature envelope. The uprated handles used on 1 MW+ platforms extend the same approach to 1,000 A and above when coolant flow rate is scaled, which is the mechanism MCS relies on.
For the physical connector itself, CCS2 pins carry the same current regardless of cable cooling, but the pin-contact resistance heats up under sustained load. Liquid-cooled connectors route the coolant jacket right up to the pin backshell, keeping contact resistance stable; air-cooled connectors rely on connector-to-cable thermal mass to buffer peaks and must derate under long sessions.
4. Thermal headroom: cabinet architecture that keeps efficiency flat
Inside the cabinet, a modular rectifier stack converts AC to DC. Each 30 kW or 40 kW power module has an efficiency curve (typically 95–96% at nominal load) that drops as the module heats up: a 1% efficiency loss at 480 kW is ~4.8 kW of extra heat per cabinet, which the cooling system then has to pull out — a positive feedback loop in a hot environment.
Air-cooled architectures use front-to-back fan flow through finned heatsinks, filtered to keep dust out. Operating envelope is typically –30 °C to +45 °C intake air, with linear derating above 45 °C. Liquid-cooled modules replace the airflow path with a coolant loop that terminates at an outdoor heat exchanger (dry cooler or evaporative). Operating envelope extends to +50 °C or +55 °C intake-equivalent, and modules can be stacked more densely because they do not need airflow clearance between them.
Density is the hidden second-order gain of liquid-cooled modules: a 1 MW liquid-cooled cabinet typically occupies meaningfully less floor area than an air-cooled equivalent at the same power (the exact ratio varies by vendor and module generation), which matters when leasing highway service-area footprint. For MCS and megawatt deployments the ratio widens further — see our MCS Megawatt Charging System overview for the heavy-duty economics.
5. The 240 kW crossover: when does liquid-cooled start paying off
The crossover point is not a single number — it is a function of ambient temperature, duty cycle, and session concurrency. The table below is illustrative, based on typical site profiles and public technical literature. Actual crossover should be modelled against the specific site.
Site profile | Per-gun power | Ambient 95th percentile | Daily utilisation | Recommended cooling
---|---|---|---|---
Workplace / destination | 60–120 kW | <35 °C | <30% | Air-cooled
Urban public plaza | 120–180 kW | <35 °C | 30–50% | Air-cooled
Suburban retail | 180–240 kW | 35–40 °C | 40–60% | Liquid-cable, air-module (hybrid)
Highway service area | 240–480 kW | >40 °C or <30% but 24/7 | >50% | Full liquid-cooled
Heavy-duty depot | 400 kW–2.6 MW | Any | >60%, back-to-back | Full liquid-cooled
MCS truck corridor | 1–3.75 MW | Any | Any | Full liquid-cooled (mandatory)
Hybrid configurations — liquid-cooled cable with air-cooled modules — occupy the middle band of the 240–360 kW segment where cable ergonomics dominate the buyer’s experience but the module heat load is still manageable with forced air. Hybrid configurations are available on specific HG Power higher-power air-cooled variants on request; the exact variant list is confirmed per quotation.
6. Duty cycle and ambient temperature: the two filters that override everything else
Two site conditions override the power-rating heuristic:
- Ambient 95th percentile above 40 °C — common in Middle East, South Asia, Australia, southern US. Air-cooled modules linearly derate above intake 45 °C, meaning a nameplate 480 kW cabinet may deliver 400 kW during the hottest 8 weeks of the year. Liquid-cooled modules hold rated power to intake 50–55 °C.

Filter cleaning | Quarterly (dusty sites: monthly) | None | Air-cooled: higher routine O&M labour
Coolant replacement | None | Every 3–5 years (glycol-water) | Liquid-cooled: scheduled coolant service
Pump / heat exchanger service | None | Pump 7–10 years; HX inspection annual | Liquid-cooled: higher planned-service cost per event
Cable replacement | Mechanical wear (connector pins, strain relief) | Mechanical wear + coolant leak checks | Liquid-cooled: additional leak-check protocol

Liquid\-Cooled vs Air\-Cooled DC Fast Chargers\: Which to Buy at 240 kW and Above

DC FAST CHARGING · COOLING COMPARISON

\# Liquid\-Cooled vs Air\-Cooled DC Fast Chargers\: Which to Buy at 240 kW and Above

HG PowerAir · Hybrid · LiquidBuyer guide

\#\#\#\# Crossover

Below \~180–240 kW per gun\, air\-cooled is cheaper and simpler\. Above it\, liquid\-cooled wins on cable weight\, sustained power\, and lifetime\.

\#\#\#\# Cable Physics

A liquid\-cooled 500 A CCS2 cable uses \~95 mm² copper\; the air\-cooled equivalent needs 150–185 mm² and is twice as heavy at the handle\.

\#\#\#\# Duty Cycle

Air\-cooled connectors derate after sustained high\-current sessions\; liquid\-cooled holds rated current back\-to\-back at 40 °C ambient\.

\#\#\#\# HG Power Lineup

Air\-cooled\: Genesis 40–480 kW\, Aurora Split 180 kW–2\.6 MW\. Liquid\-cooled\: Glacier 160–480 kW\, Deepsea 600 kW–2 MW \(MCS\-capable\)\.

Direct answer\: Air\-cooled DC fast chargers remain the economic choice up to about 180–240 kW per gun\. Above that threshold\, liquid\-cooled cables and modules deliver higher sustained current in a lighter handle and hold efficiency flat under back\-to\-back sessions\. The four cost drivers are cable copper mass\, connector derating under duty cycle\, module thermal headroom\, and 10\-year maintenance mix\. HG Power’s Glacier 160–480 kW and Deepsea 600 kW–2 MW cover the liquid\-cooled range \(Deepsea is MCS\-capable\)\; Genesis 40–480 kW and Aurora Split 180 kW–2\.6 MW cover the air\-cooled baseline where ambient and duty cycle allow\.

\#\# 1\. What is a liquid\-cooled DC fast charger and what exactly is cooled

A “liquid\-cooled DC fast charger” refers to one or both of two independently engineered subsystems\. First is the liquid\-cooled charging cable and connector\, where a glycol\-water coolant loop runs through the cable alongside the power conductors to carry away I²R heat at the handle and the CCS2 \(or NACS\, GB\/T\) pins\. Second is the liquid\-cooled power module\, where the rectifier stack inside the cabinet uses a coolant loop instead of forced air to pull heat from the IGBTs and inductors\.

Vendors routinely conflate the two\. A charger marketed as “liquid\-cooled” may have liquid cables but air\-cooled modules \(common in 350–480 kW units\) or full liquid everywhere \(standard above 600 kW and in MCS platforms\)\. The decision for a buyer is which subsystem is justified at the chosen power rating\, not whether to flip a single switch\.

\#\# 2\. The four cost drivers side\-by\-side

Driver \| Air\-cooled \| Liquid\-cooled \| Impact at ≥240 kW 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Cable copper \& weight \| 150–185 mm² to carry 500 A continuously\; handle \~2\.3–3\.0 kg \| \~95 mm² with coolant loop\; handle \~1\.3–1\.8 kg \| Driver experience and ergonomic compliance \(EN 50620\) 
Sustained current under duty \| Current derates after \~15–20 min continuous at 500 A\, 40 °C ambient \| Holds 500 A continuously\; 600–1000 A possible with uprated handle \| Highway hubs and depots cannot absorb mid\-session derate 
Module thermal headroom \| Fans \+ heatsinks\; derates above \~45 °C intake air \| Coolant loop \+ heat exchanger\; stable to \~50–55 °C ambient \| Hot climates\, dust ingress\, 24\/7 duty 
10\-year lifetime maintenance \| Fan replacement every 3–5 years\, filter cleaning quarterly \| Coolant replacement every 3–5 years\, pump\/heat\-exchanger service \| Operator OPEX\, SLA uptime commitments 

Both approaches have scheduled maintenance\; neither is maintenance\-free\. The decision is which failure mode and OPEX profile the operator prefers for the site’s climate and traffic\.

\#\# 3\. Cable physics\: why 95 mm² of copper outperforms 185 mm² when it is cooled

CCS2 is rated to 500 A continuous\. Pushing 500 A through copper generates I²R losses proportional to resistance\; resistance scales inversely with cross\-sectional area\. An uncooled cable at 500 A reaches handle temperatures that exceed the handle\-surface limits set by EN 50620 and IEC 62196\-3 \(50 °C on grasped surfaces\, 60 °C on other touchable surfaces during normal use\) unless the copper mass is increased to 150–185 mm² — which pushes handle weight above the ergonomic one\-handed\-insertion threshold cited in the same standards\.

Liquid cooling flips the thermodynamics\: the cable’s coolant jacket actively removes heat\, so the copper only needs to carry the current\, not also dissipate the heat\. A \~95 mm² copper conductor paired with a glycol\-water loop sustains 500 A within the standard touch\-temperature envelope\. The uprated handles used on 1 MW\+ platforms extend the same approach to 1\,000 A and above when coolant flow rate is scaled\, which is the mechanism MCS relies on\.

For the physical connector itself\, CCS2 pins carry the same current regardless of cable cooling\, but the pin\-contact resistance heats up under sustained load\. Liquid\-cooled connectors route the coolant jacket right up to the pin backshell\, keeping contact resistance stable\; air\-cooled connectors rely on connector\-to\-cable thermal mass to buffer peaks and must derate under long sessions\.

\#\# 4\. Thermal headroom\: cabinet architecture that keeps efficiency flat

Inside the cabinet\, a modular rectifier stack converts AC to DC\. Each 30 kW or 40 kW power module has an efficiency curve \(typically 95–96\% at nominal load\) that drops as the module heats up\: a 1\% efficiency loss at 480 kW is \~4\.8 kW of extra heat per cabinet\, which the cooling system then has to pull out — a positive feedback loop in a hot environment\.

Air\-cooled architectures use front\-to\-back fan flow through finned heatsinks\, filtered to keep dust out\. Operating envelope is typically –30 °C to \+45 °C intake air\, with linear derating above 45 °C\. Liquid\-cooled modules replace the airflow path with a coolant loop that terminates at an outdoor heat exchanger \(dry cooler or evaporative\)\. Operating envelope extends to \+50 °C or \+55 °C intake\-equivalent\, and modules can be stacked more densely because they do not need airflow clearance between them\.

Density is the hidden second\-order gain of liquid\-cooled modules\: a 1 MW liquid\-cooled cabinet typically occupies meaningfully less floor area than an air\-cooled equivalent at the same power \(the exact ratio varies by vendor and module generation\)\, which matters when leasing highway service\-area footprint\. For MCS and megawatt deployments the ratio widens further — see our MCS Megawatt Charging System overview for the heavy\-duty economics\.

\#\# 5\. The 240 kW crossover\: when does liquid\-cooled start paying off

The crossover point is not a single number — it is a function of ambient temperature\, duty cycle\, and session concurrency\. The table below is illustrative\, based on typical site profiles and public technical literature\. Actual crossover should be modelled against the specific site\.

Site profile \| Per\-gun power \| Ambient 95th percentile \| Daily utilisation \| Recommended cooling 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Workplace \/ destination \| 60–120 kW \| \<35 °C \| \<30\% \| Air\-cooled 
Urban public plaza \| 120–180 kW \| \<35 °C \| 30–50\% \| Air\-cooled 
Suburban retail \| 180–240 kW \| 35–40 °C \| 40–60\% \| Liquid\-cable\, air\-module \(hybrid\) 
Highway service area \| 240–480 kW \| \>40 °C or \<30\% but 24\/7 \| \>50\% \| Full liquid\-cooled 
Heavy\-duty depot \| 400 kW–2\.6 MW \| Any \| \>60\%\, back\-to\-back \| Full liquid\-cooled 
MCS truck corridor \| 1–3\.75 MW \| Any \| Any \| Full liquid\-cooled \(mandatory\) 

Hybrid configurations — liquid\-cooled cable with air\-cooled modules — occupy the middle band of the 240–360 kW segment where cable ergonomics dominate the buyer’s experience but the module heat load is still manageable with forced air\. Hybrid configurations are available on specific HG Power higher\-power air\-cooled variants on request\; the exact variant list is confirmed per quotation\.

Event \| Air\-cooled frequency \| Liquid\-cooled frequency \| Operator impact
