2.4 Trends in materials
There has been two major trends in how polymers have developed within AM, with regards to the two types of material that are now available for 3D printing; these include both; (1) the diversity of feedstock materials to print with, and (2) the enhancement of final use performance. For example, commodity polymers (e.g. PLA, ABS, PETG) were initially used in prototyping applications for their low cost and printability, but are still being used in educational settings. In contrast, engineering polymers (e.g. PC, Nylon, PEI, PEEK) are now providing a level of structural and thermal performance that is adequate for aerospace, medical, and automotive applications. Figure 3 shows multiple examples from literature between 2018 and 2024 that illustrate the movement from prototyping to functional part production, due to improved mechanical robustness, thermal stability, and material modification techniques.
The recent literature shows an increase in the development of composite and reinforced polymer systems, such as carbon fiber-reinforced PEEK, conductive polymers, and elastomeric blends. This expanding range of materials will enable the development of flexible electronics, wearable technology, and high-temperature components. However, this trend toward more diverse materials has also increased the potential for new defect mechanisms associated with anisotropic properties, shrinkage, warping, and layer-to-layer adhesion, reiterating the need for a data-driven approach to defect detection. Therefore, the reviewed literature illustrates that the areas of materials development and sensing/monitoring of performance are increasingly becoming intertwined as polymer systems move toward their performance-critical applications.

Defect detection in 3D printing has evolved significantly from manual inspection to sophisticated machine learning techniques. Early methods as shown in the Fig. were limited by human error and lacked scalability, but machine vision and AI now provide more efficient solutions. Paraskevoudis et al. 3.1 Data-driven advances in additive manufacturing: trends in materials and techniques
The integration of data science and additive manufacturing has produced profound advances in materials, manufacturing processes, and real-time quality assurance. Through the integration of high-end sensors and monitoring systems, data-driven methods in additive manufacturing are improving defect detection, process parameter optimization, and material behavior prediction. For example, machine learning methods facilitate the analysis of large datasets obtained from in-process monitoring to enable real-time adjustments that avoid defects and product inconsistencies. This has been highly useful in sectors that need high-quality and precision, which allows for the production of parts with specially designed mechanical, thermal, or electrical characteristics for precise applications. Moreover, the capacity to simulate material performance via data analysis prior to production has greatly minimized trial-and-error processes, thereby saving time and resources.
Future evolution of additive manufacturing is built on continued integration of data-driven solutions, which promise to deliver full automation in every stage, from design to production. These developments are predicted to redefine the limits of additive manufacturing, allowing manufacturers to produce highly detailed parts with unmatched precision, while at the same time cutting costs and minimizing material waste common in most industries, including aerospace and medicine.
The field of material development has also seen a transformation of revolutionary proportions with the use of data-driven solutions. New materials such as composites, functionally graded materials, and multi-material printing are designed with improved precision to tune their properties [70,71,72,73].
3.2 Machine learning techniques and their applications in polymer additive manufacturing
Machine learning (ML) techniques used in polymer additive manufacturing (AM) can be divided into two: model complexity and data supervision.
Data Supervision: Supervised learning uses data characterized by having labels: each piece of input data has a specific outcome associated with it, which is known with conviction. The two main purposes for which this method is often applied are forecasting a continuous value, called regression, and sorting data into distinct groups, called classification. For instance, by looking at the data you already possess about the properties and behaviors of printed polymers, it is possible to use supervised learning models to ascertain the strength or flexibility of printed polymers.
Unsupervised Learning: These models work on unlabeled data to identify patterns or structures in the data without defined outcomes. Common tasks are clustering, where data points are classified as similar, and dimensionality reduction, which compresses data while preserving important information. This is useful for identifying hidden patterns in polymer properties or process parameter optimization without defined labels.
Semi-Supervised Learning: This method takes both supervised and unsupervised learning characteristics. It begins with some labelled data and a vast quantity of unlabeled data. Semi-supervised models learn from both data iteratively, frequently used when it is expensive or impossible to get labeled data. Active learning (in which the model asks for labels on the most informative points) and self-training (in which the model labels itself) are examples of this category and the Pictorial representation is given as Fig. 8.
3.2.1 Supervised learning
Machine learning, particularly in Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) and, on a broader scope, in Powder Bed Fusion (PBF), has progressed rapidly in AM. They have extensively studied how supervised machine-learning models can be integrated for real-time monitoring, optimization of processes, and defect detection. Magolon et al. [67] reviewed the supervised machine-learning approaches to detect defects in Laser-Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF) whereby they also discussed optimization algorithms for settings that achieve quality in separate works. Then in 2024, Rojek et al. examined AI models for fault detection and process automation in AM, with specific emphasis on the possibilities of FDM for rapid prototyping. Agron et al. [69] developed a machine-learning method for monitoring FDM printers based on avoiding issues with nozzles and predicting printing trouble. In 2023, Enslin conducted study work on how interpretable machine learning can inform better understanding of FDM process parameters for quality improvement by real-time adjustment. These studies emphasized that supervised learning is an increasing trend to establish more reliability into AM processes and efficiency-wise. It further highlights the consequential contributions of machine learning in developing and optimizing manufacturing technologies.
3.2.2 Unsupervised learning
Unsupervised machine learning methods continue to be embraced in recent times for process monitoring and quality control for AM. In 2023, Alatefi et al. introduced a framework in which multivariate statistical quality monitoring is used in the Fused Filament Fabrication (FFF) process; they pointed out that having multiple inter-related quality factors to assess the consistency of AM processes must be taken into account [74]. Meanwhile, work from the Baumgartl team in 2022 used unsupervised learning to detect defects. They underscore the possible merits of combining image analysis with machine learning to automatically identify defects during the production process [75]. In 2021, Narayana and his team looked into AI-supported methods, including unsupervised learning, for giving consideration to opportunities and challenges in the manufacturing sector. Their findings demonstrated significant potential for improving operational efficiency [76]. Collectively, these studies underscore the growing role of unsupervised learning in addressing key challenges in additive manufacturing.
3.2.3 Semi-supervised learning
Newer technologies in additive manufacturing (AM) apply semi-supervised learning methods to improve the detection of defects and quality control. For example, semi-supervised deep learning was demonstrated in one study to automatically check the quality of AM using both labeled and unlabeled data, thereby increasing the accuracy of AM checks. Grierson and colleagues [75] reviewed different machine learning methodologies, including semi-supervised methods, and emphasized how these approaches address problems stemming from limited availability of labeled data in AM. Furthermore, research exploring deep learning for laser additive manufacturing defect detection has also shown that semi-supervised techniques can exploit small amounts of labeled data to identify defects more efficiently. Such findings underscore the pivotal role that semi-supervised learning plays in the optimization and reliability of AM processes.
3.2.4 Deep learning models
Indeed, owing to recent advances in additive manufacturing (AM), deep learning models have become critical components in the improvement of various aspects of the manufacturing process. A comprehensive review of the 2023 literature by Peles and colleagues demonstrated how deep learning helped resolve some key problems related to understanding the quality of components in AM due to difference in process settings. This also introduced a very different method of investigating the structure of 3D-printed parts, using a technology called conditional Generative Adversarial Network (GAN). This method simulates the use of GANs to quickly predict shape and detect defects from images. Besides, progress has been made in the study of real-time quality tests with point cloud data, which makes us realize that deep learning will automatically capture defects in AM. All these things bring together a paradigm change in using deep learning in increasing the reliability, effectiveness, and quality control of AM processes [76, 77].
3.3 Model complexity
Shallow Models: Shallow models have less complicated architectures and include parametric and non-parametric approaches. Parametric models like linear regression and logistic regression have strong assumptions about the input-output relationship and can be applied to simpler problems with well-defined relationships. Non-parametric models like decision trees and k-nearest neighbors have no fixed structure and can learn from data more flexibly. Shallow models are generally applied to structured data and can be applied to classification and regression.
Deep Learning Models: They have complex architectures and are able to learn complex patterns from data. Deep learning includes: Multilayer Perceptron’s (MLPs): Fully connected networks suitable for structured and unstructured data, and are used for regression and classification operations.
tRecurrent Neural Networks (RNNs): Specifically designed for sequential data, RNNs possess a “memory” of previous inputs and are therefore most suitable for time-series forecasting. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, a type of RNN, are employed for learning long-term dependencies.
Convolution Neural Networks (CNNs): For spatial pattern data, i.e., images. CNNs utilize convolution layers to detect local patterns and are well-suited for tasks like image recognition and defect inspection in AM.

Additive manufacturing represents a new technology that produces complex shapes with very little waste. Although it can offer a lot of advantages, there are still many technical challenges. For example, manipulating many process parameters to get the right quality of the part, accommodating flexible design options, and dealing with defects have their challenges. With polymers and polymer composites, batch differences and small variations in processing and environmental conditions add to the increased complexity. Machine learning (ML) is the application that has a new technology for enclosing all these concerns and reducing the costs of experimentation and computation in a novel way. This review details a few recent advancements in polymer AM by ML, discusses the obstacles faced, presents solutions to them, and identifies potential areas of future study.
4.1 Machine learning for polymer additive manufacturing
Machine learning is changing the game in polymer additive manufacturing, a type of 3D printing. It brings improvements to the managing of process settings, material quality, and fault detection in a production environment. Neural networks and decision trees are increasingly becoming the most favorite tools of prediction on outcomes, ranging from surface smoothness and material strength to shape changes during printing. With such level of prediction accuracy, materials and processes can be fine-tuned to meet the specific application, for example, in airplanes or medical tools. Analyzing images enables the detection of impending problems layer-wise, leading to better efficiencies in production with less waste. Therefore, having evolved, this manufacturing method now requires machine learning to provide better accuracy, consistency, and material quality.
4.1.1 Machine learning for fused deposition modeling
Recent studies highlight the role of machine learning (ML) in improving Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM). In 2023, researchers Huang and others developed ML models to predict the surface smoothness of PLA prints. This helps enhance print quality by selecting the right settings. They also introduced a method using Description Logic (DL) ontology to optimize how parts are oriented in FDM. DL ontology allows for describing, representing, and reusing information about part placement, which traditionally depended on expert knowledge. The method includes steps for creating different part orientations, predicting values for different factors, and choosing the best orientation. This was tested using six different FDM parts. The results show that this method enhances the efficiency and effectiveness of part orientation, supporting automatic checking, reasoning, and further reuse of FDM data.
4.1.2 Machine learning for powder bed fusion and SLS
In the field of Powder Bed Fusion (PBF), significant research efforts have been directed towards enhanc- ing material selection, quality control, and discrete outcome prediction using various machine learning techniques. However, there is a noticeable gap in research specifically focused on in situ process parameter optimization and defect classification. Although some studies have explored in situ monitoring techniques such as CNN models for detecting defects in powder bed samples and thermal recordings, comprehensive approaches that dynamically adjust process parameters in real-time to prevent defects are still underdeveloped. The lack of advanced, data-driven methodologies for optimizing process parameters during the printing process limits the full potential of PBF technologies. Addressing this gap could significantly enhance the overall reliability, efficiency, and quality of additive manufacturing, paving the way for smarter, more adaptive manufacturing systems Table 3.
Powder Bed Fusion (PBF) is a widely used additive manufacturing technique that has revolutionized the production of complex, high-precision parts across various industries. Despite its advantages, PBF is highly sensitive to process parameters such as laser power, scan speed, and layer thickness, which significantly influence the final part quality. Defects such as porosity, warping, and surface irregularities can arise due to suboptimal process conditions, leading to reduced mechanical properties and part reliability. Traditional quality control methods often involve post-process inspections, which are time-consuming, costly, and incapable of detecting internal defects or adjusting process parameters in real-time. To address these challenges, there is an emerging need for advanced in situ process parameter optimization and real-time defect classification techniques. These approaches leverage real-time data acquisition and machine learning models to monitor the printing process, detect defects as they occur, and dynamically adjust process parameters to prevent further issues. By integrating sensor data such as thermal imaging, surface roughness Through direct measurements and acoustic signals, in situ monitoring systems can allow for immediate feedback and actions during the building process. However, recent studies have focused less on optimization of process parameters and more on defect detection. The development of true data-driven, adaptive manufacturing systems with instantaneous decision-making capabilities holds the key to genuinely transforming PBF into a highly reliable, efficient, and high-quality means to manufacture 3D-printed parts. This will actually require interdisciplinary collaboration in which advanced analytical modeling can combine with machine learning and real-time sensor integration to develop smart systems that detect defects and optimize the printing conditions in real time. Bowoto and co-authors talk about fresh technique of detecting some flaws in 3D printed components during printing. The technique applies specifically to a kind of 3D printing known as Powder Bed Fusion (PBF). Using a combination of sensor data including thermal images and measurements of surface roughness, they detect microscopic holes and surface imperfections while printing the layers themselves. It, therefore, makes immediate correction of errors possible, instead of waiting for the component to finish printing before correcting it. Computer simulation and real-world testing all demonstrated this very fact as they tested the model, which is that it very much improves the quality of the printed components by early identification of defects. The authors stress that this monitoring system increases reliability and efficiency in 3D printing. Active quality control system through live monitoring, overcomes the passive flaw detection at the end of the printing process.

In this stop, the printer head moves away from the printed object-the platform holding the object goes back to its original position. Once the analysis is complete, the printing process resumes, ensuring quality control at each step of the production.
4.2 Real-time defect detection
Recent developments in real-time defect detection in Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) 3D printing have employed machine learning methods to improve accuracy and operational effectiveness. Kadam [98] emphasizes the potential of real-time monitoring in enhancing additive manufacturing deficiencies through the utilization of machine learning for real-time defect detection, thereby reducing wastage of materials. Paraskevoudis [99] emphasizes the application of deep convolutional neural networks to identify particular defects, like “stringing,” through real-time video inspection, enabling prompt remedial measures. Likewise, Kozhaya [100] employs convolutional neural networks to identify faults like layer misalignment and over-extrusion, emphasizing the capability of the model in conducting real-time quality checks. Together, these works illustrate the potential of AI-driven defect detection to advance 3D printing quality and efficiency in industrial applications.
Future research can focus on improving real-time monitoring systems in additive manufacturing by developing advanced machine learning models that provide immediate feedback and optimize process parameters dynamically during production. The Fig. 12 highlights and is showing the trend line of real time defect detection from published articles till date.
4.3 In-situ process optimization
The application of adaptive algorithms for in-situ optimization of process parameters is under explored. This research area could lead to smarter, self-correcting systems that reduce the occurrence of defects and improve part quality in real-time.
Recent research on optimizing Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) for printing polylactic acid (PLA) components highlights diverse strategies to improve material properties and manufacturing efficiency. Raju et al. [101] explored the effect of in-situ carbon nanoparticles on the structural properties of PLA using the Taguchi technique to optimize parameters like layer thickness, fill density, and speed, resulting in improved hardness and impact resistance. Singh et al. [102] conducted a multi-objective optimization using Grey Relational Analysis (GRA), focusing on surface roughness, printing time, and filament usage. They identified an optimal setup involving a triangular infill pattern with 70% infill, a printing speed of 100 mm/h, and a layer thickness of 0.2 mm, achieving a 10% performance improvement. Finally, Patil et al. [103] investigated the influence of process parameters on PLA using the Design of Experiments (DoE) method and concluded that layer thickness and infill pattern significantly affect the dimensional accuracy and surface finish of printed components the intensity of defects as evidenced in recent literatures is illustrated through a heat map Fig. 13, is generated by considering over 250 journal articles in area of FDM from 2021 till date. It is also observed that the intensity of warping and the dimensional accuracy are severe to be addressed in further studies. These studies underscore the importance of parameter optimization in achieving desired material characteristics and manufacturing efficiency in FDM.
4.4 Multi material additive manufacturing
In the realm of multi-material additive manufacturing, researchers have made significant advances, lever- aging various materials and techniques to optimize performance in fields ranging from automotive to aerospace. Singh et al. explored the integration of ABS, PLA, and HIPS thermoplastics, assessing their mechanical and thermal properties for structural applications, underscoring FDM as a versatile platform for multi-material 3D printing [21]. Yadav et al. examined FDM process parameters with a hybrid GA-ANN approach to enhance tensile strength in multi-material components, highlighting the potential of ANN-based optimization for achieving high-performance structures [104]. Hasanov et al. reviewed the progress and challenges in additive manufacturing for multi-material parts, including issues with material compatibility and interface strength, emphasizing the need for further advancements to fully realize the potential of MMAM [105]. These studies collectively demonstrate the diverse methods and innovations that are shaping the future of multi-material additive manufacturing, with a focus on optimizing material interfaces, enhancing mechanical properties, and expanding application possibilities [106]. There is growing interest in incorporating multiple materials, such as metals, polymers, and smart materials, within a single manufacturing process. Exploring the compatibility of different materials and optimizing processes for their combined use remains a promising research direction.
These research areas offer the potential to advance additive manufacturing, pushing the boundaries of efficiency, material diversity, and system intelligence.
Table 4 provides a comparative overview of widely used machine learning methods applied in polymer additive manufacturing defect detection. It highlights the type of sensor data each model relies on, the typical dataset sizes reported in literature, and key performance metrics achieved. The summary demonstrates how different ML approaches specialize in identifying specific defect types, enabling more accurate and reliable real-time quality monitoring.
Several citations in the original manuscript were identified as secondary, non-academic, or not directly relevant to polymer AM defect detection. In the revised version, these references—such as ASTM terminology summaries, general AM history sources, news articles (e.g., The Economist), community websites, and early foundational AM overviews—have been removed or replaced with peer-reviewed and technically relevant literature. Only citations directly supporting discussions on polymer AM processes, defect mechanisms, sensing technologies, machine learning methods, and data-driven quality monitoring have been retained. Where historical context is no longer essential to the paper’s revised scope, corresponding references have also been eliminated to maintain scientific rigor and citation relevance. The manuscript now cites recent and domain-specific research (2016–2024) that contributes directly to understanding defect detection in polymer AM.
While several prior reviews have examined aspects of defect detection or monitoring in additive manufacturing, the existing literature remains fragmented, particularly for polymer-based processes. Paraskevoudis (2020) focused primarily on vision-based inspection methods without integrating thermal, acoustic, or process-sensor modalities. Khanzadeh (2020) emphasized predictive analytics for AM quality but did not link defect mechanisms to specific sensing strategies or discuss polymer-specific defect behavior. Magolon (2021) provided a broad overview of AM data analytics but did not propose a structured framework connecting data acquisition, feature extraction, machine learning model selection, and real-time quality decision-making. In contrast, the present review synthesizes these dimensions into a unified, data-driven conceptual framework specifically tailored for polymer AM, integrating defect mechanisms, multi-sensor monitoring, machine learning models, and closed-loop feedback considerations. This focused and structured integration—absent in prior reviews—constitutes the key novelty of this work and provides a clearer roadmap for advancing intelligent defect detection in polymer additive manufacturing.
Recent reviews have explored the integration of big data analytics, machine learning, and digital twin technologies in additive manufacturing, emphasizing their potential for virtual process replication, predictive modeling, and intelligent quality management. However, these studies generally adopt a broad, technology-centric perspective and do not provide a defect-specific or polymer-focused framework. Existing digital twin reviews tend to describe high-level architectures—such as cyber-physical synchronization, cloud-based data pipelines, and simulation–data fusion—but offer limited guidance on how individual defect mechanisms, sensor modalities, or machine learning models should be selected and connected within a practical monitoring workflow. In contrast, the framework proposed in this study is explicitly tailored to polymer AM defect detection, detailing how process-linked defects (e.g., warping, under-extrusion, layer separation) correspond to sensor data characteristics and which ML approaches are most appropriate for real-time detection. Unlike previous big-data and digital-twin reviews, our framework moves beyond conceptual architectures by mapping defects → sensing → feature extraction → ML model → decision support, thereby providing a more operational and application-focused structure. This comparison highlights that while digital twin literature offers valuable system-level insights, the present review uniquely contributes a defect-oriented, polymer-specific, and implementable data-driven framework not previously articulated.
5 Conclusion and future scope
Additive manufacturing (AM) has matured substantially; several critical gaps remain in the development of reliable, real-time defect detection for polymer-based processes. First, while traditional sensing techniques such as vibration analysis and acoustic emissions provide useful information, they suffer from high noise sensitivity and require extensive preprocessing. Future research should focus on developing standardized, noise-robust signal processing pipelines and benchmark datasets to enable fair comparison across studies—an issue consistently highlighted in the literature.
The rapid adoption of machine learning and AI, current implementations often rely on small, proprietary, or single-modality datasets. This limits model generalizability. Therefore, future work should advance multi-sensor data fusion frameworks that combine optical, thermal, acoustic, and machine log data, and validate them on large, open-access, polymer-AM-specific datasets. Such efforts would fill the gap in unified sensing protocols identified in this review.
Digital twin concepts have been explored at a high level, their integration into polymer AM defect detection remains limited. Existing digital twin models rarely incorporate defect mechanisms, sensor behavior, and machine learning predictions in a closed-loop manner. Future research should prioritize physics-informed and data-driven digital twins capable of real-time synchronization with the printing process, enabling predictive correction of warping, under-extrusion, and layer separation before defects propagate.
Finally, current AM systems lack autonomous decision-making. Machine learning predictions are rarely connected to active process adjustments. The field would benefit from research into adaptive control systems that transform detection algorithms into actionable control strategies, such as dynamic parameter tuning or automated re-slicing. These developments would directly address the gap between defect identification and defect mitigation, moving polymer AM toward fully autonomous, self-correcting manufacturing systems.

\# Data driven framework for defect detection in polymer additive manufacturing

\- Review
\- Open access
\- Published\:

\- Volume 5\, article number 205 \(2026\)
\- Cite this article

\#\# Abstract

Although additive manufacturing \(AM\) has enabled the production of intricate and customized polymer components\, ensuring part quality and consistency remains a major challenge\. Traditional defect detection methods rely on isolated sensing approaches and lack the ability to operate adaptively in real time\. While several studies apply machine learning \(ML\) or sensor\-based monitoring\, the existing literature remains fragmented\, with no unified framework that connects defect mechanisms\, data acquisition strategies\, ML model selection\, and feedback\-based process control\. The novelty of this study lies in proposing a structured\, data\-driven conceptual framework specifically tailored for defect detection in polymer AM\. This framework synthesizes insights from sensor fusion\, signal processing\, and machine learning into a coherent\, step\-by\-step structure that has not been formalized in prior reviews\. In addition\, the paper critically evaluates existing detection methods\, identifies unresolved gaps across sensing\, data pipelines\, and model robustness\, and outlines research opportunities such as multi\-sensor integration\, digital\-twin\-enabled monitoring\, and real\-time adaptive control\. By positioning defect detection as a closed\-loop data\-driven system\, this work provides a clear roadmap for progressing polymer AM toward more autonomous and reliable manufacturing\.

\#\#\# Graphical Abstract

\#\#\# Similar content being viewed by others

\#\# 1 Introduction

Polymer\-based additive manufacturing \(AM\) has become a widely adopted fabrication method for producing lightweight\, customized\, and geometrically complex components across engineering\, biomedical\, and consumer domains\. However\, despite its advantages\, achieving consistent part quality remains a significant challenge\. Polymer AM processes—particularly fused deposition modelling \(FDM\)\, stereolithography \(SLA\)\, selective laser sintering \(SLS\)\, and related variants—are sensitive to variations in material behavior\, thermal gradients\, environmental conditions\, and machine settings\. These variations often lead to common defects such as warping\, under\-extrusion\, dimensional inaccuracy\, incomplete fusion\, and surface inconsistencies\. Traditional quality assurance methods in AM rely heavily on manual inspection\, post\-processing measurements\, and operator experience\, making them slow\, subjective\, and unsuitable for real\-time intervention\. The increasing availability of sensors\, machine vision\, and in\-situ monitoring technologies has created an opportunity for data\-driven approaches to enhance defect detection\, predict failures earlier\, and support automated corrective actions\. Machine learning \(ML\) techniques—especially those using thermal imaging\, acoustic signatures\, layer\-wise optical data\, or extrusion dynamics—have demonstrated strong potential to detect anomalies\, classify defect types\, and evaluate process stability more reliably than conventional inspection methods\. Despite significant progress\, the literature remains fragmented\. Existing studies often address isolated aspects such as polymer material behavior\, defect mechanisms\, individual sensing methods\, or ML classifiers\, but lack a unified data\-driven framework that connects these elements into an integrated defect detection pipeline tailored specifically for polymer AM\. Furthermore\, polymer processes exhibit different defect mechanisms compared to metals\, yet many existing reviews generalize across materials without providing polymer\-specific insights\. This article contributes by\: Providing a focused review of defect types\, sensing modalities\, monitoring strategies\, and ML techniques specifically relevant to polymer AM\. Synthesizing these insights into a structured\, data\-driven conceptual framework for defect detection\, covering data acquisition\, feature extraction\, model development\, and real\-time decision support\. Identifying research gaps related to sensor fusion\, real\-time feedback control\, benchmark datasets\, and robustness across materials and printers\. Positioning defect detection as a closed\-loop intelligence problem\, enabling future developments toward autonomous\, self\-correcting polymer AM systems \[1\,2\,3\,4\,5\,6\,7\]\.

Figure 1 summarizes the evolution of monitoring and decision\-making capabilities in AM\, illustrating the shift from empirical and simulation\-based approaches to modern data\-driven analytics that can support real\-time quality assurance\.

\#\#\# 1\.1 Materials used in polymer additive manufacturing

Materials used in AM have diversified significantly\, but polymers remain the most widely adopted due to their cost\-effectiveness\, ease of processing\, and suitability for prototyping and functional applications\. Commonly used polymers include PLA\, ABS\, PETG\, Nylon\, and high\-performance materials such as PEEK and PEI\. Each material exhibits distinct thermal\, rheological\, and mechanical characteristics that influence defect formation\, interlayer bonding\, and surface quality\. While metals\, ceramics\, and composites play important roles in broader AM research\, this review focuses specifically on polymers because their defect mechanisms—such as shrinkage\-driven warping\, extrusion variability\, and anisotropic bonding—differ substantially from metal AM\. Understanding these polymer\-specific properties is essential for developing accurate prediction and detection models\. Figure 2 illustrates the increasing research activity in polymer AM materials\, reflecting growing interest in improving process reliability\, mechanical performance\, and defect monitoring strategies \[8\,9\,10\,11\,12\,13\]\.

Recent research in additive manufacturing \(AM\) over the past eight years has increasingly emphasized reliability\, real\-time monitoring\, and data\-driven quality assurance—particularly in polymer\-based processes\. Several influential studies between 2016 and 2024 have highlighted the need for improved defect detection strategies and integrated sensing approaches\. Ngo et al\. \[14\] provided a comprehensive overview of AM materials and processes\, underscoring the challenges related to process variability and the need for in\-situ monitoring systems to ensure part consistency\. Baumann and Roller \[15\] discussed the emergence of cloud\-connected AM systems and the importance of process data collection for predictive quality control\. Dilberoglu et al\. \[16\] examined AM within Industry 4\.0 frameworks\, emphasizing the role of cyber\-physical systems and smart sensors in achieving stable production\. More recent studies have directly targeted defect detection and data\-driven monitoring\. Horst et al\. \[17\] and Kumar et al\. \[18\] highlighted how sensor fusion and machine learning can be combined for real\-time anomaly identification in polymer AM\. Chang et al\. \[19\] and Mittal et al\. \[20\] discussed advancements in material\-specific process optimization and adaptive control strategies\. Singh et al\. \[21\] and Gobena and Woldeyohannes \[22\] explored the integration of advanced materials\, functional polymers\, and smart sensing technologies to enhance structural integrity and reduce defect occurrence\. Across these developments\, the literature consistently points to a research gap\: although sensors and machine learning tools are widely explored\, there is no unified framework that connects defect mechanisms\, sensing strategies\, data processing pipelines\, and machine learning model selection for polymer AM\. Addressing this gap is essential for progressing toward autonomous\, closed\-loop defect mitigation systems \[23\,24\,25\,26\,27\,28\,29\,30\]\.

\#\#\# 1\.2 Trends for material use in additive manufacturing

The radar chart in Fig\. 3 is a comparative study of different materials in additive manufacturing \(AM\) on four axes\: benefits\, uses\, current trends\, and limitations\. Composites are outstanding in their versatility\, reflecting outstanding performance across different applications based on their ability to excel in a wide range of fields\. Metals confer gigantic strengths in terms of strength and durability\; however\, they are also associated with gigantic limitations\, such as high costs and complex processing requirements\. Smart materials are the epitome of current trends\, with distinctive features to match the innovative nature of contemporary technology\. While biomaterials are characterized by the lowest limitations\, their uses are comparatively narrower compared to other types of materials\. The positioning of ceramic\-metal composites\, polymers\, and ceramics on the radar chart reflects a variety of strengths and weaknesses\.

To understand the material properties and potential applications with regards to the materials used in additive manufacturing \(AM\) methods\, the review by Kumar et al\. \(2021\) is very useful \[18\]\. The article explains several AM methods\, the materials used\, and the respective applications in industries\, presenting a clear overview of the mechanical properties of components manufactured using different AM methods\. The authors indicate the benefits of AM technologies\, such as the ability to personalize\, freedom to design\, minimization of waste\, and the ability to generate complex geometries\. Moreover\, the review by Gobena and Woldeyohannes \(2024\) explains the development of AM technologies\, such as rapid prototyping and 3D printing\, which have greatly revolutionized traditional manufacturing methods \[22\]\. The paper discusses the transition from rapid prototyping to AM and highlights its role in creating fully customized products\, optimizing topologies\, and fabricating complex designs\, especially in industries such as aerospace\, medical\, automotive\, defense\, energy\, and food\.

\#\#\# 1\.3 Brief introduction on techniques used in additive manufacturing

3D printing\, or additive manufacturing \(AM\)\, has advanced significantly in recent years\, particularly in the development of polymer\-based printing techniques\. As shown in Fig\. 4\, several studies published between 2018 and 2023 highlight technological improvements across major polymer AM processes\. In 2018\, Smith et al\. examined enhancements in Fused Deposition Modelling \(FDM\)\, reporting increased material availability\, improved print accuracy\, and faster deposition rates that have enabled FDM to transition from basic prototyping to the production of functional end\-use components \[31\]\. Around the same period\, Brown and colleagues investigated advances in Stereolithography \(SLA\)\, demonstrating how newer photopolymer resins and refined curing mechanisms have contributed to higher precision\, smoother surfaces\, and reduced post\-processing requirements \[32\]\. Further developments were noted by Lee et al\. \[33\]\, who analyzed Selective Laser Sintering \(SLS\) for polymer powders and highlighted its capability to fabricate complex geometries with enhanced mechanical performance while benefiting from ongoing innovations in polymer powder formulations \[34\]\. Patel et al\. \[35\] explored the progress of Digital Light Processing \(DLP\) in fabricating intricate polymer microstructures\, emphasizing improved resolution\, faster layer curing\, and the broadened use of high\-performance photopolymer materials \[35\,36\,37\]\. Other notable contributions include Wang et al\. \(2020\)\, who reviewed advancements in Direct Ink Writing \(DIW\) for polymer and composite inks\, showing its versatility in printing conductive inks\, elastomers\, and bio\-compatible materials for applications ranging from flexible electronics to biomedical scaffolds \[38\]\. Martin et al\. \(2021\) discussed improvements in Multi Jet Fusion \(MJF\) that have resulted in higher production throughput and more uniform mechanical properties in printed polymer parts \[39\]\. Nguyen et al\. \(2021\) highlighted the growth of Robocasting for polymer\-derived ceramics and functional polymer pastes\, demonstrating its ability to produce precise\, complex structures using controlled extrusion pathways \[40\]\. More recently\, Miller et al\. \(2023\) presented an extensive review of Vat Photopolymerization technologies\, showing how innovations in resin chemistry and exposure control have achieved exceptional print resolution and enhanced thermal and mechanical properties for advanced polymer applications \[41\]\. Likewise\, Lee et al\. \(2022\) examined the role of Laminated Object Manufacturing \(LOM\) in the polymer domain\, particularly in large\-scale fabrication using polymer sheets and improved interlayer bonding techniques \[42\]\. Overall\, these recent studies demonstrate rapid advancements across polymer AM technologies\, driven by improved material systems\, higher\-resolution printing mechanisms\, and process optimizations that support increasingly demanding engineering applications\[41\, 43\, 44\]\.

\#\#\# 1\.4 Trends in additive manufacturing technologies

Additive manufacturing \(AM\)\, or 3D printing\, has gained significant momentum in recent years due to its adaptability\, material efficiency\, and ability to produce customized polymer components across a broad range of industries\. As illustrated in Fig\. 5\, recent literature highlights the growing integration of AM within digital and intelligent manufacturing environments\. Horst \(2018\) \[45\] reviewed AM within the context of Industry 4\.0\, emphasizing how polymer AM processes benefit from improved connectivity\, smart sensors\, and real\-time data utilization to enhance flexibility and reduce production costs\. Ngo et al\. \(2018\) \[46\] provided a comprehensive overview of material and process developments in AM\, particularly focusing on polymer applications in biomedical devices\, consumer products\, and construction formwork\, while also outlining the challenges of maintaining process consistency and part quality\. Kumar \[47\] and \[48\] further discussed how polymer AM systems are increasingly coupled with Internet of Things \(IoT\) architectures and embedded sensors\, enabling more responsive and adaptive manufacturing workflows\. Chang \(2018\) \[49\] explored emerging polymer\-related material strategies—such as smart materials and conductive polymers—that expand the functionality of additively manufactured parts\, particularly for soft robotics\, electronics\, and biomaterials\. Baumann \(2017\) \[50\] examined the role of cloud\-based AM platforms in supporting distributed polymer printing environments\, emphasizing their potential for collaborative design\, remote monitoring\, and scalable production\. Dilberoglu \(2017\) \[51\] highlighted advancements in AM technologies within smart manufacturing systems\, noting how polymer AM has benefited from improved design optimization tools and cyber–physical integration\. Mittal \(2017\) \[52\] similarly emphasized AM as a key enabler within intelligent manufacturing\, identifying polymer AM processes as essential for achieving rapid prototyping\, real\-time customization\, and agile production\. Attaran \(2017\) \[53\] underscored AM’s advantages—such as low waste generation and mass customization—which are particularly applicable to polymer components in consumer\, medical\, and industrial sectors\. Eyers \(2017\) \[54\] analyzed AM adoption in industrial environments\, focusing on system\-level considerations such as workflow optimization and digital production planning for polymer\-based systems\. Thoben \(2017\) \[55\] also reviewed the integration of AM within Industry 4\.0 ecosystems\, discussing research challenges and future scenarios for digitally\-driven polymer manufacturing\. Singh \(2017\) \[56\] examined challenges related to polymer biomaterials and highlighted the emerging field of additive bio\-manufacturing\. More recently\, Ponis et al\. \(2021\) \[57\] emphasized the role of polymer AM in enabling circular economy practices through recyclability and reduced material waste\. Comprehensive reviews by Bandyopadhyay \[58\] and by Gibson\, Rosen\, and Stucker \(2020\) \[59\] illustrate broader trends in AM technologies and materials\, with substantial emphasis on developments in polymer processes and their expanding engineering applications\. Overall\, these studies demonstrate the rapid advancement of polymer AM technologies as they intersect with smart manufacturing\, sustainability initiatives\, and emerging digital tools\, reinforcing the need for robust\, data\-driven defect detection methods to support high\-quality production \[60\]\.

This seven\-year period analysis traces the uptake paths of ten polymer additive manufacturing \(AM\) technologies\. Major observations\:

Predominant Technologies\: FDM \(Fused Deposition Modeling\) records steady growth\, a testament to its dominant position as the industry standard for cost\-efficiency and material adaptability\.SLA \(Stereo\-lithography\) demonstrates gradual decline\, likely attributable to competition from faster\, higher\-throughput technologies like DLP \(Digital Light Processing\)\.

Emergent Trends\: SLS \(Selective Laser Sintering\) and Material Jetting show moderate growth\, reflecting increased adoption for functional prototyping and multi\-material applications\, respectively\.

EBM \(Electron Beam Melting\) and DED \(Directed Energy Deposition\) remains niche\, with marginal usage due to their specialization in high\-performance polymers and composites\.

\#\# 2 Background and review methodology

Polymers have become foundational to additive manufacturing \(AM\)\, enabling the production of lightweight\, complex\, and highly customized parts across various sectors\, including aerospace\, automotive\, health\- care\, and consumer products\. The diversity of polymers used in AM is extensive\, ranging from common thermoplastics like PLA and ABS to more advanced materials such as high\-performance polymers \(e\.g\.\, PEEK\, PEI\) and elastomers that bring specific benefits\, such as flexibility or thermal resistance\. Ther\- moplastics are especially popular for rapid prototyping and are known for their ease of processing and reusability\, while thermosetting polymers provide greater rigidity and are often chosen for applications requiring high thermal stability\, though they are less recyclable\.

The techniques used to print polymers continue to evolve\, with processes like Fused Deposition Modeling \(FDM\) widely accessible and ideal for creating detailed parts with complex geometries\. Stere\- olithography \(SLA\) and Digital Light Processing \(DLP\) offer high\-resolution prints with smooth finishes\, making them highly suitable for applications in the medical and dental fields\, where precision is essential\. On the other hand\, processes like Selective Laser Sintering \(SLS\) and Multi Jet Fusion \(MJF\) allow the production of parts with robust mechanical properties\, which makes them fit for functional prototyping as well as parts to be used\.

\#\#\# 2\.1 Background on polymer AM

Recent developments in additive manufacturing \(AM\) have more and more utilized polymeric materials\, each with distinct behavior that influences print quality as well as performance upon use\. Tensile strength\, a key requirement for bearing loads\, has been the subject of wide investigation\; research highlights the superior performance of PEEK under high stresses owing to high tensile properties\, as reported in the work of Smith et al\. \[61\] in Fig\. 6\. Flexibility\, essential for functional applications like wearable tech\, has been predominantly associated with TPU and Nylon\, as Lee et al\. \[62\] demonstrated their resilience under cyclic stress conditions\. The need for high\-temperature resistance in industrial applications has led to studies on PC and PEEK polymers\, as Jones et al\. \[63\] found them particularly suited for thermal stability\. Printability\, or ease of use in 3D printing setups\, remains a challenge with materials like ABS\, which Brown and Clark \[64\] reported often exhibit warping but can be mitigated with optimized bed temperatures\. Finally\, warping tendency\, a factor affecting print accuracy\, has been thoroughly assessed\, with Wang et al\. \[65\] confirming PLA’s stability during cooling\, reducing deformation risks\. Each property plays a pivotal role\, shaping the selection of polymers based on application needs and 3D printing technologies\.

\#\#\# 2\.2 Review methodology

In additive manufacturing of polymers\, several common defects can significantly impact the quality and functionality of printed parts\. Poor bridging occurs when the printer fails to adequately support larger bridging regions\, leading to sagging or collapse between support structures\. Dimensional accuracy defects are caused by many factors\, including thermal contraction\, incorrect extrusion speeds\, filament quality\, and first\-layer nozzle misalignment\, resulting in parts that do not meet precise specifications\. Differences between infill and outline are often caused by the same reasons\, such as variable extrusion or thermal contraction\, which weaken the part’s structural integrity\. Splitting and layer separation result from infill extrusion at speeds that are too high\, preventing bonding with outline perimeters\. Elastic deformation is usually the result of a layer height that is too great or an undersupply of cooling\, often a result of printing at high temperatures\. Misalignments are most often caused by over\-extrusion\, while layer shifting can be caused by tool head speeds that are too high or mechanical\/electrical printer malfunctions\. Blobs and zits are usually a result of incorrect retraction or coasting values\. Incoherence of print quality can be caused by many issues\, such as filament tangling\, clogged extruders\, or incorrect extrusion values\, ultimately resulting in variable results\. Finally\, stringing or oozing results when too much filament is extruded during non\-print movements\, most often due to low retraction settings or high printing temperatures\. Correction of these flaws involves precise calibration of printer settings\, rigid quality control of materials\, and particular adjustments based on the specific conditions of the printing process\.

Bowoto et al\. \[66\] designed a MATLAB\-based algorithm for in situ layer\-wise defect detection in 3D\-printed parts\. The algorithm detects porosity and other defects that can impact both the mechanical properties and aesthetic quality of 3D\-printed components\. Tested on different geometries\, the method successfully identified defects in real\-time\, reducing material wastage\. The study highlights the need for such real\-time monitoring systems to improve the efficiency and quality of additive manufacturing processes and the Defects are showing in the Table 1\.

The defect types observed in polymer AM\, particularly PLA printing\, are not only descriptive phenomena but are directly linked to quantifiable process deviations\, measurable sensor indicators\, and predictable impacts on part performance\. Poor bridging typically occurs when unsupported spans exceed 5–10 mm or cooling rates are insufficient\, and can be detected using optical imaging or thermal sensors that highlight filament sagging\; such defects weaken interlayer bonding and reduce structural reliability\. Dimensional inaccuracy arises from thermal contraction \(0\.2–0\.8\%\)\, nozzle misalignment \(± 0\.1–0\.2 mm\)\, or extrusion deviations \(5–15\%\)\, and is commonly identified through 3D scanning or machine\-vision\-based contour measurements\, often resulting in poor tolerance fit and functional mismatch\. Gaps between infill and outline occur when under\-extrusion drops below 90\% or print speeds exceed 60–80 mm\/s\; image\-based gap detection or acoustic monitoring can reveal these defects\, which decrease density and mechanical strength by 10–30\%\. Layer separation\, caused by insufficient interlayer bonding time or low extrusion temperatures\, is detectable through thermal imaging or CNN\-based delamination classification\, and can reduce tensile strength by up to 60\%\. Elastic deformation often associated with excessive temperatures or large layer heights can be captured through curvature\-tracking algorithms or thermal gradient analysis and typically results in warping and dimensional instability\. Misalignment defects arise from motor backlash or extrusion inconsistencies and can be identified using position\-tracking sensors or motor current analysis\, leading to geometric inaccuracies\. Finally\, layer shifting caused by high acceleration rates or mechanical faults is detectable via vibration analytics or image\-based layer comparison and results in severe dimensional distortion or total print failure\. Together\, these quantitative relationships highlight the need for integrated sensing and data\-driven monitoring frameworks to ensure reliable polymer AM quality\.

A structured literature screening was performed across Scopus\, Web of Science\, IEEE Xplore\, and Google Scholar to identify studies linking polymer AM\, defect mechanisms\, and data\-driven monitoring\. Boolean keyword combinations included\: \(“polymer” OR “FDM” OR “SLA” OR “SLS”\) AND \(“3D printing” OR “additive manufacturing”\) AND \(“defect” OR “quality monitoring” OR “in\-situ”\) AND \(“machine learning” OR “deep learning” OR “sensor fusion”\)\. The search window was limited to 2016–2025\, and only peer\-reviewed English publications were considered\.

Inclusion criteria\: \(i\) polymer AM focus\, \(ii\) defect\/quality analysis\, \(iii\) sensing or ML involvement\.

Exclusion criteria\: \(i\) non\-polymer AM without polymer comparison\, \(ii\) descriptive overviews without defect content\, \(iii\) purely hardware studies lacking monitoring analytics\, \(iv\) non\-peer\-reviewed material\.

Screening Procedure\: Records were screened in three stages\: \(i\) title\/keyword filtering\, \(ii\) abstract review\, and \(iii\) full\-text assessment\. Backward snowballing was additionally performed to capture frequently cited studies\. A PRISMA\-style trace is shown in Fig\. 7a\. Dataset\: From 312 identified records\, 75 articles were retained for synthesis after deduplication and screening\.

\#\#\# 2\.3 Dataset summary

A total of 75 peer\-reviewed papers were used for a thorough analysis based on the screening methodology described in Sect\. 2\.2\, covering the time range of 2016–2025 for this analysis\; they represent research into polymer Additive Manufacturing \(AM\)\, detection of defects\, and Data\-Driven modeling\. \#\#\# 2\.4 Trends in materials

There has been two major trends in how polymers have developed within AM\, with regards to the two types of material that are now available for 3D printing\; these include both\; \(1\) the diversity of feedstock materials to print with\, and \(2\) the enhancement of final use performance\. For example\, commodity polymers \(e\.g\. PLA\, ABS\, PETG\) were initially used in prototyping applications for their low cost and printability\, but are still being used in educational settings\. In contrast\, engineering polymers \(e\.g\. PC\, Nylon\, PEI\, PEEK\) are now providing a level of structural and thermal performance that is adequate for aerospace\, medical\, and automotive applications\. Figure 3 shows multiple examples from literature between 2018 and 2024 that illustrate the movement from prototyping to functional part production\, due to improved mechanical robustness\, thermal stability\, and material modification techniques\.

The recent literature shows an increase in the development of composite and reinforced polymer systems\, such as carbon fiber\-reinforced PEEK\, conductive polymers\, and elastomeric blends\. This expanding range of materials will enable the development of flexible electronics\, wearable technology\, and high\-temperature components\. However\, this trend toward more diverse materials has also increased the potential for new defect mechanisms associated with anisotropic properties\, shrinkage\, warping\, and layer\-to\-layer adhesion\, reiterating the need for a data\-driven approach to defect detection\. Therefore\, the reviewed literature illustrates that the areas of materials development and sensing\/monitoring of performance are increasingly becoming intertwined as polymer systems move toward their performance\-critical applications\.

Technologies relating to Polymer Additive Manufacturing \(Polymer AM\) have matured significantly in the last several years with improvements made in terms of accuracy\, speed\, and functional integration\. Improvements made between 2018 and 2023 in technologies such as Fused Deposition Modeling \(FDM\)\, Stereolithography \(SLA\)\, Selective Laser Sintering \(SLS\)\, Digital Light Processing \(DLP\)\, Direct Ink Writing \(DIW\)\, and Multi Jet Fusion \(MJF\) are depicted visually in the following figure \(Fig\. 4\)\. These advancements will be critical in supporting the ability to detect defects in real time\, monitor processes during production\, and adaptively control variable factors\, which is explained in further detail in Sects\. 3 and 4 of this article\. \#\# 3 Defect detection techniques in polymer additive manufacturing

Defect detection in 3D printing has evolved significantly from manual inspection to sophisticated machine learning techniques\. Early methods as shown in the Fig\. were limited by human error and lacked scalability\, but machine vision and AI now provide more efficient solutions\. Paraskevoudis et al\. \(2020\) introduced a real\- time defect detection system using deep neural networks to analyze live video feeds\, enabling instant identification of issues such as stringing in fused filament fabrication\, enhancing real\-time feedback for corrective actions \[67\]\. Saidy et al\. \(2021\) utilized the PointNet neural network to classify defects in 3D\- printed objects using 3D point cloud data\, achieving an accuracy of 87\.5\%\, and demonstrated how supervised learning can improve defect detection in diverse 3D printing scenarios \[68\]\. Additionally\, Khanzadeh et al\. \(2020\) applied machine learning models\, including support vector machines and CNNs\, to predict and classify defects based on sensor data and thermal imaging\, showing the importance of data fusion for comprehensive defect analysis in additive manufacturing \[69\]\.

\#\#\# 3\.1 Data\-driven advances in additive manufacturing\: trends in materials and techniques

The integration of data science and additive manufacturing has produced profound advances in materials\, manufacturing processes\, and real\-time quality assurance\. Through the integration of high\-end sensors and monitoring systems\, data\-driven methods in additive manufacturing are improving defect detection\, process parameter optimization\, and material behavior prediction\. For example\, machine learning methods facilitate the analysis of large datasets obtained from in\-process monitoring to enable real\-time adjustments that avoid defects and product inconsistencies\. This has been highly useful in sectors that need high\-quality and precision\, which allows for the production of parts with specially designed mechanical\, thermal\, or electrical characteristics for precise applications\. Moreover\, the capacity to simulate material performance via data analysis prior to production has greatly minimized trial\-and\-error processes\, thereby saving time and resources\.

Future evolution of additive manufacturing is built on continued integration of data\-driven solutions\, which promise to deliver full automation in every stage\, from design to production\. These developments are predicted to redefine the limits of additive manufacturing\, allowing manufacturers to produce highly detailed parts with unmatched precision\, while at the same time cutting costs and minimizing material waste common in most industries\, including aerospace and medicine\.

The field of material development has also seen a transformation of revolutionary proportions with the use of data\-driven solutions\. New materials such as composites\, functionally graded materials\, and multi\-material printing are designed with improved precision to tune their properties \[70\,71\,72\,73\]\.

\#\#\# 3\.2 Machine learning techniques and their applications in polymer additive manufacturing

Machine learning \(ML\) techniques used in polymer additive manufacturing \(AM\) can be divided into two\: model complexity and data supervision\.

Data Supervision\: Supervised learning uses data characterized by having labels\: each piece of input data has a specific outcome associated with it\, which is known with conviction\. The two main purposes for which this method is often applied are forecasting a continuous value\, called regression\, and sorting data into distinct groups\, called classification\. For instance\, by looking at the data you already possess about the properties and behaviors of printed polymers\, it is possible to use supervised learning models to ascertain the strength or flexibility of printed polymers\.

Unsupervised Learning\: These models work on unlabeled data to identify patterns or structures in the data without defined outcomes\. Common tasks are clustering\, where data points are classified as similar\, and dimensionality reduction\, which compresses data while preserving important information\. This is useful for identifying hidden patterns in polymer properties or process parameter optimization without defined labels\.

Semi\-Supervised Learning\: This method takes both supervised and unsupervised learning characteristics\. It begins with some labelled data and a vast quantity of unlabeled data\. Semi\-supervised models learn from both data iteratively\, frequently used when it is expensive or impossible to get labeled data\. Active learning \(in which the model asks for labels on the most informative points\) and self\-training \(in which the model labels itself\) are examples of this category and the Pictorial representation is given as Fig\. 8\.

\#\#\#\# 3\.2\.1 Supervised learning

Machine learning\, particularly in Fused Deposition Modeling \(FDM\) and\, on a broader scope\, in Powder Bed Fusion \(PBF\)\, has progressed rapidly in AM\. They have extensively studied how supervised machine\-learning models can be integrated for real\-time monitoring\, optimization of processes\, and defect detection\. Magolon et al\. \[67\] reviewed the supervised machine\-learning approaches to detect defects in Laser\-Powder Bed Fusion \(L\-PBF\) whereby they also discussed optimization algorithms for settings that achieve quality in separate works\. Then in 2024\, Rojek et al\. examined AI models for fault detection and process automation in AM\, with specific emphasis on the possibilities of FDM for rapid prototyping\. Agron et al\. \[69\] developed a machine\-learning method for monitoring FDM printers based on avoiding issues with nozzles and predicting printing trouble\. In 2023\, Enslin conducted study work on how interpretable machine learning can inform better understanding of FDM process parameters for quality improvement by real\-time adjustment\. These studies emphasized that supervised learning is an increasing trend to establish more reliability into AM processes and efficiency\-wise\. It further highlights the consequential contributions of machine learning in developing and optimizing manufacturing technologies\.

\#\#\#\# 3\.2\.2 Unsupervised learning

Unsupervised machine learning methods continue to be embraced in recent times for process monitoring and quality control for AM\. In 2023\, Alatefi et al\. introduced a framework in which multivariate statistical quality monitoring is used in the Fused Filament Fabrication \(FFF\) process\; they pointed out that having multiple inter\-related quality factors to assess the consistency of AM processes must be taken into account \[74\]\. Meanwhile\, work from the Baumgartl team in 2022 used unsupervised learning to detect defects\. They underscore the possible merits of combining image analysis with machine learning to automatically identify defects during the production process \[75\]\. In 2021\, Narayana and his team looked into AI\-supported methods\, including unsupervised learning\, for giving consideration to opportunities and challenges in the manufacturing sector\. Their findings demonstrated significant potential for improving operational efficiency \[76\]\. Collectively\, these studies underscore the growing role of unsupervised learning in addressing key challenges in additive manufacturing\.

\#\#\#\# 3\.2\.3 Semi\-supervised learning

Newer technologies in additive manufacturing \(AM\) apply semi\-supervised learning methods to improve the detection of defects and quality control\. For example\, semi\-supervised deep learning was demonstrated in one study to automatically check the quality of AM using both labeled and unlabeled data\, thereby increasing the accuracy of AM checks\. Grierson and colleagues \[75\] reviewed different machine learning methodologies\, including semi\-supervised methods\, and emphasized how these approaches address problems stemming from limited availability of labeled data in AM\. Furthermore\, research exploring deep learning for laser additive manufacturing defect detection has also shown that semi\-supervised techniques can exploit small amounts of labeled data to identify defects more efficiently\. Such findings underscore the pivotal role that semi\-supervised learning plays in the optimization and reliability of AM processes\.

\#\#\#\# 3\.2\.4 Deep learning models

Indeed\, owing to recent advances in additive manufacturing \(AM\)\, deep learning models have become critical components in the improvement of various aspects of the manufacturing process\. A comprehensive review of the 2023 literature by Peles and colleagues demonstrated how deep learning helped resolve some key problems related to understanding the quality of components in AM due to difference in process settings\. This also introduced a very different method of investigating the structure of 3D\-printed parts\, using a technology called conditional Generative Adversarial Network \(GAN\)\. This method simulates the use of GANs to quickly predict shape and detect defects from images\. Besides\, progress has been made in the study of real\-time quality tests with point cloud data\, which makes us realize that deep learning will automatically capture defects in AM\. All these things bring together a paradigm change in using deep learning in increasing the reliability\, effectiveness\, and quality control of AM processes \[76\, 77\]\.

\#\#\# 3\.3 Model complexity

Shallow Models\: Shallow models have less complicated architectures and include parametric and non\-parametric approaches\. Parametric models like linear regression and logistic regression have strong assumptions about the input\-output relationship and can be applied to simpler problems with well\-defined relationships\. Non\-parametric models like decision trees and k\-nearest neighbors have no fixed structure and can learn from data more flexibly\. Shallow models are generally applied to structured data and can be applied to classification and regression\.

Deep Learning Models\: They have complex architectures and are able to learn complex patterns from data\. Deep learning includes\: Multilayer Perceptron’s \(MLPs\)\: Fully connected networks suitable for structured and unstructured data\, and are used for regression and classification operations\.

tRecurrent Neural Networks \(RNNs\)\: Specifically designed for sequential data\, RNNs possess a “memory” of previous inputs and are therefore most suitable for time\-series forecasting\. Long Short\-Term Memory \(LSTM\) networks\, a type of RNN\, are employed for learning long\-term dependencies\.

Convolution Neural Networks \(CNNs\)\: For spatial pattern data\, i\.e\.\, images\. CNNs utilize convolution layers to detect local patterns and are well\-suited for tasks like image recognition and defect inspection in AM\.

Additive manufacturing represents a new technology that produces complex shapes with very little waste\. Although it can offer a lot of advantages\, there are still many technical challenges\. \#\#\# 4\.1 Machine learning for polymer additive manufacturing

Machine learning is changing the game in polymer additive manufacturing\, a type of 3D printing\. It brings improvements to the managing of process settings\, material quality\, and fault detection in a production environment\. Neural networks and decision trees are increasingly becoming the most favorite tools of prediction on outcomes\, ranging from surface smoothness and material strength to shape changes during printing\. With such level of prediction accuracy\, materials and processes can be fine\-tuned to meet the specific application\, for example\, in airplanes or medical tools\. Analyzing images enables the detection of impending problems layer\-wise\, leading to better efficiencies in production with less waste\. Therefore\, having evolved\, this manufacturing method now requires machine learning to provide better accuracy\, consistency\, and material quality\.

\#\#\#\# 4\.1\.1 Machine learning for fused deposition modeling

Recent studies highlight the role of machine learning \(ML\) in improving Fused Deposition Modeling \(FDM\)\. In 2023\, researchers Huang and others developed ML models to predict the surface smoothness of PLA prints\. This helps enhance print quality by selecting the right settings\. They also introduced a method using Description Logic \(DL\) ontology to optimize how parts are oriented in FDM\. DL ontology allows for describing\, representing\, and reusing information about part placement\, which traditionally depended on expert knowledge\. The method includes steps for creating different part orientations\, predicting values for different factors\, and choosing the best orientation\. This was tested using six different FDM parts\. The results show that this method enhances the efficiency and effectiveness of part orientation\, supporting automatic checking\, reasoning\, and further reuse of FDM data\.

\#\#\#\# 4\.1\.2 Machine learning for powder bed fusion and SLS

In the field of Powder Bed Fusion \(PBF\)\, significant research efforts have been directed towards enhanc\- ing material selection\, quality control\, and discrete outcome prediction using various machine learning techniques\. However\, there is a noticeable gap in research specifically focused on in situ process parameter optimization and defect classification\. Although some studies have explored in situ monitoring techniques such as CNN models for detecting defects in powder bed samples and thermal recordings\, comprehensive approaches that dynamically adjust process parameters in real\-time to prevent defects are still underdeveloped\. The lack of advanced\, data\-driven methodologies for optimizing process parameters during the printing process limits the full potential of PBF technologies\. Addressing this gap could significantly enhance the overall reliability\, efficiency\, and quality of additive manufacturing\, paving the way for smarter\, more adaptive manufacturing systems Table 3\.

Powder Bed Fusion \(PBF\) is a widely used additive manufacturing technique that has revolutionized the production of complex\, high\-precision parts across various industries\. Despite its advantages\, PBF is highly sensitive to process parameters such as laser power\, scan speed\, and layer thickness\, which significantly influence the final part quality\. Defects such as porosity\, warping\, and surface irregularities can arise due to suboptimal process conditions\, leading to reduced mechanical properties and part reliability\. Traditional quality control methods often involve post\-process inspections\, which are time\-consuming\, costly\, and incapable of detecting internal defects or adjusting process parameters in real\-time\. To address these challenges\, there is an emerging need for advanced in situ process parameter optimization and real\-time defect classification techniques\. These approaches leverage real\-time data acquisition and machine learning models to monitor the printing process\, detect defects as they occur\, and dynamically adjust process parameters to prevent further issues\. By integrating sensor data such as thermal imaging\, surface roughness Through direct measurements and acoustic signals\, in situ monitoring systems can allow for immediate feedback and actions during the building process\. However\, recent studies have focused less on optimization of process parameters and more on defect detection\. The development of true data\-driven\, adaptive manufacturing systems with instantaneous decision\-making capabilities holds the key to genuinely transforming PBF into a highly reliable\, efficient\, and high\-quality means to manufacture 3D\-printed parts\. This will actually require interdisciplinary collaboration in which advanced analytical modeling can combine with machine learning and real\-time sensor integration to develop smart systems that detect defects and optimize the printing conditions in real time\.
