While several prior reviews have examined aspects of defect detection or monitoring in additive manufacturing\, the existing literature remains fragmented\, particularly for polymer\-based processes\. Paraskevoudis \(2020\) focused primarily on vision\-based inspection methods without integrating thermal\, acoustic\, or process\-sensor modalities\. Khanzadeh \(2020\) emphasized predictive analytics for AM quality but did not link defect mechanisms to specific sensing strategies or discuss polymer\-specific defect behavior\. Magolon \(2021\) provided a broad overview of AM data analytics but did not propose a structured framework connecting data acquisition\, feature extraction\, machine learning model selection\, and real\-time quality decision\-making\. In contrast\, the present review synthesizes these dimensions into a unified\, data\-driven conceptual framework specifically tailored for polymer AM\, integrating defect mechanisms\, multi\-sensor monitoring\, machine learning models\, and closed\-loop feedback considerations\. This focused and structured integration—absent in prior reviews—constitutes the key novelty of this work and provides a clearer roadmap for advancing intelligent defect detection in polymer additive manufacturing\.

Recent reviews have explored the integration of big data analytics\, machine learning\, and digital twin technologies in additive manufacturing\, emphasizing their potential for virtual process replication\, predictive modeling\, and intelligent quality management\. However\, these studies generally adopt a broad\, technology\-centric perspective and do not provide a defect\-specific or polymer\-focused framework\. Existing digital twin reviews tend to describe high\-level architectures—such as cyber\-physical synchronization\, cloud\-based data pipelines\, and simulation–data fusion—but offer limited guidance on how individual defect mechanisms\, sensor modalities\, or machine learning models should be selected and connected within a practical monitoring workflow\. In contrast\, the framework proposed in this study is explicitly tailored to polymer AM defect detection\, detailing how process\-linked defects \(e\.g\.\, warping\, under\-extrusion\, layer separation\) correspond to sensor data characteristics and which ML approaches are most appropriate for real\-time detection\. Unlike previous big\-data and digital\-twin reviews\, our framework moves beyond conceptual architectures by mapping defects → sensing → feature extraction → ML model → decision support\, thereby providing a more operational and application\-focused structure\. This comparison highlights that while digital twin literature offers valuable system\-level insights\, the present review uniquely contributes a defect\-oriented\, polymer\-specific\, and implementable data\-driven framework not previously articulated\.

\#\# 5 Conclusion and future scope

Additive manufacturing \(AM\) has matured substantially\; several critical gaps remain in the development of reliable\, real\-time defect detection for polymer\-based processes\. First\, while traditional sensing techniques such as vibration analysis and acoustic emissions provide useful information\, they suffer from high noise sensitivity and require extensive preprocessing\. Future research should focus on developing standardized\, noise\-robust signal processing pipelines and benchmark datasets to enable fair comparison across studies—an issue consistently highlighted in the literature\.

The rapid adoption of machine learning and AI\, current implementations often rely on small\, proprietary\, or single\-modality datasets\. This limits model generalizability\. Therefore\, future work should advance multi\-sensor data fusion frameworks that combine optical\, thermal\, acoustic\, and machine log data\, and validate them on large\, open\-access\, polymer\-AM\-specific datasets\. Such efforts would fill the gap in unified sensing protocols identified in this review\.

Digital twin concepts have been explored at a high level\, their integration into polymer AM defect detection remains limited\. Existing digital twin models rarely incorporate defect mechanisms\, sensor behavior\, and machine learning predictions in a closed\-loop manner\. Future research should prioritize physics\-informed and data\-driven digital twins capable of real\-time synchronization with the printing process\, enabling predictive correction of warping\, under\-extrusion\, and layer separation before defects propagate\.

Finally\, current AM systems lack autonomous decision\-making\. Machine learning predictions are rarely connected to active process adjustments\. The field would benefit from research into adaptive control systems that transform detection algorithms into actionable control strategies\, such as dynamic parameter tuning or automated re\-slicing\. These developments would directly address the gap between defect identification and defect mitigation\, moving polymer AM toward fully autonomous\, self\-correcting manufacturing systems\.

records.title: Hierarchically porous copper–graphene current collectors via material extrusion additive manufacturing for dendrite free lithium metal batteries
records.abstract: A previous study demonstrated that, 3D porous copper current collector (3DP-CCC) fabricated using ME-AM process exhibited average CE of 95.5% with cycling time of more than 450 h at CD of 1 mAcm−2 with plated capacity 5 mAhcm−2 [17]. ... In this work, we address this ... 3DP-Copper Graphene Current Collector(3DP-CGCC) through ME-AM.
records.summary: This paper reports a 3D porous copper–graphene current collector (3DP-CGCC) for lithium metal batteries, fabricated by material extrusion additive manufacturing (ME-AM). A high-solid-loading ink containing ≥95 wt.% Cu powder, 0.2 wt.% graphene, and PLA binder was formulated and shown to be shear-thinning and printable, yielding collectors with uniform pore size of 190 ± 3 μm. Graphene incorporation reportedly increased electrical conductivity by ~9% versus a graphene-free 3DP-Cu collector, and the 3DP-CGCC reportedly delivered ~98.8% coulombic efficiency over 700 h at 1 mA cm⁻² with 5 mAh cm⁻² plating, lower charge-transfer resistance by EIS, and COMSOL-simulated homogeneous Li deposition at 1 and 3 mA cm⁻². A Li@3DP-CGCC||LFP full cell reportedly delivered ~139 mAh g⁻¹ at 0.5C with ~99% efficiency and good rate capability. The summary is based on an accessible excerpt (abstract, highlights, introduction, and partial sections); figures, tables, and full experimental details were not available.
records.why_it_matters: The work indicates that combining ME-AM geometric control of pore architecture with a small graphene addition to a Cu ink is a plausible route to scalable, dendrite-suppressing current collectors, since pore uniformity and conductivity both directly affect local current density and Li plating homogeneity.

records.body_text:
Published by: Elsevier
Published by
Highlights
- •Developed a high solid loading (≥95 wt%) Cu–Gr ink.
- •Material Extrusion Additive Manufacturing fabricated 3DP Cu–Gr current collectors.
- •Current collector showed 98.8% efficiency over 700 h at 1mAcm⁻2, plating 5mAhcm−2.
- •Full cell showed 139mAhg⁻1, ~99% efficiency at 0.5C and excellent rate performance.
- •COMSOL simulation results confirmed homogeneous Li deposition at 1 and 3 mAcm⁻2.
Abstract
Porous copper current collectors help mitigate key challenges in Lithium Metal Batteries (LMB), including volume changes, unstable SEI formation, and dendritic lithium growth. However, further structural optimization along with manufacturing innovation is required to achieve improved electrochemical performance and long-term stability. Hence, this work presents a high-performance 3D Porous Copper Graphene Current Collector (3DP-CGCC) fabricated via Material Extrusion Additive Manufacturing (ME-AM) for advanced LMB applications. A novel Copper-Graphene ink with high copper particle loading (≥95
wt.%) and graphene loading (0.2 wt.%) has been formulated for ME-AM process. Rheological investigations revealed pronounced shear-thinning and viscoelastic characteristics, enabling excellent printability and shape retention. This optimized ink facilitated the fabrication of a 3DP-CGCC with uniform pore size of 190 ± 3 μm, providing precise regulation of Li-ions transport. Furthermore, incorporation of graphene resulted in ~9% increase in electrical conductivity compared with 3D Porous Copper Current Collector (3DP-CCC). Owing to this synergistic architectural and compositional design, 3DP-CGCC delivered exceptional electrochemical performance, achieving a coulombic efficiency of ~98.8% for over 700 h with CD 1 mAcm⁻2 at plating capacity 5 mAhcm⁻2. The EIS results reveal lower charge transfer resistance compared with 3DP-CCC and Cu Foil. COMSOL simulations confirmed homogeneous current distribution and uniform Li deposition at 1 and 3 mAcm⁻2. The Li@3DP-CGCC||LFP full cell delivered stable cycling (~139 mAhg⁻1 at 0.5C) and superior rate capability, demonstrating excellent practical applicability. Overall, this study demonstrates an advanced 3DP-CGCC integrated with a scalable manufacturing strategy, offering a promising pathway toward the development of next-generation LMB systems.

Introduction
Lithium (
Li) metal is one of most advanced anode material for next-generation Lithium Metal Battery (LMB) due to its exceptionally high specific capacity (~3860 mAhg−1) and low reduction potential of −3.04 V versus SHE. Despite its potential, key limitations like volume fluctuation during charging and discharging, unstable Solid Electrolyte Interface (SEI) and uncontrollable Lidendrites growth hinder its practical applications [1], [2], [3]. The current collector typically a flat copper (Cu) foil is widely used in LMBs due to its high electrical conductivity, better mechanical robustness, and stability with Li-ions. However, its flat surface provides limited Li-ions nucleation sites, localized Current Density (CD) and unstable SEI formation resulting in aforesaid mentioned problems with LMBs and poor Coulombic Efficiency (CE) [4], [5]. To overcome these limitations, researchers have explored 3D structured Cu current collectors such as foams, meshes, and scaffolds [6], [7]. Commonly used manufacturing techniques for preparing such structures includes hydrogen bubble dynamic template process [8], asymmetric coating strategy process [9], pulsed electrodeposition process [10], chemical etching [11], alloying/dealloying processes [6], [7]. and NaCl-templated/powder-sintering method [12]. While these 3D structured Cu current collectors reduce local CD and accommodate Li deposition, they often suffer from low mechanical robustness and limited electrical conductivity. Also, these methods can involve multiple processing steps, specialized equipment, and corrosive or hazardous chemicals, which may increase fabrication complexity, and challenges associated with achieving tuned porosity. This problem can be addressed by use of additive manufacturing (AM) process for the fabricating of 3D porous Cu current collectors.
Different AM techniques, such as laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), electron beam melting (EBM), and directed energy deposition (DED), have been employed to fabricate complex Cu components. However, the high equipment and processing costs, together with the challenges associated with processing Cu due to its high laser reflectivity and thermal conductivity, limit the suitability of these techniques for fabricating 3DP Cu current collectors [13], [14], [15]. Moreover, powder handling issues with these AM processes further restrict their use for battery application. To address these limitations, beamless AM techniques, particularly binder jetting and material extrusion additive manufacturing (ME-AM) have emerged as alternative approaches for fabricating 3DP Cu current collectors' structures for LMB applications [8]. Although binder jetting offers considerable geometric freedom, challenges associated with powder handling, achieving sufficient green strength, and the need for de-binding and sintering can complicate the fabrication of self-supporting porous Cu architectures [16]. In contrast, ME-AM enables the direct deposition of highly loaded, viscous Cu-based inks, facilitating the fabrication of self-supporting structures with interconnected pores and tuneable architectures. Its relatively simple equipment requirements, efficient material utilization, and digital design flexibility make ME-AM a promising approach for producing 3DP Cu current collectors for LMB applications [17]. Nevertheless, its scalability and overall cost-effectiveness depend on printing throughput, ink formulation, and post-processing requirements.
Hierarchically porous three-dimensional Cu current collectors fabricated via ME-AM have demonstrated more uniform current distribution, homogeneous Li-ion transport, suppressed dendritic Li growth, and improved coulombic efficiency (CE) [18], [19]. A previous study demonstrated that, 3D porous copper current collector (3DP-CCC) fabricated using ME-AM process exhibited average CE of 95.5% with cycling time of more than 450
h at CD of 1 mAcm−2 with plated capacity 5 mAhcm−2 [17]. Though 3DP-CCC exhibited good electrochemical performance (CE and cyclic stability), but still, there is considerable scope for improvement. This improvement in electrochemical performance can be achieved by the incorporation of highly electrically conductive carbon additives likes carbon nanofibers, carbon nanotubes (CNT) and Graphene (Gr) [20], [21], [22]. Among these additives, Gr is often the superior filler for Cu matrix because of its ultra-high electrical conductivity (105–107 Sm⁻1), 2D sheet structure (very high specific surface area 2630 m2/g), very high mechanical strength (130 GPa), and less loading requirement to achieve percolation [23], [24], [25], [26]. Addition of Gr into Cu scaffold, effectively improves the electrical conductivity owing to bridging of the gap between Cu particles. Moreover, the large specific surface area of Gr sheets provides abundant electrochemically active sites for Li-ion deposition, effectively reducing the local CD and promoting uniform Li plating. This ultimately leads to reduced Li dendrite formation, improved electron mobility, enhanced electron transport kinetics and overall percolation network [27], [28], [29]. Some studies have reported notable improvements in CE with Gr-integrated Cu based anode [27], [30], [31]. The r-GO modified Cu foam achieved ~98.5% CE over 350 cycles, attributed to its porous conductive network and uniform Li deposition behaviour. Similarly, (Cu3P)/r-GO and CuO/GO hybrid anodes exhibited rapid CE stabilization (>98% and > 90%, respectively), driven by enhanced electron transport, SEI stability, and effective suppression of parasitic reaction. However, aforesaid mentioned Gr-integrated Cu current collectors were fabricated using conventional techniques that suffers from similar issues such as poor scalability and limited design flexibility.
Based on existing literature, it can be inferred that Gr-integrated Cu-based porous current collectors offer a highly promising solution to overcoming the long-standing challenges associated with LMBs. The incorporation of ME-AM technique has the potential to further elevate their performance by enabling precise structural control and material distribution. This capability allows the fabrication of optimized structures that facilitate uniform Li-ion transport, improve electron conduction, and promote stable Li plating/stripping. However, to the best of our knowledge, very limited work has been conducted on the development of graphene-integrated porous Cu current collectors through ME-AM for LMBs applications, leaving significant scope for further investigation. In this work, we address this critical gap by developing a high-performance 3DP-Copper Graphene Current Collector(3DP-CGCC) through ME-AM. A high-solid-loading Copper–Graphene (Cu-Gr) composite ink containing 95
wt.% Cu and Gr contents (0.2 wt.%) was successfully formulated with optimized rheological characteristics to ensure stable extrusion, excellent printability, and high shape fidelity. The developed ink enabled the fabrication of hierarchically porous Cu–Gr current collectors with well-defined architectures, offering improved electrical conductivity and electrochemical performance. The effect of Gr on the rheological behaviour, printability, microstructure, electrical conductivity was systematically investigated. Comprehensive structural, morphological, electrical, and electrochemical characterizations demonstrated that the optimized 3DP-CGCC effectively regulates Li deposition, and enables highly reversible Li plating/stripping, highlighting its potential as a durable current collector for high-performance LMBs. Hence, through this study, a viable approach and scalable pathway toward next-generation LMB technologies have been presented.

\#\# Published by\: Elsevier

\#\#\# Published by

\#\# Highlights

\- •Developed a high solid loading \(≥95 wt\%\) Cu–Gr ink\.
\- •Material Extrusion Additive Manufacturing fabricated 3DP Cu–Gr current collectors\.
\- •Current collector showed 98\.8\% efficiency over 700 h at 1mAcm⁻2\, plating 5mAhcm−2\.
\- •Full cell showed 139mAhg⁻1\, \~99\% efficiency at 0\.5C and excellent rate performance\.
\- •COMSOL simulation results confirmed homogeneous Li deposition at 1 and 3 mAcm⁻2\.

\#\# Abstract

Porous copper current collectors help mitigate key challenges in Lithium Metal Batteries \(LMB\)\, including volume changes\, unstable SEI formation\, and dendritic lithium growth\. However\, further structural optimization along with manufacturing innovation is required to achieve improved electrochemical performance and long\-term stability\. Hence\, this work presents a high\-performance 3D Porous Copper Graphene Current Collector \(3DP\-CGCC\) fabricated via Material Extrusion Additive Manufacturing \(ME\-AM\) for advanced LMB applications\. A novel Copper\-Graphene ink with high copper particle loading \(≥95
wt\.\%\) and graphene loading \(0\.2 wt\.\%\) has been formulated for ME\-AM process\. Rheological investigations revealed pronounced shear\-thinning and viscoelastic characteristics\, enabling excellent printability and shape retention\. This optimized ink facilitated the fabrication of a 3DP\-CGCC with uniform pore size of 190 ± 3 μm\, providing precise regulation of Li\-ions transport\. Furthermore\, incorporation of graphene resulted in \~9\% increase in electrical conductivity compared with 3D Porous Copper Current Collector \(3DP\-CCC\)\. Owing to this synergistic architectural and compositional design\, 3DP\-CGCC delivered exceptional electrochemical performance\, achieving a coulombic efficiency of \~98\.8\% for over 700 h with CD 1 mAcm⁻2 at plating capacity 5 mAhcm⁻2\. The EIS results reveal lower charge transfer resistance compared with 3DP\-CCC and Cu Foil\. COMSOL simulations confirmed homogeneous current distribution and uniform Li deposition at 1 and 3 mAcm⁻2\. The Li\@3DP\-CGCC\|\|LFP full cell delivered stable cycling \(\~139 mAhg⁻1 at 0\.5C\) and superior rate capability\, demonstrating excellent practical applicability\. Overall\, this study demonstrates an advanced 3DP\-CGCC integrated with a scalable manufacturing strategy\, offering a promising pathway toward the development of next\-generation LMB systems\.

\#\# Introduction

Lithium \(
Li\) metal is one of most advanced anode material for next\-generation Lithium Metal Battery \(LMB\) due to its exceptionally high specific capacity \(\~3860 mAhg−1\) and low reduction potential of −3\.04 V versus SHE\. Despite its potential\, key limitations like volume fluctuation during charging and discharging\, unstable Solid Electrolyte Interface \(SEI\) and uncontrollable Lidendrites growth hinder its practical applications \[1\]\, \[2\]\, \[3\]\. The current collector typically a flat copper \(Cu\) foil is widely used in LMBs due to its high electrical conductivity\, better mechanical robustness\, and stability with Li\-ions\. However\, its flat surface provides limited Li\-ions nucleation sites\, localized Current Density \(CD\) and unstable SEI formation resulting in aforesaid mentioned problems with LMBs and poor Coulombic Efficiency \(CE\) \[4\]\, \[5\]\. To overcome these limitations\, researchers have explored 3D structured Cu current collectors such as foams\, meshes\, and scaffolds \[6\]\, \[7\]\. Commonly used manufacturing techniques for preparing such structures includes hydrogen bubble dynamic template process \[8\]\, asymmetric coating strategy process \[9\]\, pulsed electrodeposition process \[10\]\, chemical etching \[11\]\, alloying\/dealloying processes \[6\]\, \[7\]\. and NaCl\-templated\/powder\-sintering method \[12\]\. While these 3D structured Cu current collectors reduce local CD and accommodate Li deposition\, they often suffer from low mechanical robustness and limited electrical conductivity\. Also\, these methods can involve multiple processing steps\, specialized equipment\, and corrosive or hazardous chemicals\, which may increase fabrication complexity\, and challenges associated with achieving tuned porosity\. This problem can be addressed by use of additive manufacturing \(AM\) process for the fabricating of 3D porous Cu current collectors\.
Different AM techniques\, such as laser powder bed fusion \(LPBF\)\, electron beam melting \(EBM\)\, and directed energy deposition \(DED\)\, have been employed to fabricate complex Cu components\. However\, the high equipment and processing costs\, together with the challenges associated with processing Cu due to its high laser reflectivity and thermal conductivity\, limit the suitability of these techniques for fabricating 3DP Cu current collectors \[13\]\, \[14\]\, \[15\]\. Moreover\, powder handling issues with these AM processes further restrict their use for battery application\. To address these limitations\, beamless AM techniques\, particularly binder jetting and material extrusion additive manufacturing \(ME\-AM\) have emerged as alternative approaches for fabricating 3DP Cu current collectors\' structures for LMB applications \[8\]\. Although binder jetting offers considerable geometric freedom\, challenges associated with powder handling\, achieving sufficient green strength\, and the need for de\-binding and sintering can complicate the fabrication of self\-supporting porous Cu architectures \[16\]\. In contrast\, ME\-AM enables the direct deposition of highly loaded\, viscous Cu\-based inks\, facilitating the fabrication of self\-supporting structures with interconnected pores and tuneable architectures\. Its relatively simple equipment requirements\, efficient material utilization\, and digital design flexibility make ME\-AM a promising approach for producing 3DP Cu current collectors for LMB applications \[17\]\. Nevertheless\, its scalability and overall cost\-effectiveness depend on printing throughput\, ink formulation\, and post\-processing requirements\.

Hierarchically porous three\-dimensional Cu current collectors fabricated via ME\-AM have demonstrated more uniform current distribution\, homogeneous Li\-ion transport\, suppressed dendritic Li growth\, and improved coulombic efficiency \(CE\) \[18\]\, \[19\]\. A previous study demonstrated that\, 3D porous copper current collector \(3DP\-CCC\) fabricated using ME\-AM process exhibited average CE of 95\.5\% with cycling time of more than 450
h at CD of 1 mAcm−2 with plated capacity 5 mAhcm−2 \[17\]\. Though 3DP\-CCC exhibited good electrochemical performance \(CE and cyclic stability\)\, but still\, there is considerable scope for improvement\. This improvement in electrochemical performance can be achieved by the incorporation of highly electrically conductive carbon additives likes carbon nanofibers\, carbon nanotubes \(CNT\) and Graphene \(Gr\) \[20\]\, \[21\]\, \[22\]\. Among these additives\, Gr is often the superior filler for Cu matrix because of its ultra\-high electrical conductivity \(105–107 Sm⁻1\)\, 2D sheet structure \(very high specific surface area 2630 m2\/g\)\, very high mechanical strength \(130 GPa\)\, and less loading requirement to achieve percolation \[23\]\, \[24\]\, \[25\]\, \[26\]\. Addition of Gr into Cu scaffold\, effectively improves the electrical conductivity owing to bridging of the gap between Cu particles\. Moreover\, the large specific surface area of Gr sheets provides abundant electrochemically active sites for Li\-ion deposition\, effectively reducing the local CD and promoting uniform Li plating\. This ultimately leads to reduced Li dendrite formation\, improved electron mobility\, enhanced electron transport kinetics and overall percolation network \[27\]\, \[28\]\, \[29\]\. Some studies have reported notable improvements in CE with Gr\-integrated Cu based anode \[27\]\, \[30\]\, \[31\]\. The r\-GO modified Cu foam achieved \~98\.5\% CE over 350 cycles\, attributed to its porous conductive network and uniform Li deposition behaviour\. Similarly\, \(Cu3P\)\/r\-GO and CuO\/GO hybrid anodes exhibited rapid CE stabilization \(\>98\% and \> 90\%\, respectively\)\, driven by enhanced electron transport\, SEI stability\, and effective suppression of parasitic reaction\. However\, aforesaid mentioned Gr\-integrated Cu current collectors were fabricated using conventional techniques that suffers from similar issues such as poor scalability and limited design flexibility\.
Based on existing literature\, it can be inferred that Gr\-integrated Cu\-based porous current collectors offer a highly promising solution to overcoming the long\-standing challenges associated with LMBs\. The incorporation of ME\-AM technique has the potential to further elevate their performance by enabling precise structural control and material distribution\. This capability allows the fabrication of optimized structures that facilitate uniform Li\-ion transport\, improve electron conduction\, and promote stable Li plating\/stripping\. However\, to the best of our knowledge\, very limited work has been conducted on the development of graphene\-integrated porous Cu current collectors through ME\-AM for LMBs applications\, leaving significant scope for further investigation\. In this work\, we address this critical gap by developing a high\-performance 3DP\-Copper Graphene Current Collector\(3DP\-CGCC\) through ME\-AM\. A high\-solid\-loading Copper–Graphene \(Cu\-Gr\) composite ink containing 95
wt\.\% Cu and Gr contents \(0\.2 wt\.\%\) was successfully formulated with optimized rheological characteristics to ensure stable extrusion\, excellent printability\, and high shape fidelity\. The developed ink enabled the fabrication of hierarchically porous Cu–Gr current collectors with well\-defined architectures\, offering improved electrical conductivity and electrochemical performance\. The effect of Gr on the rheological behaviour\, printability\, microstructure\, electrical conductivity was systematically investigated\. Comprehensive structural\, morphological\, electrical\, and electrochemical characterizations demonstrated that the optimized 3DP\-CGCC effectively regulates Li deposition\, and enables highly reversible Li plating\/stripping\, highlighting its potential as a durable current collector for high\-performance LMBs\. Hence\, through this study\, a viable approach and scalable pathway toward next\-generation LMB technologies have been presented\.

records.title: Analytical and Experimental Assessment of the Effect of Current Harmonics on the Heating of a Flat Rectangular Busbar
records.abstract: Higher harmonics can increase conductor temperature even when the total current root mean square (RMS) value remains unchanged, because Joule losses depend on frequency and the spatial distribution of current density. This study develops a compact analytical model of the heating of an isolated, flat rectangular copper busbar and assesses its predictions against laboratory measurements. A one-dimensional solution of the electromagnetic field and heat conduction equation yields a dimensionless heating coefficient for each harmonic and a weighted superposition rule for an arbitrary spectrum. The experimental assessment was limited to a copper busbar with a cross-section of 40 mm × 10 mm at a current of approximately 400 A with temperature rise predictions referenced to the 50 Hz experiment. Eight measurement tests covered four spectra with a fundamental frequency of 50 Hz and single-frequency excitations from 100 to 250 Hz. Nine temperature channels and the actual current spectra were recorded. For the controlled mixed spectra, the relative error of the analytical prediction with respect to the measured relative temperature rise ranged from −3.1% to +0.4%. Under excitation at 100–250 Hz, the analytical model underestimated the measured rise by 3.4–8.8%. The model can be useful for rapidly assessing the effect of harmonic spectra on the ampacity of strip conductors.
records.summary: This paper develops a compact one-dimensional analytical model of the heating of an isolated flat rectangular copper busbar carrying distorted (harmonic) current, and assesses it against laboratory measurements. A 1D solution of the electromagnetic field and heat conduction equations yields a dimensionless heating coefficient for each harmonic and a weighted superposition rule for an arbitrary spectrum, so that the temperature rise can be referenced to that produced by a DC current of the same RMS value. The experimental assessment used a 40 mm × 10 mm copper busbar at approximately 400 A, with eight tests covering four 50 Hz-based spectra and single-frequency excitations from 100 to 250 Hz, recording nine temperature channels and the actual current spectra. For the controlled mixed spectra, the relative error of the analytical prediction with respect to the measured relative temperature rise ranged from −3.1% to +0.4%; under 100–250 Hz excitation the model underestimated the measured rise by 3.4–8.8%. The authors conclude the model can support rapid preliminary assessment of harmonic effects on strip-conductor ampacity, while noting it was not validated for arbitrary spectra, other geometries, or different cooling conditions.
records.why_it_matters: The model gives a closed-form, spectrum-weighted heating coefficient that lets engineers quickly flag when equal-RMS harmonic currents are not thermally equivalent, indicating when detailed numerical modeling or direct temperature testing is warranted for busbar ampacity.

Analytical and Experimental Assessment of the Effect of Current Harmonics on the Heating of a Flat Rectangular Busbar
and
Faculty of Electrical Engineering, Częstochowa University of Technology, 42-201 Częstochowa, Poland
Author to whom correspondence should be addressed.
Abstract
Higher harmonics can increase conductor temperature even when the total current root mean square (RMS) value remains unchanged, because Joule losses depend on frequency and the spatial distribution of current density. This study develops a compact analytical model of the heating of an isolated, flat rectangular copper busbar and assesses its predictions against laboratory measurements. A one-dimensional solution of the electromagnetic field and heat conduction equation yields a dimensionless heating coefficient for each harmonic and a weighted superposition rule for an arbitrary spectrum. The experimental assessment was limited to a copper busbar with a cross-section of 40 mm × 10 mm at a current of approximately 400 A with temperature rise predictions referenced to the 50 Hz experiment. Eight measurement tests covered four spectra with a fundamental frequency of 50 Hz and single-frequency excitations from 100 to 250 Hz. Nine temperature channels and the actual current spectra were recorded. For the controlled mixed spectra, the relative error of the analytical prediction with respect to the measured relative temperature rise ranged from −3.1% to +0.4%. Under excitation at 100–250 Hz, the analytical model underestimated the measured rise by 3.4–8.8%. The model can be useful for rapidly assessing the effect of harmonic spectra on the ampacity of strip conductors.
1. Introduction
The growth of power electronic energy conversion has increased the importance of analyzing distorted currents in industrial distribution systems. Relationships between circuit parameters and current distortion have been considered in an analytical model of a single-phase circuit with an inductance and a rectifier bridge [1] in a simulation analysis of a single-phase circuit with a nonlinear load [2]. Radwan-Pragłowska et al. [3] analyzed the effect of harmonics on active power losses and temperature distribution in power cables. IEEE 519-2022 [4] specifies requirements for limiting harmonic distortion at the point of common coupling, while IEEE 1459-2025 [5] defines the quantities used in power measurements under sinusoidal and non-sinusoidal conditions. From a thermal design perspective, however, both waveform distortion and the frequency-dependent losses associated with individual current components are relevant. Thus, two currents with the same root mean square (RMS) value can produce different conductor losses and different steady-state temperatures.
Under direct current, the current density in a homogeneous conductor is approximately uniform away from connections and geometric discontinuities. As frequency increases, the skin effect shifts the current toward the surface, while nearby conductors and return paths cause additional nonuniformity in current density through the proximity effect. The effective AC resistance therefore depends on frequency, conductor shape, material properties, and the electromagnetic environment. Classical solutions for winding layers and isolated rectangular conductors established the basic analytical framework for this problem [6,7], and improved loss models for windings in magnetic components explained how field solutions can be translated into engineering resistance factors [8]. These results remain directly applicable to busbars because a wide strip can be treated locally as a one-dimensional (1D) slab when its width is much greater than its thickness and the return conductor is sufficiently far away.
Early studies of cables carrying harmonic currents showed that an assessment based solely on total RMS current can underestimate the effect of distortion on temperature and ampacity. Meliopoulos and Martin presented a simplified procedure for calculating additional losses and cable ampacity in the presence of harmonics [9], while O’Connell et al. described correction factors and heating tests for cables carrying harmonic currents [10]. Subsequent studies using finite element and thermal methods considered insulation systems and cable configurations under non-sinusoidal currents [11]. Recent measurement studies emphasize the need for a frequency-dependent resistance model in harmonic power flow analysis [12]. These studies share a common conclusion: Parseval’s relation correctly determines the total RMS current but does not assign the same loss multiplier to all spectral components.
Research on busbars has developed in several complementary directions. Coneybeer et al. formulated steady-state and transient busbar ampacity models [13]. Du et al. combined experiments with numerical analysis of busbar system impedance [14]. Plesca analyzed heat transfer in a high-current power supply system [15]. Measurements and simulations of a low-voltage switchgear showed that airflow within the enclosure, joints, supports, and three-dimensional geometry strongly affect the resulting temperatures [16]. More recent multiphysics studies determined electrothermal field distributions in busbars under various operating conditions [17]. Alboyaci et al. directly investigated non-sinusoidal operation of a busbar system, demonstrating that both the current waveform and the construction affect thermal performance [18].
Studies of round conductors provide additional context: Jabłoński et al. presented an analytical–numerical solution for the skin and proximity effects in two parallel conductors [19], Zaręba et al. analyzed the thermal field of such a system [20], and Jabłoński et al. considered the thermal field in three-phase systems with flat and triangular arrangements [21]. These studies concern geometries other than the busbar considered here but indicate the range of issues associated with accounting for adjacent conductors.
Issues extending beyond a single-busbar model also include the effect of contact resistance on joint temperature monitoring in an insulated busbar system [22], coupled thermal processes in laboratory switchgear [23], and methods for conducting temperature rise tests on switchgear assemblies [24]. IEC 60287-1-1:2023 [25] provides standardized calculations of steady-state cable ampacity and losses; its scope concerns cables and does not provide a direct verification procedure for the busbar analyzed here.
Most detailed busbar studies, however, use the finite element method, computational fluid dynamics, or lumped thermal networks. These approaches are essential for the final design of an actual assembly but do not always reveal the contribution of a specific harmonic order to the resulting temperature. Closed-form field solutions, in turn, provide transparent scaling laws, but are often presented as AC resistance relationships rather than as a temperature rise coefficient for an arbitrary measured spectrum.
This study addresses that gap. A 1D electromagnetic and thermal model is developed in analytical form for a single wide rectangular busbar, the contribution of each harmonic is expressed relative to the temperature rise caused by a direct current of the same RMS value, and the resulting superposition rule is experimentally verified. The derived coefficient can serve as a rapid and physically interpretable preliminary assessment tool: it indicates when currents of equal RMS value cease to be thermally equivalent and identifies spectra that require more detailed modeling or direct temperature tests.
Section 2 presents the modeling assumptions, test specimen, test program, and data processing method. Section 3 derives the analytical relationships and illustrates them with examples. Section 4 presents the experimental results and compares them with the theory. Section 5 provides detailed conclusions from the work completed to date.
2. Modeling Assumptions, Methodology, and Test Specimen
This study was conducted in two stages. First, the 1D electromagnetic field and heat conduction problem was solved for a single wide busbar, yielding relationships that can be applied to a measured spectrum. Next, a series of heating tests was performed on a 40 mm × 10 mm copper busbar, temperatures and current waveforms were recorded, normalized harmonic spectrum amplitudes were determined, and relative temperature rises were compared. Detailed derivations are presented in Section 3, and the experimental results are reported in Section 4.

2.2. Laboratory Setup and Tests
The test specimen was a bare copper busbar with a cross-section of 40 mm × 10 mm, mounted on insulating supports with its longitudinal axis horizontal and its wider cross-sectional dimension vertical (Figure 2). The strip conductor (1) was supplied by a programmable distorted-voltage source N4L N4A30 (Newton4th Ltd., Leicester, UK) (6) through a single-phase isolation transformer (3) to step down the voltage. The current was measured with a 1146B KEY S probe (Keysight Technologies, Santa Rosa, CA, USA) and monitored with a Benning CM8 true RMS meter (BENNING, Bocholt, Germany), while the voltage, reference signal, and current waveforms were recorded with a DS1054Z digital oscilloscope (RIGOL Technologies Co., Ltd., Suzhou, China) (4). Temperature was measured using a nine-channel logger (PMP-201/EMT-200, CZAKI Thermo-Product Sp. z o.o., Raszyn-Rybie, Poland) (5) with thermocouples (2) positioned at different points on the busbar. The busbar was 4 m long, and the thermocouples were placed uniformly along the busbar starting 1 m from the ends of the busbar (supply joints). Three insulating supports were positioned 0.8 m from the busbar ends and in the busbar middle.
Figure 2. Laboratory setup: 1—40 mm × 10 mm copper busbar under test; 2—nine temperature measurement points; 3—single-phase isolation transformer; 4—Rigol DS1054Z oscilloscope; 5—Czaki PMP 201/EMT 200 multichannel temperature meter and logger; 6—N4L N4A30 programmable voltage source; 7—high-current circuit conductors; 8—hps SystemTechnik 8626 isolation transformer.
Type B uncertainty contributions were estimated from the manufacturers’ specifications, assuming rectangular distributions within the stated error limits. The CZAKI EMT-200 temperature meter has a resolution of 0.1 °C and a specified indication error limit of ±0.47 °C at approximately 35 °C, corresponding to a standard uncertainty of 0.27 K. For the BENNING CM8, the standard uncertainty contributions at 400 A are 3.75 A (0.94%) for 50 Hz and 6.06 A (1.52%) for 100–250 Hz.
The experiments were conducted in a laboratory with the windows and doors closed and without air conditioning. The ambient temperature was determined based on the initial busbar temperature reading. The busbar was cooled under natural convection conditions. The sensing tips of the nine temperature probes were in direct contact with the copper surface of the busbar and were secured using strips of electrical insulating tape.
Each test lasted approximately three hours and included 272–287 temperature samples, corresponding to a sampling interval of approximately 38 s. Four tests used a 50 Hz fundamental component with different harmonic combinations. Further tests were performed with single-frequency excitation at 100, 150, 200, and 250 Hz (Table 1). Oscilloscope records were available at the beginning, middle, and/or end of each test. After removal of the DC component, the measured current was decomposed by the least squares method into harmonics up to order 10 relative to 50 Hz. This approach reduces the effect of a slight mismatch between the record length and an integer number of periods and allows the RMS value to be reconstructed. For each harmonic, the average across the available measurement stages was calculated. The standard deviation between stages describes the short-term repeatability of the measured current rather than the full uncertainty of the instrumentation.

For the four experiments with a 50 Hz fundamental frequency and the 100 Hz experiment, the exported data sampling frequency was 20 kHz and the record duration was 60 ms. For the 150, 200, and 250 Hz experiments, these values were 50 kHz and 24 ms, respectively. Record duration was defined as the number of samples multiplied by the sampling interval. The corresponding oscilloscope hardware sampling frequencies were 50 and 125 MHz.

4.2. Interpretation of the Results and Discussion of the Discrepancies
For the mixed spectra at 50 Hz, the relative error of the predictions with respect to the measurements are approximately 0.43%, −3.08%, and −0.18%. For these spectra, the model predicts a small increase in heating of approximately 0.13%, 0.21%, and 0.17%, respectively, relative to the reference test. For excitations at 100–250 Hz, the errors are negative and range from approximately −8.80% to −3.42%, with the largest absolute value at 250 Hz. The model reproduces the direction of the frequency effect but underestimates the temperature rise in these tests. Equation (19) sums the contributions of the individual frequencies after the losses are averaged over time. The phase angles do not appear in the result under the assumed constant properties and linear heat equation.
Differences between measurements and calculations may result from deflections from the assumptions of the 1D model:
- Finite width and current crowding at the edges;
- Losses and heat flow in connections and joints;
- The increase in copper resistance with temperature;
- Neglecting the heat exchange across the shorter sides and nonlinear natural convection and radiation;
- The proximity effect caused by transformer leads, the return path, and neighboring conductors;
- Longitudinal nonuniformity of the system sampled by the nine sensors.
Some of the limitations were removed due to referencing the results to those for pure sinusoid 50 Hz. Most of the limitations can be removed by using suitable numerical calculations. However, they make it impossible to obtain analytical formulas, which was the aim of the paper. Therefore, being aware of the limitations, we will briefly discuss each of them.

Ad. 3. The predictions in Table 3 are referenced to the measured temperature rise at 50 Hz. The temperature differences between particular test configurations were up to 3.4 K; therefore, the change in resistance was below 1.5%:

Ad. 5. The proximity effects due to the return conductor and other equipment were eliminated due to placing the busbar far from them (around 1 m; see Figure 2).

Hou et al. [17] investigated the busbar system of a 500 kA aluminum electrolysis cell and reported temperature calculation errors within 8% for riser busbars and below 6% for cast busbars. Alboyacı et al. [18] reported harmonic current loading limits of 20–25% for a single-neutral configuration, 22–39% for a double-neutral configuration, and 39–44% for conductors with cross-sections increased by 25%, depending on phase arrangement. In the present study, the relative errors of the predictions with respect to the measured temperature rises were −3.08% to +0.43% for the mixed spectra and −8.80% to −3.42% for the 100–250 Hz tests. These results concern different geometries, operating conditions, and reported quantities; therefore, they provide quantitative context rather than a direct ranking of model accuracy.
5. Conclusions
The following conclusions can be drawn from the study:
- Sinusoidal current flowing through a strip conductor produces a temperature rise times that produced by a DC current equal to the RMS value of the current under consideration. This is caused by the nonuniform current density resulting from the skin effect.
- The coefficient depends on the dimensionless parameter , which is determined by the frequency, material properties, and conductor thickness. For , the heating is close to that produced by DC current, whereas for ,  holds.
- Distorted current flowing through a strip conductor produces a temperature rise times that produced by a DC current equal to the RMS value of the current under consideration. The heating coefficient  is a weighted sum of the expressions , with weights equal to the squares of the normalized RMS values of the harmonic currents, while  is the relative dimensionless skin-effect parameter for the fundamental harmonic.
- The derived heating coefficient shows that equal RMS currents are generally not thermally equivalent. Total harmonic distortion (THD) is not a sufficient indicator either. This is because different harmonics yield different values of and, consequently, a different heating coefficient . For distorted current, the heating coefficient is a function of both the dimensionless skin-effect parameter and the entire current harmonic spectrum.
- The experimental comparisons were limited to the investigated 40 mm × 10 mm copper busbar, the eight tested excitation conditions, and the laboratory cooling arrangement. Predictions were referenced to the 50 Hz experiment. For the mixed spectra, the relative errors of the predictions with respect to the measurements ranged from −3.08% to +0.43%; for the 100–250 Hz tests, they ranged from −8.80% to −3.42%. The results support the observed frequency dependence of heating but do not conclusively resolve the small predicted changes of approximately 0.13–0.21% between the mixed spectra and the reference case. The experimental assessment therefore does not establish validity for arbitrary spectra, other conductor geometries, or different cooling conditions. The DC reference and ampacity relationships remain as theoretical predictions that were not directly tested experimentally.
The analytical 1D model assumes constant material properties, a 1D current density distribution, 1D heat conduction, equal heat transfer coefficients at both surfaces, and negligible cooling at the narrower sides of the conductor. Therefore, one should not expect that its predictions will be very accurate, especially when
A natural next step is a 2D electromagnetic solution coupled to a reduced thermal network and calibrated using the same measured spectra. Further research should include other current spectra, conductors with different cross-sections, and controlled arrangements of neighboring conductors to enable assessment of the proximity effect.

Early studies of cables carrying harmonic currents showed that an assessment based solely on total RMS current can underestimate the effect of distortion on temperature and ampacity\. Meliopoulos and Martin presented a simplified procedure for calculating additional losses and cable ampacity in the presence of harmonics \[9\]\, while O’Connell et al\. described correction factors and heating tests for cables carrying harmonic currents \[10\]\. Subsequent studies using finite element and thermal methods considered insulation systems and cable configurations under non\-sinusoidal currents \[11\]\. Recent measurement studies emphasize the need for a frequency\-dependent resistance model in harmonic power flow analysis \[12\]\. These studies share a common conclusion\: Parseval’s relation correctly determines the total RMS current but does not assign the same loss multiplier to all spectral components\.

Research on busbars has developed in several complementary directions\. Coneybeer et al\. formulated steady\-state and transient busbar ampacity models \[13\]\. Du et al\. combined experiments with numerical analysis of busbar system impedance \[14\]\. Plesca analyzed heat transfer in a high\-current power supply system \[15\]\. Measurements and simulations of a low\-voltage switchgear showed that airflow within the enclosure\, joints\, supports\, and three\-dimensional geometry strongly affect the resulting temperatures \[16\]\. More recent multiphysics studies determined electrothermal field distributions in busbars under various operating conditions \[17\]\. Alboyaci et al\. directly investigated non\-sinusoidal operation of a busbar system\, demonstrating that both the current waveform and the construction affect thermal performance \[18\]\.

Studies of round conductors provide additional context\: Jabłoński et al\. presented an analytical–numerical solution for the skin and proximity effects in two parallel conductors \[19\]\, Zaręba et al\. analyzed the thermal field of such a system \[20\]\, and Jabłoński et al\. considered the thermal field in three\-phase systems with flat and triangular arrangements \[21\]\. These studies concern geometries other than the busbar considered here but indicate the range of issues associated with accounting for adjacent conductors\.

Issues extending beyond a single\-busbar model also include the effect of contact resistance on joint temperature monitoring in an insulated busbar system \[22\]\, coupled thermal processes in laboratory switchgear \[23\]\, and methods for conducting temperature rise tests on switchgear assemblies \[24\]\. IEC 60287\-1\-1\:2023 \[25\] provides standardized calculations of steady\-state cable ampacity and losses\; its scope concerns cables and does not provide a direct verification procedure for the busbar analyzed here\.

Most detailed busbar studies\, however\, use the finite element method\, computational fluid dynamics\, or lumped thermal networks\. These approaches are essential for the final design of an actual assembly but do not always reveal the contribution of a specific harmonic order to the resulting temperature\. Closed\-form field solutions\, in turn\, provide transparent scaling laws\, but are often presented as AC resistance relationships rather than as a temperature rise coefficient for an arbitrary measured spectrum\.

This study addresses that gap\. A 1D electromagnetic and thermal model is developed in analytical form for a single wide rectangular busbar\, the contribution of each harmonic is expressed relative to the temperature rise caused by a direct current of the same RMS value\, and the resulting superposition rule is experimentally verified\. The derived coefficient can serve as a rapid and physically interpretable preliminary assessment tool\: it indicates when currents of equal RMS value cease to be thermally equivalent and identifies spectra that require more detailed modeling or direct temperature tests\.

Section 2 presents the modeling assumptions\, test specimen\, test program\, and data processing method\. Section 3 derives the analytical relationships and illustrates them with examples\. Section 4 presents the experimental results and compares them with the theory\. Section 5 provides detailed conclusions from the work completed to date\.

\#\# 2\. Modeling Assumptions\, Methodology\, and Test Specimen

This study was conducted in two stages\. First\, the 1D electromagnetic field and heat conduction problem was solved for a single wide busbar\, yielding relationships that can be applied to a measured spectrum\. Next\, a series of heating tests was performed on a 40 mm × 10 mm copper busbar\, temperatures and current waveforms were recorded\, normalized harmonic spectrum amplitudes were determined\, and relative temperature rises were compared\. Detailed derivations are presented in Section 3\, and the experimental results are reported in Section 4\.

\#\#\# 2\.2\. Laboratory Setup and Tests

The test specimen was a bare copper busbar with a cross\-section of 40 mm × 10 mm\, mounted on insulating supports with its longitudinal axis horizontal and its wider cross\-sectional dimension vertical \(Figure 2\)\. The strip conductor \(1\) was supplied by a programmable distorted\-voltage source N4L N4A30 \(Newton4th Ltd\.\, Leicester\, UK\) \(6\) through a single\-phase isolation transformer \(3\) to step down the voltage\. The current was measured with a 1146B KEY S probe \(Keysight Technologies\, Santa Rosa\, CA\, USA\) and monitored with a Benning CM8 true RMS meter \(BENNING\, Bocholt\, Germany\)\, while the voltage\, reference signal\, and current waveforms were recorded with a DS1054Z digital oscilloscope \(RIGOL Technologies Co\.\, Ltd\.\, Suzhou\, China\) \(4\)\. Temperature was measured using a nine\-channel logger \(PMP\-201\/EMT\-200\, CZAKI Thermo\-Product Sp\. z o\.o\.\, Raszyn\-Rybie\, Poland\) \(5\) with thermocouples \(2\) positioned at different points on the busbar\. The busbar was 4 m long\, and the thermocouples were placed uniformly along the busbar starting 1 m from the ends of the busbar \(supply joints\)\. Three insulating supports were positioned 0\.8 m from the busbar ends and in the busbar middle\.

\#\#\# 2\.3\. Processing of Current and Temperature Records

Oscilloscope records were available at the beginning\, middle\, and\/or end of each test\. After removal of the DC component\, the measured current was decomposed by the least squares method into harmonics up to order 10 relative to 50 Hz\. This approach reduces the effect of a slight mismatch between the record length and an integer number of periods and allows the RMS value to be reconstructed\. For each harmonic\, the average across the available measurement stages was calculated\. The standard deviation between stages describes the short\-term repeatability of the measured current rather than the full uncertainty of the instrumentation\.

\#\#\# 4\.2\. Interpretation of the Results and Discussion of the Discrepancies

For the mixed spectra at 50 Hz\, the relative error of the predictions with respect to the measurements are approximately 0\.43\%\, −3\.08\%\, and −0\.18\%\. For these spectra\, the model predicts a small increase in heating of approximately 0\.13\%\, 0\.21\%\, and 0\.17\%\, respectively\, relative to the reference test\. For excitations at 100–250 Hz\, the errors are negative and range from approximately −8\.80\% to −3\.42\%\, with the largest absolute value at 250 Hz\. The model reproduces the direction of the frequency effect but underestimates the temperature rise in these tests\. Equation \(19\) sums the contributions of the individual frequencies after the losses are averaged over time\. The phase angles do not appear in the result under the assumed constant properties and linear heat equation\.

Differences between measurements and calculations may result from deflections from the assumptions of the 1D model\:

\- Finite width and current crowding at the edges\;
\- Losses and heat flow in connections and joints\;
\- The increase in copper resistance with temperature\;
\- Neglecting the heat exchange across the shorter sides and nonlinear natural convection and radiation\;
\- The proximity effect caused by transformer leads\, the return path\, and neighboring conductors\;
\- Longitudinal nonuniformity of the system sampled by the nine sensors\.

Some of the limitations were removed due to referencing the results to those for pure sinusoid 50 Hz\. Most of the limitations can be removed by using suitable numerical calculations\. However\, they make it impossible to obtain analytical formulas\, which was the aim of the paper\. Therefore\, being aware of the limitations\, we will briefly discuss each of them\.

\#\# 5\. Conclusions

The following conclusions can be drawn from the study\:

\- Sinusoidal current flowing through a strip conductor produces a temperature rise times that produced by a DC current equal to the RMS value of the current under consideration\. This is caused by the nonuniform current density resulting from the skin effect\.
\- The coefficient depends on the dimensionless parameter \, which is determined by the frequency\, material properties\, and conductor thickness\. For \, the heating is close to that produced by DC current\, whereas for \,  holds\.
\- Distorted current flowing through a strip conductor produces a temperature rise times that produced by a DC current equal to the RMS value of the current under consideration\. The heating coefficient  is a weighted sum of the expressions \, with weights equal to the squares of the normalized RMS values of the harmonic currents\, while  is the relative dimensionless skin\-effect parameter for the fundamental harmonic\.
\- The derived heating coefficient shows that equal RMS currents are generally not thermally equivalent\. Total harmonic distortion \(THD\) is not a sufficient indicator either\. This is because different harmonics yield different values of and\, consequently\, a different heating coefficient \. For distorted current\, the heating coefficient is a function of both the dimensionless skin\-effect parameter and the entire current harmonic spectrum\.
\- The experimental comparisons were limited to the investigated 40 mm × 10 mm copper busbar\, the eight tested excitation conditions\, and the laboratory cooling arrangement\. Predictions were referenced to the 50 Hz experiment\. For the mixed spectra\, the relative errors of the predictions with respect to the measurements ranged from −3\.08\% to \+0\.43\%\; for the 100–250 Hz tests\, they ranged from −8\.80\% to −3\.42\%\. The results support the observed frequency dependence of heating but do not conclusively resolve the small predicted changes of approximately 0\.13–0\.21\% between the mixed spectra and the reference case\. The experimental assessment therefore does not establish validity for arbitrary spectra\, other conductor geometries\, or different cooling conditions\. The DC reference and ampacity relationships remain as theoretical predictions that were not directly tested experimentally\.

The analytical 1D model assumes constant material properties\, a 1D current density distribution\, 1D heat conduction\, equal heat transfer coefficients at both surfaces\, and negligible cooling at the narrower sides of the conductor\. Further research should include other current spectra\, conductors with different cross\-sections\, and controlled arrangements of neighboring conductors to enable assessment of the proximity effect\.

records.body_text:
Celestica DS6005: 102.4-Tbit/s Switch with Co-Packaged Optics and Full Liquid Cooling
For network hardware used in AI clusters, simply adding more ports is no longer enough. Bandwidth, power consumption, cooling, and electrical signal paths are so closely interrelated that conventional switch architectures are increasingly reaching their technical limits. Celestica therefore introduced the DS6005 on October 12, 2026. The system combines the Broadcom Tomahawk 6 Davisson with Co-Packaged Optics, full liquid cooling, and a form factor designed for OCP Open Rack V3. According to the manufacturer, the DS6005 delivers 102,4 Tbit/s of switching capacity and provides 64 optical ports, each with a bandwidth of 1,6 Tbit/s. The platform is intended for AI data centers in which large accelerator clusters must communicate with high bandwidth and the lowest possible latency. Unlike conventional switches, the optical components are integrated directly next to the network chip.
The key difference lies in the optical architecture. Conventional network switches often use replaceable transceivers on the front of the device. Electrical signals must therefore travel from the switch ASIC along circuit-board traces to the corresponding modules. As data rates increase, this transmission path becomes increasingly demanding. Signal loss, electrical interference, and the signal conditioning required can increase power consumption. For the DS6005, Celestica uses Co-Packaged Optics, or CPO. The optical engines are located directly next to the switch ASIC. This shortens the electrical connection, while optical links carry signals over longer distances.
The manufacturer associates this architecture with higher bandwidth density, lower latency, and improved energy efficiency. No concrete independent measurements of the actual advantage over conventional 102,4-Tbit/s switches have been published to date. Celestica uses the Broadcom Tomahawk 6 Davisson as the central network chip. The switch provides 64 optical Ethernet ports, each with a bandwidth of 1,6 Tbit/s. This results in an aggregate interface capacity of 102,4 Tbit/s.
Feature | Celestica DS6005
---|---
Switch ASIC | Broadcom Tomahawk 6 Davisson
Switching capacity | 102,4 Tbit/s
Optical ports | 64 × 1,6 TbE
Optical architecture | Co-Packaged Optics
Form factor | 1,5 OU
Rack standard | OCP Open Rack V3
Cooling | Full liquid cooling
Network software | SONiC support
Laser modules | External and replaceable
Applications | AI data centers and AI fabrics
Power consumption | Not disclosed
However, optical integration introduces new requirements for packaging, cooling, and maintenance. While conventional transceivers can be replaced individually, integrated optical engines are more closely coupled to the network hardware itself. Celestica therefore uses external, replaceable laser modules. This is intended to keep at least part of the optical infrastructure serviceable. The system also supports software management tailored to the CPO architecture.
The DS6005 is fully liquid-cooled and was developed for the Open Compute Project’s Open Rack V3 concept. Its height is just 1,5 Open Units. This compact design is notable because the switch must accommodate both a high-performance network chip and numerous optical components. The resulting heat is intended to be removed by liquid cooling, enabling high rack density. Thermal integration is particularly important with Co-Packaged Optics. Optical engines and electronic circuits have different temperature requirements, so the cooling architecture must be designed accordingly.
Celestica has not yet disclosed either the total power consumption or the required coolant volume. As a result, the system’s energy efficiency cannot currently be compared independently with that of other high-performance switches. On the software side, the DS6005 supports the open network operating system SONiC. This is already used in large data centers and enables standardized management of different network platforms. This is an important consideration for operators, since new hardware should not necessarily require a completely new management system. Automated configuration, monitoring, and integration into existing workflows are just as relevant in large AI clusters as transmission speed itself.
Celestica explicitly positions the DS6005 for scale-up and scale-out networks. These require numerous accelerators and servers to communicate with high bandwidth. However, the actual requirements vary depending on the cluster architecture and the communication protocols used. The DS6005 demonstrates that Co-Packaged Optics is increasingly being integrated into actual system products. Its introduction does not, however, mean that conventional pluggable optical modules will disappear in the short term.
Serviceability, cost, and long-term reliability remain particularly important factors. Replacing individual transceivers is comparatively straightforward in conventional network equipment. More highly integrated optical components, by contrast, require different service concepts. Actual savings in power consumption and latency also depend on the complete system architecture. Without corresponding comparative measurements, the announced benefits remain manufacturer claims for now.
Conclusion
I consider the DS6005 an interesting development because Celestica brings together several important technologies in a concrete network platform. A switching capacity of 102,4 Tbit/s, Co-Packaged Optics, full liquid cooling, and SONiC support form a technically coherent combination for large AI clusters.
Whether this approach gains wider adoption, however, will depend on more than bandwidth alone. Serviceability and the energy efficiency actually achieved will be particularly important. Nevertheless, the DS6005 shows that networking technology for modern AI data centers is increasingly moving away from conventional switch concepts.

Celestica introduced a data-centre switch that uses co-packaged optics for AI networking fabrics, an approach that moves optical components much closer to the switching chip than in conventional designs.
This article explains the technology behind the launch, why AI workloads are pushing networking toward new designs and what must happen before the product matters commercially. It does not make a share-price call. The update also adds context for readers tracking the broader S&P/TSX Composite Index, where technology hardware has become a more prominent source of leadership.
Why Celestica Matters Now
AI workloads increase the demands placed on connections between processors, memory and storage. Training large models requires vast numbers of chips to exchange data constantly, and the network linking them can become a bottleneck if it cannot keep pace.
Celestica's switch launch is a confirmed product event. It shows the company applying its hardware-design capabilities to among the most technically demanding areas of data-centre infrastructure, rather than only manufacturing to customer specifications.
As data centres expand, networking equipment becomes an important factor in power use, heat and throughput. Operators facing limits on electricity supply are looking closely at every component that consumes power without directly performing computation.
The launch therefore lands in a conversation that extends well beyond Celestica, touching on how the entire industry plans to scale AI infrastructure over the next several years.
The Technology Link Explained Simply
In a conventional switch, data travels as electrical signals from the switching chip to pluggable optical modules at the front of the equipment, where it is converted to light for transmission over fibre. That electrical path consumes power and degrades signals at very high speeds.
Co-packaged optics places optical components on or very near the same package as the switching silicon. Shortening the electrical path can reduce power consumption and help maintain signal quality as data rates continue to rise.
For technology stocks readers, the link is that co-packaged optics represents a potential architectural shift. Companies able to design and build such systems reliably may be well placed if the approach becomes widely adopted.
The approach is not new as a concept, but commercial deployment at scale has been limited. Product launches like Celestica's indicate that the industry is moving closer to practical use.
Delivery Matters for Celestica
Adoption depends on customer qualification, system integration, reliability and manufacturing readiness. Data-centre operators typically test new networking hardware extensively before deploying it across production environments.
Serviceability is a practical concern. Pluggable optics can be replaced individually when they fail, while co-packaged designs may require different maintenance approaches, which operators will weigh carefully before committing.
Manufacturing complexity is another test. Integrating optics and electronics in a single package demands precise assembly, thermal management and testing, and yields need to be high enough to make volume production economical.
Readers can watch for disclosures on customer engagements, early deployments and production timelines as signs that the technology is moving from demonstration toward commercial use.
Readers following Celestica alongside other Canadian technology names can use the Technology Stocks page to explore related coverage without losing the focus on AI networking hardware.
How Technology Peers Are Positioned
Several semiconductor companies, networking vendors and hardware manufacturers are developing co-packaged optics products. Competition spans chip designers, optical component makers and system builders.
Comparisons are most useful when they consider power savings demonstrated in real deployments, reliability data and the breadth of customer adoption, rather than specifications announced at launch.
Some large technology companies design networking hardware in-house, which can limit the market for outside suppliers or create opportunities for partners able to manufacture those designs.
Industry standards will also influence competition. If common specifications emerge, they may broaden adoption while reducing the advantage of any single proprietary approach.
What Celestica Reveals Next
Quarterly results and investor commentary may include updates on customer interest, qualification milestones or early shipments related to the new switch.
Industry conferences and announcements from switching-chip suppliers can provide signals about the readiness of the broader co-packaged optics ecosystem.
Statements from large data-centre operators about network architecture choices will indicate how quickly demand for this type of equipment could grow.
Capital spending and capacity disclosures will show whether Celestica is preparing for volume production.
Uncertainty Facing Technology Names Now
New architectures often take longer to adopt than early enthusiasm suggests. Operators may continue using pluggable optics if they meet requirements at lower risk or cost.
Competitors with deeper resources or established customer relationships may capture a large share of early deployments.
Supply-chain constraints for specialised optical and semiconductor components could slow production ramp-ups.
Demand for AI networking depends on continued investment in data centres, which can shift with economic conditions and corporate priorities.
Celestica on Investor Radars
AI networking announcements draw strong search interest, and co-packaged optics has become a widely discussed term. The company's own releases provide the most reliable description of what has been launched.
The company name, ticker and co-packaged optics theme create a clear path into the story. Following later customer and revenue disclosures is the most useful next step.
Readers can also follow technical commentary from the wider industry, which helps place individual product claims in context.
Comparing announced capabilities with independently reported deployment results will eventually show how the technology performs in practice.
Long View for Technology Stocks
Over time, the significance of the switch will depend on whether co-packaged optics becomes a mainstream architecture and whether Celestica captures a meaningful share of that market.
For now, Celestica Inc. (TSX:CLS) Technology Celestica Inc. The strongest follow-up will draw on qualification milestones, deployment evidence and segment results over several quarters.
Readers may find it useful to track those measures rather than reacting to the launch announcement itself.

Lubrication Engineers Acquires BioBlend Renewable Resources
WICHITA, Kan. (October 19, 2026) – Lubrication Engineers, Inc. (“LE”), a leading developer and manufacturer of high-performance industrial lubricants and asset reliability solutions, today announced that it has acquired BioBlend Renewable Resources, LLC (“BioBlend”), an innovator of high-performance, bio-based lubricants.
BioBlend, with its comprehensive portfolio of bio-based and hybrid lubricants, helps its mining, marine, drilling and industrial customers reduce environmental impact without compromising performance. Its proprietary formulations, developed over nearly two decades, are used in demanding applications ranging from underground mining and dredging to fire-resistant hydraulic systems, and are trusted by customers who require reliability and regulatory compliance in sensitive operating environments.
This is LE’s fourth acquisition since partnering with Aurora Capital Partners in September 2023, following its acquisitions of Royal Purple Industrial, SWEPCO and RSC Bio Solutions. During this time, LE has significantly expanded its lubrication expertise with powerful new synthetic and sustainable product offerings. Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed.
About BioBlend Renewable Resources
Founded in 2007, BioBlend Renewable Resources, LLC develops and manufactures high-performance, bio-based lubricants for the mining, marine, drilling, food grade, and industrial markets. BioBlend’s proprietary hybrid and fully biodegradable formulations are engineered to match or exceed the performance of conventional petroleum-based products, giving customers a viable path to reduce environmental impact across demanding applications. The company operates from its manufacturing facility in Grundy Center, Iowa. For more information about BioBlend, visit: www.bioblend.com.

records.title: Data-Driven Modelling of an Electroplating Process
records.abstract: Electroplated zinc-nickel (Zn-Ni) coatings are commonly applied as corrosion protection for steel components in demanding industrial environments.
records.summary: This article reports a data-driven machine-learning study of an alkaline zinc-nickel (Zn-Ni) barrel electroplating process, aimed at improving process transparency and predictive control where process complexity and irregular chemical monitoring make resource efficiency difficult. The authors built a cyber-physical production system framework linking a controlled 20 L test bath (186 experiments with systematic variation of current density, temperature, Zn/Ni concentrations, barrel speed and coating time) to an industrial 13,000 L plant (151 coating batches across 43 part types). Supervised models (Random Forest, XGBoost, SVR, MLP, Linear Regression, Gaussian Process Regression, 1D-CNN) were trained using only routinely available industrial inputs to predict post-coating Zn and Ni bath concentrations (process level) and coating thickness, nickel ratio and a binary OK/NOK quality indicator (product level). In the test environment, reported best results included R2 = 87% (MAE 0.28 g/L) for Zn concentration, R2 = 91% (MAE 0.04 g/L) for Ni concentration, R2 = 88% (MAE 0.45 µm) for coating thickness, R2 = 86% (MAE 0.53%) for nickel ratio, and 92% accuracy for the binary quality classifier. On the industrial dataset alone, process-level Gaussian Process models reached R2 = 92% (Zn) and 94% (Ni), but augmenting with test data was not feasible because unrecorded zinc dosing from immersed anodes changed concentration dynamics; at product level, augmentation improved Random Forest performance (e.g., coating thickness R2 from 61% to 74%, nickel ratio from 35% to 74%, and quality ROC from 0.75 to 0.95).
records.why_it_matters: The study shows that transferability of ML models from lab to plant depends on whether the causal mechanism behind the target is recorded in both environments: product-level targets can benefit from experimental data augmentation, while process-level bath-concentration models require explicit logging of dosing interventions such as zinc anode immersion.
