Introduction
Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) is a Direct Energy Deposition (DED) method that uses an electric arc as a heat source to melt metal and create customized structures by depositing material layer by layer [1]. In recent years, there has been growing academic and industrial interest in research related to WAAM, highlighting its potential applications in the metal-mechanical industry, as well as its alignment with the principles of Industry 4.0 (I4.0) and Circular Economy [2], [3], [4], [5]. The advantages of this method include high deposition rates, energy and material efficiency, besides lower initial investment and material costs compared to other DED methods such as Powder Bed Fusion [6], [7], [8], [9].
However, at present, a full integration of the WAAM technique into the industry is still limited by different factors, some of them related to the mechanical properties of the manufactured parts [10], [11]. Due to the constant heat input during the deposition process, these components are subject to distortions and residual stress distribution [12], [13], [14] and exhibit heterogeneous areas with non-uniform microstructures and anisotropic properties which compromise their integrity [15], [16], [17], [18], [19]. Considering this, solutions have been sought to improve the microstructure and mechanical properties of parts printed using WAAM, with the aim of certifying such components for critical industrial applications [20], [21], [22]. These solutions range from the optimization of deposition parameters [23] to the application of post-heat treatments [24] and surface modification techniques such as Friction Stir Processing [25], Laser Shock Peening [26] or Plasma Spray Coating [27].
One of the most attractive applications offered by the WAAM method is tools manufacturing [28], [29], [30], [31]. Nevertheless, some steels used for tools and molds, such as AISI 4140, D2, or H13, have a carbon content greater than 0.3% which reduces the weldability and toughness of the parts at the end of the Additive Manufacturing (AM) process [32], making strict parameter controls necessary [33]. For instance, in the case of H13 steel manufactured via the WAAM method, inhomogeneity has been observed in different areas of the resulting parts [34], along with pores and voids [35] and anisotropic behavior. In response to this, other material options have been considered. For instance, Alimov et al. [36] used Maraging/precipitation-hardened steel 17-4PH, as an alternative for traditional hot-working steels, to manufacture hot-forming dies using WAAM method. To evaluate their performance, these molds were mounted on an SMS SPPE 6.3 screw press, and hot-forming processes were carried out with different levels of blow energy (50%, 70%, and 100%) and blows. At the end of the processes, no signs of wear or warping were detected on the dies.
Surface modification technologies can extend the service life of industrial machinery components by reducing potential failures caused by corrosion or wear, even increasing their surface hardness. Aluminizing, for example, is a surface modification treatment in which an aluminized layer is obtained, primarily enhancing the corrosion properties of the material where it is applied. This treatment is highly relevant for components where an increase in high-temperature oxidation resistance is desired. The first studies on the effect of aluminizing on parts manufactured using the WAAM technique have been reported in the literature. Such is the case of Gürol et al. [37], who evaluated the effect of the powder-pack aluminizing treatment on ER307 stainless steel components fabricated by the aforementioned method. The authors observed an increase in surface hardness and elastic modulus as well as an improvement in oxidation resistance in the range of 46–70%. Bölükbaşi et al. [38], on the other hand, evaluated the effect of aluminizing on Inconel 625, manufactured using the WAAM method, and also observed improvements in oxidation resistance. Both works reported stability of aluminide phases at temperatures exceeding 1000 °C.
Boriding, another example of surface modification technology, is a thermochemical process in which a boride layer is formed on the surface of a substrate through boron diffusion [39], [40]. Due to the growing interest in AM processes, research has begun to explore the feasibility and performance of this process in parts manufactured using WAAM methods. Günen et al. [41] performed a boriding process (980 °C for 1 h) on Inconel 625 superalloy parts produced by WAAM method and evaluated their hardness and tribological performance. They found that, after this treatment, there was an increase in surface hardness and an improvement in wear resistance, both at room temperature and elevated temperatures (500 °C). Additionally, there was a reduction in the coefficient of friction (CoF) compared to untreated samples. In a different study, Günen et al. [42] carried out a thermochemical treatment (1000 °C for 1 h) on 307ER stainless steel parts manufactured using WAAM method. This led to an improvement in tribological performance, with wear resistance increasing nearly 32 times at room temperature and 8 times at 500 °C. Balhara et al. [43] used ultra-fast boriding technique (1000 °C for 15 min) on 316 L stainless steel samples fabricated using a laser-based DED technique. They evaluated how different printing parameters (300 W and 450 W laser power with 40 J/mm and 95 J/mm linear energy, respectively) affect the morphology of the generated coatings and the hardness distribution in the samples. The sample printed at 300 W showed more uniform substrate hardness but greater coating variations, while the sample printed at 450 W exhibited higher surface hardness uniformity but greater substrate variation. Resendiz-Calderon et al. [44] simulated a WAAM-based repair process on AISI D2 tool steel by depositing ER308L stainless steel using Gas Tungsten Arc Welding, followed by a boriding treatment at 950 °C for 3 h to evaluate the resulting surface and tribological performance. It was found that the boride layer promotes a more homogeneous mechanical response between the repaired and unrepaired zones, as it reduces the hardness difference between both surfaces from 57% to less than 9%. Additionally, in reciprocating sliding tests, there was a reduction in total wear volume by approximately 80% and in the CoF by 25% due to the boriding process.
Low-carbon steels offer great potential for microstructure control through parameter adjustments in the WAAM process due to their low carbon content [45], [46]. However, their relatively low hardness results in reduced wear resistance and, consequently, inferior tribological performance compared to similar steels manufactured using conventional methods. Treatments such as boriding or aluminizing can enhance the surface hardness of treated components, however, the boride layer allows for achieving significantly higher values [47], [48], [49]. This substantial increase in hardness is desirable for improving wear resistance. Consequently, boriding was chosen as the treatment for this work because it focuses on studying tribological performance. Some studies on the effect of boriding on low-carbon steels have been conducted, evaluating their mechanical properties and corrosion resistance [50], [51]. On the other hand, Farfan-Cabrera et al. [52], evaluated the tribological behavior of AISI 1018, low-carbon steel, parts repaired via material deposition (ER70S-6 wire) and subjected to a boriding process (950 °C for 2 h). The authors observed the formation of a monophasic Fe₂B coating in both the unwelded and welded zones, which led to a reduction in wear volume loss by 33% and 44%, respectively. Additionally, both regions exhibited an approximately sixfold increase in surface hardness.
The previously presented information provides important background for research on the effect of boriding on parts manufactured using the WAAM method and on repaired low-carbon steels. However, a gap still exists regarding the effect of this surface modification treatment on parts made entirely of this material using the WAAM method. Therefore, this study aims to evaluate and compare the tribological performance of low-carbon steel samples, fully manufactured via the WAAM method and those fabricated by conventional methods (AISI 1018), subjected to a thermochemical boriding process. The ultimate goal is to determine whether the borided WAAM samples achieve tribological performance comparable to that of the borided AISI 1018 samples.

WAAM system
The WAAM 3D printing system used in this work is shown in Fig. 1. It is based on the Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW) process, for which a Millermatic 140 (115 V Wire Welder) welding machine was used to provide the electrical power required to generate the electric arc necessary to melt and subsequently deposit the welding wire. Microstructure analysis
The surface microstructures of the WU and WL samples are presented in Fig. 6, a typical microstructure of low carbon steel deposited by WAAM was found [67], [68]. Fig. 6a shows the final deposited layer (WU), which consisted primarily of acicular ferrite and bainite, along with polygonal ferrite grains in localized regions. The formation of these microstructural constituents is largely attributed to factors such as the absence of subsequent thermal refinement and cooling at room temperature.
Conclusions
In this work, low-carbon steel samples manufactured using the WAAM method and a conventional manufacturing method were subjected to a thermochemical boriding treatment. The morphology, phase composition, and hardness of the generated layer, as well as the tribological performance of samples, were evaluated and compared. \#\# Published by\: Elsevier

\#\#\# Published by

\#\# Highlights

\- •Low\-carbon steel samples were fabricated via GMAW\-based WAAM with 100\% CO₂\.
\- •Boriding was applied to low\-carbon steel samples manufactured via WAAM\.
\- •Boride layer degradation was found for boriding treatment at 1000 °C for 6 h\.
\- •Surface hardness improved significantly in all WAAM samples\, except at 1000 °C \- 6 h\.
\- •Borided WAAM samples matched borided AISI 1018 samples in tribological performance\.

\#\# Abstract

Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing \(WAAM\) method enables the fabrication of customized layer\-by\-layer structures\. Low\-carbon steels are particularly attractive feedstock materials for WAAM because of their low cost\, excellent weldability\, and reliable deposition behavior\. However\, their inherently low surface hardness and poor wear resistance restrict their use in tribological applications\. Surface modification techniques offer a potential solution to address these limitations\. This study evaluates the effect of boriding on the surface properties and tribological performance of low\-carbon steel samples manufactured via WAAM\. Low\-carbon steel \(ER70S\-6\) plates were fabricated using a voltage of \~19\.7 V\, a current of \~67 A\, and a gas flow rate of 20 L\/min of 100\% CO₂\. Samples were extracted from the upper and lower regions of the WAAM\-built plates to evaluate possible variations in the response to boriding along the build direction\. AISI 1018 steel samples manufactured by conventional processing were used as a reference material\. Powder pack boriding treatment was performed at 900 °C and 1000 °C for 2 h and 6 h\. The morphology\, phase composition\, hardness\, and tribological performance of the boride layers formed on WAAM\-fabricated low\-carbon steel were evaluated and compared with those formed on conventionally manufactured AISI 1018 steel\. The results indicate that borided WAAM samples can achieve performance on par with AISI 1018 samples\. However\, at higher temperatures and longer exposure times during boriding \(1000 °C for 6 h\)\, degradation of the boride layer was observed in all samples\.

\#\# Introduction

Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing \(WAAM\) is a Direct Energy Deposition \(DED\) method that uses an electric arc as a heat source to melt metal and create customized structures by depositing material layer by layer \[1\]\. In recent years\, there has been growing academic and industrial interest in research related to WAAM\, highlighting its potential applications in the metal\-mechanical industry\, as well as its alignment with the principles of Industry 4\.0 \(I4\.0\) and Circular Economy \[2\]\, \[3\]\, \[4\]\, \[5\]\. The advantages of this method include high deposition rates\, energy and material efficiency\, besides lower initial investment and material costs compared to other DED methods such as Powder Bed Fusion \[6\]\, \[7\]\, \[8\]\, \[9\]\.

However\, at present\, a full integration of the WAAM technique into the industry is still limited by different factors\, some of them related to the mechanical properties of the manufactured parts \[10\]\, \[11\]\. Due to the constant heat input during the deposition process\, these components are subject to distortions and residual stress distribution \[12\]\, \[13\]\, \[14\] and exhibit heterogeneous areas with non\-uniform microstructures and anisotropic properties which compromise their integrity \[15\]\, \[16\]\, \[17\]\, \[18\]\, \[19\]\. Considering this\, solutions have been sought to improve the microstructure and mechanical properties of parts printed using WAAM\, with the aim of certifying such components for critical industrial applications \[20\]\, \[21\]\, \[22\]\. These solutions range from the optimization of deposition parameters \[23\] to the application of post\-heat treatments \[24\] and surface modification techniques such as Friction Stir Processing \[25\]\, Laser Shock Peening \[26\] or Plasma Spray Coating \[27\]\.

One of the most attractive applications offered by the WAAM method is tools manufacturing \[28\]\, \[29\]\, \[30\]\, \[31\]\. Nevertheless\, some steels used for tools and molds\, such as AISI 4140\, D2\, or H13\, have a carbon content greater than 0\.3\% which reduces the weldability and toughness of the parts at the end of the Additive Manufacturing \(AM\) process \[32\]\, making strict parameter controls necessary \[33\]\. For instance\, in the case of H13 steel manufactured via the WAAM method\, inhomogeneity has been observed in different areas of the resulting parts \[34\]\, along with pores and voids \[35\] and anisotropic behavior\. In response to this\, other material options have been considered\. For instance\, Alimov et al\. \[36\] used Maraging\/precipitation\-hardened steel 17\-4PH\, as an alternative for traditional hot\-working steels\, to manufacture hot\-forming dies using WAAM method\. To evaluate their performance\, these molds were mounted on an SMS SPPE 6\.3 screw press\, and hot\-forming processes were carried out with different levels of blow energy \(50\%\, 70\%\, and 100\%\) and blows\. At the end of the processes\, no signs of wear or warping were detected on the dies\.

Surface modification technologies can extend the service life of industrial machinery components by reducing potential failures caused by corrosion or wear\, even increasing their surface hardness\. Aluminizing\, for example\, is a surface modification treatment in which an aluminized layer is obtained\, primarily enhancing the corrosion properties of the material where it is applied\. This treatment is highly relevant for components where an increase in high\-temperature oxidation resistance is desired\. The first studies on the effect of aluminizing on parts manufactured using the WAAM technique have been reported in the literature\. Such is the case of Gürol et al\. \[37\]\, who evaluated the effect of the powder\-pack aluminizing treatment on ER307 stainless steel components fabricated by the aforementioned method\. The authors observed an increase in surface hardness and elastic modulus as well as an improvement in oxidation resistance in the range of 46–70\%\. Bölükbaşi et al\. \[38\]\, on the other hand\, evaluated the effect of aluminizing on Inconel 625\, manufactured using the WAAM method\, and also observed improvements in oxidation resistance\. Both works reported stability of aluminide phases at temperatures exceeding 1000 °C\.

Boriding\, another example of surface modification technology\, is a thermochemical process in which a boride layer is formed on the surface of a substrate through boron diffusion \[39\]\, \[40\]\. Due to the growing interest in AM processes\, research has begun to explore the feasibility and performance of this process in parts manufactured using WAAM methods\. Günen et al\. \[41\] performed a boriding process \(980 °C for 1 h\) on Inconel 625 superalloy parts produced by WAAM method and evaluated their hardness and tribological performance\. They found that\, after this treatment\, there was an increase in surface hardness and an improvement in wear resistance\, both at room temperature and elevated temperatures \(500 °C\)\. Additionally\, there was a reduction in the coefficient of friction \(CoF\) compared to untreated samples\. In a different study\, Günen et al\. \[42\] carried out a thermochemical treatment \(1000 °C for 1 h\) on 307ER stainless steel parts manufactured using WAAM method\. This led to an improvement in tribological performance\, with wear resistance increasing nearly 32 times at room temperature and 8 times at 500 °C\. Balhara et al\. \[43\] used ultra\-fast boriding technique \(1000 °C for 15 min\) on 316 L stainless steel samples fabricated using a laser\-based DED technique\. They evaluated how different printing parameters \(300 W and 450 W laser power with 40 J\/mm and 95 J\/mm linear energy\, respectively\) affect the morphology of the generated coatings and the hardness distribution in the samples\. The sample printed at 300 W showed more uniform substrate hardness but greater coating variations\, while the sample printed at 450 W exhibited higher surface hardness uniformity but greater substrate variation\. Resendiz\-Calderon et al\. \[44\] simulated a WAAM\-based repair process on AISI D2 tool steel by depositing ER308L stainless steel using Gas Tungsten Arc Welding\, followed by a boriding treatment at 950 °C for 3 h to evaluate the resulting surface and tribological performance\. It was found that the boride layer promotes a more homogeneous mechanical response between the repaired and unrepaired zones\, as it reduces the hardness difference between both surfaces from 57\% to less than 9\%\. Additionally\, in reciprocating sliding tests\, there was a reduction in total wear volume by approximately 80\% and in the CoF by 25\% due to the boriding process\.

Low\-carbon steels offer great potential for microstructure control through parameter adjustments in the WAAM process due to their low carbon content \[45\]\, \[46\]\. However\, their relatively low hardness results in reduced wear resistance and\, consequently\, inferior tribological performance compared to similar steels manufactured using conventional methods\. Treatments such as boriding or aluminizing can enhance the surface hardness of treated components\, however\, the boride layer allows for achieving significantly higher values \[47\]\, \[48\]\, \[49\]\. This substantial increase in hardness is desirable for improving wear resistance\. Consequently\, boriding was chosen as the treatment for this work because it focuses on studying tribological performance\. Some studies on the effect of boriding on low\-carbon steels have been conducted\, evaluating their mechanical properties and corrosion resistance \[50\]\, \[51\]\. On the other hand\, Farfan\-Cabrera et al\. \[52\]\, evaluated the tribological behavior of AISI 1018\, low\-carbon steel\, parts repaired via material deposition \(ER70S\-6 wire\) and subjected to a boriding process \(950 °C for 2 h\)\. The authors observed the formation of a monophasic Fe₂B coating in both the unwelded and welded zones\, which led to a reduction in wear volume loss by 33\% and 44\%\, respectively\. Additionally\, both regions exhibited an approximately sixfold increase in surface hardness\.

The previously presented information provides important background for research on the effect of boriding on parts manufactured using the WAAM method and on repaired low\-carbon steels\. However\, a gap still exists regarding the effect of this surface modification treatment on parts made entirely of this material using the WAAM method\. Therefore\, this study aims to evaluate and compare the tribological performance of low\-carbon steel samples\, fully manufactured via the WAAM method and those fabricated by conventional methods \(AISI 1018\)\, subjected to a thermochemical boriding process\. The ultimate goal is to determine whether the borided WAAM samples achieve tribological performance comparable to that of the borided AISI 1018 samples\.

\#\#\# Microstructure analysis

The surface microstructures of the WU and WL samples are presented in Fig\. 6\, a typical microstructure of low carbon steel deposited by WAAM was found \[67\]\, \[68\]\. Fig\. 6a shows the final deposited layer \(WU\)\, which consisted primarily of acicular ferrite and bainite\, along with polygonal ferrite grains in localized regions\. The formation of these microstructural constituents is largely attributed to factors such as the absence of subsequent thermal refinement and cooling at room temperature\.

\#\#\# Conclusions

In this work\, low\-carbon steel samples manufactured using the WAAM method and a conventional manufacturing method were subjected to a thermochemical boriding treatment\. records.summary: The article proposes an integrated framework for securing digital file transfer in distributed additive manufacturing (AM) by combining GIT version control, Neo4j graph-based product lifecycle management, IPFS decentralized storage, and an Ethereum-based blockchain with a smart contract. Approved G-code files are hashed with SHA-256, uploaded to IPFS, and registered on-chain; a receiver node retrieves the file and cross-verifies the CID, hash, GIT commit, revision, approval status, and receiver authorization, after which a print gateway checks printer authorization and machine compatibility before dispatch. The authors report a single proof-of-concept run printing a drone arm on an Elegoo Centauri Carbon printer with PETG, with a recurring workflow time of 8.4 s (3.69 s sender, 2.38 s receiver verification, 2.33 s gateway) and 15.68 s aggregate including a one-time 7.28 s smart-contract deployment. Two failure cases were demonstrated: a tampered file (CID/SHA-256/GIT-content mismatch, detected in 4.34 s) and an unauthorized printer selection rejected at the gateway. The authors explicitly frame this as functional feasibility rather than scalability or statistical performance benchmarking.
records.why_it_matters: The design separates digital authentication from physical execution via a device-level print gateway, so a file that passes integrity checks can still be blocked from an unauthorized printer—addressing IP leakage and unapproved manufacturing in distributed AM workflows.

score_details.reason: Full article text supplied. It directly addresses a tracked Additive Manufacturing problem: securing distributed AM file transfer and printer authorization. The architecture (GIT version control, Neo4j PLM, IPFS storage, Ethereum smart contract, SHA-256 integrity, print gateway) is concretely described with an algorithm, threat model, and a single proof-of-concept run printing a drone arm. Measured timings (3.69 s sender, 2.38 s receiver, 2.33 s gateway, 7.28 s deployment) and two failure cases (CID/hash mismatch, unauthorized printer) are reported. However, validation is a single run with one sender/receiver/printer, no repeated trials or latency statistics, and several security claims (receiver authorization, replay, key compromise, DoS) are explicitly untested. Novelty is integration of existing components rather than new mechanism; the authors themselves frame it as combining otherwise separate mechanisms.

Receiver authorization, GIT revision, and approval-status failure conditions implemented but not independently tested
Replay, credential/key compromise, malicious insiders, node compromise, and DoS are in the threat model but not experimentally evaluated

No printer-side execution feedback loop; traceability ends at dispatch

Abstract
Owing to the dispersed and data-driven nature of additive manufacturing (AM), various new cybersecurity-related threats have emerged regarding digital file transfer, data trustworthiness, intellectual property (IP) protection, and traceability. The issues mentioned above can be resolved by utilizing GIT, Neo4j, IPFS, and Ethereum-based blockchain technology (BT). Here, version control can be managed with GIT, product lifecycle management with Neo4j, and data storage across decentralized locations with IPFS. The proposed interconnected architecture determines a digital thread by utilizing BT for immutable registration and transaction provenance for the IPFS file reference, authorization rules, and permitted manufacturing resources, while SHA-256 hashing is applied for file integrity. In addition, in this framework, a print gateway has been executed at the device level to verify the file credentials before execution. To test the proposed framework experimentally, a drone arm was printed. The results demonstrated effective implementation of the smart contract, safe file transmission, integrity verification, approved printer validation, and traceable manufacturing implementation. In the reported single proof-of-concept run, the recurring operational workflow comprising sender processing, receiver-side retrieval and integrity verification, and print-gateway authorization and dispatch required 8.4 s. Including the one-time 7.28 s smart contract deployment, the aggregate processing time for the initial execution was 15.68 s. The framework was also able to detect file tampering and unauthorized printer access activities. The proposed GIT-Neo4j-IPFS-Blockchain-based framework provides the feasibility of an integrated approach for improving cybersecurity, traceability, and trust in distributed AM workflows.
1. Introduction
Additive manufacturing (AM) offers two key benefits: (a) mass level customization with the capacity for economic feasibility, and (b) substantial unrestricted design freedom compared to traditional manufacturing [1]. These characteristics have facilitated various industries to resolve application-specific and niche needs efficiently. For instance, in the pharmaceutical industry, AM has enabled the manufacturing of patient-specific drug doses tailored to individual body requirements, such as body mass index and metabolism [2]. In the biomedical field, the AM has aided the industry in producing patient-specific medical devices such as implants, valves, and splints [3,4]. Likewise, the electronics, aerospace and automotive sectors have accepted AM to utilize the geometric customization freedom within their production systems [5,6]. Continued research and developments in materials science advance these abilities, permitting the development of customized parts without depreciating the functional performance owing to the process-induced design limitations [7,8].
AM integration into industrial manufacturing systems applies transformative impacts on supply chain (SC) architecture and functioning [9]. By facilitating distributed along with on-demand fabrication, AM enables the expansion of agile and environmentally sustainable supply chains. AM technology decreases dependency on multi-tiered distributed networks by moving manufacturing closer to the end consumers, thus reducing hauling requirements, inventory, and corresponding complex logistics [10]. Additionally, the dispersed and digitally piloted nature of AM has stirred the growth of the maker movement, such as the RepRap open-source project, advocating for combined and open-source manufacturing ecosystems [11,12]. Such expansions show the AM potential to democratize manufacturing abilities and redefine established production–consumption patterns.
AM facilitates manufacturing at diverse locations within a supply network rather than being restricted to a central facility, which reduces the structural constraints associated with conventional supply chain planning and configuration, thereby contributing to better environmental performance and cost-effectiveness. When strategically employed, AM centers can leverage underutilized capacity in conventional manufacturing facilities, establishing combined production approaches that integrate additive and traditional processes [13]. AM integration can lower the dependency on massive parts of stockpiling, dedicated tooling supplies, and intricate multi-level supplier structures inherent to conventional manufacturing systems [14]. As an alternative to transferring finished goods through multiple dispersed stages, digital designs can be transmitted and manufactured closer to the point of demand [15]. Such manufacturing models can reduce last-mile distribution limitations and decrease the likelihood of stockouts by enabling manufacturing at the point of consumption. A distributed, on-demand manufacturing technique enables on-site and responsive manufacturing, which strengthens supply chain responsiveness by improving service performance and reducing lead times, while reducing inventory-related risk and stock levels [16].
As AM systems continue to advance into data-centric cyber-physical systems (CPSs) integrated using IoT platforms and digital twins (DTs), their exposure to cyber threats elevates notably. The increasing dependency on digital design archives, firmware-driven hardware, cloud-based supervision, and interconnected manufacturing infrastructures presents liabilities that may jeopardize part quality, proprietary assets, and process safety. Studies have been carried out to analyze such risks within the AM workflow. In a study by Pearce et al. [17], a Trojan-based malware attack was exhibited to control AM firmware, causing mechanical defects within the manufactured parts. To mitigate risks associated with digital data transfer, an ultralight-weight encryption scheme was proposed by Yasmin and Gupta [18] to safeguard CAD file transmission between the slicer and AM printers, thus protecting data integrity and privacy under limited computing capacity.
Blockchain technology (BT) has been progressively explored as an added cybersecurity layer within networked manufacturing environments [19]. Due to its dispersed and tamper-resistant ledger structure, BT facilitates protected and tamper-proof logging of operating conditions, toolpath planning, and post-fabrication logs, thus augmenting end-to-end traceability throughout the AM process [20]. In a study by Banerjee [21], BT was applied to incorporate design and manufacturing systems, comprising CAD/CAM, quality inspection, and 3D-printing systems, with enterprise resource planning to enable safe data sharing, accountability, and product traceability across manufacturing nodes. Tao et al. [22] used a BT-based architecture to promote confidence in smart factory settings and enable ongoing supervision. In BT systems, smart contracts (SCs) offer a fundamental tool for implementing rule-based control logics. SCs have been used in AM to implement role-based access control for trusted asset management [23]. Furthermore, in order to improve identity certification and access governance in a dispersed manufacturing environment, an adaptive SC framework was presented to manage login policies vigorously based on operator identification and system conditions [24].
Process provenance (PPR) is critical to safeguard AM printing processes. Alkhader et al. [25] extended the BT-based PPR outline to record the part’s printing process parameters, including sensor data, post-printing inspection results, and part design data. A BT-based system has also been integrated to monitor, validate, and regulate compliance in manufacturing operations. In the study by Yousef et al. [26], defect generation was assessed by implementing BT in the casting process, resulting in excellent traceability and part qualification. BT was integrated with ASTM-52900 by Westphal et al. [27] to support automated part assessment with certification. Abebe et al. [28] devised a layer to monitor and record data exchange activities via BT. This technique results in an absolute log configuration that can be applied to a large-scale digital manufacturing environment.
For counterfeit inhibition and anomaly identification, BT has also been explored in complex manufacturing systems. Wang et al. [29] applied BT within a modular service architecture to advance transaction efficacy and production management in dispersed systems. In a study by Kurpjuweit et al. [30], a BT-supported trust evaluation model was developed for distributed AM supply chains. Intellectual property protection and counterfeiting prevention approaches for AM-ed parts were studied by Holland et al. [31]. Access and identity control within a dispersed environment was improved by Geng et al. [32] by leveraging composite signature-based mechanisms. In another study by Jadidi et al. [33], a BT-enabled log management and abnormality recognition framework was explored by integrating sandbox mechanisms to limit cyber-physical attacks. Song and Diao [34] integrated federated learning with BT to facilitate safe model updates without disclosing proprietary design information. Hang and Kim [35] proposed BT-based runtime device verification and permission control frameworks for IoT-enabled manufacturing systems.
Unlike existing studies that primarily address blockchain-based traceability, access control, or data integrity individually, this work integrates GIT-based version control, Neo4j-based lifecycle and authorization management, IPFS-based distributed storage, and blockchain-based immutable transaction records within a single end-to-end AM workflow. The framework further connects file approval, version verification, receiver authorization, printer authorization, integrity verification, and manufacturing execution. In contrast to centralized systems, this architecture is aimed at safeguarding transaction logs, cryptographic authentication of digital resources, regulated access governance, and end-to-end traceability of process events. With the proposed integration, the outline is intended to improve cybersecurity, maintain data reliability, and ensure verifiable traceability across dispersed AM environments.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the proposed secure and traceable AM data-transfer framework, including the overall system architecture and the specific roles of GIT, Neo4j, IPFS, blockchain, the sender and receiver nodes, the integrity verification module, and the print gateway. This section also describes the secure file transfer algorithm, experimental printing setup, and cybersecurity threat model used to evaluate the framework. Section 3 presents and discusses the experimental results, including smart-contract deployment, sender and receiver side processing, blockchain transaction registration, integrity verification, printer authorization, lifecycle traceability, and the successful manufacturing of the test component. Representative failure cases, including file integrity violations and unauthorized printer selection, are also evaluated, followed by a comparison with existing blockchain-based additive manufacturing frameworks. Finally, Section 4 summarizes the main findings of this study, discusses the current limitations of the proof-of-concept implementation, and identifies directions for future work related to scalability, resilience, printer-side feedback, and broader distributed manufacturing deployment.
2. Materials and Methods
2.1. System Architecture for Secure and Traceable AM Data Transfer
Figure 1 shows the proposed framework for achieving safe and traceable AM log transmission. The given framework integrates four technologies, including (a) GIT to regulate version, (b) Neo4j to manage the product lifecycle, which utilizes a graph-based scheme, (c) IPFS to store files in a decentralized location, and (d) Ethereum-based BT to register and authorize the transactions. In this framework, Neo4j PLM is designated as the Single Source of Truth for the current product lifecycle and authorization state, while GIT maintains file-version history and the blockchain provides immutable evidence of authorized transactions. Concurrently, the elements mentioned above govern a digital thread that couples file creation, authorization, transfer, confirmation, and manufacturing operation execution through dispersed nodes. The framework is proposed to guarantee that only approved and integrity-assured files are permitted to enter the AM process.
Figure 1. Integrated architecture of the proposed GIT-Neo4j-IPFS-BT framework for secure additive manufacturing data transfer.
The process flows with the operator, who works with the system through a user interface linked to the GIT layer. At this step, the approved G-code manufacturing file, generated from the CAD model through the slicing process, is administered under a hybrid data governance ecosystem in which GIT controls the version history while Neo4j preserves the end-to-end lifecycle. It is important to mention here that GIT is primarily responsible for conserving the meticulous file history via commit-based versioning, while Neo4j retains the metadata such as part IDs, revisions, operational stages, authorization stage, user links, envisioned receiver, and approved AM printer details. This separation is critical as GIT alone can uphold the technical revision history but cannot support adequate lifecycle control for manufacturing. Furthermore, Neo4j acts as a lightweight PLM layer that regulates whether a file is qualified for transmission and printing.
The main technical contribution is the integration of these otherwise separate mechanisms into a closed-loop workflow that maintains the file version, lifecycle approval, distributed storage, immutable transaction evidence, receiver-side integrity verification, and authorized printer execution.
2.2. Core Technologies and Associated Roles
Figure 2 illustrates the process flow of the proposed framework and focuses on the performance during an actual file transfer and execution. The workflow initiates with an approved G-code manufacturing file at the sender node (N1), proceeds through the receiver node (N2) for retrieval and integrity verification, and subsequently passes through the print gateway before being dispatched to the authorized AM printer. The receiver node and the physical printer are treated as separate entities in the proposed architecture. Traceability throughout the process is achieved via Neo4j, and reliability is maintained using BT. The framework can be classified into seven blocks, including (a) Neo4j PLM/GIT layer, (b) N1, (c) IPFS, (d) BT integrated with smart contract (SC), (e) N2, (f) reliability check, and (g) print gateway along with AM execution. All blocks have been explained below.
Figure 2. Operational workflow for receiver-side validation, integrity verification, print authorization, and manufacturing execution in the proposed framework.
2.2.1. Neo4j PLM/GIT Layer
Within the framework, this layer is depicted as the trustworthy engineering source that integrates lifecycle administration and version management. Neo4j serves as the authoritative source for the current lifecycle state, including revision, approval status, authorized receiver, and approved printer. Its graph structure enables these evolving relationships to be efficiently maintained and queried. Here, GIT conserves the file version via commit-based tracing and facilitates deterministic reclamation of the file. Hence, this block decides whether the given file is qualified for transmission as well as execution. If the file has not attained the released state, it is not allowed to exit the PLM ecosystem. This principle ensures that the workflow consistently starts with a monitored engineering artifact rather than an arbitrary local file.
In the current proof-of-concept implementation, GIT and Neo4j are deployed as trusted centralized services. The framework assumes the availability and integrity of these off-chain components, as their compromise or unavailability could affect file version retrieval and lifecycle authorization decisions. Although blockchain provides immutable transaction records, it does not eliminate risks associated with centralized off-chain services. Production deployment would require additional mechanisms, such as access control, backup, replication, monitoring, and failover strategies to improve system availability and resilience.

2.2.7. Print Gateway
This block serves as the definitive policy-compliance layer before execution. This layer acts as a gateway between the integrity check layer and the printer in such a way that even if the file has passed the integrity check, the proposed framework does not allow the explicit printer execution. In fact, the authorized file is transmitted via the print gateway, which verifies whether the requested printer (
The proposed gateway also applies printer compatibility controls, file format verification, and policies of execution. This design is critical for AM, where unauthorized AM printer utilization can result in intellectual-property (IP) leakage along with unidentified manufacturing and process exploitation. Hence, the print gateway presents a decisive control stage that splits the digital authentication from the actual manufacturing execution.
After successful gateway authorization, the verified file is released to the authorized physical printer through the printer interface. The gateway therefore represents the final blockchain-controlled authorization stage before off-chain printer execution.
2.3. AM Printer Execution: Algorithm for Secure File Transfer, Verification, and Controlled Manufacturing
Following successful receiver-side verification and print-gateway authorization, the verified G-code file is dispatched to the authorized AM printer interface. At this point, the blockchain-controlled portion of the workflow is complete. The verified file is subsequently transferred off-chain to the authorized physical printer for manufacturing. In the present proof-of-concept, the printer executes the verified G-code file; however, printer-generated execution information such as job start/end time, printer status, completion status, and process data is not automatically returned to the blockchain or Neo4j.
The feedback as well as the logging path, as shown in Figure 2, are crucial as they transform the proposed framework from one-way to a closed-loop traceability system. Neo4j obtains PLM metadata and print logs, thus permitting post-process assessment, auditability, and lifecycle management. The proposed framework not only supports safe transfer but also provides complete accountability from part design authorization to complete part production.
Algorithm 1 discusses the algorithm for the workflow illustrated in Figure 2. Within the table, steps 1–2 show the Neo4j PLM authorization step, where the system verifies that the particular file has been approved in the Neo4j block. The workflow will be terminated if the file is not approved. Steps 3–7 relate to the N1-side requirement and registration phase, where the file is recovered from GIT via an authorized commit. At this stage, the hash is processed and uploaded to IPFS to acquire the content ID. As a result, the accompanying metadata is uploaded to Neo4j, and the transaction is registered on BC, confirming protected storage and absolute traceability. Steps 8–10 describe the retrieval phase at N2, where the reference data is acquired from BT, the file is downloaded from IPFS, and the metadata from Neo4j is recovered. In Steps 11–12, the integrity check is carried out, and the consistency is validated. Here, the hash is recomputed along with the GIT commit and PLM approval state verification. The transaction will be terminated if any mismatch results are identified. Step 13 imposes printer approval, guaranteeing that an authorized machine is utilized for the printing process. Steps 14–15 relate to supervised manufacturing operation, where the verified file is transmitted to the printer through the gateway, and printing results are recorded within Neo4j.

Approved file record from Neo4j/GIT
Output:
Verified file executed on authorized printer or rejected
- Query Neo4j PLM for approved file, metadata, receiver, and printer
- If status ≠ Approved → Terminate
- Retrieve file f from Git using commit Cg
- Compute hash Hf = SHA-256(f)
- Upload f to IPFS → obtain CID (C\_IPFS)
- Store metadata in Neo4j
- Register {C\_IPFS, Hf, Cg, Rev, Receiverauth, Gatewayauth, Printerauth, MachineProfile} on blockchain
- At N2, retrieve the immutable blockchain reference values for the Transfer ID
- Compare the user-supplied CID with the blockchain reference CID

- Send verified file to printer via gateway

- End Algorithm
2.4. Framework Testing Using AM Printer
The framework was tested to print the F450 Drone arm. The CAD model was prepared using Siemens NX software at N1. After CAD model generation, the file was transferred using the framework explained above and was received at N2. At N2, the file was retrieved and was sent to an Elegoo Centauri Carbon AM printer equipped with a 0.4 mm Hardened Steel Nozzle. For printing, Elegoo Rapid PETG filament was utilized. Throughout the printing, two perimeter walls and 15% infill density were maintained. Furthermore, the arm was printed with the layer lines running parallel to the length of the arm, necessary to hold inter-layer stresses stable throughout the part.
The present validation was conducted as proof-of-concept using one sender, one receiver, one printer, and one representative manufacturing file. Therefore, the experiment evaluates functional feasibility rather than system scalability.
2.5. Cybersecurity Threat Model
A formal cybersecurity threat model was developed to define protected assets, trusted components, attacker capabilities, trust boundaries, attack surfaces, and security assumptions of the proposed AM file-transfer framework. As illustrated in Figure 3, the framework consists of five primary components: the sender/developer node, off-chain services comprising GIT, IPFS, and Neo4j PLM, the blockchain network and smart contract, the receiver node, and the authorized AM printer. Trust boundaries exist between these components because manufacturing data, authorization information, and control decisions are exchanged across different services, networks, and endpoints.
Figure 3. Threat model and trust boundaries of the proposed secure AM file-transfer framework.
The protected assets include the AM build file, SHA-256 file hash, IPFS CID, GIT revision information, PLM authorization and approval records, blockchain transaction records, printer authorization information, and cryptographic credentials. The primary attack surfaces include network communication channels, sender and receiver applications, GIT and Neo4j interfaces, IPFS storage and retrieval interfaces, blockchain RPC interfaces, smart-contract functions, blockchain private keys, and the printer authorization interface.
The adversary is assumed to be capable of intercepting network traffic; modifying, replacing, or manipulating manufacturing files and associated metadata; replaying previously valid transactions or requests; compromising authentication credentials or cryptographic keys; acting as a malicious authorized user; compromising sender, receiver, or blockchain nodes; and attempting denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. These capabilities represent potential threats to confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, traceability, and availability of manufacturing data and associated authorization information.
The current prototype assumes that authorized users, sender and receiver hosts, blockchain validator nodes, and their associated private keys remain trusted and uncompromised. Therefore, attacks involving private-key theft, endpoint compromise, malicious authorized users, or validator compromise are included in the threat model but are outside the present experimental validation scope. GIT and Neo4j PLM are assumed to operate under controlled access, while IPFS is not relied upon as a trusted source of file integrity. Instead, files retrieved from IPFS are independently verified using their SHA-256 hashes before being accepted for manufacturing. Similarly, blockchain records are treated as immutable audit references under the assumption that the validator nodes and transaction-signing keys remain uncompromised.
Under these assumptions, the implemented framework provides file-integrity verification through SHA-256 hash comparison, authorization enforcement through PLM and smart-contract checks, and immutable blockchain logging for traceability. At the receiver, the retrieved manufacturing file is verified against its registered SHA-256 hash, and the corresponding authorization information, receiver identity, file status, and printer authorization are checked before manufacturing is permitted.
Table 1 summarizes the identified security threats, corresponding protection mechanisms, and their validation status in the current implementation. The present experimental validation focuses on two representative failure scenarios: file-integrity violation and unauthorized printer selection. File tampering was evaluated by introducing mismatches in the registered and current CID/SHA-256 values, while the unauthorized-printer case was evaluated by selecting a printer different from the authorized manufacturing resource. Receiver authorization, GIT revision, approval status, and machine compatibility are implemented as verification checks within the successful workflow, but their corresponding failure conditions were not independently tested. Blockchain private-key theft, credential compromise, malicious authorized users, compromised sender or receiver nodes, compromised blockchain validators, replay attacks, and denial-of-service attacks are included in the threat model but were not experimentally evaluated in the present prototype. The current implementation therefore assumes that cryptographic credentials, endpoint hosts, and validator nodes remain trusted and uncompromised. Accordingly, the security claims of this study are limited to the mechanisms that were implemented and experimentally demonstrated.
Table 1. Threats, implemented security mechanisms, and validation scope of the proposed framework.
3. Results and Discussion
3.1. Smart Contract Migration
The “AMTransferRegistry” SC was employed over the localized Ethereum-based network at N1 via Truffle for compilation and deployment. A unique contract address was allocated as presented in Figure 4 and documented in block 261 along with the subsequent hash for traceability. This deployment used 0.01874063 ETH (10 gwei), representing an effective implementation. The whole process was fulfilled in 7.28 s, confirming successful deployment and readiness of the blockchain layer for subsequent file transfer operations.
Figure 4. The smart contract deployment over a localized Ethereum network with the corresponding contract address, hashing, and time.
3.2. Sender Node Output
As illustrated in Figure 5, the N1 initiates the process flow by querying the Neo4j PLM/GIT layer to retrieve an endorsed file (PLM-AM-0001, Revision R3) and its GIT commit ID, ensuring that version-controlled data is selected. The file is then fetched locally, and a SHA-256 hash is computed to generate a deterministic integrity fingerprint. A unique content ID (QmS5hhtM…) is generated as the file is uploaded to IPFS. In Neo4j, an identical check is also carried out before the metadata is stored and the graph-based relationships are developed among the N1, transfer, and authorized nodes. Following on, this transfer is registered on the BT via the employed SC. Here, the fundamental characteristics, such as content ID, generated hash, version number, and consent details, are recorded through an immutable transaction (0x a668c8195…). Hence, the sending process is fulfilled with an event recording in Neo4j. It can be seen that the entire process was completed in 3.69 s following coordinated communication among PLM, IPFS, Neo4j, and BT.
Figure 5. The execution at N1 through a series of events, including GIT PLM confirmation, hash calculation, IPFS content ID creation, Neo4j relationship development, and BT transaction registration.
3.3. Receiver Node Output: Success Case
N2 utilizes the “TR-20260919-0013” transfer ID to retrieve the transaction record from the BT network, as presented in Figure 6. The record includes content ID, hash, GIT commit, version number, and endorsement information. Following on, the framework validates that the hash received at N2 matches the hash at N1 to ensure the dependability of the BT logs. At this stage, N2 permission is verified with the address stored in the BT network. The metadata is then retrieved from the GIT PLM layer, with a hash, content-ID, version number, GIT commit, and authorization status. The retrieved information is then cross-verified with the BT data, and the resultant file is downloaded from IPFS using the content ID and the recomputed localized SHA-256 hash. The framework performs a thorough integrity inspection by assessing the downloaded file against BT records, and confirms the hash, content ID, GIT commit, version number, approval status, and approval constraints across the BT network. Upon validation, the integrity result is logged to the blockchain transfer record, and a receiver transaction hash is recorded. The corresponding verification relationships and status are also recorded in Neo4j. It, in turn, links the N2, transfer, and integrity to check nodes. It can be seen that the whole process is completed in 2.38 s, which demonstrates uniform data certification and harmonization across a dispersed network.
Figure 6. Receiver node output showing blockchain verification, Neo4j metadata retrieval, IPFS file download, multi-layer integrity validation, and blockchain status update.
3.4. Print Gateway Output
As displayed in Figure 7, the print gateway receives the verified transfer package (TR-20260919-0013) after successful integrity validation at the receiver stage. It first confirms that the selected printer matches the authorized printer defined on the blockchain, then validates machine compatibility using the required machine profile. A secure dispatch package is then created, encapsulating the transfer of ID, file path, and associated integrity token. An integrity-verified dispatch package is created after the gateway confirms printer authorization, machine compatibility, and the pre-dispatch file hash. Following on, the file is progressed to the printer interface, and the transmission event is recorded on the BT transfer along with a timestamp. Furthermore, the operation is recorded in Neo4j by the gateway that captures events such as “PRINT\_GATEWAY\_APPROVED” and “FILE\_DISPATCHED\_TO\_PRINTER”. The gateway records the authorization and dispatch result through a new blockchain transaction linked to the existing Transfer ID. It can be found that the whole gateway operation is completed in 2.33 s, indicating monitored and endorsed handling of validated manufacturing data.
Figure 7. Output from the printer gateway, illustrating validation, dispatch organization, data transfer to interface, and blockchain status update.
3.5. Final Lifecycle Status
The final lifecycle status consolidates information from all system layers, PLM/Git, IPFS, blockchain, and Neo4j, providing an end-to-end verification of the transfer process. As shown in Figure 8, the output confirms that the file corresponds to an approved PLM record (PLM-AM-0001, Revision R3) with a valid GIT commit ID, ensuring correct selection. It is important to note that the file data remains available in IPFS via the content ID, indicating successful distributed storage. From the BT perspective, the registered transfer is associated with a PASSED integrity status and a DISPATCHED execution status. The N2 validation verifies effective endorsement and hash pairing, while the gateway confirms endorsement and machine compatibility, along with file dispatch creation. The registration, integrity-verification, and gateway-dispatch stages generated three distinct blockchain transactions linked to the same Transfer ID.
Figure 8. Final lifecycle status showing consolidated traceability across PLM/Git, IPFS, blockchain, receiver verification, and successful dispatch to the authorized printer interface.
For timing interpretation, the one-time blockchain initialization is distinguished from the recurring operational workflow. Smart-contract deployment required 7.28 s and is performed only during initial system setup. The recurring transfer workflow consisted of 3.69 s for sender processing, 2.38 s for receiver-side retrieval and integrity verification, and 2.33 s for print-gateway authorization and dispatch. Therefore, the recurring operational processing time is
Accordingly, the reported 15.68 s represents the aggregate measured processing time for initial deployment plus one operational workflow cycle, whereas 8.4 s represents the cumulative measured software-processing time of the recurring operational workflow. These aggregate values exclude manual user-input and inter-stage handoff delays. These timing values are based on a single proof-of-concept execution and are reported to demonstrate workflow feasibility rather than statistical performance benchmarking. Repeated trials and detailed latency characterization were not conducted in the present study.
3.6. Failure Case: Integrity Check Failed
In the failure case, as exhibited in Figure 9, the receiver retrieves the original content ID and SHA-256 hash from the blockchain for the given transfer. For controlled integrity-failure validation, a modified manufacturing file with a different IPFS CID is supplied to the receiver. The receiver first compares the user-supplied CID with the immutable CID stored on the blockchain, resulting in a CID mismatch. The substituted file is then retrieved from IPFS, and its SHA-256 digest is recomputed and compared with the registered blockchain reference. During integrity verification, the CID comparison, SHA-256 comparison, and GIT-authorized content comparison fail, whereas the receiver authorization, revision, and PLM approval checks pass. Consequently, the integrity status is marked as FAILED, while the original blockchain registration record remains the immutable reference for the authorized file. The failure is recorded in Neo4j through events such as CID\_MISMATCH\_DETECTED and INTEGRITY\_CHECK\_FAILED, and further processing toward the print gateway is terminated. For this controlled validation experiment only, retrieval of the substituted CID was permitted after detection of the CID mismatch so that the downstream SHA-256 and GIT-content checks could also be evaluated; in the normal operational workflow, a CID mismatch results in rejection. The failure-detection process required 4.34 s in the reported proof-of-concept run.
Figure 9. Integrity-failure case showing mismatch between the user-supplied IPFS CID and the immutable blockchain reference, followed by SHA-256 and GIT-content verification failure.
3.7. Failure Case: Unauthorized Printer
In this case as shown in Figure 10, a valid integrity status “PASSED” is received by the gateway, which verifies that the file has already been validated at the N2 node. Nevertheless, during the endorsement stage, the framework assesses the endorsed printer defined in both the BT and the PLM (PRINTER\_01) against the user-defined printer (PRINTER\_02). Printer endorsement declines because both printers are different. Consequently, the framework instantly rejects the file dispatch process. The resultant rejection is recorded in Neo4j under “PRINT\_GATEWAY\_REJECTED” and “UNAUTHORIZED\_PRINTER” events, and the gateway records the rejection through a new gateway/dispatch transaction linked to the existing Transfer ID. This exhibits that even with authorized data integrity, the framework implements precise device-level endorsement, thus avoiding unauthorized production execution.
Figure 10. Failure case presenting denial at the gateway owing to the divergence between the approved and selected printers.
The present proof-of-concept evaluates two representative failure scenarios: file integrity violation and unauthorized printer selection. The verification logic also includes GIT revision, receiver authorization, and approval-status checks; however, these failure conditions were not independently tested in the present study.
3.8. Printer Outputs
Figure 11a–c show the CAD model and actual fabricated drone arm. The arm design was prepared using Siemens NX and subsequently prepared for additive manufacturing through slicing to generate the executable G-code file. In the reported experiment, the approved G-code file (approved\_build\_file.gcode) was retrieved at N1, hashed using SHA-256, and uploaded to IPFS, and its associated metadata were registered in Neo4j and on the blockchain. At N2, the same G-code file was retrieved from IPFS and verified against the reference hash, GIT commit, revision, approval status, and authorization information. Following successful gateway approval, the verified G-code file was dispatched to the authorized printer for fabrication of the drone arm. The resulting physical part demonstrates the capability of the proposed framework to maintain data integrity, traceability, and controlled manufacturing from approved digital artifact to physical execution.
Figure 11. Drone arm manufacturing workflow showing (a) the CAD model developed at N1, (b) dimensional verification of the fabricated part using a digital caliper, and (c) the fabricated part produced after gateway authorization using the verified G-code manufacturing file.
3.9. Comparison with Existing Blockchain-Based AM Frameworks
To further evaluate the contribution of the proposed architecture, Table 2 compares its performance and functional capabilities with representative blockchain-based AM security and traceability frameworks reported in the literature. The comparison considers latency, storage strategy, traceability coverage, access control, integrity verification, decentralization, version control, and manufacturing-level enforcement.
Table 2. Comparison of the proposed framework with representative blockchain-based AM security and traceability approaches.
4. Conclusions
In this study, a secure and traceable digital thread has been proposed for a distributed AM network by integrating GIT PLM, Neo4j, IPFS, and Ethereum-based BT. The proposed outline combines file version administration, lifecycle management and control, disseminated data storage, absolute transaction record, integrity verification, and printer-level endorsement to create a secure pathway from design formation to manufacturing execution.
Experimental validation using a drone arm established successful smart contract disposition, safe file transmission, dispersed storage retrieval, integrity verification, and authorized manufacturing execution. In the reported single proof-of-concept run, the recurring operational workflow required 8.4 s, comprising 3.69 s for sender processing, 2.38 s for receiver-side retrieval and integrity verification, and 2.33 s for print-gateway authorization and dispatch. Including the one-time 7.28 s smart-contract deployment, the aggregate processing time for the initial execution was 15.68 s. In addition, the framework was also evaluated against tampered files, such as hash mismatches, to prevent unauthorized printer access. These results reveal that the presented framework can efficiently preserve data integrity, attribution, and access control in distributed AM environments.
The current evaluation is limited to one sender, one receiver, one printer, and a representative file. Since the file itself is transferred through IPFS and only the CID, SHA-256 hash, and associated metadata are registered on the blockchain, the file size primarily affects hashing and IPFS transfer rather than the blockchain payload size. The present proof-of-concept also evaluates two representative failure scenarios: file integrity violation and unauthorized printer access. Although the verification logic includes GIT revision, receiver authorization, and approval-status checks, these cases were not independently tested. Future work will extend the proposed digital thread beyond authorized printer dispatch by integrating printer-side execution feedback, including the job ID, printer ID, print start/end timestamps, completion status, and relevant process data, and linking these records to the corresponding Transfer ID in Neo4j and, where appropriate, the blockchain. In addition, the scalability and resilience of the framework will be further evaluated through experiments involving additional nodes, concurrent transactions, repeated runs, and broader distributed network configurations. These evaluations will include performance characterization through repeated trials, measurement of mean execution time and variability, and analysis of component-level latency, including blockchain transaction processing, IPFS retrieval, gateway processing, and the failure detection response time. Additional failure scenarios, such as outdated GIT revisions, unauthorized receivers, Neo4j metadata manipulation, replay attacks, and communication failures, will also be investigated.
Future work will further examine distributed deployment strategies, redundancy mechanisms, and fault-tolerant operation of off-chain components, including GIT and Neo4j, to improve system availability and resilience.
The established framework provides a basis for securing digital manufacturing ecosystems and supports the growing adoption of distributed manufacturing networks. Future work will focus on leveraging real-time printer process parameters, digital twins, multi-node manufacturing networks, and advanced access-control mechanisms to further improve cybersecurity, scalability, and operational trust in AM systems.
