\#\# Abstract

Owing to the dispersed and data\-driven nature of additive manufacturing \(AM\)\, various new cybersecurity\-related threats have emerged regarding digital file transfer\, data trustworthiness\, intellectual property \(IP\) protection\, and traceability\. The issues mentioned above can be resolved by utilizing GIT\, Neo4j\, IPFS\, and Ethereum\-based blockchain technology \(BT\)\. Here\, version control can be managed with GIT\, product lifecycle management with Neo4j\, and data storage across decentralized locations with IPFS\. The proposed interconnected architecture determines a digital thread by utilizing BT for immutable registration and transaction provenance for the IPFS file reference\, authorization rules\, and permitted manufacturing resources\, while SHA\-256 hashing is applied for file integrity\. In addition\, in this framework\, a print gateway has been executed at the device level to verify the file credentials before execution\. To test the proposed framework experimentally\, a drone arm was printed\. The results demonstrated effective implementation of the smart contract\, safe file transmission\, integrity verification\, approved printer validation\, and traceable manufacturing implementation\. In the reported single proof\-of\-concept run\, the recurring operational workflow comprising sender processing\, receiver\-side retrieval and integrity verification\, and print\-gateway authorization and dispatch required 8\.4 s\. Including the one\-time 7\.28 s smart contract deployment\, the aggregate processing time for the initial execution was 15\.68 s\. The framework was also able to detect file tampering and unauthorized printer access activities\. The proposed GIT\-Neo4j\-IPFS\-Blockchain\-based framework provides the feasibility of an integrated approach for improving cybersecurity\, traceability\, and trust in distributed AM workflows\.

\#\# 1\. Introduction

Additive manufacturing \(AM\) offers two key benefits\: \(a\) mass level customization with the capacity for economic feasibility\, and \(b\) substantial unrestricted design freedom compared to traditional manufacturing \[1\]\. These characteristics have facilitated various industries to resolve application\-specific and niche needs efficiently\. For instance\, in the pharmaceutical industry\, AM has enabled the manufacturing of patient\-specific drug doses tailored to individual body requirements\, such as body mass index and metabolism \[2\]\. In the biomedical field\, the AM has aided the industry in producing patient\-specific medical devices such as implants\, valves\, and splints \[3\,4\]\. Likewise\, the electronics\, aerospace and automotive sectors have accepted AM to utilize the geometric customization freedom within their production systems \[5\,6\]\. Continued research and developments in materials science advance these abilities\, permitting the development of customized parts without depreciating the functional performance owing to the process\-induced design limitations \[7\,8\]\.

AM integration into industrial manufacturing systems applies transformative impacts on supply chain \(SC\) architecture and functioning \[9\]\. By facilitating distributed along with on\-demand fabrication\, AM enables the expansion of agile and environmentally sustainable supply chains\. AM technology decreases dependency on multi\-tiered distributed networks by moving manufacturing closer to the end consumers\, thus reducing hauling requirements\, inventory\, and corresponding complex logistics \[10\]\. Additionally\, the dispersed and digitally piloted nature of AM has stirred the growth of the maker movement\, such as the RepRap open\-source project\, advocating for combined and open\-source manufacturing ecosystems \[11\,12\]\. Such expansions show the AM potential to democratize manufacturing abilities and redefine established production–consumption patterns\.

AM facilitates manufacturing at diverse locations within a supply network rather than being restricted to a central facility\, which reduces the structural constraints associated with conventional supply chain planning and configuration\, thereby contributing to better environmental performance and cost\-effectiveness\. When strategically employed\, AM centers can leverage underutilized capacity in conventional manufacturing facilities\, establishing combined production approaches that integrate additive and traditional processes \[13\]\. AM integration can lower the dependency on massive parts of stockpiling\, dedicated tooling supplies\, and intricate multi\-level supplier structures inherent to conventional manufacturing systems \[14\]\. As an alternative to transferring finished goods through multiple dispersed stages\, digital designs can be transmitted and manufactured closer to the point of demand \[15\]\. Such manufacturing models can reduce last\-mile distribution limitations and decrease the likelihood of stockouts by enabling manufacturing at the point of consumption\. A distributed\, on\-demand manufacturing technique enables on\-site and responsive manufacturing\, which strengthens supply chain responsiveness by improving service performance and reducing lead times\, while reducing inventory\-related risk and stock levels \[16\]\.

As AM systems continue to advance into data\-centric cyber\-physical systems \(CPSs\) integrated using IoT platforms and digital twins \(DTs\)\, their exposure to cyber threats elevates notably\. The increasing dependency on digital design archives\, firmware\-driven hardware\, cloud\-based supervision\, and interconnected manufacturing infrastructures presents liabilities that may jeopardize part quality\, proprietary assets\, and process safety\. Studies have been carried out to analyze such risks within the AM workflow\. In a study by Pearce et al\. \[17\]\, a Trojan\-based malware attack was exhibited to control AM firmware\, causing mechanical defects within the manufactured parts\. To mitigate risks associated with digital data transfer\, an ultralight\-weight encryption scheme was proposed by Yasmin and Gupta \[18\] to safeguard CAD file transmission between the slicer and AM printers\, thus protecting data integrity and privacy under limited computing capacity\.

Blockchain technology \(BT\) has been progressively explored as an added cybersecurity layer within networked manufacturing environments \[19\]\. Due to its dispersed and tamper\-resistant ledger structure\, BT facilitates protected and tamper\-proof logging of operating conditions\, toolpath planning\, and post\-fabrication logs\, thus augmenting end\-to\-end traceability throughout the AM process \[20\]\. In a study by Banerjee \[21\]\, BT was applied to incorporate design and manufacturing systems\, comprising CAD\/CAM\, quality inspection\, and 3D\-printing systems\, with enterprise resource planning to enable safe data sharing\, accountability\, and product traceability across manufacturing nodes\. Tao et al\. \[22\] used a BT\-based architecture to promote confidence in smart factory settings and enable ongoing supervision\. In BT systems\, smart contracts \(SCs\) offer a fundamental tool for implementing rule\-based control logics\. SCs have been used in AM to implement role\-based access control for trusted asset management \[23\]\. Furthermore\, in order to improve identity certification and access governance in a dispersed manufacturing environment\, an adaptive SC framework was presented to manage login policies vigorously based on operator identification and system conditions \[24\]\.

Process provenance \(PPR\) is critical to safeguard AM printing processes\. Alkhader et al\. \[25\] extended the BT\-based PPR outline to record the part’s printing process parameters\, including sensor data\, post\-printing inspection results\, and part design data\. A BT\-based system has also been integrated to monitor\, validate\, and regulate compliance in manufacturing operations\. In the study by Yousef et al\. \[26\]\, defect generation was assessed by implementing BT in the casting process\, resulting in excellent traceability and part qualification\. BT was integrated with ASTM\-52900 by Westphal et al\. \[27\] to support automated part assessment with certification\. Abebe et al\. \[28\] devised a layer to monitor and record data exchange activities via BT\. This technique results in an absolute log configuration that can be applied to a large\-scale digital manufacturing environment\.

For counterfeit inhibition and anomaly identification\, BT has also been explored in complex manufacturing systems\. Wang et al\. \[29\] applied BT within a modular service architecture to advance transaction efficacy and production management in dispersed systems\. In a study by Kurpjuweit et al\. \[30\]\, a BT\-supported trust evaluation model was developed for distributed AM supply chains\. Intellectual property protection and counterfeiting prevention approaches for AM\-ed parts were studied by Holland et al\. \[31\]\. Access and identity control within a dispersed environment was improved by Geng et al\. \[32\] by leveraging composite signature\-based mechanisms\. In another study by Jadidi et al\. \[33\]\, a BT\-enabled log management and abnormality recognition framework was explored by integrating sandbox mechanisms to limit cyber\-physical attacks\. Song and Diao \[34\] integrated federated learning with BT to facilitate safe model updates without disclosing proprietary design information\. Hang and Kim \[35\] proposed BT\-based runtime device verification and permission control frameworks for IoT\-enabled manufacturing systems\.

Unlike existing studies that primarily address blockchain\-based traceability\, access control\, or data integrity individually\, this work integrates GIT\-based version control\, Neo4j\-based lifecycle and authorization management\, IPFS\-based distributed storage\, and blockchain\-based immutable transaction records within a single end\-to\-end AM workflow\. The framework further connects file approval\, version verification\, receiver authorization\, printer authorization\, integrity verification\, and manufacturing execution\. In contrast to centralized systems\, this architecture is aimed at safeguarding transaction logs\, cryptographic authentication of digital resources\, regulated access governance\, and end\-to\-end traceability of process events\. With the proposed integration\, the outline is intended to improve cybersecurity\, maintain data reliability\, and ensure verifiable traceability across dispersed AM environments\.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows\. Section 2 presents the proposed secure and traceable AM data\-transfer framework\, including the overall system architecture and the specific roles of GIT\, Neo4j\, IPFS\, blockchain\, the sender and receiver nodes\, the integrity verification module\, and the print gateway\. This section also describes the secure file transfer algorithm\, experimental printing setup\, and cybersecurity threat model used to evaluate the framework\. Section 3 presents and discusses the experimental results\, including smart\-contract deployment\, sender and receiver side processing\, blockchain transaction registration\, integrity verification\, printer authorization\, lifecycle traceability\, and the successful manufacturing of the test component\. Representative failure cases\, including file integrity violations and unauthorized printer selection\, are also evaluated\, followed by a comparison with existing blockchain\-based additive manufacturing frameworks\. Finally\, Section 4 summarizes the main findings of this study\, discusses the current limitations of the proof\-of\-concept implementation\, and identifies directions for future work related to scalability\, resilience\, printer\-side feedback\, and broader distributed manufacturing deployment\.

\#\# 2\. Materials and Methods

\#\#\# 2\.1\. System Architecture for Secure and Traceable AM Data Transfer

Figure 1 shows the proposed framework for achieving safe and traceable AM log transmission\. The given framework integrates four technologies\, including \(a\) GIT to regulate version\, \(b\) Neo4j to manage the product lifecycle\, which utilizes a graph\-based scheme\, \(c\) IPFS to store files in a decentralized location\, and \(d\) Ethereum\-based BT to register and authorize the transactions\. In this framework\, Neo4j PLM is designated as the Single Source of Truth for the current product lifecycle and authorization state\, while GIT maintains file\-version history and the blockchain provides immutable evidence of authorized transactions\. Concurrently\, the elements mentioned above govern a digital thread that couples file creation\, authorization\, transfer\, confirmation\, and manufacturing operation execution through dispersed nodes\. The framework is proposed to guarantee that only approved and integrity\-assured files are permitted to enter the AM process\.

Figure 1\. Integrated architecture of the proposed GIT\-Neo4j\-IPFS\-BT framework for secure additive manufacturing data transfer\.

The process flows with the operator\, who works with the system through a user interface linked to the GIT layer\. At this step\, the approved G\-code manufacturing file\, generated from the CAD model through the slicing process\, is administered under a hybrid data governance ecosystem in which GIT controls the version history while Neo4j preserves the end\-to\-end lifecycle\. It is important to mention here that GIT is primarily responsible for conserving the meticulous file history via commit\-based versioning\, while Neo4j retains the metadata such as part IDs\, revisions\, operational stages\, authorization stage\, user links\, envisioned receiver\, and approved AM printer details\. This separation is critical as GIT alone can uphold the technical revision history but cannot support adequate lifecycle control for manufacturing\. Furthermore\, Neo4j acts as a lightweight PLM layer that regulates whether a file is qualified for transmission and printing\.

The main technical contribution is the integration of these otherwise separate mechanisms into a closed\-loop workflow that maintains the file version\, lifecycle approval\, distributed storage\, immutable transaction evidence\, receiver\-side integrity verification\, and authorized printer execution\.

\#\#\# 2\.2\. Core Technologies and Associated Roles

Figure 2 illustrates the process flow of the proposed framework and focuses on the performance during an actual file transfer and execution\. The workflow initiates with an approved G\-code manufacturing file at the sender node \(N1\)\, proceeds through the receiver node \(N2\) for retrieval and integrity verification\, and subsequently passes through the print gateway before being dispatched to the authorized AM printer\. The receiver node and the physical printer are treated as separate entities in the proposed architecture\. Traceability throughout the process is achieved via Neo4j\, and reliability is maintained using BT\. The framework can be classified into seven blocks\, including \(a\) Neo4j PLM\/GIT layer\, \(b\) N1\, \(c\) IPFS\, \(d\) BT integrated with smart contract \(SC\)\, \(e\) N2\, \(f\) reliability check\, and \(g\) print gateway along with AM execution\. All blocks have been explained below\.

Figure 2\. Operational workflow for receiver\-side validation\, integrity verification\, print authorization\, and manufacturing execution in the proposed framework\.

\#\#\#\# 2\.2\.1\. Neo4j PLM\/GIT Layer

Within the framework\, this layer is depicted as the trustworthy engineering source that integrates lifecycle administration and version management\. Neo4j serves as the authoritative source for the current lifecycle state\, including revision\, approval status\, authorized receiver\, and approved printer\. Its graph structure enables these evolving relationships to be efficiently maintained and queried\. Here\, GIT conserves the file version via commit\-based tracing and facilitates deterministic reclamation of the file\. Hence\, this block decides whether the given file is qualified for transmission as well as execution\. If the file has not attained the released state\, it is not allowed to exit the PLM ecosystem\. This principle ensures that the workflow consistently starts with a monitored engineering artifact rather than an arbitrary local file\.

In the current proof\-of\-concept implementation\, GIT and Neo4j are deployed as trusted centralized services\. The framework assumes the availability and integrity of these off\-chain components\, as their compromise or unavailability could affect file version retrieval and lifecycle authorization decisions\. Although blockchain provides immutable transaction records\, it does not eliminate risks associated with centralized off\-chain services\. Production deployment would require additional mechanisms\, such as access control\, backup\, replication\, monitoring\, and failover strategies to improve system availability and resilience\.

\#\#\#\# 2\.2\.7\. Print Gateway

This block serves as the definitive policy\-compliance layer before execution\. This layer acts as a gateway between the integrity check layer and the printer in such a way that even if the file has passed the integrity check\, the proposed framework does not allow the explicit printer execution\. In fact\, the authorized file is transmitted via the print gateway\, which verifies whether the requested printer \(

The proposed gateway also applies printer compatibility controls\, file format verification\, and policies of execution\. This design is critical for AM\, where unauthorized AM printer utilization can result in intellectual\-property \(IP\) leakage along with unidentified manufacturing and process exploitation\. Hence\, the print gateway presents a decisive control stage that splits the digital authentication from the actual manufacturing execution\.

After successful gateway authorization\, the verified file is released to the authorized physical printer through the printer interface\. The gateway therefore represents the final blockchain\-controlled authorization stage before off\-chain printer execution\.

\#\#\# 2\.3\. AM Printer Execution\: Algorithm for Secure File Transfer\, Verification\, and Controlled Manufacturing

Following successful receiver\-side verification and print\-gateway authorization\, the verified G\-code file is dispatched to the authorized AM printer interface\. At this point\, the blockchain\-controlled portion of the workflow is complete\. The verified file is subsequently transferred off\-chain to the authorized physical printer for manufacturing\. In the present proof\-of\-concept\, the printer executes the verified G\-code file\; however\, printer\-generated execution information such as job start\/end time\, printer status\, completion status\, and process data is not automatically returned to the blockchain or Neo4j\.

The feedback as well as the logging path\, as shown in Figure 2\, are crucial as they transform the proposed framework from one\-way to a closed\-loop traceability system\. Neo4j obtains PLM metadata and print logs\, thus permitting post\-process assessment\, auditability\, and lifecycle management\. The proposed framework not only supports safe transfer but also provides complete accountability from part design authorization to complete part production\.

Algorithm 1 discusses the algorithm for the workflow illustrated in Figure 2\. Within the table\, steps 1–2 show the Neo4j PLM authorization step\, where the system verifies that the particular file has been approved in the Neo4j block\. The workflow will be terminated if the file is not approved\. Steps 3–7 relate to the N1\-side requirement and registration phase\, where the file is recovered from GIT via an authorized commit\. At this stage\, the hash is processed and uploaded to IPFS to acquire the content ID\. As a result\, the accompanying metadata is uploaded to Neo4j\, and the transaction is registered on BC\, confirming protected storage and absolute traceability\. Steps 8–10 describe the retrieval phase at N2\, where the reference data is acquired from BT\, the file is downloaded from IPFS\, and the metadata from Neo4j is recovered\. In Steps 11–12\, the integrity check is carried out\, and the consistency is validated\. Here\, the hash is recomputed along with the GIT commit and PLM approval state verification\. The transaction will be terminated if any mismatch results are identified\. Step 13 imposes printer approval\, guaranteeing that an authorized machine is utilized for the printing process\. Steps 14–15 relate to supervised manufacturing operation\, where the verified file is transmitted to the printer through the gateway\, and printing results are recorded within Neo4j\.

Algorithm 1\: Secure File Transfer and Controlled Execution 

Input\:
Approved file record from Neo4j\/GIT

Output\:

Verified file executed on authorized printer or rejected

\- Query Neo4j PLM for approved file\, metadata\, receiver\, and printer
\- If status ≠ Approved → Terminate
\- Retrieve file f from Git using commit Cg
\- Compute hash Hf \= SHA\-256\(f\)
\- Upload f to IPFS → obtain CID \(C\_IPFS\)
\- Store metadata in Neo4j
\- Register \{C\_IPFS\, Hf\, Cg\, Rev\, Receiverauth\, Gatewayauth\, Printerauth\, MachineProfile\} on blockchain
\- At N2\, retrieve the immutable blockchain reference values for the Transfer ID
\- Compare the user\-supplied CID with the blockchain reference CID
\- Verify that the receiving node matches the authorized receiver
\- Download file f’ from IPFS
\- Fetch metadata from Neo4j
\- Compute Hf’ \= SHA\-256\(f’\)
\- If OR Hf’ ≠ Hf\(ref\) OR Cg’ ≠ Cg\(ref\) OR status ≠ Approved → Reject
\- If requested printer Pr ≠ authorized printer Pauth → Reject
\- Send verified file to printer via gateway
\- Execute print on authorized printer
\- End Algorithm

\#\#\# 2\.4\. Framework Testing Using AM Printer

The framework was tested to print the F450 Drone arm\. The CAD model was prepared using Siemens NX software at N1\. After CAD model generation\, the file was transferred using the framework explained above and was received at N2\. At N2\, the file was retrieved and was sent to an Elegoo Centauri Carbon AM printer equipped with a 0\.4 mm Hardened Steel Nozzle\. For printing\, Elegoo Rapid PETG filament was utilized\. Throughout the printing\, two perimeter walls and 15\% infill density were maintained\. Furthermore\, the arm was printed with the layer lines running parallel to the length of the arm\, necessary to hold inter\-layer stresses stable throughout the part\.

The present validation was conducted as proof\-of\-concept using one sender\, one receiver\, one printer\, and one representative manufacturing file\. Therefore\, the experiment evaluates functional feasibility rather than system scalability\.

\#\#\# 2\.5\. Cybersecurity Threat Model

A formal cybersecurity threat model was developed to define protected assets\, trusted components\, attacker capabilities\, trust boundaries\, attack surfaces\, and security assumptions of the proposed AM file\-transfer framework\. As illustrated in Figure 3\, the framework consists of five primary components\: the sender\/developer node\, off\-chain services comprising GIT\, IPFS\, and Neo4j PLM\, the blockchain network and smart contract\, the receiver node\, and the authorized AM printer\. Trust boundaries exist between these components because manufacturing data\, authorization information\, and control decisions are exchanged across different services\, networks\, and endpoints\.

Figure 3\. Threat model and trust boundaries of the proposed secure AM file\-transfer framework\.

The protected assets include the AM build file\, SHA\-256 file hash\, IPFS CID\, GIT revision information\, PLM authorization and approval records\, blockchain transaction records\, printer authorization information\, and cryptographic credentials\. The primary attack surfaces include network communication channels\, sender and receiver applications\, GIT and Neo4j interfaces\, IPFS storage and retrieval interfaces\, blockchain RPC interfaces\, smart\-contract functions\, blockchain private keys\, and the printer authorization interface\.

The adversary is assumed to be capable of intercepting network traffic\; modifying\, replacing\, or manipulating manufacturing files and associated metadata\; replaying previously valid transactions or requests\; compromising authentication credentials or cryptographic keys\; acting as a malicious authorized user\; compromising sender\, receiver\, or blockchain nodes\; and attempting denial\-of\-service \(DoS\) attacks\. These capabilities represent potential threats to confidentiality\, integrity\, authenticity\, traceability\, and availability of manufacturing data and associated authorization information\.

The current prototype assumes that authorized users\, sender and receiver hosts\, blockchain validator nodes\, and their associated private keys remain trusted and uncompromised\. Therefore\, attacks involving private\-key theft\, endpoint compromise\, malicious authorized users\, or validator compromise are included in the threat model but are outside the present experimental validation scope\. GIT and Neo4j PLM are assumed to operate under controlled access\, while IPFS is not relied upon as a trusted source of file integrity\. Instead\, files retrieved from IPFS are independently verified using their SHA\-256 hashes before being accepted for manufacturing\. Similarly\, blockchain records are treated as immutable audit references under the assumption that the validator nodes and transaction\-signing keys remain uncompromised\.

Under these assumptions\, the implemented framework provides file\-integrity verification through SHA\-256 hash comparison\, authorization enforcement through PLM and smart\-contract checks\, and immutable blockchain logging for traceability\. At the receiver\, the retrieved manufacturing file is verified against its registered SHA\-256 hash\, and the corresponding authorization information\, receiver identity\, file status\, and printer authorization are checked before manufacturing is permitted\.

Table 1 summarizes the identified security threats\, corresponding protection mechanisms\, and their validation status in the current implementation\. The present experimental validation focuses on two representative failure scenarios\: file\-integrity violation and unauthorized printer selection\. File tampering was evaluated by introducing mismatches in the registered and current CID\/SHA\-256 values\, while the unauthorized\-printer case was evaluated by selecting a printer different from the authorized manufacturing resource\. Receiver authorization\, GIT revision\, approval status\, and machine compatibility are implemented as verification checks within the successful workflow\, but their corresponding failure conditions were not independently tested\. Blockchain private\-key theft\, credential compromise\, malicious authorized users\, compromised sender or receiver nodes\, compromised blockchain validators\, replay attacks\, and denial\-of\-service attacks are included in the threat model but were not experimentally evaluated in the present prototype\. The current implementation therefore assumes that cryptographic credentials\, endpoint hosts\, and validator nodes remain trusted and uncompromised\. Accordingly\, the security claims of this study are limited to the mechanisms that were implemented and experimentally demonstrated\.

A unique contract address was allocated as presented in Figure 4 and documented in block 261 along with the subsequent hash for traceability\. This deployment used 0\.01874063 ETH \(10 gwei\)\, representing an effective implementation\. \#\#\# 3\.2\. Sender Node Output

As illustrated in Figure 5\, the N1 initiates the process flow by querying the Neo4j PLM\/GIT layer to retrieve an endorsed file \(PLM\-AM\-0001\, Revision R3\) and its GIT commit ID\, ensuring that version\-controlled data is selected\. The file is then fetched locally\, and a SHA\-256 hash is computed to generate a deterministic integrity fingerprint\. A unique content ID \(QmS5hhtM…\) is generated as the file is uploaded to IPFS\. In Neo4j\, an identical check is also carried out before the metadata is stored and the graph\-based relationships are developed among the N1\, transfer\, and authorized nodes\. Following on\, this transfer is registered on the BT via the employed SC\. Here\, the fundamental characteristics\, such as content ID\, generated hash\, version number\, and consent details\, are recorded through an immutable transaction \(0x a668c8195…\)\. Hence\, the sending process is fulfilled with an event recording in Neo4j\. It can be seen that the entire process was completed in 3\.69 s following coordinated communication among PLM\, IPFS\, Neo4j\, and BT\.

\#\#\# 3\.3\. Receiver Node Output\: Success Case

N2 utilizes the “TR\-20260919\-0013” transfer ID to retrieve the transaction record from the BT network\, as presented in Figure 6\. The record includes content ID\, hash\, GIT commit\, version number\, and endorsement information\. Following on\, the framework validates that the hash received at N2 matches the hash at N1 to ensure the dependability of the BT logs\. At this stage\, N2 permission is verified with the address stored in the BT network\. The metadata is then retrieved from the GIT PLM layer\, with a hash\, content\-ID\, version number\, GIT commit\, and authorization status\. The retrieved information is then cross\-verified with the BT data\, and the resultant file is downloaded from IPFS using the content ID and the recomputed localized SHA\-256 hash\. The framework performs a thorough integrity inspection by assessing the downloaded file against BT records\, and confirms the hash\, content ID\, GIT commit\, version number\, approval status\, and approval constraints across the BT network\. Upon validation\, the integrity result is logged to the blockchain transfer record\, and a receiver transaction hash is recorded\. The corresponding verification relationships and status are also recorded in Neo4j\. It\, in turn\, links the N2\, transfer\, and integrity to check nodes\. It can be seen that the whole process is completed in 2\.38 s\, which demonstrates uniform data certification and harmonization across a dispersed network\.

Figure 6\. Receiver node output showing blockchain verification\, Neo4j metadata retrieval\, IPFS file download\, multi\-layer integrity validation\, and blockchain status update\.

\#\#\# 3\.4\. Print Gateway Output

As displayed in Figure 7\, the print gateway receives the verified transfer package \(TR\-20260919\-0013\) after successful integrity validation at the receiver stage\. It first confirms that the selected printer matches the authorized printer defined on the blockchain\, then validates machine compatibility using the required machine profile\. A secure dispatch package is then created\, encapsulating the transfer of ID\, file path\, and associated integrity token\. An integrity\-verified dispatch package is created after the gateway confirms printer authorization\, machine compatibility\, and the pre\-dispatch file hash\. Following on\, the file is progressed to the printer interface\, and the transmission event is recorded on the BT transfer along with a timestamp\. Furthermore\, the operation is recorded in Neo4j by the gateway that captures events such as “PRINT\_GATEWAY\_APPROVED” and “FILE\_DISPATCHED\_TO\_PRINTER”\. The gateway records the authorization and dispatch result through a new blockchain transaction linked to the existing Transfer ID\. \#\#\# 3\.6\. Failure Case\: Integrity Check Failed

In the failure case\, as exhibited in Figure 9\, the receiver retrieves the original content ID and SHA\-256 hash from the blockchain for the given transfer\. For controlled integrity\-failure validation\, a modified manufacturing file with a different IPFS CID is supplied to the receiver\. The receiver first compares the user\-supplied CID with the immutable CID stored on the blockchain\, resulting in a CID mismatch\. The substituted file is then retrieved from IPFS\, and its SHA\-256 digest is recomputed and compared with the registered blockchain reference\. During integrity verification\, the CID comparison\, SHA\-256 comparison\, and GIT\-authorized content comparison fail\, whereas the receiver authorization\, revision\, and PLM approval checks pass\. Consequently\, the integrity status is marked as FAILED\, while the original blockchain registration record remains the immutable reference for the authorized file\. The failure is recorded in Neo4j through events such as CID\_MISMATCH\_DETECTED and INTEGRITY\_CHECK\_FAILED\, and further processing toward the print gateway is terminated\. For this controlled validation experiment only\, retrieval of the substituted CID was permitted after detection of the CID mismatch so that the downstream SHA\-256 and GIT\-content checks could also be evaluated\; in the normal operational workflow\, a CID mismatch results in rejection\. The failure\-detection process required 4\.34 s in the reported proof\-of\-concept run\.

Figure 9\. Integrity\-failure case showing mismatch between the user\-supplied IPFS CID and the immutable blockchain reference\, followed by SHA\-256 and GIT\-content verification failure\.

\#\#\# 3\.7\. Failure Case\: Unauthorized Printer

In this case as shown in Figure 10\, a valid integrity status “PASSED” is received by the gateway\, which verifies that the file has already been validated at the N2 node\. Nevertheless\, during the endorsement stage\, the framework assesses the endorsed printer defined in both the BT and the PLM \(PRINTER\_01\) against the user\-defined printer \(PRINTER\_02\)\. Printer endorsement declines because both printers are different\. Consequently\, the framework instantly rejects the file dispatch process\. The resultant rejection is recorded in Neo4j under “PRINT\_GATEWAY\_REJECTED” and “UNAUTHORIZED\_PRINTER” events\, and the gateway records the rejection through a new gateway\/dispatch transaction linked to the existing Transfer ID\. This exhibits that even with authorized data integrity\, the framework implements precise device\-level endorsement\, thus avoiding unauthorized production execution\.

Figure 10\. Failure case presenting denial at the gateway owing to the divergence between the approved and selected printers\.

The present proof\-of\-concept evaluates two representative failure scenarios\: file integrity violation and unauthorized printer selection\. The verification logic also includes GIT revision\, receiver authorization\, and approval\-status checks\; however\, these failure conditions were not independently tested in the present study\.

\#\# 4\. Conclusions

In this study\, a secure and traceable digital thread has been proposed for a distributed AM network by integrating GIT PLM\, Neo4j\, IPFS\, and Ethereum\-based BT\. The proposed outline combines file version administration\, lifecycle management and control\, disseminated data storage\, absolute transaction record\, integrity verification\, and printer\-level endorsement to create a secure pathway from design formation to manufacturing execution\.

Experimental validation using a drone arm established successful smart contract disposition\, safe file transmission\, dispersed storage retrieval\, integrity verification\, and authorized manufacturing execution\. In the reported single proof\-of\-concept run\, the recurring operational workflow required 8\.4 s\, comprising 3\.69 s for sender processing\, 2\.38 s for receiver\-side retrieval and integrity verification\, and 2\.33 s for print\-gateway authorization and dispatch\. Including the one\-time 7\.28 s smart\-contract deployment\, the aggregate processing time for the initial execution was 15\.68 s\. In addition\, the framework was also evaluated against tampered files\, such as hash mismatches\, to prevent unauthorized printer access\. These results reveal that the presented framework can efficiently preserve data integrity\, attribution\, and access control in distributed AM environments\.

The current evaluation is limited to one sender\, one receiver\, one printer\, and a representative file\. Since the file itself is transferred through IPFS and only the CID\, SHA\-256 hash\, and associated metadata are registered on the blockchain\, the file size primarily affects hashing and IPFS transfer rather than the blockchain payload size\. The present proof\-of\-concept also evaluates two representative failure scenarios\: file integrity violation and unauthorized printer access\. Although the verification logic includes GIT revision\, receiver authorization\, and approval\-status checks\, these cases were not independently tested\. Future work will extend the proposed digital thread beyond authorized printer dispatch by integrating printer\-side execution feedback\, including the job ID\, printer ID\, print start\/end timestamps\, completion status\, and relevant process data\, and linking these records to the corresponding Transfer ID in Neo4j and\, where appropriate\, the blockchain\. In addition\, the scalability and resilience of the framework will be further evaluated through experiments involving additional nodes\, concurrent transactions\, repeated runs\, and broader distributed network configurations\. These evaluations will include performance characterization through repeated trials\, measurement of mean execution time and variability\, and analysis of component\-level latency\, including blockchain transaction processing\, IPFS retrieval\, gateway processing\, and the failure detection response time\. Additional failure scenarios\, such as outdated GIT revisions\, unauthorized receivers\, Neo4j metadata manipulation\, replay attacks\, and communication failures\, will also be investigated\.

Future work will further examine distributed deployment strategies\, redundancy mechanisms\, and fault\-tolerant operation of off\-chain components\, including GIT and Neo4j\, to improve system availability and resilience\.

The established framework provides a basis for securing digital manufacturing ecosystems and supports the growing adoption of distributed manufacturing networks\. Future work will focus on leveraging real\-time printer process parameters\, digital twins\, multi\-node manufacturing networks\, and advanced access\-control mechanisms to further improve cybersecurity\, scalability\, and operational trust in AM systems\.

A Year-End Reflection from the Editor-in-Chief
- Editorial
- Published:
As 2026 draws to a close, I would like to extend my sincere gratitude to the Experimental Mechanics community—our authors, reviewers, Technical Editors, International Advisory Board members, Guest Editors, publishing staff, and readers—whose dedication and contributions continue to strengthen the journal and advance our field.
This has been an exciting year for Experimental Mechanics. The journal continues to attract high-quality contributions spanning both established and emerging areas of experimental mechanics. We were also pleased to see the journal's Impact Factor reach 2.9, its highest level to date. While metrics are only one measure of a journal's influence, this milestone reflects the quality of the research published in Experimental Mechanics and the collective efforts of our authors, reviewers, editors, and broader community.
At the same time, the field of experimental mechanics itself continues to evolve. Advances in full-field measurements, high-speed and high-resolution characterization, additive manufacturing and architectured materials, soft and biological systems, and artificial intelligence and data-driven methods are expanding both what we can measure and what we can learn from experiments. Increasingly, experiments are also being integrated with theory, computation, and data science to provide deeper understanding of material and structural behavior. Experimental Mechanics seeks to embrace these developments while maintaining its foundation in rigorous experimentation and innovation in experimental methods.
Special Issues
Special Issues continue to provide an important forum for highlighting emerging research directions and bringing together communities across experimental mechanics. Several collections highlighted in last year's year-end message reached important milestones in 2026, while new Special Issues have been launched to further broaden the journal's reach. I am deeply grateful to all of our Guest Editors for their vision, leadership, and considerable efforts in developing and managing these collections.
Published in 2026
Celebrating Prof. Cesar Sciammarella’s 100th Anniversary and Contributions Guest Editors: Cosme Furlong, Horacio Espinosa, Kyung-Suk Kim, Gordon A. Shaw, and Mike Sutton Published: First issue of 2026
Recent Progress in Chemomechanics Guest Editors: Emilio Martínez-Pañeda and Kejie Zhao Published: 7th issue of 2026
Completed and Scheduled for Publication in 2027
Mechanics of Soft and Living Matter Guest Editors: Xueju “Sophie” Wang, Ruobing Bai, and Christian Franck Publication: 2027
Emerging Frontiers in Experimental Mechanics: Collection of the 2025 International Symposium on Experimental Mechanics (ISEM 2025) Guest Editors: Ming-Tzer Lin, Yu-Lung Lo, and Wei-Chung Wang Publication: 2027
New and Upcoming Special Issues
Machine Learning for Full-field Experimental Mechanics Guest Editors: Hanxun Jin, Jin Yang, Kshitiz Upadhyay, Christos Athanasiou, and Samantha Daly Submissions open through January 31, 2027
Mechanics of Porous and Architectured Materials Guest Editors: Ameya Rege, Anastasiia Krushynska, and Atul Bhaskar Submissions open through March 31, 2027
Recent Advances in Nanoindentation and Instrumented Indentation: From Fundamentals to AI-Driven Characterization Guest Editors: Ill Ryu, Gi-Dong Sim, and Eun-chae Jeon Submissions open December 1, 2026 through March 31, 2027
Together, these Special Issues reflect the breadth of contemporary experimental mechanics—from foundational measurement and characterization to emerging applications in chemomechanics, soft and living matter, architectured materials, and machine learning. They also illustrate our commitment to ensuring that Experimental Mechanics remains a welcoming venue for new directions at the frontiers of the field.
Our Editorial Community
The success of the journal depends fundamentally on the people who generously contribute their time and expertise to the editorial process. I am especially grateful to our Technical Editors, whose judgment, scientific expertise, and commitment are essential to maintaining the journal quality and efficiency.
I would like to express my sincere appreciation to Janice Barton, Adrian DeWald, Shelby Hutchens, Michael Keller, Jamie Kimberley, John Kolinski, Kunal Mishra, and Luoyu (Roy) Xu, who completed their terms as Technical Editors at the end of 2025. I am deeply grateful for their dedicated service and many contributions to the journal. I am also pleased that Janice Barton continues her service to Experimental Mechanics as a member of our International Advisory Board.
We also welcomed four new Technical Editors in 2026: Frank DelRio (returned after a short break), Xinglong Gong, Chenglin Wu, and Mohammad Naraghi. I thank them for their contributions during their first year on the Editorial Board and look forward to continuing to work with them in the years ahead.
I would also like to offer a special thank you to our reviewers. Peer review is essential to the quality and integrity of the journal, yet it is work performed largely behind the scenes. Every thoughtful review represents a generous contribution of time and expertise. Your careful assessments not only help us make sound editorial decisions but also help authors strengthen their work. On behalf of the entire editorial team, thank you for this invaluable service.
Most importantly, I thank our authors for choosing Experimental Mechanics as a home for your research and our readers for your continued engagement with the journal. I am also grateful to the Society for Experimental Mechanics and our publishing team at Springer Nature for their continued support and partnership.
Looking Ahead
As we look toward 2027, our priorities remain clear: to publish rigorous and impactful research, maintain an efficient and thoughtful peer-review process, increase the visibility and reach of the journal, and continue to broaden our engagement with emerging areas of mechanics.
The field of experimental mechanics is changing rapidly, but its fundamental role remains as important as ever. New instrumentation, imaging and measurement capabilities, together with advances in computation and artificial intelligence, are creating unprecedented opportunities to observe, quantify, and understand mechanical behavior across scales. I am excited about the role that Experimental Mechanics can play in bringing these developments together and in helping define the future of our field.
On behalf of the entire editorial team, thank you for your continued support, and for everything you have contributed during 2026. I look forward to another exciting year of discoveries, innovations, and collaborations in 2027.
Junlan Wang Editor-in-Chief, Experimental Mechanics.

records.body_text:
Intel Makes AI Optical Interconnect Push, Claims to Be Sole Volume Producer of 300mm Indium Phosphide Wafers
Intel laid out its full silicon photonics technology blueprint at the OCP 2026 conference, positioning the technology as the core architecture for next-generation high-performance computing and AI data centers. Nic Dubé, Intel's vice president of data center systems and solutions, described silicon photonics as a "golden hammer" and claimed Intel is the only wafer fab in the industry capable of integrating indium phosphide (InP) on a 300mm silicon wafer platform and producing it at volume.
Dubé noted that discussions about silicon photonics becoming an industry standard have been going on for years, and that Intel's team is fully committed, with the goal of making the technology truly take hold within the next two years. He explained that traditional copper interconnects are approaching physical limits on three fronts — transmission distance, bandwidth density at the package edge, and energy per bit — and that silicon photonics can solve all three problems at once.
Indium phosphide is a III-V compound semiconductor capable of producing laser light sources, and can be integrated with silicon photonics platforms to provide the light source needed for optical data transmission. Compared with designs that rely entirely on external light sources, integrated lasers help reduce the complexity of packaging and optical connections. Intel said its integrated laser design uses a highly reliable light source requiring no additional maintenance, while also supporting industry standards for external light sources, preserving design flexibility across different system architectures and providing the industry with a U.S. wafer fab source for multi-wavelength light sources.
It is worth noting that Intel's "300mm indium phosphide" refers to InP integrated on a 300mm silicon wafer platform (InP on 300mm Silicon), not the use of a full 300mm indium phosphide crystal as the substrate. The industry's standard InP substrates remain predominantly 150mm (6-inch), with 3-inch and 4-inch still widely used; InP crystals are brittle, grow slowly and are difficult to control for defects, limiting the number of laser dies that can be produced per wafer. Intel's approach integrates InP lasers into its existing 300mm silicon photonics volume manufacturing platform, leveraging the economies of scale of silicon processes to cut costs and expand capacity.
On deployment, Intel uses near-packaged optics (NPO) and co-packaged optics (CPO) to push optical components as close as possible to compute chips and network switch chips, shortening the transmission path for high-speed electrical signals and easing the signal attenuation and power burden of copper wiring in high-speed, long-distance scenarios.
Intel's energy target is to drive the transmission energy of optical interconnect systems below 5 picojoules per transmitted bit (5pJ/bit). The semiconductor industry has long viewed this as a key threshold for commercializing optical interconnects, though what Intel has disclosed so far remains a technology development goal, with no volume production timeline yet.
Intel is not starting from scratch in this field. Since 2016, the company has shipped more than 8 million photonic integrated circuits (PICs) containing over 32 million integrated lasers, mainly for pluggable optical transceiver modules used by large cloud providers. In June 2024, Intel demonstrated an optical I/O chiplet (OCI) co-packaged with a CPU: 4Tbps bidirectional in total, with 64 channels at 32Gbps each, and at 5pJ/bit versus roughly 15pJ/bit for pluggable modules — about one-third of the latter. Intel also noted at the time that while the OCI can reach 100 meters over fiber, optical propagation delay means practical application scenarios may be only tens of meters.
The company stresses that the value of silicon photonics lies not only in raising bandwidth but also in changing the logic of how compute resources are allocated. Future data centers will be able to link different CPUs, GPUs and memory pools through high-speed optical interconnects, scheduling resources in real time according to AI workload demands and reducing the idle capacity caused by the fixed configurations of traditional servers. Intel will also provide advanced interconnect topologies and runtime resource orchestration capabilities to keep pace with the continued expansion of AI models.
Intel Silicon Photonics Technology Highlights | Details
---|---
Volume manufacturing capability | InP integrated on a 300mm silicon wafer platform; claimed to be the industry's only volume producer
Packaging technology | Near-packaged optics (NPO), co-packaged optics (CPO)
Light source approach | Integrated lasers, plus support for industry standards for external light sources
Energy target | Below 5pJ/bit per transmitted bit
System value | Supports dynamic resource scheduling across CPUs, GPUs and memory pools
Note: 5pJ/bit is a technology target Intel has consistently disclosed since its 2024 OCI demonstration, not a volume production specification.
However, CPO and NPO still face multiple hurdles before large-scale commercialization. Long-term light-source reliability, thermal design, packaging yields, failure repair methods, and cross-vendor industry standard-setting are all issues that must be overcome. Although Intel has secured a position in wafer-level manufacturing, the supply chain involved in optical packaging is far more complex than that of traditional chips, and any link falling short of expected yields will drag down the overall cost structure.
Testing is another bottleneck for volume production. Although optical alignment time has been shortened to within seconds, a complete test of a single photonic integrated circuit can still take more than 100 seconds, shifting the bottleneck from alignment to test speed and cost. Research firm TrendForce therefore expects 2027 to be the key year for CPO test system integration, and 2028 to be the critical period for determining whether large-scale volume production can be achieved.
From an industry competition perspective, silicon photonics is already seen as the key bottleneck solution for scaling AI clusters. As the number of GPUs in a single rack continues to climb, copper cabling's disadvantages in bandwidth density and power consumption are becoming increasingly obvious, and both network chip makers and wafer foundries have already invested in related efforts. By putting its ability to volume-manufacture InP integrated on 300mm silicon wafers on the table, Intel aims to turn its wafer fab assets into a differentiating advantage and win AI infrastructure customers over to its platform.
Vendor | CPO Solution | Key Specifications | Progress (October 2026)
---|---|---|---
NVIDIA | Spectrum-X CPO switches (co-developed with TSMC, using COUPE packaging) | Switching capacity up to 400Tb/s | Shipping to select partners; capacity to expand further in the second half of 2026
Broadcom | Tomahawk 6-Davisson third-generation CPO | 102.4Tb/s, 200Gbps per lane | Showcased at OCP 2026; Bailly 51.2T already in volume production with limited shipments, saving up to 70% power versus pluggable solutions
TSMC | COUPE-on-substrate advanced packaging | Power efficiency doubled, latency 10x lower than board-level pluggable optics (company claim) | Entering production in 2026
Huawei | Ascend 960 supernode (NPO) | For large-scale AI training and inference | Announced September 2026
Lightmatter | 204.8Tb/s CPO switch tray (with Flex) | 204.8Tb/s | Announced October 2026, used to validate volume production processes
The table shows that CPO competition has expanded from individual chips to advanced packaging. NVIDIA's Spectrum-X CPO switches were co-developed with TSMC and use its COUPE packaging, and TSMC plans to bring COUPE-on-substrate into production in 2026, claiming twice the power efficiency and ten times lower latency than board-level pluggable optics. This also means the key to AI optical interconnects lies not only in upstream photonic chips but also in the advanced packaging capacity controlled by TSMC; industry analysis notes that CPO switches must compete with AI chips and HPC processors for the same pool of 2.5D/3D packaging resources.
In Japan, NTT is advancing its own photonics-electronics convergence path through the IOWN architecture. Each PEC-2 module delivers 3.2Tb/s — equivalent to the bandwidth of eight 400G pluggable optical transceivers — with 87% less volume and power consumption cut from about 96W to 48W; a 51.2Tb/s photonics-electronics convergence switch prototype equipped with PEC-2 occupies just 2RU and ran continuously for six months from April to October 2025 at Expo 2025 Osaka-Kansai, distributing venue camera footage in real time to multiple GPUs for AI analysis. NTT plans to offer commercial samples in 2026 and is developing a 6.4Tb/s version to match 102.4Tb/s switch chips, targeting 50% power savings versus pluggable solutions. Addressing the difficulty of repairing failed CPO units, NTT has also proposed a pluggable socket-type package that allows photonics modules to be swapped like conventional transceivers.
For data center operators, if optical interconnects can drive energy per transmitted bit below 5pJ/bit, it will directly affect the power provisioning and thermal design of large-scale AI clusters, which in turn will influence rack density and total cost of ownership. However, before industry standards are settled and repair models are validated, most operators are expected to first verify reliability through small-scale deployments before gradually scaling up adoption.

records.title: Navigating the Shift: Trivalent Chromium Plating in the Automotive Steel Market - Products Finishing
records.abstract: Navigating the Shift: Trivalent Chromium Plating in the Automotive Steel Market Products Finishing
records.summary: This Products Finishing article previews a SUR/FIN 2026 presentation by MKS Atotech on adopting decorative trivalent chromium plating for automotive steel bumpers and exterior components. It frames the problem as long-standing industry hurdles: decorative trivalent processes have existed for decades, but widespread adoption has been slowed by debate over chloride-based versus sulfate-based chemistries and by rigorous interior and exterior performance requirements that complicate decisions for suppliers, applicators and OEMs. The article states it reviews the strategic transition of automotive steel into the trivalent chromium market, examining barriers to entry and the technical evolution of these processes, and outlines how the industry is navigating regulatory and performance demands toward sustainable, high-quality plating solutions. Only a short article preview is available, so no specific process parameters, test data or measured outcomes are reported in the supplied text.

Navigating the Shift: Trivalent Chromium Plating in the Automotive Steel Market
MKS Atotech details the path to success to adopting trivalent chromium plating for automotive steel bumpers and exterior components.
Share
Read Next
This paper is based on a presentation originally given at SUR/FIN 2026 in Rosemont, Illinois on June 2, 2026, in Session 3: Automotive Surface Finishing. Decorative trivalent plating processes have been available for several decades, yet widespread adoption has faced significant industry hurdles. Debates regarding chloride-based chemistries versus sulfate-based chemistries, coupled with rigorous requirements for interior and exterior performance, have created a complex landscape for suppliers, applicators and OEMs alike.
This article reviews the strategic transition of automotive steel into the trivalent chromium market. By examining barriers to entry and the technical evolution of these processes, it outlines how the industry is successfully navigating regulatory and performance demands to implement sustainable, high-quality plating solutions.
The full presentation can be accessed and printed at short.pfonline.com/NASF26-Nov2.

Oct 19, 2026 View: 108 Leave a message
How thick should the gold plating on a pogo pin be?
Alice Smith
Alice is a senior R&D engineer at Dongguan Xinteng Electronics Co., Ltd. With over 8 years of experience in the field of Pogo Pin connectors, she specializes in the research of high - current and miniaturization scenarios. She has contributed to many of the company's patented products and more than 300 solutions.
Gold thickness is often written in microinches, shown as µin or µ". One microinch equals 0.0254 micrometers (µm), so the differences between 1 µin, 3 µin and 5 µin are extremely small. They still matter: a thin coating can wear through or develop pores sooner than a thicker one under the same conditions.
Thickness is only part of the specification. The type of gold deposit, nickel underplate, mating pad, contact force and movement during connection all affect service life. There is no reliable rule that assigns one gold thickness to all consumer products and another to all industrial or medical products.
What do 1, 3, 5 and 10 microinches mean?
Nominal gold thickness | Metric equivalent | How to assess it
---|---|---
1 µin | 0.0254 µm | A very thin finish. Consider it only after checking wear and corrosion requirements.
3 µin | 0.0762 µm | Still a thin finish. Its suitability depends on the mating design and expected use.
5 µin | 0.127 µm | Provides more gold than a 1 or 3 µin finish, but does not establish a cycle-life rating.
10 µin | 0.254 µm | May be considered when more coating thickness is needed at the contact area; testing remains necessary.
These figures describe thickness, not guaranteed performance grades. In particular, a 3 to 5 µin finish should not be described as a universal "industrial standard," and 10 µin cannot be translated into tens of thousands of mating cycles without test results for the specific connector.
Start with the way the contact is used
A pogo pin that touches a pad a few times during factory testing has a different duty from a charging contact used several times each day. Count both the expected connections and what happens during each one. A pin that lands squarely on a pad experiences different wear from one that slides across the pad as a device settles into a dock.
The environment changes the decision too. Humidity, skin oils and cleaning residues can affect exposed contacts. Gold helps maintain a conductive surface because it does not readily form an insulating oxide in air, but a thin gold layer may contain pores. The nickel beneath it and the quality of the plating process therefore matter alongside the stated gold thickness.
For a magnetic connector, attraction and alignment also need review. If the magnets pull the two halves together with sideways movement, the contacts may wipe across their pads on every connection. That motion can be useful for clearing minor surface contamination, but it also changes the wear pattern. The required plating should be chosen with the assembled connector in mind.
Specify the surface that actually makes contact
A drawing that says only "gold plated, 5 µin" leaves several questions unanswered. Is 5 µin a nominal value or the minimum permitted thickness? Is it required at the tip, on the mating pad or across the entire part? What nickel underplate is specified? Is the gold finish intended for repeated electrical contact?
These details affect both cost and inspection. Gold applied to areas that never make contact may add expense without improving performance. Conversely, a thickness measured on an accessible area of the part may not describe the coating at the point where the pin meets its pad. The internal plunger-to-barrel interface also deserves consideration because it can form part of the current path.
When a customer provides a drawing, we can review these contact areas together with the pin stroke, tip geometry and mating arrangement, then develop a pogo pin or magnetic connector solution for the intended application. Sample testing can help resolve the plating specification before it is applied to a production order.
Test the complete contact pair
The most useful comparison is between candidate finishes tested under the same conditions. Measure contact resistance at the intended working stroke, cycle the pin against the specified mating pad, then measure resistance again and inspect both surfaces. Where the product may encounter moisture or contaminants, add environmental testing that reflects its expected use.
A thicker gold deposit may be justified if the thinner candidate wears through or its resistance becomes unstable. If both candidates meet the requirement, the thinner finish may be a reasonable cost choice. The result belongs to that pin, pad and test setup; it should not be treated as a rating for every product with the same plating thickness.
FAQ
Is 1 µin of gold enough for a consumer product?
It may be enough for a particular low-use design, but the product category alone cannot answer the question. Check the mating frequency, contact motion, environment and test results before specifying such a thin finish.
Is 3 to 5 µin the standard for industrial or medical pogo pins?
No universal thickness applies to either category. The required finish follows the device's contact design, expected service life and applicable qualification requirements.
Will 10 µin of gold support tens of thousands of connections?
Thickness alone cannot guarantee that. Tip shape, spring force, alignment, mating pad finish and the type of gold deposit all affect wear. A cycle-life claim needs testing on the finished contact pair.
What should be included on a custom pogo pin drawing?
Identify the contact areas and state whether the specified gold thickness is nominal or minimum. Include the underplate, mating pad finish, working stroke, expected connection cycles and operating environment so the design can be sampled and checked against its intended use.

records.body_text:
Near-Packaged Optics NPO: A Comprehensive Guide
The demand for bandwidth in AI computing clusters is surging, driving the large-scale deployment of 800G, 1.6T, and even higher-speed interconnects. In traditional setups, pluggable optical modules are positioned on the front panels of switches or servers; this requires high-speed electrical signals—output by ASICs or GPUs—to travel across long copper traces on the PCB to reach the optical modules.
These long copper traces create three primary bottlenecks: significant high-speed signal attenuation, crosstalk, and degraded signal integrity. To compensate for these losses, the link must incorporate a Digital Signal Processor (DSP), which keeps power consumption high. Furthermore, the limited physical space on the front panel constrains port density and hinders effective airflow for cooling. While LPO (Linear-Drive Pluggable Optics) simplifies the internal DSP, it fails to eliminate the signal loss inherent in the long electrical path from the chip to the front panel. Against this backdrop, NPO (Near-Package Optics) has emerged as an intermediate solution that balances performance, maintainability, and implementation feasibility. By relocating the optoelectronic conversion unit closer to the chip package, NPO effectively resolves the high-speed interconnect bottlenecks caused by long copper traces on the front panel.
What exactly is an NPO?
Definition
NPO stands for "Near-Packaged Optics." In an NPO configuration, the optical engine is placed on the motherboard in the vicinity of the ASIC/GPU chip package. The optical engine remains a separate, independent package—distinct from the chip’s own package substrate—and is connected to the chip via short-reach, high-speed electrical interconnects. In this setup, optical fibers emerge from the optical engine rather than from the device's front panel.
Working principle
Concept: Minimize the transmission distance of high-speed electrical signals.
High-speed electrical signals output by switching or computing chips travel only a few centimeters—via short PCB traces—to an adjacent NPO (Near-Packaged Optics) light engine. Within the light engine, electrical-to-optical and optical-to-electrical conversions take place; the signals are then transmitted externally via an optical fiber array. This significantly reduces losses in the short electrical link, potentially eliminating the need for a DSP (Digital Signal Processor) in certain scenarios by utilizing linear drive instead, thereby lowering interconnect power consumption. The light engine is designed as an independent, detachable unit, allowing for individual replacement in the event of a failure without requiring the replacement of the entire motherboard or the main chip.
The problem to be solved
● Significantly shorten the copper trace length between the chip and the optoelectronic conversion unit, reducing high-frequency signal loss and crosstalk, while improving signal integrity;
● Reduce or eliminate the need for a DSP, thereby lowering power consumption per bit transmitted;
● Free up space on the device's front panel, increasing the port bandwidth density of the entire system;
● Provide an engineering compromise between the high integration complexity of CPO (Co-Packaged Optics) and the high power consumption of traditional pluggable modules, balancing performance with operational and maintenance requirements.
What constitutes the system: Hardware overview
A complete NPO system mainly includes the following hardware components, with the signal flow as follows: ASIC/GPU chip → board-level high-speed electrical interconnect → NPO optical engine → fiber optic array → peer optical interconnect device.
● ASIC/GPU main chip : computing/switching core, outputting high-speed serial electrical signals;
● Onboard high-speed interconnect substrate/socket : connects the main chip and NPO optical engine, provides a short-distance high-speed electrical interface, and supports optical engine installation and removal;
● NPO optical engine (core unit) : integrates light emission, light reception, driving, and TIA components to complete electro-optical/photoelectric conversion;
● Fiber Array (FAU) : High-density fiber optic cabling, drawn from the optical engine, responsible for optical signal transmission;
● Supporting passive components : fiber optic connectors, alignment structures, heat dissipation components, and shielding structures;
● System motherboard PCB : contains chips, NPO optical engine, power supply and control circuitry.
Signal Path
The chip generates a high-speed electrical signal, which is sent to the NPO optical engine via a short-distance onboard power-on link; the optical engine modulates the electrical signal into an optical signal, which is then transmitted to the NPO engine at the other end via an optical fiber array; the receiving optical engine restores the optical signal into an electrical signal and sends it back to the receiving chip.
Product Type and Category Differentiation
NPO products can be classified according to light source solution, optical technology architecture, and bandwidth specifications.
Classified by light source/light technology
● CW continuous wave light source solution : external continuous laser, the optical engine is only responsible for modulation and reception; the light source is centrally deployed, which facilitates heat dissipation and wavelength management, and is suitable for high-density large-scale clusters;
● Integrated light source type optical engine : The laser is integrated inside the optical engine, resulting in higher overall integration, but the optical engine generates more heat and the thermal management becomes more difficult.
Classified by bandwidth specifications
Mainstream options are 800G, 1.6T, and 3.2T single-engine bandwidth, and specifications are divided into 100G/lane, 200G/lane, etc., based on channel rate.
Classification by installation method
● Plug-in NPO optical engine: can be individually disassembled and replaced on site, is maintenance-friendly, and is the current mainstream commercial form;
● Surface mount NPO light engine: directly mounted on the motherboard, with higher integration density, but increased maintenance difficulty.
Mainstream NPO-Related Vendors and Products
Corning: GlassBridge™ Glass-Based Optical Interconnect Components
Corning does not manufacture NPO optical engines directly; instead, it provides passive coupling components for NPO architectures that connect Photonic Integrated Circuits (PICs) to fiber arrays. Utilizing glass optical waveguides for passive alignment, these components offer low coupling loss and support high-density parallel channels. They simplify the micron-level optical assembly of optical engines and serve as an essential interconnect solution for NPO systems from various vendors.
Coherent: 1.6T VCSEL NPO Optical Engine
A socketable, pluggable optical engine based on VCSEL technology with an integrated laser source. It supports linear, DSP-free links. Designed for ease of deployment—eliminating the need for external light-source cabinets—it is targeted at AI supernodes and short-reach intra-rack interconnects, with a clear upgrade path to higher-bandwidth optical engine platforms.
Broadcom: 3.2T VCSEL NPO Optical Engine
Featuring a VCSEL-based architecture, this ultra-low-power, socketable optical engine can be arranged in arrays around a switching ASIC. With a per-channel data rate of 128 Gbps, it leverages the native NPO electrical interfaces of Broadcom’s Tomahawk switching chips. It is intended for next-generation AI leaf-spine switches and is currently a key solution under evaluation by major overseas cloud service providers.
Lightmatter: Passage L20 Optical Engine
A silicon photonics-based solution compatible with both NPO and CPO architectures, utilizing an external continuous-wave (CW) light source. By relocating the heat source externally, it reduces thermal stress around the chip. ● Point-to-point paired deployment : NPOs must be used in pairs – transmitting optical engine + fiber array + receiving optical engine, with one end converting electrical to optical and the other end converting optical to electrical, for direct connection between GPU-GPU and ASIC-ASIC devices.

Step 3: Establishing Fiber Optic Connections: The fiber optic array is led out from the optical engine, and the cabling is completed inside the chassis and connected to the NPO optical engine at the other end. The two ends are paired for transmitting and receiving.

● Process and Standards: Micron-level coupling precision affects mass production yield, and cross-vendor interface standards need to be unified.
● Complex troubleshooting and debugging: The optoelectronic system requires joint debugging and testing, and there are many steps involved in fault location.

Near-Package Optics (NPO) achieves an engineering balance among power consumption, bandwidth density, and maintainability by positioning the optical engine close to the chip package, thereby shortening the copper traces used for high-speed electrical signals. Far from being a mere transitional solution, NPO is a practical, viable technology roadmap designed for AI super-node interconnects. Situated between traditional pluggable optical modules and Co-Packaged Optics (CPO), it avoids the high manufacturing risks associated with CPO while resolving the bottlenecks caused by high-speed traces on the front panel. Consequently, NPO stands as a core optical interconnect choice for high-density computing networks in the coming years.
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)
What is the core difference between NPO and CPO?
CPO optical devices and ASICs are on the same package substrate; NPO optical engines are independent and placed on the motherboard next to the chip, with a removable socket, and the optoelectronics do not share the same substrate.
Does NPO necessarily not need DSP?
Not absolutely. In short-link scenarios, the DSP can be removed and a linear drive LPO architecture can be adopted; in some longer on-board link scenarios, a lightweight DSP is still retained.
Can NPO only be used for AI switches?
It is mainly used for interconnection between intelligent computing switches and super node servers. It can also be used for high-density data center switches. In ordinary cloud data center traditional rack scenarios, pluggable modules are preferred.
The NPO light engine is broken. Do I need to replace the entire motherboard?
No. The standard NPO uses a socket-type structure, with the light engine as an independent unit that can be individually plugged in and replaced. The motherboard and main chip are retained.
Where does the NPO fiber optic cable originate?
The optical fiber is led out from the NPO optical engine on the motherboard inside the chassis, and no longer goes through the optical port on the front panel of the device. Dedicated optical fiber cabling management is required inside the chassis.
