\#\# Near\-Packaged Optics NPO\: A Comprehensive Guide

The demand for bandwidth in AI computing clusters is surging\, driving the large\-scale deployment of 800G\, 1\.6T\, and even higher\-speed interconnects\. In traditional setups\, pluggable optical modules are positioned on the front panels of switches or servers\; this requires high\-speed electrical signals—output by ASICs or GPUs—to travel across long copper traces on the PCB to reach the optical modules\.

These long copper traces create three primary bottlenecks\: significant high\-speed signal attenuation\, crosstalk\, and degraded signal integrity\. To compensate for these losses\, the link must incorporate a Digital Signal Processor \(DSP\)\, which keeps power consumption high\. Furthermore\, the limited physical space on the front panel constrains port density and hinders effective airflow for cooling\. While LPO \(Linear\-Drive Pluggable Optics\) simplifies the internal DSP\, it fails to eliminate the signal loss inherent in the long electrical path from the chip to the front panel\. Against this backdrop\, NPO \(Near\-Package Optics\) has emerged as an intermediate solution that balances performance\, maintainability\, and implementation feasibility\. By relocating the optoelectronic conversion unit closer to the chip package\, NPO effectively resolves the high\-speed interconnect bottlenecks caused by long copper traces on the front panel\.

\#\# What exactly is an NPO\?

\#\# Definition

NPO stands for \"Near\-Packaged Optics\.\" In an NPO configuration\, the optical engine is placed on the motherboard in the vicinity of the ASIC\/GPU chip package\. The optical engine remains a separate\, independent package—distinct from the chip’s own package substrate—and is connected to the chip via short\-reach\, high\-speed electrical interconnects\. In this setup\, optical fibers emerge from the optical engine rather than from the device\'s front panel\.

\#\# Working principle

Concept\: Minimize the transmission distance of high\-speed electrical signals\.

High\-speed electrical signals output by switching or computing chips travel only a few centimeters—via short PCB traces—to an adjacent NPO \(Near\-Packaged Optics\) light engine\. Within the light engine\, electrical\-to\-optical and optical\-to\-electrical conversions take place\; the signals are then transmitted externally via an optical fiber array\. This significantly reduces losses in the short electrical link\, potentially eliminating the need for a DSP \(Digital Signal Processor\) in certain scenarios by utilizing linear drive instead\, thereby lowering interconnect power consumption\. The light engine is designed as an independent\, detachable unit\, allowing for individual replacement in the event of a failure without requiring the replacement of the entire motherboard or the main chip\.

\#\# The problem to be solved

● Significantly shorten the copper trace length between the chip and the optoelectronic conversion unit\, reducing high\-frequency signal loss and crosstalk\, while improving signal integrity\;

● Reduce or eliminate the need for a DSP\, thereby lowering power consumption per bit transmitted\;

● Free up space on the device\'s front panel\, increasing the port bandwidth density of the entire system\;

● Provide an engineering compromise between the high integration complexity of CPO \(Co\-Packaged Optics\) and the high power consumption of traditional pluggable modules\, balancing performance with operational and maintenance requirements\.

\#\# What constitutes the system\: Hardware overview

A complete NPO system mainly includes the following hardware components\, with the signal flow as follows\: ASIC\/GPU chip → board\-level high\-speed electrical interconnect → NPO optical engine → fiber optic array → peer optical interconnect device\.

● ASIC\/GPU main chip \: computing\/switching core\, outputting high\-speed serial electrical signals\;

● Onboard high\-speed interconnect substrate\/socket \: connects the main chip and NPO optical engine\, provides a short\-distance high\-speed electrical interface\, and supports optical engine installation and removal\;

● NPO optical engine \(core unit\) \: integrates light emission\, light reception\, driving\, and TIA components to complete electro\-optical\/photoelectric conversion\;

● Fiber Array \(FAU\) \: High\-density fiber optic cabling\, drawn from the optical engine\, responsible for optical signal transmission\;

● Supporting passive components \: fiber optic connectors\, alignment structures\, heat dissipation components\, and shielding structures\;

● System motherboard PCB \: contains chips\, NPO optical engine\, power supply and control circuitry\.

\#\# Signal Path

The chip generates a high\-speed electrical signal\, which is sent to the NPO optical engine via a short\-distance onboard power\-on link\; the optical engine modulates the electrical signal into an optical signal\, which is then transmitted to the NPO engine at the other end via an optical fiber array\; the receiving optical engine restores the optical signal into an electrical signal and sends it back to the receiving chip\.

\#\# Product Type and Category Differentiation

NPO products can be classified according to light source solution\, optical technology architecture\, and bandwidth specifications\.

\#\# Classified by light source\/light technology

● CW continuous wave light source solution \: external continuous laser\, the optical engine is only responsible for modulation and reception\; the light source is centrally deployed\, which facilitates heat dissipation and wavelength management\, and is suitable for high\-density large\-scale clusters\;

● Integrated light source type optical engine \: The laser is integrated inside the optical engine\, resulting in higher overall integration\, but the optical engine generates more heat and the thermal management becomes more difficult\.

\#\# Classified by bandwidth specifications

Mainstream options are 800G\, 1\.6T\, and 3\.2T single\-engine bandwidth\, and specifications are divided into 100G\/lane\, 200G\/lane\, etc\.\, based on channel rate\.

\#\# Classification by installation method

● Plug\-in NPO optical engine\: can be individually disassembled and replaced on site\, is maintenance\-friendly\, and is the current mainstream commercial form\;

● Surface mount NPO light engine\: directly mounted on the motherboard\, with higher integration density\, but increased maintenance difficulty\.

\#\# Mainstream NPO\-Related Vendors and Products

\#\# Corning\: GlassBridge™ Glass\-Based Optical Interconnect Components

Corning does not manufacture NPO optical engines directly\; instead\, it provides passive coupling components for NPO architectures that connect Photonic Integrated Circuits \(PICs\) to fiber arrays\. Utilizing glass optical waveguides for passive alignment\, these components offer low coupling loss and support high\-density parallel channels\. They simplify the micron\-level optical assembly of optical engines and serve as an essential interconnect solution for NPO systems from various vendors\.

\#\# Coherent\: 1\.6T VCSEL NPO Optical Engine

A socketable\, pluggable optical engine based on VCSEL technology with an integrated laser source\. It supports linear\, DSP\-free links\. Designed for ease of deployment—eliminating the need for external light\-source cabinets—it is targeted at AI supernodes and short\-reach intra\-rack interconnects\, with a clear upgrade path to higher\-bandwidth optical engine platforms\.

\#\# Broadcom\: 3\.2T VCSEL NPO Optical Engine

Featuring a VCSEL\-based architecture\, this ultra\-low\-power\, socketable optical engine can be arranged in arrays around a switching ASIC\. With a per\-channel data rate of 128 Gbps\, it leverages the native NPO electrical interfaces of Broadcom’s Tomahawk switching chips\. It is intended for next\-generation AI leaf\-spine switches and is currently a key solution under evaluation by major overseas cloud service providers\.

\#\# Lightmatter\: Passage L20 Optical Engine

A silicon photonics\-based solution compatible with both NPO and CPO architectures\, utilizing an external continuous\-wave \(CW\) light source\. By relocating the heat source externally\, it reduces thermal stress around the chip\. It supports bandwidths ranging from 800G to 6\.4T and features a detachable socket\, making it well\-suited for high\-speed interconnects within AI GPU supernodes\.

The greatest value of NPO is that it can achieve the low power consumption and high density benefits of short power links without incurring the extremely high packaging and yield costs of CPO\, while retaining the maintainability of the optical engine\.

\#\# NPO One\-Step Solution\: Select Scenario\, Assemble Architecture\, Run Links

\#\# Typical application scenarios

● AI Intelligent Computing Super Node Cluster \(Core\) \: GPU pooling and high\-bandwidth interconnection within the switch reduce overall power consumption and increase computing power density\.

● High\-density data center switches \: The optical engine is moved next to the ASIC\, freeing up front panel space to support high\-density interconnects in a leaf\-ridge architecture\.

● In\-rack short\-distance interconnect \: Point\-to\-point high\-speed interconnect between servers in the same rack\, reducing DSP power consumption\.

● High\-performance computing \(HPC\) clusters \: reduce interconnection latency between nodes\.

\#\# Deployment Architecture

● Point\-to\-point paired deployment \: NPOs must be used in pairs – transmitting optical engine \+ fiber array \+ receiving optical engine\, with one end converting electrical to optical and the other end converting optical to electrical\, for direct connection between GPU\-GPU and ASIC\-ASIC devices\.

● Parallel multi\-engine array \: Multiple NPO optical engines are arranged around the switching\/computing chip\, enabling high\-speed external transmission through multiple ports in parallel\, supporting the high bandwidth of the entire switch\.

● Light source selection \: centralized light source \(external CW laser\, good heat dissipation\, suitable for large\-scale\) or built\-in light source \(simple deployment\, suitable for small and medium\-sized scale\)\.

\#\# Usage process

Step 1\: Prepare a complete set of link units\. An NPO link consists of a pair of transmit\/receive optical engines\, a fiber optic array \(FAU\)\, and a light source\. First\, select and prepare the necessary components as needed\.

Step 2\: Complete the assembly by inserting the light engine into the dedicated socket on the motherboard\. The engine is an independent\, pluggable unit that does not share a package with the main chip and can be replaced separately later\.

Step 3\: Establishing Fiber Optic Connections\: The fiber optic array is led out from the optical engine\, and the cabling is completed inside the chassis and connected to the NPO optical engine at the other end\. The two ends are paired for transmitting and receiving\.

Step 4\: Power\-on Link Establishment\: The high\-speed interface \(SerDes\) of the chip directly drives the optical engine\. In most scenarios\, linear drive is used\, eliminating the need for a DSP\. High\-speed interconnection is established upon power\-on\, replacing the front panel optical module\.

\#\# Precautions

● Significant architectural changes\: The motherboard and structural components need to be redeveloped\, resulting in a long verification cycle\.

● Stringent thermal management\: Optical devices are sensitive to heat and require thermal isolation to prevent wavelength drift\.

● Increased maintenance difficulty\: The fiber optic cable is inside the chassis\, making troubleshooting and replacement more complex than with panel modules\.

● Process and Standards\: Micron\-level coupling precision affects mass production yield\, and cross\-vendor interface standards need to be unified\.

● Complex troubleshooting and debugging\: The optoelectronic system requires joint debugging and testing\, and there are many steps involved in fault location\.

\#\# Conclusion

Near\-Package Optics \(NPO\) achieves an engineering balance among power consumption\, bandwidth density\, and maintainability by positioning the optical engine close to the chip package\, thereby shortening the copper traces used for high\-speed electrical signals\. Far from being a mere transitional solution\, NPO is a practical\, viable technology roadmap designed for AI super\-node interconnects\. Situated between traditional pluggable optical modules and Co\-Packaged Optics \(CPO\)\, it avoids the high manufacturing risks associated with CPO while resolving the bottlenecks caused by high\-speed traces on the front panel\. Consequently\, NPO stands as a core optical interconnect choice for high\-density computing networks in the coming years\.

\#\# Frequently Asked Questions \(FAQs\)

\#\# What is the core difference between NPO and CPO\?

CPO optical devices and ASICs are on the same package substrate\; NPO optical engines are independent and placed on the motherboard next to the chip\, with a removable socket\, and the optoelectronics do not share the same substrate\.

\#\# Does NPO necessarily not need DSP\?

Engineering Review: 2000W 6-Axis Collaborative Welder – Antwerp, Belgium
Field Report: Deployment of 2000W 6-Axis Collaborative Welder for Copper Component Fabrication
1. Project Overview and Site Context
This report documents the technical deployment and process optimization of a 2000W 6-Axis Collaborative Welder at a specialized maritime electrical facility in Antwerp, Belgium. The facility focuses on the production of high-current busbars and heat exchange assemblies, where copper components welding has historically been a bottleneck due to the material’s high thermal conductivity and reflective properties. The objective was to transition from manual TIG processes to a fully Automated Welding workflow to improve throughput and reduce the high rate of thermal distortion common in manual copper fabrication.
2. Technical Specifications and System Integration
The system comprises a 2000W continuous wave (CW) fiber laser source integrated with a high-dexterity 6-axis collaborative arm. Unlike traditional industrial robots, this 6-axis collaborative welder allows for a “lead-through” programming approach, which is critical in the Antwerp workshop where batch sizes vary, and rapid re-tasking is required.
2.1. The Synergy of the 6-Axis Collaborative Welder and Automated Welding
The core advantage observed during this deployment is the synergy between the collaborative interface and the rigors of automated welding. In copper applications, the margin for error regarding the Tool Center Point (TCP) and travel speed is exceptionally narrow. A 6-axis system provides the necessary degrees of freedom to maintain a constant 90-degree torch angle (or a specific lead angle to manage back-reflection) across complex geometries. When we talk about automated welding in this context, we aren’t just discussing a “set and forget” machine; we are discussing a system that maintains a consistent energy density—critical for overcoming the latent heat of fusion in copper.
3. Challenges in Copper Components Welding
Copper (specifically C11000 and C10100 grades used on-site) presents a unique set of challenges for any 6-axis collaborative welder. With a thermal conductivity roughly ten times that of carbon steel, the “heat sink” effect is the primary enemy. At 2000W, the energy input must be concentrated and delivered with extreme precision.
3.1. Overcoming Reflectivity and Thermal Dissipation
Initial tests in the Antwerp facility showed that manual intervention struggled with the “start-stop” crater cracks caused by rapid cooling. By moving to automated welding, we implemented programmed ramp-down sequences for the laser power. The 6-axis arm allowed us to execute a “wobble” pattern—a high-frequency oscillation of the beam—which increases the effective width of the weld pool and helps in degassing the melt, significantly reducing porosity in the copper components welding process.
4. Process Optimization: The Antwerp Field Observations
4.1. Shielding Gas Dynamics
In the humid maritime environment of Antwerp, hydrogen embrittlement is a legitimate concern for copper welds. We transitioned from pure Argon to an Argon-Helium mix (70/30). While more expensive, the Helium component provides a hotter arc/plasma environment, assisting the 2000W laser in maintaining a stable keyhole. The 6-axis collaborative welder was programmed to maintain a specialized trailing gas lens, ensuring the copper remained shielded until it cooled below the oxidation threshold.
4.2. Jigging and Fixturing for Automated Welding
A lesson learned during the second week of deployment: automated welding is only as good as the fixturing. Copper expands significantly when heated. If the jigs are too rigid, the weld cracks during solidification; if too loose, the 6-axis path becomes misaligned. We developed “floating” toggle clamps that allow for lateral thermal expansion while maintaining vertical alignment. This is where the “collaborative” aspect of the welder shone—operators could safely adjust clamps in proximity to the arm without the need for extensive light-curtain resets.
5. Programming and Pathing Strategy
The 6-axis collaborative welder utilizes a software stack that allows for G-code interpolation. For the copper components welding, we utilized a “continuous path” strategy. Because copper dissipates heat so quickly, stopping the weld to reposition a 3-axis gantry would result in cold-lap at the join. The 6-axis range of motion allowed us to weld three sides of a busbar assembly in a single, uninterrupted movement, maintaining the thermal equilibrium of the workpiece.
5.1. Wobble Parameters and Frequency
We found the “sweet spot” for 2mm copper sheet to be a 1.5mm circular wobble at 180Hz, with a travel speed of 12mm/s. The 2000W power was utilized at an 85% duty cycle. This prevented the “burn-through” that occurs when the copper finally reaches its liquidus state and the reflectivity drops sharply.
6. Safety and Compliance in the Belgian Industrial Context
Operating a 2000W laser-based 6-axis collaborative welder in Antwerp requires strict adherence to CE standards and local Belgian safety regulations (revolving around the wellbeing of workers). Although the arm is “collaborative,” the laser radiation is not. We implemented a Class 4 enclosure with interlocked viewing windows. The “collaborative” benefit shifted from “working side-by-side during the weld” to “ultra-fast setup and teaching” between cycles.
7. Lessons Learned and Practical Recommendations
7.1. Thermal Management of the Laser Head
One unforeseen issue in the field was the back-reflection from the copper. Despite the 6-axis arm being able to tilt the head, high-angle reflections occasionally tripped the internal sensors of the 2000W laser source.
Lesson: Always program a 5-to-10 degree “push” angle when automated welding highly reflective copper to protect the optical fiber.
7.2. Surface Preparation is Non-Negotiable
In manual welding, an experienced welder can “burn through” slight oxidation. In automated welding, specifically with copper components welding, any surface oxide leads to immediate coupling inconsistencies. We integrated a pre-weld mechanical abrasion step into the workflow. The repeatability of the 6-axis collaborative welder means it expects the same material conditions every time; it cannot “feel” the puddle like a human can.
7.3. Power Stability

\# Engineering Review\: 2000W 6\-Axis Collaborative Welder – Antwerp\, Belgium

\#\# Field Report\: Deployment of 2000W 6\-Axis Collaborative Welder for Copper Component Fabrication

\#\#\# 1\. Project Overview and Site Context

This report documents the technical deployment and process optimization of a 2000W 6\-Axis Collaborative Welder at a specialized maritime electrical facility in Antwerp\, Belgium\. The facility focuses on the production of high\-current busbars and heat exchange assemblies\, where copper components welding has historically been a bottleneck due to the material’s high thermal conductivity and reflective properties\. The objective was to transition from manual TIG processes to a fully Automated Welding workflow to improve throughput and reduce the high rate of thermal distortion common in manual copper fabrication\.

\#\#\# 2\. Technical Specifications and System Integration

The system comprises a 2000W continuous wave \(CW\) fiber laser source integrated with a high\-dexterity 6\-axis collaborative arm\. Unlike traditional industrial robots\, this 6\-axis collaborative welder allows for a “lead\-through” programming approach\, which is critical in the Antwerp workshop where batch sizes vary\, and rapid re\-tasking is required\.

\#\#\#\# 2\.1\. The Synergy of the 6\-Axis Collaborative Welder and Automated Welding

The core advantage observed during this deployment is the synergy between the collaborative interface and the rigors of automated welding\. In copper applications\, the margin for error regarding the Tool Center Point \(TCP\) and travel speed is exceptionally narrow\. A 6\-axis system provides the necessary degrees of freedom to maintain a constant 90\-degree torch angle \(or a specific lead angle to manage back\-reflection\) across complex geometries\. When we talk about automated welding in this context\, we aren’t just discussing a “set and forget” machine\; we are discussing a system that maintains a consistent energy density—critical for overcoming the latent heat of fusion in copper\.

\#\#\# 3\. Challenges in Copper Components Welding

Copper \(specifically C11000 and C10100 grades used on\-site\) presents a unique set of challenges for any 6\-axis collaborative welder\. With a thermal conductivity roughly ten times that of carbon steel\, the “heat sink” effect is the primary enemy\. At 2000W\, the energy input must be concentrated and delivered with extreme precision\.

\#\#\#\# 3\.1\. Overcoming Reflectivity and Thermal Dissipation

Initial tests in the Antwerp facility showed that manual intervention struggled with the “start\-stop” crater cracks caused by rapid cooling\. By moving to automated welding\, we implemented programmed ramp\-down sequences for the laser power\. The 6\-axis arm allowed us to execute a “wobble” pattern—a high\-frequency oscillation of the beam—which increases the effective width of the weld pool and helps in degassing the melt\, significantly reducing porosity in the copper components welding process\.

\#\#\# 4\. Process Optimization\: The Antwerp Field Observations

\#\#\#\# 4\.1\. Shielding Gas Dynamics

In the humid maritime environment of Antwerp\, hydrogen embrittlement is a legitimate concern for copper welds\. We transitioned from pure Argon to an Argon\-Helium mix \(70\/30\)\. While more expensive\, the Helium component provides a hotter arc\/plasma environment\, assisting the 2000W laser in maintaining a stable keyhole\. The 6\-axis collaborative welder was programmed to maintain a specialized trailing gas lens\, ensuring the copper remained shielded until it cooled below the oxidation threshold\.

\#\#\#\# 4\.2\. Jigging and Fixturing for Automated Welding

A lesson learned during the second week of deployment\: automated welding is only as good as the fixturing\. Copper expands significantly when heated\. If the jigs are too rigid\, the weld cracks during solidification\; if too loose\, the 6\-axis path becomes misaligned\. We developed “floating” toggle clamps that allow for lateral thermal expansion while maintaining vertical alignment\. This is where the “collaborative” aspect of the welder shone—operators could safely adjust clamps in proximity to the arm without the need for extensive light\-curtain resets\.

\#\#\# 5\. Programming and Pathing Strategy

The 6\-axis collaborative welder utilizes a software stack that allows for G\-code interpolation\. For the copper components welding\, we utilized a “continuous path” strategy\. Because copper dissipates heat so quickly\, stopping the weld to reposition a 3\-axis gantry would result in cold\-lap at the join\. The 6\-axis range of motion allowed us to weld three sides of a busbar assembly in a single\, uninterrupted movement\, maintaining the thermal equilibrium of the workpiece\.

\#\#\#\# 5\.1\. Wobble Parameters and Frequency

We found the “sweet spot” for 2mm copper sheet to be a 1\.5mm circular wobble at 180Hz\, with a travel speed of 12mm\/s\. The 2000W power was utilized at an 85\% duty cycle\. This prevented the “burn\-through” that occurs when the copper finally reaches its liquidus state and the reflectivity drops sharply\.

\#\#\# 6\. Safety and Compliance in the Belgian Industrial Context

Operating a 2000W laser\-based 6\-axis collaborative welder in Antwerp requires strict adherence to CE standards and local Belgian safety regulations \(revolving around the wellbeing of workers\)\. Although the arm is “collaborative\,” the laser radiation is not\. We implemented a Class 4 enclosure with interlocked viewing windows\. The “collaborative” benefit shifted from “working side\-by\-side during the weld” to “ultra\-fast setup and teaching” between cycles\.

\#\#\# 7\. Lessons Learned and Practical Recommendations

\#\#\#\# 7\.1\. Thermal Management of the Laser Head

One unforeseen issue in the field was the back\-reflection from the copper\. Despite the 6\-axis arm being able to tilt the head\, high\-angle reflections occasionally tripped the internal sensors of the 2000W laser source\.
Lesson\: Always program a 5\-to\-10 degree “push” angle when automated welding highly reflective copper to protect the optical fiber\.

\#\#\#\# 7\.2\. Surface Preparation is Non\-Negotiable

In manual welding\, an experienced welder can “burn through” slight oxidation\. In automated welding\, specifically with copper components welding\, any surface oxide leads to immediate coupling inconsistencies\. We integrated a pre\-weld mechanical abrasion step into the workflow\. The repeatability of the 6\-axis collaborative welder means it expects the same material conditions every time\; it cannot “feel” the puddle like a human can\.

\#\#\#\# 7\.3\. Power Stability

The power grid in the Antwerp industrial zone is generally stable\, but we noticed fluctuations during peak hours \(10\:00 AM\) that affected the 2000W output\. We installed a dedicated voltage stabilizer to ensure the laser beam’s consistency\. For copper\, a 5\% drop in power can be the difference between a full\-penetration weld and a surface bead\.

\#\#\# 8\. Conclusion and ROI Analysis

The deployment of the 6\-axis collaborative welder in Antwerp has resulted in a 40\% increase in production speed for copper busbar assemblies\. The transition to automated welding has virtually eliminated the rework necessitated by the inconsistent thermal management of manual TIG\.

Key to this success was recognizing that copper components welding requires more than just raw power\; it requires the precise\, multi\-axis pathing and consistent speed that only a 6\-axis system can provide\. For future deployments\, the focus should remain on perfecting the “wobble” geometries and ensuring that the collaborative interface is used to minimize downtime between different component runs\. The technical synergy between the 2000W fiber source and the collaborative robotic arm represents the current “gold standard” for mid\-tier copper fabrication in high\-precision environments\.

NovaEuris provides industrial equipment, instruments, food processing systems and green energy solutions for manufacturers and engineering companies across European markets.
Contact Info
- Gustav Mahlerplein 29, 1082 MA Amsterdam, Netherlands
- support@novaeuris.com
News
2026 Energy Storage PACK Busbar Selection Guide: Conductive Copper Components for Battery Packs
Energy storage systems are moving from pilot projects to gigawatt-scale deployment across Europe, and the battery pack remains the cost and safety center of gravity. Inside every PACK, copper busbars and conductive connecting components carry hundreds of amps between cells, modules and terminals. A busbar that is undersized, poorly plated or sourced from an unqualified supplier can drive contact resistance up, create hot spots and, in the worst case, contribute to thermal runaway. This guide sets out what procurement and engineering teams should evaluate in 2026 when selecting copper busbars for energy storage PACKs, from material specification through supplier vetting, compliance, logistics and in-service maintenance.
The market context matters. European buyers are balancing cost pressure from Chinese and Southeast Asian suppliers against the incoming requirements of the EU Batteries Regulation, which tightens documentation, carbon footprint disclosure and due diligence across the battery value chain. At the same time, PACK designs are converging on higher current densities, more compact module layouts and liquid-cooled architectures, all of which raise the demands on busbar geometry, insulation and joint quality. Buyers who treat busbars as a commodity item rather than an engineered component tend to discover the cost of that assumption during commissioning or, worse, in the field.
Use the table below as a starting checklist when building a technical specification or evaluating quotations from competing suppliers.
Selection Area | What to Specify | Procurement and Risk Notes
---|---|---
Copper material | T2 or TU1 oxygen-free copper; conductivity typically ≥ 99.9% IACS; hardness and temper stated on the drawing | Request mill certificates and conductivity test reports per lot; verify that the grade on the certificate matches the purchase order
Surface treatment | Nickel plating (typical 3–8 µm), tin plating, or bare copper with antioxidant treatment depending on joint design and environment | Plating thickness and adhesion should be measurable; thin or porous plating is a common cause of rising contact resistance in humid or coastal installations
Cross-section and current rating | Current-carrying capacity with defined temperature rise limit (for example ≤ 65 K above ambient), plus short-circuit withstand | Do not accept supplier ratings without test conditions; confirm the calculation basis and request thermal test data
Insulation and spacing | Heat-shrink or powder coating, dielectric strength, creepage and clearance distances for the system voltage class | Insulation must be compatible with the cooling method (air or liquid) and with the PACK's expected operating temperature range
Joint and connection design | Bolt size, torque values, contact surface flatness, use of Belleville washers, anti-seize or conductive paste | Define torque in the assembly work instruction and audit it at the supplier; loose joints are a leading field failure mode
Dimensional tolerances | Hole position, bend radius, flatness and twist limits tied to the module stack-up | Request first-article inspection reports and CMM data; tolerance stack-up errors cause assembly line stoppages
Compliance and documentation | RoHS and REACH declarations, material traceability, UL 1973 or IEC 62619 alignment at system level, IEC 61439 where applicable to assemblies | Keep declarations on file per shipment; EU Batteries Regulation due diligence expectations are increasing, so supplier documentation quality is a selection criterion
Supplier capability | In-house stamping, bending, plating and inspection; ISO 9001 and preferably IATF 16949 where automotive-grade discipline is required | Audit plating lines in person or by video; outsourced plating is a frequent weak point in the supply chain
Logistics and packaging | Anti-oxidation wrapping, moisture barrier bags, shock-resistant cartons, pallet configuration | Copper is a theft target and plating is sensitive to humidity; agree Incoterms, insurance and packaging standards in the contract
Maintenance and service life | Inspection intervals for torque and thermal imaging, spare parts availability, replacement part traceability | Build busbar inspection into the PACK maintenance schedule; require the supplier to hold spare capacity or stock for the contract term
On material selection, T2 and TU1 copper grades are the common baseline for energy storage busbars, with conductivity verified against the ≥ 99.9% IACS expectation. Buyers should insist on lot-level mill certificates and, for high-current joints, independent conductivity or resistance testing. Plating choice depends on the joint and environment: nickel plating offers good wear and corrosion resistance for bolted joints, tin plating supports solderability and lower contact resistance in some designs, and bare copper with antioxidant treatment can be acceptable in sealed, dry enclosures. The specification should state plating thickness with a tolerance band and a measurable adhesion test, because plating quality varies widely between suppliers and is difficult to assess from a datasheet alone.
Sizing is where many procurement errors originate. Suppliers frequently quote a current rating without stating the allowable temperature rise, ambient conditions, mounting orientation or cooling assumptions. A defensible specification defines the temperature rise limit, the short-circuit withstand current and duration, and the test method used to verify both. For liquid-cooled PACKs, the busbar and insulation must be qualified for direct or indirect contact with the coolant and for the operating temperature window. For high-voltage systems, creepage and clearance distances should be calculated for the system voltage class and confirmed against the relevant standards rather than copied from a previous project.
Joint design deserves the same rigor as the busbar itself. Bolt size, torque, contact surface flatness and the use of Belleville washers or conductive paste all influence long-term contact resistance. Procurement teams should require the supplier to document torque values and to demonstrate that assembly instructions are controlled and audited. Where possible, request joint resistance and thermal cycling test data, since a busbar that passes a static resistance test can still degrade under repeated thermal cycling in the field.
Supplier selection in 2026 should combine commercial and technical due diligence. Look for manufacturers with in-house stamping, bending and plating, because outsourced plating is one of the most common sources of quality escapes. ISO 9001 is the minimum; IATF 16949 certification signals automotive-grade process discipline that transfers well to energy storage. Ask for first-article inspection reports, CMM dimensional data, plating thickness measurements and references from comparable PACK projects. Where possible, audit the plating line and the final inspection station in person or by live video. Established connector and busbar specialists, as well as tier-one automotive suppliers expanding into storage, are worth shortlisting, but verify capability rather than relying on brand recognition alone.
Compliance documentation is now a selection criterion, not an afterthought. RoHS and REACH declarations should accompany every shipment, and material traceability should allow a finished busbar to be linked back to a copper mill lot. At system level, UL 1973 and IEC 62619 alignment is expected by many European customers, and IEC 61439 applies where busbars form part of an assembly. The EU Batteries Regulation is raising expectations for carbon footprint disclosure and supply chain due diligence, so suppliers who can provide consistent environmental and traceability documentation will be easier to onboard and less likely to create compliance gaps later.
Logistics and packaging protect both quality and margin. Copper is a theft target in transit, and plated surfaces are sensitive to humidity, so contracts should specify moisture-barrier packaging, anti-oxidation wrapping and shock-resistant cartons, along with Incoterms, insurance and inspection rights. For European buyers sourcing from Asia, build in incoming inspection for plating thickness, dimensions and conductivity on the first lots, and consider a pre-shipment inspection for high-value orders.
Finally, plan for maintenance. Busbar joints should be included in the PACK inspection schedule, with periodic torque checks and thermal imaging to detect rising resistance before it becomes a failure. Agree spare parts availability and replacement lead times in the supply contract, and keep replacement busbars traceable to the original specification. Teams that treat busbars as engineered, documented and maintained components rather than commodity hardware will see fewer commissioning delays, lower field failure rates and a cleaner compliance position as European requirements tighten through 2026 and beyond.

records.title: Research Progress and Prospects for Lubricant Additives for Water-Based Hydraulic Fluids in Hydraulic Supports
records.abstract: This paper provides a systematic review of research progress on lubricant additives ... focusing on two main categories: liquid and nanoparticle lubricant additives. records.summary: This review article surveys lubricant additives for water-based hydraulic fluids used in coal-mine hydraulic supports, where water's low viscosity shifts lubrication from fluid to mixed/boundary regimes and makes additive molecular structure critical. It organizes liquid additives into fatty alcohol ethers (including carboxylated variants), vegetable-oil-derived additives (fatty acids and amidation products), and ionic liquids (protic and polymeric), and nanoparticle additives into inorganic and organic–inorganic composites. For each class it discusses molecular design strategies, proposed lubrication mechanisms (adsorption films, tribochemical films, nanoscale rolling), and performance regulation pathways, citing reported laboratory results such as friction and wear reductions for modified nanoparticles and ionic liquids. The authors argue that future additives should integrate lubrication, hard-water resistance, and corrosion inhibition to enable single- or few-component fluids, supported by improved dilution-water quality and cylinder anticorrosion technology. The article is a review, so reported numbers are drawn from cited primary studies rather than new experiments by the authors.
