Research Progress and Prospects for Lubricant Additives for Water-Based Hydraulic Fluids in Hydraulic Supports
,
and
1
Coal Science (Beijing) New Materials Technology Co., Ltd., Beijing 100013, China
2
CCTEG China Coal Research Institute, Beijing 100013, China
3
School of Chemical and Environmental Engineering, Shanghai Institute of Technology, Shanghai 201400, China
Authors to whom correspondence should be addressed.
Abstract
Water-based hydraulic fluids serve as the power transmission medium for hydraulic support systems in coal mines, and the performance of their lubricant additives directly affects the stable operation of the supports. This paper provides a systematic review of research progress on lubricant additives for water-based hydraulic fluids in China, focusing on two main categories: liquid and nanoparticle lubricant additives. Liquid lubricant additives are categorized into fatty alcohol ether-based, vegetable oil-based, and ionic liquid-based additives; nanoparticle-based additives include inorganic nanoparticles and organic–inorganic composite particles. This article analyzes the molecular structure design strategies, lubrication mechanisms, and performance regulation pathways of various additives. In response to the demands of intelligent coal mining and green mine construction, it is proposed that the development of lubricant additives for water-based hydraulic fluids should target multifunctional integration and environmental friendliness. Improvements in the quality of the dilution water and the maturity of cylinder anticorrosion technology will create favorable conditions for the development of single-component (or few-component) hydraulic fluids. In the future, research should deepen understanding of the structure–performance relationships of lubricant additives, so as to facilitate the engineering application of high-performance, low-dose, degradable green lubricant additives and provide technical support for intelligent coal mine construction and ecological protection in the Yellow River Basin.
1. Introduction
In 2025, China’s coal production accounted for 54.8% of the global total (International Energy Agency (IEA) data: 8.85 billion tons), with underground coal mining accounting for approximately 75% of this output [1]. Hydraulic supports serve as the safety shield for fully mechanized mining faces in underground coal mines: they are responsible for supporting the roof, propelling the scraper conveyor, and advancing autonomously to guarantee the safety of the working spaces [2]. The hydraulic fluid supply system is the power source for hydraulic supports, and the hydraulic fluid is the medium for power transmission within the hydraulic system. The development of hydraulic fluids has mainly undergone four technical stages, transitioning gradually from oil-based to water-based fluids. Initially, mineral oil was used as the hydraulic fluid for coal mine hydraulic supports. Owing to its low biodegradability and the flammability of the mist formed from leaks under high pressure, it posed significant safety risks. In the 1970s, dispersed mineral-oil-in-water emulsion systems (approximately 50%) were developed, addressing the safety concerns of hydraulic fluids in underground mines. However, due to their thermodynamic instability, oil–soap separation could easily occur during service [3]. In the 1990s, with increased automation of hydraulic supports and the application of electro-hydraulic control systems, the filtration precision of electro-hydraulic control systems reached 25 μm, while traditional emulsion-type hydraulic fluids were prone to oil and soap separation, posing a risk of system clogging. The adoption of micro-emulsion technology reduced droplet size and yielded micro-emulsion hydraulic fluids with greatly improved stability, although these formulations still contained a small amount of mineral oil (about 5%) [4]. At the beginning of the 21st century, mineral oil-free concentrated fluids using water-soluble lubricants (e.g., modified vegetable oils) as the core components were successfully developed. These fluids not only completely eliminated mineral oil-related contamination, but also met the cleanliness and stability requirements of hydraulic fluids for electro-hydraulic control systems [5].
According to China’s coal industry standard KA 76-2011 [6] ‘Emulsifying oil, concentrate fluid and high-water content hydraulic fluid used for powered support,’ hydraulic fluids include emulsified oils (HFAEs), concentrate fluid (HFASs), and high water content hydraulic fluid. High water content hydraulic fluid is mainly prepared by mixing the corresponding emulsion oil or concentrate fluid with water (generally purified mine water) as the diluent at a mass ratio of 3–5%; this fluid circulates within the hydraulic system to provide power [7]. Water-based lubricants are a cheaper, safer, and more environmentally friendly alternative to mineral oil lubricants for coal mine hydraulic support systems. However, compared to mineral oils, water itself is a poor lubricant. Due to its low viscosity, the lubrication mechanism shifts from fluid lubrication to mixed or boundary lubrication. In this case, the rheological properties of the lubricant become less important, and friction and wear are mainly determined by the physico-chemical properties of the friction surfaces, the lubricant, and the interactions between them [8]. Under fixed friction surface conditions, the molecular structure of the lubricant becomes particularly important [9]. Therefore, the development of high-efficiency lubricants is required to achieve better tribological performance.
Research shows that, compared with mineral oils, improving the tribological performance of water-based lubricants can minimize the shear resistance between friction pairs, reduce the power required for operating machinery, and thus save energy [10]. In addition, water-based lubricants have excellent cooling capabilities and environmentally friendly properties [11], making them very effective as cutting fluids, drilling fluids, and hydraulic fluids [12]. Research reports on water-based lubricant additives mainly focus on the fields of cutting fluids [13,14] and drilling fluids [15,16,17]. Although water-based lubricant additives are also key components for enhancing the overall performance of hydraulic fluids, few relevant systematic reviews have been published. This paper reviews the research progress of lubricant additives for water-based hydraulic fluids and, against the background of intelligent coal mining and green mine construction, discusses the development trends of lubricant additives for water-based hydraulic fluids, aiming to promote the better and faster development of high-performance environmentally friendly hydraulic fluids.
2. Lubricant for Water-Based Hydraulic Fluids
Lubricant additives for water-based hydraulic fluids not only need to have good dispersibility and lubricity, but also must be compatible with other additives in the hydraulic fluid; this is a necessary condition for the lubricant additives to fully exert their activity. In addition, because high water content hydraulic fluids contain a large proportion of mine water, and mine water has a certain hardness (Ca2+, Mg2+), water-based lubricant additives should also have a certain level of hard water resistance. Furthermore, sufficient raw material availability, environmental friendliness, and reasonable cost are important factors in determining whether lubricant additives for water-based hydraulic fluids can be widely applied. To satisfy these performance requirements, researchers have developed different types of lubricant additives for water-based hydraulic fluids. According to their physical state, they mainly fall into two categories: liquid lubricants and nanoparticle lubricant additives. Nanoparticles include inorganic particles and organic–inorganic composite particles.
2.1. Liquid Lubricant Additives
2.1.1. Alcohol Ether Lubricants
Alkyl ether lubricant additives are formed by the condensation of alcohol compounds and epoxy compounds. The alcohol compounds include polyols (such as glycerol) and fatty alcohols. Based on the type of alcohol compound, corresponding polyether polyols and fatty alcohol ethers can be synthesized. Both are non-ionic surfactants and have excellent resistance to hard water. Compared with polyols, fatty alcohols contain long alkyl chains as lipophilic groups, presenting a lower hydrophilic–lipophilic balance (HLB) value, which delivers better lubrication and load-bearing capacity, making them more suitable for serving as lubricant additives in hydraulic fluid.
Fatty Alcohol Ether Lubricants
Fatty alcohol ether lubricants generally consist of alkyl chains (C8–C18) and alcohol ether segments. The structure of fatty alcohol ether lubricants contains both hydrophobic long alkyl chains and a hydrophilic polyether structure. They dissolve in water via intermolecular hydrogen bonds formed between the oxygen atoms in the ether chains and hydrogen atoms in water. Therefore, the hydrophilic–lipophilic balance can be adjusted by changing the number and structure of ether chains [18] or by selecting alkyl chains with different structures and lengths [19]. Furthermore, the foaming properties of hydraulic fluids can be modulated by choosing straight-chain or branched-chain alkyl alcohols [20]. As shown in Figure 1a, Pan [21] investigated extended surfactants of different structures and performed interfacial tension measurement. The results indicate that increasing the number of PO groups, lengthening the alkyl chain, and introducing branching in the hydrophobic group exert only a minor influence on interfacial tension-reducing capacity. PO groups can enlarge the hydrophobic group size via molecular curling to match the dimension of the hydrophilic head group. Under suitable hydrophilic–lipophilic balance conditions, these surfactants can lower interfacial tension to ultra-low levels (<10−2 mN/m). However, excessively long EO chains can stretch into the aqueous phase, disrupting the close packing of the interfacial film and causing an increase in interfacial tension. As shown in Figure 1b, Li et al. [22] synthesized linear alcohol ether (AEO3) and isomeric alcohol ether (IAEO3) with three EO adducts using C12–14 linear alcohol and C13 isomeric alcohol and evaluated the foaming performance of these two alcohol ethers. The results showed that, at the same EO adduct number, AEO3 exhibited slightly higher initial foam height but faster foam decay, whereas IAEO3 produced a lower initial foam height than AEO3, yet the foam was more stable and did not easily collapse.
Figure 1. Extended surfactants with different structures (a) and straight-chain (isomeric) alcohol ethers (b) (adapted from [21,22]).
Fatty Alcohol Ether Carboxylic Acid Lubricants
Generally, the molecular structure of organic lubricants largely determines their lubrication performance. Lubrication efficiency is influenced by various factors such as the length of the alkyl hydrophobic chain, heteroatoms, the presence of electron-donating or electron-withdrawing substituents, and the size of heterocycles. Heteroatoms represented by P, N, S, B, etc. can be introduced into lubricant molecules as extreme pressure and anti-wear elements to improve lubrication performance. Other studies have reported that oxygen-containing functional groups enhance lubrication in the following order: COOH > CHO > OH > COOCH3 > C=O > C-O-C [23]. These functional groups can form intra- or intermolecular hydrogen bonds to regulate the adsorption layer [24]. Fatty alcohol ether lubricants have good water solubility and hard water resistance [25], but because ethers have limited enhancement effects on lubrication performance, researchers have further modified fatty alcohol ethers by carboxylation to achieve superior lubrication performance.
Carboxylation modification involves introducing carboxyl groups into the structure of fatty alcohol ethers to obtain fatty alcohol ether carboxylates. Fatty alcohol ether carboxylates are anionic amphiphilic surfactants that contain both EO/PO and carboxyl hydrophilic groups. The introduction of carboxyl groups improves salt tolerance, emulsifying properties, and lubricating properties. As shown in Figure 2a, Zhang [26] synthesized isomeric alcohol ether carboxylates using tridecyl isomeric alcohol ether as the substrate and studied the wetting, emulsifying, and foaming properties of isomeric alcohol ether carboxylates with different EO numbers and linear alcohol ether carboxylates. It was found that a lower EO number resulted in relatively better wetting and emulsifying performance; compared with linear analogs, branched analogs exhibited superior wetting, emulsifying, and decontamination performance on carbon black cloth, but poorer foam stability. As shown in Figure 2b, Lin [27] synthesized alcohol ether carboxylates with eight PO segments and with both 20 PO segments and 10 EO segments using linear alcohol C18OH and isomeric alcohol C12+8OH as initiators. Compared with the (PO)8 series products, the inclusion of EO segments significantly improved water solubility and salt tolerance. C18(PO)20(EO)10OCH2COONa tolerated Na+ and Ca2+ concentrations exceeding 200,000 mg/L. Huang et al. [28] introduced alcohol ether carboxylates as calcium soap dispersants to develop a hydraulic support emulsion that can withstand Grade 40 hard water (per standard KA 76-2011). Industrial validation demonstrates that the emulsion satisfies field service (Grade 40 hard water); the hydraulic support system runs smoothly without filter clogging or valve sticking. Similarly, commercial oil-free water-based hydraulic fluids adopt alcohol ether carboxylates as lubricant additives, yet such fluids generally produce excessive foam. Foaming performance is also an important property of hydraulic fluids; the less the fluid foams, the more favorable it is for the operation of the hydraulic support. Anticorrosion relies primarily on added corrosion inhibitors.
Figure 2. Heterogeneous alcohol ether carboxylates embedded with different amounts of EO (a) and heterogeneous alcohol ether carboxylates embedded with different amounts of EO and PO (b) (adapted from [26,27]).
2.1.2. Vegetable Oil Lubricant Additives
China’s major coal-producing areas are mainly distributed along the Yellow River Basin. Guided by the national ecological protection in the Yellow River Basin, vegetable oil-based hydraulic fluids exhibit distinct advantages over mineral oils, including wide raw material availability, superior biodegradability, and low toxicity. They can effectively address the water and soil pollution problems caused by traditional mineral oil-based hydraulic fluids and are a type of renewable green lubricant [29,30].
Vegetable Oil Lubricants
There are numerous reports on the development and application of vegetable oil lubricants [31,32,33], mainly focusing on the study of the structure–property relationship of vegetable oil molecules and their lubricating properties, including the effects of alkyl chain length [34], degree of unsaturation [35], and branching [36] on lubrication performance. The alkyl chain structure in vegetable oil molecules directly affects the viscosity characteristics of lubricants. The length of the alkyl chain mainly affects the lateral cohesion of the lubricating film; as the alkyl chain length increases, the lateral cohesion gradually rises, and viscosity increases. Typically, vegetable oils with long alkyl chains have higher viscosity and can bear higher loads, whereas short-chain vegetable oils have lower viscosity, and under high load or high temperature conditions their pressure–viscosity and viscosity–temperature characteristics are insufficient, impairing the lubrication effect [33]. As shown in Figure 3a, Gusain et al. [34] synthesized fatty acids with different alkyl chain lengths (C10, C12, C14, C16, C18-1) as anions, with tetrabutylammonium as the cation in ionic liquids, and investigated their friction performance. With the increase of the alkyl chain length of the anion, the viscosity of the ionic liquid gradually increased. This is because longer alkyl chains exhibit larger molecular volumes and stronger intermolecular interactions, which hinder the relative movement of molecules and thus increase internal friction [37].
Figure 3. Ionic liquids with alkyl chains of different lengths (a) and isopropylation of soybean oil (b) (adapted from [34,36]).
For saturated vegetable oils, their lubrication performance increases with the length of the alkyl chain. However, when the alkyl chain length exceeds 16, the friction resistance and wear resistance of the resulting lubricating film reach a peak and are no longer affected by chain length [38]. In contrast, for unsaturated vegetable oils, the adsorption effect of double bonds makes the arrangement of the adsorption film less dense. At this point, the lateral cohesion between molecules becomes the key factor affecting lubrication performance. Since cohesion is proportional to the length of the alkyl chain, longer alkyl chains can compensate for this adverse effect and enhance intermolecular cohesion. Additionally, when the number of double bonds is greater than one, the lubrication performance tends to decrease as the number of double bonds increases. This may be because the increase in double bonds increases the interaction sites of the π-electron cloud with the metal substrate, effectively shortening the length of the non-polar alkyl chains, making the lubricating film thinner and reducing its load-bearing capacity. Long et al. [35] studied oleic acid and ricinoleic acid, each containing one double bond, which both showed excellent lubrication performance, whereas linoleic acid, containing two double bonds, resulted in relatively higher friction and wear.
The presence of branches in the structure of vegetable oils enhances the ability to separate non-polar alkyl chains from polar functional groups, increasing the tendency of polar functional groups to attach to metal surfaces. At the same time, this tendency increases with the degree of branching of the alkyl chains, making it easier to form dense lubricating films on friction surfaces. Moreover, calculations of adsorption energy show that adsorption energy gradually increases with the degree of branching, which also confirms that the formed lubricating film is denser. As shown in Figure 3b, Bhowmik et al. [36] carried out isopropylation of the double bonds of soybean oil fatty chains, converting the double bonds into single bonds, while also achieving isomerization of the fatty chains. The isomerized regular soybean oil reduced the wear volume by 35% at room temperature and by 15% at high temperature, whereas high-oleic soybean oil reduced wear volume by about 10% at both room and high temperatures. Finally, Table 1 summarizes the influences of alkyl chain structures on the lubricating performance of vegetable oil lubricants.
Table 1. Effects of different alkyl chains on the performance of vegetable oil lubricants.
Vegetable Oil-Based Modified Lubricant Additive
Compared with vegetable oil lubricants, downstream products of vegetable oils, such as fatty acids (oleic acid, ricinoleic acid, etc.), contain carboxyl structures, which can undergo further chemical modification at the carboxyl group to design higher-performance or even multifunctional lubricant additives. Fatty acid molecules contain both polar and non-polar groups; the polar groups can bind to metal surfaces through adsorption, while the non-polar alkyl chains influence the load-bearing capacity and lubrication performance of the oil film through intermolecular forces, allowing them to act as oil-based lubricants themselves. However, since hydraulic fluids are water-based systems, fatty acids need to be modified to be suitable for aqueous conditions. The simplest modification method is to convert fatty acids into salts, but fatty acid salts are sensitive to hard water, and the adsorption ability of a single carboxyl polar group on metal surfaces is limited. Therefore, further structural modification of fatty acids is particularly important.
Since the chemical structure of the non-polar region of fatty acids derived from vegetable oils is mainly influenced by the type of vegetable oil and is relatively fixed, the carboxyl group at the polar end becomes the key active site for chemical modification. Based on the carboxyl group, more polar groups, such as hydroxyl, amino, and sulfonic groups, can be introduced. The polar atoms in the functional groups (N, O, S, P, etc.) not only enhance intermolecular interactions through hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, and other interactions, but also have strong affinity with metal surfaces, forming high-strength lubricating oil films and reducing friction and wear. At the same time, the introduction of polar groups also improves other properties of hydraulic fluids. For example, lone pairs on heteroatoms can coordinate and chelate with Ca2+/Mg2+, enhancing resistance to hard water [39]. Compared with ester bonds, amide bonds have stronger adsorption and are more stable in aqueous solutions, so researchers mainly perform chemical modification through amidation. Amino acids themselves are effective small-molecule corrosion inhibitors [40,41,42,43], and, when reacted with fatty acids through amidation to form alkyl amides, they can reduce the hardness sensitivity of fatty acids while introducing more groups with adsorption and coordination chelation activity [44,45]. Our research group [46] prepared alkyl amide surfactants by reacting fatty acids with amino acids and found that, compared with fatty acids, the introduction of amino acids greatly improved the low-temperature stability of water-based fluids and increased hard water resistance by 30.50%, while also exhibiting excellent corrosion inhibition performance [47]. The corrosion inhibition mechanism is shown in Figure 4.
Figure 4. Corrosion inhibition mechanism of alkylamide [47].
2.1.3. Ionic Liquid Lubricant Additives
Conventional Ionic Liquid Lubricant Additives
Ionic liquids consist of organic cations and inorganic/organic anions and remain liquid at room temperature or near room temperature. Since their first application in the field of friction in 2001 [48], researchers have systematically studied their development and optimization as lubricants [49,50] and lubricant additives [51,52], showing a significant effect in improving the friction performance of oil- and water-based lubricants [53]. Traditional ionic liquids, due to their high cost, have limited feasibility when applied alone as lubricants, and are therefore generally used as lubricant additives. Ionic liquids can effectively reduce friction and wear and, to a certain extent, mitigate the corrosiveness of water-based lubrication systems [54]. As lubricant additives, the advantage of ionic liquids lies in the designability of their molecular structure; by precisely controlling the cationic and anionic groups of the ionic liquids, their adsorption ability on friction surfaces can be enhanced, thereby improving their tribological performance [55].
Protic Ionic Liquids Lubricant Additives
Protic ionic liquids (PILs) are typically formed from a Lewis base and a Brønsted acid via a neutralization reaction, undergoing proton transfer to produce a cation (protonated Lewis base) and an anion (conjugate base of the Brønsted acid). The reaction conditions are relatively mild, the preparation procedure is straightforward, and raw materials are readily available and inexpensive. When using fatty acids (such as carboxylic acids) as the anion, PILs can usually be synthesized at room temperature under solvent-free conditions. Due to the presence of proton exchange, studies have shown that, in oil-based systems, the structure of the anion has a significant impact on the viscosity of PILs, while variations in the cation have relatively little effect [56]. Similarly, Oliver Jarvik et al. [57] studied the structure, properties, and structure–activity relationship of amine ammonium salts and carboxylate-type PILs–H2O mixtures, suggesting that the strength of the interaction between PILs and H2O depends on the anion, while the cation only affects the position of water within the PILs–H2O cosolvent network. As shown in Figure 5, Dong et al. [58] synthesized four water-soluble PILs as water-based additives, and results from physicochemical property assessments and friction tests indicated that PILs not only exhibit high viscosity and certain corrosion resistance, but also have excellent lubrication performance. Lubrication mechanism and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation analyses revealed that PILs form double-layer structures in aqueous solutions through self-assembly and simultaneously induce continuous boundary protective films through tribochemical reactions at the friction interface, thereby effectively reducing shear resistance. PILs have high structural tunability, simple production processes, excellent dispersibility in water, and strong adaptability to both high and low temperatures, making them a class of high-performance water-based functional additives.
Figure 5. Structures of four water-soluble PILs [58].
Polymeric Ionic Liquid Lubricant Additives
Water-based polymer lubricant additives are mainly composed of water-soluble or dispersible polymeric materials. Compared with lubricating oil, water exhibits low viscosity and difficulty forming robust lubricating film on surfaces, which greatly restricts its industrial application. Polymer additives not only have excellent viscosity-enhancing effects, but also have high molecular design flexibility, allowing the introduction of active elements or target functional groups into the structure, thereby obtaining multifunctional water-based lubricant additives [59,60]. Poly(ionic liquid)s (PILs) are a type of multifunctional lubricant additives that can simultaneously increase viscosity, reduce friction, and resist wear, while maintaining superior environmental friendliness. Through clever molecular design, they combine the lubricating properties of ionic liquids with the high viscosity characteristics of polymers. They are a current research hotspot in the field of water-based lubrication and are expected to address the performance limitations of traditional water-based lubricants [61]. As shown in Figure 6a, Yang et al. [62] used polyethyleneimine as the cation and fatty acids of different chain lengths as the anion to design a series of polymeric protic ionic liquids (PLPILs) that serve as green lubricants for steel substrates with excellent lubricating performance. Notably, the PLPILs based on nonanoic acid, with medium alkyl chain length, exhibit a low coefficient of friction (COF) and wear volume under high load conditions (2.15 kN), mainly due to the formation of a dense, ordered, and relatively thick protective layer on the contact surface. As shown in Figure 6b, Liu et al. [63] synthesized polymeric protic ionic liquids (PLPILs) using a copolymer of poly(ethylene glycol) methyl ether methacrylate and dimethylaminoethyl methacrylate as the cation and octanoylglycine as the anionic counterpart. Adding the PLPILs to water-based fluids significantly improves the viscosity, anticorrosion, and tribological performance of the water-based lubricants. As shown in Figure 6c, Liu et al. [64] developed two polyurea-type ionic liquid water-based lubricant additives based on the hydrogen-bonding effect of urea groups. The urea moieties enable polymers to form stronger interfacial adsorption layers, substantially enhancing the friction-reducing, wear-resistant performance and extreme pressure load-bearing capacity of water-based lubrication systems. When the mass fraction of the PILIPs is 2%, the COF of the water-based lubrication system is as low as 0.12, the extreme pressure load capacity reaches 1 kN, and metal corrosion is significantly reduced. PLIL lubricant additives do not contain sulfur, phosphorus, or halogen elements, combine friction-reducing and anticorrosion properties, are environmentally friendly, can stably disperse in water-based fluids, and show great application potential in water-based hydraulic fluids for hydraulic supports. Finally, Table 2 summarizes the lubrication and anticorrosion performance of different ionic liquids, as well as their corresponding action mechanisms. The basic principles of both the lubrication and anticorrosion performance of hydraulic fluids are based on the interfacial behavior of additive molecules with metals.
Figure 6. Polyethyleneimine-based polymeric protic ionic liquids (PLPILs) (a), octanoylglycine-based polymeric protic ionic liquids (PLPILs) (b), and polyurea-based ionic liquids (c) (adapted from [62,63,64]).
Table 2. Lubrication and anticorrosion properties of different ionic liquids.
2.2. Nano-Lubricant Additives
Nanoparticles, owing to their high specific surface area, superior mechanical properties, and excellent chemical stability, provide new insights into the development of advanced lubricating materials [65]. Common nano-lubricant additives for water-based lubricant systems can be classified into inorganic nano-additives and organic–inorganic composite nano-additives, according to their components. Spherical or quasi-spherical nanoparticles possess rigid structures. When entering the friction contact region, these particles function as nanoscale ball bearings, converting pure sliding friction into a mixed rolling–sliding friction state [66]. This strategy avoids direct contact between friction pairs and effectively prevents severe tribological failures such as seizure. At the same time, high-performance nanoparticles with active surface groups are restricted within the friction contact area due to their ideal embedding stability [67], thereby providing excellent friction-reducing and wear-resistant performance [68].
2.2.1. Inorganic Nano-Additives
Nano-lubricants are suspensions formed by dispersing nanoparticles in conventional fluids and possess unique physicochemical properties that can significantly reduce the coefficient of friction (COF) and wear, effectively enhancing lubrication performance [69,70]. Common inorganic nano-lubricant materials mainly include metals [71,72], metal oxides [73,74,75], molybdenum disulfide [76,77], carbon-based materials [78,79], and so on. Benefiting from the inherent viscosity of oil-based systems, nanoparticles can be readily dispersed stably and have found successful applications as lubricant additives [80]. However, nanoparticle aggregation in water-based fluid media restricts their practical deployment [81].
2.2.2. Organic–Inorganic Composite Additives
Owing to their ultrafine particle size, nano-lubricating additives exhibit superior comprehensive advantages compared with conventional solid lubricants. However, the direct utilization of nano-additives yields limited tribological improvement due to poor dispersion stability, especially in water-based systems. Surface modification can enhance the dispersion of nanoparticles in the aqueous phase and their adsorption on friction surfaces, thereby improving lubrication performance [82].
Metal Lubricant Additives
Metal nanoparticles possess extremely high surface energy and can strongly adsorb onto frictional interfaces during friction, undergoing tribochemical reactions to form a protective film with excellent anti-friction and anti-wear properties. However, metal nanoparticles are chemically unstable and easily oxidized, are also prone to oxidation, and corrode in water-based fluids. Therefore, chemical coating modification is particularly important. As shown in Figure 7, Yang et al. [83] synthesized three types of PILs with alkyl chains of different lengths. Water-soluble Cu nanoparticles were coated with PILs and used as lubricant additives in water–ethylene glycol, and their lubricating performance was studied. The results show that the composite of water-soluble PILs and water-soluble Cu nanoparticles exhibits excellent anti-friction, wear-resistant, and extreme pressure performance as lubricant additives in water–ethylene glycol.
Figure 7. Protic ionic liquids of alkanolamines with three different alkyl chain lengths (adapted from [83]).
Oxide Lubricant Additives
Oxide nanoparticles are superior to metal nanoparticles, owing to their superior chemical stability [84], and mainly include titanium dioxide (TiO2), silicon dioxide (SiO2), and copper oxide (CuO), etc. [74]. Zhao et al. [85] prepared water-based titanium dioxide nanoparticles (TiO2) with dual coating using a silane coupling agent (KH-570) and OP-10 and studied the tribological performance and application performance of the nanoparticles as water-based lubricant additives in Q235 steel processing on an MSR-10D four-ball wear tester and a benchtop drilling machine. The results showed that surface-modified TiO2 nanoparticles can significantly enhance the load-bearing capacity of pure water and reduce friction and wear. During drilling, the water-based lubricant containing TiO2 nanoparticles consumed less power and produced smoother machined surfaces than the lubricant without nanoparticles. Liu et al. [86] designed polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE)-modified SiO2 nanoparticles. The newly prepared PTFE@silica Janus nanoparticles (JNs) meet the requirements of water-based lubricant additives, and, due to their unique amphiphilic structure, they exhibit excellent dispersion stability in water. By introducing a mass concentration of 0.5% JNs into water-based lubricants, compared with pure water lubrication, the coefficient of friction (COF) and wear volume decreased by 63.8% and 94.2%, respectively. Similarly, compared with commercial silica and PTFE suspensions, the JN suspension also demonstrated better lubrication and wear resistance performance.
Sulfide Lubricant Additives
Sulfur atoms within sulfides can react at the friction interface to form a high-performance protective film, thereby performing anti-friction and anti-wear functions. Representative include MoS2 [87], WS2 [88], and CuS [89]. Liang et al. [90] used urea to modify MoS2 to improve its compatibility with polar lubricants, preparing U–MoS2 water-based lubricant additives. In a water-based system, when the mass concentration of U–MoS2 was 0.25%, the COF decreased by 84%, and wear was reduced by 81%. Zhang et al. [88] modified CuS nanoparticles with bis(2-hydroxyethyl) dithiocarbamate (HDA) as a surface modifier to prepare water-soluble lubricant additives (HDA-CuS). The prepared HDA-CuS nanoparticles can effectively improve the tribological behavior and thermal conductivity of distilled water. When the additive mass concentration was 0.8%, the COF and wear rate decreased by 78.3% and 93.7%, respectively.
Carbon-Based Lubricant Additives
Common carbon-based nano-lubricant additives include nanodiamonds [91], carbon nanotubes [92], graphene [93], fullerenes [94], and carbon quantum dots [95,96]. Although carbon-based nanomaterials have good anti-friction and anti-wear effects when used directly as lubricant additives, functionalization of carbon-based nanomaterials can endow them with superior physicochemical, mechanical, and tribological properties. Gu et al. [97] chemically activated the carboxyl groups on graphene oxide (GO) to enable reactions with the hydroxyl groups at the terminals of oleic acid triethanolamine (MDLO), synthesizing GO-grafted modified oleic acid triethanolamine ester (MDLO-GO). When applied in hydraulic liquid, at a GO loading of 0.004%, the non-seizure load of the hydraulic fluid reached 481 N. Compared with hydraulic liquid without GO modification, the lubrication was improved by 11.9%, while high- and low-temperature performance were also significantly enhanced. Wang et al. [67] developed a simpler one-step pyrolysis method to prepare IL-functionalized CQDs as water-based lubricant additives. At an optimal mass fraction of 0.015%, the average COF and wear were reduced by 57.5% and 64%, respectively, showing excellent tribological performance. The friction reduction and anti-wear performance of the composite additive were far superior to that of CDs and IL, demonstrating the synergistic lubricating effect between the IL groups and the carbon core. Some researchers have also studied the bonding of amino acids with carbon dots to generate multifunctional amino acid-based carbon dots, which can effectively prevent carbon steel corrosion and enhance lubrication performance in water-based cutting fluids [98].
3. Development Trends of Lubricants for Water-Based Hydraulic Fluids
At present, the technical development of hydraulic fluids remains at the stage of compounding various specific-function additives for lubrication, corrosion inhibition, and hard water resistance. These fluids are sensitive to fluctuations in the quality of dilution water, and the compatibility among multiple additives is poor, making the system equilibrium easy to disrupt and affecting the online intelligent monitoring of the fluid supply system. In the construction of intelligent fully mechanized mining face, optical–electric signals from sensors, such as concentration sensors, are often used for online monitoring of indicators like hydraulic fluid concentration to achieve intelligent sensing, decision-making, and automated execution in fluid supply technology [99,100]. When the cleanliness and stability of hydraulic fluids decline, this affects the accurate capture and transmission of optical–electric signals by sensors. The main methods for maintaining hydraulic fluid stability fall into two categories: one involves controlling the stability of the hydraulic fluid from the perspective of usage methods and the quality of diluted water, mainly by pre-treating the diluted water to meet the KA 76-2011 industry standard for water quality. However, fluctuations in underground water quality are difficult to avoid, often leading to issues such as saponification of the hydraulic fluid, filter clogging, and valve corrosion. Another category is the development of lubricant additives that are inherently resistant to hard water and also have corrosion-inhibiting functions, thereby preventing declines in hydraulic fluid stability caused by saponification and valve rust, ensuring the normal operation of intelligent working faces. At the same time, multifunctional and highly efficient lubricants can reduce additive usage, mitigate environmental impact, and promote the construction of green mines.
Performance tuning of corrosion inhibition and tribological properties of small molecule compounds is ultimately governed by interfacial adsorption (chemical/physical) effects [101,102]. For alkylamide lubricants, the non-polar segment consists of alkyl chain with relatively low reactivity; therefore, the performance regulation strategy mainly involves introducing characteristic functional groups at the polar end. Based on the introduced heteroatoms and the coordination of the amide bond with alkaline earth metal ions, the hard water resistance can be adjusted, and the adsorption (monolayer/multilayer) behavior of the molecules on the metal surface can be controlled through changes in hydrogen bonding and steric hindrance. Overall, the polar groups of alkylamides affect the comprehensive performance of lubricants in multiple ways, including lubrication, corrosion inhibition, and sensitivity to hard water. The combination and interaction of different polar groups determine the overall performance of the lubricant and its suitability under various operating conditions.
With the advancement of intelligent and green coal mining, hydraulic fluids for hydraulic supports will develop in the direction of stability, reliability, greenness, and efficiency. High-efficiency multifunctional lubricants with the combined properties of hard water resistance, lubrication, and corrosion inhibition will become an important research direction for next-generation additives. Whether based on fatty alcohol ethers, ionic liquids, or alkylamides, introducing different functional groups at the polar end while balancing corresponding properties can achieve synergistic enhancement. The development and use of multifunctional additives can mitigate issues such as the large consumption and insufficient stability of multiple additive blends, allowing for the development of single- (or few-) component hydraulic fluids, meeting the transmission requirements of optoelectronic signals in intelligent fluid supply systems, reducing the amount of hydraulic fluid additives, and supporting the construction of green mines. As shown in Figure 8a, Yang et al. [103] used borate esters as extreme pressure components, introducing fatty acid diethanolamides containing active groups such as hydroxyl and amide bonds into the borate esters to prepare alkylamide borate esters. The introduction of amide bonds can circumvent their hard water sensitivity while enhancing adsorption on metal surfaces, and the introduction of fatty chains can improve their lubrication and load-bearing capacity. As shown in Figure 8b, Yang et al. [104] used 1,3-diamino-2-propanol as the substrate to synthesize 1,3-dioleoylamide-2-oleate propyl ester (DOAPO), containing polar amide and ester groups as well as non-polar alkyl chains, similarly providing hard water resistance, lubrication, and corrosion inhibition properties. In addition, introducing nanoparticles into water-based hydraulic fluid systems can not only improve the product’s lubrication performance, but also reduce the foaming tendency of hydraulic fluids and enhance the operational stability of hydraulic supports [105].
Figure 8. Preparation process of fatty acid diethanolamide borate ester (a) and DOAPO (b) (adapted from [103,104]).
In addition, our research team analyzed 1146 water samples collected in 2025 from coal bases in Shendong, Jinbei, Jinzhong, Jindong, Luxi, Lianghuai, Huanglong, Jizhong, Ningdong, and northern Shaanxi, primarily testing their hardness (Ca2+ + Mg2+), SO42−, Cl−, and HCO3−, and statistical analyses were conducted for the concentration distribution of each ion, as summarized in Table 3. Currently, most mainstream mines in China are equipped with pre-treatment devices for dilution water. Although the water quality indicators of blending water still fluctuate, the overall water quality has significantly improved. Compared with the 2015 statistical data [106], the proportion of water samples with hardness below 200 mg/L increased by 21.52%, the proportion with SO42− content below 200 mg/L increased by 38.50%, the proportion with Cl− content below 200 mg/L increased by 7.18%, and the proportion with HCO3− content below 200 mg/L increased by 393.33%. With the maturation of corrosion-resistant technologies such as ultra-high-speed laser cladding [107,108], the corrosion resistance of hydraulic support cylinders has been improved. The improvement in the quality of blending water and the corrosion resistance of cylinders, along with research on the structural design and performance balance of multifunctional additives such as alkyl amides, provide a solid foundation for the development of single- (or low-) component hydraulic fluids.
Table 3. Water sample data statistics in 2025 and 2015.
4. Conclusions and Outlook
As the power transmission media for coal mine hydraulic supports, water-based hydraulic fluids have seen the development of their lubricant additives evolve from alcohol ether types and vegetable oils to ionic liquids and nanoparticles, with continuous improvement in lubrication performance and multifunctionality. Alcohol ether lubricants, with their excellent resistance to hard water and tunable hydrophilicity and lipophilicity, have become one of the most widely used water-based lubricant additives today. Vegetable oil lubricants, derived from renewable resources, provide a solid theoretical foundation for the molecular design of green lubricants through systematic studies on the unsaturation, alkyl chain length, and branching degree of fatty acid molecular structures. Ionic liquid lubricant additives, particularly protic ionic liquids and polymeric ionic liquids, exhibit good synergistic effects in reducing friction, resisting wear, and inhibiting corrosion in water-based systems through precise molecular-level design and self-assembly behavior. Nano-lubricant additives, leveraging their unique rolling effects and interfacial reaction activity, open new avenues for overcoming performance bottlenecks of conventional water-based lubricants. Each type of lubricant has its own advantages, but it is difficult for a single type to fully meet the comprehensive demands for lubrication, hard water resistance, corrosion inhibition, and stability under complex operating conditions.
Driven by the dual goals of intelligent coal mining and the construction of green mines, lubricant additives for water-based hydraulic fluids are rapidly developing toward multifunctional integration, single-component formulation, and environmental friendliness. Currently, hydraulic fluids commonly adopt a technology route that blends multiple functional additives, which makes them sensitive to fluctuations in the quality of dilution water, easily compromising system stability and thus affecting the photonic signal transmission accuracy of online monitoring devices such as concentration sensors in intelligent fluid supply systems. Developing highly efficient multifunctional additives with lubrication, hard water tolerance, and corrosion inhibition properties to achieve single- (or few-) component hydraulic fluid formulations has become a consensus in the industry, as it fundamentally simplifies the system and enhances stability. Molecular design strategies, such as those involving alkylamides and polymeric ionic liquids, can simultaneously regulate molecular adsorption behavior on metal surfaces and coordination capabilities with calcium and magnesium ions by introducing amide bonds or heteroatom active groups at the polar end, providing a feasible path for the construction of multifunctional additives. Meanwhile, the incorporation of nanoparticles can not only improve lubrication performance, but also potentially reduce the foaming tendency of hydraulic fluids, further enhancing system operational reliability.
It is noteworthy that the overall dilution water quality at major national coal bases has improved markedly in recent years, with greatly elevated compliance rates for key indicators including hardness and sulfate, chloride, and bicarbonate contents. Furthermore, the mature deployment of anticorrosion technologies such as ultrahigh-speed laser cladding for powered support cylinders has established favorable external prerequisites for developing single-component hydraulic fluids. In the future, research should further deepen the understanding of the structure–activity relationship of lubricating additives. Theoretical tools such as molecular dynamics simulations can be adopted to uncover the synergistic mechanisms of multifunctional groups, facilitating the shift in additive molecular design from empirical to rational design. Researchers should develop multifunctional additives that integrate lubrication, corrosion inhibition, and hard water resistance to cater the demands of intelligent and green mine construction. In parallel, systematical evaluations are required for long-cycle and repeated-operation stability of newly developed lubricant additives, their compatibility with electro-hydraulic control systems, and their full life-cycle environmental impacts. It is essential to accelerate the engineering application of high-performance, low-dosage, and easily degradable green lubricating additives.

\# Research Progress and Prospects for Lubricant Additives for Water\-Based Hydraulic Fluids in Hydraulic Supports

\,

and

1

Coal Science \(Beijing\) New Materials Technology Co\.\, Ltd\.\, Beijing 100013\, China

CCTEG China Coal Research Institute\, Beijing 100013\, China

School of Chemical and Environmental Engineering\, Shanghai Institute of Technology\, Shanghai 201400\, China

Authors to whom correspondence should be addressed\.

\#\# Abstract

Water\-based hydraulic fluids serve as the power transmission medium for hydraulic support systems in coal mines\, and the performance of their lubricant additives directly affects the stable operation of the supports\. This paper provides a systematic review of research progress on lubricant additives for water\-based hydraulic fluids in China\, focusing on two main categories\: liquid and nanoparticle lubricant additives\. Liquid lubricant additives are categorized into fatty alcohol ether\-based\, vegetable oil\-based\, and ionic liquid\-based additives\; nanoparticle\-based additives include inorganic nanoparticles and organic–inorganic composite particles\. This article analyzes the molecular structure design strategies\, lubrication mechanisms\, and performance regulation pathways of various additives\. In response to the demands of intelligent coal mining and green mine construction\, it is proposed that the development of lubricant additives for water\-based hydraulic fluids should target multifunctional integration and environmental friendliness\. Improvements in the quality of the dilution water and the maturity of cylinder anticorrosion technology will create favorable conditions for the development of single\-component \(or few\-component\) hydraulic fluids\. In the future\, research should deepen understanding of the structure–performance relationships of lubricant additives\, so as to facilitate the engineering application of high\-performance\, low\-dose\, degradable green lubricant additives and provide technical support for intelligent coal mine construction and ecological protection in the Yellow River Basin\.

\#\# 1\. Introduction

In 2025\, China’s coal production accounted for 54\.8\% of the global total \(International Energy Agency \(IEA\) data\: 8\.85 billion tons\)\, with underground coal mining accounting for approximately 75\% of this output \[1\]\. Hydraulic supports serve as the safety shield for fully mechanized mining faces in underground coal mines\: they are responsible for supporting the roof\, propelling the scraper conveyor\, and advancing autonomously to guarantee the safety of the working spaces \[2\]\. The hydraulic fluid supply system is the power source for hydraulic supports\, and the hydraulic fluid is the medium for power transmission within the hydraulic system\. The development of hydraulic fluids has mainly undergone four technical stages\, transitioning gradually from oil\-based to water\-based fluids\. Initially\, mineral oil was used as the hydraulic fluid for coal mine hydraulic supports\. Owing to its low biodegradability and the flammability of the mist formed from leaks under high pressure\, it posed significant safety risks\. In the 1970s\, dispersed mineral\-oil\-in\-water emulsion systems \(approximately 50\%\) were developed\, addressing the safety concerns of hydraulic fluids in underground mines\. However\, due to their thermodynamic instability\, oil–soap separation could easily occur during service \[3\]\. In the 1990s\, with increased automation of hydraulic supports and the application of electro\-hydraulic control systems\, the filtration precision of electro\-hydraulic control systems reached 25 μm\, while traditional emulsion\-type hydraulic fluids were prone to oil and soap separation\, posing a risk of system clogging\. The adoption of micro\-emulsion technology reduced droplet size and yielded micro\-emulsion hydraulic fluids with greatly improved stability\, although these formulations still contained a small amount of mineral oil \(about 5\%\) \[4\]\. At the beginning of the 21st century\, mineral oil\-free concentrated fluids using water\-soluble lubricants \(e\.g\.\, modified vegetable oils\) as the core components were successfully developed\. These fluids not only completely eliminated mineral oil\-related contamination\, but also met the cleanliness and stability requirements of hydraulic fluids for electro\-hydraulic control systems \[5\]\.

According to China’s coal industry standard KA 76\-2011 \[6\] ‘Emulsifying oil\, concentrate fluid and high\-water content hydraulic fluid used for powered support\,’ hydraulic fluids include emulsified oils \(HFAEs\)\, concentrate fluid \(HFASs\)\, and high water content hydraulic fluid\. High water content hydraulic fluid is mainly prepared by mixing the corresponding emulsion oil or concentrate fluid with water \(generally purified mine water\) as the diluent at a mass ratio of 3–5\%\; this fluid circulates within the hydraulic system to provide power \[7\]\. Water\-based lubricants are a cheaper\, safer\, and more environmentally friendly alternative to mineral oil lubricants for coal mine hydraulic support systems\. However\, compared to mineral oils\, water itself is a poor lubricant\. Due to its low viscosity\, the lubrication mechanism shifts from fluid lubrication to mixed or boundary lubrication\. In this case\, the rheological properties of the lubricant become less important\, and friction and wear are mainly determined by the physico\-chemical properties of the friction surfaces\, the lubricant\, and the interactions between them \[8\]\. Under fixed friction surface conditions\, the molecular structure of the lubricant becomes particularly important \[9\]\. Therefore\, the development of high\-efficiency lubricants is required to achieve better tribological performance\.

Research shows that\, compared with mineral oils\, improving the tribological performance of water\-based lubricants can minimize the shear resistance between friction pairs\, reduce the power required for operating machinery\, and thus save energy \[10\]\. In addition\, water\-based lubricants have excellent cooling capabilities and environmentally friendly properties \[11\]\, making them very effective as cutting fluids\, drilling fluids\, and hydraulic fluids \[12\]\. Research reports on water\-based lubricant additives mainly focus on the fields of cutting fluids \[13\,14\] and drilling fluids \[15\,16\,17\]\. Although water\-based lubricant additives are also key components for enhancing the overall performance of hydraulic fluids\, few relevant systematic reviews have been published\. This paper reviews the research progress of lubricant additives for water\-based hydraulic fluids and\, against the background of intelligent coal mining and green mine construction\, discusses the development trends of lubricant additives for water\-based hydraulic fluids\, aiming to promote the better and faster development of high\-performance environmentally friendly hydraulic fluids\.

\#\# 2\. Lubricant for Water\-Based Hydraulic Fluids

Lubricant additives for water\-based hydraulic fluids not only need to have good dispersibility and lubricity\, but also must be compatible with other additives in the hydraulic fluid\; this is a necessary condition for the lubricant additives to fully exert their activity\. In addition\, because high water content hydraulic fluids contain a large proportion of mine water\, and mine water has a certain hardness \(Ca2\+\, Mg2\+\)\, water\-based lubricant additives should also have a certain level of hard water resistance\. Furthermore\, sufficient raw material availability\, environmental friendliness\, and reasonable cost are important factors in determining whether lubricant additives for water\-based hydraulic fluids can be widely applied\. To satisfy these performance requirements\, researchers have developed different types of lubricant additives for water\-based hydraulic fluids\. According to their physical state\, they mainly fall into two categories\: liquid lubricants and nanoparticle lubricant additives\. Nanoparticles include inorganic particles and organic–inorganic composite particles\.

\#\#\# 2\.1\. Liquid Lubricant Additives

\#\#\#\# 2\.1\.1\. Alcohol Ether Lubricants

Alkyl ether lubricant additives are formed by the condensation of alcohol compounds and epoxy compounds\. The alcohol compounds include polyols \(such as glycerol\) and fatty alcohols\. Based on the type of alcohol compound\, corresponding polyether polyols and fatty alcohol ethers can be synthesized\. Both are non\-ionic surfactants and have excellent resistance to hard water\. Compared with polyols\, fatty alcohols contain long alkyl chains as lipophilic groups\, presenting a lower hydrophilic–lipophilic balance \(HLB\) value\, which delivers better lubrication and load\-bearing capacity\, making them more suitable for serving as lubricant additives in hydraulic fluid\.

\#\#\#\#\# Fatty Alcohol Ether Lubricants

Fatty alcohol ether lubricants generally consist of alkyl chains \(C8–C18\) and alcohol ether segments\. The structure of fatty alcohol ether lubricants contains both hydrophobic long alkyl chains and a hydrophilic polyether structure\. They dissolve in water via intermolecular hydrogen bonds formed between the oxygen atoms in the ether chains and hydrogen atoms in water\. Therefore\, the hydrophilic–lipophilic balance can be adjusted by changing the number and structure of ether chains \[18\] or by selecting alkyl chains with different structures and lengths \[19\]\. Furthermore\, the foaming properties of hydraulic fluids can be modulated by choosing straight\-chain or branched\-chain alkyl alcohols \[20\]\. As shown in Figure 1a\, Pan \[21\] investigated extended surfactants of different structures and performed interfacial tension measurement\. The results indicate that increasing the number of PO groups\, lengthening the alkyl chain\, and introducing branching in the hydrophobic group exert only a minor influence on interfacial tension\-reducing capacity\. PO groups can enlarge the hydrophobic group size via molecular curling to match the dimension of the hydrophilic head group\. Under suitable hydrophilic–lipophilic balance conditions\, these surfactants can lower interfacial tension to ultra\-low levels \(\<10−2 mN\/m\)\. However\, excessively long EO chains can stretch into the aqueous phase\, disrupting the close packing of the interfacial film and causing an increase in interfacial tension\. As shown in Figure 1b\, Li et al\. \[22\] synthesized linear alcohol ether \(AEO3\) and isomeric alcohol ether \(IAEO3\) with three EO adducts using C12–14 linear alcohol and C13 isomeric alcohol and evaluated the foaming performance of these two alcohol ethers\. The results showed that\, at the same EO adduct number\, AEO3 exhibited slightly higher initial foam height but faster foam decay\, whereas IAEO3 produced a lower initial foam height than AEO3\, yet the foam was more stable and did not easily collapse\.

Figure 1\. Extended surfactants with different structures \(a\) and straight\-chain \(isomeric\) alcohol ethers \(b\) \(adapted from \[21\,22\]\)\.

\#\#\#\#\# Fatty Alcohol Ether Carboxylic Acid Lubricants

Generally\, the molecular structure of organic lubricants largely determines their lubrication performance\. Lubrication efficiency is influenced by various factors such as the length of the alkyl hydrophobic chain\, heteroatoms\, the presence of electron\-donating or electron\-withdrawing substituents\, and the size of heterocycles\. Heteroatoms represented by P\, N\, S\, B\, etc\. can be introduced into lubricant molecules as extreme pressure and anti\-wear elements to improve lubrication performance\. Other studies have reported that oxygen\-containing functional groups enhance lubrication in the following order\: COOH \> CHO \> OH \> COOCH3 \> C\=O \> C\-O\-C \[23\]\. These functional groups can form intra\- or intermolecular hydrogen bonds to regulate the adsorption layer \[24\]\. Fatty alcohol ether lubricants have good water solubility and hard water resistance \[25\]\, but because ethers have limited enhancement effects on lubrication performance\, researchers have further modified fatty alcohol ethers by carboxylation to achieve superior lubrication performance\.

Carboxylation modification involves introducing carboxyl groups into the structure of fatty alcohol ethers to obtain fatty alcohol ether carboxylates\. Fatty alcohol ether carboxylates are anionic amphiphilic surfactants that contain both EO\/PO and carboxyl hydrophilic groups\. The introduction of carboxyl groups improves salt tolerance\, emulsifying properties\, and lubricating properties\. As shown in Figure 2a\, Zhang \[26\] synthesized isomeric alcohol ether carboxylates using tridecyl isomeric alcohol ether as the substrate and studied the wetting\, emulsifying\, and foaming properties of isomeric alcohol ether carboxylates with different EO numbers and linear alcohol ether carboxylates\. It was found that a lower EO number resulted in relatively better wetting and emulsifying performance\; compared with linear analogs\, branched analogs exhibited superior wetting\, emulsifying\, and decontamination performance on carbon black cloth\, but poorer foam stability\. As shown in Figure 2b\, Lin \[27\] synthesized alcohol ether carboxylates with eight PO segments and with both 20 PO segments and 10 EO segments using linear alcohol C18OH and isomeric alcohol C12\+8OH as initiators\. Compared with the \(PO\)8 series products\, the inclusion of EO segments significantly improved water solubility and salt tolerance\. C18\(PO\)20\(EO\)10OCH2COONa tolerated Na\+ and Ca2\+ concentrations exceeding 200\,000 mg\/L\. Huang et al\. \[28\] introduced alcohol ether carboxylates as calcium soap dispersants to develop a hydraulic support emulsion that can withstand Grade 40 hard water \(per standard KA 76\-2011\)\. Industrial validation demonstrates that the emulsion satisfies field service \(Grade 40 hard water\)\; the hydraulic support system runs smoothly without filter clogging or valve sticking\. Similarly\, commercial oil\-free water\-based hydraulic fluids adopt alcohol ether carboxylates as lubricant additives\, yet such fluids generally produce excessive foam\. Foaming performance is also an important property of hydraulic fluids\; the less the fluid foams\, the more favorable it is for the operation of the hydraulic support\. Anticorrosion relies primarily on added corrosion inhibitors\.

Figure 2\. Heterogeneous alcohol ether carboxylates embedded with different amounts of EO \(a\) and heterogeneous alcohol ether carboxylates embedded with different amounts of EO and PO \(b\) \(adapted from \[26\,27\]\)\.

\#\#\#\# 2\.1\.2\. Vegetable Oil Lubricant Additives

China’s major coal\-producing areas are mainly distributed along the Yellow River Basin\. Guided by the national ecological protection in the Yellow River Basin\, vegetable oil\-based hydraulic fluids exhibit distinct advantages over mineral oils\, including wide raw material availability\, superior biodegradability\, and low toxicity\. They can effectively address the water and soil pollution problems caused by traditional mineral oil\-based hydraulic fluids and are a type of renewable green lubricant \[29\,30\]\.

\#\#\#\#\# Vegetable Oil Lubricants

There are numerous reports on the development and application of vegetable oil lubricants \[31\,32\,33\]\, mainly focusing on the study of the structure–property relationship of vegetable oil molecules and their lubricating properties\, including the effects of alkyl chain length \[34\]\, degree of unsaturation \[35\]\, and branching \[36\] on lubrication performance\. The alkyl chain structure in vegetable oil molecules directly affects the viscosity characteristics of lubricants\. The length of the alkyl chain mainly affects the lateral cohesion of the lubricating film\; as the alkyl chain length increases\, the lateral cohesion gradually rises\, and viscosity increases\. Typically\, vegetable oils with long alkyl chains have higher viscosity and can bear higher loads\, whereas short\-chain vegetable oils have lower viscosity\, and under high load or high temperature conditions their pressure–viscosity and viscosity–temperature characteristics are insufficient\, impairing the lubrication effect \[33\]\. As shown in Figure 3a\, Gusain et al\. \[34\] synthesized fatty acids with different alkyl chain lengths \(C10\, C12\, C14\, C16\, C18\-1\) as anions\, with tetrabutylammonium as the cation in ionic liquids\, and investigated their friction performance\. With the increase of the alkyl chain length of the anion\, the viscosity of the ionic liquid gradually increased\. This is because longer alkyl chains exhibit larger molecular volumes and stronger intermolecular interactions\, which hinder the relative movement of molecules and thus increase internal friction \[37\]\.

Figure 3\. Ionic liquids with alkyl chains of different lengths \(a\) and isopropylation of soybean oil \(b\) \(adapted from \[34\,36\]\)\.

For saturated vegetable oils\, their lubrication performance increases with the length of the alkyl chain\. However\, when the alkyl chain length exceeds 16\, the friction resistance and wear resistance of the resulting lubricating film reach a peak and are no longer affected by chain length \[38\]\. In contrast\, for unsaturated vegetable oils\, the adsorption effect of double bonds makes the arrangement of the adsorption film less dense\. At this point\, the lateral cohesion between molecules becomes the key factor affecting lubrication performance\. Since cohesion is proportional to the length of the alkyl chain\, longer alkyl chains can compensate for this adverse effect and enhance intermolecular cohesion\. Additionally\, when the number of double bonds is greater than one\, the lubrication performance tends to decrease as the number of double bonds increases\. This may be because the increase in double bonds increases the interaction sites of the π\-electron cloud with the metal substrate\, effectively shortening the length of the non\-polar alkyl chains\, making the lubricating film thinner and reducing its load\-bearing capacity\. Long et al\. \[35\] studied oleic acid and ricinoleic acid\, each containing one double bond\, which both showed excellent lubrication performance\, whereas linoleic acid\, containing two double bonds\, resulted in relatively higher friction and wear\.

The presence of branches in the structure of vegetable oils enhances the ability to separate non\-polar alkyl chains from polar functional groups\, increasing the tendency of polar functional groups to attach to metal surfaces\. At the same time\, this tendency increases with the degree of branching of the alkyl chains\, making it easier to form dense lubricating films on friction surfaces\. Moreover\, calculations of adsorption energy show that adsorption energy gradually increases with the degree of branching\, which also confirms that the formed lubricating film is denser\. As shown in Figure 3b\, Bhowmik et al\. \[36\] carried out isopropylation of the double bonds of soybean oil fatty chains\, converting the double bonds into single bonds\, while also achieving isomerization of the fatty chains\. The isomerized regular soybean oil reduced the wear volume by 35\% at room temperature and by 15\% at high temperature\, whereas high\-oleic soybean oil reduced wear volume by about 10\% at both room and high temperatures\. Finally\, Table 1 summarizes the influences of alkyl chain structures on the lubricating performance of vegetable oil lubricants\.

Table 1\. Effects of different alkyl chains on the performance of vegetable oil lubricants\.

\#\#\#\#\# Vegetable Oil\-Based Modified Lubricant Additive

Compared with vegetable oil lubricants\, downstream products of vegetable oils\, such as fatty acids \(oleic acid\, ricinoleic acid\, etc\.\)\, contain carboxyl structures\, which can undergo further chemical modification at the carboxyl group to design higher\-performance or even multifunctional lubricant additives\. Fatty acid molecules contain both polar and non\-polar groups\; the polar groups can bind to metal surfaces through adsorption\, while the non\-polar alkyl chains influence the load\-bearing capacity and lubrication performance of the oil film through intermolecular forces\, allowing them to act as oil\-based lubricants themselves\. However\, since hydraulic fluids are water\-based systems\, fatty acids need to be modified to be suitable for aqueous conditions\. The simplest modification method is to convert fatty acids into salts\, but fatty acid salts are sensitive to hard water\, and the adsorption ability of a single carboxyl polar group on metal surfaces is limited\. Therefore\, further structural modification of fatty acids is particularly important\.

Since the chemical structure of the non\-polar region of fatty acids derived from vegetable oils is mainly influenced by the type of vegetable oil and is relatively fixed\, the carboxyl group at the polar end becomes the key active site for chemical modification\. Based on the carboxyl group\, more polar groups\, such as hydroxyl\, amino\, and sulfonic groups\, can be introduced\. The polar atoms in the functional groups \(N\, O\, S\, P\, etc\.\) not only enhance intermolecular interactions through hydrogen bonds\, ionic bonds\, and other interactions\, but also have strong affinity with metal surfaces\, forming high\-strength lubricating oil films and reducing friction and wear\. At the same time\, the introduction of polar groups also improves other properties of hydraulic fluids\. For example\, lone pairs on heteroatoms can coordinate and chelate with Ca2\+\/Mg2\+\, enhancing resistance to hard water \[39\]\. Compared with ester bonds\, amide bonds have stronger adsorption and are more stable in aqueous solutions\, so researchers mainly perform chemical modification through amidation\. Amino acids themselves are effective small\-molecule corrosion inhibitors \[40\,41\,42\,43\]\, and\, when reacted with fatty acids through amidation to form alkyl amides\, they can reduce the hardness sensitivity of fatty acids while introducing more groups with adsorption and coordination chelation activity \[44\,45\]\. Our research group \[46\] prepared alkyl amide surfactants by reacting fatty acids with amino acids and found that\, compared with fatty acids\, the introduction of amino acids greatly improved the low\-temperature stability of water\-based fluids and increased hard water resistance by 30\.50\%\, while also exhibiting excellent corrosion inhibition performance \[47\]\. \#\#\#\# 2\.1\.3\. Ionic Liquid Lubricant Additives

\#\#\#\#\# Conventional Ionic Liquid Lubricant Additives

Ionic liquids consist of organic cations and inorganic\/organic anions and remain liquid at room temperature or near room temperature\. Since their first application in the field of friction in 2001 \[48\]\, researchers have systematically studied their development and optimization as lubricants \[49\,50\] and lubricant additives \[51\,52\]\, showing a significant effect in improving the friction performance of oil\- and water\-based lubricants \[53\]\. Traditional ionic liquids\, due to their high cost\, have limited feasibility when applied alone as lubricants\, and are therefore generally used as lubricant additives\. Ionic liquids can effectively reduce friction and wear and\, to a certain extent\, mitigate the corrosiveness of water\-based lubrication systems \[54\]\. As lubricant additives\, the advantage of ionic liquids lies in the designability of their molecular structure\; by precisely controlling the cationic and anionic groups of the ionic liquids\, their adsorption ability on friction surfaces can be enhanced\, thereby improving their tribological performance \[55\]\.

\#\#\#\#\# Protic Ionic Liquids Lubricant Additives

Protic ionic liquids \(PILs\) are typically formed from a Lewis base and a Brønsted acid via a neutralization reaction\, undergoing proton transfer to produce a cation \(protonated Lewis base\) and an anion \(conjugate base of the Brønsted acid\)\. The reaction conditions are relatively mild\, the preparation procedure is straightforward\, and raw materials are readily available and inexpensive\. When using fatty acids \(such as carboxylic acids\) as the anion\, PILs can usually be synthesized at room temperature under solvent\-free conditions\. Due to the presence of proton exchange\, studies have shown that\, in oil\-based systems\, the structure of the anion has a significant impact on the viscosity of PILs\, while variations in the cation have relatively little effect \[56\]\. Similarly\, Oliver Jarvik et al\. \[57\] studied the structure\, properties\, and structure–activity relationship of amine ammonium salts and carboxylate\-type PILs–H2O mixtures\, suggesting that the strength of the interaction between PILs and H2O depends on the anion\, while the cation only affects the position of water within the PILs–H2O cosolvent network\. As shown in Figure 5\, Dong et al\. \[58\] synthesized four water\-soluble PILs as water\-based additives\, and results from physicochemical property assessments and friction tests indicated that PILs not only exhibit high viscosity and certain corrosion resistance\, but also have excellent lubrication performance\. Lubrication mechanism and molecular dynamics \(MD\) simulation analyses revealed that PILs form double\-layer structures in aqueous solutions through self\-assembly and simultaneously induce continuous boundary protective films through tribochemical reactions at the friction interface\, thereby effectively reducing shear resistance\. PILs have high structural tunability\, simple production processes\, excellent dispersibility in water\, and strong adaptability to both high and low temperatures\, making them a class of high\-performance water\-based functional additives\.

Figure 5\. Structures of four water\-soluble PILs \[58\]\.

\#\#\#\#\# Polymeric Ionic Liquid Lubricant Additives

Water\-based polymer lubricant additives are mainly composed of water\-soluble or dispersible polymeric materials\. Compared with lubricating oil\, water exhibits low viscosity and difficulty forming robust lubricating film on surfaces\, which greatly restricts its industrial application\. Polymer additives not only have excellent viscosity\-enhancing effects\, but also have high molecular design flexibility\, allowing the introduction of active elements or target functional groups into the structure\, thereby obtaining multifunctional water\-based lubricant additives \[59\,60\]\. Poly\(ionic liquid\)s \(PILs\) are a type of multifunctional lubricant additives that can simultaneously increase viscosity\, reduce friction\, and resist wear\, while maintaining superior environmental friendliness\. Through clever molecular design\, they combine the lubricating properties of ionic liquids with the high viscosity characteristics of polymers\. They are a current research hotspot in the field of water\-based lubrication and are expected to address the performance limitations of traditional water\-based lubricants \[61\]\. As shown in Figure 6a\, Yang et al\. \[62\] used polyethyleneimine as the cation and fatty acids of different chain lengths as the anion to design a series of polymeric protic ionic liquids \(PLPILs\) that serve as green lubricants for steel substrates with excellent lubricating performance\. Notably\, the PLPILs based on nonanoic acid\, with medium alkyl chain length\, exhibit a low coefficient of friction \(COF\) and wear volume under high load conditions \(2\.15 kN\)\, mainly due to the formation of a dense\, ordered\, and relatively thick protective layer on the contact surface\. As shown in Figure 6b\, Liu et al\. \[63\] synthesized polymeric protic ionic liquids \(PLPILs\) using a copolymer of poly\(ethylene glycol\) methyl ether methacrylate and dimethylaminoethyl methacrylate as the cation and octanoylglycine as the anionic counterpart\. Adding the PLPILs to water\-based fluids significantly improves the viscosity\, anticorrosion\, and tribological performance of the water\-based lubricants\. As shown in Figure 6c\, Liu et al\. \[64\] developed two polyurea\-type ionic liquid water\-based lubricant additives based on the hydrogen\-bonding effect of urea groups\. The urea moieties enable polymers to form stronger interfacial adsorption layers\, substantially enhancing the friction\-reducing\, wear\-resistant performance and extreme pressure load\-bearing capacity of water\-based lubrication systems\. When the mass fraction of the PILIPs is 2\%\, the COF of the water\-based lubrication system is as low as 0\.12\, the extreme pressure load capacity reaches 1 kN\, and metal corrosion is significantly reduced\. PLIL lubricant additives do not contain sulfur\, phosphorus\, or halogen elements\, combine friction\-reducing and anticorrosion properties\, are environmentally friendly\, can stably disperse in water\-based fluids\, and show great application potential in water\-based hydraulic fluids for hydraulic supports\. Finally\, Table 2 summarizes the lubrication and anticorrosion performance of different ionic liquids\, as well as their corresponding action mechanisms\. The basic principles of both the lubrication and anticorrosion performance of hydraulic fluids are based on the interfacial behavior of additive molecules with metals\.
