\#\#\# 2\.2\. Nano\-Lubricant Additives

Nanoparticles\, owing to their high specific surface area\, superior mechanical properties\, and excellent chemical stability\, provide new insights into the development of advanced lubricating materials \[65\]\. Common nano\-lubricant additives for water\-based lubricant systems can be classified into inorganic nano\-additives and organic–inorganic composite nano\-additives\, according to their components\. Spherical or quasi\-spherical nanoparticles possess rigid structures\. When entering the friction contact region\, these particles function as nanoscale ball bearings\, converting pure sliding friction into a mixed rolling–sliding friction state \[66\]\. This strategy avoids direct contact between friction pairs and effectively prevents severe tribological failures such as seizure\. At the same time\, high\-performance nanoparticles with active surface groups are restricted within the friction contact area due to their ideal embedding stability \[67\]\, thereby providing excellent friction\-reducing and wear\-resistant performance \[68\]\.

\#\#\#\# 2\.2\.1\. Inorganic Nano\-Additives

Nano\-lubricants are suspensions formed by dispersing nanoparticles in conventional fluids and possess unique physicochemical properties that can significantly reduce the coefficient of friction \(COF\) and wear\, effectively enhancing lubrication performance \[69\,70\]\. Common inorganic nano\-lubricant materials mainly include metals \[71\,72\]\, metal oxides \[73\,74\,75\]\, molybdenum disulfide \[76\,77\]\, carbon\-based materials \[78\,79\]\, and so on\. Benefiting from the inherent viscosity of oil\-based systems\, nanoparticles can be readily dispersed stably and have found successful applications as lubricant additives \[80\]\. However\, nanoparticle aggregation in water\-based fluid media restricts their practical deployment \[81\]\.

\#\#\#\# 2\.2\.2\. Organic–Inorganic Composite Additives

Owing to their ultrafine particle size\, nano\-lubricating additives exhibit superior comprehensive advantages compared with conventional solid lubricants\. However\, the direct utilization of nano\-additives yields limited tribological improvement due to poor dispersion stability\, especially in water\-based systems\. Surface modification can enhance the dispersion of nanoparticles in the aqueous phase and their adsorption on friction surfaces\, thereby improving lubrication performance \[82\]\.

\#\#\#\#\# Metal Lubricant Additives

Metal nanoparticles possess extremely high surface energy and can strongly adsorb onto frictional interfaces during friction\, undergoing tribochemical reactions to form a protective film with excellent anti\-friction and anti\-wear properties\. However\, metal nanoparticles are chemically unstable and easily oxidized\, are also prone to oxidation\, and corrode in water\-based fluids\. Therefore\, chemical coating modification is particularly important\. As shown in Figure 7\, Yang et al\. \[83\] synthesized three types of PILs with alkyl chains of different lengths\. Water\-soluble Cu nanoparticles were coated with PILs and used as lubricant additives in water–ethylene glycol\, and their lubricating performance was studied\. The results show that the composite of water\-soluble PILs and water\-soluble Cu nanoparticles exhibits excellent anti\-friction\, wear\-resistant\, and extreme pressure performance as lubricant additives in water–ethylene glycol\.

Figure 7\. Protic ionic liquids of alkanolamines with three different alkyl chain lengths \(adapted from \[83\]\)\.

\#\#\#\#\# Oxide Lubricant Additives

Oxide nanoparticles are superior to metal nanoparticles\, owing to their superior chemical stability \[84\]\, and mainly include titanium dioxide \(TiO2\)\, silicon dioxide \(SiO2\)\, and copper oxide \(CuO\)\, etc\. \[74\]\. Zhao et al\. \[85\] prepared water\-based titanium dioxide nanoparticles \(TiO2\) with dual coating using a silane coupling agent \(KH\-570\) and OP\-10 and studied the tribological performance and application performance of the nanoparticles as water\-based lubricant additives in Q235 steel processing on an MSR\-10D four\-ball wear tester and a benchtop drilling machine\. The results showed that surface\-modified TiO2 nanoparticles can significantly enhance the load\-bearing capacity of pure water and reduce friction and wear\. During drilling\, the water\-based lubricant containing TiO2 nanoparticles consumed less power and produced smoother machined surfaces than the lubricant without nanoparticles\. Liu et al\. \[86\] designed polytetrafluoroethylene \(PTFE\)\-modified SiO2 nanoparticles\. The newly prepared PTFE\@silica Janus nanoparticles \(JNs\) meet the requirements of water\-based lubricant additives\, and\, due to their unique amphiphilic structure\, they exhibit excellent dispersion stability in water\. By introducing a mass concentration of 0\.5\% JNs into water\-based lubricants\, compared with pure water lubrication\, the coefficient of friction \(COF\) and wear volume decreased by 63\.8\% and 94\.2\%\, respectively\. Similarly\, compared with commercial silica and PTFE suspensions\, the JN suspension also demonstrated better lubrication and wear resistance performance\.

\#\#\#\#\# Sulfide Lubricant Additives

Sulfur atoms within sulfides can react at the friction interface to form a high\-performance protective film\, thereby performing anti\-friction and anti\-wear functions\. Representative include MoS2 \[87\]\, WS2 \[88\]\, and CuS \[89\]\. Liang et al\. \[90\] used urea to modify MoS2 to improve its compatibility with polar lubricants\, preparing U–MoS2 water\-based lubricant additives\. In a water\-based system\, when the mass concentration of U–MoS2 was 0\.25\%\, the COF decreased by 84\%\, and wear was reduced by 81\%\. Zhang et al\. \[88\] modified CuS nanoparticles with bis\(2\-hydroxyethyl\) dithiocarbamate \(HDA\) as a surface modifier to prepare water\-soluble lubricant additives \(HDA\-CuS\)\. The prepared HDA\-CuS nanoparticles can effectively improve the tribological behavior and thermal conductivity of distilled water\. When the additive mass concentration was 0\.8\%\, the COF and wear rate decreased by 78\.3\% and 93\.7\%\, respectively\.

\#\#\#\#\# Carbon\-Based Lubricant Additives

Common carbon\-based nano\-lubricant additives include nanodiamonds \[91\]\, carbon nanotubes \[92\]\, graphene \[93\]\, fullerenes \[94\]\, and carbon quantum dots \[95\,96\]\. Although carbon\-based nanomaterials have good anti\-friction and anti\-wear effects when used directly as lubricant additives\, functionalization of carbon\-based nanomaterials can endow them with superior physicochemical\, mechanical\, and tribological properties\. Gu et al\. \[97\] chemically activated the carboxyl groups on graphene oxide \(GO\) to enable reactions with the hydroxyl groups at the terminals of oleic acid triethanolamine \(MDLO\)\, synthesizing GO\-grafted modified oleic acid triethanolamine ester \(MDLO\-GO\)\. When applied in hydraulic liquid\, at a GO loading of 0\.004\%\, the non\-seizure load of the hydraulic fluid reached 481 N\. Compared with hydraulic liquid without GO modification\, the lubrication was improved by 11\.9\%\, while high\- and low\-temperature performance were also significantly enhanced\. Wang et al\. \[67\] developed a simpler one\-step pyrolysis method to prepare IL\-functionalized CQDs as water\-based lubricant additives\. At an optimal mass fraction of 0\.015\%\, the average COF and wear were reduced by 57\.5\% and 64\%\, respectively\, showing excellent tribological performance\. The friction reduction and anti\-wear performance of the composite additive were far superior to that of CDs and IL\, demonstrating the synergistic lubricating effect between the IL groups and the carbon core\. Some researchers have also studied the bonding of amino acids with carbon dots to generate multifunctional amino acid\-based carbon dots\, which can effectively prevent carbon steel corrosion and enhance lubrication performance in water\-based cutting fluids \[98\]\.

\#\# 3\. Development Trends of Lubricants for Water\-Based Hydraulic Fluids

At present\, the technical development of hydraulic fluids remains at the stage of compounding various specific\-function additives for lubrication\, corrosion inhibition\, and hard water resistance\. These fluids are sensitive to fluctuations in the quality of dilution water\, and the compatibility among multiple additives is poor\, making the system equilibrium easy to disrupt and affecting the online intelligent monitoring of the fluid supply system\. In the construction of intelligent fully mechanized mining face\, optical–electric signals from sensors\, such as concentration sensors\, are often used for online monitoring of indicators like hydraulic fluid concentration to achieve intelligent sensing\, decision\-making\, and automated execution in fluid supply technology \[99\,100\]\. When the cleanliness and stability of hydraulic fluids decline\, this affects the accurate capture and transmission of optical–electric signals by sensors\. The main methods for maintaining hydraulic fluid stability fall into two categories\: one involves controlling the stability of the hydraulic fluid from the perspective of usage methods and the quality of diluted water\, mainly by pre\-treating the diluted water to meet the KA 76\-2011 industry standard for water quality\. However\, fluctuations in underground water quality are difficult to avoid\, often leading to issues such as saponification of the hydraulic fluid\, filter clogging\, and valve corrosion\. Another category is the development of lubricant additives that are inherently resistant to hard water and also have corrosion\-inhibiting functions\, thereby preventing declines in hydraulic fluid stability caused by saponification and valve rust\, ensuring the normal operation of intelligent working faces\. At the same time\, multifunctional and highly efficient lubricants can reduce additive usage\, mitigate environmental impact\, and promote the construction of green mines\.

Performance tuning of corrosion inhibition and tribological properties of small molecule compounds is ultimately governed by interfacial adsorption \(chemical\/physical\) effects \[101\,102\]\. For alkylamide lubricants\, the non\-polar segment consists of alkyl chain with relatively low reactivity\; therefore\, the performance regulation strategy mainly involves introducing characteristic functional groups at the polar end\. Based on the introduced heteroatoms and the coordination of the amide bond with alkaline earth metal ions\, the hard water resistance can be adjusted\, and the adsorption \(monolayer\/multilayer\) behavior of the molecules on the metal surface can be controlled through changes in hydrogen bonding and steric hindrance\. Overall\, the polar groups of alkylamides affect the comprehensive performance of lubricants in multiple ways\, including lubrication\, corrosion inhibition\, and sensitivity to hard water\. The combination and interaction of different polar groups determine the overall performance of the lubricant and its suitability under various operating conditions\.

With the advancement of intelligent and green coal mining\, hydraulic fluids for hydraulic supports will develop in the direction of stability\, reliability\, greenness\, and efficiency\. High\-efficiency multifunctional lubricants with the combined properties of hard water resistance\, lubrication\, and corrosion inhibition will become an important research direction for next\-generation additives\. Whether based on fatty alcohol ethers\, ionic liquids\, or alkylamides\, introducing different functional groups at the polar end while balancing corresponding properties can achieve synergistic enhancement\. The development and use of multifunctional additives can mitigate issues such as the large consumption and insufficient stability of multiple additive blends\, allowing for the development of single\- \(or few\-\) component hydraulic fluids\, meeting the transmission requirements of optoelectronic signals in intelligent fluid supply systems\, reducing the amount of hydraulic fluid additives\, and supporting the construction of green mines\. As shown in Figure 8a\, Yang et al\. \[103\] used borate esters as extreme pressure components\, introducing fatty acid diethanolamides containing active groups such as hydroxyl and amide bonds into the borate esters to prepare alkylamide borate esters\. The introduction of amide bonds can circumvent their hard water sensitivity while enhancing adsorption on metal surfaces\, and the introduction of fatty chains can improve their lubrication and load\-bearing capacity\. As shown in Figure 8b\, Yang et al\. \[104\] used 1\,3\-diamino\-2\-propanol as the substrate to synthesize 1\,3\-dioleoylamide\-2\-oleate propyl ester \(DOAPO\)\, containing polar amide and ester groups as well as non\-polar alkyl chains\, similarly providing hard water resistance\, lubrication\, and corrosion inhibition properties\. In addition\, introducing nanoparticles into water\-based hydraulic fluid systems can not only improve the product’s lubrication performance\, but also reduce the foaming tendency of hydraulic fluids and enhance the operational stability of hydraulic supports \[105\]\.

Figure 8\. Preparation process of fatty acid diethanolamide borate ester \(a\) and DOAPO \(b\) \(adapted from \[103\,104\]\)\.

In addition\, our research team analyzed 1146 water samples collected in 2025 from coal bases in Shendong\, Jinbei\, Jinzhong\, Jindong\, Luxi\, Lianghuai\, Huanglong\, Jizhong\, Ningdong\, and northern Shaanxi\, primarily testing their hardness \(Ca2\+ \+ Mg2\+\)\, SO42−\, Cl−\, and HCO3−\, and statistical analyses were conducted for the concentration distribution of each ion\, as summarized in Table 3\. Currently\, most mainstream mines in China are equipped with pre\-treatment devices for dilution water\. Although the water quality indicators of blending water still fluctuate\, the overall water quality has significantly improved\. Compared with the 2015 statistical data \[106\]\, the proportion of water samples with hardness below 200 mg\/L increased by 21\.52\%\, the proportion with SO42− content below 200 mg\/L increased by 38\.50\%\, the proportion with Cl− content below 200 mg\/L increased by 7\.18\%\, and the proportion with HCO3− content below 200 mg\/L increased by 393\.33\%\. With the maturation of corrosion\-resistant technologies such as ultra\-high\-speed laser cladding \[107\,108\]\, the corrosion resistance of hydraulic support cylinders has been improved\. The improvement in the quality of blending water and the corrosion resistance of cylinders\, along with research on the structural design and performance balance of multifunctional additives such as alkyl amides\, provide a solid foundation for the development of single\- \(or low\-\) component hydraulic fluids\.

\#\# 4\. Conclusions and Outlook

As the power transmission media for coal mine hydraulic supports\, water\-based hydraulic fluids have seen the development of their lubricant additives evolve from alcohol ether types and vegetable oils to ionic liquids and nanoparticles\, with continuous improvement in lubrication performance and multifunctionality\. Alcohol ether lubricants\, with their excellent resistance to hard water and tunable hydrophilicity and lipophilicity\, have become one of the most widely used water\-based lubricant additives today\. Vegetable oil lubricants\, derived from renewable resources\, provide a solid theoretical foundation for the molecular design of green lubricants through systematic studies on the unsaturation\, alkyl chain length\, and branching degree of fatty acid molecular structures\. Ionic liquid lubricant additives\, particularly protic ionic liquids and polymeric ionic liquids\, exhibit good synergistic effects in reducing friction\, resisting wear\, and inhibiting corrosion in water\-based systems through precise molecular\-level design and self\-assembly behavior\. Nano\-lubricant additives\, leveraging their unique rolling effects and interfacial reaction activity\, open new avenues for overcoming performance bottlenecks of conventional water\-based lubricants\. Each type of lubricant has its own advantages\, but it is difficult for a single type to fully meet the comprehensive demands for lubrication\, hard water resistance\, corrosion inhibition\, and stability under complex operating conditions\.

Driven by the dual goals of intelligent coal mining and the construction of green mines\, lubricant additives for water\-based hydraulic fluids are rapidly developing toward multifunctional integration\, single\-component formulation\, and environmental friendliness\. Currently\, hydraulic fluids commonly adopt a technology route that blends multiple functional additives\, which makes them sensitive to fluctuations in the quality of dilution water\, easily compromising system stability and thus affecting the photonic signal transmission accuracy of online monitoring devices such as concentration sensors in intelligent fluid supply systems\. Developing highly efficient multifunctional additives with lubrication\, hard water tolerance\, and corrosion inhibition properties to achieve single\- \(or few\-\) component hydraulic fluid formulations has become a consensus in the industry\, as it fundamentally simplifies the system and enhances stability\. Molecular design strategies\, such as those involving alkylamides and polymeric ionic liquids\, can simultaneously regulate molecular adsorption behavior on metal surfaces and coordination capabilities with calcium and magnesium ions by introducing amide bonds or heteroatom active groups at the polar end\, providing a feasible path for the construction of multifunctional additives\. Meanwhile\, the incorporation of nanoparticles can not only improve lubrication performance\, but also potentially reduce the foaming tendency of hydraulic fluids\, further enhancing system operational reliability\.

It is noteworthy that the overall dilution water quality at major national coal bases has improved markedly in recent years\, with greatly elevated compliance rates for key indicators including hardness and sulfate\, chloride\, and bicarbonate contents\. Furthermore\, the mature deployment of anticorrosion technologies such as ultrahigh\-speed laser cladding for powered support cylinders has established favorable external prerequisites for developing single\-component hydraulic fluids\. In the future\, research should further deepen the understanding of the structure–activity relationship of lubricating additives\. Theoretical tools such as molecular dynamics simulations can be adopted to uncover the synergistic mechanisms of multifunctional groups\, facilitating the shift in additive molecular design from empirical to rational design\. Researchers should develop multifunctional additives that integrate lubrication\, corrosion inhibition\, and hard water resistance to cater the demands of intelligent and green mine construction\. In parallel\, systematical evaluations are required for long\-cycle and repeated\-operation stability of newly developed lubricant additives\, their compatibility with electro\-hydraulic control systems\, and their full life\-cycle environmental impacts\. It is essential to accelerate the engineering application of high\-performance\, low\-dosage\, and easily degradable green lubricating additives\.

records.title: Stagewise multi-material topology optimization reducing material switching in additive manufacturing
records.abstract: This paper presented a stagewise multi-material topology optimization framework to mitigate the substantial overheads associated with frequent material switching in multi-material additive manufacturing. ... References (83) - W. Gao et al. ... Additive manufacturing (3D printing): A review of materials...
records.summary: The paper proposes a stagewise multi-material topology optimization framework that internalizes material-switching costs into the structural design phase rather than addressing them only in post-processing (slicing/path planning). Building on a pseudo-time field, it maps spatial material distributions onto discretized time stages via an alternating material-stage mapping and a stage elimination mechanism, aiming to enable continuous deposition and reduce material switches versus conventional layer-by-layer processes. Spatial manufacturing constraints—material-dependent overhang angles, nozzle collision avoidance, and minimum length scales—are integrated to ensure printability. Numerical examples are reported to suppress material switching while satisfying constraints, with extensions to multi-axis AM, explicit switching minimization, and multiple material phases. The authors report experimental fabrication on a multi-material AM system showing simultaneous reductions in material switching, purging waste, and production time versus conventional layer-by-layer fabrication; specific quantitative values are not given in the available text.
records.why_it_matters: It moves material-switch minimization from a downstream slicing/path-planning problem into the topology optimization formulation, so designers can trade structural performance against deposition-sequence overhead before geometry is fixed.

Introduction
Additive manufacturing (AM) is a layer-by-layer fabrication process that can realize structures with complex geometry and topology, which are difficult to produce using conventional machining techniques [1], [2]. A prominent application is a multi-material structure, in which materials with distinct properties are distributed within a single component [3], [4], [5], [6]. Manufacturing of such structures necessitates multi-material additive manufacturing that deposits multiple materials during a single process. The fabrication of such multi-material structures is being actively explored across various AM technologies, including fused deposition modeling (FDM) and directed energy deposition (DED), primarily through alternating material deposition strategies [7], [8], [9]. This capability provides a high degree of design freedom for developing advanced structures with customized functionalities and superior mechanical performance.
Despite these advantages in geometric flexibility, the practical implementation of multi-material processes faces significant challenges regarding process efficiency due to the mechanics of switching between multiple materials. In typical multi-material systems, a purge operation is required whenever a material needs to be alternated within a single layer, removing residual material within the nozzle and resetting process parameters [10], [11]. These operations not only cause delays in overall production time but also result in unnecessary material waste [12], [13]. Furthermore, the frequent interruption and resumption of material supply induce extrusion instability, which is a primary cause of surface defects and dimensional inaccuracies at the transition zones [14], [15]. Although hardware improvements such as multi-nozzle systems have been introduced, their compatibility with existing equipment is limited [16], [17], [18]. Consequently, minimizing the number of material switches remains a critical challenge to ensuring the productivity and quality of multi-material additive manufacturing.
To date, efforts to mitigate the issues associated with material switching have predominantly focused on process planning stages, such as slicing and path planning, aiming to reduce the purging waste by reordering deposition paths through grouping same-material regions or localizing transition zones [13], [19], [20]. However, these post-processing approaches face a fundamental limitation as they operate under the premise of an already fixed design. Moreover, in the approaches that group same-material layers into batches, the height deposited in a single batch is restricted by potential collisions between the nozzle and the previously deposited neighboring regions, which limits the attainable reduction in tool changes [13]. If the initial geometric design inherently requires highly fragmented material distributions and frequent intersections, process optimization alone cannot effectively reduce the number of material switches without altering the design intent. Therefore, to fundamentally alleviate the burden of material switching, this issue must be addressed directly during the structural design phase rather than being treated solely as a post-processing task in manufacturing [21].
Topology optimization has been actively adopted as a core methodology for determining complex multi-material distributions during the structural design phase [22], [23], [24], [25], [26]. It enables the derivation of optimal material layouts that satisfy given conditions. However, conventional multi-material topology optimization techniques tend to focus primarily on maximizing structural performance [27], [28], [29], [30]. To achieve these theoretical optima, these approaches often create fragmented material layouts, leading to highly scattered or frequently alternating material distributions. This tendency fundamentally disregards the cost of transitioning between material phases. Consequently, these complex layouts significantly increase the required number of material switches during the multi-material manufacturing process, thereby hindering manufacturability and escalating production costs. To ensure manufacturability, various geometric and process considerations [31], [32], [33], [34], such as overhangs [35], [36], [37], [38], [39], build orientations [40], [41], [42], length scales [43], [44], [45], collisions [46], [47], [48], and build volume limits [49], [50], [51], have been widely integrated. However, these considerations act only on the spatial geometry of the design and thus do not explicitly account for the operational overheads arising from material switching during deposition. A similar limitation applies to spatial regularization strategies such as perimeter control [52], which restrict the total interface length of the design and can thereby suppress the fragmentation of the material layout. The number of material switches is nevertheless determined by where the materials coexist along the build orientation and by the order in which they are deposited, which cannot be captured by such spatial regularizations alone. While recent process-aware multi-material formulations have begun to reflect process-specific restrictions, including the dimensional limits on material components and the build volume [53], [54], as well as the interfacial behavior between different materials [55], [56], the deposition sequence and the number of material transitions have yet to be incorporated into the design formulation, and research addressing material switching in multi-material environments thus remains limited.
Recently, space–time topology optimization has been developed to incorporate the fabrication process into the structural design by introducing a pseudo-time field as an additional design variable, enabling the concurrent optimization of the structural layout and the fabrication sequence [57], [58]. Building upon this concept, the fabrication sequence has been designed to account for process-dependent structural conditions, including the self-weight of intermediate structures and deposition-induced material anisotropy [47], [59], [60], to control process-induced thermomechanical effects, such as distortion and residual stresses [61], [62], [63], and to ensure manufacturability in multi-axis and hybrid manufacturing environments through stagewise build orientations, curved-layer slicing, and the scheduling of additive and subtractive operations [46], [64], [65], [66]. Related sequence-aware formulations have also been extended to fiber-reinforced composites, in which curved layers and deposition paths are optimized concurrently with the structural topology [67], [68]. As summarized in Table 1, however, all of these formulations design the fabrication sequence of a single prescribed material system. Consequently, neither the deposition sequence of multiple materials nor the number of material transitions has been treated as a design quantity in existing sequence-aware formulations.
To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel stagewise multi-material topology optimization framework that directly internalizes material switching into the structural design formulation. As conceptually compared in Fig. 1, unlike conventional layer-by-layer approaches that inevitably require frequent material switching to avoid nozzle collisions, the proposed approach proactively optimizes the structural geometry to ensure that the feature angle
θ does not exceed the nozzle angle ᾱ. This spatial consideration prevents interference and creates an environment where continuous deposition is geometrically feasible. To systematically realize and control this continuous printing process, this study employs the pseudo-time field as a design variable during the optimization process to determine the fabrication sequence of alternating multi-material depositions. By doing so, the framework naturally induces the continuous deposition of each material in a single stage wherever possible, thereby effectively tuning and restricting the number of material switches, as depicted in Fig. 2. In this process, an alternating mapping between materials and stages, a stage elimination mechanism, and a differentiable switching measure are newly introduced. Furthermore, essential geometric constraints specific to multi-material processes, including material-dependent overhang limitations, nozzle collision avoidance, and minimum feature sizes, are concurrently integrated into the optimization problem to prevent potential manufacturing defects in advance. As a result, the proposed methodology derives optimized multi-material designs that balance process efficiency and structural performance. Physical fabrication using a multi-material AM system further confirms these benefits, reducing material switching, purging waste, and production time compared to conventional layer-by-layer processes.

Section 6 experimentally validates the manufacturing efficiency of the proposed framework using a multi-material AM system. records.summary: This in vitro study investigated how intaglio surface microstructure morphology and depth affect shear bond strength (SBS) and fracture load of nanoparticle jetting (NPJ) 3D printed zirconia restorations, aiming to optimize surface topography for ultrathin (0.5 mm) fixed prosthodontics. Zirconia specimens with four texture types (circular, triangular, concentric circular, undercut circular) at four depths (40, 60, 80, 100 μm) were fabricated by NPJ additive manufacturing and compared with conventionally milled zirconia; SBS and fracture load were tested mechanically, with debonding modes and interfacial composition analyzed by SEM and EDS, and one-way ANOVA with Tukey HSD used for comparisons. Nontextured NPJ zirconia performed similarly to milled zirconia (P=.984), while surface microstructures significantly increased bond strength, with circular and undercut circular textures performing best; bond strength rose with depth and plateaued at 80–100 μm. For 0.5-mm crowns, fracture load decreased significantly with increasing depth (P<.001), and a 60-μm circular microstructure balanced favorable SBS with mechanical stability, with all groups meeting ISO 6872 graded clinical mechanical criteria. The authors concluded that NPJ enables precise control of zirconia surface topography and that the 60-μm circular design was optimal for ultrathin prostheses.
records.why_it_matters: For ultrathin NPJ-printed zirconia crowns, intaglio texture depth is a trade-off variable: deeper features improve bonding but reduce fracture load, so a 60-μm circular texture is proposed as the design point that preserves both adhesion and structural integrity.

ABSTRACT
Statement of problem
Ultrathin 3-dimensionally (3D) printed zirconia restorations require optimized intaglio microstructures to balance bonding performance and fracture resistance; however, systematic data regarding surface morphology and depth for nanoparticle jetting (NPJ)-fabricated zirconia are lacking.
Purpose
The purpose of this in vitro study was to investigate the effects of surface-microstructural morphology and depth on the shear bond strength (SBS) and fracture load of NPJ 3D printed zirconia restorations and to optimize the surface-topography design for clinical use.
Material and methods
Zirconia specimens with 4 surface textures (circular, triangular, concentric circular, and undercut circular) and 4 depths (40, 60, 80, and 100 μm) were fabricated by NPJ additive manufacturing and conventional milling. Ultrathin zirconia complete crowns (0.5 mm thick) were prepared. The SBS and fracture load were tested with a universal material testing machine. The debonding modes and interfacial elemental composition were analysed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) coupled with the Tukey HSD test was adopted for intergroup comparisons (α=.05).
Results
The bonding performance and mechanical strength of nontextured NPJ-printed zirconia were similar to those of milled zirconia (P=.984). The surface microstructures significantly increased the bond strength, with the circular and undercut circular textures performing the best. The bond strength increased with depth and plateaued at 80 to 100 μm. For the 0.5-mm crowns, the fracture load decreased significantly with increasing depth (P<.001). The 60-μm circular microstructure balanced favorable SBS and mechanical stability, and all the groups satisfied clinical mechanical criteria under the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 6872 graded standards.
Conclusions
NPJ technology enables precise control of the zirconia surface topography to increase bonding. For ultrathin prostheses, the 60-μm circular microstructure represented the optimal design that provided high bond strength and sufficient fracture resistance for clinical application.

\#\# ABSTRACT

\#\#\# Statement of problem

Ultrathin 3\-dimensionally \(3D\) printed zirconia restorations require optimized intaglio microstructures to balance bonding performance and fracture resistance\; however\, systematic data regarding surface morphology and depth for nanoparticle jetting \(NPJ\)\-fabricated zirconia are lacking\.

\#\#\# Purpose

The purpose of this in vitro study was to investigate the effects of surface\-microstructural morphology and depth on the shear bond strength \(SBS\) and fracture load of NPJ 3D printed zirconia restorations and to optimize the surface\-topography design for clinical use\.

\#\#\# Material and methods

Zirconia specimens with 4 surface textures \(circular\, triangular\, concentric circular\, and undercut circular\) and 4 depths \(40\, 60\, 80\, and 100 μm\) were fabricated by NPJ additive manufacturing and conventional milling\. Ultrathin zirconia complete crowns \(0\.5 mm thick\) were prepared\. The SBS and fracture load were tested with a universal material testing machine\. The debonding modes and interfacial elemental composition were analysed by scanning electron microscopy \(SEM\) and energy\-dispersive X\-ray spectroscopy \(EDS\)\. One\-way analysis of variance \(ANOVA\) coupled with the Tukey HSD test was adopted for intergroup comparisons \(α\=\.05\)\.

\#\#\# Results

The bonding performance and mechanical strength of nontextured NPJ\-printed zirconia were similar to those of milled zirconia \(P\=\.984\)\. The surface microstructures significantly increased the bond strength\, with the circular and undercut circular textures performing the best\. The bond strength increased with depth and plateaued at 80 to 100 μm\. For the 0\.5\-mm crowns\, the fracture load decreased significantly with increasing depth \(P\<\.001\)\. The 60\-μm circular microstructure balanced favorable SBS and mechanical stability\, and all the groups satisfied clinical mechanical criteria under the International Organization for Standardization \(ISO\) 6872 graded standards\.

\#\#\# Conclusions

NPJ technology enables precise control of the zirconia surface topography to increase bonding\. For ultrathin prostheses\, the 60\-μm circular microstructure represented the optimal design that provided high bond strength and sufficient fracture resistance for clinical application\.

Riley Surface World has recently won a six-figure order for the supply of pre-owned nickel plating, anodising, cleaning and water treatment plants from a specialist metal finishing company in Mexico.
The equipment had all been declared surplus to requirements by a large, international provider of safety products to the nuclear power generation sector. Riley Surface World was selected to dispose of the plants due to its specialist knowledge of the global surface finishing industry. The various items have now been shipped from their original home in Birmingham, UK to their new location in Toluca, near Mexico City.
The new owner is Ecoplating SA, part of a group of eight companies that comprises the largest metal finishing organisation in Mexico. It was formed 70 years ago by Ramon Pages Snr., who is still active in the company. It has a workforce of 1550 employees and two of the companies have joint ventures in the USA and Germany. Its services include nickel, copper, zinc, chrome, tin and precious metal plating, passivation, phosphating and other ancillary activities.
Ecoplating enjoys an excellent strategic location in one of Mexico's most vibrant manufacturing areas, with neighbouring companies that include Chrysler, Mercedes Benz, BMW, Nissan, Honda, Valeo, Schneider and Siemens. It supplies the automotive, electronics, oil, gas and consumer products sectors. Future expansion plans include new factories in Monterrey and Queretaro to support the expansion of the Mexican automobile industry.
The equipment supplied by Riley Surface World comprised an 8-stage nickel plating line with two rectifiers, four modern 4-stage anodising lines with rectifiers, fume extraction and product suspension, two cleaning lines including transporters and drying ovens and a 5m3 demineralised water generation plant.
All of the machinery is in immaculate condition and can be easily re-configured for other process finishing and cleaning applications.
The current CEO of Ecoplating SA, Ramon Pages Jnr., says that the purchase of such valuable and versatile equipment will make an important contribution to his company's future expansion plans, as it stands to benefit from the expected upturn in the Central and North American economies over the next few years. He also paid tribute to the professionalism and technical expertise of all the staff at Riley Surface World, who worked very hard to complete the project on budget and on time.

E-Archive
VOL. 21 September ISSUE YEAR 2020
Good Vibrations
in Vol. 21 - September Issue - Year 2020
Quality Assurance In Mass Finishing – The Present And Future
control panel of a mass finishing system
quality check - media sticking in a work piece
quality check - corrosion after mass finishing operation
quality check after mass finishing operation
Series production on an industrial scale requires stable and reproducible processes. The key factors are traceability, reproducibility and complete logging of processing data. In order to identify and assess risks and avoid complaints, it is necessary to plan processes with foresight. In the best-case scenario, measures should be derived from this data to make sure that all process sequences are completely monitored. Is mass finishing at a good state of development in 2020?
What has been established for decades in electroplating technology is only gradually becoming known and put into practice in mass finishing: Continuous logging and documentation of all quality-relevant parameters throughout the process in order to make processes stable and reproducible, identify risks and derive measures from them.
Galvanic processes in series production are closely monitored: The bath temperature, cycle times, chemical analysis of the electrolytes, movement of goods and other quality-relevant parameters are continuously monitored. After the last work step of a batch, a log with all important information is generated from the central control system. This can be used as evidence during the batch process, and the QA is then immediately available as a verification tool to evaluate the process. In the event of deviations or complaints, it is easy to trace the point in the process at which problems occurred.
At what state of development is mass finishing? Has development progressed in the same way in recent decades? To put it mildly: There is still room for improvement. In many cases, vibratory finishing processes are underrated. The complex interrelationships between machine/drive, water/chemistry and abrasive media are often only discovered when systems are installed in an industrial environment and run unsatisfactorily. This leads to frustration, complaints, disputes and incalculable costs. Once a system has been put into operation, it has to run and often it is a year-long battle between Manufacturing and QA before effective measures to improve process stability are implemented.
Some examples from practice:
Which system is used to indicate when abrasive particles have reached a critical size due to wear? In the best-case scenario, it is the machine operator, when he discovers workpieces with abrasive particles stuck to them. In the worst case, it is the customer who complains about exactly this appearance. One solution is precisely coordinated and systematically developed separation or detection systems (e.g. camera systems) that remove abrasive particles from the process or sound the alarm if they reach a critical size or shape. Established suppliers of automated vibratory finishing systems/processes offer solutions that can be used for specific applications and tailored to the process.
Which system is used to indicate a defective dosing pump for cleaning and corrosion protection agents? Usually it is the first employee discovering soiled or corroded workpieces in the process chain. This is unpleasant and can turn out to be expensive.
A solution is a system that constantly monitors the flow of all media together with the flow rates in parallel with the process, logs the recorded information in a batch log via the control system, and triggers an alarm or interrupts the process if necessary. Such a system makes the peripheral equipment of the vibratory finishing system considerably more complex and also more expensive, but if the complaint rate and quality costs can be reduced as a result, the extra cost can be quickly amortised.
Which system is used to indicate when the filling level of the abrasive media in a vibratory finishing system does not meet the specifications? Usually it is the employee who discovers damaged workpieces and is surprised why. Even a reduction of the filling level by only 10 % can lead to changes in the process which cannot be detected with the naked eye, but which can influence the quality of the workpieces. Especially when it comes to multi-shift operation, nobody tends to feel responsible for specific control tasks that are required on a regular basis, and it is precisely then that it can be important to develop and establish aids or semi-automated control equipment in order to get things running smoothly in production.
As a solution, the system could also be monitored by a camera system or alternative technical tools that monitor the fill level. Through the integration with the control system and the system specific to the company, machine operators and also QA can monitor the process at any time with regard to such criteria.
How can the machine operator see at a glance all setting parameters of the machine, including the drive motor imbalance setting? In some cases, this can be successfully done via the control system, because some parameters are entered there and can be called up at any time. In some cases, however, the parameters that can be called up and logged via the control system are incomplete. The truth in many departments: A colleague from the night shift takes a note of how he has adjusted the machine on a piece of paper. It is possible that the writing cannot be understood well or he forgets important information. Mistakes, fluctuations and a disturbance of the process stability are unavoidable in this case. Even if it is only a simple deburring process, the chain of consequences cannot be calculated. In any case, the bottom line is that nothing good comes out of it.
Generally speaking, the better solution would be an override control system, which only releases the machine for machining if all machining steps and parameters previously defined and described in detail by QA have been entered. The safest variant is of course a program with all this data stored within the control system. However, this requires a suitable control system, which not every vibratory finishing system has.
When investing in a vibratory finishing system, the user should not only have the machine price and the installation location in mind, but he should also delve deeper into the process technology right from the planning phase. It is important to understand that this is a technology and not some simple operation that performs more or less by itself.
Well-known and established suppliers operate departments that are primarily concerned with application technology. Even before launching series production, application engineers can optimise all production conditions, both in the planning phase and on-site at the operator's premises, so that frustrating experiences with vibratory finishing processes are avoided wherever possible.
Good Vibrations

Business Conditions Are Improving; Outlook Remains Cautiously Positive - vdma.eu
Universal article viewer
Business performance over the past twelve months has been significantly better than in previous years.
© shutterstock
In the fall of 2026, the additive manufacturing industry views its current business performance somewhat more positively than it did a year ago. The latest VDMA survey shows an improved business situation and predominantly stable to positive expectations for the coming years. At the same time, costs, technological advancements, and the industrial implementation of additive manufacturing remain key issues for the industry.
In the fall of 2026, the additive manufacturing industry is in a generally more stable position than in previous years. “The results of the fall survey show that the situation for many companies has improved. However, it would be premature to speak of a fundamental turnaround. Companies are cautiously assessing their current situation but continue to see good prospects for the development of additive manufacturing in the coming years,” explains Dr. Markus Heering, Managing Director of the Additive Manufacturing Working Group at the VDMA. The working group brings together manufacturers and users across the entire additive value chain. Member companies work with various additive manufacturing processes and different materials, applying them to mass-produced products, prototypes, assembly aids, and other applications.
Business performance over the past twelve months has been significantly better than in previous years. Only 15 percent of the surveyed companies report declining sales, while 64 percent report positive growth. By comparison: In the fall of 2025, 29 percent of companies still reported declining revenue, while only 45 percent reported growth. This marks a continuation of the improvement that was already evident in the spring 2026 survey.
Positive Expectations, but No Sense of Optimism
Positive expectations prevail regarding the future development of the German additive manufacturing market. For the coming twelve months, 40 percent of companies anticipate increasing market demand, while 53 percent expect stable growth. Only 6 percent expect a decline. The outlook remains predominantly positive even over a two-year horizon: 67 percent expect market growth, while 28 percent anticipate stable development. Expectations have hardly changed since the spring. The generally positive sentiment persists.
International markets remain important
Most companies expect their export business to remain stable or grow. For the next twelve months, 52 percent expect rising export sales, while 39 percent anticipate no change. Looking ahead two years, 63 percent expect rising foreign sales. At the same time, only a small minority expresses expectations of a decline. The European Union remains the most important sales market, cited by 73 percent of respondents. In addition, the U.S., cited by 71 percent, continues to play a central role in the industry’s international business. At the same time, Asian markets are gaining in importance. China, in particular, is cited significantly more often as a relevant export market than in previous surveys. International competition remains intense. Particularly striking is the growing importance of American competitors.
Companies Are Holding Steady on Investments
Despite a still challenging economic environment, companies’ investment plans remain stable. For the coming twelve months, 72 percent of respondents plan to maintain their investment levels in additive manufacturing. Another 22 percent expect investments to rise, while only 7 percent intend to reduce their spending. This indicates that, despite ongoing economic uncertainties, companies continue to prioritize the technological advancement of their additive manufacturing activities.
Companies cite new applications (53 percent), technological developments (51 percent), and new markets (42 percent) as the most important positive factors influencing their own business. Research and development, as well as the expansion into additional international markets, also remain relevant.
Focus on Technological Development and Industrialization
The most important future topics for the industry include technological development (61 percent), costs (57 percent), process stability and reproducibility (50 percent), mass production (48 percent), new applications (46 percent), and market acceptance (43 percent).
When it comes to application areas, respondents cited mechanical engineering as the dominant field of application less frequently than in previous surveys. Additive manufacturing processes, on the other hand, are more widespread, particularly in the aerospace and medical technology sectors. “The survey shows that additive manufacturing is further solidifying its position as an industrial technology. The key now will be to scale up new applications economically and to exploit the technology’s potential even more fully in industrial practice,” Heering summarizes.

Dr. Markus Heering

Supercritical CO2 and kitchen-shelf lubricants could transform titanium machining
When carbon dioxide is squeezed past 74 bar and warmed above 31 degrees Celsius, it stops behaving like an ordinary gas or liquid and enters a strange middle state known as the supercritical phase. A team of French researchers at the Arts et Métiers Institute of Technology has now harnessed this exotic fluid to attack one of manufacturing’s most stubborn problems: the friction and heat that plague the machining of Ti6Al4V, the titanium alloy that holds together much of the aerospace industry. Their findings, published in Frontiers in Manufacturing Technology, suggest that cheap, sustainable additives dissolved in supercritical CO2 could rival industrial mineral oils, with ionic liquids delivering the most dramatic friction reductions of all.
The machining industry has long relied on flood coolants, minimum quantity lubrication, and cryogenic sprays such as liquid nitrogen to keep cutting tools alive and machined parts intact. These methods aim to tame the intense friction and heating that occur at the chip-tool and tool-part contact zones, where temperatures can soar high enough to soften the workpiece and destroy the tool edge. Supercritical CO2 has emerged as an intriguing alternative because it acts as a green solvent and, when delivered to the cutting zone, expands with a phase transformation that drops its temperature sharply, cooling both the tool and the part. Previous studies have shown that pairing supercritical CO2 with dissolved soybean oil roughly halved flank wear compared with emulsion flood cooling when milling compacted graphite iron, and that supercritical CO2 plus minimum quantity lubrication outperformed flood coolant in milling Ti6Al4V and turning AISI 1045 steel.
Yet supercritical CO2 alone often performs worse than flood cooling, which is why the lubricant carried within it matters so much. The research team, led by Koffi Samuel Koulekpa, set out to systematically test what happens when different lubricants are introduced into supercritical CO2 and delivered to a titanium-carbide contact under conditions mimicking real machining. They selected ionic liquids, vegetable oils, mineral oil, water, and polyethylene glycol, chosen for their solubility in supercritical CO2, their sustainable character, or their previous performances in machining-related friction analysis. The two ionic liquids tested, BMIM-PF6 and BMIM-BF4, are salts that stay liquid at room temperature and boast negligible volatility, high thermal stability, and non-flammability, making them fascinating candidates for machining applications.
Order Lab Supplies
To deliver these exotic mixtures, the researchers designed and built a dedicated machine that feeds CO2 from pressurized bottles, cools it to ensure a liquid phase before compression, then squeezes it to pressures up to 350 bar and heats it with four cartridges to reach the supercritical state in a mixing chamber. There, lubricants are injected at user-specified rates before the mixture sprays through a 0.25 mm round jet nozzle. For the experiments, the pressure was limited to 100 bar and the temperature set to 40 degrees Celsius, guaranteeing a supercritical state while minimizing CO2 consumption. The supercritical CO2 flowed at 0.185 kg/min, while lubricants were delivered at 1 mL/min and 4 mL/min, rates common in minimum quantity lubrication applications.
Shop Motor Oils
The friction tests themselves took place on a CNC lathe fitted with a Hedenqvist-type pin-on-cylinder tribometer, a setup chosen for easy and quick execution. Cylindrical carbide pins, instrumented with K-type thermocouples connected to a data acquisition system sampling at 2 kHz, pressed against a rotating Ti6Al4V bar with an initial diameter of 120 mm. The normal loads of 100 N, 250 N, and 400 N were selected based on a contact pressure of 1,300 MPa derived from finite element simulations, while sliding velocities of 20 m/min and 100 m/min covered the range of chip sliding velocities typical when machining difficult-to-cut alloys such as Ti6Al4V or Inconel 718. After each test, the workpiece surface was refreshed by a fresh machining pass to obtain a theoretical roughness of Ra 0.5 µm, and the pins were rotated by 25 degrees to expose a new contact surface.
The results revealed a striking pattern. At 20 m/min, adding lubricants to supercritical CO2 decreased friction, but the mixtures never outperformed the dry condition, with friction coefficients staying above the dry baseline for almost all loads. At 100 m/min, however, the story changed dramatically. The team observed a mean decrease of 0.1 in the apparent friction coefficient, and increasing the lubricant flow rate from 1 mL/min to 4 mL/min produced further reductions. The ionic liquids showed their lubricating prowess most clearly at 100 m/min with significant friction decreases at 4 mL/min and 400 N, demonstrating that the combined effect of lubrication by the additives and cooling from supercritical CO2 works best under the most demanding conditions.
The adhesive behavior of Ti6Al4V, notorious for sticking to counter-materials during friction, provided another revealing metric. After each test, the researchers examined the friction zone under an optical microscope and calculated the sticking area by assimilating it to an ellipse. Once again, the effects of the lubricants were clearly visible at 100 m/min. The ionic liquids, together with polyethylene glycol, led to the lowest sticking area values, with surface reductions of 54 percent and 55 percent for BF4 and PF6 respectively at the 1 mL/min rate. These values climbed to 74 percent at 4 mL/min, showing how strongly the delivery flow rate influences the protective action. The researchers attribute this to an adsorption layer that reduces direct contact between the two materials, and for the ionic liquids, to tribochemical reactions between the liquids and the tool-workpiece materials that form remarkably effective protective films.
Temperature measurements confirmed the cooling credentials of supercritical CO2. Pin temperatures dropped significantly compared with dry tests, with a maximum reduction of 80 degrees Celsius. Interestingly, no significant difference in cooling was provided by the presence of the lubricants compared with supercritical CO2 alone, suggesting that the additives’ contribution to heat removal was not activated under the tested speed conditions, possibly due to suboptimal delivery techniques or solubility issues that the team plans to investigate further.
Perhaps the most commercially significant finding concerns the cheap lubricants. Water, rapeseed oil, and sunflower oil performed similarly to the commonly used machining mineral oil when paired with supercritical CO2, and these biological alternatives are less expensive and less health-threatening than traditional emulsions. This could help develop future low-cost yet effective cooling and lubrication methods for the machining industry, a prospect with real sustainability appeal given that cryogenic minimum quantity lubrication methods have already been highlighted as superior to conventional flood coolants when considering toxicity, power consumption, and ozone depletion. The researchers caution that these lubricants would not suit applications where cleanliness is crucial, such as the biomedical and agri-food industries, but for aerospace-grade titanium machining the outlook is bright.
The study also demonstrates the fundamental need for lubrication when using supercritical CO2 in friction-related applications, since supercritical CO2 alone had almost no lubrication effect. The measured apparent friction coefficients could prove useful for supercritical CO2-assisted finite element simulations of machining processes, helping engineers model cutting operations more accurately. Solubility studies are already under investigation to find suitable supercritical conditions for better dissolving oils in supercritical CO2 and defining new efficient cutting fluids. If successful, this work could usher in a new generation of cutting fluids that combine the cooling power of an abundant, recyclable gas with the lubricating finesse of kitchen-shelf oils or laboratory-designed ionic liquids, transforming how the industry machines its most valuable alloys.

HanWei Releases Blue Light Laser Welding Head for High Reflectivity Materials
HanWei Laser has officially released its blue light laser welding head, a 450nm blue diode laser torch designed specifically for metals that infrared laser cannot weld reliably. The product is fully developed, manufactured and sold by HanWei Laser, covering optical path design, wobble control, wire feeding and the control system, which means every unit leaves the factory with matched parameters and direct factory support behind it.
The launch answers a long standing production problem in copper, gold and silver processing: infrared laser energy is reflected away by these metals at room temperature, so welders are forced into unstable processes with heavy spatter, porosity and frequent lens damage.
Key advantages of the blue light laser welding head
- Independent research, manufacturing and sales: optical path, wobble unit, wire feeder and control software are all self developed by HanWei Laser, so weld parameters can be customized to individual customer processes without third party bottlenecks.
- Reliable welding of high reflectivity materials: copper, gold, silver, as well as nickel, aluminium can be welded with stable penetration, low porosity and repeatable quality batch after batch.
- Spatter free and highly stable: closed loop process control together with an optimized beam profile keeps the keyhole steady, cutting spatter to almost zero, protecting the protective lens and keeping long shifts consistent.
- Smooth seams with good appearance: the finished bead is uniform with fine ripples and requires little or no post grinding, which directly reduces polishing labor and scrap rate.
- Single side welding, double side forming: full penetration is achieved from one accessible side while both sides show a clean formed seam, ideal for busbars, battery tabs, tubes and thin plate overlap joints.
Where it is used
The head is already running in copper busbar and laminated busbar welding, battery tab and module interconnection, motor hairpin and stator winding welding, connectors and heat sinks, sensor housings, thin wall copper tubes, and gold and silver jewelry repair and joining. Customers switching from infrared only welding typically report fewer reworked parts, longer lens life and a shorter parameter tuning cycle, because blue light gives a much wider process window on reflective surfaces.
Availability and support
Standard configurations are available in 7 to 15 working days. HanWei Laser provides welding sample testing before shipment and remote parameter setup. Spare protective lenses, focus lenses and nozzles are kept in stock for fast after sales response.
"Our goal with the blue light welding head was simple: give production engineers a welding tool that behaves the same on copper as it does on stainless steel. Self development from the optical module to the control software is what makes that stability possible."
HanWei Laser, technical team
For welding samples, quotations or a process consultation, contact the HanWei Laser sales team and share your material, thickness and joint type. We will recommend the blue light laser welding head configuration that fits your production line.

records.body_text:
Effects of vacuum annealing, build direction, and wall thickness on the mechanical anisotropy of SLS polyamide 12
- Original Article
- Published:
Abstract
Polyamide 12 (PA12) parts produced by selective laser sintering (SLS) are known to exhibit anisotropic mechanical behavior governed by the build direction, wall thickness, and residual porosity inherent to the process. The objective of the present study is to determine whether short-term vacuum annealing reduces this anisotropy and to establish the role of wall thickness as a modulating factor. A full 3³ factorial design was used to evaluate the combined influence of the build direction (vertical, horizontal, and transverse), wall thickness (2.0, 2.5, and 3.0 mm), and vacuum annealing time (0, 3, and 4 h at 140 °C) on the tensile, hardness, surface, thermal, structural, and defect-related response of SLS-manufactured PA12. Atmosphere was not a factor in the design, so the results are attributable to annealing at 140 °C under vacuum rather than to the vacuum itself. After 3 h, the average degree of crystallinity, recomputed from the archived thermograms, was 33.37% in the control condition, 34.25% after 3 h and 32.45% after 4 h, a variation that is not statistically significant when the build-direction and wall-thickness cells are treated as blocks (p = 0.551). Partial closure of the cross-sectional porosity was significant, with the cross-sectional area density increasing from 96.58% to 98.21%, whereas the reduction in mean pore diameter (76.17 to 69.63 μm) was at most marginal when the specimen was used as the unit of analysis (p = 0.032), with no pairwise comparison between annealing levels surviving correction. These structural changes were accompanied by small increases in the ultimate tensile strength (+ 1.6% on average, + 2.3% at best in any single condition) and hardness (+ 0.7 Shore D) and by a reduction in elongation at break (− 14.1% overall) after 3 h of annealing. The build direction remained the dominant source of anisotropy after treatment: the vertical samples consistently showed the lowest strength and ductility regardless of the annealing condition. Elongation at break was the only property whose anisotropy responded to the treatment, and it did so because the horizontal direction lost ductility (− 24.9%, p < 0.001) while the transverse (− 5.6%) and vertical (− 2.1%) directions did not change significantly; the anisotropy of ultimate tensile strength and hardness was unaffected, and that of the dynamic elastic modulus increased rather than decreased with annealing time (1.7%, 3.2% and 3.7% under the bounded index for 0, 3 and 4 h). XRD and FTIR analyses showed no new crystalline phases and no chemical change detectable within the sensitivity of those techniques. These results indicate that short-term vacuum annealing produces only marginal gains in the strength of SLS-manufactured PA12 and does not reduce its build-direction anisotropy; the apparent reduction in ductility anisotropy reflects degradation of the stronger directions rather than improvement of the weaker one.
