records.body_text:
Combined Environmental Reliability Testing for EV Busbars: Temperature, Humidity, and 3-Axis Random Vibration
Oct 17, 2026 View: 112
EV battery-pack busbars cannot be qualified reliably through temperature, humidity, or vibration tests performed in isolation. A combined environmental profile exposes the actual interaction between thermal expansion, moisture, mechanical preload loss, fretting at bolted interfaces, and insulation stress, allowing failure mechanisms to be identified before vehicle-level durability testing.
For high-voltage battery applications, Apollo evaluates busbar assemblies under customer-defined combined profiles that can include -40°C to 125°C temperature cycling, up to 95% RH, and 3-axis random vibration, with vibration methodology referenced to ISO 16750-3 where applicable. Electrical resistance, fastening integrity, insulation condition, and post-test dimensional characteristics are correlated with the environmental load history.
-40°C to 125°C Thermal Cycling and 95% RH: Why Single-Factor Testing Misses Busbar Failures
Thermal Expansion at ΔT = 165°C: Copper, Aluminum, Insulation, and Fasteners
A busbar assembly contains materials with different coefficients of thermal expansion (CTE).
A temperature range from -40°C to 125°C produces a thermal span of 165°C. Copper, aluminum, polymer insulation, stainless-steel fasteners, and plated interfaces respond differently to this temperature change.
This differential expansion can generate:
Bolt preload variation
Contact-interface shear
Localized bending stress
Insulation movement
Cracking around formed sections
Fretting at bolted joints
A busbar that passes a static resistance test at 23°C may therefore show a different resistance profile after repeated thermal cycling.
95% RH and Condensation: Corrosion and Interface Degradation
High relative humidity creates an additional mechanism at exposed interfaces.
Potential failure locations include:
Plated copper terminals
Bolt and washer interfaces
Exposed conductor edges
Insulation defects
Crimped or welded transition areas
Moisture combined with temperature variation can accelerate surface oxidation and corrosion products. At a bolted electrical interface, even a small increase in contact resistance becomes significant at hundreds of amperes because
That 16 W is generated locally at the connection rather than distributed along the entire busbar.
ISO 16750-3 Vibration and Environmental Interaction: Mechanical Loading
ISO 16750-3 addresses mechanical loads for road vehicles and provides vibration-test approaches according to component location and vehicle application.
For an EV battery-pack busbar, the relevant mechanical environment may contain:
Broadband random vibration
Multiple vibration axes
Road-induced shocks
Resonance amplification
Fastener excitation
Local bending of flexible sections
The test profile must be established from the vehicle location, mounting structure, mass, and customer durability specification rather than assigning one universal vibration spectrum to every battery busbar.
3-Axis Random Vibration and 165°C Thermal Span: Combined Test Architecture
Three-Axis Excitation at X/Y/Z: Replicating Battery-Pack Mechanical Loads
A production busbar assembly should be mounted using the same:
Fasteners
Torque specification
Insulation components
Support brackets
Connector interfaces
Mounting points
used in the vehicle or battery-pack configuration.
The three principal directions are normally evaluated as:
Axis | Typical Mechanical Concern | Busbar Failure Mechanism
---|---|---
X-axis | Longitudinal excitation | Terminal/interface shear
Y-axis | Lateral excitation | Fastener loosening and bending
Z-axis | Vertical excitation | Support fatigue and resonance
Combined sequence | Multi-directional loading | Interaction of thermal and mechanical stresses
The objective is not simply to demonstrate that the copper conductor survives vibration. The complete assembly must maintain electrical and mechanical functionality.
Random Vibration PSD at Vehicle-Specific Frequencies: Resonance Control
Random vibration is normally defined using a power spectral density (PSD) profile in:
The highest mechanical stress may occur near a natural frequency rather than at the highest nominal acceleration.
For this reason, engineering validation should identify:
Natural frequency
Resonance frequency
Damping ratio
Mode shape
Acceleration response
Relative displacement between mounting points
A busbar with a long unsupported copper span can exhibit significantly higher dynamic displacement than a short rigid conductor.
Thermal-Vibration Interaction at -40°C and 125°C: Structural Resonance Shift
Temperature changes can alter polymer modulus, copper stress state, insulation flexibility, and joint stiffness.
At low temperature:
Polymer insulation may become less compliant
Flexible support elements can stiffen
Thermal contraction increases interface displacement
At high temperature:
Polymer modulus can decrease
Insulation may soften
Fastener preload can change
Differential thermal expansion increases
The vibration test should therefore include temperature states representative of the intended vehicle environment rather than relying exclusively on room-temperature vibration.
Fastener Preload at 400–800V and mΩ Resistance: Monitoring Bolted Busbar Interfaces
Belleville Washer Preload at High Vibration: Preventing Joint Loosening
Bolted busbar connections depend on stable clamping force.
A typical joint consists of:
Bolt → Belleville washer → terminal → busbar → mating terminal → nut
The preload creates the normal force required to maintain a low-resistance electrical interface.
A Belleville washer can provide controlled elastic displacement as the joint stack-up changes through thermal expansion and vibration.
Compared with a rigid flat washer, the spring characteristic of a Belleville washer can provide greater compensation for small changes in joint compression.
Preload Loss After 3-Axis Vibration: Torque Is Not Enough
Initial bolt torque does not prove long-term joint integrity.
Torque is an indirect indicator of preload because friction at the thread and bearing surface consumes a large portion of applied torque.
For reliability validation, Apollo can correlate:
Initial tightening torque
Initial bolt preload
Thermal cycling
Vibration exposure
Final preload
Contact resistance
Interface wear
A useful engineering acceptance criterion is therefore based on measured preload retention and electrical resistance, not torque alone.
Fretting Wear at <1 mΩ Interfaces: Resistance Growth Detection
Microscopic relative movement between two contacting surfaces can cause fretting.
The process may generate:
Removal of plating
Oxide formation
Metallic debris
Reduced real contact area
Increased contact resistance
Localized Joule heating
The failure can develop gradually, making continuous or periodic four-wire resistance measurement more informative than visual inspection alone.
For high-current EV busbars, resistance changes should be tracked against:
Cycle count
Temperature
Vibration axis
RMS acceleration
Joint preload
Interface condition
Flexible Copper Foil and Braided Transition Sections: Reducing Resonance-Induced Shear Stress
Multi-Layer Copper Foil at High Flexibility: Strain Distribution
Rigid copper busbars are efficient for short, fixed-distance connections but can transmit mechanical displacement directly between mounting points.
A flexible transition section changes the mechanical load path.
Common structures include:
Multi-layer copper foil
Laminated copper foil
Copper braided conductor
Stamped flexible links
Braided copper expansion connectors
The flexible section absorbs relative displacement between battery modules, busbar terminals, and structural supports.
Flexible Braided Copper at 100% IACS-Class Conductivity: Electrical and Mechanical Trade-Off
Electrical conductivity and mechanical flexibility must be evaluated together.
Structure | Electrical Path | Flexibility | Vibration Accommodation | Typical Use
---|---|---|---|---
Rigid C1100 copper bar | Low resistance | Low | Low | Fixed connection
Multi-layer copper foil | Low resistance | High | High | Battery interconnect
Braided copper conductor | Low resistance | Very high | Very high | Expansion/vibration transition
Laminated busbar | Low inductance potential | Medium | Medium | Power electronics
Flexible stamped copper link | Low resistance | Medium–High | High | Compact battery modules
High-purity copper such as C1100 can provide conductivity approaching 100% IACS, depending on material condition and specification.
Stray Inductance <10nH: Flexible Geometry in High-Speed Power Switching
For high-current switching systems, mechanical flexibility does not remove electrical design requirements.
A laminated or closely coupled conductor geometry can reduce loop area and associated parasitic inductance.
Even a small inductance becomes relevant when (di/dt) is high.
Therefore, flexible sections used around inverter or battery switching structures should be evaluated for both:
Mechanical strain relief
Electrical loop geometry
The final geometry depends on current rating, switching frequency, insulation system, mounting envelope, and customer electromagnetic compatibility requirements.
Insulation Sleeve at 125°C and Dielectric Strength >15kV/mm: Detecting Environmental Cracking
Thermal Stress at -40°C to 125°C: Polymer Insulation Failure Points
Busbar insulation can fail even when the copper conductor remains electrically functional.
High-risk locations include:
Sharp stamped edges
Formed corners
Bolt holes
Terminal transitions
Molded supports
Areas under mechanical compression
Repeated thermal expansion and contraction can produce tensile strain in the polymer.
At the same time, random vibration can create cyclic bending around the same location.
The combined mechanism is more severe than either load alone.
UL 94 V-0 Insulation and High-Voltage Dielectric Testing
For EV battery applications, insulation material selection may involve:
Operating temperature rating
Dielectric strength
Flame resistance
Chemical resistance
Tracking resistance
Environmental aging
Where specified by the material system, UL 94 V-0 can be used as a flammability classification.
A dielectric strength specification such as >15 kV/mm must be treated as a material or system-specific requirement and verified under the applicable test method.
The test program should also examine insulation after environmental exposure for:
Cracks
Pinholes
Delamination
Edge lifting
Abrasion
Carbonized areas
Post-Test Insulation Resistance at 400–800V: Electrical Safety Verification
Environmental testing should be followed by electrical inspection.
Depending on the customer's validation specification, measurements can include:
Insulation resistance
Dielectric withstand
Leakage current
Hi-pot test
Visual insulation inspection
Continuity testing
The electrical acceptance limits should be established from the vehicle architecture and applicable safety standard.
CMM Inspection at ±0.01mm and Resistance Mapping: Pre-Test and Post-Test Correlation
CMM Measurement at ±0.01mm: Detecting Permanent Deformation
Environmental testing should not end with a pass/fail electrical result.
A busbar may retain electrical continuity while experiencing permanent mechanical deformation.
CMM inspection can measure:
Terminal position
Hole-to-hole distance
Flatness
Bend angle
Mounting height
Flexible-section geometry
Connector alignment
Pre-test and post-test measurements are compared to identify permanent dimensional drift.
Four-Wire Resistance at mΩ Resolution: Mapping Joint Degradation
A four-wire Kelvin measurement separates voltage-sensing leads from current-carrying leads, reducing measurement error caused by lead resistance.
For busbar qualification, resistance should be recorded:
Before test → during defined intervals → after test
This creates a resistance-versus-cycle profile.
A resistance increase should then be correlated with:
Fastener preload loss
Fretting marks
Oxidation
Plating wear
Copper deformation
Thermal exposure
Cross-Section Analysis and Microscopy: Identifying Fretting and Fatigue
When resistance increases after vibration, destructive analysis can locate the failure mechanism.
Typical analysis includes:
Optical microscopy
Metallographic cross-section
SEM where required
Plating thickness measurement
Surface morphology analysis
Joint fracture analysis
The objective is to distinguish between electrical interface degradation and bulk conductor fatigue.
ISO 16750-3 Vibration and EV Battery Validation: From Component Test to Vehicle Durability
Battery-Pack Mounting at -40°C to 125°C: Test Fixture Fidelity
A test fixture must reproduce the mechanical boundary conditions of the production installation.
Fixture design should account for:
Mounting-point stiffness
Fastener type
Torque
Support spacing
Cable routing
Busbar mass
Connector constraints
An overly rigid fixture can suppress real vibration modes. An overly flexible fixture can introduce artificial resonance.
Therefore, fixture modal behavior should be checked before interpreting component test data.
Combined Environmental Test Matrix: Temperature × Humidity × Vibration
A structured validation matrix may be organized as follows:
Test Stage | Temperature | Humidity | Vibration | Primary Measurement
---|---|---|---|---
Baseline | 23°C | Ambient | None | Resistance + dimensions
Low-temperature exposure | -40°C | Defined by profile | Defined PSD | Resistance + function
High-temperature exposure | 125°C | Defined by profile | Defined PSD | Resistance + insulation
High-RH exposure | Defined by profile | Up to 95% RH | Defined PSD | Corrosion + insulation
Combined profile | -40°C to 125°C | Up to 95% RH | X/Y/Z random | Full electrical/mechanical data
Post-test | 23°C | Ambient | None | CMM + resistance + visual
Not every program requires simultaneous maximum temperature, maximum humidity, and maximum vibration. The test matrix should reflect the vehicle duty cycle and customer specification.
Failure Mode Analysis at IATF 16949: PFMEA-Driven Reliability Testing
Environmental reliability testing becomes more useful when each test condition is linked to a predefined failure mode.
For an automotive busbar program, PFMEA can identify:
Joint loosening
Fretting corrosion
Conductor fatigue
Insulation cracking
Plating degradation
Terminal deformation
Resistance increase
Dielectric failure
The Control Plan can then define the corresponding production controls and inspection frequencies.
This creates a closed engineering loop:
Design → FEA → Prototype → Environmental Test → Failure Analysis → DFM → Tooling → SPC → PPAP Level 3 → Mass Production
Apollo EV Busbar Reliability Engineering: C1100 Copper, Flexible Links, and PPAP Level 3
C1100 Copper at High Conductivity: Material and Forming Control
Apollo's EV busbar manufacturing process can incorporate precision copper stamping, bending, forming, surface treatment, insulation, and flexible transition structures according to the customer's drawing and electrical specification.
Typical engineering inputs include:
C1100/C10200 copper grades
Copper thickness
Plating specification
Bend radius
Hole diameter
Mounting pitch
Insulation requirement
Current rating
Temperature rise limit
Precision Stamping at ±0.01mm: Geometry and Assembly Fit
Critical busbar dimensions can be monitored using:
CMM inspection
Optical measurement
Go/no-go gauges
Flatness measurement
Burr inspection
SPC
Dimensional tolerances should be assigned according to functional requirements rather than applying ±0.01mm indiscriminately to every feature.
PPAP Level 3 and IATF 16949: Production Validation Documentation
For automotive programs, Apollo can structure project quality documentation around customer PPAP requirements, including:
Process Flow Diagram
PFMEA
Control Plan
Dimensional Inspection Report
Material Certification
MSA documentation
SPC data
Capability studies
Functional test results
Sample submission records
The final submission level and specific documents remain subject to the customer's purchasing and quality requirements.
FAQ
What temperature range should an EV busbar environmental reliability test use?
A customer-defined profile may include -40°C to 125°C for EV battery applications. The actual temperature limits, dwell time, transition rate, and number of cycles should be based on the battery-pack location and vehicle validation specification.
How is EV busbar random vibration testing performed?
The busbar assembly is mounted in its production configuration and exposed to vehicle-specific vibration profiles, commonly including X/Y/Z excitation. ISO 16750-3 can provide the mechanical test framework, while the customer defines the applicable PSD and duration.
How can Apollo detect busbar failure after combined thermal and vibration testing?
Apollo can compare pre- and post-test CMM dimensions, four-wire resistance, fastener preload, insulation condition, and interface wear. Metallographic analysis can then identify fretting, fatigue, corrosion, or joint degradation.

Repeated thermal expansion and contraction can produce tensile strain in the polymer\.

At the same time\, random vibration can create cyclic bending around the same location\.

The combined mechanism is more severe than either load alone\.

UL 94 V\-0 Insulation and High\-Voltage Dielectric Testing

For EV battery applications\, insulation material selection may involve\:

Operating temperature rating

Dielectric strength

Flame resistance

Chemical resistance

Tracking resistance

Environmental aging

Where specified by the material system\, UL 94 V\-0 can be used as a flammability classification\.

A dielectric strength specification such as \>15 kV\/mm must be treated as a material or system\-specific requirement and verified under the applicable test method\.

The test program should also examine insulation after environmental exposure for\:

Cracks

Pinholes

Delamination

Edge lifting

Abrasion

Carbonized areas

Post\-Test Insulation Resistance at 400–800V\: Electrical Safety Verification

Environmental testing should be followed by electrical inspection\.

Depending on the customer\'s validation specification\, measurements can include\:

Insulation resistance

Dielectric withstand

Leakage current

Hi\-pot test

Visual insulation inspection

Continuity testing

The electrical acceptance limits should be established from the vehicle architecture and applicable safety standard\.

\#\# CMM Inspection at ±0\.01mm and Resistance Mapping\: Pre\-Test and Post\-Test Correlation

CMM Measurement at ±0\.01mm\: Detecting Permanent Deformation

Environmental testing should not end with a pass\/fail electrical result\.

A busbar may retain electrical continuity while experiencing permanent mechanical deformation\.

CMM inspection can measure\:

Terminal position

Hole\-to\-hole distance

Flatness

Bend angle

Mounting height

Flexible\-section geometry

Connector alignment

Pre\-test and post\-test measurements are compared to identify permanent dimensional drift\.

Four\-Wire Resistance at mΩ Resolution\: Mapping Joint Degradation

A four\-wire Kelvin measurement separates voltage\-sensing leads from current\-carrying leads\, reducing measurement error caused by lead resistance\.

For busbar qualification\, resistance should be recorded\:

Before test → during defined intervals → after test

This creates a resistance\-versus\-cycle profile\.

A resistance increase should then be correlated with\:

Fastener preload loss

Fretting marks

Oxidation

Plating wear

Copper deformation

Thermal exposure

Cross\-Section Analysis and Microscopy\: Identifying Fretting and Fatigue

When resistance increases after vibration\, destructive analysis can locate the failure mechanism\.

Typical analysis includes\:

Optical microscopy

Metallographic cross\-section

SEM where required

Plating thickness measurement

Surface morphology analysis

Joint fracture analysis

The objective is to distinguish between electrical interface degradation and bulk conductor fatigue\.

\#\# ISO 16750\-3 Vibration and EV Battery Validation\: From Component Test to Vehicle Durability

Battery\-Pack Mounting at \-40°C to 125°C\: Test Fixture Fidelity

A test fixture must reproduce the mechanical boundary conditions of the production installation\.

Fixture design should account for\:

Mounting\-point stiffness

Fastener type

Torque

Support spacing

Cable routing

Busbar mass

Connector constraints

An overly rigid fixture can suppress real vibration modes\. An overly flexible fixture can introduce artificial resonance\.

Therefore\, fixture modal behavior should be checked before interpreting component test data\.

Combined Environmental Test Matrix\: Temperature × Humidity × Vibration

A structured validation matrix may be organized as follows\:

Test Stage \| Temperature \| Humidity \| Vibration \| Primary Measurement 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Baseline \| 23°C \| Ambient \| None \| Resistance \+ dimensions 
Low\-temperature exposure \| \-40°C \| Defined by profile \| Defined PSD \| Resistance \+ function 
High\-temperature exposure \| 125°C \| Defined by profile \| Defined PSD \| Resistance \+ insulation 
High\-RH exposure \| Defined by profile \| Up to 95\% RH \| Defined PSD \| Corrosion \+ insulation 
Combined profile \| \-40°C to 125°C \| Up to 95\% RH \| X\/Y\/Z random \| Full electrical\/mechanical data 
Post\-test \| 23°C \| Ambient \| None \| CMM \+ resistance \+ visual 

Not every program requires simultaneous maximum temperature\, maximum humidity\, and maximum vibration\. The test matrix should reflect the vehicle duty cycle and customer specification\.

records.title: Application and Adaptation of Arc-Based Welding Processes to Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing: A Review
records.abstract: Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) has emerged as one of the most industrially scalable arc-based metal additive manufacturing (AM) technologies, using established Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW), Gas Tungsten Arc Welding (GTAW), and Plasma Arc Welding (PAW) processes to deposit metallic material layer-by-layer into near-net-shape components. This review presents a physics-based examination of the adaptation of traditional welding processes for AM applications, with emphasis on: (i) the thermodynamic and metallurgical principles governing melt pool formation, solidification, and solid-state transformations; (ii) the thermal and solidification features that WAAM shares with multi-pass welding and those that are distinctive to WAAM, with particular attention to the temperature gradient-to-solidification-rate ratio (G/R) and its role in controlling grain morphology; (iii) deposition path strategies and their influence on heat distribution and microstructural homogeneity; (iv) arc metal transfer modes and their thermal implications for AM; and (v) mechanisms of defect formation including porosity, solidification cracking, residual stress, and geometric deviation. Unlike general WAAM reviews, this article specifically positions conventional arc welding processes as the metallurgical and thermal foundation of WAAM and critically examines how their operating principles are transformed under repeated layer-by-layer deposition. Key governing equations linking process parameters to microstructure and properties are presented. Among GMAW variants, Cold Metal Transfer (CMT) provides low heat input, controlled droplet transfer, and low spatter, whereas GTAW and PAW allow wire feed and arc power to be set independently; the preferred process therefore depends on the alloy, required deposition rate, geometry, and surface quality. A synthesis of findings across ferrous and non-ferrous alloy systems is presented, together with knowledge gaps and future directions toward closed-loop adaptive WAAM systems.
records.summary: This review examines how conventional arc welding processes—GMAW (including MIG/MAG), GTAW, and PAW—are adapted for Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing, treating welding metallurgy as the thermal and metallurgical foundation of WAAM. It presents governing equations linking process parameters to melt-pool thermodynamics, solidification (the G/R and G·R framework), phase transformation, residual stress, and defect formation, and contrasts WAAM's free-standing, layer-by-layer thermal conditions with those of single-pass and multi-pass welding. The authors compare arc process variants, noting that CMT offers low heat input, controlled droplet transfer, and low spatter, while GTAW and PAW decouple wire feed from arc power; process choice depends on alloy, deposition rate, geometry, and surface quality. Reported quantitative results from cited primary studies are compiled, including a porosity minimum at 100 A hot-wire current in aluminum (relative density 96.8% to 99.6%), CMT/CMT Pulse thermal differences in ER309LSi walls, and grain refinement and hardness increases with hybrid WAAM–FSP in ER4043. The review is a critical narrative review, not a systematic one, and its figures are largely author-drawn conceptual schematics rather than measured data.
records.why_it_matters: For process engineers, the review frames G/R and G·R as diagnostic variables: because the heat-extraction path lengthens as a WAAM wall grows, the thermal gradient at the solidification front tends to fall with build height, so achieving microstructural homogeneity requires active compensation (e.g., reducing heat input with height, inter-pass cooling, or inter-layer deformation) rather than fixed welding parameters.

Abstract
Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) has emerged as one of the most industrially scalable arc-based metal additive manufacturing (AM) technologies, using established Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW), Gas Tungsten Arc Welding (GTAW), and Plasma Arc Welding (PAW) processes to deposit metallic material layer-by-layer into near-net-shape components. This review presents a physics-based examination of the adaptation of traditional welding processes for AM applications, with emphasis on: (i) the thermodynamic and metallurgical principles governing melt pool formation, solidification, and solid-state transformations; (ii) the thermal and solidification features that WAAM shares with multi-pass welding and those that are distinctive to WAAM, with particular attention to the temperature gradient-to-solidification-rate ratio (G/R) and its role in controlling grain morphology; (iii) deposition path strategies and their influence on heat distribution and microstructural homogeneity; (iv) arc metal transfer modes and their thermal implications for AM; and (v) mechanisms of defect formation including porosity, solidification cracking, residual stress, and geometric deviation. Unlike general WAAM reviews, this article specifically positions conventional arc welding processes as the metallurgical and thermal foundation of WAAM and critically examines how their operating principles are transformed under repeated layer-by-layer deposition. Key governing equations linking process parameters to microstructure and properties are presented. Among GMAW variants, Cold Metal Transfer (CMT) provides low heat input, controlled droplet transfer, and low spatter, whereas GTAW and PAW allow wire feed and arc power to be set independently; the preferred process therefore depends on the alloy, required deposition rate, geometry, and surface quality. A synthesis of findings across ferrous and non-ferrous alloy systems is presented, together with knowledge gaps and future directions toward closed-loop adaptive WAAM systems.
1. Introduction
Metal additive manufacturing (AM) has reshaped the design, prototyping, and production landscape for complex metallic components across aerospace, defense, energy, automotive, and biomedical sectors. Unlike subtractive manufacturing processes that begin with bulk material and remove material to reveal a final geometry, AM processes build components layer-by-layer directly from digital models, offering substantial reductions in material waste, tooling costs, and lead times, alongside greater design freedom for topology-optimized and internally featured structures [1,2,3].
Within the broad family of metal AM processes encompassing Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF), Directed Energy Deposition (DED), binder jetting, and sheet lamination, Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) occupies a distinctive and growing niche defined by its use of electric arc welding as the heat source and metallic wire as feedstock. WAAM is a DED-family process in the ASTM/ISO classification framework, and its defining advantage over powder-based AM is the combination of high deposition rate (1–10 kg/h), near-100% material utilization, and industrial scalability to component dimensions of several meters, capabilities that remain difficult and economically impractical for most powder-bed processes [2,3,4,5,6,7].
WAAM draws directly on the rich industrial heritage and established process science of GMAW (including its MIG and MAG variants), GTAW (TIG), and PAW processes, which have been refined over more than seven decades of industrial application. The conceptual roots of arc-based shape deposition trace to Baker’s 1925 patent on the deposition of successive weld beads to produce solid objects [8]. However, modern computer-controlled WAAM emerged in earnest during the 1990s and 2000s, with pioneering contributions from Cranfield University (the WAAM/WAAMMat program), aerospace research institutions, and other groups developing three-dimensional welding and hybrid welding–milling systems [9,10,11,12], targeting the fabrication of large titanium and high-strength steel aerospace structures with markedly reduced buy-to-fly ratios [13,14]. The comparison between traditional manufacturing and the WAAM route is shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1. Comparison of traditional subtractive and WAAM additive manufacturing routes, illustrating the reduction in material waste and buy-to-fly (BTF) ratio achievable with WAAM. Conceptual schematic generated with ChatGPT (GPT-5) from author-specified content; material fractions and ratios are illustrative.
Welding science and WAAM share a common metallurgical foundation, not merely the convenience of available equipment. From a physical metallurgy standpoint, WAAM and fusion welding share closely related governing phenomena: arc-driven metal melting, melt pool dynamics under electromagnetic, buoyancy, and Marangoni forces, solidification governed by local temperature gradient G and solidification rate R, solid-state phase transformations upon cooling, and the generation of residual stresses under constrained thermal conditions [15,16]. Yet WAAM imposes thermal conditions that differ from those of single-pass welding. Heat accumulation and repeated reheating of prior deposits also occur in multi-pass welding of thick sections, which may require hundreds of passes, so they are not unique to WAAM; what distinguishes WAAM is that the deposit is a free-standing structure that grows away from its only heat sink. The progressive increase in thermal resistance between the melt pool and the substrate, together with the evolving geometry of the build, produces microstructural heterogeneity, residual stress fields, and dimensional deviations that have no exact analog in conventional welding practice.
Although several reviews have addressed WAAM process development, alloy-specific properties, and defect mitigation [17,18], fewer studies have explicitly examined WAAM as a direct metallurgical extension of traditional arc welding processes. This review therefore emphasizes the transition from conventional welding to layer-wise additive manufacturing, focusing on how heat input, metal transfer, melt-pool solidification, repeated thermal cycling, and defect formation are altered when GMAW, GTAW, and PAW are adapted for WAAM.
The closest precedent is the review of Oliveira et al. [19], which revisited fundamental welding concepts for fusion-based additive manufacturing as a whole, including laser, electron-beam, and arc processes; identified the similarities in solidification, chemical reactions, thermal effects, residual stress, and distortion; and proposed geometric, energetic, and thermal criteria for process optimization together with a dimensionless energy-density parameter. The present review differs from it, and from recent general WAAM reviews [20,21], in three respects. First, it is restricted to arc-based wire deposition and treats the arc processes themselves, including metal transfer physics and the coupling between wire feed and heat input in GMAW and CMT, which is absent in GTAW and PAW. Second, it separates the thermal and solidification features that WAAM shares with multi-pass welding from those that are distinctive to WAAM and uses the G/R and G·R framework to state which microstructural outcomes arise from each. Third, it links these principles to quantitative data verified against the original publications, to hybrid deformation strategies, and to the barriers to industrial qualification.
Understanding these similarities and differences from first principles is the central intellectual challenge of WAAM process science and the primary motivation for this review. The objective of this review is threefold: (i) to provide a comparative analysis of GMAW, GTAW, and PAW in the context of WAAM applicability; (ii) to critically examine the physical mechanisms of melt pool formation, solidification, phase transformation, and defect generation in WAAM relative to traditional welding, supported by governing equations; and (iii) to synthesize the current understanding of microstructural evolution and defect formation across alloy systems, while identifying open research challenges and future directions. The review is structured to serve both researchers entering the field and practitioners seeking to optimize WAAM for industrial deployment.
2. Scope and Literature Selection
This article is a critical narrative review. It is not a systematic review: the literature was selected for its relevance to the process–structure–property questions addressed here, not through a protocol-driven search with documented record counts, and no meta-analysis was performed. The scope and organization of the review are summarized in Figure 2.
Figure 2. Scope and organization of this review, linking the arc heat sources and process control (Section 3, Section 4 and Section 5) to welding metallurgy, microstructure, and defects (Section 6 and Section 7), alloy-specific synthesis (Section 8), and industrial transfer and hybrid strategies (Section 9 and Section 10). Schematic drawn with Python 3.12 with Matplotlib 3.10; no data are shown.
2.1. Literature Identification and Selection Principles
The review addresses the literature published between 2005 and March 2025 on arc-based wire additive manufacturing, together with earlier foundational works on welding metallurgy, solidification, and three-dimensional welding (from 1925 onward) where these are needed to explain the governing physics; during the revision of this article in 2026, the literature base was updated with publications from 2025 and 2026, including recent reviews and studies on WAAM feedstock, process configuration, and hybrid deformation processing. The searches combined three concept areas: (i) the process (wire arc additive manufacturing); (ii) the arc heat source (GMAW, including MIG and MAG; GTAW; PAW; and CMT); and (iii) process–structure outcomes (heat input, deposition path, solidification, microstructure, porosity, and residual stress). The literature was identified mainly through Google Scholar searches, and full texts were obtained through the library resources of Wayne State University. Further references were provided by the co-authors through the library resources of their institutions. Conceptual schematic illustrations were generated with ChatGPT (GPT-5, OpenAI, San Francisco, CA, USA) from content specified by the authors and were reviewed and revised by the authors; the plotted figures and the graphical abstract were drawn with Python 3.12 (Python Software Foundation, Wilmington, DE, USA) and Matplotlib 3.10 code prepared with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic, San Francisco, CA, USA). The method used is stated in the caption of each figure. None of these figures presents measured, digitized, or extracted data; the inter-pass cooling curves in Section 5.2 are calculated from Equation (14).
Studies were selected according to the following principles: (i) peer-reviewed journal articles and conference papers in English form the primary evidence base, and theses are cited only where the corresponding data have not been published in journal form; (ii) experimental, computational, and combined studies were considered if they address GMAW-, GTAW-, or PAW-based wire deposition of steels, aluminum alloys, titanium alloys, nickel-based superalloys, or copper alloys; (iii) review articles, textbooks, standards, and patents are cited for context and background but are not used as sources of quantitative data; and (iv) studies reporting only qualitative observations are used for mechanistic discussion, whereas quantitative values are taken only from studies that meet the criteria in Section 2.3.
Because the literature was identified through relevance-ranked Google Scholar searches, whose ranking and coverage are not fully transparent, and because the search dates and record counts were not documented, this review does not claim complete or reproducible coverage of the WAAM literature. To limit selection bias in the quantitative synthesis, every numerical value reported in the table of verified quantitative data in Section 8.1 was verified against the original publication, and figures that show trends without numerical data are identified as conceptual schematics.
2.2. Data Extraction and Quality Assessment
For each study considered for the quantitative comparison, the following information was recorded where reported: alloy system and composition, WAAM process variant (GMAW, GTAW, PAW, CMT), linear heat input H (J/mm), travel speed, wire feed rate, inter-pass temperature, resulting grain size (µm), porosity fraction (%), Vickers hardness (HV), and ultimate tensile strength (MPa). Studies that reported only qualitative microstructural observations without quantitative data were retained for mechanistic discussion but excluded from the quantitative comparison in Section 8.1. The quality of each study was screened against three author-defined criteria: physical consistency of reported data, sample size and statistical treatment, and independent validation of key claims.
The WAAM literature suffers from important methodological heterogeneity: significant variations in reporting standards, specimen geometry, measurement locations within builds, and testing protocols make direct quantitative comparisons challenging. Accordingly, quantitative values extracted from the literature were used for representative comparison rather than direct statistical normalization across studies. The consequences of this limitation for the quantitative synthesis are addressed in Section 8.1 and considered further in Section 10.1.
2.3. Criteria for the Quantitative Comparison
A study was used as a data source for the quantitative comparison in Section 8.1 only if it (i) was a primary experimental study rather than a review, textbook, or schematic source; (ii) identified the alloy and the arc-process variant; (iii) reported the quantity numerically in its text or tables together with the process condition to which the value refers; and (iv) was available in full text for verification. Values were transcribed as reported; no values were digitized from plots, interpolated, or converted other than as stated in the table. Where a study reported several conditions, the controlled variable and the condition supporting each value are identified in the table. Figures in this review that show trends without numerical data are identified in their captions as author-drawn schematics.
3. WAAM Process Architecture and Comparison with Laser-Based AM
3.1. WAAM System Architecture and Governing Heat Input
A WAAM system comprises five principal sub-systems [22], as shown schematically in Figure 3 and Figure 4: (i) a welding power source, such as a constant-voltage GMAW inverter, GTAW unit, or plasma power supply; (ii) a wire feeding mechanism delivering feedstock at controlled rates; (iii) a motion system typically a 6-axis industrial robot or CNC gantry that controls torch position, travel speed and deposition trajectory; (iv) a shielding gas delivery system; and (v) a process control and monitoring system coordinating all sub-systems [23]. The quality and geometric accuracy of WAAM parts are governed by a complex interplay of process parameters, physical phenomena, and geometrical features, as classified by Jafari et al. [24]. The importance of this system architecture in WAAM is that each sub-system influences not only bead formation, as in conventional welding, but also the accumulated thermal history and dimensional stability of the entire build.
Figure 3. Schematic of the WAAM layer-by-layer deposition process showing the welding torch, power supply, shielding gas nozzle, filler wire feed, weld pool, and the growing multi-layer deposit structure on the substrate. The deposition direction and layered build geometry are indicated. Conceptual schematic generated with ChatGPT (GPT-5) from author-specified content.
Figure 4. Schematic of a WAAM system showing the five principal sub-systems: welding power source, wire feed mechanism, motion system, shielding gas delivery, and process control. Conceptal schematic generated with ChatGPT (GPT-5) from author-specified content.
Tooling and support structures play different roles in welding and in WAAM. In welding, fixtures and clamps locate the parent members, control fit-up and distortion, and backing bars or strips support the root, while the parent plates themselves provide most of the heat sink. In WAAM, the substrate is the only initial support and heat sink, and it becomes part of the thermal and mechanical boundary condition of the build: its thickness, clamping, and preheat set the early-layer cooling rate, and the distortion that develops during deposition is partly released when the part is unclamped [25,26]. As the deposit grows, its stiffness, heat-extraction path, and exposed surface area change continuously, so the thermal boundary conditions evolve during manufacturing instead of remaining fixed as they do for a joint. Active cooling of the substrate has therefore been used to control heat accumulation in WAAM [27], and overhanging or inclined features are usually produced by torch inclination, positioner rotation, or deposition sequence rather than by sacrificial support structures [21].
The deposition process is described at the most fundamental level by the net heat input per unit length, which represents the primary process-level control variable linking power source settings to thermal conditions in the deposit. The quasi-steady temperature field around a moving arc can be approximated by the analytical solutions of Rosenthal [28], whose form depends on the assumed heat-flow geometry. For a point source moving over a thick (semi-infinite) substrate, heat flow is three-dimensional and the solution is Equation (2); for a line source moving through a thin plate of thickness d, heat flow is two-dimensional and the solution is Equation (3):
3.2. Comparison of WAAM with Laser-Based Additive Manufacturing
WAAM is most frequently contrasted with LPBF and Laser DED. While laser-based processes excel in geometric resolution and surface finish, WAAM offers clear advantages in deposition rate, component scale, material utilization and economic accessibility. Table 1 presents a process-level comparison based on the work of Ding (2012) [30] and subsequent contributions from the literature.
Table 1. Process comparison between WAAM and laser-based AM processes [30,31,32].
As shown in Table 1, WAAM’s combination of high energy efficiency (>80%), high deposition rate (up to 10 kg/h), near-100% material utilization, and large-scale build capability positions it as a strong candidate for structural applications where gross material removal and complex internal features are not required. The compromise in surface finish and maximum component complexity compared to powder-bed processes is typically addressed through hybrid additive–subtractive machining, which has emerged as WAAM’s natural complement in industrial practice [9,10].
A commonly overlooked comparison metric is the buy-to-fly (BTF) ratio, defined as the mass of raw material consumed per unit mass of finished component. For machined aerospace titanium components, BTF ratios of 12:1 to 20:1 are common, whereas WAAM can reduce this to 1.5:1 to 3:1 for equivalent geometries, representing substantial material cost savings and corresponding reductions in machining time and energy consumption [1,14].
4. Arc Welding Processes and Metal Transfer Modes in WAAM
Having established the basic WAAM system architecture and heat-input framework, the next step is to examine how conventional arc welding processes operate when they are adapted for layer-wise additive deposition. GMAW, GTAW, and PAW provide the principal arc-based heat sources for WAAM, but they differ markedly in heat input, deposition rate, arc stability, shielding control, equipment complexity and alloy suitability [35].
4.1. GMAW, GTAW and PAW as WAAM Heat Sources
Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW) is the most widely employed heat source in WAAM. GMAW denotes the process category: it is designated metal inert gas (MIG) welding when the shielding gas is inert (Ar, He, or Ar–He mixtures, as used for aluminum, copper, and nickel alloys) and metal active gas (MAG) welding when the shielding gas contains an active component such as CO2 or O2 (e.g., Ar–CO2 mixtures for carbon and low-alloy steels) [16,36]. The general term GMAW is used in this review unless a cited study specifically employed MIG or MAG conditions. Commercially introduced in the late 1940s, GMAW establishes an arc between a continuously fed consumable wire electrode and the workpiece, which serves as the substrate or previously deposited layer in AM terminology, melting both to form the melt pool. Shielding is provided coaxially through the torch nozzle using argon, helium, or Ar–CO2 mixtures [36]. Key process parameters in GMAW-WAAM are arc voltage V, welding current I (or wire feed rate WFR, which determines I in constant-voltage mode), travel speed v, wire stick-out distance L, wire diameter d, and shielding gas composition X. The relationship between WFR and the resulting bead dimensions has been studied extensively [37,38,39].
Dickens et al. [40] conducted parameter studies on mild steel WAAM using Fe–C (0.08%)–Si (0.9%)–Mn (1.5%) wire and documented the influence of voltage, WFR, stick-out, wire diameter, and travel speed on arc current, bead width Wb, and bead height Hb. Response surface methodology (RSM) and analysis of variance (ANOVA) are commonly used to rank the influence of these parameters on bead width and height, and empirical second-order regression models of the following form are widely applied [37,38,39]:
The industrial appeal of GMAW for WAAM rests on broad alloy compatibility, suitability for multiple welding positions, high productivity, ready automation, and considerably lower capital and operating costs than laser or electron beam systems. The coupling of a GMAW torch to a CNC milling machine, creating a hybrid additive–subtractive system, has been demonstrated by multiple research groups and represents one of the most economically accessible routes to metallic AM for small and medium enterprises [11,41].
Gas Tungsten Arc Welding (GTAW), or TIG welding, employs a non-consumable tungsten electrode to generate the arc and delivers filler wire separately into the melt pool, as shown in Figure 5. In WAAM, GTAW is employed where deposit quality, arc stability, and shielding control are prioritized over deposition rate, particularly for reactive metals such as titanium and nickel-base superalloys where oxygen pickup must be minimized [32].

Plasma Arc Welding (PAW) constricts the arc through a fine orifice in the nozzle, producing a highly concentrated plasma jet with energy densities higher than those typically obtained in GMAW or GTAW arcs. The constriction increases the power density and produces a deeper and narrower melt pool than an unconstricted arc at the same power [16]. The resulting solidification conditions (G, R, and the cooling rate G·R) depend on the travel speed and deposit geometry and must be evaluated for the specific process window rather than inferred from arc constriction alone [32]. In WAAM, PAW is preferred for applications where high travel speed, high-quality deposits, and reduced distortion are simultaneously required.

A further difference that governs process selection is whether material feed and heat input can be set independently. In GMAW and CMT, the wire is the electrode: in constant-voltage operation the wire feed speed sets the current, so the deposition rate, the arc power, and therefore the linear heat input H are coupled, and commercial synergic programs further tie voltage and waveform to a single wire-feed setting. Deposition rate, bead geometry, and thermal conditions therefore cannot always be optimized separately when productivity, geometric accuracy, and thermal requirements conflict. In GTAW and PAW, the filler wire is fed independently of the arc current, so the energy delivered per unit mass of deposited metal can be varied at a fixed deposition rate. In PAW-based deposition, wire feed speed, arc current, and plasma gas flow rate each influence droplet transfer and bead formation [45], and hot-wire feeding adds resistive preheating of the wire that raises the deposition rate without increasing the arc power [44]. This flexibility is one reason why GTAW and PAW are used for titanium alloys [13,46], whereas the coupled but more productive GMAW and CMT processes dominate the deposition of steels and aluminum alloys.
4.3. Metal Transfer Physics in GMAW-WAAM
In GMAW, molten metal is transferred from the consumable wire electrode to the melt pool by mechanisms governed by the competition among arc pressure, electromagnetic (Lorentz) force, surface tension, and gravity. The detachment of a droplet occurs when the sum of detaching forces exceeds the retaining surface tension force. The dominant retaining force for a droplet of radius rd hanging from a wire of radius rw at its tip is the surface tension force Fγ:
The key point for WAAM is that the heat input requirement for additive deposition differs from that for conventional fusion welding. In traditional fusion welding, high heat input is required to achieve full penetration and complete fusion of base plates. In WAAM, the objective is controlled fusion with the previously deposited layer, usually through shallow remelting sufficient to achieve metallurgical bonding rather than full plate penetration. This requirement favors operation in a lower heat input regime than many conventional welding applications, shifting the optimal GMAW operating mode toward short-circuit transfer and, where available, Cold Metal Transfer. In Short Circuit Transfer (SCT), the energized wire periodically contacts the melt pool at 90–200 Hz. At each contact, the arc extinguishes and a short-circuit current flows. Cold Metal Transfer (CMT), developed by Fronius International, is among the most thermally efficient GMAW modes currently used for WAAM. In CMT, the wire feed motion and welding current are electronically synchronized: as the wire approaches the melt pool and makes contact, the current is reduced to near zero and the wire is retracted to mechanically assist droplet detachment at up to 70 Hz. This controlled retraction eliminates the uncontrolled arc-off phase associated with conventional SCT, thereby lowering heat input, spatter, and distortion in many GMAW-WAAM applications [49].
Galeazzi et al. [51] compared conventional GMAW with the CMT, CMT Advanced, and CMT Pulse variants for thin walls of AISI 420 martensitic stainless steel and found that CMT Advanced and CMT Pulse lay at opposite extremes of the tested range: CMT Advanced gave the lowest heat input and the best wall-height performance, whereas CMT Pulse lay at the high-heat-input end. The metallurgical consequence of such differences can be interpreted through the inverse dependence of grain size, or of the scale of the transformation products, on the cooling rate:
A higher cooling rate shortens the time available for grain-boundary migration and for coarsening of transformation products. A variant that raises the energy delivered per unit length, such as CMT Pulse, is therefore expected to enlarge the melt pool, extend the time spent at high temperature, and lower the cooling rate through the relevant temperature range, all of which favor coarser structures; conversely, a low-heat-input variant such as CMT Advanced is expected to favor finer structures. Grain size must therefore be interpreted together with the heat input per cycle and the reheating history, and a larger grain size should not be associated with a higher cooling rate unless an additional mechanism, such as reheating by subsequent layers, is demonstrated. This interpretation is consistent with infrared measurements on ER309LSi thick walls by Silva et al. [52]: at the same wire feed rate, CMT Pulse delivered a higher power than CMT; without interlayer idle time, the area above 900 °C in the last layer was 1013 mm2 for CMT Pulse and 400.8 mm2 for CMT, and the mean interlayer temperature was on average 15.0% higher for CMT Pulse; interlayer idle times of up to 300 s controlled heat accumulation for both variants. Separately, Luo et al. [53] compared pulsed and non-pulsed arcs in WAAM of aluminum alloys and found that the pulsed arc gave a higher droplet-transfer frequency, smaller droplets, and a higher deposition efficiency at similar arc power; because the arc force on the droplet also increased with arc power and could cause collapse of the deposited layer, they recommended the lowest pulsed arc power compatible with the required productivity.
Despite its thermal advantages in many WAAM applications [54], CMT adoption remains constrained by higher equipment cost, approximately two to three times that of conventional GMAW, and greater system complexity. As CMT technology matures and competition reduces costs, its adoption in WAAM is expected to increase considerably. Metal-transfer-mode selection in GMAW-WAAM is therefore a thermal and geometric control strategy rather than only a droplet detachment mechanism, because transfer stability directly affects heat input, remelting depth, bead regularity, spatter, and defect formation.
5. Deposition Path Planning and Thermal Management in WAAM
Beyond heat-source selection, WAAM build quality is strongly affected by the path followed by the torch and by the thermal state retained between successive layers. Deposition path strategy determines not only geometric fidelity, but also local reheating, cooling intervals, residual stress distribution and microstructural uniformity. For this reason, path planning and inter-pass temperature control should be considered together as coupled thermal-management strategies.
5.1. Path Planning Fundamentals and Deposition Patterns
Deposition path planning is among the most consequential decisions in WAAM process design. The path determines not only geometric fidelity, but also the thermal history experienced at each material location, which in turn governs microstructure, residual stress distribution, and mechanical properties. Jafari et al. [24] identified deposition path strategy as a primary determinant of WAAM microstructure. Ding et al. [55] demonstrated that, for thin-walled structures, optimal step-over distance dSO can more than double material efficiency relative to an unoptimized baseline. The step-over distance governs the overlap ratio ω:
Four classical deposition path patterns are used in WAAM, each with distinct thermal, geometric, and efficiency characteristics, as shown in Figure 8.
Figure 8. Classical WAAM deposition path patterns: (a) Raster parallel bidirectional lines; (b) zigzag continuous single bidirectional pass; (c) spiral-in inward continuous spiral; (d) contour successive boundary offsets.
- Raster: Parallel lines are deposited in alternating directions. Its advantages include reduced heat accumulation due to cooling intervals between adjacent lines. Its limitations include frequent arc starts and stops, which may introduce bead-height variability, and boundary discretization errors that reduce geometric accuracy at perimeter regions [57].
- Zigzag: Parallel lines are connected into a single continuous bidirectional pass. Its advantages include fewer arc-start and arc-stop instabilities and improved bead continuity. Its limitations include possible localized heat accumulation at path reversals in complex geometries, while boundary accuracy remains similar to raster strategies.
- Spiral-in: Smooth inward spiraling paths distribute thermal gradients more evenly. Its advantages include improved thermal uniformity for circular or ovoid cross-sections and smoother continuous motion. Its limitation is that it is not readily generalizable to arbitrary polygonal cross-sections.
- Contour: Successive offsets are deposited parallel to the part boundary. Its advantages include high boundary accuracy and regular direction changes that can reduce distortion and anisotropy. Its limitations include the possibility of overfill or underfill in regions where cross-section geometry diverges from the regular contour spacing.
These path strategies should therefore be interpreted not merely as geometric toolpaths, but as thermal-management strategies that determine local reheating, cooling intervals, residual stress distribution, and microstructural uniformity.
Hybrid strategies combining contour perimeter passes with interior zigzag fill, which are widely used in WAAM path planning software, represent the current best practice for geometrically complex parts. 5.2. Inter-Pass Temperature Control and Heat Accumulation
Because deposition path controls local reheating and cooling intervals, path planning must be considered together with inter-pass temperature management. As WAAM builds progress in height, the thermal resistance between the melt pool and the heat sink increases because the deposited material progressively separates the active melt pool from the substrate and because the geometrical heat-sink area does not increase proportionally with deposited volume. In H13 tool-steel walls deposited with pulsed MIG at a controlled inter-layer temperature of 150 °C, Wang et al. [58] attributed the variety of microstructures observed at different locations to the different thermal histories of those regions.
Two principal inter-pass temperature management strategies exist. The first is fixed dwell time, in which deposition of each new layer is delayed by a fixed time after completion of the previous layer. This approach is simple to implement but does not ensure a consistent thermal state because cooling is non-linear. The second is fixed inter-pass temperature, TIP, in which deposition begins only when the deposit surface reaches a target temperature. Montevecchi et al. [59] advocated fixed TIP control as better suited to maintaining thermal consistency. However, Geng et al. [60] cautioned that identifying the appropriate TIP is largely empirical, and the analytical process model of Rios et al. [61] for Ti-6Al-4V deposition showed that the inter-pass temperature must be included to predict layer height and wall width, confirming that the thermal state at the start of each layer is a process variable in its own right. 6. Welding Metallurgy of WAAM: Melt Pool, Solidification, Phase Transformation and Residual Stress
The process-level variables discussed above ultimately affect WAAM performance through their influence on melt-pool behavior, solidification, phase transformation, and residual stress development.
6.1. Melt-Pool Thermodynamics and Heat-Source Modeling
Traditional fusion welding and WAAM are governed by the closely related fundamental thermodynamic and fluid-dynamics principles. In both cases, the arc creates a localized heat source that raises the material above the liquidus temperature TL, forming a melt pool that is bounded by the solidification front at TL and the fusion boundary at TS (solidus). The heat flux distribution from the arc is commonly modeled using Goldak’s double-ellipsoidal heat source model [29]:
Within the melt pool, fluid flow is driven by four competing forces: Marangoni or thermocapillary convection, buoyancy-driven convection, electromagnetic or Lorentz forces, and arc pressure. The Marangoni number Ma characterizes the dominance of surface-tension-driven flow:
The Reynolds number Re = ρl · vfl · Lmp/μ of the melt-pool flow characterizes the ratio of inertial to viscous forces; together with Ma, it governs how strongly the flow redistributes solute and affects gas escape and porosity formation.
6.2. Solidification and the G/R Framework
The microstructural outcome of solidification is controlled by two parameters: the temperature gradient G (K/m) at the solidification front and the solidification velocity R (m/s). Their ratio G/R governs the stability of the solid–liquid interface and hence the resulting solidification mode, as established by the constitutional undercooling criterion [15]:
The product G·R equals the local cooling rate Ṫ (K/s) at the solidification front and governs the primary dendrite arm spacing (PDAS) λ1:
The significance of the G/R framework in WAAM is therefore not only predictive but diagnostic, because it explains why identical nominal arc parameters can produce different microstructures at different build heights as the thermal boundary condition evolves.
6.3. Welding Versus WAAM: Repeated Thermal Cycling and Microstructural Consequences
While WAAM and welding share the physics described above, they differ in several important ways that have direct consequences for microstructure and properties:
- Repeated thermal cycling: In single-pass welding, each material point generally experiences one dominant heating-cooling cycle. In WAAM, each point experiences multiple thermal cycles from the deposition of subsequent layers, with the number of cycles depending on build height and layer thickness. Each cycle reheats the material to a peak temperature Tpeak that decreases with distance from the torch. These repeated cycles drive: (a) grain growth, following the isothermal kinetic relationn − 0n = K0·t·exp[−Qg/(Rg·T)] (Table 4), with n = 2 for ideal parabolic growth and n > 2 when boundaries are pinned, integrated over the thermal history, (b) precipitation/dissolution of secondary phases, (c) recovery and partial recrystallization, and (d) microstructural banding due to alternating coarse/fine zones corresponding to Tpeak above and below the recrystallization temperature Trex.
- Thermal gradient directionality: In welding, the dominant heat extraction direction is often lateral into the parent plates, whereas in WAAM, heat is extracted primarily downward through the substrate and previously deposited material, especially in the early build stages. This promotes epitaxial columnar grain growth along the build direction (BD). The result is often a strong crystallographic texture, typically <001> parallel to BD in cubic metals, which may persist across the build height unless disrupted by allotropic transformations, as in Ti-6Al-4V, where the β→α transformation partially randomizes texture, or by active grain refinement strategies [67].
- Chemical composition freedom: In single-pass welding of two bulk components with filler wire, the resulting deposit chemistry is strongly influenced by dilution with the base material. In WAAM, material is deposited onto a flat substrate or prior layer, allowing the deposit chemistry to be varied spatially by switching wire feedstock or using multiple feed wires, thereby enabling functionally graded structures with tailored property distributions; twin-wire WAAM has been used to fabricate intermetallic alloys and functionally graded materials [35].
- Process automation and precision: Welding may be manual, mechanized, or automated, whereas WAAM is typically computer-controlled, enabling improved reproducibility of melt-pool placement, layer thickness, and deposition trajectory compared with manual welding and comparable to advanced automated welding systems [16].
- Melt pool aspect ratio and penetration: Welding often requires a relatively high depth-to-width melt-pool ratio to achieve joint penetration, whereas WAAM usually requires controlled remelting of the prior layer rather than full plate penetration. This generally produces shallower melt pools and different G/R distributions at the solidification front, which can alter dendritic growth, fusion-boundary morphology, and inter-layer bonding compared with conventional welding at equivalent power levels.

Several of the characteristics listed above are shared with multi-pass welding. Thick-section joints, such as reactor pressure vessel welds that may require hundreds of passes, also experience repeated reheating, heat accumulation, tempering or re-transformation of earlier passes, and residual stress build-up, and the metallurgy of reheated multi-pass weld metal applies directly to WAAM [16,19]. The distinctive features of WAAM arise from its geometry and boundary conditions rather than from repetition itself. (i) In a joint, each pass is bounded by the groove faces of the parent plates, which act as lateral heat sinks and epitaxial substrates, whereas a WAAM wall is free-standing, so heat is conducted downward through a lengthening path of previously deposited material and lost from two free side surfaces. (ii) In a joint, the bead sequence, bead placement, and groove geometry change the direction of the thermal gradient from pass to pass, whereas in a WAAM wall the fusion boundary advances upward in the same direction layer after layer, so the thermal gradient remains aligned with the build direction while its magnitude decreases with height [66]. (iii) The deposit forms the whole component rather than a joint between wrought members, so the reheated as-deposited microstructure and its build-height gradient determine the properties of the entire part. (iv) Inter-pass conditions in WAAM are usually set by productivity and geometric stability rather than by a qualified welding procedure, and they change as the build grows.
The different microstructures arising from these distinct thermal conditions can be described conceptually across the build height. Moving from the substrate toward the top of a WAAM build, one may observe a gradient from a remelted or refined near-substrate region, through a thermally cycled mid-build region characterized by banded microstructures, to a columnar-dominated near-top region that has experienced the fewest reheating cycles. Wang et al. [58] likewise reported location-dependent microstructures in H13 walls, although the hardness remained within 300–360 HV from top to bottom and the as-deposited tensile properties were anisotropic.
6.4. Phase Transformations and Residual Stress Development
In steels and titanium alloys, solid-state phase transformations during cooling from the melt pool strongly influence the final room-temperature microstructure. In single-pass welding of ferritic steels, the weld metal cools from the austenite (γ) field through the Ac3 temperature and transforms to ferrite morphologies such as allotriomorphic ferrite, Widmanstätten ferrite, acicular ferrite, bainite, or martensite depending on cooling rate and alloy composition, as represented by continuous cooling transformation (CCT) diagrams [16]. In WAAM, the same transformation may occur during the first cooling cycle; however, subsequent layers reheat the prior deposit to peak temperatures that may partially or fully austenitize it again, driving repeated transformation cycling that progressively homogenizes the microstructure in mid-build regions while leaving the topmost layers in a more as-deposited transformation state [12,40].
For Ti-6Al-4V, the dominant high-temperature phase is body-centered cubic β, which transforms on cooling to hexagonal close-packed α, forming lamellar colonies or Widmanstätten α, or to α′ martensite at higher cooling rates. In WAAM, the primary β columnar grains form by epitaxial solidification and persist through the β-field on cooling. The β → α transformation then partitions the columnar β into a microstructure of α laths, whose morphology, including coarse lamellae, fine basketweave, or acicular martensite, is controlled by the local cooling rate through the β transus [13,62,68]. Repeated reheating below the β transus in subsequent layers partially homogenizes this microstructure but does not fully eliminate prior-β columnar grain inheritance, a limitation that hybrid deformation strategies such as rolling and FSP are designed to overcome [69].
In aluminum alloys, which lack allotropic transformations, the solid-state microstructural evolution in WAAM is controlled primarily by precipitation, dissolution, coarsening kinetics, and grain-boundary migration. Repeated thermal cycling can dissolve strengthening precipitates, such as θ′-Al2Cu in 2xxx series alloys and β″-Mg2Si in 6xxx series alloys, in the heat-affected region of each deposited layer, creating over-aged or solution-annealed zones that degrade local strength. This precipitate heterogeneity, characterized by alternating zones of fresh precipitation and dissolution, is one of the primary sources of the banded hardness profiles characteristic of aluminum WAAM builds [70]. In addition to phase transformation, residual stress development is another major metallurgical consequence of repeated WAAM thermal cycling.

7. Microstructural Evolution and Defect Formation in WAAM
The metallurgical mechanisms discussed in Section 6 provide the basis for understanding the microstructural gradients and defects that develop during WAAM.
7.1. Columnar Grain Growth, Epitaxy and Build-Height Heterogeneity
The macrostructure of WAAM deposits is commonly characterized by epitaxial columnar grains that nucleate on the solid substrate or prior layer and grow preferentially along the maximum thermal gradient, often aligned with the build direction (BD). This epitaxial growth occurs because the nucleation barrier ΔG* for heterogeneous nucleation on an existing grain is zero when the growth direction is crystallographically aligned with the thermal gradient [15]:
The resulting microstructure varies as a function of build position. In the remelted zone immediately adjacent to the fusion boundary with the substrate, grains nucleate epitaxially on the substrate grain structure and grow rapidly into the melt pool. In the mid-build region, columnar grains may span multiple layers, periodically interrupted by the remelted zone of each subsequent pass but generally maintaining directional continuity. In the near-top region, typically the topmost few layers, depending on layer thickness and thermal history, grains are less affected by reheating from above and therefore may exhibit a coarser, more as-solidified morphology [12,40]. Figure 13 illustrates the microstructural gradient from the substrate to the build top in a WAAM deposit. The near-substrate region contains fine equiaxed grains due to repeated remelting and reheating. In contrast, the near-top region develops coarse columnar grains because these layers experience less reheating after deposition.

For a given alloy system, these boundaries are calculated from Equation (18) and the dendrite stability criteria [15,16]. In WAAM, the G and R operating points vary continuously around the melt pool perimeter: G is highest and R is lowest at the fusion boundary (where solidification is just established), yielding high G/R values that favor planar or cellular growth; toward the pool center, G decreases and R increases, producing G/R values more characteristic of columnar-dendritic growth. This spatial variation produces the mixed microstructures, such as cellular regions near the fusion boundary and columnar-dendritic regions in the melt-pool interior, which are characteristic of many WAAM deposits [16,65].
A practical implication is that increasing the travel speed v at a fixed arc power P changes G and R simultaneously. At the trailing boundary of the melt pool, R = v·cos φ, where φ is the angle between the travel direction and the normal to the local solidification front, so R varies from approximately v at the pool centerline to nearly zero at the fusion boundary, whereas G depends on the melt-pool shape and the thermal boundary conditions [16]. Using three-dimensional heat-transfer and fluid-flow modeling of WAAM deposits, Ou et al. [65] showed that a faster travel speed increases the cooling rate G·R and decreases G/R. These two changes act on different aspects of the solidification structure and must be interpreted separately. The increase in G·R reduces the primary dendrite arm spacing according to Equation (20), i.e., it refines the dendritic length scale. The decrease in G/R reduces the stability of the solidification front and moves the operating point toward columnar-dendritic growth and, when sufficient constitutional undercooling and nucleation sites are available, toward the columnar-to-equiaxed transition (Equations (18) and (19)); this is a change in solidification morphology, not an increase in dendrite size. A faster travel speed should therefore not be equated with dendritic coarsening, and its net effect on a given deposit must be evaluated with thermal simulation because the melt-pool geometry changes at the same time.
7.2. Porosity, Solidification Cracking and Delamination
Porosity is one of the most prevalent and mechanistically complex defects in WAAM, particularly in aluminum alloys. The dominant mechanism, hydrogen porosity, arises from the dramatic change in hydrogen solubility at the melting point [42,73]. For aluminum, hydrogen solubility drops from approximately 0.65 mL/100 g in the liquid state to approximately 0.034 mL/100 g in the solid state at the melting point (a ratio of approximately 19:1) [16]. This discontinuity drives hydrogen rejection from the advancing solidification front: if the local hydrogen concentration CH exceeds the solubility in the solid CHsol and the solidification rate is sufficient to entrap rejected hydrogen, gas pores can nucleate and grow.

For hydrogen pores in liquid aluminum (ρl ≈ 2.4 × 103 kg·m−3, μl ≈ 1 × 10−3 Pa·s), Equation (25) gives vStokes ≈ 0.13 mm/s for rp = 5 µm, ≈ 0.5 mm/s for rp = 10 µm, and ≈ 13 mm/s for rp = 50 µm. Because typical solidification rates in WAAM are R ≈ 1–10 mm/s, pores smaller than approximately 10–20 µm rise more slowly than the solidification front advances and are likely to be entrapped, whereas pores of several tens of micrometers can escape if they nucleate early enough. This analysis explains why bead geometry matters: a narrow, deep bead requires pores to travel longer distances to escape, increasing entrapment probability. Optimizing bead geometry toward wider and shallower profiles through appropriate current, travel speed, and transfer-mode control can reduce hydrogen porosity [16]. Other process variables also matter: in WAAM of AlSi5 (AW4043), a higher shielding-gas flow rate increased porosity because forced convection accelerated melt-pool solidification and limited pore escape [42], whereas for 21 AA2319 panels, porosity was not strongly dependent on CMT mode, wire feed speed, or the ratio of wire feed speed to travel speed within the tested ranges but varied significantly between wire batches, reflecting differences in wire surface finish [43].
Fu et al. [44] reported a non-monotonic relationship between hot-wire current and porosity in hot-wire arc additive manufacturing of aluminum, with a minimum at 100 A. A plausible interpretation is that at lower hot-wire currents insufficient preheating leaves hydrogen-bearing surface contamination on the wire; whereas above 100 A, the enlarged melt pool increases Marangoni turbulence and extends the solidification time, both of which can increase pore entrapment. The minimum porosity at approximately 100 A corresponds to the optimal balance between pre-heating, which reduces hydrogen sources, and melt-pool size, which governs pore escape probability. 7.3. Summary of Defect Mechanisms and Governing Relationships
This subsection summarizes the main defect mechanisms and governing relationships in WAAM. Figure 18 shows two important defects related to thermal stress and inter-layer bonding. Figure 18a shows solidification cracking as a mushy-zone tearing mechanism. During solidification, liquid films remain between growing dendrites within the brittleness temperature range (BTR). This region is weak because it is not fully solidified. When tensile residual stress acts across this semi-solid zone, the liquid film can rupture and form a crack. This problem is more serious in alloys with a wide solidification range, strong solute segregation, and poor resistance to thermal contraction [16].

Figure 18b shows delamination caused by weak inter-layer bonding. In WAAM, each new layer must partially remelt the previous layer to form a sound metallurgical bond. If remelting is insufficient, or if oxidation and unsuitable inter-pass temperature affect the interface, a weak bonding zone may remain. During cooling, tensile residual stress develops due to constrained thermal contraction. If this stress exceeds the inter-layer bond strength, separation occurs along the layer interface. Therefore, delamination is both an inter-layer bonding defect and a thermomechanical failure mode.

These defects are controlled by heat input, melt-pool stability, inter-pass temperature, solidification behavior, shielding quality, and deposition path. Porosity is mainly linked to hydrogen rejection and gas entrapment. Solidification cracking is caused by tensile stress acting on semi-solid interdendritic liquid films. Residual stress forms due to constrained thermal contraction. Delamination occurs when the inter-layer bond is too weak to resist cooling stress. Columnar grain coarsening is related to epitaxial growth along the build direction. Geometric deviation is linked to bead instability and heat accumulation during multilayer deposition.
