Cold Metal Transfer \(CMT\)\, developed by Fronius International\, is among the most thermally efficient GMAW modes currently used for WAAM\. In CMT\, the wire feed motion and welding current are electronically synchronized\: as the wire approaches the melt pool and makes contact\, the current is reduced to near zero and the wire is retracted to mechanically assist droplet detachment at up to 70 Hz\. This controlled retraction eliminates the uncontrolled arc\-off phase associated with conventional SCT\, thereby lowering heat input\, spatter\, and distortion in many GMAW\-WAAM applications \[49\]\.

Galeazzi et al\. \[51\] compared conventional GMAW with the CMT\, CMT Advanced\, and CMT Pulse variants for thin walls of AISI 420 martensitic stainless steel and found that CMT Advanced and CMT Pulse lay at opposite extremes of the tested range\: CMT Advanced gave the lowest heat input and the best wall\-height performance\, whereas CMT Pulse lay at the high\-heat\-input end\. The metallurgical consequence of such differences can be interpreted through the inverse dependence of grain size\, or of the scale of the transformation products\, on the cooling rate\:

A higher cooling rate shortens the time available for grain\-boundary migration and for coarsening of transformation products\. A variant that raises the energy delivered per unit length\, such as CMT Pulse\, is therefore expected to enlarge the melt pool\, extend the time spent at high temperature\, and lower the cooling rate through the relevant temperature range\, all of which favor coarser structures\; conversely\, a low\-heat\-input variant such as CMT Advanced is expected to favor finer structures\. Grain size must therefore be interpreted together with the heat input per cycle and the reheating history\, and a larger grain size should not be associated with a higher cooling rate unless an additional mechanism\, such as reheating by subsequent layers\, is demonstrated\. This interpretation is consistent with infrared measurements on ER309LSi thick walls by Silva et al\. \[52\]\: at the same wire feed rate\, CMT Pulse delivered a higher power than CMT\; without interlayer idle time\, the area above 900 °C in the last layer was 1013 mm2 for CMT Pulse and 400\.8 mm2 for CMT\, and the mean interlayer temperature was on average 15\.0\% higher for CMT Pulse\; interlayer idle times of up to 300 s controlled heat accumulation for both variants\. Separately\, Luo et al\. \[53\] compared pulsed and non\-pulsed arcs in WAAM of aluminum alloys and found that the pulsed arc gave a higher droplet\-transfer frequency\, smaller droplets\, and a higher deposition efficiency at similar arc power\; because the arc force on the droplet also increased with arc power and could cause collapse of the deposited layer\, they recommended the lowest pulsed arc power compatible with the required productivity\.

Despite its thermal advantages in many WAAM applications \[54\]\, CMT adoption remains constrained by higher equipment cost\, approximately two to three times that of conventional GMAW\, and greater system complexity\. As CMT technology matures and competition reduces costs\, its adoption in WAAM is expected to increase considerably\. Metal\-transfer\-mode selection in GMAW\-WAAM is therefore a thermal and geometric control strategy rather than only a droplet detachment mechanism\, because transfer stability directly affects heat input\, remelting depth\, bead regularity\, spatter\, and defect formation\.

\#\# 5\. Deposition Path Planning and Thermal Management in WAAM

Beyond heat\-source selection\, WAAM build quality is strongly affected by the path followed by the torch and by the thermal state retained between successive layers\. Deposition path strategy determines not only geometric fidelity\, but also local reheating\, cooling intervals\, residual stress distribution and microstructural uniformity\. For this reason\, path planning and inter\-pass temperature control should be considered together as coupled thermal\-management strategies\.

\#\#\# 5\.1\. Path Planning Fundamentals and Deposition Patterns

Deposition path planning is among the most consequential decisions in WAAM process design\. The path determines not only geometric fidelity\, but also the thermal history experienced at each material location\, which in turn governs microstructure\, residual stress distribution\, and mechanical properties\. Jafari et al\. \[24\] identified deposition path strategy as a primary determinant of WAAM microstructure\. Ding et al\. \[55\] demonstrated that\, for thin\-walled structures\, optimal step\-over distance dSO can more than double material efficiency relative to an unoptimized baseline\. Four classical deposition path patterns are used in WAAM\, each with distinct thermal\, geometric\, and efficiency characteristics\, as shown in Figure 8\.

Figure 8\. Classical WAAM deposition path patterns\: \(a\) Raster parallel bidirectional lines\; \(b\) zigzag continuous single bidirectional pass\; \(c\) spiral\-in inward continuous spiral\; \(d\) contour successive boundary offsets\.

\- Raster\: Parallel lines are deposited in alternating directions\. Its advantages include reduced heat accumulation due to cooling intervals between adjacent lines\. Its limitations include frequent arc starts and stops\, which may introduce bead\-height variability\, and boundary discretization errors that reduce geometric accuracy at perimeter regions \[57\]\.
\- Zigzag\: Parallel lines are connected into a single continuous bidirectional pass\. Its advantages include fewer arc\-start and arc\-stop instabilities and improved bead continuity\. Its limitations include possible localized heat accumulation at path reversals in complex geometries\, while boundary accuracy remains similar to raster strategies\.
\- Spiral\-in\: Smooth inward spiraling paths distribute thermal gradients more evenly\. Its advantages include improved thermal uniformity for circular or ovoid cross\-sections and smoother continuous motion\. Its limitation is that it is not readily generalizable to arbitrary polygonal cross\-sections\.
\- Contour\: Successive offsets are deposited parallel to the part boundary\. Its advantages include high boundary accuracy and regular direction changes that can reduce distortion and anisotropy\. Its limitations include the possibility of overfill or underfill in regions where cross\-section geometry diverges from the regular contour spacing\.

These path strategies should therefore be interpreted not merely as geometric toolpaths\, but as thermal\-management strategies that determine local reheating\, cooling intervals\, residual stress distribution\, and microstructural uniformity\.

Hybrid strategies combining contour perimeter passes with interior zigzag fill\, which are widely used in WAAM path planning software\, represent the current best practice for geometrically complex parts\. \#\#\# 5\.2\. Inter\-Pass Temperature Control and Heat Accumulation

Because deposition path controls local reheating and cooling intervals\, path planning must be considered together with inter\-pass temperature management\. As WAAM builds progress in height\, the thermal resistance between the melt pool and the heat sink increases because the deposited material progressively separates the active melt pool from the substrate and because the geometrical heat\-sink area does not increase proportionally with deposited volume\. In H13 tool\-steel walls deposited with pulsed MIG at a controlled inter\-layer temperature of 150 °C\, Wang et al\. \[58\] attributed the variety of microstructures observed at different locations to the different thermal histories of those regions\.

Two principal inter\-pass temperature management strategies exist\. The first is fixed dwell time\, in which deposition of each new layer is delayed by a fixed time after completion of the previous layer\. This approach is simple to implement but does not ensure a consistent thermal state because cooling is non\-linear\. The second is fixed inter\-pass temperature\, TIP\, in which deposition begins only when the deposit surface reaches a target temperature\. Montevecchi et al\. \[59\] advocated fixed TIP control as better suited to maintaining thermal consistency\. However\, Geng et al\. \[60\] cautioned that identifying the appropriate TIP is largely empirical\, and the analytical process model of Rios et al\. \[61\] for Ti\-6Al\-4V deposition showed that the inter\-pass temperature must be included to predict layer height and wall width\, confirming that the thermal state at the start of each layer is a process variable in its own right\. \#\# 6\. Welding Metallurgy of WAAM\: Melt Pool\, Solidification\, Phase Transformation and Residual Stress

The process\-level variables discussed above ultimately affect WAAM performance through their influence on melt\-pool behavior\, solidification\, phase transformation\, and residual stress development\.

\#\#\# 6\.1\. Melt\-Pool Thermodynamics and Heat\-Source Modeling

Traditional fusion welding and WAAM are governed by the closely related fundamental thermodynamic and fluid\-dynamics principles\. In both cases\, the arc creates a localized heat source that raises the material above the liquidus temperature TL\, forming a melt pool that is bounded by the solidification front at TL and the fusion boundary at TS \(solidus\)\. The heat flux distribution from the arc is commonly modeled using Goldak’s double\-ellipsoidal heat source model \[29\]\:

Within the melt pool\, fluid flow is driven by four competing forces\: Marangoni or thermocapillary convection\, buoyancy\-driven convection\, electromagnetic or Lorentz forces\, and arc pressure\. The Marangoni number Ma characterizes the dominance of surface\-tension\-driven flow\:

The Reynolds number Re \= ρl · vfl · Lmp\/μ of the melt\-pool flow characterizes the ratio of inertial to viscous forces\; together with Ma\, it governs how strongly the flow redistributes solute and affects gas escape and porosity formation\.

\#\#\# 6\.2\. Solidification and the G\/R Framework

The microstructural outcome of solidification is controlled by two parameters\: the temperature gradient G \(K\/m\) at the solidification front and the solidification velocity R \(m\/s\)\. Their ratio G\/R governs the stability of the solid–liquid interface and hence the resulting solidification mode\, as established by the constitutional undercooling criterion \[15\]\:

The product G·R equals the local cooling rate Ṫ \(K\/s\) at the solidification front and governs the primary dendrite arm spacing \(PDAS\) λ1\:

The significance of the G\/R framework in WAAM is therefore not only predictive but diagnostic\, because it explains why identical nominal arc parameters can produce different microstructures at different build heights as the thermal boundary condition evolves\.

\#\#\# 6\.3\. Welding Versus WAAM\: Repeated Thermal Cycling and Microstructural Consequences

While WAAM and welding share the physics described above\, they differ in several important ways that have direct consequences for microstructure and properties\:

\- Repeated thermal cycling\: In single\-pass welding\, each material point generally experiences one dominant heating\-cooling cycle\. In WAAM\, each point experiences multiple thermal cycles from the deposition of subsequent layers\, with the number of cycles depending on build height and layer thickness\. Each cycle reheats the material to a peak temperature Tpeak that decreases with distance from the torch\. These repeated cycles drive\: \(a\) grain growth\, following the isothermal kinetic relationn − 0n \= K0·t·exp\[−Qg\/\(Rg·T\)\] \(Table 4\)\, with n \= 2 for ideal parabolic growth and n \> 2 when boundaries are pinned\, integrated over the thermal history\, \(b\) precipitation\/dissolution of secondary phases\, \(c\) recovery and partial recrystallization\, and \(d\) microstructural banding due to alternating coarse\/fine zones corresponding to Tpeak above and below the recrystallization temperature Trex\.
\- Thermal gradient directionality\: In welding\, the dominant heat extraction direction is often lateral into the parent plates\, whereas in WAAM\, heat is extracted primarily downward through the substrate and previously deposited material\, especially in the early build stages\. This promotes epitaxial columnar grain growth along the build direction \(BD\)\. The result is often a strong crystallographic texture\, typically \<001\> parallel to BD in cubic metals\, which may persist across the build height unless disrupted by allotropic transformations\, as in Ti\-6Al\-4V\, where the β→α transformation partially randomizes texture\, or by active grain refinement strategies \[67\]\.
\- Chemical composition freedom\: In single\-pass welding of two bulk components with filler wire\, the resulting deposit chemistry is strongly influenced by dilution with the base material\. In WAAM\, material is deposited onto a flat substrate or prior layer\, allowing the deposit chemistry to be varied spatially by switching wire feedstock or using multiple feed wires\, thereby enabling functionally graded structures with tailored property distributions\; twin\-wire WAAM has been used to fabricate intermetallic alloys and functionally graded materials \[35\]\.
\- Process automation and precision\: Welding may be manual\, mechanized\, or automated\, whereas WAAM is typically computer\-controlled\, enabling improved reproducibility of melt\-pool placement\, layer thickness\, and deposition trajectory compared with manual welding and comparable to advanced automated welding systems \[16\]\.
\- Melt pool aspect ratio and penetration\: Welding often requires a relatively high depth\-to\-width melt\-pool ratio to achieve joint penetration\, whereas WAAM usually requires controlled remelting of the prior layer rather than full plate penetration\. This generally produces shallower melt pools and different G\/R distributions at the solidification front\, which can alter dendritic growth\, fusion\-boundary morphology\, and inter\-layer bonding compared with conventional welding at equivalent power levels\.

Table 4\. Summary of governing equations for WAAM process–microstructure–defect relationships\.

Several of the characteristics listed above are shared with multi\-pass welding\. Thick\-section joints\, such as reactor pressure vessel welds that may require hundreds of passes\, also experience repeated reheating\, heat accumulation\, tempering or re\-transformation of earlier passes\, and residual stress build\-up\, and the metallurgy of reheated multi\-pass weld metal applies directly to WAAM \[16\,19\]\. The distinctive features of WAAM arise from its geometry and boundary conditions rather than from repetition itself\. \(i\) In a joint\, each pass is bounded by the groove faces of the parent plates\, which act as lateral heat sinks and epitaxial substrates\, whereas a WAAM wall is free\-standing\, so heat is conducted downward through a lengthening path of previously deposited material and lost from two free side surfaces\. \(ii\) In a joint\, the bead sequence\, bead placement\, and groove geometry change the direction of the thermal gradient from pass to pass\, whereas in a WAAM wall the fusion boundary advances upward in the same direction layer after layer\, so the thermal gradient remains aligned with the build direction while its magnitude decreases with height \[66\]\. \(iii\) The deposit forms the whole component rather than a joint between wrought members\, so the reheated as\-deposited microstructure and its build\-height gradient determine the properties of the entire part\. \(iv\) Inter\-pass conditions in WAAM are usually set by productivity and geometric stability rather than by a qualified welding procedure\, and they change as the build grows\.

The different microstructures arising from these distinct thermal conditions can be described conceptually across the build height\. Moving from the substrate toward the top of a WAAM build\, one may observe a gradient from a remelted or refined near\-substrate region\, through a thermally cycled mid\-build region characterized by banded microstructures\, to a columnar\-dominated near\-top region that has experienced the fewest reheating cycles\. Wang et al\. \[58\] likewise reported location\-dependent microstructures in H13 walls\, although the hardness remained within 300–360 HV from top to bottom and the as\-deposited tensile properties were anisotropic\.

\#\#\# 6\.4\. Phase Transformations and Residual Stress Development

In steels and titanium alloys\, solid\-state phase transformations during cooling from the melt pool strongly influence the final room\-temperature microstructure\. In single\-pass welding of ferritic steels\, the weld metal cools from the austenite \(γ\) field through the Ac3 temperature and transforms to ferrite morphologies such as allotriomorphic ferrite\, Widmanstätten ferrite\, acicular ferrite\, bainite\, or martensite depending on cooling rate and alloy composition\, as represented by continuous cooling transformation \(CCT\) diagrams \[16\]\. In WAAM\, the same transformation may occur during the first cooling cycle\; however\, subsequent layers reheat the prior deposit to peak temperatures that may partially or fully austenitize it again\, driving repeated transformation cycling that progressively homogenizes the microstructure in mid\-build regions while leaving the topmost layers in a more as\-deposited transformation state \[12\,40\]\.

For Ti\-6Al\-4V\, the dominant high\-temperature phase is body\-centered cubic β\, which transforms on cooling to hexagonal close\-packed α\, forming lamellar colonies or Widmanstätten α\, or to α′ martensite at higher cooling rates\. In WAAM\, the primary β columnar grains form by epitaxial solidification and persist through the β\-field on cooling\. The β → α transformation then partitions the columnar β into a microstructure of α laths\, whose morphology\, including coarse lamellae\, fine basketweave\, or acicular martensite\, is controlled by the local cooling rate through the β transus \[13\,62\,68\]\. Repeated reheating below the β transus in subsequent layers partially homogenizes this microstructure but does not fully eliminate prior\-β columnar grain inheritance\, a limitation that hybrid deformation strategies such as rolling and FSP are designed to overcome \[69\]\.

In aluminum alloys\, which lack allotropic transformations\, the solid\-state microstructural evolution in WAAM is controlled primarily by precipitation\, dissolution\, coarsening kinetics\, and grain\-boundary migration\. Repeated thermal cycling can dissolve strengthening precipitates\, such as θ′\-Al2Cu in 2xxx series alloys and β″\-Mg2Si in 6xxx series alloys\, in the heat\-affected region of each deposited layer\, creating over\-aged or solution\-annealed zones that degrade local strength\. This precipitate heterogeneity\, characterized by alternating zones of fresh precipitation and dissolution\, is one of the primary sources of the banded hardness profiles characteristic of aluminum WAAM builds \[70\]\. In addition to phase transformation\, residual stress development is another major metallurgical consequence of repeated WAAM thermal cycling\.

\#\# 7\. Microstructural Evolution and Defect Formation in WAAM

The metallurgical mechanisms discussed in Section 6 provide the basis for understanding the microstructural gradients and defects that develop during WAAM\.

\#\#\# 7\.1\. Columnar Grain Growth\, Epitaxy and Build\-Height Heterogeneity

The macrostructure of WAAM deposits is commonly characterized by epitaxial columnar grains that nucleate on the solid substrate or prior layer and grow preferentially along the maximum thermal gradient\, often aligned with the build direction \(BD\)\. This epitaxial growth occurs because the nucleation barrier ΔG\* for heterogeneous nucleation on an existing grain is zero when the growth direction is crystallographically aligned with the thermal gradient \[15\]\:

The resulting microstructure varies as a function of build position\. In the remelted zone immediately adjacent to the fusion boundary with the substrate\, grains nucleate epitaxially on the substrate grain structure and grow rapidly into the melt pool\. In the mid\-build region\, columnar grains may span multiple layers\, periodically interrupted by the remelted zone of each subsequent pass but generally maintaining directional continuity\. In the near\-top region\, typically the topmost few layers\, depending on layer thickness and thermal history\, grains are less affected by reheating from above and therefore may exhibit a coarser\, more as\-solidified morphology \[12\,40\]\. Figure 13 illustrates the microstructural gradient from the substrate to the build top in a WAAM deposit\. The near\-substrate region contains fine equiaxed grains due to repeated remelting and reheating\. In contrast\, the near\-top region develops coarse columnar grains because these layers experience less reheating after deposition\.

For a given alloy system\, these boundaries are calculated from Equation \(18\) and the dendrite stability criteria \[15\,16\]\. In WAAM\, the G and R operating points vary continuously around the melt pool perimeter\: G is highest and R is lowest at the fusion boundary \(where solidification is just established\)\, yielding high G\/R values that favor planar or cellular growth\; toward the pool center\, G decreases and R increases\, producing G\/R values more characteristic of columnar\-dendritic growth\. This spatial variation produces the mixed microstructures\, such as cellular regions near the fusion boundary and columnar\-dendritic regions in the melt\-pool interior\, which are characteristic of many WAAM deposits \[16\,65\]\.

A practical implication is that increasing the travel speed v at a fixed arc power P changes G and R simultaneously\. At the trailing boundary of the melt pool\, R \= v·cos φ\, where φ is the angle between the travel direction and the normal to the local solidification front\, so R varies from approximately v at the pool centerline to nearly zero at the fusion boundary\, whereas G depends on the melt\-pool shape and the thermal boundary conditions \[16\]\. Using three\-dimensional heat\-transfer and fluid\-flow modeling of WAAM deposits\, Ou et al\. \[65\] showed that a faster travel speed increases the cooling rate G·R and decreases G\/R\. These two changes act on different aspects of the solidification structure and must be interpreted separately\. The increase in G·R reduces the primary dendrite arm spacing according to Equation \(20\)\, i\.e\.\, it refines the dendritic length scale\. The decrease in G\/R reduces the stability of the solidification front and moves the operating point toward columnar\-dendritic growth and\, when sufficient constitutional undercooling and nucleation sites are available\, toward the columnar\-to\-equiaxed transition \(Equations \(18\) and \(19\)\)\; this is a change in solidification morphology\, not an increase in dendrite size\. A faster travel speed should therefore not be equated with dendritic coarsening\, and its net effect on a given deposit must be evaluated with thermal simulation because the melt\-pool geometry changes at the same time\.

\#\#\# 7\.2\. Porosity\, Solidification Cracking and Delamination

Porosity is one of the most prevalent and mechanistically complex defects in WAAM\, particularly in aluminum alloys\. The dominant mechanism\, hydrogen porosity\, arises from the dramatic change in hydrogen solubility at the melting point \[42\,73\]\. For aluminum\, hydrogen solubility drops from approximately 0\.65 mL\/100 g in the liquid state to approximately 0\.034 mL\/100 g in the solid state at the melting point \(a ratio of approximately 19\:1\) \[16\]\. This discontinuity drives hydrogen rejection from the advancing solidification front\: if the local hydrogen concentration CH exceeds the solubility in the solid CHsol and the solidification rate is sufficient to entrap rejected hydrogen\, gas pores can nucleate and grow\.

Pore nucleation is governed by Sieverts’s law \[16\]\:

The pore escape criterion is also important\: a hydrogen pore of radius rp in the melt pool will escape to the surface before solidification only if the Stokes velocity vStokes exceeds the solidification front velocity R \[16\]\:

For hydrogen pores in liquid aluminum \(ρl ≈ 2\.4 × 103 kg·m−3\, μl ≈ 1 × 10−3 Pa·s\)\, Equation \(25\) gives vStokes ≈ 0\.13 mm\/s for rp \= 5 µm\, ≈ 0\.5 mm\/s for rp \= 10 µm\, and ≈ 13 mm\/s for rp \= 50 µm\. Because typical solidification rates in WAAM are R ≈ 1–10 mm\/s\, pores smaller than approximately 10–20 µm rise more slowly than the solidification front advances and are likely to be entrapped\, whereas pores of several tens of micrometers can escape if they nucleate early enough\. This analysis explains why bead geometry matters\: a narrow\, deep bead requires pores to travel longer distances to escape\, increasing entrapment probability\. Optimizing bead geometry toward wider and shallower profiles through appropriate current\, travel speed\, and transfer\-mode control can reduce hydrogen porosity \[16\]\. Other process variables also matter\: in WAAM of AlSi5 \(AW4043\)\, a higher shielding\-gas flow rate increased porosity because forced convection accelerated melt\-pool solidification and limited pore escape \[42\]\, whereas for 21 AA2319 panels\, porosity was not strongly dependent on CMT mode\, wire feed speed\, or the ratio of wire feed speed to travel speed within the tested ranges but varied significantly between wire batches\, reflecting differences in wire surface finish \[43\]\.

Fu et al\. \[44\] reported a non\-monotonic relationship between hot\-wire current and porosity in hot\-wire arc additive manufacturing of aluminum\, with a minimum at 100 A\. A plausible interpretation is that at lower hot\-wire currents insufficient preheating leaves hydrogen\-bearing surface contamination on the wire\; whereas above 100 A\, the enlarged melt pool increases Marangoni turbulence and extends the solidification time\, both of which can increase pore entrapment\. The minimum porosity at approximately 100 A corresponds to the optimal balance between pre\-heating\, which reduces hydrogen sources\, and melt\-pool size\, which governs pore escape probability\. \#\#\# 7\.3\. Summary of Defect Mechanisms and Governing Relationships

This subsection summarizes the main defect mechanisms and governing relationships in WAAM\. Figure 18 shows two important defects related to thermal stress and inter\-layer bonding\. Figure 18a shows solidification cracking as a mushy\-zone tearing mechanism\. During solidification\, liquid films remain between growing dendrites within the brittleness temperature range \(BTR\)\. This region is weak because it is not fully solidified\. When tensile residual stress acts across this semi\-solid zone\, the liquid film can rupture and form a crack\. This problem is more serious in alloys with a wide solidification range\, strong solute segregation\, and poor resistance to thermal contraction \[16\]\.

Figure 18b shows delamination caused by weak inter\-layer bonding\. In WAAM\, each new layer must partially remelt the previous layer to form a sound metallurgical bond\. If remelting is insufficient\, or if oxidation and unsuitable inter\-pass temperature affect the interface\, a weak bonding zone may remain\. During cooling\, tensile residual stress develops due to constrained thermal contraction\. If this stress exceeds the inter\-layer bond strength\, separation occurs along the layer interface\. Therefore\, delamination is both an inter\-layer bonding defect and a thermomechanical failure mode\.

As summarized in Table 5\, WAAM defects include porosity\, solidification cracking\, residual stress\, delamination\, columnar grain coarsening\, and geometric deviation\. These defects are controlled by heat input\, melt\-pool stability\, inter\-pass temperature\, solidification behavior\, shielding quality\, and deposition path\. Porosity is mainly linked to hydrogen rejection and gas entrapment\. Solidification cracking is caused by tensile stress acting on semi\-solid interdendritic liquid films\. Residual stress forms due to constrained thermal contraction\. Delamination occurs when the inter\-layer bond is too weak to resist cooling stress\. Columnar grain coarsening is related to epitaxial growth along the build direction\. Geometric deviation is linked to bead instability and heat accumulation during multilayer deposition\.

\#\# 8\. Quantitative and Alloy\-Specific Synthesis of WAAM Performance

The preceding sections show that WAAM performance is governed by coupled process\, thermal\, microstructural\, and defect\-related mechanisms\. A quantitative synthesis is therefore useful\, but it must be interpreted cautiously because reported values across the literature differ in alloy condition\, build geometry\, testing direction\, measurement location\, and post\-processing state\.

\#\#\# 8\.1\. Representative Quantitative Trends Across the Literature

With this caveat in mind\, Table 6 compiles quantitative results that could be traced to the original publications according to the criteria in Section 2\.3\. For each entry\, the controlled variable and the condition to which each value refers are stated\, so that values are compared within\, not across\, studies\.

Although the entries in Table 6 cannot be pooled statistically\, three observations are consistent with the mechanisms discussed in Section 4\, Section 5\, Section 6 and Section 7\. First\, when the heat input or the inter\-pass temperature is varied within a single study\, the defect or property response is non\-monotonic\, with optima at intermediate conditions\: porosity passed through a minimum at an intermediate hot\-wire current \[44\]\, and tensile strength peaked at an intermediate inter\-pass temperature before the wall collapsed at the highest one \[63\]\. Second\, the transfer\-mode variant changes the heat input at nominally similar deposition conditions\, as shown for CMT variants in martensitic stainless steel \[51\]\. Third\, inter\-layer or post\-deposition treatments act on features that the arc process alone does not remove\, such as the coarse as\-deposited grain structure of aluminum walls \[74\] or Laves phase retained near a dissimilar interface \[75\]\.

Build\-height gradients in grain size and hardness follow from the same thermal history\. As a wall grows\, heat accumulates and the effective temperature gradient at the solidification front decreases \(Section 6\.2\)\, so grain size tends to increase and hardness to fluctuate along the build direction\, with bands corresponding to regions reheated above and below the relevant transformation or precipitation temperatures \[40\,70\]\. The magnitude of these gradients is alloy\- and geometry\-specific and should be quantified by layer\-resolved measurements within a given build rather than inferred from values compiled across studies\. More generally\, the underlying mechanisms are strongly alloy\-dependent\. Although the heat\-source and solidification principles discussed above are common to all WAAM processes\, their microstructural consequences differ considerably among alloy families because phase transformation behavior\, thermal conductivity\, solidification range\, hydrogen solubility\, and precipitation kinetics vary significantly\.

\#\#\# 8\.2\. Ferrous and Stainless Steels

In mild steels and low\-alloy steels\, WAAM deposits may exhibit columnar prior austenite grains in as\-solidified regions\, which subsequently transform into ferrite–pearlite\, bainite\, or martensite depending on alloy composition and cooling rate\. The continuous cooling transformation \(CCT\) diagram governs the transformation product for a given cooling rate\. Dickens et al\. \[40\] documented a wall microstructure comprising large equiaxed ferrite \(α\) and pearlite \(α \+ Fe3C\) with grain sizes of approximately 60 µm in reheated mid\-wall regions\. In unreheated top\-layer regions\, columnar austenite grains transformed to coarser Widmanstätten ferrite colonies\, with reported dimensions of approximately 600 µm × 1000 µm\. The practical implication is that the uppermost layers of a WAAM steel component may exhibit lower toughness and ductility than the thermally cycled bulk\, requiring consideration of post\-process heat treatment\, surface machining\, or location\-specific property qualification in toughness\-critical applications \[12\,32\,40\]\.

For 316L stainless steel WAAM\, solidification is commonly described as austenitic or austenite\-dominant depending on composition and thermal history\. The deposit may exhibit columnar austenite grains with residual ferrite stringers along grain boundaries\, produced by segregation of ferrite\-stabilizing elements such as Cr and Mo during solidification\. Repeated reheating cycles in mid\-build regions can partially homogenize this segregation pattern\, but may also promote secondary\-phase precipitation at grain boundaries under certain thermal exposure conditions\, which is a concern for corrosion resistance and embrittlement in elevated\-temperature service \[32\,78\,79\]\.

\#\#\# 8\.3\. Aluminum and Titanium Alloys

Aluminum alloys present the most complex suites of WAAM microstructural challenges owing to\: \(i\) the high hydrogen solubility ratio at the melting point\, which drives porosity\; \(ii\) wide solidification temperature ranges in high\-solute alloys\, which increase hot\-cracking susceptibility\; \(iii\) sensitivity of strengthening precipitates to dissolution or over\-aging during reheating\; \(iv\) high thermal conductivity\, which modifies the thermal gradient at the solidification front\; and \(v\) the stable refractory oxide layer that rapidly re\-forms on exposed aluminum surfaces and can reduce inter\-layer bonding unless disrupted by arc action\.

The microstructure of WAAM aluminum alloys is commonly characterized by columnar grains with cellular or columnar\-dendritic substructures\. The inter\-dendritic eutectic constituents depend on alloy series\: β\-Al3Mg2 in 5xxx alloys\, θ\-Al2Cu in 2xxx alloys\, and eutectic Si in 4xxx alloys \[16\]\. The 4xxx series silicon\-bearing alloys often show better WAAM processability than many higher\-solute aluminum alloys because their narrower solidification temperature range reduces the brittleness temperature range \[16\]\. In GMAW\-based deposition of common aluminum filler alloys\, the 4000\-series wires gave better bead width\, porosity\, strength\, and defect sensitivity than ER1100 and ER5356\, and ER5356 showed the highest porosity \[77\]\. With variable\-polarity CMT\, Zhang et al\. \[80\] obtained equiaxed grains of 20\.6–28\.5 µm with random orientation in Al\-6Mg deposits\, whereas other arc modes produced larger columnar grains\; the tensile strength reached 333 MPa but was 8–27\% anisotropic because of micropores in the interlayer regions\. In AlMg5Mn deposited with the CMT\, CMT Advanced\, and CMT Pulse Advanced modes\, Gierth et al\. \[81\] controlled the layer geometry and kept the porosity area fraction below 1\% by adjusting the energy input per unit length\, which also changed the tensile strength and hardness\.

Vimal et al\. \[70\] reviewed WAAM of aluminum alloys and\, consistent with other reviews \[7\,14\,82\]\, identified six primary challenges\: \(i\) porosity from hydrogen rejection\; \(ii\) tensile residual stress\; \(iii\) cracks and deformation when σres \> σUTS\; \(iv\) delamination\; \(v\) difficulty in processing 7xxx series alloys by single\-wire WAAM\; and \(vi\) turbulent melt pool development in 7xxx and 6xxx series due to high vapor pressure of volatile alloying elements such as Zn and Mg\. For the 7xxx and 6xxx alloys specifically\, a turbulent melt pool promotes oxide film entrainment and bifilm defects\, which can be difficult to detect using conventional ultrasonic inspection and can considerably reduce ductility and fatigue life \[70\]\. The sensitivity of fatigue life to pore geometry has been quantified for additively manufactured Ti\-6Al\-4V\, for which finite element analysis gave stress concentration factors of 2\.08 for internal spherical pores and 2\.5 for internal oblate pores and identified subsurface pores as the most critical \[83\]\.

Ti\-6Al\-4V is the most studied titanium alloy in WAAM because of its widespread aerospace applications \[46\,84\,85\]\. Using PAW\-based WAAM in an argon atmosphere\, Artaza et al\. \[46\] deposited Ti\-6Al\-4V walls at 2 kg\/h with oxygen levels below 100 ppm\, and the annealed material met the AMS 4928 yield and tensile strength requirements whether heat treatment was performed in vacuum\, air\, or argon\. In WAAM\, Ti\-6Al\-4V solidifies as body\-centered cubic β\, forming columnar β grains with a strong \<001\> texture parallel to the build direction\. These columnar β grains are stable above the β transus\, approximately 995 °C\, and transform on cooling to α \+ β microstructures\, including lamellar α colonies or Widmanstätten α within the β matrix\, with the specific morphology governed by local cooling rate\. In Jominy end\-quench experiments on Ti\-6Al\-4V\, cooling rates above 410 °C\/s produced a fully martensitic microstructure\; a massive transformation occurred between 410 and 20 °C\/s\, and this was progressively replaced by diffusion\-controlled Widmanstätten α as the cooling rate decreased further \[68\]\; the rates prevailing in a given WAAM deposit depend on the heat input and on the reheating history \[13\,85\]\.

The repeated thermal cycling of WAAM reheats prior β columnar grains below the β transus\, driving solid\-state transformation without re\-solidification\. Progressive decomposition of as\-formed martensite α’ to equilibrium α \+ β\, and coarsening of α laths with increasing thermal exposure\, produce the characteristic banded microstructure of WAAM Ti\-6Al\-4V\. This banding can include alternating regions of finer α morphologies in zones that experienced higher thermal exposure and coarser lamellar α colonies in regions subjected to lower thermal exposure\. Because the mechanical properties of Ti\-6Al\-4V are strongly dependent on α morphology and prior\-β grain structure\, these microstructural bands produce property gradients that remain a significant challenge for certification of WAAM titanium components for aerospace applications\.

\#\#\# 8\.4\. Nickel\-Based Superalloys and Cross\-Alloy Performance Comparison

Nickel\-based superalloys\, including Inconel 625\, Inconel 718\, and Hastelloy\-type alloys\, are challenging materials for WAAM because of their high alloying content\, strong segregation tendency\, potential formation of Laves and other secondary phases\, high residual stress generation\, and sluggish recrystallization kinetics that can limit grain refinement\. In WAAM of Inconel 625 and Inconel 718\, columnar γ grains with a strong ⟨001⟩ texture are commonly reported\, and Laves phase enriched in Nb \(and Mo in Inconel 625\) can form in interdendritic regions because of solidification segregation \[75\,76\]\. In GTAW\-based deposition of Inconel 625\, Wang et al\. \[76\] observed cellular grains near the substrate\, upward\-oriented columnar dendrites in the layer bands\, and a transition to equiaxed grains in the top region\; Nb and Mo segregation strengthened with deposit height\, the primary dendrite arm spacing correlated with the Laves content\, and the near\-substrate region had the highest microhardness and tensile strength\.

The Laves phase in nickel\-superalloy WAAM is particularly detrimental because it can raise local hardness\, reduce toughness\, and serve as a crack\-initiation site under thermal or mechanical cycling\. Post\-WAAM solution treatment above the Laves solvus can dissolve this phase and redistribute segregating elements more homogeneously\, but such high\-temperature treatments must be balanced against undesirable grain growth\. Hasani et al\. \[75\] used elastic\-field models\, informed by neutron diffraction and nanohardness data collected across a WAAM IN718\/S275 interface\, to interpret how heat treatment changes dislocation mobility and the Peierls–Nabarro stress\, and reported that Laves phase persisted near the interface even after solution treatment at 1080 °C for 1 h\.

\#\#\# 8\.5\. Comparison with Multi\-Pass Weld Metal

A systematic comparison of WAAM deposits with multi\-pass weld metal of the same alloy\, process\, and heat input would show directly which characteristics are distinctive to WAAM\. Matched datasets of this kind\, with the same filler wire\, process\, heat input\, and test orientation\, are rarely reported\; most WAAM studies compare their results with wrought material \[21\,78\]\. The mechanisms discussed in Section 6 and Section 7 nevertheless allow the characteristics to be classified\. Shared with multi\-pass weld metal are the dendritic solidification structure and microsegregation governed by G\, R\, and the solidification range\; δ\-ferrite and its transformation products in austenitic stainless steels \[78\]\; tempering and re\-transformation of earlier passes in steels\; and hydrogen porosity in aluminum alloys\. Distinctive to WAAM\, or more pronounced in it\, are columnar grains and crystallographic texture aligned with the build direction over the full height of the component \[75\]\, and the resulting anisotropy\; build\-height gradients in grain size\, segregation\, and hardness caused by the evolving heat\-extraction path \[66\,76\]\; the absence of dilution\, so that the deposit chemistry equals the wire chemistry and cannot be adjusted by a parent metal\; and residual stress fields that develop in a free\-standing wall and redistribute when it is released from the substrate \[25\,26\]\. Establishing these differences quantitatively requires matched WAAM and multi\-pass weld specimens\, which remains a research need\.

\#\#\# 8\.6\. WAAM\-Specific Feedstock

Most WAAM wires are conventional welding consumables\, whose compositions were designed to give sound joints after dilution with the parent metal in one or a few passes \[21\]\. In WAAM\, the wire alone forms the component\; there is no dilution\, and the deposit is reheated many times\, so compositions that are adequate for joining can be unsuitable for bulk deposition\. Feedstock tailored for WAAM has followed three routes\. For aluminum alloys\, wires micro\-alloyed with Sc and Zr form Al3\(Sc\,Zr\) particles that nucleate equiaxed grains and reduce hot\-cracking susceptibility\, and tailored fillers have enabled the deposition of high\-strength Al–Zn–Mg–Cu compositions that crack when deposited with standard wires \[21\,86\]\. For titanium and nickel alloys\, modified chemistries\, such as β\-stabilizer additions to refine prior\-β grains in Ti\-6Al\-4V and reduced Nb in 718\-type wires to limit Laves formation\, and impurity limits stricter than those for welding consumables have been proposed \[21\]\. For duplex stainless steels\, wires with adjusted N\, Ni\, and Mn contents are used to maintain the ferrite–austenite balance under repeated reheating \[21\]\. These modifications address the WAAM\-specific conditions discussed in Section 6 and Section 7\: the absence of dilution\, the columnar growth promoted by directional heat extraction\, and the cumulative reheating of the deposit\.

\#\# 9\. Industrial Readiness\, Advantages\, Limitations and Qualification Challenges

The process and metallurgical characteristics discussed above explain why WAAM is attractive for large\-scale metallic component production\. At the same time\, they also explain why industrial qualification remains challenging\. WAAM offers clear advantages in deposition rate\, material utilization\, component scale and cost\, but these benefits must be balanced against surface finish limitations\, microstructural heterogeneity\, residual stress\, porosity\, process complexity and certification requirements\.

\#\#\# 9\.1\. Industrial Advantages and Persistent Technical Limitations

The technical trends discussed in Section 3\, Section 4\, Section 5\, Section 6\, Section 7 and Section 8 explain why WAAM is attractive for industrial manufacturing\, but they also show why qualification remains challenging\.

\- Near\-net\-shape capability\: WAAM can reduce buy\-to\-fly \(BTF\) ratios to approximately 1\.5\:1 to 3\:1 for aerospace titanium components\, compared with 12\:1 to 20\:1 by conventional machining \[1\,14\]\.
\- Scalability\: WAAM can fabricate components ranging from sub\-kilogram prototypes to multi\-tonne structural parts several meters in dimension\, a scale that remains difficult and economically impractical for most powder\-based AM processes\.
\- High deposition rate\: WAAM can achieve deposition rates of approximately 1–10 kg\/h\, typically 2–4 kg\/h for GMAW\-WAAM\, which is appreciably higher than powder\-bed fusion processes\.
\- Low capital and operating costs\: WAAM uses standard industrial welding equipment\, widely available wire feedstock\, and established maintenance infrastructure\.
\- Near\-100\% material utilization\: Wire feedstock is fully consumed\, unlike powder processes requiring powder recycling and contamination management\.
\- Multi\-axis deposition flexibility\: Multi\-axis robotic systems enable deposition on non\-planar surfaces and complex fixture geometries\, although the achievable geometric resolution remains lower than powder\-bed processes\.
\- Broad feedstock availability\: Standard welding wires in steel\, aluminum\, titanium\, nickel\, copper\, and intermetallic alloys are commercially available at low cost\.
\- Established metallurgical knowledge base\: The extensive body of welding metallurgy science provides a direct foundation for WAAM process development and defect understanding\.

Despite these advantages\, WAAM also presents several persistent challenges that must be addressed before wider industrial qualification and certification\.

\- Surface finish\: Bead\-on\-bead deposition produces surface waviness\, commonly with Ra values of approximately 10–50 µm\, requiring post\-deposition machining in most structural applications\.
\- Microstructural heterogeneity\: The layered thermal history produces non\-uniform microstructures from base to top\, including columnar grain continuity and property anisotropy that complicate structural design and certification\.
\- Residual stress and distortion\: Cyclic thermal loading can generate residual stresses approaching yield strength\, driving distortion and\, in severe cases\, cracking or delamination\.
\- Porosity\: Porosity is particularly severe in aluminum alloys\, driven by the high liquid\-to\-solid hydrogen solubility ratio and compounded by turbulent melt pool dynamics\.
\- Process parameter complexity\: The large parameter space requires systematic design of experiments\, response surface methods\, or data\-driven optimization to achieve consistent part quality\.
\- Certification gap\: The lack of mature\, process\-specific qualification standards for WAAM components remains the primary barrier to adoption in regulated industries\.

Taken together\, these advantages and disadvantages show that WAAM is not limited by deposition capability alone\, but by the ability to control the process–structure–property relationship across large volumes\. This is why thermal management\, inter\-pass control\, hybrid post\-processing\, and qualification standards remain central to the transition from laboratory\-scale deposition to certified industrial production\.

\#\#\# 9\.2\. Technology Readiness and Certification Barriers

After considering WAAM’s technical advantages and limitations\, the next question is whether the process is mature enough for reliable industrial deployment \[87\]\. The Technology Readiness Level \(TRL\) framework\, originally developed by NASA and subsequently adopted by organizations such as the European Space Agency\, the US Department of Defense\, and the European Commission for Horizon research programs\, provides a standardized nine\-level scale for assessing the maturity of a technology from basic research principles \(TRL 1\) to fully deployed\, flight\-proven systems \(TRL 9\) \[87\]\. Applying this framework to WAAM enables a structured assessment of where the technology currently stands and which technical\, industrial\, and regulatory barriers must be overcome to advance toward routine deployment\.

Figure 20 presents the TRL progression for WAAM from its conceptual origins in Baker’s 1925 patent \[8\] to the current state of the art\. Based on the literature reviewed and selected industrial case studies\, WAAM may be considered to have reached approximately TRL 6–7 for selected steel and titanium alloy applications\, whereas many aluminum and nickel\-based superalloy applications remain closer to TRL 5–6\. Specific applications\, such as WAAM\-fabricated titanium brackets\, structural frames\, and selected large\-scale demonstrator components reported by Cranfield University and aerospace industrial partners\, may approach higher TRL levels\, but these examples should be interpreted as application\-specific rather than representative of all WAAM materials and geometries\. While TRL provides a useful maturity indicator\, certification readiness depends on whether WAAM components can meet reproducible property allowables\, defect acceptance criteria\, and inspection requirements\.

The TRL assessment presented here is intended as a qualitative\, application\-dependent maturity map rather than a fixed universal rating\; TRL depends on the material\, component geometry\, qualification route\, and end\-use sector \[87\]\.

The primary barrier preventing the broader transition of WAAM from demonstrated capability toward routine qualification in regulated industries\, particularly aerospace\, nuclear\, and pressure\-containing applications\, is not only technical performance but also regulatory qualification\. Current aviation certification frameworks\, such as FAR Part 25 and CS\-25\, were developed primarily for conventionally manufactured metallic components and do not yet provide WAAM\-specific qualification pathways\. The key certification challenges are\:

\- Microstructural heterogeneity and anisotropy\: Certification requires demonstration of consistent properties meeting minimum allowables across the relevant part volume\. WAAM’s inherent base\-to\-top microstructural gradient and build\-direction anisotropy make this demonstration difficult without extensive sampling\, process control\, and location\-specific property assessment\.
\- Porosity detection and acceptance criteria \[88\,89\]\: Non\-destructive evaluation \(NDE\) of WAAM components for porosity using conventional ultrasonic testing can be complicated by anisotropic grain structures\, which scatter ultrasound and reduce flaw\-detection sensitivity\. The smallest detectable defect depends on grain size\, anisotropy\, surface condition\, and section thickness\; phased\-array ultrasonic testing has detected defects of 0\.6–1 mm in aluminum WAAM components\, whereas X\-ray computed tomography\, although capable of finer resolution\, is too slow for real\-time or in\-line assessment \[89\]\.
\- Residual stress qualification\: No universally adopted production\-scale method currently exists for qualifying WAAM components against residual\-stress\-related failure modes\. Neutron diffraction and synchrotron X\-ray diffraction can map residual stress in three dimensions\, but they are not accessible for routine production inspection \[90\,91\]\.
\- Fatigue design allowables\: Fatigue allowables for WAAM\, analogous to established allowables for conventional alloys\, remain insufficient for many alloy\/process combinations\. The sensitivity of WAAM fatigue performance to microstructural heterogeneity\, surface waviness\, porosity\, and residual stress requires systematic\, statistically robust S\-N curve development before routine certification in safety\-critical structural applications\.

International standardization bodies are actively developing and updating AM and DED\-related standards\. ISO\/ASTM 52900\:2021 remains the current terminology standard for additive manufacturing\, while ASTM F3187\-16\(2023\) provides guidance for directed energy deposition of metals\, including systems using laser beam\, electron beam\, and arc\/plasma\-based energy sources \[92\,93\]\. These standards provide important terminology and process\-guidance frameworks\, but they do not by themselves establish complete material allowables\, fatigue databases\, or component\-specific qualification routes for all WAAM applications\. Ongoing work by the ASTM F42 and ISO\/TC 261 committees\, and by aerospace materials committees\, is therefore essential\, but progress in standardization remains slower than the pace of WAAM process development\.

\#\#\# 9\.3\. Industrial Case Studies and Deployment Status

Despite the certification gap\, WAAM has achieved meaningful industrial deployment in several application domains\. In aerospace\, Cranfield University’s WAAMMat \(Wire \+ Arc Additive Manufacturing Materials\) program demonstrated multi\-meter titanium spars and wing ribs with buy\-to\-fly ratios below 3\:1\, validated against conventional machined counterparts \[1\,14\,84\]\. Airbus and Spirit AeroSystems have reported exploratory programs for WAAM titanium brackets\. In defense\, BAE Systems and Lockheed Martin have evaluated WAAM for the repair and fabrication of naval and aerospace components \[84\]\.

In the energy sector\, where qualification routes may be less restrictive than aerospace depending on component criticality\, WAAM has been explored for the manufacture and repair of large valve bodies\, impellers\, propellers\, and pressure\-vessel\-related components in oil and gas applications \[7\,31\]\. The marine sector has also demonstrated one of the most visible WAAM qualification examples\: the WAAMpeller project\, a nickel–aluminum bronze ship propeller fabricated by Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing and unveiled in 2017 after testing verified by Bureau Veritas \[94\]\. These examples indicate that WAAM is already viable for selected high\-value and large\-scale components\, but broader adoption still depends on repeatable process control\, defect acceptance criteria\, property allowables\, and application\-specific certification routes\.

\#\# 10\. Discussion\: Critical Contradictions\, Hybrid Strategies and Future Research Priorities

The preceding sections establish the process\, metallurgical\, defect\, alloy and industrial contexts of WAAM\. The scientific value of interpreting WAAM through traditional welding principles lies not in treating WAAM as repeated welding\, but in identifying where the welding framework remains valid and where it breaks down under layer\-wise thermal accumulation\. This distinction provides the basis for discussing unresolved contradictions\, hybrid process strategies and future research priorities\.

\#\#\# 10\.1\. Critical Contradictions and Process\-Microstructure Interpretation

A careful review should not only synthesize areas of agreement but also identify genuine scientific disagreements that define the most productive frontiers for future research\. Several important contradictions exist in the WAAM literature\.

Travel speed and solidification structure\: Ou et al\. \[65\] predicted that a faster travel speed increases the cooling rate G·R and decreases G\/R\. The first effect refines the dendrite arm spacing \(Equation \(20\)\)\, whereas the second shifts the solidification morphology toward columnar\-dendritic or equiaxed growth \(Equations \(18\) and \(19\)\)\. Apparent disagreements on whether faster travel coarsens or refines WAAM microstructures usually arise because studies report different length scales \(primary dendrite arm spacing\, columnar grain width\, or equiaxed grain size\) and because travel speed is rarely varied at constant arc power and deposition rate\: reducing the bead cross\-section at a higher speed also changes the number of layers\, the heat accumulation\, and the reheating history of the wall\. A meaningful comparison therefore requires that the measured length scale and the co\-varied parameters be stated explicitly\.

Inter\-pass temperature and defect formation\: Geng et al\. \[60\] reported that lower inter\-pass temperature reduces heat accumulation and improves dimensional accuracy in aluminum WAAM\. Conversely\, an excessively low inter\-pass temperature reduces the effective preheat of the prior layer surface and can increase the risk of insufficient remelting and delamination \[70\]\. Rios et al\. \[61\] further showed that the inter\-pass temperature enters the prediction of deposit geometry\. These findings indicate that inter\-pass temperature is a critical but difficult\-to\-standardize variable\, and that a single optimal value cannot be defined without specifying alloy system\, deposit geometry\, process variant\, and environmental conditions\.

CMT variants versus pulsed GMAW\: Galeazzi et al\. \[51\] found that CMT Advanced and CMT Pulse lay at opposite extremes of heat input among the CMT variants for AISI 420 martensitic stainless\-steel walls\, whereas Luo et al\. \[53\] found that a pulsed arc outperformed a non\-pulsed arc in aluminum WAAM because of its higher droplet\-transfer frequency and deposition efficiency\. These studies differ in alloy\, thermal conductivity\, transfer mode\, and evaluation criteria \(wall geometry and heat input versus droplet transfer and deposition efficiency\)\, so they do not constitute a direct contradiction\; they do show that the ranking of CMT and pulsed GMAW variants is material\- and criterion\-specific and must be established for the alloy and component of interest\.

Porosity and heat input optima\: While many studies agree on the non\-monotonic porosity–heat\-input relationship\, the location of the optimum differs considerably among alloy systems and process variants\. Fu et al\. \[44\] identified a porosity minimum at a hot\-wire current of 100 A in hot\-wire arc additive manufacturing of aluminum\, while Haselhuhn et al\. \[77\] found that\, under common GMAW printing conditions\, porosity remained below 2\% for all tested aluminum filler alloys but was highest for ER5356\, with the 4000\-series alloys performing best\. These discrepancies confirm that porosity management protocols are alloy\-specific and cannot be transferred across systems without experimental re\-validation\.

The most important conceptual unification emerging from this review is the central role of the G\/R ratio as the governing parameter linking WAAM process conditions to microstructural outcome\. As demonstrated through Equations \(18\)–\(20\)\, G\/R controls the solidification mode ranging from planar to equiaxed\-dendritic\, while G·R controls cooling rate and dendrite arm spacing\. Both parameters vary continuously in three dimensions around the melt pool\, meaning that a single deposited WAAM bead can contain a gradient of microstructures from planar or cellular regions near the fusion boundary to columnar\-dendritic regions in the melt\-pool interior\, as represented schematically in Figure 15\.

The transition between columnar and equiaxed solidification is controlled by the local thermal gradient G\, solidification rate R\, cooling rate G·R\, and the degree of constitutional undercooling ahead of the solidification front\. Higher G\/R generally favors planar or columnar growth\, whereas lower G\/R combined with sufficient undercooling and available nucleation sites can promote equiaxed growth \[33\,71\,72\]\.

Cumulative effects of repeated deposition on G and R are not unique to WAAM\; they also occur in multi\-pass welding\. The difference lies in the geometry and boundary conditions\. In a multi\-pass joint\, each bead solidifies against the groove faces and the previous beads\, so the direction of G changes with bead placement and the columnar grains change orientation from pass to pass\, while the parent plates maintain a lateral heat sink throughout\. In a WAAM wall\, the fusion boundary advances continuously upward\, G remains aligned with the build direction\, and its magnitude decreases as the heat\-extraction path lengthens \[66\]\, so grains can grow epitaxially through many layers with a common orientation\. As build height increases\, the effective heat sink distance from the melt pool to the external boundary increases\, often reducing G at the solidification front and shifting the operating point on the solidification map toward a different dendritic regime\. This progressive reduction in G with build height is the physical basis for the commonly observed increase in grain size from the base to the top of WAAM builds\.

The practical implication for WAAM process engineers is that achieving microstructural homogeneity across build height requires active compensation for this evolving thermal boundary condition\. Possible strategies include decreasing H with build height through adaptive process control\, increasing substrate or inter\-pass cooling\, or introducing external perturbations to the melt pool\, such as arc oscillation\, ultrasonic assistance\, magnetic\-field assistance\, grain refiners\, or inter\-layer deformation\, to promote equiaxed nucleation or disrupt columnar growth\. These approaches are active research areas\, but their robustness across alloy systems\, build geometries\, and industrial\-scale production remains insufficiently established\.

A recurring and practically important finding across the reviewed literature is the non\-monotonic relationship between heat input and porosity in aluminum WAAM\. At low heat input\, insufficient preheating of the wire and substrate may leave hydrogen\-bearing surface contamination intact\, increasing the hydrogen source term in Sieverts’ law\. At high heat input\, the enlarged melt pool increases Marangoni\-driven flow\, extends the solidification time\, and promotes oxide\-film entrainment\, all of which can increase pore entrapment\. An intermediate optimum therefore exists\, such as the hot\-wire current of 100 A reported by Fu et al\. \[44\]\, at which preheating and melt\-pool size are balanced\.

This optimal window is alloy\-specific\, feedstock\-condition\-specific\, and geometry\-specific\, which explains the persistent difficulty of transferring WAAM porosity solutions from one application to another\. A physics\-informed approach to porosity management must address all three hydrogen source categories\: \(i\) surface contamination\, controlled by wire and substrate cleaning protocols\; \(ii\) shielding gas moisture\, controlled by gas quality\, line dryness\, and purging\; and \(iii\) melt pool hydrodynamics\, controlled by process parameters and bead geometry optimization\.

The analysis in Section 6\.4 shows that the thermal strain driving residual stress is αCTE·ΔT\, so E·αCTE alone does not rank alloys\; the temperature change must be included\, and the tendency toward plastic flow and distortion is best expressed as E·αCTE·ΔT\/σy\. For a deposit that cools from the temperature at which it begins to support stress to the inter\-layer temperature\, the upper bound of ΔT is TS − TIP\, where TS is the solidus temperature\, and this bound differs strongly between alloys\. For an aluminum alloy with TS ≈ 580 °C and TIP ≈ 100 °C\, ΔT ≲ 480 K and E·αCTE·ΔT ≈ 0\.8 GPa \(E ≈ 70 GPa\, αCTE ≈ 23 × 10−6 K−1\)\; for Ti\-6Al\-4V with TS ≈ 1600 °C and TIP ≈ 200 °C\, ΔT ≲ 1400 K and E·αCTE·ΔT ≈ 1\.4 GPa \(E ≈ 110 GPa\, αCTE ≈ 9 × 10−6 K−1\)\. Both values exceed the room\-temperature yield strength\, so the residual stress is limited by the temperature\-dependent yield strength rather than by the elastic estimate\; because E and σy fall steeply as the solidus is approached\, the effective ΔT over which stress accumulates is smaller than TS − TIP\. For aluminum\, the low yield strength of the as\-deposited material means that thermal strains exceed the elastic limit readily\, as shown by longitudinal tensile residual stresses reaching the flow strength in 2319 aluminum walls \[25\]\, whereas in nickel superalloys the high E·αCTE combined with high elevated\-temperature strength is expected to produce large residual stresses\. In both cases residual stresses can approach the yield strength\, driving distortion and\, in susceptible alloys\, cracking\. This thermomechanical constraint cannot always be eliminated by process\-parameter adjustment alone and provides a rationale for hybrid WAAM approaches incorporating inter\-layer rolling\, peening\, friction stir processing\, or other mechanical treatments that introduce plastic strain\, refine grains\, and partially counteract the tensile residual\-stress field\.

\#\#\# 10\.2\. Hybrid WAAM Strategies\: Deformation\, Machining\, and Low\-Heat\-Input Transfer

Hybrid WAAM strategies couple arc deposition with a second\, non\-fusion operation that acts on the deposit between layers or after deposition\. They can be grouped by the mechanism through which they modify the as\-deposited state\: \(i\) mechanical deformation of each layer or of the completed wall \(inter\-layer rolling\, peening\, and friction stir processing\)\, which introduces plastic strain that disrupts epitaxial columnar growth on reheating and redistributes residual stress\; \(ii\) machining between or after layers\, which restores geometric accuracy but does not change the microstructure\; and \(iii\) thermal or field\-assisted control of solidification\, such as forced inter\-pass cooling\, arc oscillation\, and ultrasonic or magnetic assistance\, which acts on the melt pool rather than on the solid deposit\. Table 8 compares the principal deformation\- and machining\-based strategies on a common basis\.

Rolling\, peening\, and magnetic fields are also used in conventional welding\, but with different purposes\, timing\, and effects\. In welding\, they are usually applied once\, after the joint is complete\, to reduce distortion or residual stress or to improve the fatigue strength of the weld toe\, or\, in the case of electromagnetic stirring\, during a single solidification event to refine the fusion\-zone grains\. In WAAM\, they are applied layer by layer\, so each treated layer becomes the substrate for the next one and is reheated by it\. The imposed plastic strain must therefore survive\, or be released by\, this reheating to produce the intended effect\: in Ti\-6Al\-4V\, the strain stored by rolling or hammer peening leads to new β grains when the next layer reheats the material \[67\,95\]\, and the refinement accumulates through the build rather than being confined to a surface layer \[20\]\. The treatment must also reach the top of a growing wall and be synchronized with the inter\-pass temperature\, which in turn changes the thermal history of the subsequent layers\.

Inter\-layer rolling is the most extensively studied deformation\-assisted route\. Rolling each layer of WAAM steel walls reduced distortion\, which was eliminated with a slotted roller\, lowered the residual stress\, particularly near the baseplate\, and refined the grains when the rolled material was reheated by the next pass \[26\]\; in Ti\-6Al\-4V\, rolling each layer refined the centimetre\-scale columnar prior\-β grains to below 100 µm and weakened both the β and α textures to near random\, which Donoghue et al\. \[67\] attributed to new β orientations formed at deformation heterogeneities acting as nuclei on reheating\; high\-pressure interpass rolling produced equiaxed prior\-β grains of 56–139 µm \[85\]\, and larger roller radii gave more uniform recrystallization while higher loads increased refinement\, with most of the strain generated within 3 mm of the rolled surface \[69\]\; and in 2319 \(Al–Cu\) walls\, vertical inter\-pass rolling virtually eliminated distortion and side rolling produced fairly uniform longitudinal compressive stresses \[25\]\, while inter\-layer rolling at 45 kN raised the ultimate tensile and yield strengths to 314 and 244 MPa\, respectively \[96\]\. The principal limitations of rolling are the high contact loads required\, the need for a roller path that follows the deposit\, and the resulting restriction to simple\, accessible geometries such as straight or gently curved walls\.

Peening introduces compressive residual stress and plastic strain from the surface\. Laser shock peening of WAAM 2319 aluminum converted the tensile residual stress to compressive \(maximum about 100 MPa\)\, reduced the average grain size from 59\.7 to 46\.7 µm\, and increased the yield strength by 72\% \[97\]\. Because the plastically affected depth is limited\, peening is most effective when applied between layers or to critical surfaces\, and it has little influence on the bulk columnar structure of thick sections\.

Inter\-layer friction stir processing imposes severe plastic deformation below the solidus\, producing a dynamically recrystallized\, fine equiaxed stir zone\, fragmenting interdendritic eutectic networks\, and closing porosity within the stirred volume \[74\,98\]\. Compared with rolling\, FSP produces a much finer stir\-zone grain size but is limited by tool wear and process forces in high\-melting\-point alloys\, by the requirement that the stir\-zone depth exceed the layer thickness to avoid unprocessed interlayer bands\, and by exit holes and geometric access\; it is therefore currently most mature for aluminum alloys\. Pore closure by FSP also depends on the thermal history of each layer\: in three\-layer Al 4043 walls\, the upper layer retained higher porosity \(2\.90 ± 1\.18\%\) than the bottom layer despite a lower peak FSP surface temperature\, which was associated with its lower post\-peak cooling rate \(−12\.3 versus −16\.2 °C\/s\) \[99\]\.

Inter\-layer or final machining in hybrid additive–subtractive systems removes surface waviness and stair\-stepping and provides a flat reference surface for the next layer \[10\,11\,41\]\, but it leaves the as\-deposited microstructure and residual\-stress state essentially unchanged and adds cycle time\.

The authors’ Additive–Deformation–Machining \(ADM\) process\, also reported as the unified additive–deformation manufacturing process \(UAMFSP\) \[100\]\, is one implementation of the FSP\-based route in which GMAW deposition\, inter\-layer FSP\, and CNC milling are performed sequentially within one CNC workcell \(Figure 21\)\. The GMAW \(MIG\) torch is mounted on a multi\-purpose CNC machine adjacent to the FSP spindle\; after each layer cools to the inter\-pass temperature\, the FSP tool traverses the bead\, and the milling tool can then restore a flat reference surface for the next layer\. In ER4043 aluminum walls\, infrared thermography showed peak layer temperatures of approximately 870–1000 °C for MIG\-only deposition\, whereas the MIG \+ FSP walls maintained more uniform sub\-solidus temperature profiles below approximately 400 °C\; the mean grain area decreased from approximately 314 µm2 to 10\.9 µm2\, and the Vickers microhardness \(HV0\.2\) increased from 52\.0 ± 1\.3 to 75\.8 ± 7\.7 \[74\,101\]\. These results were obtained on single aluminum walls\; residual stress\, fatigue performance\, and transfer to high\-melting\-point alloys and complex geometries are not addressed in \[74\] and remain to be established for this route\, which shares the tool\-wear\, stir\-depth\, and access limitations of the other FSP\-based hybrids in Table 8\.
