Co\-packaged optics emerged as a concept around the start of the decade\, when the data center industry began discussing the need for a solution to the power and bandwidth bottlenecks it was increasingly experiencing\.

“In the old days\, your electrical connections were copper\. Your data center networks were connected by Ethernet\, and everything was good\,” says Roy Chua\, founder and industry analyst at AvidThink\. “Then\, as speeds increased\, copper became unable to handle the volume of traffic\, so the industry turned to fiber optics\,” which Chua notes was also good\, until it wasn’t quite good enough anymore\.

Fiber optics requires the use of lasers to convert electrical signals into optics\, or photons\, so they can be transported over the glass fiber\, then reconverted from optical signals back to electrical ones when they reach the other side\. “So that\'s all wonderful\, except that all takes a certain amount of energy\,“ Chua says\.

In today’s data center environments\, most electrical\-to\-optical conversions take place via pluggable optical transceivers\, known as digital signal processors \(DSPs\)\, which connect to the switch\. However\, DSPs are expensive and power\-hungry\, meaning that although they have clear benefits over copper interconnects\, they are not quite the power\-efficient option the industry is looking for\.

Enter\: Co\-packaged optics\. On a very basic level\, unlike pluggable optics\, where the transceivers are kept separate from the main chips\, CPO integrates optical and electrical components\, such as optical engines and switching ASICs\, on a single packaged substrate\.

“What co\-packaged optics does is move the conversion onto the actual silicon itself\. It moves those lasers onto the silicon\, eliminating the need for any external units\,” Chua explains\. “And by putting those lasers inside the silicon\, you are able to save power\. By co\-packaging these elements\, it allows for more consolidation while lowering costs and energy use\.”

However\, while the concept might seem relatively straightforward\, the practicalities are less so\. “As you can imagine\, manufacturing of co\-packaged optics can be complicated because you have to manufacture everything – your wave guides and your modulators – all together\.”

Therefore\, it\'s unsurprising that another early concern regarding the technology was its potential cost\, with Chua noting that “people felt it would not be sufficiently reliable and cost\-effective enough to produce and take to market\. “

The reliability of the technology has also come under scrutiny from customers\, with questions arising as to how to go about replacing a laser that has failed when it\'s part of a monolithic structure\, particularly given the so\-called blast radius of optics\, and the high failure rate of lasers\.

The industry has responded by developing a hot\-swappable laser source known as an External Laser Small Form\-Factor Pluggable \(or ELSFP\) while keeping everything monolithically integrated\. Gartner says that although this solution certainly helps to address the challenge\, it’s something of a half\-measure that doesn’t succeed in solving the issue entirely\.

\#\# The shifting optical landscape

According to AvidThink’s Data Center Networking in 2026 report\, CPO is one of several new architectures that are driving a “structural shift” in the optical interconnect landscape\, namely removing the need for DSPs from optical transceiver modules\.

In addition to CPO\, there’s what Chua describes as a half\-step\, known as linear pluggable optics \(LPO\)\, and a three\-quarter step called near\-packaged optics\, with LPO currently the most popular of the three\. There’s also eXtra\-dense pluggable optics\, or XPO\, which was developed by Arista but described by Chua as less of a pure technology and more of a packaging form factor\. \[See Box Out\]\.

While co\-packaged optics is not a new concept\, AvidThink’s report notes that the technology reached a milestone this year\, transitioning from “perpetual promise to production deployment\,” with both Chua and Gartner agreeing this has been largely driven by announcements made by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at GTC 2026\.

At the March conference\, Huang indicated that Nvidia’s Spectrum\-X CPO switches would be in production in H2 2026\, and officially announced that the chip giant’s 2028 Feynman architecture would introduce NVLink 8 CPO\, bringing silicon photonics directly to the GPU\-to\-GPU scale\-up interconnect for the first time\.

AvidThink says this is architecturally significant as\, until now\, CPO has been applied to scale\-out switch\-to\-switch connections\. Applying it to the latency\-critical scale\-up domain signals that CPO technology has achieved the maturity and performance required for the most demanding interconnect tier\.

“Until Jensen said CPO\, no one cared about CPO\. No one had any idea what CPO was\, and now I get asked that question all the time\,” Chua laughs\. He also questions whether anyone in the industry would have been saying widespread adoption of the technology would take place in 2028 had Huang not gotten on stage and made the Feynman announcement\.

“Without Jensen sort of stoking the fire\, I think it would have been the 2027 \- 2028 conversation\, and Jensen basically made it the 2025 \- 2026 conversation\,” Chua says\, adding that “to be frank\, I wasn\'t expecting it\.”

While Chua says Huang has put a rocket under the industry – with Broadcom in particular being incredibly aggressive around its timelines for deployment in the wake of Huang’s comments – the AvidThink report does highlight that there have been a number of other notable CPO announcements from the last 18 months\.

These include AMD’s January 2025 acquisition of Enosemi\; Lightmatter unveiling Passage L200\, the world’s first 3D co\-packaged optics product\; Broadcom announcing its Tomahawk 6 CPO variant ‘Davisson’\; Marvell’s acquisition of Celestial AI\; Coherent demonstrating multi\-technology CPO at OFC 2026\; and Ayar Labs and Wiwynn announcing a joint reference design for optically connected\, rack\-scale AI systems\.

Furthermore\, in March 2026\, Ciena\, Coherent\, Marvell\, Molex\, Samtec\, and TeraHop announced the formation of the Open CPX MSA \(Open Co\-packaging Multi\-Source Agreement\) to develop the specifications for optical engines “required to enable a broad ecosystem of interoperable co\-packaged and near\-package interconnect solutions\.”

\#\# Where are we now\?

While all of these announcements appear to indicate significant demand\, Gartner says it\'s important to note that a lot of work in the CPO space was initially vendor\, not customer\, driven\, as demonstrated by those poor early responses\.

“\[In 2023\] Cisco and Broadcom announced these CPO demos and didn\'t get a great customer response\. Then Nvidia announced that they were going to deploy CPO and\, quite honestly\, stimulated a lot of excitement in the industry – I think maybe irrational exuberance is the way I would characterize it though\.”

Although Cisco had already demoed a co\-packaged optics prototype back in 2023\, Gartner says the company has not yet announced a commercial CPO line\, although he says that it does have CPO technology under development\.

“We\'re playing this a bit cautiously\,” he explains\. “We don\'t want to come across to our customers like we\'re not going to give them a choice\.”

Gartner says Cisco’s initial CPO offering will likely be in the 100\-terabit switch capacity range\, and the company will continue to give customers a choice between pluggables and an embedded option\, be that CPO or NPO\.

“Again\, we have not announced a product yet\; this is something that\'s under development\, and we\'re really going to be cautious about launching it based on customer demand\. We want to see the customers are really pulling for this\, as opposed to it being a vendor push\.”

In the meantime\, the company is developing LPO options for its Silicon One portfolio\, with the first commercially available 800G LPO modules for its Nexus 9000 series switches and 8000 series routers released in February 2026\.

“I think the challenge that we have to acknowledge here is that the industry ecosystem is evolving around CPO\, but it’s not mature\. The ecosystem around silicon is highly mature – we know how to put a package and substrates around silicon\, and we know how to do that around optics\, and build a pluggable optics module\, but we don’t have an ecosystem that’s mature and can put those two together\,” Gartner says\.

“There\'s a lot of invention right now around things like connectors for CPO\, substrates that support the optics\, and optical chiplets\, but that\'s an immature ecosystem\, and it really has to mature pretty significantly before we\'ll see this technology make sense at volume\. Anybody can produce a hundred of these things\, but when we have to talk about delivering thousands or millions\, that ecosystem really needs to be mature\, and that\'s going to take some time\.”

Despite all the excitement\, Chua also acknowledges that\, at the moment\, CPO is being deployed at “a very small scale\.” However\, he says all early signs are promising\, and the data show that the technology will be able to scale up and be deployed into production\.

In particular\, Meta’s deployment of the Broadcom Tomahawk 5 ‘Bailly’ CPO switch in its data centers resulted in a 0\.34 percent annual link failure rate during the first million hours of testing\, making it roughly five times more reliable than traditional pluggable transceivers that were used as control groups\.

As a result\, Chua says he can’t see anything on the horizon that would block the mass adoption of co\-packaged optics in the near future\, and he expects to see some level of volume shipments from Broadcom of its Tomahawk 6 ‘Davisson’ CPO variant\.

For Gartner\, however\, whether the reality of CPO lives up to the hype remains to be seen\, especially with regard to the timelines being touted by vendors such as Nvidia and Broadcom\. While shiny and new will be enough for some people to jump on board the co\-packaged optics train\, for him\, the real turning point for the technology will be when all the other technologies currently on offer hit their ceiling\, making CPO a necessity\.

“Today\, the SerDers rate coming off the silicon is 200G per line\, and at that rate\, in my view\, it\'s a toss\-up as to whether CPO or LPO makes sense\,” he says\. “Once we get to 400G per line\, then LPO becomes much more challenging \.\.\. that is where the ability for LPO to continue serving the market diminishes\, and the need for CPO becomes more real\.”

records.body_text:
Thermal Co-Simulation Testing Of Co-Packaged Optics
Ensuring optical engines can operate reliably alongside high-power AI processors in multi-chip packages.
By Vladimir Stojanovic and Igor Elkanovich
The CPO revolution is at our doorstep. But transforming data center interconnects requires overcoming new challenges in architecture, power delivery, mechanical design, and thermal management. Of these, thermal management has emerged as one of the most critical areas for successfully deploying co-packaged optics (CPO) in hyperscale AI environments.
Thermal instability has been a concern for CPO technology. Ayar Labs and Global Unichip Corp. (GUC) jointly conducted thermal co-simulation of the advanced package design and determined the thermal floor map for the package and subsequent chiplets, including air- and liquid-cooled environments.
Since thermal stability has been raised as a concern for micro-ring-based CPO, we want to address it head-on. Our co-simulation data show that CPO can operate reliably within the thermal envelope of advanced multi-chip packages. We’re sharing these results to give hyperscalers the confidence to move forward with CPO deployments at scale.
Novel design enables over 100 Tbps speeds
Let’s start with the new multi-chip package (MCP) design that integrates Ayar Labs’ TeraPHY optical engines into GUC’s advanced packaging and ASIC workflow. The new XPU MCP design replaces traditional electrical interconnects with Ayar Labs’ optical engines, which are attached directly to the MCP organic substrate. This architecture enables a full-duplex optical interface of more than 100 Tbps from the XPU package, an improvement of more than an order of magnitude over current XPUs.
UCIe-S provides bandwidth between the optical engines and the I/O chiplets over the MCP substrate. UCIe-A, on the other hand, is used for communication between the I/O chiplet and the main AI die over local silicon interconnect (LSI) bridges.
The scale of this design creates thermal challenges we must address. The complete package measures 105mm x 140mm, housing:
- 2 XPUs (25.69mm x 32.40mm each)
- 8 HBM4 memory modules
- 4 I/O chiplets
- 8 TeraPHY optical engines (12.5mm x 13.0mm each)
The +3 kW power envelope in a single package underscores the importance of thermal management and the need for optical engines to operate reliably alongside high-power AI processors. This complex multi-chip architecture requires sophisticated packaging. The design uses a 9-2-9 layer substrate structure to handle the complex routing requirements.
The design also addresses signal and power integrity challenges associated with the large-scale package. We perform thermal optimization at the XPU MCP level, while a stiffener design incorporates optical engines’ requirements and enables detachable fiber connections that meet mechanical stress and warpage requirements.
What is thermal co-simulation and why is it important?
Thermal co-simulation is the combined simulation of electrical behavior and heat flow across a chip. It lets designers predict temperatures, hotspots, and reliability issues in integrated circuits (ICs) and packages under realistic operating conditions. The data ensures the entire system operates within required temperature specifications. This is critical for successful deployment.
In GUC’s thermal integrity design flow, we consider every chip’s power maps and perform thermal crosstalk and dynamic thermal co-simulation to ensure the MCP’s thermal integrity from early-stage through sign-off. This allows us to identify local thermal hotspots and the impact of thermal crosstalk on the optical engine.
Thermal co-simulation is crucial for GUC’s advanced ASIC workflows. In our joint analysis, the MCP includes multiple chiplets to analyze thermal crosstalk between adjacent chiplet dies. Any heat generated by the entire interposer complex may affect the optical engine’s performance.
Thermal modeling is needed to optimize optical engine performance. This joint technical exercise deliberately probes thermal hotspots and thermal crosstalk to evaluate overall CPO thermal stability in a realistic customer package form factor. Rather than avoiding the hard questions, we designed the simulation to stress the system and raise any potential concerns.
These findings are invaluable for assessing advanced packaging designs and collaborating with ecosystem partners to design optimal cooling solutions for AI server and switch applications at the most demanding Thermal Design Power levels. This testing allows us to do just that.
Thermal co‑sim testing
We performed three simulations: an analysis to determine thermal resistance targets for each chip component, plus testing of two different cooling solutions. One solution met spec, and one did not.
3D VC heatsink test
We tested a standard air fin heatsink at airspeeds of 5 m/s and 6 m/s at 25ºC.
Fig. 1: GUC + Ayar Labs CoWoS-L CPO simulation using heatsink.
This did not meet spec, as the temperature significantly exceeded spec for all components except the I/O die.
Thermal resistance analysis
We analyzed the maximum junction temperature versus resistance curve to determine suitable resistance for the Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate with Local Silicon Interconnect (CoWoS-L) advanced packaging and optical engine to meet the temperature spec.
Fig. 2: GUC + Ayar Labs CoWoS-L CPO Thermal Resistance (Rsa) analysis.
The system-level thermal solution successfully meets the specification when RSA-ASIC is ≤ 0.008 K/W and RSA-OE is ≤ 0.15 K/W. The cold plate design achieves these targets with pressure drops of 11.2 kPa for the ASIC cold plate and 18.8 kPa for the optical engine cold plate. This ensures efficient coolant flow while maintaining thermal performance.
Cold plate test
Finally, we tested an impingement-type cold plate thermal solution at 4.5 LPM.
Fig. 3: GUC + Ayar Labs CoWoS-L CPO simulation using cold plate.
This solution did meet spec. All components were below the temperature specifications.
Cold plate details
We selected the impingement-type cold plate for this application because it enables higher heat flux removal than conventional parallel-channel designs. The design uses optimized fin dimensions (thickness: 0.15mm, height: 2.4mm for the ASIC and 3.0mm for the optical engine) with thermal interface materials (K=5.2 W/mK) to achieve the required thermal performance.
This approach effectively dissipates the concentrated heat from multiple high-power chiplets while maintaining the optical engines within their operational temperature limits.
Key Results
- Determined the thermal resistance design targets for each chiplet for thermal sign-off constraints:
- HBM4 < 95ºC
- SoC < 125ºC
- Optical Engine < 100ºC
- Mapped the location of thermal hotspots.
- Showed that a traditional air heatsink does not work for this solution.
- Demonstrated that a real-world liquid cooling device meets the specifications needed.
These results point to a significant breakthrough in CPO deployment. Successfully maintaining optical engines under 100ºC while dissipating over 3kW TDP from a single package (with 1,500W coming from the AI processors alone) shows that CPO operates reliably with ample junction-temperature headroom, paving the way for the most demanding thermal environments.
Future plans
Our next step will focus on dynamic workload simulation to further analyze thermal impact on CPO under real-world operating conditions. The tests we’ve shared here were based on static power assumptions, where each component’s power consumption remains constant. Systems ramp up from idle, spike during training or booting, and fluctuate based on user demand during normal operations.
Large numbers of users can cause heat spikes. A dynamic workload simulation will allow us to test our design under conditions more accurate to the real world. This will help us understand how the optics respond to sudden temperature changes and ensure the systems operate efficiently.
These thermal co-simulation test results demonstrate that CPO can operate reliably in high-power AI systems when paired with appropriate cooling solutions. As the industry continues to push the boundaries of compute performance and thermal design power, CPO will play a significant role in overcoming bandwidth and power limitations.
Igor Elkanovich is the CTO of GUC.
Vladimir Stojanovic
(all posts)
Vladimir Stojanovic is the CTO and co-founder of Ayar Labs. Prior to founding Ayar Labs, he led the team that designed the world’s first processor to communicate using light. Stojanovic was recently a professor of EECS at UC Berkeley, and was one of the key developers of the Rambus high-speed link technology. He holds a PhD from Stanford University.

\- 2 XPUs \(25\.69mm x 32\.40mm each\)
\- 8 HBM4 memory modules
\- 4 I\/O chiplets
\- 8 TeraPHY optical engines \(12\.5mm x 13\.0mm each\)

This complex multi\-chip architecture requires sophisticated packaging\. The design uses a 9\-2\-9 layer substrate structure to handle the complex routing requirements\.

The design also addresses signal and power integrity challenges associated with the large\-scale package\. We perform thermal optimization at the XPU MCP level\, while a stiffener design incorporates optical engines’ requirements and enables detachable fiber connections that meet mechanical stress and warpage requirements\.

\#\# What is thermal co\-simulation and why is it important\?

Thermal co\-simulation is the combined simulation of electrical behavior and heat flow across a chip\. It lets designers predict temperatures\, hotspots\, and reliability issues in integrated circuits \(ICs\) and packages under realistic operating conditions\. The data ensures the entire system operates within required temperature specifications\. This is critical for successful deployment\.

In GUC’s thermal integrity design flow\, we consider every chip’s power maps and perform thermal crosstalk and dynamic thermal co\-simulation to ensure the MCP’s thermal integrity from early\-stage through sign\-off\. This allows us to identify local thermal hotspots and the impact of thermal crosstalk on the optical engine\.

Thermal co\-simulation is crucial for GUC’s advanced ASIC workflows\. In our joint analysis\, the MCP includes multiple chiplets to analyze thermal crosstalk between adjacent chiplet dies\. Any heat generated by the entire interposer complex may affect the optical engine’s performance\.

Thermal modeling is needed to optimize optical engine performance\. This joint technical exercise deliberately probes thermal hotspots and thermal crosstalk to evaluate overall CPO thermal stability in a realistic customer package form factor\. Rather than avoiding the hard questions\, we designed the simulation to stress the system and raise any potential concerns\.

These findings are invaluable for assessing advanced packaging designs and collaborating with ecosystem partners to design optimal cooling solutions for AI server and switch applications at the most demanding Thermal Design Power levels\. This testing allows us to do just that\.

\#\# Thermal co‑sim testing

We performed three simulations\: an analysis to determine thermal resistance targets for each chip component\, plus testing of two different cooling solutions\. One solution met spec\, and one did not\.

\#\#\# 3D VC heatsink test

We tested a standard air fin heatsink at airspeeds of 5 m\/s and 6 m\/s at 25ºC\.

Fig\. 1\: GUC \+ Ayar Labs CoWoS\-L CPO simulation using heatsink\.

This did not meet spec\, as the temperature significantly exceeded spec for all components except the I\/O die\.

\#\#\# Thermal resistance analysis

We analyzed the maximum junction temperature versus resistance curve to determine suitable resistance for the Chip\-on\-Wafer\-on\-Substrate with Local Silicon Interconnect \(CoWoS\-L\) advanced packaging and optical engine to meet the temperature spec\.

The cold plate design achieves these targets with pressure drops of 11\.2 kPa for the ASIC cold plate and 18\.8 kPa for the optical engine cold plate\. This ensures efficient coolant flow while maintaining thermal performance\.

\#\#\# Cold plate test

\- HBM4 \< 95ºC
\- SoC \< 125ºC
\- Optical Engine \< 100ºC

The tests we’ve shared here were based on static power assumptions\, where each component’s power consumption remains constant\. These thermal co\-simulation test results demonstrate that CPO can operate reliably in high\-power AI systems when paired with appropriate cooling solutions\. records.abstract: Celestica DS6005 Puts 102.4Tbps of Co-Packaged Optics and 64 1.6TbE Ports in a 1.5OU Liquid-Cooled ORv3 Switch StorageReview.com
records.summary: StorageReview reports that Celestica introduced the DS6005 at the OCP Global Summit, a co-packaged optics (CPO) data center switch delivering 102.4Tbps of non-blocking switching capacity and 64 optically enabled 1.6TbE ports in a 1.5OU, fully liquid-cooled chassis for Open Rack v3. The system is built on Broadcom's Tomahawk 6 Davisson, the CPO version of the 102.4T Tomahawk 6, which integrates optical engines onto the switch package so the front panel carries fiber connectors and laser modules instead of pluggable transceivers. Celestica states that co-packaging removes discrete DSPs and long copper traces between the ASIC and pluggable modules, reducing link-level power and latency, while 16 field-replaceable ELSFP external laser modules keep lasers outside the package. The switch targets AI/ML scale-up and scale-out fabrics and runs SONiC with ONIE. Celestica DS6005 Puts 102.4Tbps of Co-Packaged Optics and 64 1.6TbE Ports in a 1.5OU Liquid-Cooled ORv3 Switch
by Harold Fritts on October 15, 2026
Celestica introduced the DS6005 at the OCP Global Summit, a co-packaged optics (CPO) data center switch that puts 102.4Tbps of switching capacity and 64 optically enabled 1.6TbE ports in a 1.5OU, fully liquid-cooled chassis for Open Rack v3. It is built on Broadcom’s Tomahawk 6 Davisson, the CPO version of the 102.4T Tomahawk 6, which integrates the optical engines onto the switch package so the front panel carries fiber connectors and laser modules in place of pluggable transceivers. Celestica is aiming it at AI/ML scale-up and scale-out fabrics.
The DS6005 lands in the same week as two other Tomahawk 6 CPO systems. Micas Networks put Davisson in a 1RU box with a Q1 2027 production date, and Supermicro’s 2OU CPO switch takes busbar power in an ORv3 rack. Celestica’s version is the one built for the OCP high-power rack from the start, with liquid cooling as the only cooling option and a chassis labeled for 46 to 56V DC input at 76A on the rear.
Optical Engine Integration
Co-packaging moves the optical engines from the faceplate onto the Tomahawk 6 Davisson package, which Celestica says removes the discrete digital signal processors and the long copper traces between the ASIC and a pluggable module, cutting link-level power and latency.
The lasers stay outside the package: the DS6005 carries 16 ELSFP external laser modules on the front panel that can be swapped in the field, so a failed laser does not take the switch out of service, and the 64 1.6TbE ports terminate in 16 MMC-16 fiber connectors. Celestica also cites CPO-aware software management for the platform, though it has not described what that covers.
“AI infrastructure is driving unprecedented demand for bandwidth, while power, thermal management, latency, and reach are becoming increasingly important constraints,” said Gavin Cato, SVP & GM Portfolio Solutions & AI Platform Engineering at Celestica. “The DS6005 brings co-packaged optics, liquid cooling, field-replaceable external laser modules, and CPO-aware software management together in a compact platform designed to help customers build scalable and power-efficient AI fabrics.”
Celestica has not published power or latency figures for the DS6005, so the savings over a pluggable-optics switch remain something to investigate further. Broadcom’s Manish Mehta, vice president of marketing and operations for its Optical Systems Division, said the partnership covers silicon, optical engines, packaging, thermal design, manufacturing, and system integration, and Dell’Oro Group’s Sameh Boujelbene noted in the same announcement that pluggable, near-package, and co-packaged optics will coexist as the ecosystem matures.
Thermal Management
The DS6005 is fully liquid-cooled in a 1.5OU chassis for ORv3-HPR, the OCP high-power rack, with the coolant quick-disconnects and the DC input on the rear panel. Celestica says the cooling keeps switch-level temperature stable, which improves reliability and allows denser racks, and its product page claims the design prevents thermal throttling. Beyond the switch ASIC and optics, the system runs an AMD Ryzen x86 host CPU with a BMC, carries TPM 2.0, a hardware root of trust, and post-quantum cryptography support, and has IEEE 1588 and SyncE timing hardware.
The switch runs SONiC with ONIE for installation, though Celestica has not named a SONiC release, and its specifications are preliminary and subject to change. The announcement and product documentation do not give sampling, shipping, or general-availability dates.

records.body_text:
JIT Industries Acquires Birmingham-Based Chrome Plating Facility
JIT Industries, a full-service diversified company specializing in fluid power manufacturing and repair, large-scale machining, engineering support, and automation, has acquired Precision Plating in Birmingham, Alabama.
Precision Plating specializes in industrial hard chrome plating, machining, grinding, roll repair, and surface restoration. The facility can also chrome large components up to 23 feet long and up to 28 inches in outside diameter.
Precision Plating has served Birmingham and the surrounding region for more than 40 years. As part of JIT Industries, Precision Plating continues to expand its capabilities and provide customers with additional hydraulic and fluid power support.
Precision Plating is led by Operations Manager Charlie Butler, who brings more than 40 years of experience in the chrome plating industry. Together, the Precision Plating team has more than 90 years of industry experience.
“I’m proud to lead this new chapter for Precision Plating,” Butler says. “I believe we can accomplish a lot as part of JIT Industries, and I’m excited to see what the future holds as we continue to grow and support our customers in new ways.”
Matt McComb, COO of JIT Industries, was happy with the agreement.
"We are thrilled to welcome Precision Plating to the JIT Industries team as we continue our aggressive expansion focused on providing localized, immediate support and expanded capabilities across our network," McComb says.
The addition of Precision Plating expands JIT Industries’ industrial hard chrome plating capabilities while strengthening its ability to provide comprehensive fluid power solutions. Precision Plating is one of seven locations owned and operated by JIT Industries across four states.
Founded in 2001 in Hartselle, Alabama, JIT Industries began as a local hydraulic repair shop. Over the past 25 years, the company has grown into a full-service fluid power provider with seven Southeast locations. JIT Industries provides cylinder manufacturing, fluid power repair, CNC machining, engineering, research and development, and industrial hard chrome plating services to customers across heavy and critical industries.

records.title: Silver Plating For Conductive Applications: Benefits And Limitations
records.abstract: It also has limits, mainly tarnish and silver migration, and both are worth planning for before a part goes into production. ... Tarnish Silver reacts with sulfur compounds in the air, such as hydrogen sulfide, and forms a dark film of silver sulfide. The film can raise contact resistance, especially on low-force contacts that cannot wipe through it, and it can reduce solderability.
records.summary: This ProPlate article explains why silver plating is used for conductive surfaces and what limits its use. Silver has the highest electrical conductivity of any metal, slightly ahead of copper and well ahead of gold, and it provides low contact resistance, good high-frequency performance via the skin effect, and good solderability when fresh, at lower cost than gold. The article states that silver tarnishes by reacting with airborne sulfur compounds such as hydrogen sulfide to form silver sulfide, which can raise contact resistance, especially on low-force contacts, and reduce solderability. It also describes silver migration under DC voltage with moisture, where silver ions form dendritic deposits that can bridge gaps and short circuits, with risk rising at closer spacing, higher humidity, and higher voltage. Additional limitations covered are wear and galling on sliding contacts, and the need for a silver strike and sometimes a nickel underplate for adhesion and diffusion barrier. The article is a vendor technical explainer, not a peer-reviewed study, and reports no measured performance data.
records.why_it_matters: For power and high-current contacts with enough force to break through a light tarnish film, silver offers the best conductivity at lower cost than gold; for low-force signal contacts or fine-pitch circuitry exposed to moisture, tarnish and silver migration make silver a poorer fit and gold or another finish may be preferable.

Silver Plating for Conductive Applications: Benefits and Limitations
Why Silver Shows Up in Conductive Work
When a part has to carry current with as little loss as possible, silver is one of the first finishes engineers consider. It conducts electricity better than any other metal and costs far less than gold.
That is why silver plating turns up on bus bars, switchgear contacts, and RF connectors. It also has limits, mainly tarnish and silver migration, and both are worth planning for before a part goes into production. Knowing those limits up front is what makes silver electroplating a sound choice and keeps it from becoming an expensive surprise.
Benefits of Silver Plating for Conductive Applications
Highest conductivity of any metal
Silver conducts electricity better than any other metal, slightly ahead of copper and well ahead of gold. As a plated surface, it gives current a low-resistance path right where parts meet. That surface is where losses can show up first, so finishing it with the best available conductor can make a real difference on parts that carry high current.
Low contact resistance
Clean silver has low contact resistance, which matters most at joints carrying high current. Less resistance at a joint means less heat, and less heat means less stress on the joint over time. In switchgear and power connectors, that can help a connection stay stable through years of service.
Performance at high frequencies
At high frequencies, current crowds into a thin layer near the surface of a conductor. This is called the skin effect. On RF and microwave parts, that surface layer may be the plating itself, so a silver finish can lower signal loss even when the base metal underneath conducts less well.
Solderability
Fresh silver plating solders well, which is one reason it is used on electronic parts that need a solderable surface. Solder wets clean silver readily, which helps form a sound joint. That advantage fades as the surface tarnishes, so parts meant for soldering are best soldered while the finish is fresh or protected as described later in this article.
Cost
Silver costs far less than gold. For larger parts, or for thicker deposits where gold would be too expensive, that difference can decide the finish. Bus bars are a good example: plating the whole surface of a large conductive part in gold would rarely make sense.
Where Silver Plating Is Used
As a conductive plating, silver shows up wherever the surface carries the current:
- Bus bars and power distribution components
- Switchgear and circuit breaker contacts
- High-current connectors, including battery and electric vehicle connections
- RF and microwave components, such as coaxial connectors and waveguides
- Electronic parts that need a solderable surface
- Medical devices, including electrosurgical electrodes, RF ablation devices, MRI and RF coil components, and contacts in wearable monitors
In each case, conductivity at the surface matters more than any other property of the finish. That is the job silver does best as an electrical contact plating. On medical devices, silver can also be applied selectively, so only the conductive areas of a part are plated.
Limitations of Silver Plating
Tarnish
Silver reacts with sulfur compounds in the air, such as hydrogen sulfide, and forms a dark film of silver sulfide. The film can raise contact resistance, especially on low-force contacts that cannot wipe through it, and it can reduce solderability.
Higher-force contacts may break through a light film on their own. That is part of why silver works well in power applications and less well on delicate signal contacts.
Silver migration
Under a DC voltage with moisture present, silver ions can move from one conductor toward another and grow thin, branching deposits called dendrites. If a dendrite bridges the gap, it can short the circuit. The risk rises with closer spacing, higher humidity, and higher voltage, so silver may be a poor fit for fine-pitch circuitry that will see moisture in service.
Wear and galling
Silver is soft. On sliding contacts that cycle many times, it can wear through or gall, which is when the two surfaces stick and tear. A harder bright silver deposit or a contact lubricant can extend life. For high-cycle sliding contacts, another finish may be a better match.
Underplate and adhesion
Silver plating normally starts with a silver strike, a thin first layer from a dilute bath that helps the deposit bond. On copper and copper alloys, a nickel underplate may be added as a barrier. Without it, copper can diffuse into the silver at elevated temperatures and weaken the bond.
RF parts call for more care. Nickel is magnetic and can add signal loss if the silver layer above it is thin, so some designers skip the nickel, specify enough silver to keep the current out of it, or use palladium as the underplate instead, since palladium is not magnetic.
Specifying Silver Plating
Standards
Engineering silver plating is commonly specified to ASTM B700, which classifies silver deposits by purity (type), appearance (grade), and whether a supplementary tarnish treatment is applied (class). Older drawings may still call out the federal spec QQ-S-365, and aerospace work may reference AMS 2410 or AMS 2411. Our article on the evolution of silver plating standards covers how these specs relate.
What a complete callout covers
A drawing that spells out these points gives the plater what it needs to quote and plate the part correctly:
- The specification, with type, grade, and class
- Minimum thickness, and where on the part it is measured
- Underplate, if any
- Packaging requirements
Leaving any of these open means the plater has to guess, and a guess on packaging can show up as tarnished parts at receiving inspection. Thickness deserves particular care, since it can drive both the cost and how long the finish holds up to wear.
Protecting parts from tarnish
Anti-tarnish treatments applied after plating can slow the reaction, and on an ASTM B700 callout the class sets whether one is used. Packaging matters too. Sulfur-free paper and sealed bags help, and plated parts should be kept away from rubber bands and some cardboard, which can give off sulfur compounds. A part that leaves the plater clean can still arrive tarnished if it is packed wrong.
Silver or Gold?
Gold does not tarnish, so it is a common choice for low-force signal contacts and for parts that may sit in storage before use. Silver conducts better and costs less, which makes it a strong option for power and high-current contacts with enough force to break through a light film. The better fit depends on contact force, current, operating environment, and how long parts will sit before they go into service.
Silver Plating at ProPlate
ProPlate provides medical silver plating and industrial silver plating, with a nickel underplate where the base metal calls for it and a tarnish-resistant treatment for parts that need one. Work can be done to specifications including ASTM B700, QQ-S-365, AMS 2410, and AMS 2411. If you are weighing silver against another finish, ask an expert early, while the spec can still be shaped around the part.

Integrated Laser Cleaning and Welding System for Automotive Busbars
- October 16, 2026
Copper busbars are essential components in electric vehicle (EV) power distribution systems and electronic control units. They carry high currents between batteries, power electronics, and electrical connections. Consistent weld quality is critical to electrical conductivity, connection reliability, and overall system safety.
However, laser welding copper presents two major challenges: surface contamination and the material’s high thermal conductivity and reflectivity at infrared wavelengths. Oxide layers, oil residues, paint, and insulating coatings can interfere with laser energy absorption and weld formation. Copper also dissipates heat rapidly, making stable energy input and precise positioning essential.
Han’s Laser Integrated Laser Cleaning and Welding Gantry System for Automotive Busbars combines surface cleaning and laser welding in one machine. By integrating both processes with dual workstations, laser distance measurement, and welding data tracking, the system helps streamline production and improve process consistency.
Integrated Laser Cleaning and Welding
The system combines a laser cleaning unit and a laser welding unit on a single gantry platform. Before welding, the cleaning station removes paint, oxide layers, or other specified surface coatings from the busbar. The workpiece can then proceed directly to welding without intermediate transfer or secondary clamping.
This integrated approach reduces handling steps and repeated positioning, helping minimize alignment errors between cleaning and welding. It also supports a more efficient production sequence for busbars with multiple welding points.
Dual-Station Layout for Flexible Production
The left-right dual-station configuration allows cleaning and welding operations to be organized in alternating or coordinated production cycles, depending on the application.
This layout helps improve equipment utilization and supports continuous production across different product types. It is particularly useful for manufacturers processing multiple busbar designs or components that require both surface preparation and precision welding.
Gantry Design and Real-Time Distance Measurement
The gantry structure features a vertically downward-facing welding station, providing flexibility for different component geometries and fixture arrangements.
Laser distance measurement is integrated at each station to detect workpiece position and height variations in real time. This capability helps compensate for incoming-part variation and reduces the risk of welding deviations caused by inconsistent workpiece positioning.
For busbars with multiple weld locations, accurate positioning is especially important for maintaining consistent joint placement across production batches.
Semi-Automated Operation and Process Traceability
The system uses a semi-automated production approach that combines operator-assisted handling with automated cleaning and welding operations. This configuration helps balance production flexibility with repeatable processing.
Key capabilities include:
- Integrated process flow: Combines cleaning and welding within one machine.
- Reduced handling: Eliminates intermediate transfer and secondary clamping between the two processes.
- Real-time distance measurement: Detects workpiece position variations at both stations.
- Automated data recording: Saves welding data and uploads it to the designated system for traceability.
- Quality analysis: Provides historical welding parameters to support investigation of quality issues and process improvement.
- User-friendly operation: An intuitive human-machine interface simplifies routine operation and maintenance.
Data availability and system integration can be configured according to production management requirements.
Applications in EV Manufacturing and Beyond
Automotive Busbar Welding
The laser cleaning and welding system is designed for copper busbars used in EV battery packs, electronic control units, power distribution units (PDUs), and battery module connections. Online cleaning before welding helps prepare coated or oxidized surfaces for the joining process.
Laser Welding
Copper-to-Copper and Terminal Connections
It can be configured for overlapping copper busbars and connections between copper busbars and terminals. The downward-facing welding arrangement supports different workpiece orientations and joint configurations, subject to fixture and process validation.
Other Metal Components Requiring Pre-Weld Cleaning
The integrated architecture can also be evaluated for other metal components that require paint removal, coating removal, or oxide cleaning before laser welding.
Laser Cleaning
The system is particularly relevant to applications involving multiple weld points, variable incoming-part dimensions, frequent product changeovers, or production traceability requirements.
A More Integrated Approach to Busbar Welding
Reliable busbar welding depends not only on laser parameters but also on surface condition, positioning accuracy, and coordination between process steps.
By integrating laser cleaning and welding with dual-station operation, real-time distance measurement, and welding data tracking, Han’s Laser provides a coordinated solution for automotive busbar manufacturing. The system helps reduce unnecessary handling, manage workpiece variation, and support more consistent, traceable production.
Contact Han’s Laser to discuss an integrated cleaning and welding solution for your busbar components and production requirements.

records.title: Material extrusion-based additive manufacturing of aluminum feedstocks with a focus on the debinding process
records.abstract: Abstract This study investigates the printability, debinding, and sinterability of aluminum-based (AA6061) feedstocks prepared with three different commercial thermoplastic binder compositions, with focus on the effect of the post-processing on microstructure and densification during sintering. Two debinding approaches were studied: (i) solvent debinding followed by thermal debinding, and (ii) single-step wick debinding, in which the green parts were embedded in a powder bed. Debinding is the most challenging stage for Al-containing feedstocks. The strong tendency of aluminum to oxidize significantly restricts the choice of solvent and limits debinding in an oxygen-containing atmosphere. To avoid oxidation of aluminum powder, the solvent type and debinding temperature in air must be restricted. This limitation can leave residues of carbon in the structure during sintering in a nitrogen atmosphere. Based on simultaneous thermal gravimetric analysis, the onset oxidation temperature for the 6061 aluminum powder used in this study was determined to be approximately 400 °C; therefore, the thermal debinding temperature under air was selected below this limit. The results showed that with both debinding methods, binder removal of ≥ 96% could be achieved. However, optical microscopy and density measurements after sintering indicated that even high-purity acetone as a solvent medium resulted in slight oxidation, particularly at the printed sample surfaces. Interestingly, wick debinding without previous solvent debinding resulted in samples with higher post-sintering density. The effect of sintering dwell time was also examined. Increasing the holding time from 2 h to 10 h improved the relative density from ~ 97% to ~ 98%.
records.summary: This study investigates material extrusion (MEX-AM) printing of AA6061 aluminum feedstocks made with three commercial thermoplastic binders (EnCeram, Kcmix, EmbemouldCC), focusing on debinding and sintering. Because aluminum oxidizes readily, the authors used simultaneous thermal analysis to find an oxidation onset near 400 °C and limited air thermal debinding below this temperature. records.body_text:
Material extrusion-based additive manufacturing of aluminum feedstocks with a focus on the debinding process
- Research
- Open access
- Published:
Abstract
This study investigates the printability, debinding, and sinterability of aluminum-based (AA6061) feedstocks prepared with three different commercial thermoplastic binder compositions, with focus on the effect of the post-processing on microstructure and densification during sintering. Two debinding approaches were studied: (i) solvent debinding followed by thermal debinding, and (ii) single-step wick debinding, in which the green parts were embedded in a powder bed. Debinding is the most challenging stage for Al-containing feedstocks. The strong tendency of aluminum to oxidize significantly restricts the choice of solvent and limits debinding in an oxygen-containing atmosphere. To avoid oxidation of aluminum powder, the solvent type and debinding temperature in air must be restricted. This limitation can leave residues of carbon in the structure during sintering in a nitrogen atmosphere. Based on simultaneous thermal gravimetric analysis, the onset oxidation temperature for the 6061 aluminum powder used in this study was determined to be approximately 400 °C; therefore, the thermal debinding temperature under air was selected below this limit. The results showed that with both debinding methods, binder removal of ≥ 96% could be achieved. However, optical microscopy and density measurements after sintering indicated that even high-purity acetone as a solvent medium resulted in slight oxidation, particularly at the printed sample surfaces. Interestingly, wick debinding without previous solvent debinding resulted in samples with higher post-sintering density. The effect of sintering dwell time was also examined. Increasing the holding time from 2 h to 10 h improved the relative density from ~ 97% to ~ 98%.
