records.body_text:
Four Generations, One Specialty: Jersey Chrome Builds Its Legacy on Hard Chrome
For many finishers, growth means adding processes.
A zinc line leads to electroless nickel. Powder coating leads to liquid coating. Anodizing leads to passivation, conversion coatings, or another complementary finishing technology. As customers seek fewer suppliers and more capabilities, the temptation to become a one-stop finishing source can be considerable.
At Jersey Chrome Plating in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, the strategy has largely been the opposite.
For more than seven decades at its current location, the company has concentrated overwhelmingly on one demanding specialty: industrial hard chrome plating.
Today, fourth-generation owner and President Alan Jersey sees no compelling reason to abandon an approach that has worked for his family for decades.
“For the time being anyhow, we’re content to just master chrome plating and to try to be the best,” Jersey says. “Not the biggest. I don’t care about being the biggest, but I want us to be the best at chrome plating.”
This deceptively simple philosophy explains much about the company’s longevity.
Jersey Plating remains a small operation, employing 10 people and combining industrial hard chrome and thin dense chrome capabilities with an extensive precision grinding operation. The company’s size is intentional, its specialization deliberate, and its chrome-plating knowledge built through generations of experience.
“I worked with my dad on my summer breaks in high school and college,” Jersey says. “I always enjoyed it. I enjoyed working here on my summer breaks. It was something I looked forward to.”
And while Jersey is now the fourth generation overseeing the business, his path to its presidency wasn’t necessarily predetermined.
It took him away from Pittsburgh, into the U.S. Marine Corps and eventually back onto the shop floor, where he spent years learning the trade before taking responsibility for a company whose roots stretch back to his great-grandfather.
A Chrome Plating History That Began in the 1920s
The Jersey family’s history in the finishing industry predates the current company.
Jersey says his great-grandfather began chrome plating in Beaver County, about an hour outside Pittsburgh, during the 1920s. The Great Depression eventually forced him to close the plating operation, although he continued operating other businesses, including, according to Jersey, a gas station and restaurant.
His great-grandfather had several sons, including Jersey’s grandfather. Like millions of men of their generation, the brothers served during World War II. When they returned, the eldest son put the family’s knowledge of chrome plating back to work.
In 1949, Jersey Chrome Plating Company opened at its current Pittsburgh location.
“We’ve been here ever since,” Jersey says.
His great-uncle served as the first president of the Pittsburgh operation. Ownership eventually passed to Jersey’s grandfather around 1960, then to his father in 1980.
His father would oversee the company for more than 40 years, remaining at the helm until he died in 2021. That means much of Jersey Plating's history isn't simply family history told through photographs, memorabilia, and stories passed between generations. It exists inside the same facility where the company has operated since 1949.
Alan grew up about 15 minutes away. Like many children raised around family manufacturing businesses, he grew up with the shop as a familiar part of his life long before it became his career.
“I worked with my dad on my summer breaks in high school and college,” Jersey says. “I always enjoyed it. I enjoyed working here on my summer breaks. It was something I looked forward to.”
But joining the company permanently was not always the plan.
The Long Way Back to the Family Business
After college, Jersey chose a dramatically different career. He joined the Marine Corps and became an infantry officer, ultimately serving approximately six years and rising to the rank of captain. For a time, he seriously considered making the military his career.
Then his priorities began to change.
“After a few years of doing that, once I had my first child, I thought maybe being in the Marine Corps in the infantry wasn’t the most family-friendly line of work to be in,” Jersey says.
The family business was never far from his thoughts.
“It’s always been in the back of my mind,” he says. “I’ve always been drawn to it. So even while serving in the Marine Corps, I felt the pull to come back here and get back into the family business, and I’m glad I did.”
He returned to Jersey Plating full time in 2014. What happened next matters for understanding how Jersey eventually became the owner. He didn’t immediately move into the front office. He went to the shop floor. And he stayed there.
Learning Hard Chrome From the Shop Floor Up
For years after coming back to the company, Jersey says he worked almost exclusively in production.
“Before 2020, 2021, I worked exclusively on the shop floor,” he says. “Fifty, 60, 70 hours a week exclusively on the shop floor, just mastering everything myself.”
For a company of Jersey Plating’s size and specialization, Jersey says there wasn’t really an alternative.
“A business our size and as specialized as it is, that was necessary,” he says. “So I just really poured myself into the trade and just mastered it as best I could, and really got a good understanding of it.”
After several years, Jersey essentially became the shop foreman under his father, taking on increasing responsibility for day-to-day production. He officially became his father’s business partner in 2020. When his father died in 2021, Alan assumed full control.
The transition was emotionally and professionally different from what happens at many multigenerational businesses. The former owner didn't stay nearby as an adviser who could be called when an unfamiliar problem surfaced.
Jersey had to rely on the knowledge he had already acquired. Fortunately, that preparation had been extensive.
“By the time it was time for me to sit in the big chair, from that aspect I was certainly ready,” Jersey says. “I’d already been running the shop. But you’re right, it is different once the buck stops with you.”
Leadership Lessons From the Marine Corps
Jersey also brought something previous generations of his family had not necessarily possessed: six years of leadership training and experience as a Marine Corps officer.
He had served as a platoon commander and company executive officer before leaving the service as a captain.
The environments are very different, but Jersey says the lessons he learned about responsibility, leadership, and management translated well to operating a manufacturing company.
“Joining the Marine Corps was one of the best things I ever did,” he says. “I really did enjoy my service a lot.”
Becoming an officer meant extensive preparation.
“To be a Marine Corps officer, you spend your first year in training, learning not just tactics and that sort of thing, but also leadership and management,” Jersey says.
“With a heavy buildup, you often have to grind after plating in order to achieve your tolerance.”
That experience proved valuable when everything at Jersey Plating ultimately became his responsibility.
“When it was time for me to fill the big seat, I certainly did not feel overwhelmed or intimidated,” Jersey says.
Technical competence mattered, but so did the ability to make decisions and own them. For a 10-person plating company, there aren’t layers of management separating the president from what is happening at a tank, grinder, or piece of equipment. Problems can’t simply be passed to another department.
The owner has to understand the operation.
Why Hard Chrome Remains the Specialty
Jersey Plating’s core business is industrial hard chrome plating, including thin dense chrome, rather than the decorative chrome work consumers often associate with the word “chrome.”
“We do industrial chrome plating and precision grinding,” Jersey says. “We don’t offer decorative chrome plating, although we certainly get a lot of phone calls for it.”
Precision grinding has become essential to the company's service. Hard chrome can involve substantial deposits, and those heavy buildups may need to be ground after plating to achieve the required dimensions.
Jersey says the company can apply chrome deposits ranging from less than one ten-thousandth of an inch to as much as 0.060 inch radial thickness. Heavy deposits create challenges familiar to experienced hard chrome platers.
“Just the nature of hard chrome is, you have your high current density areas and low current density areas just like any other type of plating,” Jersey says. “With a heavy buildup, you often have to grind after plating in order to achieve your tolerance.”
That relationship between depositing the chrome and producing the finished dimension is one reason grinding has become such an important part of Jersey Plating.
“When it comes to hard chrome, precision grinding goes hand in hand with it,” Jersey says.
Bringing Plating and Grinding Together
Jersey Plating began adding grinding capabilities shortly after Alan’s father took over in 1980.
Jersey believes his father purchased his first grinder around 1981. The company expanded its grinding department from there. More than four decades later, grinding is a major component of the business.
“It makes us, really, a one-stop shop when it comes to chrome plating and grinding,” Jersey says.
Bringing the operations together offers benefits beyond convenience.
A part requiring heavy chrome buildup may need substantial post-plate grinding. If different suppliers perform the two processes, the work must travel between facilities, and dimensional requirements must be communicated across companies.
At Jersey Plating, those operations remain under one roof.
“It saves our customers the trouble of sending things to multiple sources,” Jersey says. “We can do it all here.”
Another benefit comes when something goes wrong.
“If there’s a mistake made, if there’s a tight tolerance where the grinder takes it undersize, we can fix it all in-house,” Jersey says. “There’s no shipping costs involved in that.”
The plating and grinding departments therefore work as complementary parts of the same process rather than independent services.
Grinding Capacity Built Around Chrome
The company’s grinding capabilities have expanded significantly since the first machine arrived in the early 1980s.
Jersey Plating operates OD and ID grinding equipment as well as vertical universal grinders. It also has CNC and NC grinding equipment that Jersey says is particularly useful for higher-volume work.
“The CNC and the NC machines really come in handy,” he says. “It’s semi-automated, and it’s a big time saver, and it’s easy to hit tight tolerances with those machines.”
Vertical grinding adds versatility for parts whose configurations may not lend themselves to conventional OD or ID grinding.
“Oddly shaped items can be ground on a vertical grinder,” Jersey says. “So there’s a lot that we can grind.”
The company’s largest OD grinder can accommodate work up to 126 inches long and 19 inches in outside diameter. While the company occasionally receives requests outside its grinding envelope, Jersey says its current equipment gives the shop considerable capacity for the work it encounters.
Those capabilities also reinforce a strategy that has worked for Jersey Plating for decades: rather than continually adding unrelated coating technologies, the company has invested in services that directly strengthen its hard chrome business.
Every Hard Chrome Job Can Be Different
Ask Jersey about one of the greatest challenges in hard chrome plating, and the answer quickly comes back to people.
At its largest, Jersey says, the company had approximately 20 employees during the 1980s and 1990s. His father deliberately reduced that number.
Why intentionally become smaller? Control.
“I think the biggest we’ve ever been was around 20 employees in the ‘80s and ‘90s,” Jersey says. “My father, at the time, deliberately just downsized it to keep better quality control.”
For a specialized operation, fewer people made it easier to monitor work and maintain consistency.
“Hard chrome plating is so technical,” Jersey says. “It can be tough if you’ve got a lot of people running around who don’t know what they’re doing.”
That puts enormous importance on training.
Unlike high-volume finishing operations in which similar components travel through standardized processes repeatedly, Jersey says hard chrome frequently demands a different approach from one part to another.
“One job can vary so much from the next,” he says. “Every plating setup is pretty much custom.”
He emphasizes the distinction plainly.
“We’re not just clipping parts on a rack and putting them in a tank,” Jersey says. “Each setup really is custom.”
Capturing the Tribal Knowledge
That customization presents one of manufacturing’s oldest challenges: how do you preserve knowledge that traditionally resides in the heads of experienced employees?
Jersey readily acknowledges that hard chrome carries a substantial amount of what manufacturers often call tribal knowledge.
“There is a lot of tribal knowledge,” he says.
The company works to capture as much of that knowledge as possible.
“We record as much as we can, and we have work instructions,” Jersey says. “I generate work instructions for every job to try to make everything as easy to understand as possible.”
“Through his tutelage I’ve learned how to repair pretty much everything in here myself if I have to, and just learned a lot of mechanical knowledge from him and from my father before he passed.”
But documentation can only go so far in a process involving different component geometries, plating setups, current density considerations, buildup requirements, and final dimensions. That makes developing skilled employees one of the owner’s most important responsibilities.
“Training is one of the most important aspects of the business,” Jersey says.
In a company that has spent generations accumulating process knowledge, transferring that expertise is every bit as important as maintaining rectifiers, tanks or grinders.
Learning to Maintain the Shop, Too
Jersey has also become increasingly self-sufficient with the equipment that keeps the business operating.
He credits a longtime electrician who has serviced the plant and become an important mentor. Jersey says the relationship has helped him acquire knowledge that goes considerably beyond plating.
“He’s been doing the electrical and repairs around here for a long time,” Jersey says. “As far as just mechanical things and electrical things, he’s an absolute expert.”
Working alongside him, Jersey learned to handle many repairs himself.
“Through his tutelage I’ve learned how to repair pretty much everything in here myself if I have to, and just learned a lot of mechanical knowledge from him and from my father before he passed,” Jersey says.
For a small specialty finishing company, that versatility can be invaluable. The person running the business isn’t separated from the equipment or process.
Jersey’s education as an owner has come from multiple places: his father, years spent plating and grinding, his Marine Corps experience, and people with specialized technical knowledge who have been around the facility for years.
Resisting the Urge to Diversify
Perhaps the most interesting part of Jersey Plating’s story is what the company has not done. Over many decades, it hasn’t transformed itself into a broad finishing house offering a long menu of processes.
Jersey says his father considered other technologies at various times, including decorative chrome and nickel plating, but never completed the expansion. Alan has considered diversification as well.
Other plating technologies could eventually be possibilities, as could spray coating processes. But for now, Jersey sees little reason to add another coating to offer something new.
The existing operation stays busy.
“For the time being, we have plenty of demand, and we stay busy,” Jersey says. “We pretty much occupy all of our tank space every day for the most part.”
“Not the biggest,” he says. “I want us to be the best at chrome plating.”
That makes the strategic calculation different. Adding a coating technology would mean new equipment, new process controls and, critically, another body of technical knowledge that the company would have to master.
Jersey would rather deepen the expertise that already distinguishes the business.
“We’re content to be the master of one trade instead of a jack-of-all-trades kind of thing where we’re doing all these different coatings,” he says.
This philosophy runs counter to the traditional assumption that a manufacturer must continually add services to grow. At Jersey Plating, specialization itself is the strategy.
Not the Biggest, but the Best
In an industry where finishing companies are continually confronting demands for capital equipment, skilled employees, automation, and new technologies, Jersey Plating offers another model for longevity.
Its history has not depended on becoming a large company. It hasn’t depended on adding every finishing process customers might request.
And despite being part of a family legacy, Alan Jersey didn’t inherit his technical knowledge along with the president’s title. He spent years earning it on the shop floor.
That combination of generational knowledge and hands-on experience has carried the business from a family plating operation whose origins reach to the 1920s through the creation of Jersey Chrome Plating Company in 1949, his grandfather’s ownership, more than four decades under his father, and now into a fourth generation.
The machinery has evolved. Grinding became increasingly important. CNC and NC equipment added a measure of automation. Work instructions increasingly capture knowledge that may once have been communicated almost entirely from one experienced plater to another.
But the central business remains remarkably recognizable.
Hard chrome goes on parts. Precision grinding brings them to dimension. Experienced people learn how to handle jobs that may be different every time they come through the door.
More than seven decades after the Pittsburgh operation began, Jersey believes there is still plenty of opportunity in simply doing that work exceptionally well.

Its current president left Pittsburgh for a completely different life, became a Marine Corps officer, and still ultimately found himself drawn back to the plating tanks he had worked around as a young man.

He credits a longtime electrician who has serviced the plant and become an important mentor\. Jersey says the relationship has helped him acquire knowledge that goes considerably beyond plating\.

“He’s been doing the electrical and repairs around here for a long time\,” Jersey says\. “As far as just mechanical things and electrical things\, he’s an absolute expert\.”

\#\#\#\# Not the Biggest\, but the Best

In an industry where finishing companies are continually confronting demands for capital equipment\, skilled employees\, automation\, and new technologies\, Jersey Plating offers another model for longevity\.

Its history has not depended on becoming a large company\. It hasn’t depended on adding every finishing process customers might request\.

And despite being part of a family legacy\, Alan Jersey didn’t inherit his technical knowledge along with the president’s title\. He spent years earning it on the shop floor\.

The company has survived depressions in its family’s earlier plating history\, a world war between generations\, changes in ownership\, advancing technology and the transfer of knowledge from fathers to sons\. Its current president left Pittsburgh for a completely different life\, became a Marine Corps officer\, and still ultimately found himself drawn back to the plating tanks he had worked around as a young man\.

Now Jersey is responsible for carrying that knowledge into another generation\.

But he isn’t chasing them\, either\. For now\, there are plating tanks to keep full\, employees to train\, grinders to operate\, equipment to maintain and difficult hard chrome jobs to get right\.

“Not the biggest\,” he says\. “I want us to be the best at chrome plating\.”

For many finishers\, growth means adding processes\.

A zinc line leads to electroless nickel\. Powder coating leads to liquid coating\. Anodizing leads to passivation\, conversion coatings\, or another complementary finishing technology\. As customers seek fewer suppliers and more capabilities\, the temptation to become a one\-stop finishing source can be considerable\.

At Jersey Chrome Plating in Pittsburgh\, Pennsylvania\, the strategy has largely been the opposite\.

For more than seven decades at its current location\, the company has concentrated overwhelmingly on one demanding specialty\: industrial hard chrome plating\.

Today\, fourth\-generation owner and President Alan Jersey sees no compelling reason to abandon an approach that has worked for his family for decades\.

“For the time being anyhow\, we’re content to just master chrome plating and to try to be the best\,” Jersey says\. “Not the biggest\. I don’t care about being the biggest\, but I want us to be the best at chrome plating\.”

This deceptively simple philosophy explains much about the company’s longevity\.

Jersey Plating remains a small operation\, employing 10 people and combining industrial hard chrome and thin dense chrome capabilities with an extensive precision grinding operation\. The company’s size is intentional\, its specialization deliberate\, and its chrome\-plating knowledge built through generations of experience\.

“I worked with my dad on my summer breaks in high school and college\,” Jersey says\. “I always enjoyed it\. I enjoyed working here on my summer breaks\. It was something I looked forward to\.”

And while Jersey is now the fourth generation overseeing the business\, his path to its presidency wasn’t necessarily predetermined\.

It took him away from Pittsburgh\, into the U\.S\. Marine Corps and eventually back onto the shop floor\, where he spent years learning the trade before taking responsibility for a company whose roots stretch back to his great\-grandfather\.

\#\#\#\# A Chrome Plating History That Began in the 1920s

The Jersey family’s history in the finishing industry predates the current company\.

Jersey says his great\-grandfather began chrome plating in Beaver County\, about an hour outside Pittsburgh\, during the 1920s\. The Great Depression eventually forced him to close the plating operation\, although he continued operating other businesses\, including\, according to Jersey\, a gas station and restaurant\.

His great\-grandfather had several sons\, including Jersey’s grandfather\. Like millions of men of their generation\, the brothers served during World War II\. When they returned\, the eldest son put the family’s knowledge of chrome plating back to work\.

In 1949\, Jersey Chrome Plating Company opened at its current Pittsburgh location\.

“We’ve been here ever since\,” Jersey says\.

His great\-uncle served as the first president of the Pittsburgh operation\. Ownership eventually passed to Jersey’s grandfather around 1960\, then to his father in 1980\.

His father would oversee the company for more than 40 years\, remaining at the helm until he died in 2021\. That means much of Jersey Plating\'s history isn\'t simply family history told through photographs\, memorabilia\, and stories passed between generations\. It exists inside the same facility where the company has operated since 1949\.

Alan grew up about 15 minutes away\. Like many children raised around family manufacturing businesses\, he grew up with the shop as a familiar part of his life long before it became his career\.

“I worked with my dad on my summer breaks in high school and college\,” Jersey says\. “I always enjoyed it\. I enjoyed working here on my summer breaks\. It was something I looked forward to\.”

But joining the company permanently was not always the plan\.

\#\#\#\# The Long Way Back to the Family Business

After college\, Jersey chose a dramatically different career\. He joined the Marine Corps and became an infantry officer\, ultimately serving approximately six years and rising to the rank of captain\. For a time\, he seriously considered making the military his career\.

Then his priorities began to change\.

“After a few years of doing that\, once I had my first child\, I thought maybe being in the Marine Corps in the infantry wasn’t the most family\-friendly line of work to be in\,” Jersey says\.

The family business was never far from his thoughts\.

“It’s always been in the back of my mind\,” he says\. “I’ve always been drawn to it\. So even while serving in the Marine Corps\, I felt the pull to come back here and get back into the family business\, and I’m glad I did\.”

He returned to Jersey Plating full time in 2014\. What happened next matters for understanding how Jersey eventually became the owner\. He didn’t immediately move into the front office\. He went to the shop floor\. And he stayed there\.

\#\#\#\# Learning Hard Chrome From the Shop Floor Up

For years after coming back to the company\, Jersey says he worked almost exclusively in production\.

“Before 2020\, 2021\, I worked exclusively on the shop floor\,” he says\. “Fifty\, 60\, 70 hours a week exclusively on the shop floor\, just mastering everything myself\.”

For a company of Jersey Plating’s size and specialization\, Jersey says there wasn’t really an alternative\.

After several years\, Jersey essentially became the shop foreman under his father\, taking on increasing responsibility for day\-to\-day production\. He officially became his father’s business partner in 2020\. When his father died in 2021\, Alan assumed full control\.

The transition was emotionally and professionally different from what happens at many multigenerational businesses\. The former owner didn\'t stay nearby as an adviser who could be called when an unfamiliar problem surfaced\.

Jersey had to rely on the knowledge he had already acquired\. Fortunately\, that preparation had been extensive\.

“By the time it was time for me to sit in the big chair\, from that aspect I was certainly ready\,” Jersey says\. “I’d already been running the shop\. But you’re right\, it is different once the buck stops with you\.”

Jersey also brought something previous generations of his family had not necessarily possessed\: six years of leadership training and experience as a Marine Corps officer\.

He had served as a platoon commander and company executive officer before leaving the service as a captain\.

Becoming an officer meant extensive preparation\.

“With a heavy buildup\, you often have to grind after plating in order to achieve your tolerance\.”

Another benefit comes when something goes wrong\.

The plating and grinding departments therefore work as complementary parts of the same process rather than independent services\.

\#\#\#\# Grinding Capacity Built Around Chrome

The company’s grinding capabilities have expanded significantly since the first machine arrived in the early 1980s\.

Jersey Plating operates OD and ID grinding equipment as well as vertical universal grinders\. It also has CNC and NC grinding equipment that Jersey says is particularly useful for higher\-volume work\.

“The CNC and the NC machines really come in handy\,” he says\. “It’s semi\-automated\, and it’s a big time saver\, and it’s easy to hit tight tolerances with those machines\.”

Vertical grinding adds versatility for parts whose configurations may not lend themselves to conventional OD or ID grinding\.

The company’s largest OD grinder can accommodate work up to 126 inches long and 19 inches in outside diameter\. While the company occasionally receives requests outside its grinding envelope\, Jersey says its current equipment gives the shop considerable capacity for the work it encounters\.

Those capabilities also reinforce a strategy that has worked for Jersey Plating for decades\: rather than continually adding unrelated coating technologies\, the company has invested in services that directly strengthen its hard chrome business\.

He emphasizes the distinction plainly\.

records.body_text:
What is the NVIDIA AI Rack and Interconnect Certification (NCP-ARI)?
The NCP-ARI is an intermediate-level certification that validates a candidate's expertise in deploying high-density AI infrastructure. It covers critical competencies in high-density cabling, rack preparation, liquid-cooling interconnects/manifolds and DC busbar power delivery, safety standards, and installation troubleshooting—ensuring data center environments are optimized for peak NVIDIA platform performance.
Please carefully review our certification FAQs and exam policies before scheduling your exam.
If you have any questions, please contact us.
To access the exam, you’ll need to create a Certiverse account.
Exam Details for NCP-ARI
Duration: 2 hours
Price: $400
Certification Level: Professional
Subject: AI Hardware Installation
Number of questions: 70
Language: English
Validity: This certification is valid for two years from issuance. Recertification may be achieved by retaking the exam.
Credentials: Upon passing the exam, participants will receive a digital badge and optional certificate indicating the certification level and topic.
Who is AI Rack and Interconnect Certification for?
This exam is for Data Center Infrastructure Technicians specializing in high-density AI cluster deployments. In this role, they are responsible for the physical staging, deployment, and validation of cutting-edge NVIDIA AI systems. They bridge the gap between facility engineering (power/cooling) and network engineering, ensuring that massive computational clusters are safely racked, powered, and interconnected with absolute precision.
Related job titles
- Data Center Infrastructure Technician
- Data Center Technician
- Data Center Hardware Installation Technician
- Data Center Network Technician/Network Engineer (Physical Layer)
- Rack and Cabling Technician/Structured Cabling Technician
- AI Data Center Infrastructure Engineer
- Data Center Operations Engineer
- Data Center Facilities/Power and Cooling Engineer
What are the Key Responsibilities for Data Center Infrastructure Technicians?
- Rack Infrastructure and Space Planning: Conduct site surveys to assess floor load capacities and rack clearances. Prepare extra-wide AI racks, install horizontal/vertical containment systems, and manage precise airflow boundary zones.
- High-Density Cabling Installation: Professionally bundle, route, and dress ultra-high-density cabling layers. Install and manage InfiniBand NDR/XDR copper links (DAC/ACC) and MPO/APC fiber optic cables while strictly adhering to a 50/50 left-right routing strategy and 30 mm bend radius constraints.
- Facility Integration: Verify data center environmental readiness, including power redundancy and thermal zones. Manage and balance power distribution units (rPDUs) for high-draw AC racks, and monitor cooling distribution units (CDUs) for liquid-cooled server architectures.
- Testing and Quality Assurance: Perform meticulous fiber end-face cleaning and transceiver inspections before every insertion. Execute cable continuity, link-state verification, and bit error rate (BER) testing to differentiate and validate NVIDIA-specific cabling requirements.
- Safety and Compliance: Adhere strictly to electrical safety protocols, including lockout/tagout (LOTO) and appropriate personal protective equipment inside demanding 120 kW+ environments. Ensure all physical layouts comply with local building and electrical codes and NVIDIA installation standards (DU-10438).
What are the Recommended Qualifications for Data Center Infrastructure Technicians?
- Experience: 2+ years of experience in enterprise data center operations, specifically handling high-density computing or supercomputing infrastructure.
- Networking Mechanics: Understanding of fiber optic types (MMF vs. SMF), transceiver form factors (OSFP vs. QSFP), and optical distance variations (DR, LR, etc.).
- Physical Dexterity and Precision: Mastery of cable slack management, weight distribution support systems (trapeze/ladder racks), and structured containment compliance.
- Infrastructure Awareness: Strong foundational knowledge of hot/cold aisle containment, AC vs. DC rack power dynamics, and liquid-to-air cooling loops.
NCP-ARI Exam Preparation Topics and Recommended Reading
The information below is intended to help you prepare for this exam.
Topics covered, weight per topic, recommended training, and additional readings are provided.
AI Infrastructure Basics for Data Centers
This section covers AI infrastructure basics, focusing on verifying data center power and cooling capacity, distinguishing AC/DC racks, balancing rPDUs, checking power redundancy and grounding, and understanding various cooling systems.
AI Infrastructure Potential Exam Topics:
- Verify power and cooling capacity in the data center.
- Describe the difference between AC- and DC-powered racks.
- Balance the rPDUs for AC-powered racks.
- Verify power redundancy per rack.
- Verify the power capacity by PDU type.
- Describe CDUs for liquid-cooled racks.
- Verify grounding.
- Differentiate between hot-aisle and cold-aisle cooling.
20%
Exam Weight
Pre-Deployment Planning and Site Assessment for AI Data Centers
This exam section covers pre-deployment planning, including physical network documentation, site surveys for load capacity, and verifying environmental readiness (power, cooling, thermal zones) for AI infrastructure.
Planning and Site Assessment Potential Exam Topic:
- Describe physical network design documentation.
- Conduct site surveys for cable management infrastructure (load capacity, clearances).
- Verify environmental readiness (rack spacing, power, cooling, thermal zones).
- Describe inventory check procedures.
11%
Exam Weight
Rack Infrastructure Preparation for AI Platforms
This section covers preparing rack infrastructure for AI platforms, focusing on extra-wide rack specifications, cable management, EMI mitigation for power/data pathways, and verifying containment clearances.
Rack Infrastructure Preparation Potential Exam Topics:
- Describe extra-wide racks for AI platforms.
- Install cable management accessories (vertical/horizontal ducts, bend radius managers).
- Coordinate power and data cable pathways (EMI mitigation).
- Verify rack containment clearance (front-post to front door and front-post to rear-post or inter-rack posts).
10%
Exam Weight
High-Density Cabling Installation for AI Clusters
This section details the practical deployment of high-density cables. It covers distinguishing between NVIDIA and other cables, understanding transceiver form factors (OSFP/QSFP) and fiber types (MMF/SMF), deploying InfiniBand copper and MPO/APC fiber optic cables, implementing the 50/50 left-right routing strategy, and applying professional cable management practices, including cleaning connectors.
High-Density Cabling Installation Potential Exam Topics:
- Describe the difference between NVIDIA cables vs. others.
- Describe the different transceiver form factors (OSFP vs. QSFP).
- Describe the difference between MMF and SMF.
- Describe the transceiver requirements across the various SMF distances.
- Deploy InfiniBand NDR/XDR copper cables.
- Install MPO/APC fiber optic cables.
- Implement 50/50 left-right cable routing strategy.
- Bundle and dress cables professionally (hook and loop fasteners, soft ties, color coding).
- Install fiber optic transceivers and clean connectors.
30%
Exam Weight
Cable Support Systems and Weight Management
This section covers defining a team orientation plan for the cabling workflow, designing cable support systems for ultra-high-density loads, installing overhead cable support infrastructure, and implementing cable slack management.
Cable Support Systems Potential Exam Topics:
- Define a team orientation plan for the cabling workflow.
- Design cable support systems for ultra-high-density loads.
- Install overhead cable support infrastructure.
- Implement cable slack management.
- Understand the causes of unexpected visual results.
- Update the extent attribute of a mesh after updating its points.
7%
Exam Weight
Testing, Verification, and Documentation for AI Cabling
This section covers cable continuity/link testing, final quality inspection (bend radius, labeling, airflow), documentation with diagrams and photos, and troubleshooting signal integrity issues like BER.
Testing and Verification Potential Exam Topics:
- Perform cable continuity and link testing (optical power meter, link status, differentiate between NVIDIA vs. non-NVIDIA cabling).
- Conduct final deployment quality inspection (bend radius, labeling, airflow).
- Document cable deployment with photos and as-built diagrams.
- Troubleshoot signal integrity issues (dirty connectors, over-bending, BER, link down vs. high BER issues).
12%
Exam Weight
Safety, Standards, and Compliance for Data Centers
This section details the practical deployment of high-density cables. It covers adhering to electrical safety, LOTO, fire compliance, NVIDIA installation standards, and proper ESD protection within high-power data center environments.
Safety and Compliance Potential Exam Topics:
- Adhere to electrical safety practices (LOTO, PPE, 120 kW+ environments).
- Comply with fire safety and cable flame ratings (NEC plenum requirements).

\#\# What is the NVIDIA AI Rack and Interconnect Certification \(NCP\-ARI\)\?

The NCP\-ARI is an intermediate\-level certification that validates a candidate\'s expertise in deploying high\-density AI infrastructure\. It covers critical competencies in high\-density cabling\, rack preparation\, liquid\-cooling interconnects\/manifolds and DC busbar power delivery\, safety standards\, and installation troubleshooting—ensuring data center environments are optimized for peak NVIDIA platform performance\.

Please carefully review our certification FAQs and exam policies before scheduling your exam\.

If you have any questions\, please contact us\.

To access the exam\, you’ll need to create a Certiverse account\.

\#\#\#\# Exam Details for NCP\-ARI

Duration\: 2 hours

Price\: \$400

Certification Level\: Professional

Subject\: AI Hardware Installation

Number of questions\: 70

Language\: English

Validity\: This certification is valid for two years from issuance\. Recertification may be achieved by retaking the exam\.

Credentials\: Upon passing the exam\, participants will receive a digital badge and optional certificate indicating the certification level and topic\.

\#\# Who is AI Rack and Interconnect Certification for\?

This exam is for Data Center Infrastructure Technicians specializing in high\-density AI cluster deployments\. In this role\, they are responsible for the physical staging\, deployment\, and validation of cutting\-edge NVIDIA AI systems\. They bridge the gap between facility engineering \(power\/cooling\) and network engineering\, ensuring that massive computational clusters are safely racked\, powered\, and interconnected with absolute precision\.

\#\#\# Related job titles

\- Data Center Infrastructure Technician
\- Data Center Technician
\- Data Center Hardware Installation Technician
\- Data Center Network Technician\/Network Engineer \(Physical Layer\)
\- Rack and Cabling Technician\/Structured Cabling Technician
\- AI Data Center Infrastructure Engineer
\- Data Center Operations Engineer
\- Data Center Facilities\/Power and Cooling Engineer

\#\# What are the Key Responsibilities for Data Center Infrastructure Technicians\?

\- Rack Infrastructure and Space Planning\: Conduct site surveys to assess floor load capacities and rack clearances\. Prepare extra\-wide AI racks\, install horizontal\/vertical containment systems\, and manage precise airflow boundary zones\.
\- High\-Density Cabling Installation\: Professionally bundle\, route\, and dress ultra\-high\-density cabling layers\. Install and manage InfiniBand NDR\/XDR copper links \(DAC\/ACC\) and MPO\/APC fiber optic cables while strictly adhering to a 50\/50 left\-right routing strategy and 30 mm bend radius constraints\.

\- Facility Integration\: Verify data center environmental readiness\, including power redundancy and thermal zones\. Manage and balance power distribution units \(rPDUs\) for high\-draw AC racks\, and monitor cooling distribution units \(CDUs\) for liquid\-cooled server architectures\.
\- Testing and Quality Assurance\: Perform meticulous fiber end\-face cleaning and transceiver inspections before every insertion\. Execute cable continuity\, link\-state verification\, and bit error rate \(BER\) testing to differentiate and validate NVIDIA\-specific cabling requirements\.

\- Safety and Compliance\: Adhere strictly to electrical safety protocols\, including lockout\/tagout \(LOTO\) and appropriate personal protective equipment inside demanding 120 kW\+ environments\. Ensure all physical layouts comply with local building and electrical codes and NVIDIA installation standards \(DU\-10438\)\.

\#\# What are the Recommended Qualifications for Data Center Infrastructure Technicians\?

\- Experience\: 2\+ years of experience in enterprise data center operations\, specifically handling high\-density computing or supercomputing infrastructure\.
\- Networking Mechanics\: Understanding of fiber optic types \(MMF vs\. SMF\)\, transceiver form factors \(OSFP vs\. QSFP\)\, and optical distance variations \(DR\, LR\, etc\.\)\.

\- Physical Dexterity and Precision\: Mastery of cable slack management\, weight distribution support systems \(trapeze\/ladder racks\)\, and structured containment compliance\.

\- Infrastructure Awareness\: Strong foundational knowledge of hot\/cold aisle containment\, AC vs\. DC rack power dynamics\, and liquid\-to\-air cooling loops\.

Topics covered\, weight per topic\, recommended training\, and additional readings are provided\.

Co-Packaged Optics Moves from Promise to Production Planning
By Ayar Labs
October 14, 2026
At Ayar Labs’ CPO Summit, leaders from Meta, Broadcom, AMD, MediaTek, Lumentum, Wiwynn, and Upscale AI examined what the optical interconnect ecosystem must deliver to meet AI demand at scale.
For more than two decades, silicon photonics has been positioned as the eventual successor to copper interconnects. Ayar Labs hosted an invitation-only CPO Summit to align the ecosystem around manufacturability, under the theme “Scaling Co-Packaged Optics for the Next Era of AI Infrastructure.” The discussion centered less on whether that transition will occur and more on whether the supply chain, standards, and manufacturing base will be ready to deliver CPO at scale.
Pat Gelsinger, general partner at Playground Global, former CEO of Intel and VMware, and an Ayar Labs board member, delivered the keynote. Two panels moderated by EE Times journalist Sally Ward-Foxton followed: the first on ecosystem readiness for a surge in co-packaged optics (CPO) demand expected to begin in 2028; the second on the Optical Compute Interconnect Multi-Source Agreement (OCI MSA) and its role in aligning the industry around a common optical interface.

records.abstract: The Effect of Monovalent Cations on Electroless Nickel Plating Finishing and Coating
records.summary: This 1994 Finishing and Coating article reports an experimental study of how the monovalent cations NH4+, Li+, Na+, and K+ affect plating rate, bath stability, deposition potential, microstructure, and phosphorus content in a lactate-acetate electroless nickel (EN) bath. The authors prepared 4 L baths at 0, 3, and 6 metal turnovers (MTO), plated at 87 ± 2 °C and pH 4.6, and measured rate by deposit thickness, potential against Ag/AgCl, composition by EDS, stress by spiral contractometer, and structure by XRD. Plating rates of all baths fell about 30 percent after three turnovers; the lithium bath had the fastest initial rate but precipitated after a few turnovers, while the ammonium bath was slowest but was the only one to reach six turnovers without precipitation. The authors attribute the ammonium behavior to nickel complexing by ammonia and higher sulfate solubility, and propose that the low solubility of Li2HPO3 could be exploited to remove phosphite by hot filtration and extend bath life.
records.why_it_matters: Cation selection is a formulation lever for EN bath life: choosing ammonium salts favors stability at high turnover, while lithium salts favor initial plating rate and offer a possible phosphite-removal route via precipitation and filtration.

score_details.reason: Full-text 1994 article directly addresses electroless nickel plating bath chemistry, a tracked plating/contact-surface engineering problem. It reports concrete experiments: four monovalent cations (NH4+, Li+, Na+, K+) in a lactate-acetate EN bath, plating rates, phosphorus content, intrinsic stress, deposition potentials, salt solubility tables, and a lithium-phosphite filtration approach to extend bath life. Evidence is detailed and traceable to methods and tables, but it is a 1994 trade article with no peer-review metadata, and the retrieval status is 'unavailable' with existing evidence retained, so source integrity is uncertain. Novelty is moderate: lithium salts in EN baths are stated as not previously reported, but the contribution is incremental bath-chemistry characterization rather than a new mechanism. Engineering value is solid for bath-life extension and deposit-stress control in EN processes.

Tensile stress increased considerably with turnovers in deposits from the ammonium and potassium baths

records.body_text:
We investigated the effect of increasing concentrations of NH4+, Li+, Na+, and K+ on plating rate and bath stability in a lactate-acetate EN plating solution.
The relationship between sulfate and phosphite salt solubilities and metal turnovers was studied. We also determined deposition potentials, microstructures, and phosphorus contents.
Since its industrial development in the 1950s, electroless nickel (EN) has found increasing use on a wide variety of parts, primarily for functional engineering applications requiring corrosion and/or wear resistance. Although its growth has slowed in the last few years, the total value of EN coatings in the U.S. is estimated at $200 million.1
EN plating has three major disadvantages compared to electrolytic nickel plating:
- High chemical cost ($0.40 to 0.70/L)
- Limited plating bath life (3 to 6 MTO)
- Expensive spent bath treatment or disposal
Limited bath life results from the continuous accumulation of phosphite and sulfate salts as byproducts of the plating reaction. To maintain optimum pH, frequent alkali addition is necessary. The main reactions are:
(1) Reduction NiSO4 + 3MH2PO2 → Ni0 + 2MH2PO3 + MHSO4 + P + 1/2H2
(2) pH adjustment (4.5 to 6.0) 2MOH + MH2PO3 + MHSO4 → M2HPO3 + M2SO4 + 2H2O
Note: This article was published in 1994, and some financial data may not be adjusted.
Table 1 shows the rapid increase in salt concentration with each nickel turnover (MTO = 1, initial nickel concentration is replenished once) in a typical EN plating bath containing nickel sulfate, sodium hypophosphite, and sodium salts of organic acids, with potassium carbonate as the pH adjuster. Increased salt content increases the solution's density and viscosity, decreases the plating rate, and induces precipitation of nickel phosphite. The NiP deposit properties deteriorate, as evidenced by increasing porosity and tensile stress. Blistering on aluminum is common after three MTOs.

The solubilities of alkali phosphite and sulfate salts are shown in Tables 2 and 3. As expected, the ammonium salts are most soluble. The nickel and lithium phosphites have the lowest solubilities in water. Because a mixture of sodium and potassium sulfates is present in the used plating bath, the actual phosphite solubilities are lower than in water alone. The nickel phosphite solubility depends on the chelating acids used in the EN formulation, which control the “free nickel” ion concentration.2
Sodium and potassium sulfate often crystallize when the spent bath is stored below 5 C. The phosphite anion can precipitate as a calcium or magnesium salt; however, the plating solution will then contain calcium or magnesium cations that impair deposit properties.3 The use of lithium salts in an EN bath has not been previously reported. In an electroless copper bath, lithium hydroxide was superior to sodium and potassium hydroxide in improving the plating rate and the mechanical properties of the copper deposits.4 One early reference found a sodium glycolate bath to plate at 21 mm/hr at 97°C and an initial pH of 4.5, compared to a rate of 16 mm/hr for an ammonium glycolate bath.5
This investigation explores the effect of varying the monovalent alkali ions in an EN plating solution.
Experimental Procedure
For all plating experiments, 4L solutions were used. Deposit composition was obtained by foil analysis using an electron beam microprobe (EDS). Intrinsic stress measurements were made with a spiral contractometer. The MTO0 deposit crystal structures were examined on foils with an X-ray diffractometer. Plating solutions containing potassium salts, but no sulfate ions, were prepared and evaluated as listed in Table 5.
Fig. 1—Solubility of anhydrous phosphites; Fig. 2—Solubility of lithium phosphite; Fig. 3—Lithium phosphite removal.

The results of the initial experiments are shown in Table 6. The plating rates of all the baths decreased by about 30 percent after three metal turnovers. Surprisingly, the lithium bath showed the fastest initial plating rate and produced a deposit with relatively low potential and slightly higher phosphorus content.
The ammonium bath plated the slowest; however, it yielded six turnovers without precipitation. Both results can be attributed to the nickel complexing action of ammonia. Tensile stress increased considerably with turnovers in deposits from the ammonium and potassium baths. Comparison of X-ray diffraction diagrams of the MTO0 foils reveals no microstructural differences among the various cation deposits (Table 7).
In the absence of sulfate, the potassium plating bath initially plated at 12.5 mm/hr. After adding 68 M potassium phosphite (6 MTO), the plating rate decreased to 5 mm/hr. The deposition potential also decreased from 590 to 620 mV.
Because lithium phosphite has lower solubility than other monovalent cation phosphites (Figs. 1 and 2), we investigated the possibility of phosphite reduction in a used lithium plating bath. A 1.75 MTO solution was simulated with lithium acetate, sulfate, and hydroxide (Table 8). Filtration at 95°C through a 0.5 µm membrane reduced the phosphite content from 39 to 30 g/L. It increased the plating rate from 16.3 to 17.5 mm/hrmA/hmay be possible to remove part of the accumulating phosphite during plating by continuous filtration, as shown in the diagram of Fig. 3. The operating life of the lithium bath would thereby be extended, and the plating rate increased.

Electroless nickel plating solutions containing lactic and acetic acids as complexants and buffers were prepared with hypophosphorous acid and ammonium, lithium, sodium, or potassium hydroxide at 0, 3, and 6 metal turnovers. The ammonium bath had the slowest initial plating rate; however, it was the only solution that plated at six metal turnovers without precipitation. Further investigation is warranted into removing lithium phosphite by filtration during plating to extend the life of an EN plating bath.
Findings
The four monovalent cations investigated have diverse effects on the operation of an electroless nickel plating system. The low solubility of the accumulated potassium sulfate limits the potassium bath. Sodium ions have a similar effect on the process at greater MTOs, but for different reasons. In the all-sodium bath, nickel phosphite is the principal precipitate, at about three MTOs.
When ammonium ions are used, the amine group's complexing effect with nickel enhances nickel solubility at the expense of nickel phosphite precipitation. Also, ammonium ions increase the solubility of the sulfate anion relative to sodium and potassium sulfate. However, the deposition rate decreases with increased NH+ concentration.
Finally, the lithium ion has two positive effects on the EN plating system. First, the rate of deposition increases in the all-lithium bath. Second, and most importantly, the low solubility of dilithium phosphite (Li2HPO3) at 88°C can control the accumulation of orthophosphite in the EN plating bath to about one MTO.

The relationship between sulfate and phosphite salt solubilities and metal turnovers was studied. We also determined deposition potentials, microstructures, and phosphorus contents.
Since its industrial development in the 1950s, electroless nickel (EN) has found increasing use on a wide variety of parts, primarily for functional engineering applications requiring corrosion and/or wear resistance. Although its growth has slowed in the last few years, the total value of EN coatings in the U.S. is estimated at $200 million.1
EN plating has three major disadvantages compared to electrolytic nickel plating:
- High chemical cost ($0.40 to 0.70/L)
- Limited plating bath life (3 to 6 MTO)
- Expensive spent bath treatment or disposal
Limited bath life results from the continuous accumulation of phosphite and sulfate salts as byproducts of the plating reaction. To maintain optimum pH, frequent alkali addition is necessary. The main reactions are:

records.summary: This Finishing and Coating item relays a Fraunhofer IST press release announcing an expanded research infrastructure for localized electrochemical surface processing. The centerpiece is an Electrochemical Jet Processing (EJP) platform combining Electrochemical Jet Machining (EJM) for non-contact, micrometer-precise material removal and Electrochemical Jet Deposition (EJD) for localized layer deposition, so surfaces can be selectively structured, smoothed, repaired, or coated. Unlike bath-based electroplating of whole components, a movable electrochemical jet acts only where processing or deposition is needed, which the release says removes bath-size constraints and masking/demasking steps and reduces chemical, energy, and raw-material use and waste. No measured performance data, efficiency figures, or peer-reviewed results are reported; the content is a company/institute announcement.

idw – Informationsdienst Wissenschaft
Nachrichten, Termine, Experten
Share on:
10/14/2026 13:30
Precision instead of immersion electroplating: New platform for selective surface modification
Dr. Simone Kondruweit Presse- und Öffentlichkeitsarbeit
Fraunhofer-Institut für Schicht- und Oberflächentechnik IST
With a comprehensive expansion of its research infrastructure, the Fraunhofer Institute for Surface Engineering and Thin Films IST is establishing a new platform for localized electrochemical surface processing. The combination of proven electroplating processes with innovative technologies such as Electrochemical Jet Processing (EJP) and intelligent robotics enables precise, resource-efficient processing of complex workpieces. In doing so, the institute is creating new opportunities for industry in fields such as electronics, energy technology, medical engineering, and aerospace.
Electroplated coatings play a central role in numerous future-oriented industries. They impart specific functional properties to components, improve their durability and performance, and extend the service life of products, thereby contributing to resource conservation and the reduction of CO₂ emissions over the entire life cycle. In this context, Fraunhofer IST is specifically advancing electrochemical manufacturing technologies and combining established electroplating processes with selective approaches to surface treatment.
Expansion for the next generation of electrochemical manufacturing
At the heart of the facility expansion is the new Electrochemical Jet Processing (EJP) platform, which combines various selective electrochemical processes for the localized processing and functionalization of surfaces. These include Electrochemical Jet Machining (EJM) for non-contact, micrometer-precise material machining, as well as Electrochemical Jet Deposition (EJD) for the localized deposition of functional layers. This allows surfaces to be selectively structured, smoothed, repaired, or coated.
In contrast to conventional electroplating processes, in which entire components are treated in process baths, the EJP platform uses a movable electrochemical jet that acts only where material is actually to be processed, or layers are to be deposited. This makes it possible, in the future, to flexibly process even complex or large-scale components. Restrictions imposed by the dimensions of process baths or potential masking and demasking steps are eliminated. At the same time, the use of chemicals, energy, and raw materials – as well as the generation of waste – is minimized.
Intelligent process control for complex component geometries
The platform is complemented by a modern robotics and automation infrastructure. In addition to high-precision industrial robots, autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) are used to flexibly support material and tool logistics and navigate their environment independently. This results in highly precise and reproducible processes that adapt to different component geometries and can be integrated into automated production lines.
“With our new system design, we combine selective electrochemical processes and robotics into a comprehensive system. Unlike with conventional systems, the process adapts to the component and its requirements – not the other way around,” explains Rowena Duckstein, a research scientist at Fraunhofer IST.
Diverse applications for high-tech industries
The new system technology is relevant wherever the highest precision, flexibility, and sustainability are required. For example, it enables the material-conserving production of microstructures with high deposition rates, as well as more targeted filling and thus better coating of, for instance, micro-holes. Localized deposition eliminates the need for stencils and masking.
A look to the future
In the future, the EJP platform is to be integrated even more closely with robotics, sensor technology, and data-driven control methods. The goal is an adaptive manufacturing system that continuously optimizes processes and reduces resource consumption and scrap. In this way, Fraunhofer IST is laying the foundation for adaptive manufacturing concepts that flexibly integrate local electrochemical processes into industrial production lines and open up new possibilities for micro-machining, repair processes, and functionalized surfaces.
“Our goal is to further develop a technology platform that not only meets current industrial requirements but also actively sets new standards – more precise, more sustainable, and more application-oriented than existing solutions,” Duckstein summarizes.

The new system technology is relevant wherever the highest precision\, flexibility\, and sustainability are required\. For example\, it enables the material\-conserving production of microstructures with high deposition rates\, as well as more targeted filling and thus better coating of\, for instance\, micro\-holes\. Localized deposition eliminates the need for stencils and masking\.
A look to the future
In the future\, the EJP platform is to be integrated even more closely with robotics\, sensor technology\, and data\-driven control methods\. The goal is an adaptive manufacturing system that continuously optimizes processes and reduces resource consumption and scrap\. In this way\, Fraunhofer IST is laying the foundation for adaptive manufacturing concepts that flexibly integrate local electrochemical processes into industrial production lines and open up new possibilities for micro\-machining\, repair processes\, and functionalized surfaces\.
“Our goal is to further develop a technology platform that not only meets current industrial requirements but also actively sets new standards – more precise\, more sustainable\, and more application\-oriented than existing solutions\,” Duckstein summarizes\.
