1 Introduction
Additive manufacturing (AM) techniques such as laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) enable the fabrication of complex geometries by adding material in a layer-by-layer manner [8, 9]. Through the L-PBF, a laser beam scans the powdered materials to selectively melt the material. The build platform is then lowered and a new fresh layer of powder is deposited and spread over the previously melted layer. This process is repeated layer by layer [10].
During L-PBF processes, the final part may contain defects such as lack-of-fusion (LOF) pores and keyhole porosity [11], which can degrade its quality. To address such defects and enhance the quality of the printed object, control systems, defined as a combination of elements that work together to drive the measured controllable output toward the desired value [3], have been employed in many studies, including [12,13,14,15,16]. In these studies, the control objectives were melt pool signatures, as these signatures are closely related to part quality. The schematic of the melt pool and associated geometric characteristics are illustrated in Fig. 1.
According to [14], controlling the dimensions of the melt pool plays an important role in addressing defects. Moreover, Hussain et al. [13] highlighted that the non-uniform melt pool size is a major contributor to porosity and part distortion. For example, the inability to bond adjacent tracks due to an insufficient melt pool area results in LOF porosity [11]. The heat from previous tracks acts as a disturbance that can change the size of the melt pool. Therefore, controlling the melt pool dimensions to maintain consistent melt pool dimensions is essential for enhancing the quality of the final object. In addition to melt pool dimensions, layer by layer variations in the melt pool temperature under constant process parameters can pose challenges to obtaining uniform parts, which can be addressed by utilising an interlayer melt pool temperature control system [15].
Among the studies mentioned in the previous paragraph, the melt pool dimensions were the control objectives in [12,13,14]. For instance, in [12] the melt pool area was chosen as the control objective, and a proportional integral (PI) controller was used to regulate it by adjusting the laser power. In that work, a transfer function was modelled via system identification, and the PI controller operated based on this mathematical model. Similarly, in [13], the melt pool cross-section area was controlled using a proportional integral derivative (PID) control, with laser power as the control input. Rezaeifar and Elbestawi [14] considered melt pool width as the control objective, which was regulated by manipulating the laser power using a combination of a proportional derivative (PD) controller and an inverse model-based feedforward controller.
While the aforementioned studies [12,13,14] focused on controlling the melt pool dimensions, studies such as [15, 16] focused on controlling the melt pool temperature. Rezaeifar and Elbestawi [15] designed three controllers: a proportional controller, an adaptive proportional controller, and a sliding mode controller, with the adaptive proportional controller generally outperforming the others. These controllers were designed to control the melt pool temperature as it can significantly impact the mechanical properties and microstructure of the final objects. Furthermore, Stavropoulos et al. [16] proposed H-Infinity and H-2 controllers using linear matrix inequalities (LMIs) to enhance robustness and account for uncertainties, while controlling the melt pool temperature by adjusting the laser power. Among the control inputs used to regulate either melt pool dimensions or melt pool temperature, laser power is the most commonly selected control signal, as it has the greatest influence on melt pool signatures [12,13,14,15,16, 19,20,21]. Laser power, in particular, has been applied to different control objectives, including melt pool dimensions such as width, area, and size, as well as melt pool temperature. Therefore, laser power is the dominant control input in L-PBF.
The sensing or measurement system is an essential component of a closed-loop control system, as it provides the feedback data required by the controller [22, 23], and it can also contribute to defect detection [24, 25]. Various measurement systems have been employed to monitor the control objectives, namely, melt pool signatures in this context. For instance, Wang et al. [20] used a camera (image-based sensor) to measure melt pool cross-section area in the L-PBF process. A co-axial CMOS camera (image-based sensor) was used to measure melt pool area in L-PBF. Regarding melt pool temperature, Rezaeifar and Elbestawi [15] and Renken et al. [26] used pyrometers for directly measuring melt pool temperature [15] and for measuring the intensity of melt pool radiation as an indirect indicator of temperature in the SLM process [26]. Moreover, Wang et al. [27] employed Light-dependent resistor (LDR) for measuring the pool thermal emissions and Rezaeifar and Elbestawi [11] used an infrared thermal camera to monitor melt pool temperature.
The intensity of melt pool emissions, measured by a photodiode and used as a temperature-related proxy, has been shown to be proportional to the melt pool area [11, 28, 29]. As previously discussed, an uncontrolled melt pool area can lead to LOF porosity. Therefore, there is a correlation between melt pool temperature and LOF porosity [11], indicating that a control system that regulates melt pool emission intensity is needed. By doing so, the melt pool temperature and consequently, the melt pool area are maintained consistent, reducing LOF porosity and keyhole porosity and enhancing final part quality. Therefore, in the present study, the control of melt pool emission intensity is investigated.
Thus far, a high-level introduction to L-PBF has been provided, highlighting the importance of control systems in regulating melt pool signatures, mitigating defects, and improving part quality. Several representative studies have been discussed to outline the key challenges in process control and the approaches adopted to address them. Building on this discussion, the remainder of this section first focuses on control system design from a modelling perspective in a general context, and then reviews the literature specifically for powder bed fusion (PBF) and directed energy deposition (DED) processes, considering whether model-based or data-driven approaches have been used to control the process outputs. These two control approaches have also been used for control design in these two metal AM processes [2].
Generally, there are two main categories of control design: model-based and data-driven/model-free. Unlike model-based methods, which explicitly incorporate a process model into the controller design, data-driven approaches rely solely on system data measurements [30]. Khaki-Sedigh [30] presented five different classes to help designers decide whether model-based or data-driven control design should be adopted. In classes 1 and 2, where accurate mathematical models can be derived, either through first-principles modelling or system identification, and where the assumptions regarding the theoretically indispensable system are expected to hold, or where rough approximations of the mathematical models exist and the modelling error with known bounds can be compensated by the use of uncertainties, model-based control design is suggested. In contrast, in classes 3, 4, and 5, where the assumptions regarding the theoretically indispensable system may not hold, the model approximations are rough, uncertainties are difficult or impossible to quantify, or a mathematical model cannot be derived easily, data-driven control design is strongly recommended. In particular, for class 5, data-driven control design is the only feasible option. The model-based approach is more suitable for both simple and complicated systems, whereas the data-driven approach is better suited to some complicated systems and most complex systems.
Data-driven strategies offer several advantages. They do not require prior knowledge of the process dynamics [31], they avoid the need to address model uncertainties [32]. It should be noted that data-driven control can be considered a specific category within the broader concept of data-based control, although most researchers use the term data-driven control to refer to data-based control more generally [33]. According to [30, 33], data-based control refers more generally to control approaches in which the knowledge of process input-output data is used for controller design without directly using the parametric model of the process. Data-based control can be categorised into four classes: post-identification control, direct data-driven control, learning control, and observer-integrated control [30, 33]. In contrast, model-based control design typically requires a mathematical process model whose inaccuracies can negatively affect closed-loop performance. Considering these advantages and limitations, and in line with the designer’s rationale discussed earlier, a data-based control approach is adopted in this study. This decision is motivated by the difficulty of deriving an accurate mathematical model of the L-PBF process and ensuring that the assumptions of the theoretically indispensable system hold. Under the broader terminology discussed above, the proposed approach is classified as data-based control because an FIR representation is identified from measured process data for the purpose of predicting future melt pool emissions within the control loop. The approach can also be considered data-driven under the definition in [30, 33], in which the starting point and destination of the closed-loop control process are both data. In the proposed approach, measured input–output data are used to generate predictions of future melt pool emissions, which are then used to determine the control action. The FIR representation therefore serves as an intermediate predictive element rather than an explicit parametric model of the underlying L-PBF process dynamics.
Table 1 summarises recent studies that adopt either model-based or model-free/data-driven control approaches for PBF and DED, two of the most widely used metal AM processes. Based on the literature references in this table, it was established that data-driven control has been applied more extensively in DED than in PBF. In particular, melt pool width in [32, 34] and surface temperature in [35] were selected as control objectives and successfully controlled using data-driven control strategies in DED processes. The optimal data-driven control strategy proposed in [35] was applied to both DED and PBF processes. Most of the methods listed in the data-driven or model-free category in this table are not fully data-driven. However, since they do not incorporate an explicit process model into the controller design, they are classified as model-free, a broader term that also encompasses data-driven approaches.
As more studies have employed model-based approaches, numerous mathematical models have been developed and are available in the literature. These models can serve as reference or benchmark systems for future researchers, either as sample models for implementing controllers and developing novel theoretical control designs applicable to various engineering fields, including metal AM, or as testbeds for conducting control simulations in metal AM processes. In PBF processes, most of these models describe the relationship between melt pool signatures and laser power, whereas the controllable inputs and outputs used in DED process models vary across studies. These models have been developed either through first-principles modelling based on physical laws or via system identification methods.
As the focus of the current study is on the development of a data-driven control approach, this approach is discussed in detail in the remainder of this section through a review of data-driven strategies in PBF and DED processes. For the DED process, various data-driven and model-free control strategies have been reported. Most of these studies employ model-free approaches, such as PI control [59], fuzzy-PID control [61], Mamdani fuzzy control [66], optimal fuzzy-PID control [67], and PID control [63, 65, 70, 72], as no model has been used in their control design. A few studies, however, are purely data-driven, including adaptive iterative learning control (ILC) [64] and VRFT-based PID control [34].
ILC is a learning-based, data-driven control strategy suitable for tracking problems. It seeks to reduce tracking error at each iteration based on data from previous iterations by adjusting the control input [31, 64]. Xia et al. (2020) [64] employed adaptive ILC to control the melt pool width by adjusting the wire feed speed, used as the control signal, in a wire arc AM (WAAM) process. A model was identified using an adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system to implement the designed controller in a simulation environment and demonstrate its effectiveness. However, the model was not used in the control design itself, which remained purely data-driven.
The VRFT method is an offline, adaptive, data-driven (or more precisely, data-based control design, according to [73]) methodology suitable for cases where a mathematical model is not available [30]. This method uses a batch of input–output data measured from the system, along with a virtual reference, and minimises a 2-norm cost function to derive optimal controller parameters, the optimisation variables of the cost function, in a single step [30], as opposed to the iterative process used in ILC. Chen et al. (2020) [34] designed a VRFT-based PID controller for regulating the melt pool width by adjusting the laser voltage, which determines the laser power, as the control signal in a laser-based DED process. The role of VRFT in that study was to tune the optimal controller parameters, namely, the PID gains, through cost function optimisation.
Regarding PBF processes, only the optimal control designed by Lee and Prabhu [35] can be considered a data-driven control strategy, as the controller was developed based on simulation data for a direct metal laser sintering (DMLS) process. The control objective was the surface temperature, while the control action was implemented by adjusting the scan speed. Two optimisation problems were solved separately: one to minimise the time required to reach the target temperature and another to minimise the control signal during the transient response. The results demonstrated that the proposed control strategy was capable of reducing both the time required to reach the target temperature and the magnitude of the control signal. The control strategies utilised in other PBF studies are considered model-free approaches, as no model was used in the control design. However, they are not data-driven methods, as controller tuning was primarily performed through heuristic or trial-and-error procedures rather than systematic data-driven techniques. These include PID control [11], proportional derivative (PD) control [27], a model-free proportional controller combined with a model-based feedforward controller [26], and proportional control [58].
In L-PBF process model-based control design has predominantly been adopted, which generally involves either using physical laws based on first principles, as in [13, 20], or conducting system identification, as in [12, 15]. However, some studies have adopted model-free control approaches. Notably, these works did not implement data-driven control strategies such as ILC, data-driven model predictive control (DD-MPC), Koopman operator–based control, model-free adaptive control, the fundamental lemma–based strategy, or virtual reference feedback tuning (VRFT). Instead, studies such as [11], which applied PID control, [26], which used proportional and feedforward control, and [58], which relied on proportional control, did not incorporate any data-driven methodologies. Although these approaches did not depend on explicit mathematical models of the process, this alone does not qualify them as data-driven control. Rather, they should be categorised as model-free control methods. This distinction highlights the need for a systematic data-driven control framework specifically developed for L-PBF processes, which remains largely unexplored in the current literature.
Based on the reviewed literature, the data-driven control approaches have been rarely explored in metal AM, particularly in L-PBF. Examples include the optimal data-driven controller for the direct metal laser sintering process [35], the VRFT-based PID controller for a laser-based DED process [34], and the adaptive ILC for a WAAM process [64]. There have been no reports in the literature of a data-driven controller for L-PBF and based on the difficulty of deriving an accurate model for L-PBF, such an approach may enhance control performance. In order to evaluate this, the current study investigates the use of a data-based predictive finite impulse response (FIR)-based proportional controller to regulate the melt pool emission intensity and reduce high fluctuations by manipulating the laser energy input during the printing of individual layers, rather than making control decisions between successive layers. Based on an examination of the control literature, it was established that most authors evaluated their control approaches based on the control of a single print layer [2]. The approach taken involves estimating the Markov parameters (impulse response coefficients) directly from input–output data collected by the in-situ monitoring system and using the resulting FIR representation based on the coefficients to predict future melt pool emissions. Thus, although an input–output FIR representation is identified from process data, no first-principles or separately identified mathematical model of the L-PBF process dynamics is required for controller design. In this sense, the proposed approach follows the data-based control methodology described earlier, in which measured plant data are used to construct a predictor and subsequently determine the control action. Unlike ILC and VRFT, which are well-established data-driven control strategies that typically rely on iterative or offline procedures, the proposed data-based predictive FIR-based proportional controller (DB-PFPC) is formulated for online operation to support future online implementation and does not rely on iteration-based procedures requiring repetitive experiments. Its practical online implementation, however, depends on the availability of real-time melt pool sensing and access to the laser energy control input. Additionally, a threshold is defined to estimate defect-prone process conditions that may give rise to LOF and keyhole porosity, noting that the available dataset does not contain physical defect labels. The stability of the closed-loop system under the proposed data-based controller is also analysed to demonstrate that stable operation can be maintained during the process, followed by a sensitivity analysis of closed-loop performance and stability to changes in the control parameters. The contributions of this paper are summarised as follows:
Proposing and designing a data-based predictive controller (DB-PFPC) to control the intensity of the melt pool emissions, used as a temperature-related proxy, based on data gathered by InfiniAM Spectral in-situ monitoring system
Conducting closed-loop stability analysis under the proposed data-based controller to show that stable operation can be maintained during the process.
Performing a sensitivity analysis of closed-loop performance and stability to changes in the control design parameters.
Estimating defect-prone regions related to LOF and keyhole porosity using statistically defined thresholds.
Integrating the threshold-based identification of defect-prone signal regions into the DB-PFPC to prevent the system response, melt pool emissions in this case, from entering unsafe regions by converting output-based thresholds into corresponding control input constraints during L-PBF.
In the present work, the process input data used in the developed controller are the laser energy input and photodiode (melt pool emissions) data. However, a range of other processing parameters influence melt pool behaviour and consequently the effectiveness of the control system. For example, Renken et al. [26] reported that part geometry can alter the heat flow to neighbouring powder and already solidified regions. Furthermore, process by-products are another factor to consider [74]. Therefore, the approach adopted in the current study provides an initial approximation of melt pool control, based solely on laser energy input and melt pool emissions due to the lack of available data on these aspects and the difficulty of integrating them into a control framework. While effective within this scope, it is acknowledged that additional parameters, including part geometry and other L-PBF processing conditions, may further impact control performance and should be considered in future work. Furthermore, a key challenge in this study is that the InfiniAM Spectral data are collected after a layer is completed, whereas the controller is designed to operate within a layer (intralayer control), a paradigm widely adopted in the literature, as employed in [13, 16, 39, 75]. In this work, the InfiniAM Spectral dataset is used to develop the controller and implement the closed-loop process in a simulation environment in Matlab R2024b, assessing the feasibility and closed-loop behaviour. The experimental validation is currently limited to a simulated closed-loop implementation, as direct real-time control is not supported by the existing Renishaw RenAM 500 system. This constraint is common in commercial L-PBF systems where low-level control access is restricted. Papatheodorou et al. [76] highlighted that this constraint has led to the validation of control systems primarily through simulation or through custom L-PBF systems rather than commercial ones. For example, Wang et al. [27] built a custom L-PBF system to implement a real-time control system, noting that sensor installation and in-process printer adjustment are generally prohibited in commercial L-PBF systems. Moreover, Kim et al. [77] also highlighted that the existence of limitations in AM processes leads to the prevention of the implementation of real-time control systems. Despite this limitation, the proposed controller is formulated for future intralayer real-time deployment. The present study therefore provides a simulation-based assessment of its feasibility and closed-loop behaviour using experimentally measured data, rather than experimental validation of real-time control on the L-PBF system. Experimental implementation and validation under actual intralayer sensing and control conditions remain important directions for future work.
This paper is organised as follows: Section 2 describes the measurement system used for data collection and presents the control design along with the defect and stability analyses. Section 3 discusses the simulation results. Section 4 discusses the research findings and the theoretical and practical implications of the proposed controller for the L-PBF process. Finally, Section 5 presents the conclusions and future research directions.
2 Materials and methods
Following the review presented in the previous section, this section first describes the data acquisition procedure used to design the data-based melt pool energy control system (Subsection 2.1), followed by the controller design (Subsection 2.2).
2.1 Data acquisition
This section describes the L-PBF system and the in-situ monitoring setup used to collect laser-related and melt pool measurements. The L-PBF printing was carried out using Ti-6Al-4V powder using a Renishaw RenAM 500 system. The printing study was investigated in the printing of a medical device known as spinal cage (Fig. 2). This geometrically complex device was selected for this study as similar designs are commercially widely L-PBF printed. As highlighted earlier, previous control studies have selected a single print layer within a part to evaluate the performance of the developed control systems. In the present study, a similar approach was adopted; a layer beyond the support layers (layer 172) was selected from the available measurements as a representative example for evaluating the proposed control.
The system used to collect laser-related and melt pool photodiode measurements was the InfiniAM Spectral in-situ monitoring system [74, 78, 79]. A schematic of this monitoring system is shown in Fig. 3. It comprises two coaxial photodiodes in the MeltVIEW module, which record the optical emissions from the melt pool at a sampling rate of 100 kHz. Additionally, the LaserVIEW module, which includes a photodiode, is used to monitor the laser energy input. The input of the laser in the printer is measured by the LaserVIEW module. Accordingly, the input and output data from the LaserVIEW and MeltVIEW modules, respectively, were collected after a layer was deposited using the InfiniAM Spectral system and will be used in the following to design the data-based predictive FIR-based proportional controller.
2.2 Control design
This section presents the design of a predictive FIR-based proportional controller (DB-PFPC) as an intralayer data-based control strategy for the spinal cage, aimed at controlling the intensity of the melt pool emissions, used as a temperature-related proxy, based on data gathered by the InfiniAM Spectral in-situ monitoring system described in the preceding section. The focus on adjusting the control signal during layer printing arises from adopting an intralayer (in-layer) control approach, whereas interlayer (layer-to-layer) control adjusts control actions between successive layers. In PBF processes, the majority of control studies in the literature have adopted intralayer control strategies, with fewer works addressing interlayer control approaches [2]. Liao-McPherson et al. [80] reported that monitoring and simulating the melt pool across layers is difficult, which has contributed to the relatively limited number of interlayer control studies. Furthermore, as noted in [2], real-time control operation is not achievable in interlayer control, since the control input is adjusted only between layers, whereas intralayer control enables real-time control within a single layer. In the present study, the controller is developed for an intralayer control. However, the InfiniAM Spectral data are collected after the layer is laid down. The closed-loop controller is therefore evaluated in a MATLAB R2024b simulation using previously recorded experimental measurements. The simulation assumes that melt pool measurements would be available during layer deposition and that the laser energy input could be adjusted online. Accordingly, the results demonstrate the feasibility and closed-loop behaviour of the proposed control strategy under these assumed real-time operating conditions, rather than experimentally validated real-time performance on the L-PBF system. The objective is to regulate the melt pool behaviour in the L-PBF process by adjusting the laser energy input whenever deviations from a desired melt pool intensity setpoint are observed, given the inevitable presence of uncertainty and noise in L-PBF processes [81].
2.2.1 Model estimation using Markov parameters
This section discusses the derivation of an FIR model using laser energy input and melt pool emission output data from the L-PBF process. This model was selected due to its simplicity and its suitability for data-based control design, as it relies only on input–output data. The FIR model does not introduce Markov-parameter-dependent poles in its model structure, whereas an autoregressive with exogenous inputs (ARX) model contains an estimated denominator whose roots (open-loop poles) are directly determined by the identified parameters. Furthermore, it enables prediction of future melt pool emissions, as outlined in Section 1, without relying on an explicit physical model of the L-PBF process. As described in [82, 83], the FIR model is expressed as follows:
$$\begin{aligned} y(k) \approx \sum \_{i=1}^{n} g\_i u(k - i), \end{aligned}$$
(1)
where \(y(k)\) denotes the system output (melt pool data), \(g\_i\) represents the Markov parameters or impulse response coefficients, and \(u(k - i)\) represents the past input values (laser energy input). To estimate the Markov parameters, a least-squares regression can be performed using the gathered data. Based on the available data, the following equation predicts the output one step ahead using the estimated Markov parameters:
$$\begin{aligned} \hat{y}(k|k-1) = \sum \_{i=1}^{n} \hat{g}\_i \cdot u(k - i), \end{aligned}$$
(2)
where \(\hat{y}(k|k-1)\) denotes the predicted system output (predicted melt pool data) at time step k, based on the information up to time step \(k-1\), and \(\hat{g}\_i\) represents the estimated Markov parameters. According to Eq. 2, this prediction is made at each time step k.
2.2.2 Control law
To derive the control law based on the melt pool emission output prediction (corresponding Markov parameters) discussed in Subsection 2.2.1, the error between the predicted output and the setpoint (r) is calculated as:
$$\begin{aligned} e(k) = r - \hat{y}(k|k-1), \end{aligned}$$
(3)
which is then used to update the control input at each time step using the following incremental form:
$$\begin{aligned} u(k) = u(k-1) + k\_pe(k). \end{aligned}$$
(4)
This formulation has the capability to enable the controller to incrementally adjust the laser energy input to drive the melt pool intensity toward the setpoint. This incremental adjustment arises because the effect of past inputs is already incorporated in the predicted output used to compute e(k), which is obtained via the estimated Markov parameters in Eqs. 2 and 3. Therefore, only the corrective term \(k\_pe(k)\) needs to be added to \(u(k-1)\), the previously applied control signal. The predicted output is used instead of the measured output \(y(k)\) because the control input u(k) must be computed before the next measurement becomes available. Therefore, only past information can be used (information available up to time \(k-1\)), which leads to the use of the predicted output \(\hat{y}(k|k-1)\) in Eqs. 3 and 4. This allows the controller to determine the control input in advance based on the predicted system response. The schematic of the proposed closed-loop, data-based control strategy is illustrated in Fig. 4. Furthermore, the algorithm of the proposed controller is outlined in Algorithm 1, which provides additional details on the proposed methods.
2.2.3 Stability analysis
This section discusses the stability analysis of the closed-loop system in the presence of the proposed controller given in Eq. 4. Two scenarios are analysed: the nominal case and the uncertain case, the latter accounting for measurement noise and estimation errors.
– Nominal case
This part discusses the nominal case:
Theorem 1
Under the proposed control law given in Eq. 4, the bounded-input, bounded-output (BIBO) stability of the closed-loop system is guaranteed provided that all roots of characteristic equation \(P(z) = z^{n} - z^{n-1} + k\_p \sum \_{i=1}^{n} \hat{g}\_i z^{n - i}\) lie inside the unit circle.
Proof
Substituting Eqs. 2 and 3 into Eq. 4 yields
$$\begin{aligned} u(k) = u(k-1) + k\_p\left( r - \sum \_{i=1}^{n} \hat{g}\_i \cdot u(k - i)\right) . \end{aligned}$$
(5)
For simplicity in analysis, the terms involving the control input can be rearranged to one side:
$$\begin{aligned} u(k) - u(k-1) + k\_p\left( \sum \_{i=1}^{n} \hat{g}\_i \cdot u(k - i)\right) = k\_pr. \end{aligned}$$
(6)
Taking the z-transform of both sides yields
$$\begin{aligned} U(z) - z^{-1} U(z) + k\_p \left( \sum \_{i=1}^{n} \hat{g}\_i z^{-i} \right) U(z) = k\_pR(z) = \frac{k\_p r z}{z-1}. \end{aligned}$$
(7)
This leads to the following closed-loop expression:
$$\begin{aligned} \left[ 1 - z^{-1} + K\_p \sum \_{i=1}^{n} \hat{g}\_i z^{-i} \right] U(z) = \frac{k\_p r z}{z-1}. \end{aligned}$$
(8)
Hence, the characteristic equation is:
$$\begin{aligned} P(z) = \left[ 1 - z^{-1} + k\_p \sum \_{i=1}^{n} \hat{g}\_i z^{-i} \right] . \end{aligned}$$
(9)
The characteristic equation is the denominator of the closed-loop transfer function Y(z)/R(z) [84]. However, the denominator of U(z)/R(z) is also correct, as it provides the internal closed-loop dynamics. Therefore, both lead to the same characteristic equation. Multiplying both sides of \(P(z) = 0\) by \(z^n\) gives:
$$\begin{aligned} P(z) = z^{n} - z^{n-1} + k\_p \sum \_{i=1}^{n} \hat{g}\_i z^{n - i}. \end{aligned}$$
(10)
Utilising the control input given in Eq. 4 ensures the bounded-input, bounded-output (BIBO) stability of the closed-loop system, provided that all roots of P(z) given in Eq. 10 lie inside the unit circle. This condition can be ensured by appropriately choosing the control gain \(k\_p\) in the control law.\(\square \)
– Uncertain case
In this subsection, in contrast to the nominal scenario, the effects of estimation errors and measurement noise are considered. The following FIR model that includes measurement noise is considered:
$$\begin{aligned} y(k) = \sum \_{i=1}^{n} g\_i u(k - i) + v(k), \end{aligned}$$
(11)
where \(v(k)\) represents measurement noise.
Assumption 1
The estimation error of the identified Markov parameters \(\hat{g}\_i\) is assumed to be bounded as
$$\begin{aligned} |\Delta g\_i| \le \bar{g}\_i, \end{aligned}$$
(12)
where \(\Delta g\_i\) denotes the estimation error. Equivalently, the estimation error can be defined as
$$\begin{aligned} e\_{g\_i} = g\_i - \hat{g}\_i, \end{aligned}$$
(13)
where \(g\_i\) represents the true Markov parameter. The estimation error is assumed to be bounded such that
$$\begin{aligned} e\_{g\_i}^* = \sup |e\_{g\_i}|, \end{aligned}$$
(14)
where \(e\_{g\_i}^*\) (or equivalently \(\bar{g}\_i\)) denotes the supremum, i.e., the maximum bound of the estimation error.
Assumption 2
The measurement noise is assumed to be bounded as
$$\begin{aligned} |v(k)| \le \bar{v}. \end{aligned}$$
(15)
This assumption is required for BIBO stability, since the input to the system must be bounded.
Theorem 2
Under the proposed control law given in Eq. 4 with respect to Assumptions 1 and 2, the BIBO stability of the closed-loop system is guaranteed provided that all roots of characteristic equation \(P(z) = z^{n} - z^{n-1} + k\_p \sum \_{i=1}^{n} \left( \hat{g}\_i+\Delta g\_i\right) z^{n - i}\) lie inside the unit circle for all admissible uncertainties \(|\Delta g\_i| \le \bar{g}\_i\).
Proof
Following Eq. 6 and considering Assumption 1, which accounts for the estimation error that may occur during the the identification of the Markov parameters, and Assumption 2, which accounts for the measurement noise, the closed-loop relation becomes
$$\begin{aligned} u(k) - u(k-1) + k\_p\left( \sum \_{i=1}^{n} \left( \hat{g}\_i+\Delta g\_i\right) \cdot u(k - i)\right) = k\_pr - k\_pv(k). \end{aligned}$$
(16)
This can be rewritten as
$$\begin{aligned} u(k) - u(k-1)&+ k\_p\left( \sum \_{i=1}^{n} \hat{g}\_i \cdot u(k - i)\right) \nonumber \\&+ k\_p\left( \sum \_{i=1}^{n} \Delta g\_i \cdot u(k - i)\right) = k\_pr - k\_pv(k). \end{aligned}$$
(17)
Taking the z-transform of both sides yields
$$\begin{aligned} U(z) - z^{-1} U(z)&+ k\_p \left( \sum \_{i=1}^{n} \hat{g}\_i z^{-i} \right) U(z) \nonumber \\&+ k\_p \left( \sum \_{i=1}^{n} \Delta g\_i z^{-i} \right) U(z) = \frac{k\_p r z}{z-1} - k\_pV(z). \end{aligned}$$
(18)
Therefore,
$$\begin{aligned} \left[ 1 - z^{-1} + k\_p \sum \_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{g}\_i + \Delta g\_i) z^{-i}\right] U(z) = \frac{k\_p r z}{z-1} - k\_pV(z). \end{aligned}$$
(19)
Hence, the characteristic equation of the closed-loop system becomes
$$\begin{aligned} P(z) = \left[ 1 - z^{-1} + k\_p \sum \_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{g}\_i + \Delta g\_i) z^{-i}\right] . \end{aligned}$$
(20)
Multiplying both sides of \(P(z) = 0\) by \(z^n\) yields
$$\begin{aligned} P(z) = z^n - z^{n-1} + k\_p \sum \_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{g}\_i + \Delta g\_i) z^{n-i}. \end{aligned}$$
(21)
Similar to the nominal case, the closed-loop system remains BIBO stable provided that all roots of P(z) given in Eq. 20 lie inside the unit circle for all admissible uncertainties \(|\Delta g\_i| \le \bar{g}\_i\). This proves the stability of the closed-loop process. However, the presence of measurement noise may affect the estimation accuracy of the Markov parameters. Equation 11 can be written in matrix form as
$$\begin{aligned} y = \Phi g + v, \end{aligned}$$
(22)
where \(\Phi \) is the regression matrix. Using the least-squares method, the Markov parameters are estimated as
$$\begin{aligned} \hat{g}&= \Phi \backslash y \nonumber \\&= (\Phi ^{T}\Phi )^{-1}\Phi ^{T}y \nonumber \\&= (\Phi ^{T}\Phi )^{-1}\Phi ^{T}\left( \Phi g + v\right) \nonumber \\&= g + (\Phi ^{T}\Phi )^{-1}\Phi ^{T}v. \end{aligned}$$
(23)
Thus, the estimation error becomes
$$\begin{aligned} |e\_g| = \left| (\Phi ^{T}\Phi )^{-1}\Phi ^{T}v \right| . \end{aligned}$$
(24)
Taking norms on both sides yields
$$\begin{aligned} \Vert e\_g\Vert = \Vert (\Phi ^{T}\Phi )^{-1}\Phi ^{T}v\Vert , \end{aligned}$$
(25)
which gives
$$\begin{aligned} \Vert e\_g\Vert \le \Vert (\Phi ^{T}\Phi )^{-1}\Phi ^{T}\Vert \, \Vert v\Vert . \end{aligned}$$
(26)
Equation 26 shows that the estimation error depends on the magnitude of the measurement noise, while \((\Phi ^{T}\Phi )^{-1}\Phi ^{T}\) determines the sensitivity of the estimation error to this noise. According to Assumption 2, the measurement noise is bounded. Therefore, reducing \(\Vert (\Phi ^{T}\Phi )^{-1}\Phi ^{T}\Vert \) improves robustness to noise. This can be achieved by applying a persistently exciting input during the identification stage. Consequently, Assumption 1 is reasonable, as appropriate experimental design can ensure that the estimation error remains sufficiently small and that the estimated Markov parameters converge towards a neighbourhood of the true values.\(\square \)
2.2.4 Threshold-based anomaly detection
To identify defect-prone signal conditions during the printing of the studied layer, a threshold-based anomaly detection approach similar to [11] is utilised. The available dataset does not contain physical defect labels (e.g., confirmed keyhole porosity, LOF porosity, or defect-free regions). Therefore, the method does not directly detect or confirm physical defects. Instead, it identifies melt pool emission excursions beyond statistically defined thresholds that are associated with process conditions potentially conducive to LOF or keyhole porosity. As discussed earlier, melt pool temperature is associated with process conditions that can contribute to print defects such as LOF as well as keyhole porosity. Since melt pool emissions provide an indirect indication of melt pool temperature, the following threshold-based rule is used to identify signal excursions associated with these defect-prone conditions: an emission value exceeding the upper threshold is classified as a keyhole defect-prone condition, whereas an emission value below the lower threshold is classified as a LOF defect-prone condition, as expressed in Eq. 27.
$$\begin{aligned} \text {Status} = {\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \text {Keyhole defect-prone condition}, & \text {if } y > \text {upper threshold}, \\ \text {LOF defect-prone condition}, & \text {if } y < \text {lower threshold}, \\ \text {Within-threshold region} & \text {otherwise.} \end{array}\right. } \end{aligned}$$
(27)
The thresholds are statistically defined using the mean, \(\mu \_y\), and multiples of the standard deviation, \(K\sigma \), an approach employed in [85, 86] for threshold-based anomaly detection. Based on this, the upper and lower thresholds are defined as follows:
$$\begin{aligned} {\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \text {Upper threshold} = \mu \_y + K\_{upper}\sigma , \\ \text {Lower threshold} = \mu \_y - K\_{lower}\sigma , \end{array}\right. } \end{aligned}$$
(28)
where \(K\_{upper}\) and \(K\_{lower}\) are selected by the designer. This comes from the idea that the data are expected to deviate from the mean maximally by an amount equal to the standard deviation, or multiples thereof, depending on how conservative the designer wants to be in order to avoid entering the unsafe area.
2.2.5 Integrating defect analysis into control system
Building upon the DB-PFPC designed earlier in this paper and the proposed threshold-based anomaly detection method, this section integrates the identification of defect-prone signal excursions into the DB-PFPC to prevent the system response, represented here by melt pool emissions, from exceeding the defined thresholds and entering statistically defined out-of-threshold region, by applying saturation at the boundaries. Accordingly, based on these output thresholds, the equivalent thresholds for the control signal are calculated to determine the allowable control signal bounds. These bounds are obtained by first rewriting Eq. 2 as follows:
$$\begin{aligned} \hat{y}(k|k-1) = \hat{g}\_1u(k-1) + y\_{past}(k), \end{aligned}$$
(29)
where \(\hat{g}\_1\) is the first element of predicted Markov parameters, and \(y\_{past}\) denotes the past output that is already available for predicting the next sample, except \(\hat{g}\_1u(k-1)\):
$$\begin{aligned} y\_{past}(k) = \sum \_{i=2}^{n} \hat{g}\_i \cdot u(k - i). \end{aligned}$$
(30)
The control signal bounds (or thresholds) can then be obtained from Eq. 29 by calculating it at the output thresholds defined in Eq. 28, ensuring that the output remains between \(y\_{upper}\) and \(y\_{lower}\), which represent the upper and lower output thresholds, respectively:
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle {\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} u\_{upper} = \dfrac{y\_{upper} - y\_{past}(k)}{\hat{g}\_1}, \\ u\_{lower} = \dfrac{y\_{lower} - y\_{past}(k)}{\hat{g}\_1}. \end{array}\right. } \end{aligned}$$
(31)
Since \(\hat{g}\_1\) may be negative, the correct upper and lower bounds can be ensured by applying the following expressions:
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle {\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} u\_{upper bound}(k) = \max \{ u\_{\text {upper}}(k), u\_{\text {lower}}(k) \} \\ u\_{lower bound}(k) = \min \{ u\_{\text {upper}}(k), u\_{\text {lower}}(k) \}. \end{array}\right. } \end{aligned}$$
(32)
To prevent the output response from entering the unsafe region, a saturation function is then applied based on the upper and lower bounds obtained in Eq. 32:
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle u\_{saturation} = {\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} u\_{upper bound}, & u\_{\text {ddp}}(k) > u\_{upper bound}, \\ u\_{\text {ddp}}(k), & u\_{lower bound} \le u\_{\text {ddp}}(k) \le u\_{upper bound}, \\ u\_{lower bound}(k), & u\_{\text {ddp}}(k) < u\_{lower bound}(k). \end{array}\right. } \end{aligned}$$
(33)
Both the input and output signals are processed in their normalised form throughout the design and are denormalised at the end, as done previously in Algorithm 1.
This work presents an attempt to identify an operating region using in-process InfiniAM data, as presented in Subsection 2.2.4. This region is then used to avoid low melt pool temperatures associated with LOF porosity and high melt pool temperatures associated with keyhole porosity, as discussed in Subsection 2.2.5, by integrating threshold-based anomaly detection into the DB-PFPC strategy.
3 Simulation results
This section presents simulation results for the proposed control strategy applied to the L-PBF process, evaluating the controller performance using experimental data from a RenAM 500 metal AM system. The goal is to regulate the melt pool temperature, which is monitored through photodiodes that measure melt pool emissions that are correlated with the melt pool temperature. The control law is derived by predicting the future output (melt pool emissions) based on input-output data measured by the InfiniAM Spectral in-situ monitoring system at a sampling rate of 100 kHz, as described in Section 2.1. Then, as mentioned in Algorithm 1 and illustrated in Fig. 4, the preprocessing is done on the raw signals, using normalisation process.
The normalised data are then used to estimate the total number of 20 Markov parameters (\(n = 20\)) via least squares outlined in Algorithm 1. However, to satisfy the one step ahead prediction, only the first element of prediction is used in the control law calculation. These parameters are used to predict the melt pool emissions through convolution. The choice of the number of Markov parameters represents a trade-off between the model order, the length of memory (historical data) required to capture the thermal dynamics of the melt pool, and the amount of initial data needed to initialise the prediction. The setpoint for melt pool intensity is set to the mean of the original signal for the studied layer. This choice is aligned with the objective of reducing fluctuations in the melt pool response, as the standard deviation quantifies the variation of the measured signal around its mean. Previous closed-loop control studies have also evaluated the effectiveness of control in terms of reductions in the standard deviation of melt pool temperature or pyrometer measurements, with reductions of up to 90% reported compared with open-loop scenario [26]. Therefore, the mean of the open-loop signal is adopted as a representative reference level around which the melt pool emissions are regulated, with the aim of reducing fluctuations in the presence of process variations, including changes in surface conditions during scanning and measurement noise. This choice is not intended to imply that the mean represents an experimentally validated optimal processing condition. Rather, it provides a reference for evaluating the ability of the proposed controller to reduce signal fluctuations and serves as a nominal statistical reference for controller-feasibility assessment. The controller uses past data, including melt pool emissions as the process output and laser energy as the control input, for prediction, starting with the initial data available at the start of the process, and subsequently for the purpose of control. The results are based on one representative layer, with the setpoint chosen as the mean of the same signal being regulated. A total of 20 Markov parameters (\(n = 20\)) are used, with the first \(T\_{\text {ini}} = 20\) data samples employed for initialisation, and \(k\_p = 2\) chosen through tuning. This process will be discussed further later in Subsection 3.3 to ensure a stable closed-loop response while achieving acceptable performance. In the following, the results of regulating the output toward the setpoint, defect analysis, and stability analysis are presented.
3.1 Output regulation performance
Fig. 5 shows the open-loop data gathered by the InfiniAM Spectral system without any controllers for the studied layer. Similar to most process systems, which are inherently stable [87, 88], the open-loop melt pool emissions data is bounded and stable but exhibits large oscillations due to measurement noise and surface changes during scanning that need to be addressed by designing a control system.
Figure 6 compares the measured melt pool emissions without controllers and under DB-PFPC control, and compares the open-loop (no control) and closed-loop data in terms of laser energy input after applying the designed controller. The melt pool intensity setpoint (i.e., the desired emission level) is set to the mean of the measured open-loop melt pool emissions. As shown in Fig. 6, the controller successfully regulates the intensity of the melt pool emissions after utilising a small portion of transient data for prediction. A zoomed-in view of the transient region is included to illustrate how the controller adjusts the laser energy input to drive the melt pool emissions toward the setpoint.
To evaluate the ability of the proposed controller to perform on other layers of the printed part and to further assess its generalisability within the intralayer control approach, a different layer from those deposited above the previously studied layer (layer 372) is selected for testing. This can show how the proposed controller behaves during the printing of another layer and whether it can still provide satisfactory performance. Figure 7 shows the performance of the closed-loop system under the proposed controller during the printing of another layer. The figure shows that the proposed controller successfully regulates the output towards the setpoint. It should be noted that, due to the different melt pool emission level observed in the second tested layer, a different setpoint is adopted for this layer. The controller parameters are kept the same as those used for the previously studied layer, while satisfactory control performance is maintained.
In addition to comparing the proposed controller with the open-loop control, its performance is also compared with another controller from the PID control family. This controller also utilises the prediction component but incorporates an integral term alongside the proportional term. The proportional-only version of this predictive FIR-based controller was previously developed and simulated as the proposed controller in this paper, and its performance was presented in Fig. 6. Accordingly, the predictive-based controller incorporating the proportional and integral terms is denoted in this paper as the data-based predictive FIR-based proportional integral controller (DB-PFPIC). Figure 8 compares the closed-loop performance of the proposed controller with that of the controller incorporating proportional integral (PI) terms, including the process output (melt pool emissions) and the control signal (laser energy input). As shown in Fig. 8, the controller with PI terms and an integral gain of 500 exhibits slower regulation and a subsequent undershoot. Since the initial values are above the setpoint, the response falling below the setpoint is considered overshoot, whereas the subsequent response rising above the setpoint is considered undershoot. Both controllers exhibit overshoot as their responses fall below the setpoint. However, the DB-PFPIC experiences a subsequent undershoot of 1.06%, unlike the proposed controller, which regulates towards the setpoint after the overshoot. Furthermore, the root mean square error (RMSE) of the proposed controller is approximately 0.055, which is 6.78% lower than that of the controller with PI terms, which has an RMSE of approximately 0.059. The root mean square (RMS) of the incremental control input is 0.035 for the proposed controller, compared with 0.044 for the controller with PI terms. Regarding the reaching time, the proposed controller reaches and maintains the setpoint after approximately 0.023 time units, whereas the controller with PI terms is slower, requiring approximately 0.058 time units to reach and maintain the setpoint. Therefore, the proposed controller is preferred because it has a simpler control design, as its control law does not include an integral term, and, under the DB-PFPIC parameter settings considered in this study, provides better regulation performance under the parameter settings considered in this study, in terms of RMSE, incremental control input RMS, time required to reach and maintain the setpoint, and undershoot percentage.
Another controller investigated and compared with the proposed controller in the following is a data-based predictive ARX-based proportional controller. Similar to the FIR model, an ARX representation can be used to formulate a one-step-ahead prediction [89]. According to [90], the ARX representation can be expressed as
$$\begin{aligned} A(q^{-1})y(k) = B(q^{-1})u(k), \end{aligned}$$
(34)
where \(A(q^{-1})\) and \(B(q^{-1})\) are defined as
$$\begin{aligned} A(q^{-1}) = 1 + a\_1q^{-1} + a\_2q^{-2} + \cdots + a\_{n\_a}q^{-n\_a}, \end{aligned}$$
(35)
$$\begin{aligned} B(q^{-1}) = b\_1q^{-1} + b\_2q^{-2} + \cdots + b\_{n\_b}q^{-n\_b}. \end{aligned}$$
(36)
In the ARX model, \(q^{-1}\) denotes the backward shift operator, such that its application to \(y(k)\) or u(k) shifts the corresponding signal backward by one sampling instant. For example, \(a\_2q^{-2}y(k)\) corresponds to \(a\_2y(k-2)\), and similarly, \(b\_2q^{-2}u(k)\) corresponds to \(b\_2u(k-2)\).
According to [89], Eq. 34 can be rearranged to formulate the ARX model in a one-step-ahead prediction form as
$$\begin{aligned} \hat{y}(k|k-1) = B(q^{-1})u(k) + \left( 1-A(q^{-1})\right) y(k). \end{aligned}$$
(37)
Similar to the FIR-based controller, a proportional correction is employed, and the control input u(k) is calculated according to Eq. 4.
Figure 9 compares the closed-loop performance of the proposed controller with that of the controller incorporating the predictive ARX model. The selected values of \(n\_a = 2\) and \(n\_b = 2\) provide acceptable performance. Varying these parameters can affect the overshoot and the time required to reach and maintain the setpoint, resulting in a trade-off between these performance characteristics. As shown in Fig. 9, both controllers exhibit overshoot, although the overshoot percentages are different. The overshoot percentage of the proposed controller is approximately 4.78%, whereas that of the ARX-based controller is approximately 5.18%. The undershoot of the ARX-based controller is very small, at approximately 0.12%. Furthermore, the proposed controller reaches and maintains the setpoint after approximately 0.023 time units, whereas the ARX-based controller is slower, reaching and maintaining the setpoint after approximately 0.041 time units. The RMSE of the proposed controller is approximately 0.055, whereas that of the ARX-based controller (DB-PAPC) is approximately 0.317. Additionally, the RMS of the incremental control input is 0.035 for the proposed controller, compared with 0.2 for the DB-PAPC. Therefore, the proposed controller outperforms the DB-PAPC, under the DB-PAPC parameter settings considered in this study, in terms of regulation performance, including overshoot percentage, the time required to reach and maintain the setpoint, RMSE, and RMS of the incremental control input. Table 2 summarises the performance characteristics of all three controllers discussed in this section.
3.2 Anomaly analysis
This section presents the results of the anomaly detection method. As mentioned earlier, the parameters \(K\_{upper}\) and \(K\_{lower}\) are selected based on how conservative the designer intends to be in avoiding entry into the defect-prone region, as well as on the mean and standard deviation of the data. Accordingly, they are chosen as 1 and 2, respectively. Figure 10 shows the defect-prone region and within-threshold region in both uncontrolled and controlled scenarios. The regions above and below the upper and lower thresholds, respectively, are interpreted as defect-prone signal regions associated with keyhole porosity and LOF conditions. As shown, in the uncontrolled scenario without a control system, a large number of data points fall within the defined defect-prone signal regions (34007 data points). In contrast, with the DB-PFPC controller, only six data points exceed the upper threshold during the initial moments of the studied layer, after which the signal rapidly stabilises within the defined operating region. The controller reduces the number of samples exhibiting defect-prone signal excursions beyond the defined thresholds by 99.98% in the studied layer compared to the uncontrolled case. This result indicates the potential of the controller to reduce process conditions associated with LOF and keyhole porosity. However, experimental validation against physical defects is required to establish whether this reduction in threshold excursions translates into a reduction in actual defects. The detection is illustrated more clearly in Fig. 11, which shows binary anomaly detection, distinguishing between defect-prone and within-threshold regions.
Regarding the saturation-based controller presented in Section 2.2.5, since the output enters and remains within the safe region immediately after \(T\_{\text {ini}} = 20\) data samples used for initialisation, no saturation needs to be applied in this case, and the results are the same as those shown in Fig. 6, which shows the strength of the proposed controller. However, this saturation-based controller is beneficial to ensure that the output does not exceed the defined thresholds.
3.3 Sensitivity analysis
This section presents sensitivity analyses of the control design parameters with respect to the closed-loop stability and regulation performance. The objective is to investigate how variations in these parameters affect the regulation performance, and closed-loop stability. The first parameter analysed is proportional gain of the controller \(k\_p\), which is also helpful in tuning of the \(k\_p\). To this purpose, the characteristic equation derived in Eq. 10 in Subsection 2.2.3 must be analysed to determine suitable bounds on \(k\_p\) that ensure closed-loop stability and to investigate how changes in the gain affect stability, thereby enabling an appropriate value to be selected. For this purpose, the maximum absolute value of the closed-loop poles (i.e., the roots of the characteristic equation) is computed for \(k\_p\) in the range \([-10, 7]\), as shown in Fig. 12. Poles lying within the unit circle ensure BIBO stability, whereas poles outside the unit circle indicate instability. This figure indicates that the closed-loop system is stable when \(k\_p\) lies approximately between 0.005 and 3.6782. Outside this interval, the closed-loop system is unstable. To further show this, several \(k\_p\) values from both the stable and unstable regions are selected, and the corresponding closed-loop poles are obtained by deriving the roots of the characteristic equation. These poles are shown in Fig. 13. For \(k\_p = 7\), three poles lie outside the unit circle, while for \(k\_p = -0.5\), \(k\_p = -1.47\), \(k\_p = -5.74\), and \(k\_p = -10\), one pole lies outside the unit circle in each case, indicating instability. In contrast, for the other gains within the stable region, all poles lie inside the unit circle. The proposed controller was implemented with \(k\_p = 2\) in Fig. 6, which lies within the stable region.
Furthermore, the sensitivity of the closed-loop performance to \(k\_p\) is analysed. Figure 14 shows the regulation performance for several stable \(k\_p\) values, as well as the regulation RMSE across the stable range of \(k\_p\). The figure shows that, as \(k\_p\) increases, the melt pool emission intensity is generally regulated towards the setpoint more rapidly. The selected value, \(k\_p = 2\), provides fast regulation without undershoot, unlike \(k\_p = 3\), which exhibits undershoot in its response. All considered \(k\_p\) values exhibit overshoot. However, only \(k\_p = 3\) exhibits a subsequent undershoot. The other \(k\_p\) values do not exhibit undershoot but result in different regulation speeds, as can be observed in Fig. 14. The regulation RMSE also remains below 0.1 for \(k\_p \ge 0.3445\). Table 3 summarises the results of this analysis with respect to changes in the proportional gain.
Next, the number of Markov parameters (n) is investigated. The values \(n = [5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40]\) are considered to investigate how the number of Markov parameters affects closed-loop stability and regulation performance. \(k\_p\) is kept at 2 for each n, while \(T\_{ini}\) is selected as the maximum value of n, which is 40, to ensure a fair comparison across the different values of n, as \(T\_{ini}\) cannot be smaller than the number of Markov parameters. To perform the sensitivity analysis with respect to variations in the number of Markov parameters, the RMSE of the output, the RMS of the incremental control input, and the maximum absolute value of the closed-loop poles are calculated. Table 4 presents the results of this analysis, while Fig. 15 illustrates how the closed-loop performance and stability are affected by varying the number of Markov parameters. The results show that closed-loop stability is maintained with the same \(k\_p = 2\), and the regulation performance is not significantly affected. The output remains regulated toward the setpoint, although the transient response varies with the number of Markov parameters, as reflected in the RMSE and RMS values. Despite these variations in the transient response, the output remains within the defined threshold region, with no threshold violations occur after controller activation. Although the closed-loop system is BIBO stable for all considered numbers of Markov parameters with \(k\_p = 2\), the stability bounds vary, as also shown in Table 4. As the number of Markov parameters increases, the stability bound for \(k\_p\) generally becomes narrower, and the maximum absolute value of the closed-loop poles generally increases, with a minor deviation observed at \(n = 35\).
Regarding the parameter \(T\_{ini}\), unlike n and \(k\_p\), it is not involved in the control design. As described in Section 2.2, the controller starts operating after \(T\_{ini}\). This parameter also has no effect on the stability analysis, as it does not appear in the characteristic equation of the closed-loop system. It can, however, affect the number of samples exhibiting defect-prone signal excursions beyond the defined thresholds. Nevertheless, the selected value of \(T\_{ini}\) was found to provide satisfactory performance. To investigate its effect, several values of \(T\_{ini}\) greater than or equal to 20 are considered, and the number of data points exceeding the defined thresholds is evaluated. For \(T\_{ini}=20\), as outlined earlier, six data points exceed the upper threshold. For \(T\_{ini}=25\), seven data points exceed the upper threshold, while for \(T\_{ini}=30\), 10 data points exceed the upper threshold. For both \(T\_{ini}=35\) and \(T\_{ini}=40\), 12 data points exceed the upper threshold. For the Markov parameter sensitivity study with \(T\_{ini}=40\), no threshold violations occur after controller activation. Twelve upper-threshold exceedances are observed during the 40-sample initialisation interval, before closed-loop regulation begins, when assessing the sensitivity of the closed-loop system to \(T\_{ini}\). Similarly, the difference between the results for \(n=20\) in Table 4 and those for \(k\_p=2\) in Table 3 is due to the different values of \(T\_{ini}\) used in the two analyses.
Finally, the ability of the controller in the closed-loop configuration to regulate the output toward different setpoints is assessed to evaluate its performance under different reference values. To this end, several setpoints are considered, including the mean and the mean \(\pm \ 0.1\sigma \) and mean \(\pm \ 0.2\sigma \). Figure 16 shows the closed-loop behaviour of the proposed controller for the different setpoints. The results demonstrate that the proposed controller is capable of regulating the output not only toward the mean but also toward other setpoints.
4 Research findings and implications
This section discusses the research findings of this study and focuses on the theoretical and practical implications of the proposed controller for the L-PBF process during the fabrication of spinal cages.
4.1 Theoretical implications
From a theoretical perspective, this study contributes to the application of control systems in L-PBF process by proposing a data-based controller. Existing L-PBF controllers predominantly rely on either model-based approaches, where a process model is derived via system identification or first-principles modelling (e.g., [12, 13, 15]), or model-free approaches, which do not exploit data-driven design methodologies (e.g., [11, 26]). While model-based controllers can achieve good performance, their effectiveness is sensitive to the accuracy of the process model. In contrast, existing model-free controllers for L-PBF generally lack a systematic control design methodology. To address these limitations, this work proposed a controller that is designed using input–output data collected from the L-PBF process, thereby classifying as a data-based/data-driven controller. The proposed controller established a link between the estimation of the Markov parameters of an FIR model and the future melt pool behaviour within a layer, enabling regulation of the melt pool emission intensity, which is a temperature-related proxy. By using predictions of the melt pool emission intensity, the controller updated the control signal. Closed-loop stability analysis was conducted, which strengthened the theory of the proposed controller by guaranteeing closed-loop stability and ensuring that the melt pool temperature remains bounded.
Furthermore, this study contributes to the development of a theoretical anomaly-aware control strategy based on statistically identified defect-prone signal regions. Prior studies on defects in L-PBF have primarily focused on defect detection alone, without integrating defect information directly into the control loop, for example, [91,92,93,94]. To address this limitation, in this work potential defect-prone conditions were detected using statistically defined thresholds and subsequently integrated into the control design. Generally, when the output exceeds these thresholds, the controller acts to prevent the process from entering defect-prone regions. The results demonstrated that, in both scenarios: without defect integration and with defect-based control, the proposed controller can effectively reduce melt pool fluctuations and regulate the process output.
4.2 Practical implications
The proposed controller relies on input–output data of the L-PBF process acquired by the InfiniAM Spectral system, without requiring prior knowledge of the system dynamics or an explicit mathematical model of the L-PBF process from a control design perspective. Although an input–output FIR representation is identified from measured process data, this representation is used to predict future melt pool emissions rather than to construct an explicit mathematical model of the underlying process dynamics. Consequently, the extensive modelling effort required for conventional model-based control is avoided, facilitating practical implementation. Nevertheless, preliminary process data are required to define appropriate operating regions and thresholds, which may vary depending on the print geometry and process conditions. Additionally, in contrast to VRFT and ILC approaches, which typically involve offline controller design and, in the case of ILC, require iterative procedures and consequently repetitive experiments, the proposed controller is formulated for online operation to support future online implementation. This significantly reduces the number of experiments required for controller design. Furthermore, the integration of the threshold-based anomaly detection method within the control approach constrains the melt pool emissions from entering signal regions associated with LOF and keyhole porosity, with potential implications for part quality, subject to experimental validation.
From a practical perspective, designing a control system for the L-PBF process highlights the importance of collaboration between control engineers and manufacturing engineers. In the controller design stage, control engineers require essential process-related information from manufacturing engineers, including the selection of appropriate setpoints for melt pool signatures and the definition of acceptable operating thresholds associated with defect-prone conditions. Control engineers then utilise this information to design the controller, perform closed-loop stability analysis, and implement the controller. This highlights the need for collaborative interaction, as the proposed controller requires upper and lower anomaly thresholds as well as a desired melt pool temperature to ensure acceptable final part quality, stable operation and a reduction of defect-prone signal excursions.
5 Conclusions and future works
The objective of this study was to regulate the intensity of the melt pool emissions, which is a temperature-related proxy, during laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) using data from the InfiniAM Spectral in-situ monitoring system to reduce melt pool fluctuations. To achieve this objective, an intralayer data-based control system, called data-based predictive finite impulse response (FIR)-based proportional controller (DB-PFPC), was designed. The approach was initially investigated on a representative layer beyond the support region, with an additional layer from the same spinal-cage build used to provide a limited assessment of the controller’s applicability to another layer. The same intralayer control approach was employed, while a different setpoint was used based on the different mean melt pool emission level observed in this layer. Although this test demonstrated that the proposed controller can operate with satisfactory performance during the printing of another layer, it does not constitute comprehensive validation across different geometries, parts, or processing conditions, as interlayer effects, such as heat accumulation from previously deposited layers, were not considered. The closed-loop control proposed in this paper consists of two parts: prediction and control. The idea behind this was to first predict the future output, which is the future melt pool emissions in this case, by estimating the Markov parameters, and then update the control input accordingly. The melt pool and laser energy data were recorded by the InfiniAM Spectral system, which comprises two modules: the MeltVIEW module with two coaxial photodiodes for recording melt pool data, and the LaserVIEW module with one photodiode for recording laser energy data. These data, collected from a Renishaw RenAM 500 printer, were used to design a data-based controller intended for future real-time deployment and evaluated within a simulated environment in MATLAB R2024b.
The proposed controller aimed to reduce fluctuations in the melt pool data to decrease the likelihood of LOF and keyhole porosity, both of which can degrade the quality of spinal cages, considered in the present study. The DB-PFPC successfully reduced these fluctuations and regulated the melt pool data toward the setpoint. The melt pool intensity setpoint was selected as the mean of the open-loop signal and was used as a representative reference level for the present simulation study, with the aim of reducing fluctuations associated with measurement noise and surface changes during scanning. However, this choice does not establish the mean as an experimentally validated optimal processing condition. Instead, it is considered a nominal statistical reference for assessing the feasibility of the proposed controller in regulating the melt pool intensity and reducing its fluctuations. Nevertheless, the controller was also tested with several other setpoints, and the results showed that it successfully regulated the melt pool emissions towards the tested setpoints. Therefore, future investigations should focus on deriving an experimentally validated setpoint or determining an appropriate setpoint based on process-quality requirements. This study contributes to the application of control systems in L-PBF by introducing a data-based control design methodology that links the estimation of Markov parameters of an FIR model to the future melt pool behaviour within a layer. This predictive capability enables the controller to update the control input based on predicted process behaviour rather than solely reacting to measured deviations. It should be noted that a limitation of the present study is that the proposed controller is evaluated in a closed-loop simulation environment rather than deployed directly on the Renishaw RenAM 500 system. This is due to current hardware and software constraints that restrict real-time access to intralayer sensing and control inputs. Although the proposed controller is formulated for online intralayer operation, practical real-time implementation and experimental validation were not performed in the present study. Instead, the simulation provides a controlled assessment of the feasibility and closed-loop behaviour of the proposed approach under the assumption that melt pool measurements and laser energy control are available during the laser scanning of each layer. Experimental implementation on an L-PBF system with access to these signals is required to verify the controller’s real-time performance and its effectiveness in reducing actual defects.
The stability of the proposed closed-loop system was analysed under both nominal and uncertain cases, which helped in tuning and selecting a suitable proportional gain to ensure it remained within the stable region. Furthermore, a sensitivity analysis of the closed-loop performance and stability to variations in the control-design parameters was conducted to assess the extent to which changes in these parameters affect the closed-loop performance and stability. A threshold-based anomaly detection approach, inspired by [85, 86], was employed to identify melt pool emission excursions that may give rise to LOF and keyhole porosity, as the dataset does not contain physical defect labels. Although this study demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed DB-PFPC in regulating melt pool temperature, several aspects remain to be explored in the future. The proposed approach does not constitute direct physical defect detection. Instead, it identifies defect-prone signal conditions using statistically defined thresholds. The reduction observed in the defect-prone signal excursions demonstrates the ability of the proposed controller to maintain the melt pool emission within the statistically defined threshold region. However, it does not establish a reduction in actual defects. Therefore, experimental validation using techniques such as computed tomography (CT) scanning or other imaging methods is required to determine validated defect thresholds and assess the proposed anomaly detection method by comparing the identified defect-prone region with the actual physical defects.
Another aspect that could be considered is extending this control design into interlayer (layer-to-layer) control design, where adjustments are applied between layers by the controller. Although most studies in the literature have adopted an intralayer approach, the interlayer approach presents distinct advantages as well as challenges. This aspect warrants further investigation to assess its effectiveness, particularly given its greater compatibility with the Renishaw RenAM 500 system for practical implementation.
Beyond improving the quality of the final spinal cages, which was the primary focus of this work, future research could also consider integrating optimisation of energy consumption and CO\(\_{2}\) impact into the control design to enhance environmental sustainability. This could be achieved by designing a recommender system that serves as a supervisory controller, balancing and trading off between part quality and environmental impact.

Definition
- Control:
A discipline concerned with regulating the behaviour of dynamical systems using feedback and algorithms [1].
- Control signal:
The controller output that is calculated and applied to the system to achieve the control objective [2].
- Control system:
A group of interacting elements that work together to drive the measured variable toward the desired value (set point) [3].
- Disturbance:
An uncontrollable input that is not known accurately in advance and is not manipulable by the control designer. The control system should therefore be designed to effectively handle and mitigate its effects [4].
- Feedback:
A looped signal or process used to control a system [5].
- Reference:
A desired value of a system [5].

The set of techniques used to derive mathematical models of dynamical systems from measured input–output data [6].

Threshold-based anomaly detection uses mean ± Kσ (K_upper=1, K_lower=2) to flag keyhole-prone (above upper) and LOF-prone (below lower) signal excursions; output thresholds are converted to control-input saturation bounds.

Reported simulation results: 99.98% reduction in threshold-exceeding samples (34,007 to six) in the studied layer; RMSE ≈0.055 vs ≈0.059 (PI variant) and ≈0.317 (ARX variant); reaching time ≈0.023 time units vs ≈0.058 and ≈0.041 respectively.
limitations: Validation is limited to a closed-loop MATLAB simulation using previously recorded layer data; no real-time control was implemented on the RenAM 500, and the authors state experimental validation remains future work.

The dataset contains no physical defect labels, so threshold excursions are proxies for defect-prone conditions; no CT or other physical defect confirmation is reported, and the 99.98% figure refers to signal excursions, not actual defects.

Results are based on one representative layer plus a limited second-layer test; interlayer heat accumulation, part geometry effects and other process parameters were not modelled, and the setpoint (open-loop mean) is not an experimentally validated optimal condition.

A data-based controller is developed using photodiode signals from the melt pool emissions to predict future melt pool data and then update the control input accordingly. The prediction is achieved by estimating the Markov parameters and constructing a finite impulse response (FIR) model of the process. This controller, termed the data-based predictive FIR-based proportional controller, adjusts the laser energy input by applying a proportional correction to deviations of the melt pool emissions from their setpoint, thereby mitigating under- or overheating of the melt pool. \# Design of an intralayer data\-based controller for laser powder bed fusion processing

\- ORIGINAL ARTICLE
\- Open access
\- Published\:

\#\# Abstract

This paper proposes a data\-based approach to reduce defect\-prone process conditions during the additive manufacturing of Ti\-6Al\-4V alloy parts using the laser powder bed fusion technique\. The focus is on controlling melt pool emissions intensity used as a temperature\-related proxy generated as the laser interacts with the alloy powder to avoid processing conditions which generate defects such as lack\-of\-fusion \(LOF\) or keyhole porosity\. A data\-based controller is developed using photodiode signals from the melt pool emissions to predict future melt pool data and then update the control input accordingly\. The prediction is achieved by estimating the Markov parameters and constructing a finite impulse response \(FIR\) model of the process\. This controller\, termed the data\-based predictive FIR\-based proportional controller\, adjusts the laser energy input by applying a proportional correction to deviations of the melt pool emissions from their setpoint\, thereby mitigating under\- or overheating of the melt pool\. The developed approach is investigated for the printing of spinal cage medical devices and evaluated through a closed\-loop MATLAB simulation to assess its potential for intralayer control\. A threshold\-based anomaly detection approach is then employed to quantitatively evaluate the controller’s effectiveness in reducing defect\-prone signal excursions\.
