records.body_text:
Advanced Electronics Lubricants Engineered for Connection Reliability
PPE connector lubricants, base fluids, vacuum fluids, and optical fluids for high-reliability electronic systems.
Most electronic failures in the field start at a contact. Vibration and temperature swings wear through plating, oxide builds up, and resistance creeps until a signal drops out. SantoLubes® ACCL® connector lubricants form a stable, non-spreading PPE film that stops that cycle while leaving conductivity intact. Billions of contacts have been protected by ACCL and PPE products over more than 30 years.
Our advanced electronics portfolio includes ACCL connector lubricants, SantoLubes PPE-derived connector fluids, SantoVac® vacuum fluids for electronics manufacturing, SantoLight™ optical fluids for optoelectronic assemblies, and SantoRad™ fluids for radiation-exposed hardware. All are built on PFAS-free polyphenyl ether (PPE) chemistry.
Low, Stable Contact Resistance
30+ Years of Field Heritage
PFAS-Free PPE Chemistry
Built for the Demands of Advanced Electronics
Electronics now run in vehicles, aircraft, outdoor cabinets, and data centers, under constant vibration and thermal cycling, for service lives measured in decades. Contacts, connectors, and assemblies need protection that lasts as long as the device. SantoLubes technologies help support:
Prevent Fretting Corrosion
Maintain Low, Stable Contact Resistance
Reduce Insertion Force & Wear
Protect Precious & Base Metal Contacts
Withstand Thermal Cycling
Resist Harsh & Corrosive Environments
Support Clean Electronics Manufacturing
Reduce PFAS Exposure
Advanced Lubricant Technologies. Built for Every Connection.
Match corrosion protection, contact stability, thermal performance, and process cleanliness to each part of your electronic system.
Product Technologies for Advanced Electronics Challenges
Electronic systems need different fluid behaviors across connectors and contacts, high-temperature components, manufacturing equipment, and optoelectronic assemblies. SantoLubes offers PPE technologies matched to each.
ACCL Electronic Connector Lubricants
- PPE-based lubricants that protect contacts without hindering conductivity. A built-in UV tracer makes coverage easy to inspect.
- ACCL-52T & ACCL-54T
- Protect against insertion damage, fretting, and environmental corrosion.
- ACCL 53T
- Conforms to Telcordia GR-78, GR-317, and GR-121.
ACCL-7T
- Ready-to-apply PPE fluid for life-of-device protection up to 150°C.
SantoLubes PPE-Derived Connector Fluids
For electronics that need extreme stability in heat, oxidation, radiation, or chemical exposure.
- SantoLubes OS-124
- Exceptionally low volatility with strong resistance to heat, oxygen, radiation, and chemical attack.
- SantoLubes OS-138
- Higher viscosity grade with compatibility across most metals, plastics, and elastomers.
SantoVac PPE Vacuum Fluids
Low-backstreaming fluids for vacuum equipment in electronics manufacturing and test.
- SantoVac 5P Ultra
- High-purity grade for contamination-sensitive processes.
- SantoVac 5 PPE
- Ultra-high vacuum of 5×10⁻¹⁰ Torr at 25°C.
SantoVac 9
- Cost-effective 10⁻⁸ Torr performance for commercial pumps.
SantoLight Optical Fluids
Optical-grade PPE fluid for optoelectronic, display, and sensor assemblies.
- SantoLight SL-5262
- High refractive index, ultra-low volatility, low particulate, and low fluorescence. Rated -40°C to +150°C.
Electronics Application / Challenge | Recommended Products | Why It Fits | Electronics Relevance
---|---|---|---
Telecom & datacom connectors | ACCL 53T | Telcordia GR-78, GR-317, and GR-121 conformance. | For network equipment with decades-long service lives.
Automotive & EV electronic connectors | ACCL-52T, ACCL-54T | Stops fretting caused by constant vibration. | Reduces intermittent faults in vehicle electronics.
Avionics & defense electronics | ACCL-52T, ACCL-53T, ACCL-54T, SantoLubes OS-124 | Fretting, corrosion, and temperature-cycling protection. | For flight controls, sensors, and mission systems.
Instrumentation & control systems | ACCL family | Low, stable contact resistance over service life. | Prevents resistance drift that causes signal errors.
Life-of-device components at elevated temperature | ACCL-7T | Ready-to-apply PPE fluid rated up to 150°C. | One application for the life of the device.
Extreme-heat or radiation-exposed electronics | SantoLubes OS-124, OS-138, SantoRad 7, SantoRad 12 | Thermal, oxidative, and radiation stability. | For space, nuclear, and high-heat hardware.
Electronics manufacturing & test vacuum systems | SantoVac 5P Ultra, SantoVac 5 PPE, SantoVac 9 | Low backstreaming and stable high vacuum. | Keeps process equipment clean and productive.
Optoelectronic, display & sensor assemblies | SantoLight SL-5262 | Optical clarity and index matching with ultra-low volatility. | Protects optical signal paths in electronic devices.
Custom electronics requirements | Custom PPE formulations through SantoTolling | Tailored viscosity, film behavior, and thermal profile. | Contact SantoLubes for application guidance.
Note: Product selection depends on contact materials and plating, connector design, temperature range, vibration, environmental exposure, application method, and qualification requirements.
How Fretting Corrosion Causes Intermittent Failures
Mated contacts are never perfectly still. Vibration and thermal cycling move them against each other by microns, thousands of times a day. That motion wears through the plating and builds up oxide debris, which insulates the contact. Resistance rises until the connection drops in and out, often in a way that never shows up on the bench.
ACCL keeps a 15–20 micron PPE film between the surfaces. It reduces the friction that drives the motion, keeps out the oxygen that forms oxides, and gets displaced at the actual metal-to-metal contact points so conductivity stays intact. Depending on the product, ACCL covers -55°C to 370°C and reduces mating force by up to 60%.
Built for Electronics OEMs, Manufacturers & Technical Decision Makers
Electronics & Connector OEMs
Connector protection designed into new products from the start.
Telecom & Datacom Equipment Makers
Telcordia-conforming protection for network hardware.
Automotive & EV Electronics Suppliers
Fretting protection for connectors under constant vibration.
Aerospace & Defense Electronics Teams
Reliable contacts for avionics, sensors, and mission systems.
Contract Manufacturers & Assemblers
Easy-to-apply lubricants with UV tracer for inline inspection.
Reliability & Failure Analysis Engineers
A proven fix for intermittent contact failures in the field.
Custom Electronics Lubricant Solutions
Not every electronic assembly fits an off-the-shelf lubricant. SantoLubes can help evaluate contact materials and plating, temperature range, vibration, environmental exposure, application method, and service-life targets.
Request Application Guidance
Every electronic design has its own contacts, materials, and operating conditions. SantoLubes provides technical information, sample material, and consultation to help you qualify the right product.
Samples and Technical Support
Request a sample or connect with the SantoLubes technical team.
Application Review
Discuss your gearbox, chain, drive system, bearing, rope, or cable application with a technical specialist.
Performance Data
Review technical data for ultEbase® and SantoTrac® technologies.
FAQ
Answers to common questions about SantoLubes technologies in advanced electronics applications.
What lubricants are used in advanced electronics?
Electronic systems use connector lubricants to protect contacts from corrosion and fretting, high-stability PPE fluids for extreme-heat or radiation-exposed hardware, vacuum pump fluids for manufacturing and test equipment, and optical fluids for optoelectronic assemblies. SantoLubes covers these needs with ACCL, SantoLubes OS-124 and OS-138, SantoVac, and SantoLight technologies.
What is fretting corrosion, and how does ACCL prevent it?
Fretting corrosion happens when vibration or thermal cycling moves mated contacts against each other by tiny amounts. The motion wears through plating and builds up insulating oxide, which raises contact resistance until the connection becomes intermittent. ACCL keeps a durable PPE film between the surfaces that reduces friction, keeps out oxygen, and keeps the contact interface clean.
Will a connector lubricant interfere with electrical conductivity?
No. ACCL is displaced at the actual metal-to-metal contact points under normal mating pressure and stays in place across the surrounding surface. The result is low, stable contact resistance with long-term protection from corrosion and fretting.
Are ACCL products Telcordia compliant?
Yes. ACCL 53T conforms to Telcordia GR-78, GR-317, and GR-121, the standards for reliability and performance of telecommunications equipment and connectors.
Are SantoLubes electronics lubricants PFAS-free?
Yes. ACCL and our other electronics products are built on polyphenyl ether (PPE) chemistry, which is not a PFAS compound. As PFAS rules expand across electronics manufacturing, PPE gives teams a way to reduce fluorinated chemistry without giving up performance. Learn about PFAS Alternatives.
Can SantoLubes support custom electronics application reviews?
Yes. Our team can review contact materials, plating, temperature range, vibration, and application method to recommend or help develop the right product. Custom formulation and private-label work is available through our affiliate, SantoTolling.

Mated contacts are never perfectly still\. Vibration and thermal cycling move them against each other by microns\, thousands of times a day\. \#\# What is fretting corrosion\, and how does ACCL prevent it\?

Fretting corrosion happens when vibration or thermal cycling moves mated contacts against each other by tiny amounts\. The motion wears through plating and builds up insulating oxide\, which raises contact resistance until the connection becomes intermittent\. ACCL keeps a durable PPE film between the surfaces that reduces friction\, keeps out oxygen\, and keeps the contact interface clean\.

\#\# Will a connector lubricant interfere with electrical conductivity\?

No\. ACCL is displaced at the actual metal\-to\-metal contact points under normal mating pressure and stays in place across the surrounding surface\. The result is low\, stable contact resistance with long\-term protection from corrosion and fretting\.

Yes\. ACCL 53T conforms to Telcordia GR\-78\, GR\-317\, and GR\-121\, the standards for reliability and performance of telecommunications equipment and connectors\.

Ionizing radiation breaks down conventional hydrocarbon lubricants. They thicken, form gels, and stop protecting the parts they were applied to. SantoRad PPE fluids resist radiation up to 10¹¹ ergs/gram and keep their viscosity and film strength, which helps equipment run longer between service visits.

SantoLight SL-5262 is an optical-grade PPE fluid for medical and nuclear optical devices. Its high refractive index supports index matching between optical components, and it keeps its clarity under ionizing radiation, where conventional optical fluids can yellow or cloud.

The products on this page are intended for medical equipment and instruments, not for direct patient contact or implantable use. SantoLight SL\-5262 is an optical\-grade PPE fluid for medical and nuclear optical devices\. Its high refractive index supports index matching between optical components\, and it keeps its clarity under ionizing radiation\, where conventional optical fluids can yellow or cloud\.

\#\# Are SantoLubes products approved for patient contact\?

The products on this page are intended for medical equipment and instruments\, not for direct patient contact or implantable use\. Device manufacturers are responsible for regulatory qualification\, including biocompatibility testing where it applies\. Contact SantoLubes for the technical and safety documentation you need for your qualification process\.

\#\# Can SantoLubes support custom medical technology application reviews\?

Yes\. Our team can evaluate radiation dose\, temperature\, volatility\, optical requirements\, materials compatibility\, and connector reliability to recommend or help develop the right fluid\. Custom formulation and private\-label work is available through our affiliate\, SantoTolling\.

records.body_text:
Comparative Investigation of Autogenous and Cu-Interlayer-Assisted Laser Welding of Dissimilar Steel-Aluminum Overlap Joints
- Original Research Article
- Published:
Abstract
In this study, steel-aluminum dissimilar metals were joined with and without a Cu interlayer in an overlap configuration using a laser welding process. The mechanical performances of the welded joints were evaluated in terms of lap shear strength and microhardness. The welding performances of the steel-aluminum joints with a Cu interlayer were also compared with autogenously welded joints by maintaining the same experimental and testing conditions. The ASTM D1002 for the lap shear test and ASTM E92 for the Vickers microhardness test were followed to assess the mechanical properties of the joints. The interfacial shear strength of the Cu interlayer-added steel-aluminum joints showed ~ 14% enhancement compared to autogenously welded joints. The microhardness at the fusion zone of Cu interlayer-added joints showed a ~ 7% reduction compared to autogenously welded samples due to ductile phase formation at the joint interface. The spectroscopic and microscopic analysis also revealed that the ductile intermetallic phases, such as Al-Cu and Al2-Cu, enhanced the overall mechanical performance of Cu interlayer-added joints. A needle-like dense network is visible on the Al side growing toward the steel interface. These phases are a characteristic feature of Fe-Al intermetallics formed during laser welding due to Fe diffusion into molten Al. Cracks are generated along the reaction layer due to these brittle phases.

\#\# Abstract

In this study\, steel\-aluminum dissimilar metals were joined with and without a Cu interlayer in an overlap configuration using a laser welding process\. The mechanical performances of the welded joints were evaluated in terms of lap shear strength and microhardness\. The welding performances of the steel\-aluminum joints with a Cu interlayer were also compared with autogenously welded joints by maintaining the same experimental and testing conditions\. The ASTM D1002 for the lap shear test and ASTM E92 for the Vickers microhardness test were followed to assess the mechanical properties of the joints\. The interfacial shear strength of the Cu interlayer\-added steel\-aluminum joints showed \~ 14\% enhancement compared to autogenously welded joints\. The microhardness at the fusion zone of Cu interlayer\-added joints showed a \~ 7\% reduction compared to autogenously welded samples due to ductile phase formation at the joint interface\. The spectroscopic and microscopic analysis also revealed that the ductile intermetallic phases\, such as Al\-Cu and Al2\-Cu\, enhanced the overall mechanical performance of Cu interlayer\-added joints\. A needle\-like dense network is visible on the Al side growing toward the steel interface\. These phases are a characteristic feature of Fe\-Al intermetallics formed during laser welding due to Fe diffusion into molten Al\. Cracks are generated along the reaction layer due to these brittle phases\.

Research Lab Fluids Engineered for Clean, Repeatable Results
PPE vacuum pump fluids, radiation-resistant fluids, optical fluids, and base fluids for laboratory and research systems.
In a research lab, the fluid in the pump or the grease in the stage can end up in your data. Backstreaming vapor coats a sample surface. A lubricant that breaks down under radiation stops a beamline mechanism mid-run. SantoLubes® builds its research portfolio on polyphenyl ether (PPE) chemistry, the lowest-volatility class of synthetic fluids, with thermal stability up to 450°C (840°F) and natural resistance to radiation and chemical attack.
Our research lab portfolio includes SantoVac® diffusion pump fluids, SantoRad™ radiation-resistant fluids, SantoLight™ optical fluids, SantoLubes PPE base fluids for specialty lubricants and greases, ultEbase® base stocks for formulation research, and ACCL® connector lubricants for instrument electronics.
Ultra-High Vacuum to 5×10⁻¹⁰ Torr
Low Backstreaming & Sample Contamination
Radiation & Thermal Stability
Built for the Demands of Research Labs
Research systems run long experiments under high vacuum, high temperature, and sometimes high radiation, with little tolerance for contamination or unplanned downtime. A failed pump fluid or degraded lubricant can cost weeks of work. SantoLubes technologies help support:
Reach Ultra-High Vacuum
Minimize Backstreaming & Sample Contamination
Withstand Radiation in Physics & Nuclear Research
Keep Optics & Measurements Clear
Stay Stable at High Temperature
Resist Chemical Attack
Protect Instrument Connectors
Reduce PFAS in the Lab
Advanced Fluid Technologies. Built for Better Data.
Match vacuum performance, purity, radiation resistance, and optical clarity to each system in your lab.
Product Technologies for Research Lab Challenges
Research facilities need different fluid behaviors across vacuum pumps, radiation-exposed hardware, optical setups, precision mechanisms, and formulation studies. SantoLubes offers PPE technologies matched to each.
SantoVac PPE Vacuum Fluids
Diffusion pump fluids for high and ultra-high vacuum research systems.
- SantoVac 5 PPE
- Ultra-high vacuum of 5×10⁻¹⁰ Torr at 25°C. MIL-L-87100 compliant.
- SantoVac 5P Ultra
- High-purity grade with negligible backstreaming for contamination-free work.
- SantoVac 9
- Cost-effective 10⁻⁸ Torr performance for general lab pumps.
SantoRad Radiation-Resistant Fluids
PPE fluids for high-energy physics, nuclear, and radiation research hardware.
- SantoRad 7
- Lower viscosity grade with excellent radiation stability and low volatility.
- SantoRad 12
- Higher viscosity grade for greater film thickness. Both resist radiation up to 10¹¹ ergs/gram.
SantoLight Optical Fluids
Optical-grade PPE fluid for metrology, laser, and imaging setups.
- SantoLight SL-5262
- High refractive index, low particulate, and low fluorescence. Stable under ionizing radiation. Rated -40°C to +150°C.
PPE Base Fluids & ultEbase Base Stocks
Base fluids for lab-built lubricants, greases, and formulation research.
- OS-124, OS-138 & OS-750
- High-temperature PPE base fluids with exceptionally low volatility.
- OS-105 ADE
- Alkylated diphenyl ether base oil with broad-temperature properties.
- ultEbase
- Low EHD shear Group V base stock for formulated lubricants.
Research Application / Challenge | Recommended Products | Why It Fits | Research Relevance
---|---|---|---
Ultra-high vacuum research systems | SantoVac 5 PPE | 5×10⁻¹⁰ Torr ultimate vacuum with long fluid life. | For surface science, thin-film, and physics research.
Contamination-critical experiments | SantoVac 5P Ultra | Very high purity and negligible backstreaming. | Keeps sample surfaces and chamber walls clean.
General laboratory diffusion pumps | SantoVac 9 | Reliable 10⁻⁸ Torr performance at lower cost. | For teaching labs and routine vacuum work.
High-energy physics & radiation research | SantoRad 7, SantoRad 12, SantoVac 5 PPE | Resists ionizing radiation without thickening or gelling. | For beamlines, accelerators, and radiation sources.
Optical metrology, laser & imaging setups | SantoLight SL-5262 | Optical clarity and index matching with ultra-low volatility. | Protects measurement accuracy.
Precision stages, manipulators & mechanisms | PPE-based specialty lubricants and greases from OS-124 / OS-138 (application specific) | Low vapor pressure and broad material compatibility. | Lubricates motion inside or near vacuum chambers.
Lubricant & tribology research | ultEbase, OS-105 ADE, OS-124, OS-138 | Well-characterized base stocks for formulation work. | For studies on friction, efficiency, and thermal stability.
Instrument electronics & connectors | ACCL-52T, ACCL-53T, ACCL-54T, ACCL-7T | Low, stable contact resistance over service life. | Prevents signal drift in data acquisition hardware.
Replacing PFPE vacuum fluids | SantoVac 5P Ultra, SantoVac 5 PPE, OS-750 | PPE vacuum performance without fluorinated chemistry. | Reduces PFAS use and disposal concerns in the lab.
Custom research requirements | Custom PPE formulations through SantoTolling | Tailored viscosity, purity, and thermal or radiation profile. | Contact SantoLubes for application guidance.
Note: Product selection depends on vacuum level, pump type, temperature, radiation exposure, materials compatibility, cleanliness requirements, and experimental conditions.
Why Pump Fluid Choice Shows Up in Your Data
Every diffusion pump sends a small amount of fluid vapor back toward the chamber. In a research system, that vapor settles on samples, detectors, and optics. A thin hydrocarbon film can change surface chemistry, shift a measurement baseline, or force a bake-out that costs days.
PPE fluids have the lowest volatility of any synthetic fluid class. SantoVac 5 PPE reaches 5×10⁻¹⁰ Torr with essentially zero backstreaming, and SantoVac 5P Ultra goes further with a high-purity refinement for the most contamination-sensitive work. Because PPE resists oxidation and thermal breakdown, the fluid also stays in service longer between changes.
Built for Research Facilities, Scientists & Technical Decision Makers
University & Academic Labs
Reliable vacuum and lubrication for teaching and research systems.
National & Government Laboratories
Proven PPE fluids for large-scale and long-running programs.
Physics & Accelerator Facilities
Radiation-stable fluids for beamlines and high-energy hardware.
Analytical & Instrument Labs
Clean vacuum and stable optics for accurate measurement.
Corporate R&D Centers
Base fluids and custom formulations for product development.
Lab Managers & Facility Engineers
Longer fluid life and fewer unplanned shutdowns.
Custom Research Fluid Solutions
Not every experiment fits an off-the-shelf fluid. SantoLubes can help evaluate vacuum level, purity, temperature, radiation exposure, materials compatibility, and the formulation needs of your research program.
Request Application Guidance
Every nuclear energy application has unique operating conditions. SantoLubes can provide technical information, sample material, and consultation to help evaluate product fit.
Samples and Technical Support
Request a sample or connect with the SantoLubes technical team.
Application Review
Discuss your gearbox, chain, drive system, bearing, rope, or cable application with a technical specialist.
Performance Data
Review technical data for ultEbase and SantoTrac® technologies.
FAQ
Answers to common questions about SantoLubes technologies in research lab applications.
What fluids and lubricants are used in research labs?
Research labs use diffusion pump fluids for high-vacuum systems, radiation-resistant fluids for physics and nuclear hardware, optical fluids for metrology and imaging setups, low-volatility lubricants and greases for stages and manipulators, and base stocks for formulation research. SantoLubes covers these needs with SantoVac, SantoRad, SantoLight, SantoLubes PPE base fluids, and ultEbase technologies.
What is the best diffusion pump fluid for ultra-high vacuum research?
SantoVac 5 PPE is widely regarded as the top-performing diffusion pump fluid. It produces ultra-high vacuum of 5×10⁻¹⁰ Torr or greater at 25°C with essentially zero backstreaming. For the most contamination-sensitive work, SantoVac 5P Ultra offers a higher-purity refinement of the same chemistry.
Which SantoVac grade is right for my lab?
SantoVac 9 suits general lab pumps that need reliable 10⁻⁸ Torr performance at lower cost. SantoVac 5 PPE is the choice for ultra-high vacuum at 5×10⁻¹⁰ Torr. SantoVac 5P Ultra is for experiments where any contamination is unacceptable. Our engineers can review your pump and vacuum targets and recommend a grade.
Can SantoLubes fluids be used in radiation research environments?
Yes. PPE fluids resist ionizing radiation far better than hydrocarbon and conventional synthetic fluids. SantoRad 7 and SantoRad 12 withstand radiation up to 10¹¹ ergs/gram, which suits high-energy physics, accelerator, and nuclear research hardware.
Can we replace PFPE vacuum fluids in our lab with a PFAS-free option?
In many vacuum applications, yes. SantoVac PPE fluids match or exceed PFPE vacuum performance without fluorinated chemistry. A successful switch depends on proper cleaning and flushing, and our engineers can help plan the changeover. Learn about PFAS Alternatives.
Does SantoLubes provide samples for research evaluation?
Yes. SantoLubes provides sample quantities, Technical Data Sheets, and Safety Data Sheets so you can evaluate a fluid in your system before a full order. Custom formulation is also available through our affiliate, SantoTolling.

A VPP-printed high-precision polymer template defines through-deposition zones, enabling volumetric metal growth over large areas and complex 3D geometries with spatial control, rather than the point-by-point strategy of conventional electrochemical additive manufacturing (ECAM). records.body_text:
Low-cost metal fabrication via in-mold continuous electrochemical additive manufacturing with VPP-printed polymer templates
- Research
- Published:
Abstract
Metal additive manufacturing (AM) has long been constrained by high energy consumption, strict fabrication environment requirements, and high costs. This study introduces a scalable and sustainable hybrid manufacturing approach that integrates vat photopolymerization (VPP) with electrochemical reduction. In this method, a VPP fabricated high-precision polymer template defines through deposition zones for metal reduction, enabling volumetric growth over large areas and the fabrication of complex three-dimensional geometries with excellent spatial control. Systematic investigation of electrochemical parameters including electrolyte pH, additive concentration, and applied current density identified optimal conditions at pH 0.5 with 10 wt.% additives and a current density of 15–25 mA/cm2 facilitating uniform, fine-grained, and high-resolution copper prints. The resulting process achieves a electrochemical volumetric deposition rate approximately 10⁸ µm3/h entirely at room temperature, overcoming the limitation of point-by-point strategy and slow printing rate of current electrochemical additive manufacturing (ECAM) methods. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), structural characterization, and physical property evaluation confirm that the deposited copper exhibits high purity, an electrical conductivity of 4.92 × 105 S/m and a thermal conductivity of 178 W/m·K, together with an ultimate tensile strength of 193.7 MPa-all achieved without post-processing. Furthermore, the estimated fabrication cost was only $0.26 cm−3, representing a reduction of approximately 99% compared with conventional SLM, DMLS, and EBM processes. The integration of polymer templates with controlled electrochemical reduction establishes an energy-efficient, cost-effective, and scalable route for producing complex metallic structures. Although demonstrated here using copper, this strategy is broadly applicable to other metals, offering a promising pathway for scalable fabrication of micro/meso scales metal devices, lightweight electronics, and multifunctional components.

Energy\-dispersive X\-ray spectroscopy \(EDS\)\, structural characterization\, and physical property evaluation confirm that the deposited copper exhibits high purity\, an electrical conductivity of 4\.92 × 105 S\/m and a thermal conductivity of 178 W\/m·K\, together with an ultimate tensile strength of 193\.7 MPa\-all achieved without post\-processing\. Furthermore\, the estimated fabrication cost was only \$0\.26 cm−3\, representing a reduction of approximately 99\% compared with conventional SLM\, DMLS\, and EBM processes\. The integration of polymer templates with controlled electrochemical reduction establishes an energy\-efficient\, cost\-effective\, and scalable route for producing complex metallic structures\. Although demonstrated here using copper\, this strategy is broadly applicable to other metals\, offering a promising pathway for scalable fabrication of micro\/meso scales metal devices\, lightweight electronics\, and multifunctional components\.

records.abstract: Abstract Temperature measurement is essential in metal additive manufacturing, as the spatio-thermal profile strongly influences the microstructure and therefore the key mechanical properties of the produced components. Conventional infrared thermography is widely used for in-situ temperature monitoring. However, its quantitative interpretation is often limited by the varying and generally unknown emissivity of the metal surfaces throughout the build process. This paper presents a pipeline that combines visual and infrared imaging to obtain more physically consistent temperature fields under spatially varying emissivity conditions. A high-resolution visual imaging method is used to segment optically distinguishable process regions. These segmented regions are subsequently mapped onto the corresponding infrared images to enable region-specific effective emissivity settings, resulting in emissivity-corrected temperature fields for surfaces above approximately 600 K. The workflow is demonstrated using a laser beam directed energy deposition system and assessed by comparison with the expected solidification behavior of AISI 316L. The results indicate improved physical consistency compared with a globally fixed emissivity assumption, rather than providing an independent metrological validation of absolute temperature accuracy. Although the workflow requires careful system integration and calibration to account for process-specific factors, it provides an approach that can be adapted to other additive manufacturing systems after appropriate modifications. This supports improved process monitoring and may facilitate the development and validation of predictive process models for metal additive manufacturing.
records.summary: The paper addresses the problem that quantitative infrared thermography in metal additive manufacturing is limited by spatially and temporally varying, generally unknown surface emissivity. The authors propose a hybrid RGB/MWIR pipeline: high-dynamic-range visual images are segmented into melt pool, transition zone and background regions, these masks are mapped onto synchronized MWIR images via a planar homography, and region-specific effective emissivity values are assigned to compute corrected temperature fields above roughly 600 K. The workflow is demonstrated on single-layer AISI 316L tracks produced by laser beam directed energy deposition, with and without a 55° build-plate inclination. Corrected profiles show plateau-like regions near the expected solidification interval of AISI 316L, which the authors present as improved physical consistency relative to a globally fixed emissivity assumption, explicitly not as independent metrological validation of absolute temperature accuracy. A Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis indicates that corrected temperatures are governed mainly by emissivity assumptions and region-boundary definitions.
records.why_it_matters: For DED-LB/M process monitoring, the work shows a practical route to reduce emissivity-induced bias in spatially resolved thermography by reusing an RGB camera for region segmentation, rather than requiring multispectral or hyperspectral instrumentation; however, effective emissivities, thresholds and smoothing widths are setup-specific and would need recalibration for other machines and geometries.

Multi-camera in-situ monitoring for emissivity-corrected temperature measurement in laser beam directed energy deposition
- Research
- Open access
- Published:
Abstract
Temperature measurement is essential in metal additive manufacturing, as the spatio-thermal profile strongly influences the microstructure and therefore the key mechanical properties of the produced components. Conventional infrared thermography is widely used for in-situ temperature monitoring. However, its quantitative interpretation is often limited by the varying and generally unknown emissivity of the metal surfaces throughout the build process. This paper presents a pipeline that combines visual and infrared imaging to obtain more physically consistent temperature fields under spatially varying emissivity conditions. A high-resolution visual imaging method is used to segment optically distinguishable process regions. These segmented regions are subsequently mapped onto the corresponding infrared images to enable region-specific effective emissivity settings, resulting in emissivity-corrected temperature fields for surfaces above approximately 600 K. The workflow is demonstrated using a laser beam directed energy deposition system and assessed by comparison with the expected solidification behavior of AISI 316L. The results indicate improved physical consistency compared with a globally fixed emissivity assumption, rather than providing an independent metrological validation of absolute temperature accuracy. Although the workflow requires careful system integration and calibration to account for process-specific factors, it provides an approach that can be adapted to other additive manufacturing systems after appropriate modifications. This supports improved process monitoring and may facilitate the development and validation of predictive process models for metal additive manufacturing.

1 Introduction
Additive manufacturing (AM) enables the production of metallic components with high geometric complexity and offers greater design freedom than conventional manufacturing methods. Features such as internal cavities, undercuts, or locally adapted material distributions can be realized more easily than with subtractive processes. Among the established metal AM processes, laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) is widely used for comparatively small and complex part geometries, whereas laser beam directed energy deposition (DED-LB/M) is particularly attractive for larger structures, repair applications, and the generation of near-net-shape components [1]. In DED-LB/M, metal powder is delivered into a laser beam, which melts both the incoming powder and the underlying substrate or previously deposited material, thereby forming a metallurgical bond between subsequent tracks or layers [2].
The thermal history during metal AM is of central importance because it strongly affects solidification conditions, residual stresses, microstructure formation, and ultimately the mechanical properties of the manufactured component [3, 4]. Consequently, there is considerable interest in measuring and controlling temperature fields during the process [5]. Because of the high temperatures, the moving heat source, and the dynamic nature of the melt pool, contact-based measurements are difficult to apply during DED-LB/M. Thermocouples, for example, provide only point-wise information at fixed positions and cannot capture the spatial temperature field of the process zone. Therefore, in-situ thermal monitoring is commonly performed using contactless radiometric methods, such as pyrometers and infrared cameras [6, 7]. Pyrometers and short-wave infrared (SWIR) cameras are often integrated coaxially to monitor melt pool temperatures, whereas mid-wave infrared (MWIR) cameras are frequently used in off-axis configurations to capture larger fields of view and broader temperature distributions [8, 9].While pyrometers can provide high temporal resolution, they usually deliver only point-like or spatially averaged measurements. Infrared cameras provide spatially resolved temperature fields. However, as with other radiometric methods, their quantitative interpretation depends critically on the assumed emissivity.
A major challenge in quantitative thermography for metal AM is that emissivity is neither constant nor generally known. It can vary substantially between the melt pool, powder, substrate, and previously solidified material, and it depends on the material itself as well as on wavelength, temperature, phase state, oxidation, surface roughness, and viewing angle [10,11,12,13]. Becker et al. showed that the emissivity of 316L and AlSi10Mg surfaces in PBF-LB/M depends strongly on wavelength, material state, oxidation, and observation angle, with clear differences between powder-covered and consolidated surfaces [11]. Although this investigation was carried out for PBF-LB/M, the core conclusions also strongly apply to DED-LB/M, where changing track geometry, powder delivery, melt pool behavior, and off-axis viewing can further amplify spatial and temporal variations in emissivity. Consequently, conventional single-band thermography, in which the user sets a globally constant emissivity, can be insufficient for physically consistent temperature-field interpretation under spatially varying emissivity conditions. This restricts both process monitoring and the validation of thermal process models that rely on reliable temperature-field information.
Different strategies have been proposed to address emissivity-related uncertainties. A simple and widely used approach is to assume a fixed or only weakly varying emissivity [9, 14,15,16]. This is straightforward to implement but is often inadequate for the heterogeneous surface states encountered in metal AM. A related practical approach is single-point calibration, in which one effective emissivity value is selected such that a known reference temperature, for example the solidification plateau of the processed alloy, is reproduced at a selected location [9, 14]. While this can improve the temperature estimate locally, it does not account for spatial emissivity variations across the melt pool, transition region, and surrounding solid material. A more physically motivated approach is region-wise or state-dependent emissivity assignment, in which different emissivity values are associated with regions such as the melt pool, substrate, powder-covered areas, or previously solidified material. Such approaches depend on suitable effective emissivity values as well as reliable identification of the corresponding process regions [8].
Other approaches aim to reduce or separate the emissivity dependence more directly. Ratio pyrometry determines temperature from the intensity ratio at two wavelengths and can reduce the dependence on absolute emissivity under gray-body assumptions. It is widely used for highly dynamic melt pool monitoring in PBF-LB/M and DED-LB/M, often in coaxial configurations [7, 15, 17]. However, its accuracy depends not only on the gray-body assumption, but also on the emissivity ratio at the selected wavelengths. If this ratio varies with material state, oxidation, surface condition, or process region, the resulting temperature can remain biased, which is particularly relevant for metallic AM surfaces with wavelength-dependent emissivity [11]. Multispectral and hyperspectral thermography provide a more rigorous route toward temperature-emissivity separation, but they also require assumptions, models, or prior information about the spectral emissivity behavior over several wavelengths. Since these emissivity ratios or spectral trends can vary between the melt pool, transition region, powder-covered areas, and solidified material, region-dependent emissivity treatment may still be necessary. In addition, such methods typically require sophisticated instrumentation, radiometric calibration, and substantial adaptation to the specific process setup [10, 12, 18, 19]. Breese and Altenburg used hyperspectral SWIR thermography in PBF-LB/M and determined absolute temperatures in the range of approximately 1300–2700 K with an error of less than 6 % relative to the solidification temperature of 316L [18]. Altenburg et al. demonstrated in DED-LB/M that multispectral SWIR thermography can be used for temperature-emissivity separation and can yield more realistic temperature fields than single-point calibration [12]. Dai et al. presented a radiometrically calibrated multispectral CMOS-based approach and reported relative errors of approximately 1.6-−2.0 % after careful calibration [19]. These studies demonstrate the potential of spectral-radiometric methods and their value as reference approaches for simpler emissivity-correction workflows. However, their direct integration into standard process monitoring remains demanding due to instrumentation and calibration requirements.
Recent studies have demonstrated how process models can support the interpretation of in-situ thermal measurements in DED-LB/M. Pereira et al. coupled thermal imaging data with spatio-temporal temperature models and used a simplified emissivity compensation based on infrared melt-pool segmentation [8]. Maximenko et al. combined surface temperature measurements with analytical and finite-element-based modeling to estimate laser absorptivity from temperature data outside the melt pool [20]. These studies show that model-assisted approaches can provide complementary information on effective radiative or energy-related parameters and on the influence of heat-transfer assumptions and process conditions. However, their reliability depends on model assumptions, material data, boundary conditions, heat-source descriptions, and emissivity or absorptivity assumptions used for calibration or validation.
In parallel, visual imaging has become an established and comparatively practical tool for process monitoring in DED-LB/M. Visual cameras are used in coaxial and off-axis configurations for melt pool observation, deposition height measurement, geometric reconstruction, and defect detection [5, 21,22,23,24,25]. Compared with more specialized spectral thermographic systems, visual camera setups are often easier to integrate and can provide high spatial and temporal resolution at comparatively low system complexity. This makes them particularly attractive for segmentation and geometric interpretation of the process zone [26,27,28]. Ansari et al. reviewed visual process monitoring in DED-LB/M and emphasized its relevance for melt pool monitoring, defect detection, and geometric reconstruction [17]. Ning et al. used a machine-vision approach to detect and compensate height deviations in thin-walled DED-LB/M parts and reported an improvement in height consistency of up to 22.8 % [29]. Zhao et al. used high-speed imaging to capture transient melt pool and bead morphologies on inclined substrates and showed that increasing tilt angle and smaller laser spot diameters promote hump formation and morphological instabilities [30]. However, the use of visual imaging has mainly focused on geometric and morphological process monitoring rather than on emissivity-aware correction of infrared temperature fields.
Overall, the literature reveals a trade-off between physical rigor, measurement complexity, and practical integrability. Spectral-radiometric methods can provide more rigorous temperature-emissivity separation, but they require complex instrumentation and calibration. Region-wise emissivity correction is more practical, but depends on reliable segmentation and suitable effective emissivity values. Visual imaging, by contrast, is already widely used in DED-LB/M and provides high-resolution spatial information that can support such segmentation. Nevertheless, the systematic coupling of visual image segmentation with MWIR thermography for region-specific emissivity correction remains comparatively underexplored, especially for DED-LB/M processes with heterogeneous surface states and off-axis observation geometries.
Against this background, this study introduces a hybrid RGB/MWIR workflow for emissivity-aware temperature field correction in DED-LB/M. Simple single-layer AISI 316L structures are manufactured and monitored using a visual RGB camera and an MWIR camera. The RGB images are used to segment process regions such as the melt pool, transition zone, and surrounding material. These regions are then mapped onto the MWIR data to assign effective region-wise emissivity values and compute corrected temperature fields. The aim is not to provide full temperature-emissivity separation, which remains experimentally demanding, but to offer a practically integrable approach that improves the physical consistency of spatially resolved temperature fields compared with common fixed-emissivity thermography approaches.
The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Sect. 2 presents the DED-LB/M facility, the employed camera systems, and the image processing workflow used to compute emissivity-corrected temperature fields. Section 3 presents the manufactured structures, recorded image data, fused temperature fields, and uncertainty considerations. Finally, Sect. 4 summarizes the main findings and outlines directions for future work.
2 Experimental setup and methods
2.1 Laser beam directed energy deposition system and material
The present study was carried out at the LMD2 facility of the University of Kassel. This research infrastructure features a unique combination of a highly flexible DED-LB/M system (adAM-RD, ODeCon engineering GmbH, Kaiserslautern, Germany) and a high-performance liquid-metal X-ray source (MetalJet E1+ 160 kV, Excillum, Kista, Sweden), complemented by dedicated detectors enabling both radiographic imaging and X-ray diffraction analysis. For the investigations conducted in this study, only the DED-LB/M system of the facility was used. The DED-LB/M system operates with a 4 kW fiber laser (IPG YLS-2000-S2, IPG Photonics GmbH, Burbach, Germany) featuring a top-hat intensity profile and a wavelength of 1070 nm. Furthermore, the system was specifically designed with an open process chamber configuration to facilitate unobstructed X-ray access and to enable the flexible integration of complementary in-situ diagnostic and monitoring systems.
The diameter of the beam can be adjusted in the focal plane between 0.5 and 1.5 mm using a zoom optics system (HD Sonderoptiken für die Lasertechnik GmbH & Co. KG, Übach-Palenberg, Germany). The powder is fed into the process by a four-disk feeder (GTV PF4/4, GTV Verschleißschutz GmbH, Luckenbach, Germany), via a pneumatic powder switch, and delivered through a coaxial 6-jet nozzle (HIGHNO-13-9, HD Sonderoptiken für die Lasertechnik GmbH & Co. KG, Übach-Palenberg, Germany) with a standoff distance of 13 mm.
For the experiments presented in this paper, a constant spot diameter of 1.0 mm was selected. The laser was moved over the component at a constant speed of 10 mm/s. The powder used in this study was AISI 316L, with a particle size distribution ranging from 50 to 150 μm. The powder mass flow was maintained at a constant rate of 12 g/min, the carrier gas flow at 5 l/min, and the shielding gas flow at 9 l/min. High-purity argon (99.999 %) was used as both a carrier and a shielding gas to protect the melt pool from the atmosphere and reduce oxidation.
The experiments were designed using a simple geometry that allowed comprehensive observation with both camera systems. To clearly reveal the differences caused by table inclination, the structure was produced both with and without table inclination. For this purpose, a flat specimen consisting of ten adjacent tracks was manufactured on a stainless steel substrate plate. The process parameters are summarized in Table 1.
In order to provide the cameras with a better perspective of the process, the build plate was tilted for some experiments at an angle of 55° (see Fig. 1) to align the normal surface with the optical axes of the cameras.
2.2 Imaging system
To ensure a comprehensive observation, two cameras were used for the monitoring: one mid-wave infrared (MWIR) camera and one visual (VIS) RGB camera. The technical specifications of the cameras used are listed in Table 2.
Images in the visible spectrum were acquired using an RGB camera (ace 2 R PRO, Basler AG, Ahrensburg, Germany), equipped with a 50-mm lens (C23-5028-5 M-P, Basler AG, Ahrensburg, Germany) and a short-pass filter (900 nm) that protects the camera from laser radiation. The RGB camera was operated at 156 frames per second. Three individual images were captured successively with varying exposure times (19, 500, and 5000 μs), which were then merged into high dynamic range (HDR) images during the post-processing stage.
The MWIR imaging was performed with an infrared camera (ImageIR 8380 hp, InfraTec GmbH, Dresden, Germany), equipped with a 100-mm lens and an additional close-up optic. The image acquisition was carried out at a frame rate of 200 Hz. A fast rotating filter wheel equipped with four neutral-density filters was used during the experiments to enable HDR imaging with different integration times, allowing a temperature measurement range from 300 to 2000 °C black body temperature. The two cameras were used to record the entire build process.
Figure 2 shows the complete experimental setup at the LMD2 facility. The cameras were arranged to maximize the overlap between their fields of view (FOVs). Furthermore, all cameras were inclined by 59° ± 1° relative to the surface normal of the non-inclined build plate, resulting in a measurement distance of 50 cm ± 1 cm.
Two halogen spotlights were used to illuminate the process for visible-spectrum imaging. This was necessary because the intense visible radiation emitted by the melt pool makes it difficult to capture both the entire component and the melt pool in sufficient detail. The halogen spotlights (ELC-3, OSRAM GmbH, München, Germany) were operated at a power of 250 W each. As the radiation from the halogen spotlights is broadband and should not be detectable in the MWIR range, an additional short-pass filter (KG5, SCHOTT AG, Mainz, Germany) was placed in front of each spotlight. Since these filters are highly sensitive to heat and the spotlights generate substantial thermal load, a Plexiglass plate was inserted between each spotlight and filter. This plate absorbs the heat, is relatively inexpensive, and can be easily replaced after several experiments.
2.3 Image processing pipeline
Figure 3 illustrates the image processing pipeline of the proposed method. As illustrated, the DED-LB/M process is initially monitored, and then HDR images are produced and aligned in time. In parallel, a segmentation of the relevant regions is performed in the visual recordings. In the final step, the MWIR-, RGB-data and the \(\varepsilon \)-map are fused together. The specific methods used for each step of the workflow are described in detail in the following subsections.
2.3.1 High dynamic range and time synchronization
HDR imaging extends the dynamic range by combining images acquired with different exposure or integration times. In this work, HDR imaging was employed to cover a wider temperature range using the MWIR camera, and to clearly depict both the entire component and the melt pool in the visual spectrum using the RGB camera.
To generate the visual RGB HDR images, three individual exposures with exposure times of 19, 500, and 5000 μs were acquired in direct succession. These images were subsequently combined into an HDR image using the exposure fusion algorithm by Mertens et al. [31], implemented in Python using the OpenCV library. At the RGB camera frame rate of 156 fps, the available time per individual exposure is approximately 6410 μs. The longest selected exposure time of 5000 μs therefore remained below this limit while leaving a margin for camera readout and image transfer. Since three individual exposures were combined into one HDR image, the resulting RGB HDR image rate was approximately 52 Hz.
The exposure times were selected empirically to cover complementary intensity ranges of the process. The 19 μs exposure corresponds to the minimum exposure time of the camera and was used to avoid saturation in the hottest melt-pool region. The 5000 μs exposure was selected to capture lower-intensity component regions and the overall component geometry, while the melt pool and parts of the transition zone are overexposed. The 500 μs exposure was chosen as an intermediate compromise that provides sufficient contrast between the melt pool and the surrounding high-temperature transition region. The use of the individual exposure images for segmentation is described in Sect. 2.3.2.
For the creation of the MWIR HDR temperature images, four individual recordings were acquired with integration times of 212, 123, 88 and 402 μs. Each of these images was captured using a specific optical filter in combination with a neutral density filter KG3. The assignment of the respective integration times, calibration ranges and filters used, is shown in Table 3.
Conventional algorithms, such as the Mertens algorithm, cannot be used to combine the four images into a single HDR image because they account for varying exposure times but not for different optical filters. Therefore, the four raw images are combined with each other according to the manufacturer’s calibration. The images were not acquired simultaneously but sequentially, which may introduce errors. However, due to the low scan velocity and low process dynamics, only minor errors are expected. These errors are expected to be most significant at the transition from the melt pool to the transition zone or the solid component in the scan direction. Pixels that fall outside the valid calibration range defined by the manufacturer are skipped in the algorithm. If, after this procedure, any pixels in the HDR image remain without a valid value, they are finally assigned with NaN.
For synchronization, the frame in which the melt pool first became visible is identified in the complete recordings of each camera. This frame is designated as the starting frame and serves to temporally align the different imaging sequences. Once this common starting point was established for the cameras, a temporal linear interpolation of the image data was performed for the MWIR camera recordings. Because the MWIR data exhibited lower temporal variability than the RGB recordings, the MWIR images were interpolated to the RGB time points. To achieve this, the timestamps of the MWIR camera images were mapped to the time points of the RGB camera, so that synchronized HDR images were available for each desired moment. This approach enables a precise analysis and a temporally accurate comparison of the image data from both cameras.
2.3.2 Segmentation of RGB images
The raw RGB images were used for an approximate segmentation into three main regions: the melt pool, the transition zone, and the background. The segmentation was performed on the individual exposure images rather than on the fused RGB HDR image to retain direct control over saturation and contrast. The 5000 μs image was used to determine the outer boundary of the combined melt pool/transition zone region relative to the colder surrounding area, but not to segment the melt pool itself because the hottest region is overexposed. The 500 μs image was then used within this mask to separate the melt pool from the transition zone. The 19 μs image served as a short-exposure reference for the hottest melt pool region and was not used as the primary image for defining the final emissivity-mask boundaries.
The images were first converted to a grayscale and normalized to an intensity range of 0 to 1. Initial segmentation of the combined melt pool/transition zone region was performed on the 5000 μs image using a normalized intensity threshold of 0.85. This image provides sufficient signal from the colder component regions and was therefore used to determine the outer boundary of the thermally affected region. Since the hottest regions are overexposed at this exposure time, it was not used to separate the melt pool from the transition zone. Morphological closing with a disk-shaped structuring element of radius 3 pixels was applied to fill small holes, followed by morphological opening with the same radius to remove small isolated objects such as spatters.
Subsequently, the 500 μs image was used within the previously identified outer mask to separate the melt pool from the transition zone by applying a higher normalized intensity threshold of 0.9. The term transition zone is used here in an operational image-processing sense and denotes the visually distinguishable high-temperature region surrounding the melt pool to which an intermediate emissivity value is assigned. It should not be interpreted as an exact thermodynamic liquid–solid boundary. Candidate values for both segmentation thresholds were evaluated from 0.6 to 1.0 in increments of 0.05. This variation was used as a qualitative check of the sensitivity of the segmentation masks and to identify threshold values that yielded stable and visually plausible results for representative images, particularly with respect to the continuity of the melt pool and transition zone masks. The resulting masks were combined, and the largest connected region was retained and further refined using morphological operations. The final thresholds and morphological radii were then selected manually based on visual assessment of representative images from different tracks and process times.
The emissivity values for these regions were selected based on literature values and are interpreted as effective region-wise emissivities. For the experiments with the inclined build plate, \(\varepsilon \_{\text {melt pool}} = 0.22\) was used for the melt pool [32], \(\varepsilon \_{\text {transition}} = 0.26\) for the transition zone, and \(\varepsilon \_{\text {background}} = 0.4\) for the remaining areas, i.e. solidified tracks and the substrate plate [11, 13, 33,34,35]. For the experiments without build plate inclination, the melt pool emissivity was kept at \(\varepsilon \_{\text {melt pool}} = 0.22\) [32], while effective emissivities of \(\varepsilon \_{\text {transition}} = 0.50\) and \(\varepsilon \_{\text {background}} = 0.80\) were used [11, 13, 33,34,35]. These adjusted values were selected empirically based on the apparent RGB transition regions and the consistency of the corrected temperature profile with the expected solidification plateau of AISI 316L. The comparison with the solidification plateau was therefore used as an internal physical-consistency criterion for selecting effective emissivity parameters and should not be interpreted as an independent validation of the absolute temperature accuracy. They should therefore be understood as configuration-specific effective parameters rather than independently measured material emissivities. To avoid sharp discontinuities, sigmoid functions were used to smooth the emissivity transitions. The smoothing widths were 5 pixels and 30 pixels for the inclined configuration and 40 pixels and 60 pixels for the non-inclined configuration for the melt pool/transition and transition/background interfaces, respectively. The sigmoid widths are numerical post-processing parameters used to regularize the emissivity map and to avoid abrupt jumps in the corrected temperature field. While a gradual transition is physically plausible, the selected widths should not be interpreted as directly measured physical transition widths.
2.3.3 Fusion of RGB and MWIR images
Prior to the measurements, specific images of the calibration target were acquired for the fusion of the individual RGB and MWIR images. A detailed description of the target can be found in Schramm et al. [36]. Using these calibration images, the intrinsic distortions of both cameras, such as lens distortion and differences in focal length, were determined. In addition, an initial homography matrix was calculated, enabling a projective transformation between the image planes of the MWIR and RGB cameras. The registration workflow is illustrated in Fig. 4. It is important to note that this homography matrix is valid only for a specific plane in space [37].
Since the actual measurement setup at the LMD2 facility differs from the plane captured during the calibration images, determining an exact homography matrix for the fusion based solely on the calibration images was challenging. Therefore, the calculated matrix was used as an initial estimate and was iteratively refined using the measurement images. For this purpose, RGB and MWIR images were superimposed, and the homography matrix was adjusted until corresponding process features were spatially aligned. In addition to visual assessment, the melt pool center was segmented in both the RGB and MWIR recordings and tracked over time. The remaining registration deviation was quantified as the Euclidean distance between the melt pool center positions in the transformed MWIR image and the corresponding RGB image.
The projective transformation establishes a projective relation between the perspectives of the MWIR and RGB cameras, compensating for differences in angle of view, position, and scale [37]. In the present optical configuration, the depth of field of the MWIR camera is limited to only a few millimeters. Therefore, the image fusion was approximated by a planar homographic transformation, which is currently the most suitable approach for the available image data. This approximation is appropriate for the observed near-planar component region, but local registration errors may occur for height deviations outside the reference plane. Following this transformation, the MWIR image is geometrically mapped onto the RGB image plane so that corresponding features in both modalities are spatially matched. During this process, the spatial resolution of the MWIR image is simultaneously resampled to match that of the RGB images, as bilinear interpolation is inherently part of the transformation operation. This ensures that subsequent region-based analyses are performed on a common pixel grid, allowing for direct comparison and integration of data from both imaging modalities.
The projective transformation enabled not only the superimposition of the RGB and MWIR images, but also the assignment of the region-specific emissivity values to the corresponding segments in the MWIR images.
First, the temperature values were converted into spectral radiance L according to Planck’s law. For this conversion, a lookup table tailored to the specific spectral and temperature range of the MWIR camera was created beforehand. This lookup table was then used to transform the values of the temperature into radiance. Each pixel of the MWIR images was subsequently assigned the corresponding emissivity value. Since the lower calibration limit was set to 573.15 K, ambient radiation was not considered in the calculation of the corrected radiance, as its influence is negligible. In the next step, the corrected radiance \(L\_{i,j}\) was calculated using Eq. (1), in which \(L\_{i,j}^{\text {meas}}\) is the radiance corresponding to the measured temperature (assuming emissivity \(\varepsilon = 1\)) for pixel (i, j), and \(\varepsilon \_{i,j}\) is the emissivity assigned to pixel (i, j). Finally, the result was converted back into a temperature using the lookup table.
$$\begin{aligned} L\_{i,j} = \frac{L\_{i,j}^{\text {meas}}}{\varepsilon \_{i,j}} \end{aligned}$$
