\#\# 3 Results and discussion

\#\#\# 3\.1 Processed components

Six experimental runs were conducted using identical process parameters to assess repeatability and to investigate the applicability of the workflow for two different build plate configurations\. Three components were manufactured with a build plate inclination of 55°\, and three were manufactured without inclination \(0°\)\. Within each configuration\, the components showed a consistent appearance\, with no pronounced differences in morphology or surface quality\, indicating stable processing conditions for the selected parameter set\. All components were processed using the settings described in Sect\. 2\.

Representative examples of both configurations are shown in Fig\. 5\.

The side views show flat and uniform structures without pronounced elevations or depressions\. The inclined build plate was used to improve the viewing perspective of the cameras\, but it also affects the resulting component geometry\. Compared with the non\-inclined configuration\, the inclined setup led to a flatter geometry\, consistent with the broader and shallower melt pool expected under inclined processing conditions \[38\]\. A quantitative analysis of the influence of build plate inclination on track height and width was not performed within the scope of this work\.

\#\#\# 3\.2 Metallography

To investigate the influence of the build plate inclination on the geometry and microstructure of the coatings produced by DED\-LB\/M\, cross\-sections of two representative samples were compared\. The cross\-sections of the coatings manufactured at 55° and 0° inclination are shown in Fig\. 6\, with the 55° sample displayed in Fig\. 6a and the 0° sample in Fig\. 6b\.

The cross\-sections reveal significant differences in the resulting coating geometry\. The coating produced at 0° exhibits a greater layer height of 1\.012 mm and a comparatively lower dilution depth of 0\.27 mm\. In contrast\, the coating manufactured at 55° shows a reduced layer height of 0\.537 mm\, but a significantly increased dilution depth of 0\.58 mm\. This behavior is attributed to the altered interaction between the powder stream\, laser beam\, and melt pool caused by the inclined substrate position\. Due to the inclination\, not the entire powder stream reaches the melt pool\, resulting in a reduced powder feed into the process\. Consequently\, the deposited material volume and the resulting melt pool volume are reduced\. At the same time\, the laser beam has a more direct interaction with the substrate surface\, leading to increased energy coupling into the base material and promoting the formation of a deeper melt pool\. As a result\, both the temperature gradients and cooling rates within the melt pool increase\. The higher cooling rates and more pronounced temperature gradients are mainly attributed to the enhanced heat dissipation through the substrate\. Compared with the 0° configuration\, a larger fraction of the melt pool is surrounded by the substrate in the 55° configuration\, allowing heat to be transferred more efficiently into the base material\.

The metallographic observations qualitatively indicate differences in the resulting microstructures between the two build plate configurations\. The coating produced at 0° appears to exhibit a coarser cellular\-dendritic microstructure with larger structural spacings\, whereas the coating manufactured at 55° shows a finer columnar\-dendritic solidification structure\. In addition\, the microstructure of the 0° sample appears less directionally oriented\. These observations are consistent with different thermal conditions during processing\. However\, no quantitative grain\-size or dendrite\-arm\-spacing analysis was performed\. Therefore\, the metallographic results are used here as qualitative supporting evidence and not as a quantitative validation of the corrected temperature fields\.

\#\#\# 3\.3 Recorded images

The cameras recorded the entire processing sequence\. For clarity\, the processing steps are first discussed using one representative measurement with the inclined build plate\. A corresponding centerline temperature profile for the non\-inclined configuration is added later for comparison\. Figure 7a–d shows representative raw images captured by the MWIR camera during the beginning of the first track\. All white areas correspond to regions with NaN values\, as these are outside the camera’s calibration range\. It is evident that\, for the analysis of almost the entire cooling process\, fusion into an HDR image is essential\, as none of the individual images covers the complete dynamic range\. In Fig\. 7c and d\, small circular features can also be observed outside the melt pool\. These correspond to hot spatters ejected during processing\.

In the MWIR HDR image \(Fig\. 7e\)\, the increased dynamic range is visible\. However\, the substrate plate\, the nozzle\, and similar components are not visible\, as their temperatures are below the lower measurement limit of 573\.15 K\. These temperatures cannot be measured with the configuration used\, as the neutral density filters do not permit sufficient radiation in this range\. The basic HDR algorithm yields acceptable results\, but distinct discontinuities remain\, particularly at the boundaries between neighboring calibration ranges\. This effect is especially pronounced at higher temperatures\. More sophisticated HDR algorithms could improve the quality at these calibration boundaries\, but typically require substantially more extensive calibration effort \[39\]\.

Figure 8a–c shows representative raw images captured by the RGB camera at the end of the first track\. In the image with the shortest exposure time\, the melt pool is particularly well depicted\. In the medium\-exposure image\, the transition zone is clearly visible\. While spatter can occur during the process\, it is not present in this particular frame\. In the image with the longest exposure time\, the melt pool is overexposed\. However\, regions such as the substrate plate\, weld tracks\, and nozzle outside the region of interest \(ROI\) are well resolved and clearly identifiable\. Figure 8d displays the resulting RGB HDR image\. Although spatters can occur during the process and are visible in some individual frames\, they are not present in the shown HDR image due to the selected recording moment\. If spatters are present\, they may appear partially doubled and elongated in the HDR image due to the combination of the medium and long exposure times\. Nevertheless\, the melt pool\, transition zone\, and weld tracks are clearly depicted\. Laser\-induced artifacts are also visible\, the red spot in the image can be attributed to the laser\.

\#\#\# 3\.4 Image fusion and validation

The regions\, i\.e\. melt pool\, transition zone\, and background\, within the raw images acquired by the RGB camera were segmented using image processing techniques\, enabling the assignment of appropriate emissivity values to each region\. These segmented images were then used to calculate the corresponding emissivity map for each frame\, as described in Sect\. 2\.3\.3\. By combining the emissivity map with the HDR temperature field\, a corrected temperature field was obtained\. To illustrate this process\, Fig\. 9 presents the results for the first track of a representative component with 55° build plate inclination\.

In Fig\. 9a\, the RGB HDR image is shown\, while Fig\. 9c shows the calculated smoothed emissivity map\. By combining the emissivity map with the HDR temperature field shown in Fig\. 9b\, the corrected temperature field in Fig\. 9d was computed\. To assess the spatial registration\, the RGB and MWIR images are overlaid in Fig\. 9e\.

The registration accuracy was additionally evaluated by comparing the melt pool center positions in the RGB and transformed MWIR images over time\. The comparison showed for the inclined build plate a mean center\-position deviation of approximately 3 pixels\, corresponding to approximately 0\.1 mm on the RGB image grid\. This value characterizes the residual alignment error of the melt pool position after transformation\. Its influence on the corrected temperature field is expected to be most relevant near the boundaries between emissivity regions\, where small spatial offsets can change the assigned emissivity\. In contrast\, pixels located well inside one emissivity region are less sensitive to such residual registration errors\.

The planar homography assumes that the relevant image features lie approximately in one plane\. This is a limitation for DED\-LB\/M components with pronounced height variations\, which can cause local mapping errors between RGB and MWIR images\. In the present study\, this effect is expected to be limited due to the comparatively flat single\-layer geometry\. However\, small local registration errors may still occur near track edges and emissivity\-region boundaries and can locally affect the corrected temperature field\.

For comparison\, a line through the melt pool center was selected in one frame of the inclined build plate configuration\. This is shown in Fig\. 10a\. The line of interest is indicated in the RGB image\, where the melt pool boundaries can be identified\. Figure 10b shows the corresponding temperature and emissivity profiles\.

It is evident that the temperature curve for \\\(\\varepsilon \= 1\\\) shows a distinct solidification plateau\, which slightly decreases behind the laser \(scan direction 18\.5 \- 20\.5 mm\)\. This decrease occurs because the emissivity was assumed to be constant \(\\\(\\varepsilon \= 1\\\)\)\, which is not fully representative of the local surface state\. Compared with the one\-point correction using a constant emissivity of \\\(\\varepsilon \= 0\.26\\\)\, the region\-specific correction yields higher temperatures in the melt pool region and exhibits a shorter solidification plateau \(scan direction 20\.0 \- 20\.5 mm\) followed by an exponential temperature decay\. The one\-point correction shows a longer apparent plateau\, indicating that a spatially constant emissivity can influence the apparent width and shape of the solidification plateau\. Consequently\, local emissivity variations affect the interpretation of the solidification behavior \[12\]\. Methods such as temperature\-emissivity separation \(TES\) could be helpful in this context \[12\]\.

To assess the applicability of the correction workflow under a different observation and process geometry\, the same centerline evaluation was performed for a representative experiment without build plate inclination\. The corresponding profile is shown in Fig\. 11\. Similar to the inclined configuration\, the corrected temperature profile \(red curve\) exhibits a pronounced solidification plateau in the expected temperature range of AISI 316L and a physically plausible cooling behavior\. This comparison should be interpreted as an applicability check for the non\-inclined configuration rather than as a full parametric validation\, since the material\, layer number\, and main process parameters were kept constant\. In contrast\, the one\-point correction using a constant emissivity of \\\(\\varepsilon \= 0\.50\\\) \(green curve\) clearly underestimates the melt pool temperature\.

Depending on the selected frame and position\, local temperatures below the nominal solidification plateau may occur between the melt pool maximum and the plateau region\. These deviations may originate from measurement uncertainties\, residual registration errors\, local emissivity variations\, powder interaction\, or limitations of the present region\-wise emissivity model\. Qualitatively similar temperature\-profile shapes in uncorrected or single\-emissivity thermographic evaluations have also been reported in previous studies \[9\, 40\]\. A possible thermophysical explanation is local undercooling\, where the liquid phase remains metastable below the equilibrium solidification temperature until nucleation starts\. However\, distinguishing such thermophysical effects from apparent effects caused by emissivity variations would require further investigation\, for example using high\-fidelity simulations and complementary spectral approaches such as temperature\-emissivity separation\. These methods can provide additional insight\, but also require careful calibration and are subject to uncertainty\. Configuration\-specific effective emissivity values and smoothing widths were required\, indicating that the present three\-zone emissivity model depends on the observation and process geometry\. In addition\, slightly different temperature profiles may result from different choices of the width and steepness of the sigmoid transition between emissivity regions\, particularly near region boundaries\.

The differences in the extent of the plateau\-like region within the solidification interval in the corrected temperature profiles can also be related to the observed microstructural differences\. The plateau\-like region may be associated with the formation of initial nuclei after sufficient undercooling\, followed by subsequent grain growth\. Compared with the non\-inclined configuration\, the 55° configuration shows a shorter solidification interval along the scan direction\. Assuming a constant scan speed\, this corresponds to a shorter dwell time within the solidification temperature range\. As a result\, the undercooling required for nucleation is reached and exceeded more rapidly\, causing nucleation to dominate over the further growth of existing nuclei\. This promotes the formation of a finer columnar\-dendritic microstructure with reduced structural spacings\.

In contrast\, the plateau\-like region is more pronounced for the non\-inclined 0° configuration\, indicating a longer dwell time within the solidification temperature range\. Consequently\, more time is available for the growth of already formed nuclei\, causing grain growth to dominate over nucleation\. As a result\, larger grains and a coarser cellular\-dendritic microstructure with larger structural spacings are formed\, which is consistent with the observations in the corresponding metallographic cross\-section\.

In addition to the centerline evaluation for the inclined configuration\, an edge\-oriented line profile was considered to assess the behavior of the emissivity correction in peripheral track regions\, where cooling rates\, surface roughness\, and oxidation conditions may differ from the center of the melt pool\. The corresponding profile is shown in Fig\. 12\.

These regions are more challenging for the present three\-zone emissivity model\, because small segmentation or registration errors can shift pixels between emissivity regions and therefore locally affect the corrected temperature\.

The edge\-oriented profile exhibits a lower maximum temperature than the centerline profile\, while still showing a pronounced solidification plateau\. This indicates that the emissivity correction remains physically plausible in the peripheral track region\. However\, the edge region is more sensitive to segmentation\, smoothing\, and registration uncertainties\, because the line crosses emissivity\-region boundaries over a short spatial distance\.

To investigate the influence of position within the inclined configuration\, seven different time points were selected for the first track\, as shown in Fig\. 13\. These points are distributed such that edge regions are also included\. The maximum temperature remains highly consistent across all points\. Furthermore\, the cooling after the solidification plateau becomes slower as time progresses\, which can be attributed to the overall heating of the component\.

In the region of the solidification plateau\, various effects become apparent\. For points \\\(t\_\{1\}\\\)\, \\\(t\_\{4\}\\\)\, and \\\(t\_\{5\}\\\)\, the selected emissivity in this range appears to be too high\. At points \\\(t\_\{2\}\\\)\, \\\(t\_\{3\}\\\)\, and \\\(t\_\{7\}\\\)\, the plateau shows a slightly undulating rather than a strictly horizontal behavior\. This can be explained by the assumption of constant emissivity within each region\, which does not account for local variations\. For example\, the formation of oxide islands can locally alter the emissivity and thus affect the corrected temperature values \[40\]\. In addition\, local cooling dynamics could also contribute to deviations within the solidification plateau\.

To further investigate the influence of the different tracks in the inclined configuration\, an analysis was carried out to determine whether differences can be observed between individual tracks for a measurement point along the scan direction \(see Fig\. 14\)\. The measurement point remains at the same position along the scan direction and is shifted only with respect to the hatching direction from track to track\. The exponential temperature decrease becomes progressively slower with an increasing number of printed tracks\, as the component heats up continuously due to the ongoing thermal input\. Furthermore\, differences in the maximum\-temperature region are visible between individual tracks\, which can be attributed to variations in melt pool dynamics\. In the region of the solidification plateau\, both flat and undulating plateaus occur\, as also observed in Fig\. 13\.

\#\#\# 3\.5 Limitations and sensitivity analysis

It should be stressed that the expected solidification interval of AISI 316L was used as an internal physical\-consistency criterion for assessing the effective emissivity assignment\. Consequently\, the agreement with the solidification plateau does not constitute an independent metrological validation of the absolute temperature accuracy\. No independent reference temperature measurement with known local emissivity was available during the DED\-LB\/M process\. Therefore\, the corrected temperature fields should not be interpreted as fully validated absolute temperature values\. Rather\, the presented correction approach improves the physical consistency of the thermographic evaluation compared with the assumption of a globally fixed emissivity\.

In the following\, two aspects are distinguished\: first\, limitations related to the model assumptions of the emissivity correction\, and second\, the sensitivity of the corrected temperature field to selected uncertain input parameters\. The Monte Carlo\-based analysis therefore quantifies parameter\-induced variations within the chosen correction framework\, but does not represent a full metrological uncertainty budget\.

A central model limitation is the simplified three\-zone emissivity description\. Constant emissivity values were assigned to the melt pool\, transition zone\, and background\, although the actual emissivity in DED\-LB\/M depends on temperature\, phase state\, wavelength\, surface roughness\, oxidation\, viewing angle\, and temporal process dynamics\. In particular\, the effective viewing angle can vary spatially due to the off\-axis camera configuration and\, for the inclined experiments\, due to the build plate inclination\. The selected emissivity values should therefore be understood as effective region\-wise parameters rather than locally exact material properties\.

The RGB\-based transition zone should also be interpreted as an optically defined emissivity region rather than as an exact thermodynamic liquid–solid boundary\. A direct segmentation based on MWIR temperature thresholds was not used because the apparent MWIR temperature field is initially evaluated assuming \\\(\\varepsilon \= 1\\\) and is therefore biased by the unknown local emissivity\. Using solidus or liquidus thresholds before emissivity correction would introduce a circular dependency\. Instead\, the segmented emissivity regions were derived from RGB images acquired with different exposure times\. In the present workflow\, the 19 μs image served as a short\-exposure reference for the hottest melt pool region\, the 500 μs image was used to separate the melt pool from the transition zone\, and the 5000 μs image was used to determine the outer extent of the combined melt pool\/transition zone region\. As a consistency check\, the apparent melt pool masks obtained from the 19 and 500 μs images were compared quantitatively and showed comparable overlap\, with a mean Intersection over Union \(IoU\) of 0\.82 and a mean Dice coefficient of 0\.89\. Alternative exposure settings\, for example 50\, 1000\, and 5000 μs\, would mainly affect the intensity distribution and saturation behavior\. If the same thresholds were applied\, the segmented emissivity regions could change\, especially near region boundaries\. If the thresholds were re\-adjusted and the relevant regions remained unsaturated and sufficiently visible\, the main spatial features would be expected to remain qualitatively similar\. Nevertheless\, local changes in emissivity assignment and therefore in the corrected temperature field cannot be excluded\.

The sigmoid smoothing of the emissivity transitions was introduced to avoid discontinuous changes between adjacent emissivity regions\. This is physically motivated by the fact that surface state\, phase fraction\, oxidation\, roughness\, and apparent optical response do not change discontinuously at a single pixel during solidification and cooling\. However\, the selected smoothing widths are empirical regularization parameters rather than directly measured physical transition widths\. They were chosen to avoid abrupt emissivity\-induced temperature jumps and to obtain physically plausible profiles\. Their influence was included in the Monte Carlo\-based sensitivity analysis by varying the smoothing widths within predefined ranges\.

To estimate the influence of selected input parameters within the proposed correction framework\, a simplified Monte Carlo\-based sensitivity analysis with 500 samples was performed for the first track of each configuration\. The analysis should be interpreted as a sensitivity study rather than as a complete metrological uncertainty budget\. The region\-wise emissivity values\, the widths of the smoothed transition regions\, and the residual registration offset were varied within predefined uniform perturbation ranges listed in Table 4\. These ranges were selected as plausible bounds around the effective baseline parameters and were not derived from statistically identified probability distributions\. For each sample\, the corrected temperature field was recalculated and compared pixel\-wise with the baseline correction obtained using the nominal parameter set\. The reported values therefore represent parameter\-induced deviations relative to this baseline correction and not errors with respect to an independent reference temperature\.

The emissivity ranges were chosen to cover plausible variations around the literature\-based and empirically adjusted effective emissivity values used in the baseline correction\. The comparatively broad background ranges account for the uncertainty of the effective emissivity of solidified tracks\, substrate material\, and surrounding solid regions\. The sigmoid\-width ranges reflect the empirical nature of the smoothing parameters and cover narrower as well as broader transitions between neighboring emissivity regions\. The registration shift range of \[− 5\, 5\] pixels was selected as a conservative bound based on the observed residual RGB–MWIR registration deviations\. Thus\, the analysis quantifies the sensitivity of the corrected temperature field to plausible parameter perturbations\, but does not provide a full uncertainty propagation\.

The selected parameter ranges were intended to represent plausible bounds for a simplified sensitivity estimate and should not be interpreted as a full metrological uncertainty budget\. The deviation metrics were evaluated within a fixed ROI around the process zone\, including regions with measurable temperatures above the lower calibration limit of the MWIR camera\. The median and 95th percentile values were calculated within each segmented region and averaged over all Monte Carlo samples\. The relative deviations refer to the corresponding baseline\-corrected temperature values\. The resulting parameter\-induced deviations are summarized in Table 5\.

The Monte Carlo\-based sensitivity analysis shows that the parameter\-induced deviations of the corrected temperature field depend strongly on the segmented region and on the build plate configuration\. The melt pool region shows comparable median deviations for both configurations\, whereas the transition zone\, i\.e\. the optically defined region associated with the solidification plateau\, exhibits large P95 deviations\, especially for the non\-inclined configuration\. This indicates that the plateau region is particularly sensitive to the selected effective emissivity and to the smoothing of the neighboring emissivity transitions\. For the 55° configuration\, the largest deviations occur in the background region\, which can be attributed to the broad range assigned to the effective background emissivity and to local boundary effects\. Overall\, the sensitivity of the corrected temperature field is mainly governed by emissivity assumptions and region\-boundary definitions rather than being uniformly distributed across the temperature field\. Therefore\, the reported values should be interpreted as parameter\-induced deviations relative to the baseline correction and not as a full metrological uncertainty budget\.

Numerical process simulations could provide additional support for interpreting the measured temperature fields and estimating process\-dependent effective emissivity or radiative parameters\. However\, such models introduce their own uncertainties through assumptions on material data\, boundary conditions\, heat\-source description\, powder interaction\, and calibration strategy\. Consequently\, model\-derived parameters require careful validation before they can be used to support quantitative temperature assessment\. Therefore\, numerical modeling is considered a valuable complementary tool for future work\, but not a substitute for dedicated emissivity\-aware measurement or validation\.

The utilized setup is a laboratory configuration with open optical access and external illumination\. Thus\, the direct transferability of the presented results to industrial DED\-LB\/M systems is limited\. However\, several methodological elements of the workflow are transferable in principle\, including synchronized RGB\/MWIR acquisition\, geometric image fusion\, RGB\-based region segmentation\, and region\-wise emissivity assignment\. In contrast\, several parameters are setup\-specific and would require recalibration for an industrial implementation\. These include the camera arrangement and homography\, illumination conditions\, RGB exposure times\, segmentation thresholds\, effective emissivity values\, and the smoothing widths between emissivity regions\. The additional non\-inclined data set provides an applicability check under a different observation and process geometry\, but it does not constitute a full parametric validation of the method\. The material\, layer number\, laser power\, scan speed\, and powder feed rate were kept constant\. Further studies with varied process parameters\, materials\, geometries\, and more industrially representative optical access are therefore required to assess the robustness of the workflow across a broader process window\.

\#\# 4 Conclusions and outlook

A workflow for deriving emissivity\-corrected temperature fields in laser beam directed energy deposition \(DED\-LB\/M\) was introduced\. The process was monitored using high dynamic range imaging with both an MWIR camera and an RGB camera\, enabling an extended temperature range and improved visibility of the component and melt pool region\.

By fusing the MWIR and RGB data through a projective transformation\, the segmented RGB regions were transferred to the thermal images and used to assign region\-specific effective emissivity values\. This enabled the calculation of corrected temperature fields that were more physically consistent than those obtained using a globally fixed emissivity assumption\. In particular\, the region\-wise correction better accounts for the spatially varying optical and thermal conditions in the melt pool\, transition zone\, and background region\.

The corrected temperature profiles showed pronounced plateau\-like regions close to the expected solidification interval of AISI 316L for both inclined and non\-inclined build plate configurations\. This supports the physical plausibility of the workflow for the investigated flat single\-layer geometries\. However\, this comparison should be interpreted as a plausibility check rather than as an independent validation of absolute temperature accuracy\, since no independent reference temperature measurement with known local emissivity was available\. The different extents of the plateau\-like regions are qualitatively consistent with the observed microstructural differences\. Shorter plateau\-like regions were associated with finer columnar\-dendritic structures and reduced structural spacings\, whereas more pronounced plateau\-like regions were observed together with coarser cellular\-dendritic structures\.

A simplified Monte Carlo\-based sensitivity analysis showed that the corrected temperatures are mainly affected by the chosen emissivity values and by the definition of the emissivity regions\. The largest effects occurred in different regions depending on the build plate configuration\: in the transition zone near the solidification plateau for the 0° configuration and in the background region for the 55° configuration\.

The quantitative interpretation and transferability of the corrected temperature fields remain limited by the simplified static emissivity model\, the RGB\-threshold\-based segmentation\, empirical smoothing widths\, and residual registration uncertainties\.

Future work should therefore focus on transferring the approach to more industrially representative DED\-LB\/M configurations and on replacing the static region\-wise emissivity assignment with spatially and temporally resolved emissivity models\. In addition\, high\-fidelity process simulations and temperature\-emissivity separation approaches could provide complementary support for further evaluating the corrected temperature fields and distinguishing true thermophysical effects from apparent emissivity\-related artifacts\. Dedicated validation experiments with independent temperature references would be required to quantify the absolute temperature accuracy of the proposed correction approach\. Overall\, the presented workflow provides a practical basis for combining visual segmentation and infrared thermography for emissivity\-aware thermal process monitoring in metal additive manufacturing\.

records.title: Effect of Micro-Structure and Mechanical Properties on 309L Austenitic Stainless Steel Deposition by Cold Metal Transfer Wire-Arc Additive Manufacturing
records.abstract: Wire-arc additive manufacturing based on cold metal transfer (CMT-WAAM) is a high-precision forming technology suitable for thin-wall stainless steel parts, yet the unclear correlations between linear energy density, forming stability, microstructure evolution and mechanical anisotropy restrict the precision forming and performance control of 309L austenitic stainless steel components. Aiming at the scientific problems of end collapse defects and mechanical performance anisotropy in multi-layer thin-wall WAAM forming of 309L stainless steel, this study systematically explores the regulation mechanism of process parameters and deposition path on forming quality, microstructure characteristics and mechanical properties. The optimal single-track forming process window (wire-feeding speed of 5 m/min, welding speed of 3 mm/s) for 309L deposits is determined using single-track single-layer experiments. Compared with unidirectional deposition, the reciprocating deposition path effectively balances inter-layer temperature field distribution, solves the end collapse problem of multi-layer thin-wall structures, and controls the collapse height within 5 mm after 35 layers of continuous deposition. The variation of linear energy density is the core factor dominating microstructure evolution and performance difference: with an increase in linear energy density, the retained delta ferrite in the matrix transforms from a discrete vermicular to continuous skeletal structure, and austenite grains are significantly coarsened. In terms of mechanical properties, the longitudinal tensile performance of the deposits is stable and less affected by heat input, while the improvement of inter-layer metallurgical bonding quality significantly improves the transverse tensile strength and elongation, effectively weakening the mechanical anisotropy of the formed parts. Meanwhile, grain coarsening and the reduction of delta ferrite content led to a gradual decrease in the average Vickers hardness of the deposits. This study reveals the inherent process–structure–performance correlations of CMT-WAAM formed 309L austenitic stainless steel, clarifies the key mechanism for suppressing forming defects and regulating anisotropic performance, and provides theoretical and technical support for the high-quality forming and engineering application of stainless steel WAAM manufacturing and component repair.
records.summary: This study investigates cold metal transfer wire-arc additive manufacturing (CMT-WAAM) of 309L austenitic stainless steel thin walls, targeting end-collapse defects and mechanical anisotropy in multi-layer deposition. Using 22 single-track single-layer trials, the authors identified an optimal process window of 5 m/min wire-feeding speed and 3 mm/s welding speed, then built ~40 mm walls (35 layers) at four linear energy densities from 348.40 to 824.47 J/mm with inter-layer temperature held at 200 °C. A reciprocating deposition path balanced inter-layer heat and limited end collapse to within 5 mm after 35 layers, whereas unidirectional deposition produced severe end collapse. Increasing linear energy density coarsened austenite grains and shifted retained delta ferrite from discrete vermicular to continuous skeletal morphology. Longitudinal tensile strength stayed near 550 MPa and elongation at 41–45%, while transverse strength rose from 495 to 581 MPa and elongation from 33% to 50% with increasing heat input, attributed mainly to improved inter-layer metallurgical bonding; average Vickers hardness fell from 185.5 to 168.0 HV.
records.why_it_matters: For thin-wall 309L CMT-WAAM, switching from unidirectional to reciprocating deposition is a low-cost path-strategy change that suppresses end collapse, while raising linear energy density trades matrix hardness for stronger inter-layer bonding and reduced transverse anisotropy.

Abstract
Wire-arc additive manufacturing based on cold metal transfer (CMT-WAAM) is a high-precision forming technology suitable for thin-wall stainless steel parts, yet the unclear correlations between linear energy density, forming stability, microstructure evolution and mechanical anisotropy restrict the precision forming and performance control of 309L austenitic stainless steel components. Aiming at the scientific problems of end collapse defects and mechanical performance anisotropy in multi-layer thin-wall WAAM forming of 309L stainless steel, this study systematically explores the regulation mechanism of process parameters and deposition path on forming quality, microstructure characteristics and mechanical properties. The optimal single-track forming process window (wire-feeding speed of 5 m/min, welding speed of 3 mm/s) for 309L deposits is determined using single-track single-layer experiments. Compared with unidirectional deposition, the reciprocating deposition path effectively balances inter-layer temperature field distribution, solves the end collapse problem of multi-layer thin-wall structures, and controls the collapse height within 5 mm after 35 layers of continuous deposition. The variation of linear energy density is the core factor dominating microstructure evolution and performance difference: with an increase in linear energy density, the retained delta ferrite in the matrix transforms from a discrete vermicular to continuous skeletal structure, and austenite grains are significantly coarsened. In terms of mechanical properties, the longitudinal tensile performance of the deposits is stable and less affected by heat input, while the improvement of inter-layer metallurgical bonding quality significantly improves the transverse tensile strength and elongation, effectively weakening the mechanical anisotropy of the formed parts. Meanwhile, grain coarsening and the reduction of delta ferrite content led to a gradual decrease in the average Vickers hardness of the deposits. This study reveals the inherent process–structure–performance correlations of CMT-WAAM formed 309L austenitic stainless steel, clarifies the key mechanism for suppressing forming defects and regulating anisotropic performance, and provides theoretical and technical support for the high-quality forming and engineering application of stainless steel WAAM manufacturing and component repair.
1. Introduction
Wire-arc additive manufacturing (WAAM) adopts electric arc as the welding/metal-transfer process and realizes near-net-shape forming of components by layer-by-layer deposition of metal wires. Compared with laser-based and electron beam-based additive manufacturing technologies, WAAM possesses outstanding advantages of high material utilization rate, short manufacturing cycle, low equipment cost and high deposition efficiency up to several kilograms per hour [1,2]. These merits make WAAM particularly suitable for the rapid fabrication and repair of large and complex metallic components, and it has been widely applied in aerospace, marine engineering and energy equipment fields in recent years [3,4].
Cold metal transfer (CMT) is an advanced short-circuit welding technology that realizes droplet transfer using wire reciprocating motion, enabling precise low-heat-input deposition with low spatter, minimal deformation and excellent process stability [5,6]. Widely applied in nuclear and hydraulic equipment owing to superior corrosion and high-temperature resistance, 309L austenitic stainless steel is highly heat-sensitive, and its thin walls are prone to thermal deformation, grain coarsening and collapse defects during wire-arc additive manufacturing (WAAM) [7,8]. Compared with TIG, plasma and laser-arc welding, CMT avoids the excessive heat accumulation of conventional arc processes and the high cost and poor adaptability of laser-arc hybrid technology. Its intermittent heat input stabilizes the molten pool and suppresses forming defects and microstructure deterioration, making CMT optimal for high-quality WAAM of 309L thin-wall structures. Process parameters critically govern its molten pool behavior, microstructure evolution and final mechanical properties [9,10].
Extensive investigations have been conducted on the WAAM of austenitic stainless steels in recent years. Previous studies have demonstrated that heat input level exerts a significant influence on the forming accuracy and microstructure-mechanical properties of WAAM components [11,12]. Chen et al. [13] examined the microstructure and mechanical anisotropy of wire-arc additively manufactured austenitic stainless steels (304, 308L, 316L) using EBSD and 60 tensile tests across five orientations and two surface conditions, with DIC employed to capture stress–strain responses. Zheng et al. [14] studied the cyclic behavior of wire-arc additively manufactured stainless-steel shear plates for seismic energy dissipation, showing that WAAM specimens matched hot-rolled counterparts in energy absorption; topology-optimized plates achieved superior stiffness and dissipation, and a validated hysteretic model was established. Kannan et al. [15] fabricated 321 steel by wire-arc additive manufacturing with equiaxed, columnar and elongated grains (3.6–5.9 FN ferrite), achieving higher hardness and tensile strength than conventional 321 steel; although properties declined from room temperature to 900 °C, the WAAM alloy retained 135 ± 7 MPa versus 108 ± 6 MPa, with serrated yielding at 600 °C due to dynamic strain aging. Tanwar et al. [16] produced 316L-309 duplex thin-walled parts by wire-arc additive manufacturing and heat-treated them at 400, 950 and 1200 °C for 2 h. As-built samples contained acicular ferrite in a finer austenite matrix, and 400 °C induced negligible changes, whereas 950 and 1200 °C markedly reduced strength. At 1200 °C, elongation nearly doubled, while strength fell by 14.3%, and hardness dropped 25–35 HV. Rahimi et al. [17] characterized 310 austenitic stainless steel made by cold-metal-transfer wire-arc additive manufacturing, finding epitaxially grown columnar grains with interdendritic and grain-boundary ferrite—unlike the fully austenitic, fine grains of hot-rolled AISI 310; dendrite spacing varied with cooling rate and inter-layer remelting, and the anisotropic microstructure governed direction-dependent tensile and Charpy impact properties.
Despite these research advances, most existing studies on stainless steel WAAM focus on 304 and 316L alloys. For 309L stainless steel, which is widely used for dissimilar steel welding and component repair [18,19], relevant research is still limited. Although several investigations have been carried out on the solidification mode and ferrite morphology evolution of CMT-deposited 309L stainless steel, the intrinsic effects under the coupling effect of different key process parameters still require further in-depth exploration. In addition, the collapse mechanism during thin-wall fabrication and the effect of deposition path strategy still need further investigation to guide practical production.
In view of the above research gaps, this work takes 309L austenitic stainless steel as the research object. Single-track single-layer deposition experiments are first performed to optimize the process parameter window by evaluating bead geometry and surface morphology. On this basis, single-track multi-layer thin-wall specimens under different process parameter combinations are fabricated. The effects of wire-feeding speed, welding speed and deposition path on the forming characteristics of thin-wall specimens are systematically analyzed, and the evolution of the microstructure and mechanical properties as a function of process parameters is revealed. The underlying mechanisms are discussed based on solidification theory and relevant strengthening mechanisms. The research results can provide a theoretical basis and technical guidance for process regulation and quality control of 309L stainless steel CMT-WAAM.
2. Experimental Materials and Methods
2.1. Experimental Materials
309L austenitic stainless steel wire with a diameter of 1.2 mm was adopted as the deposition material in this experiment. The chemical composition of the welding wire is listed in Table 1. A 304 stainless steel plate with a thickness of 10 mm was selected as the substrate. Prior to deposition, the substrate surface was ground using SiC abrasive papers to remove oxide scales and contaminants, followed by ultrasonic cleaning in ethanol for 10 min to eliminate grease. 309L stainless steel possesses favorable mechanical properties, including high compressive resistance, superior tensile strength, good ductility, and excellent weldability, as well as outstanding corrosion-resistance performance [20,21].
Table 1. Chemical composition of 309L stainless steel welding wire (mass fraction, %).
2.2. Experimental Equipment
The additive manufacturing system consists of a Fronius® VR 7000 CMT digital welding power source, a KUKA six-axis industrial robot, a wire-feeding mechanism and a shielding gas system. The welding power source enables precise control over the CMT short-circuit transfer process. The motion trajectory and travel speed of the welding torch are controlled by the robot using offline programming. A mixed gas of 97.5% Ar + 2.5% CO2 was employed as the shielding gas, with the gas flow rate set at 20 L/min.
Before deposition, no preheating was applied to the substrate. The substrate was clamped on a water-cooled copper fixture during the whole WAAM process. Inter-layer temperature was monitored by an infrared thermometer, and deposition of the subsequent layer started only when the inter-layer temperature cooled down to 100 °C. No external forced cooling was used except the water-cooled fixture.
2.3. Experimental Scheme
2.3.1. Optimization of Single-Track Single-Layer Deposition Process
The control-variable method was adopted to conduct 22 sets of single-track single-layer deposition experiments, where the wire-feeding speed and welding speed ranged from 2–6 m/min and 2–6 mm/s, respectively. The detailed experimental scheme is listed in Table 2. Parameter combinations with favorable forming quality were screened by means of macroscopic morphology observation, measurement of clad width and reinforcement height, and calculation of the reinforcement height coefficient.
Table 2. Single-track single-layer deposition test scheme.
The weld reinforcement form factor φ, a dimensionless evaluation index, is defined as the ratio of bead width W to reinforcement height H, with the mathematical expression of φ = W/H. This index can quantitatively characterize the fullness and geometric stability of single-track weld bead formation. A reasonable value of the reinforcement form factor corresponds to a smooth weld cross-section profile and superior forming quality. An excessively large factor tends to produce overly flat weld beads with insufficient cladding thickness, whereas an excessively small factor leads to prominent weld humps, which may readily induce forming defects during subsequent multi-layer deposition [22,23].
