Gold vs. Silver vs. Tin: Selecting the Correct Plating System
The correct coating depends on the electrical duty, contact geometry, substrate, environmental conditions and target service life. Gold is generally selected for stable low-level signal interfaces, silver for conductive power paths, and tin for many cost-sensitive copper connection systems.
Gold plating for low-level signals and precision connectors
Gold is useful when a contact must maintain a low and stable interface resistance under low-voltage, low-current conditions. It does not readily form the tenacious insulating oxide films associated with many base metals.
Gold plating specifications should distinguish between hard gold alloy deposits and softer, high-purity gold deposits. Hard gold, often alloyed with small quantities of other metals, is commonly used for repeated mating. Softer gold may be appropriate for applications with limited mechanical wear.
Key specification variables include:
- Minimum local gold thickness, measured in micrometres (μm).
- Gold composition and deposit hardness.
- Nickel or other qualified barrier-layer thickness where required.
- Porosity and exposed-substrate acceptance criteria.
- Mating cycles, contact force and allowable contact-resistance change.
A nominal average thickness alone may not protect edges, stamped corners or high-wear regions. The drawing should define the measurement locations and the acceptance criteria for minimum thickness.
Silver plating for relay contacts and power terminals
Silver is widely used where low electrical resistance and current-carrying capability are priorities. Silver-plated contact rivets, copper terminals and relay components can provide a conductive surface while retaining a copper-based structural substrate.
The plating specification must account for the difference between a silver-plated surface and a solid silver contact. A plated copper part has a functional surface coating over a conductive base metal; a bimetal contact rivet may instead use a silver contact layer joined to a copper shank through a forming or bonding process.
Design factor | Silver‑plated copper | Bimetal silver contact rivet | Solid silver contact
---|---|---|---
Silver distribution | Surface coating | Localized contact layer | Bulk silver
Primary cost variable | Coating area and thickness | Silver head geometry and bond integrity | Silver mass
Main qualification focus | Adhesion, porosity and thickness | Bond strength, interface integrity and contact wear | Geometry, material grade and wear
Typical use | Conductive terminals and connector parts | Relay and switch contact assemblies | Applications requiring a solid silver contact body
For switching devices, silver plating should not be treated as a substitute for the correct contact material. Arc energy, switching current, load inductance, opening speed and contact geometry may require a silver alloy such as AgSnO₂ or AgNi rather than a pure silver coating.
Tin plating for copper stamping and electrical terminals
Tin plating is widely applied to copper and copper-alloy stamped parts because it supports practical electrical joining and is compatible with many soldering and terminal-connection processes.
However, tin is not universally suitable for low-level signal contacts. Tin oxide can affect interface resistance, particularly where contact force is insufficient to disrupt the surface film. Fretting caused by vibration or thermal movement can also generate wear debris and unstable resistance.
Tin-plated copper stamping specifications should define:
- Tin deposit thickness and whether the finish is matte or bright.
- Copper substrate grade and temper.
- Underplating or barrier-layer requirements, where applicable.
- Solderability or crimping requirements for the intended connection.
- Whisker-risk assessment for susceptible geometries and operating conditions.
Tin whisker control requires particular attention in closely spaced conductors and sensitive electronic assemblies. Applicable mitigation measures should be selected through design review and qualification testing rather than assuming that a particular nominal thickness eliminates the risk.
Material selection by operating condition
Operating condition | Preferred starting point | Engineering checks
---|---|---
Low‑level signal, low contact force | Gold‑plated contact | Minimum gold thickness, porosity, mating cycles and resistance stability
High‑current conductive interface | Silver‑plated copper or a silver‑alloy contact system | Temperature rise, current density, contact force and corrosion exposure
Solderable copper terminal | Tin‑plated copper stamping | Solderability, coating thickness, storage conditions and substrate compatibility
Repeated switching with electrical arcs | Application‑qualified silver alloy contact | Arc erosion, welding tendency, transfer, temperature and endurance
Vibrating separable connection | Application‑qualified gold or tin system | Fretting, contact force, surface finish and vibration profile
These are initial selection guidelines, not universal prescriptions. Final selection should be validated against the product's electrical rating, applicable IEC requirements and the actual operating environment.
Plating Thickness, Adhesion and Corrosion Verification
Coating thickness and adhesion are separate quality characteristics. A coating can meet its nominal thickness requirement but fail because of poor surface preparation, excessive internal stress, inadequate activation or incompatibility between the coating and substrate.
Defining coating thickness and measurement locations
The engineering drawing should specify the coating material, minimum local thickness, measurement method and functional measurement locations. Where a barrier layer is used, its thickness should be controlled separately from the functional outer coating.
Verification item | Typical method or reference | What it establishes | Important limitation
---|---|---|---
Metallic coating thickness | X-ray fluorescence (XRF); ISO 3497 | Non-destructive thickness measurement where the coating system and geometry are suitable | Results depend on calibration, layer composition and measurement geometry
Cross-sectional thickness | Metallographic cross-section; ISO 1463 | Layer thickness and interface structure at the examined location | Destructive and limited to the prepared section
Adhesion of electrodeposited coatings | ISO 2819 or a specified coating-specific method | Resistance to separation under the selected test | Method suitability depends on substrate, coating and part geometry
Corrosion resistance | ASTM B117 or a specified cyclic-corrosion method | Corrosion behavior under defined exposure conditions | Does not directly establish electrical endurance in service
Solderability, where relevant | Applicable IEC 60068-2-20 method or customer specification | Wetting behavior under the specified soldering conditions | Not a substitute for contact-resistance or bond-strength testing
No single standard covers every plating system and component geometry. The drawing and inspection plan should identify the applicable edition, test conditions, sample size and acceptance limits.
XRF thickness measurement and cross-sectional analysis
XRF is suitable for routine inspection of many metallic coatings when the coating composition, substrate and measurement geometry are supported by the instrument's calibration. For multilayer systems, the measurement method must distinguish the individual layers or use a validated model.
Cross-sectional microscopy provides direct evidence of coating thickness, layer continuity and the interface between the coating and substrate. It is particularly useful during process validation, failure analysis and investigation of edge coverage or localized delamination.
A production inspection plan should specify:
- Measurement locations, including edges or contact zones where functional.
- Minimum local thickness and permitted variation.
- Calibration standards and measurement frequency.
- Cross-section preparation and evaluation criteria when required.
- Traceability between the inspection results and production lot.
Adhesion tests and bend-test limitations
Adhesion failure can originate from inadequate cleaning, incomplete activation, contamination, excessive deposit stress or poor compatibility between adjacent layers.
A bend test may be useful for suitable sheet-metal specimens, but it is not a universal acceptance method for plated electrical contacts. Bending radius, substrate thickness, ductility and coating thickness all affect the result. Small stamped parts may require a customer-approved test method or a representative process coupon.
The acceptance criteria should define the permissible condition after testing, such as no visible flaking or separation under a specified inspection method. If the functional coating is required to remain intact during deformation, that requirement must be explicit.
ASTM B117 salt spray and service-environment qualification
ASTM B117 defines a controlled salt-fog exposure procedure. It is useful for comparing corrosion behavior under specified conditions, but it does not establish a universal pass/fail duration for all gold-, silver- or tin-plated components.
For example, a salt-fog test may not reproduce silver sulfidation, mixed-gas exposure, condensation cycles or electrical arcing. Where those mechanisms govern service life, qualification should include an appropriate environmental test and, when necessary, measurements of contact resistance before and after exposure.
Cyanide-Free Electroplating and Environmental Compliance
Electroplating chemistry affects worker safety, wastewater treatment, process controls and environmental compliance. Cyanide-free processes can reduce specific cyanide-related hazards, but the term does not establish that an entire plating operation is environmentally harmless or automatically compliant with every applicable regulation.
Cyanide-free silver plating: process qualification
Conventional silver-plating processes may use cyanide-based electrolytes. Alternative chemistries are available, but their suitability depends on the substrate, deposit properties, component geometry and production requirements.
A cyanide-free process should be qualified against the same functional criteria as any other plating system:
- Coating thickness and uniformity across functional surfaces.
- Adhesion and resistance to flaking.
- Surface appearance and deposit composition.
- Electrical contact resistance and environmental stability.
- Bath stability, wastewater controls and process repeatability.
A chemistry change can affect deposit morphology, throwing power, porosity and process-window stability. Existing process parameters should not be assumed to transfer unchanged when a plating chemistry is replaced.
RoHS, REACH and substance declarations
RoHS and REACH address different regulatory requirements. RoHS restricts specified hazardous substances in electrical and electronic equipment within its scope, while REACH governs chemicals and related obligations, including applicable restrictions and substance communication requirements.
A claim of "RoHS compliant" or "REACH compliant" should be supported by relevant declarations and material information for the applicable product and market. The claim should not be inferred solely from the absence of cyanide in the plating bath.
For OEM supplier qualification, the documentation package may include:
- Plating chemistry and relevant process declarations.
- Substrate and coating material declarations.
- Applicable RoHS and REACH documentation.
- Restricted-substance information from upstream material suppliers.
- Lot identification and traceability records.
- Process-change notification and requalification requirements.
Production controls and supplier audit points
An electrical contact plating supplier should demonstrate control of the process from substrate preparation through final inspection. The audit should focus on the documented process and actual production records rather than certifications alone.
Audit item | Evidence to request | Engineering purpose
---|---|---
Pre-plating preparation | Cleaning, activation and rinse-control records | Reduce contamination and adhesion failures
Bath management | Composition, temperature, pH where applicable, and replenishment records | Maintain deposit consistency
Thickness control | XRF calibration, inspection results and sampling plan | Verify coating requirements
Adhesion and corrosion | Test procedures, results and corrective-action records | Confirm process qualification
Material compliance | Applicable RoHS/REACH declarations | Support regulatory assessment
Traceability | Lot codes, inspection records and process-change history | Enable containment and failure investigation
ISO 9001 and IATF 16949 may support documented quality management, depending on the supplier's certification scope. Neither certification by itself proves that a specific plating thickness, adhesion result or environmental test requirement has been met.
Frequently Asked Questions
How is the thickness of gold, silver or tin plating on electrical contacts measured?
X-ray fluorescence (XRF) is commonly used for non-destructive thickness measurement when the coating system and geometry are suitable. Cross-sectional microscopy can verify layer thickness and interfaces.
Which plating tests should an electrical contact manufacturer provide for OEM qualification?
The test plan depends on the application. Typical evidence includes coating-thickness measurements, adhesion tests, corrosion testing, and applicable material declarations.
Can a China electrical contact plating supplier provide RoHS/REACH documentation and production traceability?
A qualified supplier should be able to provide applicable material declarations and lot-level production records when these are included in its quality system and supply agreement.

Electrical contact plating controls surface oxidation\, contact resistance\, wear behavior and long\-term connection stability\. Gold\, silver and tin plating serve different electrical and mechanical requirements\; coating selection must account for current\, contact force\, switching frequency\, mating cycles\, base\-metal compatibility and the operating environment\. For electrical contact manufacturers and OEM purchasing teams\, coating thickness\, adhesion\, porosity and verification methods should be specified before production release\.

\#\# How Electroplating Affects Electrical Contact Performance

Electroplating deposits a controlled metallic layer onto a conductive substrate to modify its surface properties without changing the entire component\'s bulk material\. In relay contacts\, copper terminals\, stamped connectors and silver contact rivets\, the coating influences both electrical conduction at the interface and the rate at which the surface degrades\.

\#\#\# Contact resistance and surface\-film formation

Contact resistance depends on the real area of metallic contact\, contact force\, surface roughness\, contamination and the properties of the surface film\. Although a contact may have a large apparent area\, electrical current passes through a much smaller number of microscopic contact spots\.

Silver provides high electrical conductivity\, but silver sulfide can form in sulfur\-containing atmospheres\. Gold resists oxidation and is suitable for low\-level signal contacts\, while tin provides a practical surface for many separable copper connections but can develop oxide films and fretting\-related resistance under certain conditions\.

Plating material \| Typical electrical characteristic \| Main surface‑related risk \| Common engineering use 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Silver \(Ag\) \| High conductivity\; bulk resistivity approximately 1\.59 μΩ·cm at 20°C \| Sulfidation and surface tarnishing \| Power contacts\, relay contacts\, conductive terminals 
Gold \(Au\) \| High conductivity\; bulk resistivity approximately 2\.44 μΩ·cm at 20°C \| Wear‑through\, porosity and high material cost \| Low‑level signals\, precision connectors\, control circuits 
Tin \(Sn\) \| Bulk resistivity approximately 11\.5 μΩ·cm at 20°C \| Oxide formation\, fretting and tin whiskers in susceptible systems \| Copper terminals\, stamped connectors\, wire‑termination interfaces 

\#\#\# Oxidation\, sulfur exposure and corrosion testing

Coating performance depends on the chemical species present in the service environment\. Silver can tarnish in sulfur\-bearing atmospheres\; tin oxide may increase resistance at low contact forces\; and gold\'s corrosion resistance can be compromised by pores exposing the underlying substrate\.

Salt spray testing under ASTM B117 evaluates corrosion behavior in a controlled salt\-fog environment\. However\, it does not directly predict performance in sulfur\-rich industrial atmospheres\, mixed flowing gas environments or actual electrical switching duty\. Test methods should therefore match the failure mechanism expected in service\.

For electrical contact plating suppliers\, qualification should distinguish cosmetic discoloration from measurable increases in contact resistance\, corrosion through the coating and loss of mechanical integrity\.

\#\#\# Wear resistance and mating\-cycle requirements

Plating thickness must be selected against the expected mechanical and electrical duty rather than a generic coating specification\.

\- Gold\-plated signal contacts\: Define the minimum local gold thickness\, mating\-cycle target and allowable resistance change\.
\- Silver\-plated switching contacts\: Evaluate arc erosion\, transfer of material between contacts\, thermal loading and contact force\.
\- Tin\-plated copper stamping\: Evaluate insertion force\, fretting exposure\, oxide\-film behavior and the intended connection system\.

A thicker coating does not automatically provide a longer service life\. Adhesion\, porosity\, deposit hardness\, surface roughness and the distribution of contact pressure can be equally important\.

Ag\, Au\, Nickel Plated for Electrical Contact Rivet
1\-3μm Gold Plated Contact
1\-3μm Nickel Plated Contact
99\.99\% Purity Cu
99\.99\% Purity Nickel
X\-ray Fluorescence Cooling Thickness
Accurate\/draw materially Friendly Sacropolating Lines
99\.99\% Purity Ag of Electrophurils
99\.99\% Purity Cu
1\-20μm Silver Plated Contact
Bimetal Silver Contact
Trimetal Silver Contact
Solid Copper Contact

\#\# Gold vs\. Silver vs\. Tin\: Selecting the Correct Plating System

The correct coating depends on the electrical duty\, contact geometry\, substrate\, environmental conditions and target service life\. Gold is generally selected for stable low\-level signal interfaces\, silver for conductive power paths\, and tin for many cost\-sensitive copper connection systems\.

\#\#\# Gold plating for low\-level signals and precision connectors

Gold is useful when a contact must maintain a low and stable interface resistance under low\-voltage\, low\-current conditions\. It does not readily form the tenacious insulating oxide films associated with many base metals\.

Gold plating specifications should distinguish between hard gold alloy deposits and softer\, high\-purity gold deposits\. Hard gold\, often alloyed with small quantities of other metals\, is commonly used for repeated mating\. Softer gold may be appropriate for applications with limited mechanical wear\.

Key specification variables include\:

\- Minimum local gold thickness\, measured in micrometres \(μm\)\.
\- Gold composition and deposit hardness\.
\- Nickel or other qualified barrier\-layer thickness where required\.
\- Porosity and exposed\-substrate acceptance criteria\.
\- Mating cycles\, contact force and allowable contact\-resistance change\.

A nominal average thickness alone may not protect edges\, stamped corners or high\-wear regions\. The drawing should define the measurement locations and the acceptance criteria for minimum thickness\.

\#\#\# Silver plating for relay contacts and power terminals

Silver is widely used where low electrical resistance and current\-carrying capability are priorities\. Silver\-plated contact rivets\, copper terminals and relay components can provide a conductive surface while retaining a copper\-based structural substrate\.

The plating specification must account for the difference between a silver\-plated surface and a solid silver contact\. A plated copper part has a functional surface coating over a conductive base metal\; a bimetal contact rivet may instead use a silver contact layer joined to a copper shank through a forming or bonding process\.

Design factor \| Silver‑plated copper \| Bimetal silver contact rivet \| Solid silver contact 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Silver distribution \| Surface coating \| Localized contact layer \| Bulk silver 
Primary cost variable \| Coating area and thickness \| Silver head geometry and bond integrity \| Silver mass 
Main qualification focus \| Adhesion\, porosity and thickness \| Bond strength\, interface integrity and contact wear \| Geometry\, material grade and wear 
Typical use \| Conductive terminals and connector parts \| Relay and switch contact assemblies \| Applications requiring a solid silver contact body 

For switching devices\, silver plating should not be treated as a substitute for the correct contact material\. Arc energy\, switching current\, load inductance\, opening speed and contact geometry may require a silver alloy such as AgSnO₂ or AgNi rather than a pure silver coating\.

\#\#\# Tin plating for copper stamping and electrical terminals

Tin plating is widely applied to copper and copper\-alloy stamped parts because it supports practical electrical joining and is compatible with many soldering and terminal\-connection processes\.

However\, tin is not universally suitable for low\-level signal contacts\. Tin oxide can affect interface resistance\, particularly where contact force is insufficient to disrupt the surface film\. Fretting caused by vibration or thermal movement can also generate wear debris and unstable resistance\.

Tin\-plated copper stamping specifications should define\:

\- Tin deposit thickness and whether the finish is matte or bright\.
\- Copper substrate grade and temper\.
\- Underplating or barrier\-layer requirements\, where applicable\.
\- Solderability or crimping requirements for the intended connection\.
\- Whisker\-risk assessment for susceptible geometries and operating conditions\.

Tin whisker control requires particular attention in closely spaced conductors and sensitive electronic assemblies\. Applicable mitigation measures should be selected through design review and qualification testing rather than assuming that a particular nominal thickness eliminates the risk\.

\#\#\# Material selection by operating condition

Operating condition \| Preferred starting point \| Engineering checks 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Low‑level signal\, low contact force \| Gold‑plated contact \| Minimum gold thickness\, porosity\, mating cycles and resistance stability 
High‑current conductive interface \| Silver‑plated copper or a silver‑alloy contact system \| Temperature rise\, current density\, contact force and corrosion exposure 
Solderable copper terminal \| Tin‑plated copper stamping \| Solderability\, coating thickness\, storage conditions and substrate compatibility 
Repeated switching with electrical arcs \| Application‑qualified silver alloy contact \| Arc erosion\, welding tendency\, transfer\, temperature and endurance 
Vibrating separable connection \| Application‑qualified gold or tin system \| Fretting\, contact force\, surface finish and vibration profile 

These are initial selection guidelines\, not universal prescriptions\. Final selection should be validated against the product\'s electrical rating\, applicable IEC requirements and the actual operating environment\.

\#\# Plating Thickness\, Adhesion and Corrosion Verification

Coating thickness and adhesion are separate quality characteristics\. A coating can meet its nominal thickness requirement but fail because of poor surface preparation\, excessive internal stress\, inadequate activation or incompatibility between the coating and substrate\.

\#\#\# Defining coating thickness and measurement locations

The engineering drawing should specify the coating material\, minimum local thickness\, measurement method and functional measurement locations\. Where a barrier layer is used\, its thickness should be controlled separately from the functional outer coating\.

Verification item \| Typical method or reference \| What it establishes \| Important limitation 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Metallic coating thickness \| X\-ray fluorescence \(XRF\)\; ISO 3497 \| Non\-destructive thickness measurement where the coating system and geometry are suitable \| Results depend on calibration\, layer composition and measurement geometry 
Cross\-sectional thickness \| Metallographic cross\-section\; ISO 1463 \| Layer thickness and interface structure at the examined location \| Destructive and limited to the prepared section 
Adhesion of electrodeposited coatings \| ISO 2819 or a specified coating\-specific method \| Resistance to separation under the selected test \| Method suitability depends on substrate\, coating and part geometry 
Corrosion resistance \| ASTM B117 or a specified cyclic\-corrosion method \| Corrosion behavior under defined exposure conditions \| Does not directly establish electrical endurance in service 
Solderability\, where relevant \| Applicable IEC 60068\-2\-20 method or customer specification \| Wetting behavior under the specified soldering conditions \| Not a substitute for contact\-resistance or bond\-strength testing 

No single standard covers every plating system and component geometry\. The drawing and inspection plan should identify the applicable edition\, test conditions\, sample size and acceptance limits\.

\#\#\# XRF thickness measurement and cross\-sectional analysis

XRF is suitable for routine inspection of many metallic coatings when the coating composition\, substrate and measurement geometry are supported by the instrument\'s calibration\. For multilayer systems\, the measurement method must distinguish the individual layers or use a validated model\.

Cross\-sectional microscopy provides direct evidence of coating thickness\, layer continuity and the interface between the coating and substrate\. It is particularly useful during process validation\, failure analysis and investigation of edge coverage or localized delamination\.

A production inspection plan should specify\:

\- Measurement locations\, including edges or contact zones where functional\.
\- Minimum local thickness and permitted variation\.
\- Calibration standards and measurement frequency\.
\- Cross\-section preparation and evaluation criteria when required\.
\- Traceability between the inspection results and production lot\.

\#\#\# Adhesion tests and bend\-test limitations

Adhesion failure can originate from inadequate cleaning\, incomplete activation\, contamination\, excessive deposit stress or poor compatibility between adjacent layers\.

A bend test may be useful for suitable sheet\-metal specimens\, but it is not a universal acceptance method for plated electrical contacts\. Bending radius\, substrate thickness\, ductility and coating thickness all affect the result\. Small stamped parts may require a customer\-approved test method or a representative process coupon\.

The acceptance criteria should define the permissible condition after testing\, such as no visible flaking or separation under a specified inspection method\. If the functional coating is required to remain intact during deformation\, that requirement must be explicit\.

\#\#\# ASTM B117 salt spray and service\-environment qualification

ASTM B117 defines a controlled salt\-fog exposure procedure\. It is useful for comparing corrosion behavior under specified conditions\, but it does not establish a universal pass\/fail duration for all gold\-\, silver\- or tin\-plated components\.

For example\, a salt\-fog test may not reproduce silver sulfidation\, mixed\-gas exposure\, condensation cycles or electrical arcing\. Where those mechanisms govern service life\, qualification should include an appropriate environmental test and\, when necessary\, measurements of contact resistance before and after exposure\.

\#\# Cyanide\-Free Electroplating and Environmental Compliance

Electroplating chemistry affects worker safety\, wastewater treatment\, process controls and environmental compliance\. Cyanide\-free processes can reduce specific cyanide\-related hazards\, but the term does not establish that an entire plating operation is environmentally harmless or automatically compliant with every applicable regulation\.

\#\#\# Cyanide\-free silver plating\: process qualification

Conventional silver\-plating processes may use cyanide\-based electrolytes\. Alternative chemistries are available\, but their suitability depends on the substrate\, deposit properties\, component geometry and production requirements\.

A cyanide\-free process should be qualified against the same functional criteria as any other plating system\:

\- Coating thickness and uniformity across functional surfaces\.
\- Adhesion and resistance to flaking\.
\- Surface appearance and deposit composition\.
\- Electrical contact resistance and environmental stability\.
\- Bath stability\, wastewater controls and process repeatability\.

A chemistry change can affect deposit morphology\, throwing power\, porosity and process\-window stability\. Existing process parameters should not be assumed to transfer unchanged when a plating chemistry is replaced\.

\#\#\# RoHS\, REACH and substance declarations

RoHS and REACH address different regulatory requirements\. RoHS restricts specified hazardous substances in electrical and electronic equipment within its scope\, while REACH governs chemicals and related obligations\, including applicable restrictions and substance communication requirements\.

A claim of \"RoHS compliant\" or \"REACH compliant\" should be supported by relevant declarations and material information for the applicable product and market\. The claim should not be inferred solely from the absence of cyanide in the plating bath\.

For OEM supplier qualification\, the documentation package may include\:

\- Plating chemistry and relevant process declarations\.
\- Substrate and coating material declarations\.
\- Applicable RoHS and REACH documentation\.
\- Restricted\-substance information from upstream material suppliers\.
\- Lot identification and traceability records\.
\- Process\-change notification and requalification requirements\.

\#\#\# Production controls and supplier audit points

An electrical contact plating supplier should demonstrate control of the process from substrate preparation through final inspection\. The audit should focus on the documented process and actual production records rather than certifications alone\.

Audit item \| Evidence to request \| Engineering purpose 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Pre\-plating preparation \| Cleaning\, activation and rinse\-control records \| Reduce contamination and adhesion failures 
Bath management \| Composition\, temperature\, pH where applicable\, and replenishment records \| Maintain deposit consistency 
Thickness control \| XRF calibration\, inspection results and sampling plan \| Verify coating requirements 
Adhesion and corrosion \| Test procedures\, results and corrective\-action records \| Confirm process qualification 
Material compliance \| Applicable RoHS\/REACH declarations \| Support regulatory assessment 
Traceability \| Lot codes\, inspection records and process\-change history \| Enable containment and failure investigation 

ISO 9001 and IATF 16949 may support documented quality management\, depending on the supplier\'s certification scope\. Neither certification by itself proves that a specific plating thickness\, adhesion result or environmental test requirement has been met\.

\#\# Frequently Asked Questions

\#\#\# How is the thickness of gold\, silver or tin plating on electrical contacts measured\?

X\-ray fluorescence \(XRF\) is commonly used for non\-destructive thickness measurement when the coating system and geometry are suitable\. Cross\-sectional microscopy can verify layer thickness and interfaces\.

\#\#\# Which plating tests should an electrical contact manufacturer provide for OEM qualification\?

The test plan depends on the application\. Typical evidence includes coating\-thickness measurements\, adhesion tests\, corrosion testing\, and applicable material declarations\.

\#\#\# Can a China electrical contact plating supplier provide RoHS\/REACH documentation and production traceability\?

A qualified supplier should be able to provide applicable material declarations and lot\-level production records when these are included in its quality system and supply agreement\.

\#\# contact us

Submit your Gold Coating Electrical Contacts drawing\, substrate grade\, required coating metal\, minimum thickness\, and operating conditions for a technical review\. Request a quotation covering plating feasibility\, inspection methods\, sample validation\, and production capacity before finalizing your next electrical contact order\.

records.title: Lubricant-Engine Suitability Evaluation for Fuel Efficiency in Fishing VesselUsing Temperature and Color Degradation
records.source_name: Marine Fisheries : Journal of Marine Fisheries Technology and Management
records.abstract: Engine performance in fishing vessel depends on the reliability and efficiency of diesel engine, in which the lubrication system plays a key role in reducing friction, controlling operating temperature, and minimizing component wear. However, field observations in small-scale fisheries indicate that many fishermen select lubricants based on habit, price, or availability rather than manufacturer specifications, which may reduce engine efficiency and increase fuel consumption. This study evaluated the suitability of three lubricants (S40, SC SAE 15W-40, and SX SAE 15W-40), each matched to a different Mitsubishi diesel engine (6D14, 6D15, 6D16) under real purse seine fishing conditions in Majene Regency, Indonesia, using engine temperature and lubricant color degradation as practical field indicators. Because operating duration varied substantially among engines (76-180 minutes per trip), fuel consumption was expressed as a rate (L hour-1) for fair comparison. S40 produced the lowest, most stable rate (21.97 L hour-1) and lowest final temperature (36.22°C); SC SAE 15W-40 recorded the highest rate (37.51 L hour-1) despite a moderate final temperature (46.00°C); SX SAE 15W-40 showed the most fluctuating temperature (up to 50.80°C) with an intermediate rate (31.19 L hour-1). Kruskal-Wallis tests confirmed significant differences among groups (p < 0.001). Multiple regression showed operating duration and final temperature jointly explained 30.5% of the variance in total fuel consumption (R2 = 0.305, p < 0.001). These findings indicate that rate-based, engine-specific lubricant matching is essential for improving fuel efficiency and thermal stability in small-scale fishing vessels. Keywords: Fishing vessels; fuel efficiency; lubricant degradation; marine engines; operating temperature

Because trip durations varied (76–180 minutes), fuel consumption was normalized as a rate in L hour-1. Kruskal-Wallis tests indicated significant group differences (p < 0.001), and multiple regression found operating duration and final temperature jointly explained 30.5% of variance in total fuel consumption (R2 = 0.305, p < 0.001).

Lubricant-Engine Suitability Evaluation for Fuel Efficiency in Fishing VesselUsing Temperature and Color Degradation
Authors
- Etika Ariyanti Hidayat Fisheries Capture Department, Universitas Sulawesi Barat Jl. Prof. Dr. Baharuddin Lopa, SH, Talumung, Majene, West Sulawesi, Indoesia, 91412
- Sudirman Sukardi Fisheries Capture Department, Lambung Mangkurat University Jl. Ahmad Yani km 36, Loktabat Selatan, Banjarbaru Selatan, Banjarbaru City, South Kalimantan, Indonesia, 70714
- Novia Nurul Afiyah Fisheries Resoursces Management, Jenderal Sudirman University Jl. Dr Soeparno, Komplek GOR Soesilo Soedarman, Karangwangkal, Karang Bawang, Grendeng, Kec. Purwokerto Utara, Kabupaten Banyumas, Central Java, Indonesia 5312
- Zulfathri Randhi Fisheries Capture Department, Universitas Sulawesi Barat Jl. Prof. Dr. Baharuddin Lopa, SH, Talumung, Majene, West Sulawesi, Indoesia, 91412
DOI:
https://doi.org/10.29244/8sby2a58
Abstract
Engine performance in fishing vessel depends on the reliability and efficiency of diesel engine, in which the lubrication system plays a key role in reducing friction, controlling operating temperature, and minimizing component wear. However, field observations in small-scale fisheries indicate that many fishermen select lubricants based on habit, price, or availability rather than manufacturer specifications, which may reduce engine efficiency and increase fuel consumption. This study evaluated the suitability of three lubricants (S40, SC SAE 15W-40, and SX SAE 15W-40), each matched to a different Mitsubishi diesel engine (6D14, 6D15, 6D16) under real purse seine fishing conditions in Majene Regency, Indonesia, using engine temperature and lubricant color degradation as practical field indicators. Because operating duration varied substantially among engines (76-180 minutes per trip), fuel consumption was expressed as a rate (L hour-1) for fair comparison. S40 produced the lowest, most stable rate (21.97 L hour-1) and lowest final temperature (36.22°C); SC SAE 15W-40 recorded the highest rate (37.51 L hour-1) despite a moderate final temperature (46.00°C); SX SAE 15W-40 showed the most fluctuating temperature (up to 50.80°C) with an intermediate rate (31.19 L hour-1). Kruskal-Wallis tests confirmed significant differences among groups (p < 0.001). Multiple regression showed operating duration and final temperature jointly explained 30.5% of the variance in total fuel consumption (R2 = 0.305, p < 0.001). These findings indicate that rate-based, engine-specific lubricant matching is essential for improving fuel efficiency and thermal stability in small-scale fishing vessels.
Keywords: Fishing vessels; fuel efficiency; lubricant degradation; marine engines; operating temperature

\#\# Abstract

Engine performance in fishing vessel depends on the reliability and efficiency of diesel engine\, in which the lubrication system plays a key role in reducing friction\, controlling operating temperature\, and minimizing component wear\. S40 produced the lowest\, most stable rate \(21\.97 L hour\-1\) and lowest final temperature \(36\.22°C\)\; SC SAE 15W\-40 recorded the highest rate \(37\.51 L hour\-1\) despite a moderate final temperature \(46\.00°C\)\; SX SAE 15W\-40 showed the most fluctuating temperature \(up to 50\.80°C\) with an intermediate rate \(31\.19 L hour\-1\)\. Kruskal\-Wallis tests confirmed significant differences among groups \(p \< 0\.001\)\. Multiple regression showed operating duration and final temperature jointly explained 30\.5\% of the variance in total fuel consumption \(R2 \= 0\.305\, p \< 0\.001\)\. These findings indicate that rate\-based\, engine\-specific lubricant matching is essential for improving fuel efficiency and thermal stability in small\-scale fishing vessels\.

ILMA Newsroom
In Memoriam: Carol Lee Poole
In Memoriam: Carol Lee Poole
ILMA mourns the passing of Carol Lee Poole, a dedicated health and safety professional whose expertise and commitment made a lasting contribution to the lubricants industry and the Association.
As a Health and Safety Specialist at Quaker Chemical Corp. in Conshohocken, Pennsylvania, Poole worked closely with John Howell, Ike Tripp of Etna Products, and others to develop an important best practices document to minimize or prevent occurrences of occupational dermatitis sometimes associated with metal removal fluids. That document is now an ASTM standard, E2693-26, “Standard Practice for Prevention of Dermatitis in the Wet Metal Removal Environment.”
Poole’s outstanding service to ILMA was recognized in 2007 when she received the Association’s Distinguished Service Award, now known as the Bellanti Award.
In 2014, Poole joined GHS Resources Inc., where she continued sharing her extensive occupational health and safety expertise, helping organizations develop training and compliance programs under OSHA’s Globally Harmonized System (GHS) requirements.
“Carol provided our industry with clarity on subjects that were problematic,” remembered Cathy Novak, formerly of Cadillac Oil Co. and a fellow Bellanti Award recipient. “She was able to communicate, in laymen’s terms, the issues and solutions. Her superpower was her ability to stay focused on the problems, find the root cause and find a solution. Her gift to all of us was providing a safe work environment and teaching others how to achieve that.”
Poole’s dedication to workplace safety, her generous sharing of knowledge, and her service to ILMA leave a meaningful legacy. We extend our heartfelt condolences to her family, friends and colleagues. She will be remembered with gratitude and respect.
Celebration of Life
A celebration of Poole’s life will be held on Sunday, October 11, 2026, from 2:00 to 4:00 p.m. at James J. Terry Funeral Home, 736 E. Lancaster Avenue, Downingtown, Pennsylvania.
Memorial Donations
In lieu of flowers, Carol’s family requests that memorial donations be made to Oceana.

records.title: Topological Self-Locking of Hyperbranched Poly(ionic liquid)s for Impact-Stiffening Ionic Skins
records.source_name: Journal of the American Chemical Society
records.abstract: Abstract Impact-stiffening ionic skins are highly promising for bioelectronics due to their unique ability to maintain ambient softness and ionic conductivity while instantly hardening upon impact. However, the intrinsically low entropy penalty of ionic bonds typically restricts their strain-rate sensitivity, thereby dampening the overall impact-stiffening performance. To overcome this bottleneck, we report a topological self-locking strategy to exponentially boost the impact-stiffening response of ionic skins. By engineering a hyperbranched poly(ionic liquid) network, we achieved a dramatic, impact-induced transition from a viscous chain-sliding state (shear storage modulus, G′ ∼ 12 kPa at 0.1 Hz) to a rigid glassy self-locked state (G′ ∼ 70.3 MPa at 100 Hz). This topological transition yields a significant 5858-fold increase in stiffness, outperforming most state-of-the-art materials. Furthermore, the developed ionic skin demonstrates great potential for simultaneous impact resistance and high-fidelity sensing. This topological self-locking approach offers a new protective paradigm for soft materials, bypassing the need for conventional particulate jamming or specific dynamic bonds.

records.body_text:
Aluminum Busbar vs. Copper Busbar in EV Battery Modules: Weight Savings, Ampacity, and Cost Trade-offs
Oct 09, 2026 View: 118
Aluminum Busbar can reduce conductor mass and material costs in electric vehicle (EV) battery modules, but require careful evaluation of conductivity, temperature rise, joint resistance, and corrosion protection. Commercially pure aluminum has approximately 61% IACS conductivity, compared with approximately 100% IACS for standard high-conductivity copper. The final choice depends on electrical performance, installation space, manufacturing requirements, and total component cost.
Aluminum vs. Copper Busbar: Key Material Differences
Material selection affects conductor dimensions, battery pack weight, forming processes, and connection reliability. C1100 copper, 1060 aluminum, and 6061 aluminum offer different combinations of conductivity, strength, and formability.
Property
| C1100 Copper | 1060 Aluminum | 6061 Aluminum
---|---|---|---
Density | Approx. 8.9 g/cm³ | Approx. 2.70 g/cm³ | Approx. 2.70 g/cm³
Electrical conductivity | Approx. 100% IACS | Typically above 60% IACS | Generally lower than 1060
Main advantage
| High conductivity | Low mass and high conductivity among aluminum grades | Higher structural strength in suitable tempers
Main consideration | Higher density and material cost | Larger cross-section may be required | Conductivity and forming behavior depend on temper
For equal conductor length and comparable DC resistance, aluminum may require approximately 1.6 times the copper cross-sectional area. Despite the larger area, its lower density can result in a conductor mass roughly 50% lower under simplified room-temperature assumptions.
Actual savings depend on geometry, operating temperature, joint design, and thermal conditions. Engineers must validate the complete assembly rather than compare materials by density alone.
Ampacity, Temperature Rise, and Battery Pack Weight
The current-carrying capacity of an EV battery busbar depends on conductor cross-section, current duty, ambient temperature, cooling conditions, insulation, and connection resistance.
For initial sizing, conductor resistance can be estimated using:
R=ρL/A
where R is resistance, ρ is electrical resistivity, L is conductor length, and A is cross-sectional area.
A larger aluminum cross-section can compensate for its higher resistivity, but engineers must also evaluate:
- Continuous and peak current requirements.
- Temperature rise under representative operating cycles.
- Joint resistance at bolted or welded interfaces.
- Available installation space and insulation clearances.
- Mechanical loads from vibration and thermal expansion.
Weight savings at battery pack level will be smaller than the percentage reduction in busbar mass. For example, if busbars account for 2% of pack mass and their mass is reduced by 50%, the total pack mass decreases by approximately 1%, assuming other components remain unchanged.
Aluminum Busbar Plating and Corrosion Protection
Aluminum naturally forms a stable oxide film that can interfere with electrical contact. For battery applications, surface preparation and interface design are important to maintaining low contact resistance.
A qualified plating process may include:
- Degreasing and surface cleaning.
- Controlled oxide removal and pretreatment.
- Zincate treatment where required by the selected process.
- Copper or nickel underplating where specified.
- Tin plating or another approved surface finish.
- Coating inspection and electrical contact validation.
The appropriate process depends on alloy, geometry, plating chemistry, and application requirements. Tin plating can support selected contact applications, but does not eliminate all corrosion risks. Aluminum-to-copper connections require assessment of galvanic corrosion, moisture exposure, contact pressure, and coating integrity.
Recommended validation may include coating-thickness measurement, adhesion testing where applicable, four-wire joint-resistance measurement, and temperature-rise testing under defined conditions.
Stamping, Bending, and Welding for OEM Production
An Aluminum Busbar Manufacturer must control both electrical performance and manufacturing consistency. Stamping, CNC machining, bending, and joining processes affect dimensional accuracy, contact quality, and production yield.
Important design considerations include:
- Bend radius relative to material thickness.
- Burr height and direction near insulation or contact surfaces.
- Hole position, flatness, and terminal alignment.
- Cracking risk at formed edges.
- Tool wear and dimensional variation during production.
Laser welding and resistance welding may both be suitable, depending on the joint geometry and materials.
Factor
| Laser Welding | Resistance Welding
---|---|---
Heat input | Localized and controlled by laser parameters | Generated through current, resistance, and electrode force
Main process variables | Power, speed, focus, and joint fit-up | Current, force, weld time, and electrode condition
Typical risks | Porosity, lack of fusion, distortion | Inconsistent weld formation and electrode wear
Validation | Weld inspection, resistance, and mechanical testing | Weld monitoring, resistance, and mechanical testing
Copper-to-aluminum laser welding requires particular attention to brittle intermetallic compounds, cracking, and joint resistance. The process must be qualified using representative parts and agreed acceptance criteria.
For automotive programs, production documentation may include process flow, PFMEA, control plans, dimensional inspection reports, and PPAP submissions where required. ISO 9001 or IATF 16949 certification should be verified against the supplier's actual certification scope and customer requirements.
How to Select the Right Busbar Supplier
A Custom Aluminum Busbar Supplier should evaluate the drawing, material grade, electrical duty, surface finish, and production volume before confirming feasibility and pricing.

\# Aluminum Busbar vs\. Copper Busbar in EV Battery Modules\: Weight Savings\, Ampacity\, and Cost Trade\-offs

Oct 09\, 2026 View\: 118

Aluminum Busbar can reduce conductor mass and material costs in electric vehicle \(EV\) battery modules\, but require careful evaluation of conductivity\, temperature rise\, joint resistance\, and corrosion protection\. Commercially pure aluminum has approximately 61\% IACS conductivity\, compared with approximately 100\% IACS for standard high\-conductivity copper\. The final choice depends on electrical performance\, installation space\, manufacturing requirements\, and total component cost\.

\#\# Aluminum vs\. Copper Busbar\: Key Material Differences

Material selection affects conductor dimensions\, battery pack weight\, forming processes\, and connection reliability\. C1100 copper\, 1060 aluminum\, and 6061 aluminum offer different combinations of conductivity\, strength\, and formability\.

Property
 \| C1100 Copper \| 1060 Aluminum \| 6061 Aluminum 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Density \| Approx\. 8\.9 g\/cm³ \| Approx\. 2\.70 g\/cm³ \| Approx\. 2\.70 g\/cm³ 
Electrical conductivity \| Approx\. 100\% IACS \| Typically above 60\% IACS \| Generally lower than 1060 

Main advantage
 \| High conductivity \| Low mass and high conductivity among aluminum grades \| Higher structural strength in suitable tempers 
Main consideration \| Higher density and material cost \| Larger cross\-section may be required \| Conductivity and forming behavior depend on temper 

For equal conductor length and comparable DC resistance\, aluminum may require approximately 1\.6 times the copper cross\-sectional area\. Despite the larger area\, its lower density can result in a conductor mass roughly 50\% lower under simplified room\-temperature assumptions\.

Actual savings depend on geometry\, operating temperature\, joint design\, and thermal conditions\. Engineers must validate the complete assembly rather than compare materials by density alone\.

\#\# Ampacity\, Temperature Rise\, and Battery Pack Weight

The current\-carrying capacity of an EV battery busbar depends on conductor cross\-section\, current duty\, ambient temperature\, cooling conditions\, insulation\, and connection resistance\.

For initial sizing\, conductor resistance can be estimated using\:

R\=ρL\/A

where R is resistance\, ρ is electrical resistivity\, L is conductor length\, and A is cross\-sectional area\.

A larger aluminum cross\-section can compensate for its higher resistivity\, but engineers must also evaluate\:

\- Continuous and peak current requirements\.
\- Temperature rise under representative operating cycles\.
\- Joint resistance at bolted or welded interfaces\.
\- Available installation space and insulation clearances\.
\- Mechanical loads from vibration and thermal expansion\.

Weight savings at battery pack level will be smaller than the percentage reduction in busbar mass\. For example\, if busbars account for 2\% of pack mass and their mass is reduced by 50\%\, the total pack mass decreases by approximately 1\%\, assuming other components remain unchanged\.

\#\# Aluminum Busbar Plating and Corrosion Protection

Aluminum naturally forms a stable oxide film that can interfere with electrical contact\. For battery applications\, surface preparation and interface design are important to maintaining low contact resistance\.

A qualified plating process may include\:

\- Degreasing and surface cleaning\.
\- Controlled oxide removal and pretreatment\.
\- Zincate treatment where required by the selected process\.
\- Copper or nickel underplating where specified\.
\- Tin plating or another approved surface finish\.
\- Coating inspection and electrical contact validation\.

The appropriate process depends on alloy\, geometry\, plating chemistry\, and application requirements\. Tin plating can support selected contact applications\, but does not eliminate all corrosion risks\. Aluminum\-to\-copper connections require assessment of galvanic corrosion\, moisture exposure\, contact pressure\, and coating integrity\.

Recommended validation may include coating\-thickness measurement\, adhesion testing where applicable\, four\-wire joint\-resistance measurement\, and temperature\-rise testing under defined conditions\.

\#\# Stamping\, Bending\, and Welding for OEM Production

An Aluminum Busbar Manufacturer must control both electrical performance and manufacturing consistency\. Stamping\, CNC machining\, bending\, and joining processes affect dimensional accuracy\, contact quality\, and production yield\.

Important design considerations include\:

\- Bend radius relative to material thickness\.
\- Burr height and direction near insulation or contact surfaces\.
\- Hole position\, flatness\, and terminal alignment\.
\- Cracking risk at formed edges\.
\- Tool wear and dimensional variation during production\.

Laser welding and resistance welding may both be suitable\, depending on the joint geometry and materials\.

Factor
 \| Laser Welding \| Resistance Welding 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Heat input \| Localized and controlled by laser parameters \| Generated through current\, resistance\, and electrode force 
Main process variables \| Power\, speed\, focus\, and joint fit\-up \| Current\, force\, weld time\, and electrode condition 
Typical risks \| Porosity\, lack of fusion\, distortion \| Inconsistent weld formation and electrode wear 
Validation \| Weld inspection\, resistance\, and mechanical testing \| Weld monitoring\, resistance\, and mechanical testing 

Copper\-to\-aluminum laser welding requires particular attention to brittle intermetallic compounds\, cracking\, and joint resistance\. The process must be qualified using representative parts and agreed acceptance criteria\.

For automotive programs\, production documentation may include process flow\, PFMEA\, control plans\, dimensional inspection reports\, and PPAP submissions where required\. ISO 9001 or IATF 16949 certification should be verified against the supplier\'s actual certification scope and customer requirements\.

\#\# How to Select the Right Busbar Supplier

A Custom Aluminum Busbar Supplier should evaluate the drawing\, material grade\, electrical duty\, surface finish\, and production volume before confirming feasibility and pricing\.

Procurement and engineering teams should verify\:

\- Material control\: Alloy\, temper\, thickness\, and material traceability\.
\- Manufacturing capability\: Stamping\, bending\, machining\, joining\, and plating\.
\- Inspection capability\: Dimensional accuracy\, coating quality\, and electrical resistance testing\.
\- Quality documentation\: Applicable ISO 9001\, IATF 16949\, and customer\-specific requirements\.
\- Production readiness\: Sample approval\, process validation\, change control\, and PPAP where required\.

The RFQ should include a 2D drawing or 3D model\, current and voltage requirements\, temperature limits\, connection details\, surface\-finish specifications\, annual volume\, and required quality documents\. Complete specifications help suppliers evaluate manufacturability and reduce design changes during production\.

\#\# FAQ\: Aluminum Busbars for EV Battery Modules

Q\: How much lighter is an aluminum busbar than a copper busbar\?

A\: For equal length and comparable DC resistance\, a simplified calculation suggests aluminum conductor mass may be approximately 50\% lower\. Actual results depend on geometry\, operating temperature\, joints\, and thermal requirements\.

Q\: Can an aluminum busbar carry the same current as copper\?

A\: Yes\, when conductor dimensions and thermal performance are properly engineered\. Aluminum generally requires a larger cross\-section\, and the finished assembly must meet specified temperature\-rise and electrical performance limits\.

Q\: Does every aluminum busbar require tin plating\?

A\: No\. Surface treatment depends on the contact interface\, operating environment\, corrosion risk\, and customer specification\. Any selected coating system should be validated for adhesion\, thickness\, and electrical performance\.

Q\: What information is needed for an aluminum busbar quotation\?

A\: Provide drawings\, alloy and temper requirements\, current duty\, voltage\, temperature limits\, connection details\, surface finish\, annual quantity\, and applicable quality documentation\.

records.summary: This Metal Finishing News article reports that Messier Services UK, described as a global leader in landing gear maintenance, repair and overhaul, converted a former RAF hangar at Staverton, UK, into a metal finishing facility. The facility was built at a reported cost of £1.6 million and is described as operating around the clock as a one-stop shop for shot peening, grit blasting and plating. Surface Dynamics Ltd. supplied two dry blast booths: one for aluminium oxide blast treatment with walk-in, workstation and internal lance capabilities, and one for automated shot peening with an orbital external nozzle and rotary internal lance, allowing static components to receive 360º coverage. The 15,000 sq ft building houses 60 process tanks in a seven-foot-deep chemically resistant concrete pit, with plating processes including cadmium, nickel, hard chrome and stainless steel passivation, plus re-grinding, non-destructive flaw detection, stress-relieving and de-embrittlement. The article is a trade-press report based on company statements rather than a peer-reviewed study, and it provides no measured performance data.
records.why_it_matters: It illustrates an in-house MRO metal-finishing architecture that combines automated 360º shot peening and multi-process plating under one roof, which the operator expected to improve workflow control and reduce turnaround and plating costs.

E-Archive
VOL. 3 November ISSUE YEAR 2002
Articles
in Vol. 3 - November Issue - Year 2002
World Leader in Aircraft Maintenance opens new Metal Finishing Facility in England
Paul Huyton, Managing Director of Surface Dynamics
Chemical Cleaning and Plating Lines in the new Metal Finishing Facility.
Booth for Aluminium Oxide blast treatment with walk-in (left), workstation and internal lance capabilities (right)
A former RAF hangar at Staverton, UK, has been brought back into service with a brand new role …… still protecting aircraft but in a very different way. Messier Services UK - global leader in landing gear maintenance, repair and overhaul - has converted it from an historical relic to one of the UK‘s most advanced metal finishing operations.
Surface Dynamics Ltd. was the selected supplier for dry blast treatment equipment in the state-of the-art facility. The English company based in Cheltenham installed two booths. One booth for Aluminium Oxide blast treatment with walk-in, workstation and internal lance capabilities. The other booth for automated shot peening with orbital external nozzle and rotary internal lance. The equipment allows landing gear components to remain static whilst receiving 360º shot peen coverage from the blast nozzles.
Paul Huyton, managing director of Surface Dynamics, says:
”On the Messier project we were faced with the challenge of automated peening of large components within a compact space. And because of the very competitive and varied nature of MRO work it also had to be suitable for a wide range of components and repair schemes without excessive capital cost. The Messier equipment gives them great flexibility with the controlled and repeatable processing required for shot peening.”
The English manufacturer also provided full certificated training and consultancy services for the establishment of procedures and documentation.
Built at a cost of £1.6 million, the Metal Finishing Facility will operate around the clock as a dedicated one-stop shop undertaking shot peening, grit blasting and plating …… whatever is necessary to guarantee ‘as good as new’ components. The new operation has been equipped and sized to accommodate the full range of aircraft landing gears including those from such weighty customers as Airbus and Boeing. Spanning 15,000 sq feet, the building contains 60 process tanks housed in a seven feet deep chemically resistant concrete pit. The plating processes available include cadmium, nickel, hard chrome and stainless steel passivation. Re-grinding to size, non-destructive flaw detection, stress-relieving and de-embrittlement can also be undertaken.
Protection of the environment is achieved through a number of control measures. These include a purpose-built laboratory responsible for undertaking ongoing chemical analysis. All emissions, discharges and waste streams are constantly monitored to ensure full compliance with ISO 14001 and other statutory requirements.
Says Tim Rice, Managing Director of Messier Services UK:
“The advantages of bringing metal finishing in-house are substantial and we expect to secure a rapid return on our investment. Just some of the benefits will be greater control of workflow, reduced turnaround for faster delivery and reduced plating costs. In due course, owning our own finishing facility will also assist us to grasp profitable new business opportunities in aerospace, to the benefit of the business as a whole.”
The Chief of Defence Procurement, Sir Robert Walmsley, performed the official opening ceremony for the Metal Finishing Facility on June 21st 2002.

E-Archive
Articles
in Vol. 8 - September Issue - Year 2007
SURFACTS Presents Innovative Surface Technology Processes
Chromate-free corrosion protection and much more
Karlsruhe – As a showcase for innovative surface treatment processes, SURFACTS provides an overview of the latest developments in surface treatment. One particular focus is on processes for substituting corrosion protection and finishing systems containing chrome (VI) and heavy metals. The 4th International Trade Fair for Surface Technology will be held from 9 to 11 October 2007 in Karlsruhe. SURFACTS will also be integrated in INTERPART, the international supplier trade fair for the automotive, mechanical and plant construction industries. This will generate added value for both events, since many topics will interest exhibitors and visitors of both trade fairs.
As a cross-application technology, surface technology is playing an increasingly important role in almost all industrial sectors. A major factor here is corrosion protection, which will be occupying a prime position at this year's SURFACTS from 9 to 11 October in Karlsruhe. This is currently a hot topic in light of the new EU end-of-life vehicle legislation, which is set to come into effect on 1 July 2007 and bans the use of coatings containing chromate (VI) for automotive parts.
Chromate (VI)-free corrosion protection
The exhibitors at the international specialist trade fair for surface technology are to present new and modified solutions for the corrosion protection of the future. These are based on chromate (III) compounds or offered as fully chromate-free systems and include an inorganic zinc flake coating based on zinc and aluminium flakes. Free from chromate and heavy metals, this coating offers high cathodic corrosion protection without the risk of hydrogen embrittlement. This coating can be applied to the part multiple times, depending on corrosion protection requirements. The primary areas of application are connection elements and high-strength parts for the automotive and construction industries. The galvanic separation of highly corrosion resistant zinc-iron coatings combines functional corrosion protection with attractive surface design. This procedure can even be safely applied to materials which are difficult to coat, such as cast iron. Typical areas of use for zinc-iron coated components include the automotive and electrical industries, toolbuilding, mechanical engineering and sheet-metal forming. Galvanically separated zinc-nickel alloys are mainly used for components in environments which require an extremely high level of corrosion resistance at very high temperatures, such as engine compartments or the area surrounding brakes. Corrosion protection can be optimised through use organic or silica-based sealing, so-called top coats. Multifunctional layers, which set themselves apart through extremely high corrosion protection and an unusually stable wear protection at ultra-low friction coefficients, can also be created with new chromate-free coating procedures. Chemical nickel platings are distinguished by high corrosion and wear resistance, excellent strength, magnetic properties and good dimensional accuracy. In addition to the provisions of the EU end-of-life vehicles directive, they also fulfil the requirements of the German foodstuff commodities and drinking water ordinance (Lebensmittelbedarfsgegenstände- und Trinkwasserverordnung). Almost all metals and plastics used can be coated.
Surface finishing of light metals
The exhibitors at SURFACTS also offer different finishing systems for light metals such as aluminium and magnesium. These include passivations on the basis of chromate III compounds for aluminium. During this process, oxide hydrates of aluminium and chromate are generated on the surface. This coating temporarily protects the surface against oxidation and also forms a good base for varnishes and adhesives. There are also chromate-free systems available for treating aluminium and magnesium. These develop preservation layers on the surface of the material which provide good temporary corrosion protection. The layers are electroconductive and often serve as an intermediate layer for a varnish or adhesive. Anodisation and hard anodisation are further processes for finishing aluminium surfaces which will be presented at SURFACTS.
Chemical deburring and polishing
Companies are today faced with increasingly complex component geometries and the growing miniaturisation of workpieces, as well as their mechanical post-production work such as deburring and smoothing of surfaces or cleaning of laser cutting edges. SURFACTS also offers efficient solutions for these tasks. One such process is electropolishing. This procedure is, in effect, a reversal of the electroplating process. Under the influence of direct current, metal is removed from the surface of the workpiece in a special electrolyte. After the treatment, the surface is metallically pure, smooth, de-energised and free of cracks, even inside boreholes, apertures and undercuts. Even drilling and grinding burrs directed inwards are removed. These wet chemical procedures also offer advantages with dynamically loaded components, as they are able to remove defects from the surface, thereby increasing the service life of the components. New electropolishing procedures now also enable processing of aluminium die casting and "exotic" metals such as titanium, magnesium, cobalt, tantalum, tungsten, molybdenum and various others.
Added value through integration into the INTERPART supplier trade fair
This year, SURFACTS will be integrated into the INTERPART international supplier trade fair for the first time. This combination offers considerable added value over pure supplier or surface technology trade fairs, as the two events will offer information on supplier products and surface technology services from a single source at one time. In turn, this will increase the number of potential visitors and buyers for exhibitors at SURFACTS.
And alongside INTERPART and SURFACTS, the Karlsruhe Exhibition Centre is also hosting the WTT Expo, the 2nd international specialist trade fair for industrial heat exchanger and heat transfer technology - an industry sector with its own surface treatment requirements. For further information, visit www.surfacts.de.

\#\#\#\#\# in Vol\. 8 \- September Issue \- Year 2007

\# SURFACTS Presents Innovative Surface Technology Processes

Chromate\-free corrosion protection and much more

Karlsruhe – As a showcase for innovative surface treatment processes\, SURFACTS provides an overview of the latest developments in surface treatment\. One particular focus is on processes for substituting corrosion protection and finishing systems containing chrome \(VI\) and heavy metals\. The 4th International Trade Fair for Surface Technology will be held from 9 to 11 October 2007 in Karlsruhe\. SURFACTS will also be integrated in INTERPART\, the international supplier trade fair for the automotive\, mechanical and plant construction industries\. This will generate added value for both events\, since many topics will interest exhibitors and visitors of both trade fairs\.

As a cross\-application technology\, surface technology is playing an increasingly important role in almost all industrial sectors\. A major factor here is corrosion protection\, which will be occupying a prime position at this year\'s SURFACTS from 9 to 11 October in Karlsruhe\. This is currently a hot topic in light of the new EU end\-of\-life vehicle legislation\, which is set to come into effect on 1 July 2007 and bans the use of coatings containing chromate \(VI\) for automotive parts\.

Chromate \(VI\)\-free corrosion protection

The exhibitors at the international specialist trade fair for surface technology are to present new and modified solutions for the corrosion protection of the future\. These are based on chromate \(III\) compounds or offered as fully chromate\-free systems and include an inorganic zinc flake coating based on zinc and aluminium flakes\. Free from chromate and heavy metals\, this coating offers high cathodic corrosion protection without the risk of hydrogen embrittlement\. This coating can be applied to the part multiple times\, depending on corrosion protection requirements\. The primary areas of application are connection elements and high\-strength parts for the automotive and construction industries\. The galvanic separation of highly corrosion resistant zinc\-iron coatings combines functional corrosion protection with attractive surface design\. This procedure can even be safely applied to materials which are difficult to coat\, such as cast iron\. Typical areas of use for zinc\-iron coated components include the automotive and electrical industries\, toolbuilding\, mechanical engineering and sheet\-metal forming\. Galvanically separated zinc\-nickel alloys are mainly used for components in environments which require an extremely high level of corrosion resistance at very high temperatures\, such as engine compartments or the area surrounding brakes\. Corrosion protection can be optimised through use organic or silica\-based sealing\, so\-called top coats\. Multifunctional layers\, which set themselves apart through extremely high corrosion protection and an unusually stable wear protection at ultra\-low friction coefficients\, can also be created with new chromate\-free coating procedures\. Chemical nickel platings are distinguished by high corrosion and wear resistance\, excellent strength\, magnetic properties and good dimensional accuracy\. In addition to the provisions of the EU end\-of\-life vehicles directive\, they also fulfil the requirements of the German foodstuff commodities and drinking water ordinance \(Lebensmittelbedarfsgegenstände\- und Trinkwasserverordnung\)\. Almost all metals and plastics used can be coated\.

Surface finishing of light metals

The exhibitors at SURFACTS also offer different finishing systems for light metals such as aluminium and magnesium\. These include passivations on the basis of chromate III compounds for aluminium\. During this process\, oxide hydrates of aluminium and chromate are generated on the surface\. This coating temporarily protects the surface against oxidation and also forms a good base for varnishes and adhesives\. There are also chromate\-free systems available for treating aluminium and magnesium\. These develop preservation layers on the surface of the material which provide good temporary corrosion protection\. The layers are electroconductive and often serve as an intermediate layer for a varnish or adhesive\. Anodisation and hard anodisation are further processes for finishing aluminium surfaces which will be presented at SURFACTS\.

Chemical deburring and polishing

Companies are today faced with increasingly complex component geometries and the growing miniaturisation of workpieces\, as well as their mechanical post\-production work such as deburring and smoothing of surfaces or cleaning of laser cutting edges\. SURFACTS also offers efficient solutions for these tasks\. One such process is electropolishing\. This procedure is\, in effect\, a reversal of the electroplating process\. Under the influence of direct current\, metal is removed from the surface of the workpiece in a special electrolyte\. After the treatment\, the surface is metallically pure\, smooth\, de\-energised and free of cracks\, even inside boreholes\, apertures and undercuts\. Even drilling and grinding burrs directed inwards are removed\. These wet chemical procedures also offer advantages with dynamically loaded components\, as they are able to remove defects from the surface\, thereby increasing the service life of the components\. New electropolishing procedures now also enable processing of aluminium die casting and \"exotic\" metals such as titanium\, magnesium\, cobalt\, tantalum\, tungsten\, molybdenum and various others\.

Added value through integration into the INTERPART supplier trade fair

This year\, SURFACTS will be integrated into the INTERPART international supplier trade fair for the first time\. This combination offers considerable added value over pure supplier or surface technology trade fairs\, as the two events will offer information on supplier products and surface technology services from a single source at one time\. In turn\, this will increase the number of potential visitors and buyers for exhibitors at SURFACTS\.
And alongside INTERPART and SURFACTS\, the Karlsruhe Exhibition Centre is also hosting the WTT Expo\, the 2nd international specialist trade fair for industrial heat exchanger and heat transfer technology \- an industry sector with its own surface treatment requirements\. For further information\, visit www\.surfacts\.de\.
