Ionic conductivity is strongly influenced by viscosity\, but additional factors such as ion association\, charge correlations\, specific coordination\, and\, in protic ionic liquids \(ILs\)\, proton\-transfer mechanisms\, also affect charge transport\. Clough et al\. found that most of the 11 investigated IL mixture series were well described by a logarithmic conductivity–composition relation\. However\, no clear correlation was found between the non\-ideality parameters derived independently for viscosity and conductivity \[111\]\. Annat et al\. similarly observed approximately logarithmic mixing for several systems\, whereas structurally distinct mixtures showed more complex behavior\; for example\, the conductivity of \[P666\,14\]\[TFSI\]\+\[MPPyr\]\[TFSI\] remained close to that of the phosphonium parent even at xMPPyr \= 0\.5 \[109\]\. Ning et al\. found the conductivities of \[OMIm\]\[BF4\]\+\[OMIm\]\[Cl\]\, \[HMIm\]\[BF4\]\+\[HMIm\]\[Cl\]\, and \[HMIm\]\[PF6\]\+\[HMIm\]\[Cl\] to remain between those of the corresponding neat ILs and to vary inversely with viscosity\. Their fractional Walden slopes were below unity\, indicating appreciable ion association \[115\]\. More pronounced non\-additivity was reported by Zhang et al\. \[116\]\. The authors observed positive deviations for \[DEME\]x\[BMMIm\]1−x\[TFSI\]\, \[DEME\]x\[BMMIm\]1−x\[BF4\]\, and \[BMMIm\]\[TFSI\]x\[BF4\]1−x\. For the latter system\, conductivity peaked at x \= 0\.9\, exceeding the values of both parent ILs\. In contrast\, \[DEME\]\[TFSI\]x\[BF4\]1−x showed a negative deviation\, with conductivity values remaining between those of the parent compounds\. Pameté et al\. demonstrated a strong interdependence among conductivity\, viscosity\, and phase behavior\. At 293 K\, the conductivities of pure \[EMIm\]\[FSI\]\, \[EMIm\]\[BF4\]\, and \[EMIm\]\[TFSI\] were 15\.26\, 12\.16\, and 7\.14 mS cm−1\, respectively\. The mixture \[EMIm\]\[FSI\]0\.6\[BF4\]0\.4 exhibited the highest conductivity among the mixtures at 12\.62 mS cm−1 and also had the lowest viscosity\. Although the room\-temperature conductivity of the mixture was lower than that of pure \[EMIm\]\[FSI\]\, it maintained a conductivity of 0\.46 mS cm−1 at 233 K\, a temperature at which the pure FSI\-based IL was no longer in the liquid state \[71\]\. A similar benefit was observed for the \[EHIm\]\[TFO\]\+\[EHIm\]\[TFSI\] system by Abdurrokhman and Martinelli \[78\]\. They found only small changes in conductivity with composition\; however\, the addition of \[EHIm\]\[TFSI\] strongly suppressed crystallization and widened the liquid\-state temperature range\. In conclusion\, while high conductivity is typically associated with low viscosity\, the relationship is not strictly proportional\. Positive conductivity deviations are advantageous\, although exceeding the conductivity of both parent ILs is not essential\. Suppression of crystallization and preservation of ion transport over a wider temperature range may be equally important\.

\#\#\# 4\.4\. Surface Tension and Interfacial Composition

Surface tension is highly sensitive to the composition of the interfacial layer\, which may differ significantly from the bulk composition \[117\,118\]\. As a result\, IL mixtures can exhibit pronounced deviations from linear mixing behavior\, particularly when the components possess markedly different surface affinities \[40\,119\,120\,121\]\. Koller et al\. reported that adding small amounts of the fluorinated 3\-methyl\-1\-\(3\,3\,4\,4\,4\-pentafluorobutyl\)imidazolium hexafluorophosphate \(\[PFBMIm\]\[PF6\]\) to \[BMIm\]\[PF6\] led to a substantial decrease in surface tension\, consistent with preferential enrichment of the fluorinated component at the interface \[122\]\. Comparable behavior was observed for 1\,3\-bis\(2\-\(2\-methoxyethoxy\)ethyl\)imidazolium iodide \(\[\(mPEG2\)2Im\]\[I\]\)\+\[OMIm\]\[PF6\]\, for which Zhai et al\. identified a negative deviation of approximately −5\.3\% at equimolar composition \[123\]\. An even greater effect was found for the common\-cation mixture \[EMIm\]\[OAc\]\+\[EMIm\]\[TFSI\]\, for which the equimolar mixture showed a −7\.7\% deviation from linear additivity\. Angle\-resolved X\-ray photoelectron spectroscopy \(ARXPS\) confirmed preferential enrichment of \[TFSI\]− at the interface\, especially at low bulk concentrations\, thereby directly linking macroscopic surface tension to microscopic surface composition \[8\]\. Both positive and negative surface tension deviations have been reported\. Buarque et al\. observed positive surface tension deviation for \[2\-HEA\]\[OAc\]\+\[BHEA\]\[OAc\]\, while \[2\-HEA\]\[OAc\]\+\[BHEA\]\[Bu\] showed negative values across the investigated temperature range \[108\]\. Direct evidence for the microscopic origin of such non\-linear behavior was also provided by Paap et al\.\, who combined pendant\-drop measurements with angle\-resolved X\-ray photoelectron spectroscopy to correlate surface tension with surface composition \[117\]\. Overall\, surface tension cannot be reliably predicted from bulk composition alone\, because preferential interfacial segregation may allow even small amounts of a surface\-active IL to exert a disproportionately large influence on interfacial properties\. This behavior provides an additional strategy for tuning wetting\, interfacial mass transfer\, and supported\-liquid\-phase applications without necessarily inducing comparably large changes in bulk properties\.

\#\#\# 4\.5\. Hydrogen Bonding\, Polarity\, Solvatochromism\, and Acid–Base Descriptors

Polarity in ionic liquid mixtures results from Coulombic interactions\, hydrogen bonding\, polarizability\, dispersion forces\, and local ionic organization\. Mixing can redistribute cation–anion contacts and alter both the accessibility and residence time of ions around a solute\, even when macroscopic properties such as density are nearly additive\. Existing studies confirm that hydrogen\-bond structure and dynamics may vary non\-linearly with composition \[22\]\. Molecular simulations indicate that strongly coordinating anions preferentially occupy the hydrogen\-bonding sites of suitable cations and mixing may strengthen specific interactions rather than simply dilute them \[20\]\. Spectroscopic and computational results for \[BMIm\]\[TFSI\]\+\[BMPyr\]\[TFSI\] showed that imidazolium–anion hydrogen bonding is stronger than pyrrolidinium–anion coordination\. Increasing the pyrrolidinium fraction weakened the overall hydrogen\-bond network and changed the cis\/trans conformational distribution of \[TFSI\]− \[22\]\.

Solvatochromic probes offer an effective method for examining these changes\. Reichardt\-type dyes yield the normalized polarity parameter\, while multiprobe approaches provide the Kamlet–Taft parameters\: \(α\) hydrogen\-bond\-donor acidity\, \(β\) hydrogen\-bond\-acceptor basicity\, and \(π\*\) dipolarity\/polarizability\. Thawarkar et al\. reported pronounced positive deviations of the polarity parameter for mixtures of the protic ionic liquid \[HMIm\]\[OAc\] with either \[BMIm\]\[TFSI\] or \[BMPyr\]\[TFSI\]\. At intermediate compositions\, the apparent polarity exceeded that of both parent liquids\. This “hyperpolarity” was attributed to hydrogen\-bond\-mediated restructuring and preferential solvation of the dye\, whereas analogous protic–protic mixtures did not exhibit the same synergistic effect \[124\]\.

Acid–base descriptors can also be related directly to application performance\. In common\-acetate double\-salt ionic liquids containing \[EMIm\]\+\, \[Ch\]\+\, and \[N2222\]\+\, a modified multiparameter relationship incorporating \(α\)\, \(β\)\, \(π\*\)\, and Hammett basicity described catalytic activity with \(R2 \> 0\.994\)\. Hydrogen\-bond basicity was the dominant factor in two mixture families\, whereas dipolarity\/polarizability became more important in the choline–tetraethylammonium system \[82\]\.

Overall\, polarity and acid–base parameters should be treated as composition\-\, temperature\-\, water\-\, and probe\-dependent characteristics of the complete formulation\. No single descriptor fully represents the solvation environment\, and parameters obtained for the parent ionic liquids should not be assumed to mix linearly\.

\#\# 5\. Conclusions and Future Perspective

Ionic liquid \(IL\) mixtures extend the designer\-solvent concept by introducing composition as an additional\, continuously adjustable variable\. Mixing can suppress crystallization\, modify ion association and hydrogen\-bond networks\, alter preferential coordination\, and change interfacial organization\. Consequently\, the application\-optimal composition is not necessarily equimolar or eutectic and generally cannot be predicted by linear interpolation of the properties of the parent ILs\.

The most relevant composition–property relationships depend strongly on the intended application\. In low\-temperature batteries and supercapacitors\, for example\, crystallization suppression and the preservation of conductivity over a broad temperature range may be more important than achieving the highest conductivity at room temperature\. Mixed\-anion systems can additionally modify Li\+ coordination\, proton\-transfer pathways\, and ion packing within electrode pores\. In aromatic extraction and extractive distillation\, polarity and preferential solvation determine capacity and selectivity\, whereas viscosity\, phase disengagement\, and solvent recovery ultimately govern process feasibility\. In cellulose processing\, chloride and acetate can cooperatively disrupt cellulose hydrogen bonding\, although the outcome depends strongly on their relative proportions and on the cation structure\. Replacing part of the acetate with a less basic anion\, such as thiocyanate\, may improve fluidity but can substantially reduce cellulose dissolution\. In catalysis\, composition can be used to adjust acidity\, basicity\, polarity\, and the accessibility of active ions\. Electrospray propulsion depends on the combined effects of conductivity\, viscosity\, surface tension\, and cluster formation\, whereas luminescent mixtures exploit composition\-dependent nanoheterogeneity around the emitting species\. Biological activity and toxicity must likewise be assessed directly because mixtures may exhibit additive\, antagonistic\, or synergistic effects\.

Gas separation is a particularly important example of the possibilities offered by IL mixtures\, as the composition can be used to tune gas solubility\, selectivity\, phase behavior\, viscosity\, and transport properties simultaneously\. However\, the available evidence shows that the effect of mixing is highly system\-specific\. CO2 solubility may show positive deviations from linear mixing at selected compositions and pressures\, whereas CO2\/N2 or CO2\/CH4 selectivity may remain intermediate between the values of the pure ILs\. Improved CO2 uptake alone should therefore not be regarded as evidence of superior separation performance\. Instead\, capacity\, selectivity\, permeability\, diffusivity\, and regeneration behavior should be evaluated together\. A central priority for future studies is to move from pure\-gas measurements towards realistic mixed\-gas testing\. Predictions based solely on single\-gas Henry’s law constants may therefore fail to represent solvent behavior adequately in biogas upgrading\, natural\-gas sweetening\, pre\-combustion capture\, or flue\-gas treatment\. Experiments should consequently employ representative gas mixtures containing CO2\, N2\, CH4 and\, where relevant\, acid gases and water vapor\, across realistic ranges of pressure\, temperature\, and feed composition\.

A central priority for future studies is to move from pure\-gas measurements towards realistic mixed\-gas testing\. Predictions based solely on single\-gas Henry’s law constants may therefore fail to represent solvent behavior adequately in biogas upgrading\, natural\-gas sweetening\, pre\-combustion capture\, or flue\-gas treatment\. Experiments should consequently employ representative gas mixtures containing CO2\, N2\, CH4 and\, where relevant\, other feed components such as acid gases and water vapor\, across realistic ranges of pressure\, temperature\, and composition\. Because the effects of water were not systematically evaluated in the studies reviewed here\, no general conclusions regarding its influence on IL mixture performance can be drawn\. Nevertheless\, for applications involving humid gas streams\, water content should be reported and controlled so that its possible influence on phase behavior\, viscosity\, gas sorption\, and transport can be distinguished from the intrinsic effects of IL mixture composition\.

The trade\-off between reactivity and mass transfer likewise requires systematic consideration\. Basic\, acetate\-containing\, amino\-functionalized\, or otherwise reactive components can enhance CO2 affinity through chemisorption\, but may simultaneously increase viscosity\, slow transport\, complicate regeneration\, or introduce absorption–desorption hysteresis\. Less reactive components\, in contrast\, may improve fluidity and favor physical sorption\, particularly at elevated pressures\. For these reasons\, future solvent development should rely on multi\-objective optimization rather than maximizing a single equilibrium property\. Relevant objectives include CO2 capacity at the intended partial pressure\, selectivity against relevant co\-gases\, absorption and desorption kinetics\, viscosity\, diffusivity\, thermal and oxidative stability\, susceptibility to water\, liquid\-phase stability\, membrane retention where supported ionic liquid membranes are used\, and the energy required for solvent regeneration\.

Molecular\-level characterization should be integrated with macroscopic separation measurements\. Combining spectroscopic methods\, scattering techniques\, molecular simulations\, and gas\-sorption experiments would help establish direct structure–property relationships relevant to gas separation\.

The development of reliable machine learning models for IL mixtures is still limited by the amount and consistency of available experimental data\. Many datasets cover only a few compositions\, narrow temperature or pressure ranges\, or a limited number of IL families\. Future studies should therefore report the full ionic composition\, several mixture compositions including the pure\-component endpoints\, temperature\, pressure\, water content\, purity\, and experimental uncertainty\. It would also be useful to measure several relevant properties for the same compositions under the same conditions\, for example density\, viscosity\, conductivity\, phase behavior\, solubility\, selectivity\, and application performance\. Reporting both high\-performing and poor\-performing compositions is important to avoid biased datasets\. More standardized and machine\-readable data would improve model training\, validation\, and multiobjective optimization of IL mixtures\.

records.abstract: To manage heat dissipation and maintain system stability, system designers look to liquid cooling and heat sinks as effective solutions. ... compact form factors and innovative thermal management options ... This innovative approach provides a reliable, thermally efficient solution, allowing data centers to handle increasing traffic demands and achieve optimal performance.
records.summary: This Molex product page describes connector and cabling solutions intended for data center Ethernet switches, framing the engineering problem as the need for higher throughput and lower latency alongside compact, high-port-density designs and efficient heat dissipation. The described mechanisms include high-density external I/O connectors (OSFP, QSFP-DD, SFP-DD, CDFP, QSFP, SFP+, zSFP), internal high-speed connectors supporting PCIe Gen 6 and 224Gbps PAM4, backplane and mezzanine connectors, high-power connectors, and optical connectivity (MPO, LC, MDC). Molex states that its BiPass I/O system replaces lossy PCBs with high-speed twinax cabling to reduce insertion loss and improve signal integrity, and that liquid cooling and heat sinks are among the thermal approaches designers use. The page is vendor marketing material rather than a peer-reviewed experiment; it reports product specifications and supported standards but no measured performance data, test conditions, or comparisons to prior art.
records.why_it_matters: For switch interconnect selection, the page indicates that connector choice must be co-designed with thermal strategy and port density, since high-density I/O and 224Gbps-class signaling are presented alongside liquid cooling and heat-sink options rather than as independent decisions.

It is a marketing catalog with spec tables but no measured performance data, test methods, or traceable sources; thermal content is generic and not connector-specific.

records.body_text:
High-Performance Ethernet Switch Connectors
As data centers evolve, the demand for high-speed performance, reliable signal integrity and efficient heat management in Ethernet switches continues to grow. Navigating these challenges while maximizing port density requires innovative interconnect solutions. Molex delivers advanced technologies that enhance signal performance and optimize thermal efficiency, aligned with the next generation of networking infrastructure.
Overcoming Data Center Ethernet Switch Challenges with Advanced Interconnects
For data centers to meet the demands of high-speed, data-intensive applications and avoid bottlenecks, switches need to support lower latency and increased throughput. Additionally, physical space constraints often require switches and components to optimize port density and maintain compact designs. Efficient heat dissipation across the system is also critical for ensuring long-term operational reliability.
Advanced interconnects and high-performance cabling deliver the bandwidth and low latency required for next-generation data rates. High-density connectors, like QSFP-DD and SFP-DD, allow for greater port density in limited spaces. To manage heat dissipation and maintain system stability, system designers look to liquid cooling and heat sinks as effective solutions.
Molex provides the advanced Ethernet switch components that overcome these obstacles, supporting the latest standards like PCIe Gen 6 and Ethernet 224Gbps PAM4. With superior signal integrity (SI) even at high frequencies, compact form factors and innovative thermal management options, Ethernet switch components from Molex empower data centers to perform at peak efficiency.
Featured Products
High-Speed Internal I/O Connectors
As data rates increase, maintaining signal integrity becomes critical for handling high frequencies without loss or distortion. High-density connectors from Molex are designed to support leading-edge standards like PCIe Gen 6 and 224Gbps PAM4, to support reliable signal integrity and high-speed performance across complex data environments.

records.body_text:
Functionally Speaking: A Bright Future for Surface Finishing is in Our Hands
Earlier this year I wrote the article “Fabrication to Finishing to Assembly: A Stronger Voice by Aligning Affiliated Industries.”
That piece was about the metals ecosystem—fabricators, finishers, assemblers—and the strength that comes from lining up together. This one is about a different kind of voice: how our industry talks about itself.
Ask anyone in automotive, airlines, aerospace, defense, space, or medical devices where they would be without chemical surface treatment. The answer: out of luck. That’s the polite version, since I couldn’t print the F-word everyone is thinking.
Surface finishing makes the part look right, resist corrosion, and take the wear in all kinds of environments. It’s not a nice-to-have. Think about that the next time you’re driving a car, flying in a plane, talking to someone with an artificial limb, or wondering what is keeping a satellite working in space.
Why are Regulators Aggressive Towards Finishers?
If the work we provide is that essential, why do the public, regulators, and localities so often take an aggressive stance against the shops that do it? Why the hearings, the “not in my backyard,” the assumption that finishing is a problem to be contained rather than a capability manufacturing cannot fly without?
Maybe it’s because we keep inviting them into the wrong room.
Think about the finest steak restaurant. Guests don’t have the appetite for the slaughterhouse or what goes on in the kitchen. It’s all about the dining room—the plate that arrives, that well-prepared, juicy steak.
To many people, surface finishing is the slaughterhouse and the kitchen. Tanks. Chemistry. Airborne exposure. Wastewater. That is the story they already think they know. They never see the satellite, the airframe, the implant. They see the tank. Then they vote, write the rule, and tell their kids to look for work somewhere else. Sometimes we are our own worst enemy. How many times have you heard, even in the shop, “who wants to be a plater?”
There’s a story, probably embellished and maybe made up, that got me thinking about how we should be talking. During the early 1960s, as part of the space race, President Kennedy visited a NASA center and introduced himself to a janitor sweeping the floor. When Kennedy asked what he did at NASA, the janitor didn’t say he cleaned the building. He said he was helping put a man on the moon.
Why a car lasts, why a plane flies, why a satellite stays on station, why a device can go in a body. That’s our story. But telling it through public relations, marketing, and recruiting the next generation was never anyone’s main assignment.
I got a chance to try that thinking. On the way to SUR/FIN, a TSA agent asked what I was going to Chicago for. I said a trade show for surface finishing. When he asked what that was, I didn’t mention chemicals or plating. I said it was the work that helps keep aircraft doing what they are supposed to do. Much to my surprise, he started talking about how a wing flexes in flight. He got it.
It happened again in my driveway on a Saturday. A maintenance guy from one of our plating-shop customers was looking for some weekend work, and believe me, I had projects for him. My neighbor—young, family, homebrews his beer, used to jump out of planes before the kids—works for a large company that builds satellites. He saw the shop name on the guy’s shirt, came over, and said, “Hey, your company does some of our plating.” They talked for a while. He wasn’t thinking about the tanks and the processes. He saw the parts that keep a satellite on station.
What’s Missing in All of This?
A lot of good work is already happening. Suppliers are doing their part with alternative chemistries. Platers are doing their part by installing air-handling and water-treatment systems in their facilities. Associations, nationally and locally, are doing their part through advocacy, government relations, technical education, and funding sound science. The primes are doing their part by approving those alternative chemistries so shops can run them. Back to the restaurant: the kitchen is getting cleaner, safer, and easier to defend. That’s real progress. But it isn’t what’s missing.
What’s missing is something we never really had to focus on in the past: promoting and marketing surface finishing itself, and the value it delivers. You know, the dining room.
Why a car lasts, why a plane flies, why a satellite stays on station, why a device can go in a body. That’s our story. But telling it through public relations, marketing, and recruiting the next generation was never anyone’s main assignment.
The next generation—students and people early on in their careers—need to hear something else: this is a good gig, with real careers at every level
The industry around us has changed and is still changing. Surface finishing is contracting, as are other trades. Perception is part of it. So is reality: the cost of staying in compliance and the cost of doing business keep climbing. In the past, the work found you. Even today, many finishers have a website and maybe a LinkedIn or Instagram page, but they are operating without a sales force. When our associations rally members, it’s usually to fight a new regulation or a city council deciding whether to regulate us or eliminate us. We are always playing defense. It’s time to go on offense, positively.
Learning From Other Industries
If we look at other industries facing some of these same challenges, we can learn from them. Trucking still fights hours-of-service rules and the public’s view of diesel and wrecks. They also sold the dining room: if you bought it, a truck brought it—and later, Nothing Without Trucking. Beef still has packing plants. They didn’t advertise the kill floor. They advertised dinner. Mining’s association says Minerals Make Life. Paper and packaging went with How Life Unfolds. None of them stopped advocating or doing the science. They just stopped letting the plant be the only story.
We can fill the gap the same way I did with the TSA agent, and the way my neighbor did in my driveway: start with the finished product. With officials, that means jobs, tax base, defense readiness, and supply chain. The next generation—students and people early on in their careers—need to hear something else: this is a good gig, with real careers at every level. You can come in from high school, a trade program, or a four-year degree. You can stay on the line, move into quality or EHS, run a process, run a plant, or own one. Attracting them takes more than promoting the industry to the public. It means showing up at high schools, trade schools, and community colleges (counselors, CTE teachers, chem labs) with a career ladder in hand and a plant tour on the calendar.
Here’s what that ladder can look like. And that’s only the plant floor. A finishing plant also hires in sales, estimating, customer service, shipping, HR, finance, and IT. It’s a company, not a tank room.
Career Ladder: Same Plant, Many Paths
Start here: High school; 0–2 yrs | Skilled:
2–5 yrs
| Lead/Specialist:
4–8 yrs
| Manager & Up:
7+ yrs
---|---|---|---
Plating & anodizing | Racker / Masker; Entry Plater | Multi-Process Plater; Anodize Tech | Lead Plater | Production Mgr → Plant Mgr / GM → VP Ops
Paint & prep | Blast / Deburr Prep Tech | Painter (liquid or powder) | Paint Supervisor | Production Manager
Quality | Quality Inspector; NDT Level I | NDT Level II | QC Lead; Quality Engineer | Quality Manager
Lab & process | Lab Technician | Technical Service Rep | Process Engineer | Lab Manager / Chief Chemist
EHS & wastewater | Waste Treatment Assistant | Certified Wastewater Operator | Compliance Specialist | EHS Manager
Maintenance | — | Maintenance Technician | Lead Multi-Craft Tech | Maintenance Manager
How you move up | On-the-job training; safety certs (HAZWOPER) | AESF CEF; NDT Level II; CWEA wastewater cert | Supervisor training; Six Sigma Green Belt; CQE | Experience plus leadership; degree helps; not always required
Whatever Someone’s Background, There’s a Path
That’s the school packet: one table, one tour, and one sentence like the one that worked on the TSA agent. Whatever someone’s background, there’s a path. Some will be drawn to the lab, some to running the process, some to estimating, and some to keeping a satellite contractor’s parts in spec.
I wish I could snap my fingers and everyone would say this is a great industry to be in. That is not how it works. If we mean Made in the USA—and staying in the USA—local and national associations have to add promotion and the next generation to the mission. I’m not saying instead of advocacy, government relations, and the science. I’m saying in addition to.
The good news is we don’t have to invent the whole toolbox. The AESF Foundation, NASF’s education arm, already trains and certifies—CEF, CAF, MSF—and runs scholarships for students in chemistry and materials. Chapters add their own awards. Shops can pay for the course and put a bonus on passing, which some already do. Manufacturing Day is on the calendar every October: open the door, walk a class through, talk about the part that goes on the plane.
Keep the suppliers on chemistry. Keep the platers on air and water treatment. Keep the associations on advocacy, government relations, and the science. Keep the primes on approvals. Then market the value.
Other associations already invest in schools. SME’s education foundation runs PRIME—manufacturing labs, curriculum, and teacher training inside high schools, free to the school. FMA’s foundation, SparkForce, funds summer camps and scholarships that include trade school and community college, not only the four-year. AWS SENSE is the welding curriculum high schools and tech colleges use, including to line up Perkins dollars. Those programs are running now. We don’t need a new organization. We need to copy the on-ramp.
Public money is available if someone will fill out the paperwork. In California, the Employment Training Panel reimburses manufacturers for training people already on the clock and people just hired. Workforce boards under WIOA can fund on-the-job training. Perkins dollars sit in the high-school CTE and community-college system, waiting for an employer to help design the class. Registered apprenticeships exist; manufacturing is a priority sector. None of that money shows up on its own. It shows up when a shop or an association asks for it.
Promotion and Workforce Should Be in the Written Mission
So the snap-your-fingers list is actually short and doable. Put promotion and workforce in the written mission. Build a one-page school packet and a speaker list. Host a Manufacturing Day tour. Get two shops onto an ETP or WIOA contract this year. Fund a scholarship that includes trade school, not just the college junior year. Lead with the finished product, the way I did with the TSA agent, at every hearing, every counselor visit, and every plant tour. That’s not pie in the sky. That’s work.
Keep the suppliers on chemistry. Keep the platers on air and water treatment. Keep the associations on advocacy, government relations, and the science. Keep the primes on approvals. Then market the value. Cars that last. Planes that fly. Satellites that stay on station. Devices that can be implanted. If we want a future that looks like that, we have to stop leading with the kitchen.
It’s time to go on offense. Who’s in?
Dan Zinman is the Chief Commercial Officer for Miles Chemical in Arleta, California. He has been active in industry trade groups for decades, and currently sits on the board of the Metal Finishing Association of Southern California.

Some will be drawn to the lab\, some to running the process\, some to estimating\, and some to keeping a satellite contractor’s parts in spec\.

I wish I could snap my fingers and everyone would say this is a great industry to be in\. That is not how it works\. If we mean Made in the USA—and staying in the USA—local and national associations have to add promotion and the next generation to the mission\. I’m not saying instead of advocacy\, government relations\, and the science\. I’m saying in addition to\.

The good news is we don’t have to invent the whole toolbox\. The AESF Foundation\, NASF’s education arm\, already trains and certifies—CEF\, CAF\, MSF—and runs scholarships for students in chemistry and materials\. Chapters add their own awards\. Shops can pay for the course and put a bonus on passing\, which some already do\. Manufacturing Day is on the calendar every October\: open the door\, walk a class through\, talk about the part that goes on the plane\.

\#\#\#\# Keep the suppliers on chemistry\. Keep the platers on air and water treatment\. Keep the associations on advocacy\, government relations\, and the science\. Keep the primes on approvals\. Then market the value\.

Other associations already invest in schools\. SME’s education foundation runs PRIME—manufacturing labs\, curriculum\, and teacher training inside high schools\, free to the school\. FMA’s foundation\, SparkForce\, funds summer camps and scholarships that include trade school and community college\, not only the four\-year\. AWS SENSE is the welding curriculum high schools and tech colleges use\, including to line up Perkins dollars\. Those programs are running now\. We don’t need a new organization\. We need to copy the on\-ramp\.

Public money is available if someone will fill out the paperwork\. In California\, the Employment Training Panel reimburses manufacturers for training people already on the clock and people just hired\. Workforce boards under WIOA can fund on\-the\-job training\. Perkins dollars sit in the high\-school CTE and community\-college system\, waiting for an employer to help design the class\. Registered apprenticeships exist\; manufacturing is a priority sector\. None of that money shows up on its own\. It shows up when a shop or an association asks for it\.

\#\#\#\# Promotion and Workforce Should Be in the Written Mission

So the snap\-your\-fingers list is actually short and doable\. Put promotion and workforce in the written mission\. Build a one\-page school packet and a speaker list\. Host a Manufacturing Day tour\. Get two shops onto an ETP or WIOA contract this year\. Fund a scholarship that includes trade school\, not just the college junior year\. Lead with the finished product\, the way I did with the TSA agent\, at every hearing\, every counselor visit\, and every plant tour\. That’s not pie in the sky\. That’s work\.

Keep the suppliers on chemistry\. Keep the platers on air and water treatment\. Keep the associations on advocacy\, government relations\, and the science\. Keep the primes on approvals\. Then market the value\. Cars that last\. Planes that fly\. Satellites that stay on station\. Devices that can be implanted\. If we want a future that looks like that\, we have to stop leading with the kitchen\.

It’s time to go on offense\. Who’s in\?

Dan Zinman is the Chief Commercial Officer for Miles Chemical in Arleta\, California\. He has been active in industry trade groups for decades\, and currently sits on the board of the Metal Finishing Association of Southern California\.

records.summary: Rosenberger's GFC® (Glass Fiber Connector) is a company-announced fiber-optic connector standard for in-vehicle data communication, positioned as a complement to existing coaxial and differential copper solutions as automotive bandwidth demands rise. The announcement states the system supports data rates of over 50 Gbps over distances up to 40 meters and is fully IEEE 802.3cz-compliant. It is described as developed for harsh automotive environments per ISO 24581, meeting mechanical and environmental requirements of ISO 8092 and DIN 70214, and having passed Arizona dust and water tests. The connector supports OM3 and OM4 multimode fibers at 850 nm and 980 nm, is protocol-independent (Ethernet and PCIe-based applications cited), and is offered as a straight cable plug, straight cable coupler, and angled PCB connector. Robustness is attributed in part to an Expanded-Beam Principle that enlarges the optically effective surface across the fiber transition to reduce dust/contaminant sensitivity and end-face wear.
records.why_it_matters: For zonal vehicle architectures, a protocol-independent, IEEE 802.3cz-compliant multimode fiber connector rated above 50 Gbps over up to 40 m gives OEMs a candidate physical layer for backbone links between central computers and zone controllers without committing to a single upper-layer protocol.

GFC® – Optical Connectivity in Vehicles
From Copper to Fiber Optics: Rosenberger Sets New Standards for In-Vehicle Data Communication with GFC®
With a forward-looking fiber-optic standard supporting data rates of over 50 Gbps over transmission distances of up to 40 meters, Rosenberger is marking the next step in evolution
Automotive data communication is on the verge of a paradigm shift: Copper-based connections are reaching their physical limits—fiber optics takes over. Rosenberger is driving this technological transformation and, with GFC® (Glass Fiber Connector), presents a forward-looking fiber-optic standard for the automotive sector. The system enables data transfer rates of over 50 Gbps over distances of up to 40 meters, is fully IEEE 802.3cz-compliant, and marks the next evolutionary step for automotive applications—complementing proven coaxial and differential copper connection solutions.
The growing demand for in-vehicle data transmission is increasingly pushing established copper-based connectivity technologies to their limits. High-resolution camera and display systems, autonomous driving, and centralized vehicle architectures are driving the required bandwidth to unprecedented levels. As a result, both the volume of data and the requirements for signal integrity and electromagnetic compatibility are rising. Optical connections are ideally suited to meet these challenges. They offer virtually unlimited bandwidth even over long distances, excellent EMC performance, and low latency.
Robust and Designed for High-Volume Production
GFC® was specifically developed for use in harsh automotive environments in accordance with ISO 24581. Furthermore, it also meets the mechanical and environmental requirements of ISO 8092 and DIN 70214, the successor standard to the former USCAR-2 and LV 214. The system has also successfully passed the Arizona dust and water tests.
GFC® supports OM3 and OM4 multimode fibers at 850 nm and 980 nm. A key advantage is its complete protocol independence. In addition to Ethernet, PCIe-based applications, for example, can also be implemented, enabling a high degree of flexibility for future vehicle architectures. The connector system is available as a straight cable plug, a straight cable coupler, and an angled PCB connector. At the same time, it is designed for highly automated manufacturing and high-volume assembly.
EBM - The Expanded Beam Principle
The solution’s high resilience to environmental influences is achieved, in part, through the Expanded-Beam Principle. In this process, light is transmitted across the transition between fibers via an enlarged optically effective surface. This significantly reduces the impact of dust and other contaminants, enables a wear-free connection of the optical fibers, and prevents scratches on the fiber end faces. As a result, the technology is also suitable for demanding environments.
For Zonal Vehicle Architectures and Data-intensive Applications
GFC® is specifically designed for future zonal vehicle architectures. Potential applications include backbone connections between central computers and zone controllers, data aggregation and forwarding for central processing, and high-resolution camera and display connections. It also supports the implementation of data redundancy between two central processing units and applications with longer transmission distances.
In addition to automotive applications, GFC® is also suitable for heavy-duty applications—such as in mining, trucks, trailers, and agricultural machinery—due to its robustness.
“With GFC®, we are setting a fiber-optic standard that combines the performance of optical data transmission with the robustness and integration capabilities required by automotive applications. Thanks to our decades of expertise in fiber-optic technology—proven in data centers worldwide—we can adapt established network technologies into automotive-qualified solutions and support OEMs and Tier 1 suppliers from the concept phase through to series production,”
says Sebastian Mysyk, Director, Product Management Automotive Data Connectors at Rosenberger.

RI Regulators Cite Electrolizing Over Hazardous Waste Issues at Chrome Plating Facility
Rhode Island environmental regulators have issued a “Notice of Intent to Enforce” against Electrolizing Inc. following an inspection of the company's Providence chrome plating facility.
The report identified a series of alleged hazardous waste violations involving chromic acid, containment pits and waste-management practices.
The Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management (RIDEM) issued the notice Sept. 25 to Billy Brauer, general manager of Electrolizing Inc. The agency said it has reasonable grounds to believe Electrolizing and property owner B&J Properties violated statutes or regulations under RIDEM's jurisdiction.
The enforcement action provides a detailed look at hazardous waste management challenges at a working chrome plating operation. It could offer lessons for other finishing companies that generate and manage hazardous waste.
Complaints Lead to RIDEM Inspection
The investigation began after RIDEM received two anonymous complaints on Aug. 25 alleging problems with chemical containment at the facility. One alleged that a containment area holding liquids that included chromium compounds, water, alkaline materials, and acids could be leaking into the ground. Another raised concerns about changing liquid levels in a containment area.
RIDEM inspected the facility the following day. According to the agency's enforcement notice, Brauer told inspectors that in July, Tank No. 10 on an aluminum processing line had leaked approximately 100 to 200 gallons of chromic acid into a containment pit beneath the line. The company subsequently took the tank out of service while it awaited a replacement.
The document says Brauer told RIDEM that the liquid level in the containment pit had increased significantly since the tank leak. He believed chromic acid in the pit was mixing with water from sources including condensation, steam leaks, and groundwater entering the pit.
Inspectors reported observing substantial amounts of liquid waste in containment pits underneath several processing areas. In one area, the agency says Billy Brauer indicated that the employee responsible for maintaining liquid accumulation levels had resigned and that monitoring logs could not be found. According to the notice, liquid levels were measured with a stick marked in 6-inch increments.
Tests Find Chromium and Cadmium
Laboratory testing became another significant part of RIDEM's case. According to the notice, Electrolizing Inc. provided RIDEM with an Aug. 17 analytical report from Phoenix Environmental containing results for waste-liquid mixtures sampled from three containment pits underneath separate plating lines. The samples underwent Toxicity Characteristic Leaching Procedure testing.
RIDEM said the sample from the containment pit serving Tanks Nos. 1-6 exceeded the RCRA toxicity thresholds for cadmium, with a reported result of 12.7 mg/L, and chromium, reported at 546,000 mg/L. The pit serving Tanks Nos. 7-9 had reported results of 2.11 mg/L for cadmium and 25,000 mg/L for chromium, also exceeding the applicable toxicity thresholds cited by the agency.
The sample from the containment pit serving Tanks Nos. 10 and 11 exceeded the chromium toxicity threshold with a reported result of 1,070 mg/L and had a reported pH of 2, placing it at the corrosivity regulatory level cited by RIDEM.
Scrubber Leaks and Chromic Acid Also Cited
RIDEM's inspection extended beyond the containment pits. On the facility's mezzanine, inspectors observed an air scrubber connected to Chromic Acid Plating Tanks Nos. 1, 2 and 3. According to the enforcement notice, Brauer said the unit had experienced leaks over the years because of its age. Inspectors observed drip pans, containment trays, cardboard, and absorbent pads beneath the unit.
RIDEM also reported observing chromic acid on the mezzanine floor and alleged there had been no apparent effort to clean up or contain that particular release. Inspectors additionally reported finding two drip pans containing waste chromic acid that were uncovered, unlabeled, and lacked accumulation start dates.
The enforcement notice says Brauer suggested that previous leaks from the scrubber may have allowed chromic acid to enter hollow concrete blocks before eventually migrating through the wall. RIDEM directed the company to conduct analytical soil testing outside the building to determine whether hazardous materials may have reached the environment. ￼
RIDEM further alleged that Electrolizing Inc. failed to report chromic acid spills that accumulated below the scrubber and seeped through the building wall.
Waste-Management Procedures Under Scrutiny
The enforcement action also focuses heavily on the facility's hazardous waste management systems.
On Sept. 1, Brauer told RIDEM that Electrolizing Inc. did not have a procedure in place to pump out containment pits after hazardous waste was released or spilled into them, according to the notice.
RIDEM subsequently reviewed the company's hazardous waste contingency plan and personnel training program. The agency said its review found that both documents lacked required elements and did not satisfy Rhode Island's hazardous waste rules.
The state also alleged issues involving waste labeling, accumulation dates and spill records. A separate ecoRI News report says the notice identified 13 hazardous waste regulatory violations, including allegations involving labeling, recordkeeping, waste storage, and spill reporting.
Company Required to Respond
The Sept. 25 letter requires Electrolizing Inc. to submit a written response within 10 days stating its intentions to comply with RIDEM's required actions within the specified timeframes.
Importantly, the document is a Notice of Intent to Enforce, representing RIDEM's initial enforcement response to the alleged violations rather than a final adjudication of those allegations.
RIDEM also notified the company that it intends to assess administrative monetary penalties and said noncompliance in these matters could carry maximum penalties of up to $25,000 per violation, per day. The agency said the notice does not prevent it from subsequently issuing a Notice of Violation assessing administrative penalties.
Electrolizing Inc., an Armoloy company, specializes in precision surface treatments and offers processes including thin dense chrome, biocompatible chromium and several nickel coatings. Its company website says the Providence operation traces its work in surface treatment to 1945.

U.S. Lubricants Names Adam Puzach President as Pack Logix Integration Advances
U.S. Lubricants has named Adam Puzach president as the company continues integrating Pack Logix, the blending and packaging business acquired by parent company U.S. Venture earlier this year.
Puzach had served as president and CEO of Pack Logix before the April acquisition. Following the transaction, he became vice president and general manager of packaging and operations for U.S. Lubricants. His move into the president’s role places him at the center of a broader effort to combine lubricant distribution with blending, packaging, custom formulation and private-label manufacturing.
James Williams, who had been president of U.S. Lubricants, will continue to lead the division’s national sales strategy as vice president of sales, according to the company.
“The acquisition of Pack Logix has poised U.S. Lubricants uniquely in the marketplace as a fully integrated platform, providing its partners a single point of contact for all of their lubricant needs,” Puzach said in announcing his appointment.
U.S. Lubricants distributes automotive, commercial and industrial lubricants and fluids, including major branded products, while also manufacturing its proprietary THRIVE lubricant line. The addition of Pack Logix brought in-house blending and packaging, toll-blending, custom formulation and private-label capabilities.
The company says it moves nearly 14 million gallons of lubricants annually through its regional and national network.
More Than a Packaging Acquisition
When U.S. Venture announced the Pack Logix acquisition on April 16, it described the transaction as more than an expansion of packaging capacity. The combination was expected to provide greater toll-blending capacity, broader packaging options and a more integrated supply chain.
Pack Logix brought 36 employees into the organization, along with experience in custom formulations, private-label programs and specialty packaging. U.S. Lubricants said at the time that the business would be systematically integrated over the following year.
Puzach’s appointment suggests that integration is becoming an increasingly important part of the company’s strategy.
For lubricant distributors, the traditional model has centered largely on representing major brands and moving finished products from suppliers to customers. U.S. Lubricants is expanding that model by adding capabilities farther upstream in the value chain, including formulation, blending, packaging and contract manufacturing.
That can provide greater control over product availability, packaging formats, private-label programs and supply-chain response—capabilities that have taken on added significance during a year marked by substantial base-oil and finished-lubricant supply disruptions.
U.S. Lubricants said earlier this year that its growth had enabled it to secure higher contracted volumes with base-oil and additive suppliers. The company also said the Pack Logix acquisition was attracting additional supplier interest, although it remained exposed to the same market-driven price increases affecting the broader industry.
Puzach said his priorities as president will include maintaining the company’s growth, strengthening customer relationships and positioning the business for long-term success.
“We’ve built strong momentum, and I’m focused on continuing that growth, deepening our customer relationships, and positioning this team for long-term success,” he said.
Eric Kessenich, CEO of U.S. Venture, said Puzach’s experience fits what the company sees as the next stage for the lubricant division and pointed specifically to the continuing integration of Pack Logix.
The broader question now is how far U.S. Lubricants intends to take the integrated model. The combination of distribution, proprietary lubricants, blending, packaging and private-label manufacturing gives the company a broader platform than it had before the acquisition.
Whether that ultimately leads to deeper penetration in existing markets, broader geographic expansion, additional acquisitions or further growth in contract manufacturing remains to be seen.
For now, Puzach’s appointment makes clear that Pack Logix is becoming an important part of the direction of U.S. Lubricants, rather than simply operating as an acquired packaging business.
About U.S. Lubricants
U.S. Lubricants brings 50 years of experience delivering automotive, commercial and industrial fluids. The company combines authorized distribution of top-tier brands with the manufacturing of its proprietary THRIVE® lubricants, supported by in-house blending and packaging capabilities. Moving nearly 14 million gallons annually through an integrated regional and national network, U.S. Lubricants helps customers maximize performance, efficiency and supply continuity. Headquartered in Appleton, Wisconsin, U.S. Lubricants is a U.S. Venture company.
About U.S. Venture, Inc.
For more than 75 years, U.S. Venture, Inc. has been active in the distribution of renewable and traditional energy products, lubricants, tires and parts, as well as data-driven energy and logistics solutions. Its family of brands includes U.S. Energy®, U.S. AutoForce, Breakthrough®, U.S. Lubricants and IGEN®.

records.body_text:
Navigating the Shift: Trivalent Chromium Plating in the Automotive Steel Market
MKS Atotech details the path to success to adopting trivalent chromium plating for automotive steel bumpers and exterior components.
Share
Read Next
This paper is based on a presentation originally given at SUR/FIN 2026 in Rosemont, Illinois on June 2, 2026, in Session 3: Automotive Surface Finishing. Decorative trivalent plating processes have been available for several decades, yet widespread adoption has faced significant industry hurdles. Debates regarding chloride-based chemistries versus sulfate-based chemistries, coupled with rigorous requirements for interior and exterior performance, have created a complex landscape for suppliers, applicators and OEMs alike.
This article reviews the strategic transition of automotive steel into the trivalent chromium market. By examining barriers to entry and the technical evolution of these processes, it outlines how the industry is successfully navigating regulatory and performance demands to implement sustainable, high-quality plating solutions.
The full presentation can be accessed and printed at short.pfonline.com/NASF26-Nov2.

AkzoNobel Powder Coatings Earns Double Recognition at Maxion Wheels Supplier Awards
The Green Wheel 2025 Award and the Supplier of the Year 2025 Americas honors sustainability ambitions, collaborative strength and consistent performance gains derived from AkzoNobel and its teams.
Share
Read Next
AkzoNobel Powder Coatings (Reading, Pennsylvania) has earned two supplier awards from Maxion Wheels (Northville, Michigan), recognizing its role in sustainable innovation and its collaboration with the wheel manufacturer. The company;s team in the Czech Republic received the Green Wheel 2025 Award, while its Brazil team was named Supplier of the Year 2025 Americas.
“AkzoNobel has been a reliable partner and an important contributor to our success over many years,” says Pia Schuetz, VP of global purchasing at Maxion Wheels. “Their contribution goes well beyond supplying high-quality coatings. The teams bring deep technical expertise, helping us optimize application processes, achieve consistently strong coating performance and develop practical solutions that improve efficiency and support our sustainability goals. Combined with responsive technical support and dependable day-to-day service, that makes this a true partnership, and one we value enormously.”
The Green Wheel 2025 Award recognizes suppliers that support Maxion Wheels’ sustainability ambitions. For AkzoNobel, the award reflects a long-term focus on reducing emissions, advancing responsible sourcing and developing coating solutions designed to help customers reduce their environmental impact.
The Supplier of the Year 2025 Americas award celebrates the collaboration between AkzoNobel’s team in Brazil and Maxion Wheels. The partnership combines high-performing coating technologies with local technical expertise and responsive support. AkzoNobel supplies a portfolio of powder and liquid primers, basecoats and clearcoats for aluminum wheels.

records.body_text:
The course consists of 10 lessons. Each one contains a wealth of valuable, practical information. And if you score 70 or above on the optional exam, you’ll receive 1 credit toward certification as a Master Surface Finisher. MSF is the world’s most respected – and most widely recognized – designation for finishing industry professionals. Those passing 6 course exams earn the coveted MSF designation.
Dates: May: 7, 8, 14, 15, 21, 22, 28, 29
Registration Deadline: May 1, 2024
Who Benefits?
This training program is beneficial for operators and supervisors of contract and captive shops performing precious metal plating. The course is also beneficial for industry sales personnel.
Goal
The goal of this course is to provide students with a broad range of information related to preparing parts for precious metal plating and to exploring each “PM” plating process, what can go wrong and how to solve plating problems.
At the conclusion of this course, attendees can expect to:
- Have a basic understanding of methods of preparing a wide range of substrates for plating.
- Have knowledge of reel-to-reel plating technologies used for precious metals plating.
- Know the basics of the sulfamate nickel plating process which is commonly applied as an under-plate for precious metal deposits.
- Know the various types of gold plating solutions and be able to distinguish the features of each.
- Understand other precious metals plating processes such as palladium, palladium-nickel, silver, platinum and rhodium, their chemical make-up and operational conditions.
- Know the types of tin plating processes commonly used in the electronics industry, their chemical make-up and operational conditions.
- Be prepared to take the examination which is part of the Foundation MSF certification program.

records.summary: BizLink announced an ecosystem partnership with ams OSRAM to co-develop next-generation optical interconnect solutions for AI scale-up domains, targeting power, latency, density and reliability together. The proposed architecture is a "wide-and-slow" approach that distributes data across numerous parallel lower-speed channels rather than pushing data through a few complex, power-hungry high-speed channels, aiming for extended reach and ultra-low latency while preserving cost and power efficiency. At ECOC 2026 (Spain, September 21–23), the companies plan to show a connectorized multi-core fiber solution in a private room, featuring a 2D addressable microVCSEL array at 850 nm paired with BizLink's fiber-to-fiber connector and optical packaging. The announcement is a company press release describing a planned demonstrator; no measured link performance, power, latency or reliability data are provided.

BizLink Partners with ams OSRAM to Advance Photonics for AI Data Center Interconnects
FREMONT, Calif., September 21, 2026—BizLink today announced an ecosystem partnership with innovative light and sensor solutions leader ams OSRAM to co-develop next-generation optical interconnect solutions for AI scale-up domains. Leveraging its core strengths in fiber array assembly, optical packaging, optical testing, and high-volume manufacturing, BizLink is collaborating with ams OSRAM to demonstrate a revolutionary low-power, low-latency "wide-and-slow" optical link technology at the upcoming ECOC 2026 conference and exhibition.
The rise of artificial intelligence and the required training infrastructure is redefining the requirements for intra-datacenter connectivity. Bigger AI scale-up domains require interconnects designed for power, latency, density, and reliability together. To address this bottleneck, this innovative optical architecture directly targets these critical requirements. Rather than pushing ever more data through a few complex, power-hungry high-speed channels, this approach distributes data across numerous parallel, lower-speed channels, achieving extended reach and ultra-low latency while preserving cost and power efficiency.
ECOC 2026 Live Demonstration
At the upcoming ECOC 2026 conference and exhibition in Spain (September 21–23), BizLink and ams OSRAM will present a connectorized multi-core fiber solution. Shown in a private room, the optical link demonstrator features a 2D addressable microVCSEL array with an 850 nm wavelength paired with BizLink's specialized fiber-to-fiber connector and optical packaging.
“This demonstrator validates a fundamentally different optical interconnect for low power and low latency wide-and-slow interconnects. By combining ams OSRAM's addressable microVCSEL technology with BizLink's expertise in fiber-array integration, optical packaging, and manufacturing we have pushed the boundaries in optical interconnect technology,” said Hendrik Coldenstrodt, CTO of the Computing and Transportation Business Group at BizLink.
“We’re very excited to partner with BizLink to co-develop and demonstrate a high-performance optical data link based on our wide-and-slow interconnect architecture and our photonics engine. Together we’re creating a powerful ecosystem with the goal to industrialize this new architecture at scale.” said Ashkan Seyedi, Vice President and General Manager of the Optical Interconnects Business Line at ams OSRAM.
Long committed to HPC and data centers, BizLink continues to advance its leadership in high-speed and optical interconnects. This collaboration with ams OSRAM highlights BizLink’s expertise in AI optical packaging and optoelectronic manufacturing. Moving forward, BizLink remains dedicated to collaborating with global partners to empower the CPO industry for next-generation AI.
About BizLink
Founded in 1996 and headquartered in Silicon Valley, USA, BizLink is dedicated to making transformative connections that bring visionary ideas to life. We specialize in providing essential components such as wire harnesses, connectors, and cables to a broad spectrum of industries. Our global presence, with flexible production resources and R&D teams across America, Europe, and Asia, allows us to proactively drive innovation and enable future possibilities. At BizLink, our customer-centric approach and commitment to relentless advancement empower us to deliver zero-distance service and continual performance optimization, making a positive and meaningful impact worldwide. We turn possibilities into reality; furthermore, we connect possibilities to world-changing visions.

The ams OSRAM Group (SIX: AMS) is a global leader in innovative light and sensor solutions. As a specialist in Digital Photonics, we combine engineering excellence with cutting-edge global manufacturing to offer our customers the broadest portfolio of digital light and sensing technologies.
“Sense the power of light” — our success has ever since been based on a deep understanding of the potential of light. For 120 years, we have been developing innovations that move markets: from automotive applications and industrial manufacturing to medical and consumer electronics. In the anniversary year of the OSRAM brand, around 19,000 employees worldwide are working on pioneering solutions alongside societal megatrends such as smart mobility, artificial intelligence, augmented reality, smart health, and robotics. This is reflected in over 12,000 patents granted and applied for. Headquartered in Premstaetten/Graz (Austria) with co-headquarters in Munich (Germany), the group achieved EUR 3.3 billion revenues in 2025 and is listed as ams-OSRAM AG on the SIX Swiss Exchange (ISIN: AT0000A3EPA4).

Seven PPE-based product families engineered for the operating conditions where conventional mineral and PAO lubricants fail — extreme temperature, ultra-high vacuum, radiation exposure, and demanding traction environments.

Custom Formulated Solutions
ISO 9001:2015 Certified

records.title: Optical fiber insertion loss return loss test management system and method
assignees: 四川天邑康和通信股份有限公司
records.abstract: The invention relates to an optical fiber insertion loss return loss test management system and method, wherein an optical power detection module comprises an input optical power detection unit, an output optical power detection unit, a reflected optical power detection unit, an optical emission module, an optical switch matrix and a data processing module, wherein the optical emission module is a quantum dot tunable laser module, the optical switch matrix is a bionic optical switch matrix, multi-channel optical path reconstruction is realized, a multi-physical field sensing array is arranged in the optical power detection module, optical power data is detected in real time, the data processing module is used for receiving the optical power data to perform data processing, and the optical power detection system comprises a test module, acquires the optical power data based on the optical power detection module, and calculates optical fiber insertion loss and optical fiber return loss according to the acquired optical power data. The optical switch switching time is overlong, the requirement of the 5G carrier network on the rapid detection of batch optical fibers is difficult to meet, and the technical problems of inaccurate test results and the like in complex environments due to the lack of real-time sensing and compensation capability are solved.
records.summary: The disclosure describes an optical fiber insertion-loss and return-loss test management system and method intended to address slow optical-switch switching and the lack of real-time sensing/compensation in complex environments. The system combines an optical power detection module (input, output and reflected power detection units), a quantum-dot tunable laser emission module with a wavelength control unit, a bionic optical switch matrix for multi-channel optical path reconstruction, and a data processing module. A multi-physical-field sensing array integrating a distributed fiber acoustic sensor, a Brillouin optical time-domain analyzer and a micro thermal imaging unit is described for real-time optical power detection. A test module computes insertion loss and return loss from the acquired input, output and reflected optical power data. The claims present architecture and formulas; no measured performance results are supplied in the available text.
records.why_it_matters: The disclosure describes integrating real-time multi-physical-field sensing and a bionic switch matrix into an insertion-loss/return-loss test architecture, which could allow loss measurements to be compensated for temperature and environmental variation rather than relying on static calibration.

score_details.reason: The patent claims a fiber insertion-loss/return-loss test system directly relevant to high-speed connectivity test engineering: quantum-dot tunable laser source, bionic optical switch matrix with 128-channel silicon photonic crystal waveguides, multi-physical-field sensing (DAS, BOTDA, micro thermal imaging), and explicit IL/RL formulas with temperature-dependent attenuation and VOA calibration. However, the text is abstract-and-claims only, with no measured data, no comparison to prior art, and several claims (e.g., two-photon transition stabilization, photon tensor processing unit, nanosecond scheduling) are asserted without supporting evidence. The IL/RL formulas and sweep parameters (0.01 nm step, C+L band) are concrete and useful, but performance claims remain unverified.

claims: 1. The optical fiber insertion loss return loss test management system comprises an optical power detection module and is characterized in that the optical power detection module comprises an input optical power detection unit, an output optical power detection unit, a reflected optical power detection unit, an optical emission module, an optical switch matrix and a data processing module, wherein the optical emission module is connected with the input end of the optical switch matrix through an optical fiber array, the optical switch matrix is connected with a tested optical fiber link through a V-shaped groove optical fiber array, and the optical power detection module is connected with the data processing module through a designated interface; The light emitting module is a quantum dot tunable laser module, and a wavelength control unit is arranged in the light emitting module; The optical switch matrix is a bionic optical switch matrix, and multi-channel optical path reconstruction is realized; The optical power detection module is internally provided with a multi-physical-field sensing array, and is integrated with a distributed optical fiber acoustic wave sensor, a Brillouin optical time domain analyzer and a micro thermal imaging unit, so that optical power data is detected in real time; The data processing module is used for receiving the real-time optical power data detected by the optical power detection module and processing the data; The device also comprises a test module which is connected with the optical power detection module, and acquiring optical power data based on the optical power detection module, and calculating optical fiber insertion loss and optical fiber return loss according to the acquired optical power data.

2. The optical fiber insertion loss return loss test management system according to claim 1, wherein the quantum dot tunable laser module generates an ultra-narrow linewidth optical signal with a wavelength range of 1260nm-1625nm by adopting III-V group quantum dot material InAs/GaAs, and the quantum dot tunable laser module performs wavelength self-adaptive frequency hopping to avoid nonlinear effects when generating the ultra-narrow linewidth optical signal.

3. The optical fiber insertion loss return loss test management system according to claim 2, wherein the quantum dot tunable laser module adjusts a quantum dot band gap through carrier injection based on quantum dot energy separation characteristics, generates ultra-narrow linewidth laser with linewidth lower than 100kHz, and forms split exciton energy levels with energy level differences matched with a target laser frequency through stress regulation and lattice symmetry, so that a two-photon transition process is selectively enhanced when carriers are injected, stabilization of energy level layout number inversion is realized through a two-photon absorption-stimulated emission cycle, and phase random fluctuation caused by spontaneous radiation is suppressed.

4. The optical fiber insertion loss return loss test management system according to claim 2, wherein the wavelength control unit presets a wavelength tuning path optimization algorithm and sets an optimization objective function, and the expression is as follows: Wherein α i is a nonlinear weight coefficient of each wavelength point, and β=0.3 is a switching time penalty factor; and solving an optimal solution for the optimal objective function, and optimizing a wavelength tuning path based on the optimal solution.

5. The optical fiber insertion loss return loss test management system according to claim 1, wherein the bionic optical switch matrix comprises a control center, a bionic cross interconnection module, a dynamic response modulation module, an adaptive monitoring module and a bionic signal interface array, wherein the control center is connected with the bionic cross interconnection module through an optical/electrical hybrid bus, the bionic cross interconnection module is connected with the dynamic response modulation module, and the adaptive monitoring module is connected with the bionic signal interface array through a feedback control signal; the control center is used for carrying out dynamic light path reconstruction and conflict avoidance based on a distributed decision mechanism, integrating a photon tensor processing unit and realizing nanosecond optical signal scheduling decision; The bionic cross interconnection module performs bidirectional optical signal non-blocking exchange based on a topological structure, is composed of a silicon-based photonic crystal waveguide array, realizes wavelength and polarization two-dimensional multiplexing, and integrates 128 channels on a single chip; The dynamic response modulation module realizes independent regulation and control of the amplitude, the phase and the polarization state of the light waves based on the ultra-structured surface Jones matrix modulation, and simultaneously fine-adjusts the refractive index of the waveguide through piezoelectric ceramics; The self-adaptive monitoring module is integrated with a distributed optical fiber sensor and used for monitoring the optical power, the temperature and the stress distribution of the optical link to be tested in real time; the bionic signal interface array is accessed through the multimode optical fiber and the single-mode optical fiber in a mixed mode, and meanwhile low loss is achieved through the V-shaped groove optical fiber array.

6. The optical fiber insertion loss return loss test management system according to claim 1, wherein the insertion loss test process of the test module is as follows: Generating a sweep frequency optical signal based on a wavelength tuning algorithm, wherein the step length is 0.01nm, and the C+L wave band is covered; Separating forward and reverse optical power by adopting a four-quadrant detection method, and calculating an insertion loss formula; IL=10log 10 (P out /P in )+α(T)·ΔL; Wherein IL is an insertion loss value, P out is an output optical power, P in is an input optical power, α (T) is a temperature-dependent attenuation coefficient, and Δl is an optical fiber length.

7. The optical fiber insertion loss return loss test management system according to claim 6, wherein the return loss test process of the test module is as follows: Inserting an adjustable optical attenuator into the front end of the optical power meter, and adjusting attenuation values in real time to enable reflected power to be in a detection linear interval; the return loss calculation formula is as follows: RL=10log 10 [(P ref /P in )·η(V VOA )]; Wherein, P ref reflects the optical power, P in is the input optical power, and η (V VOA ) is the attenuator voltage-insertion loss calibration function.

8. The system of claim 5, wherein the control center comprises a multi-threaded task scheduling engine, performs insertion loss, return loss, polarization dependent loss testing tasks according to a priority queue, avoids inter-channel crosstalk by a collision detection algorithm built in the optical switch matrix, and generates an optical path test report including an optical fiber end face cleanliness score and connector life prediction.

9. An optical fiber insertion loss return loss test management method based on the optical fiber insertion loss return loss test management system of any one of claims 1-8, comprising the following steps: S1, the light emitting module adjusts the wavelength of output laser through a wavelength control unit and transmits the laser to the input end of an optical switch matrix through an optical fiber array; s2, the optical switch matrix realizes multi-channel optical path reconstruction through bionic characteristics, and laser is transmitted to a tested optical fiber link through a V-shaped groove optical fiber array; S3, the optical power detection module detects the input optical power entering the tested optical fiber link through the input optical power detection unit, detects the output optical power passing through the tested optical fiber link through the output optical power detection unit, detects the reflected optical power reflected from the tested optical fiber link through the reflected optical power detection unit, and detects optical power data in real time by utilizing the distributed optical fiber acoustic wave sensor, the Brillouin optical time domain analyzer and the micro thermal imaging unit which are integrated by the multi-physical field sensing array; s4, the optical power detection module transmits the detected real-time optical power data to the data processing module through a designated interface, and the data processing module processes the real-time optical power data; and S5, the test module acquires optical power data based on the optical power detection module, and calculates optical fiber insertion loss and optical fiber return loss according to the acquired input optical power, output optical power and reflected optical power data.

technical_points: Independent claim 1 recites a quantum-dot tunable laser module with a wavelength control unit, a bionic optical switch matrix, a multi-physical-field sensing array (distributed acoustic sensor, Brillouin OTDA, micro thermal imaging), and a test module computing insertion loss and return loss.
Dependent claim 2 states the laser uses III-V InAs/GaAs quantum-dot material over 1260–1625 nm and performs wavelength adaptive frequency hopping to avoid nonlinear effects.

Dependent claim 3 states linewidth below 100 kHz via quantum-dot bandgap adjustment through carrier injection, with stress/lattice-symmetry split exciton levels and a two-photon absorption–stimulated emission cycle.

Dependent claim 5 describes a bionic switch matrix with a silicon-based photonic crystal waveguide array, wavelength and polarization two-dimensional multiplexing, and 128 channels integrated on a single chip, plus photon tensor processing for nanosecond scheduling decisions.

Dependent claims 6–7 give insertion loss IL=10log10(Pout/Pin)+α(T)·ΔL with 0.01 nm sweep steps over the C+L band, and return loss RL=10log10[(Pref/Pin)·η(VVOA)] using an adjustable attenuator at the power meter front end.
limitations: Only the abstract and claims were retrieved; the description and figures are not included, so implementation details and any experimental validation cannot be assessed.
No measured insertion-loss, return-loss, switching-time or accuracy data are reported in the available text; the stated problems and benefits are framed as objectives, not demonstrated results.
The English claim text may be machine translated, and features such as the 128-channel integration and sub-100 kHz linewidth are claim recitations rather than independently verified measurements.
